en: Prosperity!
The Noble Root Manual of Mañjuśrī. Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling in a pavilion for the assembly of Bodhisattvas, which was inconceivable, marvelous, and wondrously arrayed, situated in the expanse of the sky above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
There, the Blessed One addressed the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm.

"Listen, sons of the gods! For the benefit of all sentient beings, I shall proclaim the mantra-words that fulfill the life-span, health, sovereignty, and desires of all beings, which provide sustenance for all sentient beings, and which constitute the miraculous display of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—the purity and excellence of his inconceivable, wonderful, and marvelous conduct, meditative absorptions, and the mandala of his liberations.
Listen to them; attend well and thoroughly to them, and I shall speak them to you."

Then those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm, with palms joined, [praised] the attainment of the stage of distinction, the treading upon the vajra-seat, the subduing of Māra, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, the departure from existence for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, birth among gods and humans, the pacification of all suffering, the removal of poverty, sickness, and disease, the non-surpassability of all mundane and supramundane mantra practices, the fulfillment of all hopes, and the certain retention of the words of all Tathāgatas.
Therefore, may the Blessed One, with a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit, speak out of compassion for us and for all sentient beings.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities with his Buddha-eye, entered the samādhi called "The Dispelling of the Radiance of the Pure Domain.

As soon as the Blessed One had entered that state, the Bodhisattva Saṅkusumita saw a ray of light called "The Exhortation" which was the manifestation of white light; seeing it, he became slightly smiling and addressed that assembly of bodhisattvas:
"O sons of the Conqueror, this is our ray of light for exhortation."
Come here!
May you all prepare yourselves.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, with eyes wide open and unblinking, stood facing toward where that radiance of light was.

Then that ray of light, the *sañcodanī*, having illuminated the world-system of Kusumāvatī with a great radiance, circumambulated the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, three times, and vanished into the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī. Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, rising from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, three times; bowing his head in prostration and placing his right knee upon the ground, he addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra: "The Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, has taken heed of me."

"O Blessed One, let us go from here to the Sahā world-system to see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni, in order to explain the ritual procedures for all mantra practices, accomplishments, and means, the mandala rites, the secret rituals of the manuals, the cloth-painting rites, and the secret mudrās and empowerments of the heart-essence of all Tathāgatas, so as to fulfill all the hopes of all sentient beings."
When this had been said, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, spoke thus to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Go, Mañjuśrī Kumāra, at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Furthermore, in my name, the Blessed Śākyamuni should be asked whether he is free from affliction, free from illness, light in his physical condition, and dwelling in comfort."

Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Furthermore, O Youth, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the sands of a hundred thousand Ganges rivers have spoken, will speak, and I too now speak, regarding the ultimate practice of your mantra-conduct—from the chapters on maṇḍalas, rituals, secrets, consecrations, mudrās, and procedures; from the rules for fire-offerings and recitation; from that which fulfills all hopes and satisfies all sentient beings; from the extensive chapter on the jewels of light; from the sovereignty and prophecy of the knowledge of the past, future, and present; from the turning of mantras and the finality of the place; from the chapter on the dispersal at the time of disappearance; and from the traversal of the stages of all worldly and transcendent Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, until the culmination of that conduct."
"Go, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, to offer your approval; go now to the presence of Śākyamuni, for you deem it the right time. There you shall hear this Dharma discourse face to face."
You, too, shall speak.
And there is a mantra for this occasion: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatānām acintyāpratihatashāsanānām | Oṃ ra ra smara*.
O you who possess the form of a prince whose command is unimpeded, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
Young man, this is that Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta root mantra;
it is the heart-essence of all Tathāgatas, spoken by all Tathāgatas, and will be spoken [by them].
You too shall now speak it.

Having gone to the Sahā world-system, [this mantra] was authorized by the Tathāgata Śākyamuni as the performer of all rites in detail and in its various divisions. Furthermore, the supreme heart-mantra here is: *oṃ vākye da namaḥ*.
And the *upahṛdaya* for this mantra is *hūṃ*.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having been authorized by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarāja, entered the samādhi called "Attaining the Seat of Awakening, which is the Outflow of the Bodhisattva Practice and the Ornament of All Arrays.

As soon as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had entered that samādhi, the entire world-system—extending to the four directions, the zenith, the nadir, and the intermediate points, and filling every single direction with Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—came into being.
"Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Conqueror, that you enter into this particular samādhi!

It is not possible for all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas who have entered the practice—even those established on the ten stages—to [comprehend it]. Having consulted together with the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra and those Blessed Buddhas, he spoke this supreme heart-essence, this most secret mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, which accomplishes all aims."
The single syllable, known as the supreme secret, which brings benefit to all sentient beings, is divine and is to be accomplished through other specific mantra practices as well.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, remained silent for a moment.
Having surveyed the entire world-system with his Buddha-eye and having brought those Blessed Buddhas to mind, he uttered the mantra with a mind characterized by loving-kindness:
"Homage to all Buddhas!"
This is the mantra, O Mañjuśrī; it is the supreme heart-essence that accomplishes all rites.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having arisen from that samādhi—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—in a mere instant, a flash, a moment, or a blink of an eye, through the power and vigor of his pure wisdom, entered the specific miraculous transformation of the samādhi called "The Manifestation of Renown" and returned to this Sahā world-system.
Having arrived, he established himself above in the realm of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, which rests upon great maṇi-jewels in the expanse of the sky.
Having illuminated that entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods with a great radiance of light rays, he entered the meditative absorption named "Illumination by the Ornament of Luminous Jewels."

Immediately upon entering meditative absorption, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta manifested for the sake of worshipping the Blessed One Śākyamuni a divine rain of perfumes, garlands, ointments, wreaths, and powders; he manifested a celestial palace fashioned from many varieties of jewels, adorned with jeweled parasols extending for hundreds of thousands of yojanas, beautified by divine visible arrays of great silk ribbons, and filled with divine flowers, banners, flags, and garlands, all bound together by nets of jeweled bells that produced a sweet sound proclaiming the non-retrogression and the establishment of beings in the state of a bodhisattva—having seen this marvelous, wondrous miracle and the miraculous transformation of the bodhisattva.

Then those sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa host, their hair standing on end with thrill, seeing their abode trembling, their hearts agitated and broken, cried out in great haste as if fearing, "Have we perhaps fallen away from our supernatural power? and began to shout loudly, saying: "Save us, O Blessed One! Save us, Śākyamuni!"
Then the Blessed One addressed the entire assembly of the Śuddhāvāsa deities:
"Do not fear, friends; do not be afraid!

This is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, who has come from the presence of the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarāja in the Buddha-field Saṅkusumita, in order to see, pay homage to, and attend upon [me], and to proclaim the vast, marvelous Dharma-discourse concerning the mantra-words of great purposeful practice."

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, gazed at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes, prostrated at his feet, and praised the Blessed One with these syllables, words, and summaries:
"Homage to you, the liberated one, the noble! Homage to you, the supreme among men!
Homage to you, the best of men, the accomplisher of the purpose of all conduct!"
Homage to you, O lion among men, the warder-off of all misfortunes!
May your mind be gracious, O great hero, the destroyer of all difficulties.
Homage to you, O Puruṣa of lotus-like and meritorious fragrance, infinite one! Homage to you, O Puruṣa-lotus, who purifies the mire of the three worlds!
Homage to you, the liberated one, the deliverer from all suffering;
homage to you, the peaceful one, the perfect subduer of all who are unsubdued.
Homage to you, the Siddha, who accomplishes the purpose of all mantra practices;
homage to you, the auspicious one, the most auspicious among all that is auspicious.
Homage to you, the Buddha, who has awakened to all phenomena;
homage to you, the Tathāgata, who is the suchness of all phenomena,
O teacher who has entered into the mode of non-proliferation.

"Salutations to you, the Omniscient One, who are established in the establishment of the three vehicles, the path, and nirvāṇa—both conditioned and unconditioned—among all things known by the omniscient.
By means of these syllables, phrases, summaries, and verses of praise, the Blessed One appeared face-to-face; transcending world-systems to the northeast, there was a buddha-field named Saṅkusumita."

In that regard, there is a world-system named Kusumāvatī, where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra—the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct—resides and teaches the Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end. He reveals the Buddha-way, which is beneficial for oneself and all people, entirely complete, utterly pure, and perfectly cleansed.

He currently exists, remains, and maintains himself; he teaches the Dharma—which is a protection, a shelter, a refuge, a resort, and a state of security that is the ultimate goal and the ultimate consummation for all sentient beings.

Having been granted permission by that very Blessed One, he has come here to the presence of the Blessed One at his feet. And that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, inquired after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, his lightness of body, his vigor, and his well-being.

And he spoke thus: "It is marvelous that in such a time of the five corruptions, the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, has appeared and teaches all dharmas—complete in words and syllables, leading to liberation via the three paths, and securing rebirth among gods and humans.
Marvelous is the vigor of that Blessed One Śākyamuni!"

For indeed, in this class of beings who are unfit, following a path that leads to the arising of the three realms of existence, he establishes them in devotion toward *nirvāṇa*, which follows the ultimate security and well-being.
Nevertheless, as for the mind of the Blessed Buddhas, only the Blessed Buddhas themselves shall know it.
What is possible for me to know of the Buddha-transformations of the Blessed Ones, whose miraculous displays of power and wondrous activities are inconceivable?
To know the activity that brings about the entry into the conduct of the mental dispositions, or even to describe it in brief, would take hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons.
This manifestation of the Tathāgatas—whether in its entirety, in its parts, or in all its forms—is to be seen as a conditioned phenomenon.
Regarding the conduct of those who rely on the ancient [defilements] to be abandoned by vision, or their qualities, only the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, knows this; we do not.
Then Mañjuśrī, the Youthful, sat upon a great jewel lotus created through the miraculous transformations of his own supernatural power, gazing at the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, following various discourses, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, with a Brahma-like voice—resounding like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, and possessing the thunderous resonance of a drum—with words endowed with the purpose of accomplishing the conduct of a bodhisattva that accords with the teaching of the Dharma preceded by former questions and the manifestation of the state of a Tathāgata.

Welcome to you, Mañjuśrī, Great Being! You who have accomplished the conduct empowered by all Buddhas; who brings about the welfare of all Bodhisattvas; who possesses all mantra-words along with their secrets, consecrations, mudrās, and maṇḍalas; who bestows the auspicious consecration that fulfills all hopes for long life, health, and sovereignty; who is the knowledge of all sādhanas and methods, the knowable, and the preservation of time; who, in brief, fulfills all the hopes of all beings throughout the past, future, and present; who awakens one’s own virtues, follows the practice of mantras, and causes joy in other beings; who grants invisibility, travel through the sky, swift-footedness, intelligence, summoning, entry into the netherworld (pātāla), sorcery, and the attainment of all desires; who summons Yakṣas, Yakṣiṇīs, Kiṅkaras, Piśācas, and all spirits; who restores children, the elderly, and the young to their natural state; who, in short, performs all actions and fulfills every heart’s desire; who effects sorcery, pacification, and nourishment—just as it is applied and just as it is heard, this *Mahākalparatnapaṭalavisara*, the crest-jewel of the Bodhisattvapitaka, has been authorized by us and by all the Buddhas, O Pure Being, as a treasury of Dharma for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, and for the sake of all beings, both gods and humans.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta entered the bodhisattva-samādhi called "The Array of Radiant Rays Empowered by All Buddhas, the Exhortation of Ornaments.

As soon as he had entered it, for all beings—however many there were—from the world-systems as numerous as the sands of many Ganges rivers down to the great Avīci hell, whoever was suffering in extreme misery, they all attained the pacification and stilling of their suffering.
Having exhorted all the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Blessed Buddhas, that ray of light once again vanished into the crown of the head of the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.

In the meantime, those Buddha-fields situated in the eastern direction were likewise exhorted by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, through that manifestation of the illumination of the circle of the realm of rays.

They are as follows: the Tathāgata named Jyotissaumyagandhāvabhāsaśrī; the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabharāja; the Tathāgata named Samantāvabhāsaśrī; the Tathāgata named Samudgatarāja; the Tathāgata named Śālendrarāja; the Tathāgata named Lokendrarāja; the Tathāgata named Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarāja; the Tathāgata named Anantāvabhāsarājendra; and the Tathāgata named Jyotiraśmirājendra. With these as their leaders, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones—in infinite and boundless world-systems, surrounded by hosts of Bodhisattvas, shall assemble in this Sahā world-system to see the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Awakened One Śākyamuni, who resides in the palace of the Pure Abodes and is teaching the extensive chapters on the meaning of the mantra-words for the instruction of the Bodhisattva conduct together with Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. These Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will thus gather together.

In this way, having illuminated all the Buddha-fields in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as in the intermediate directions—and thus above, below, and across—having humbled all the abodes of Māra in every Buddha-field, and being surrounded by hosts of bodhisattvas and preceded by the community of śrāvakas, they stood ready, desiring to manifest the palace of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, the miraculous power of the Buddhas, and the majesty of the bodhisattvas; and desiring to illuminate the unimpeded teaching of the Tathāgata, which consists of the extensive chapters on the specific samādhis for the accomplishment of mantra practice.

They were as follows: Subāhu, Suratna, Suvrata, Sunetra, Sūrata, Sudharma, Sarvārthasiddhi, Sarvodgata, Dharmodgata, Ratnodgata, Ratnaśrī, Meruśrī, Acintyaśrī, Prabhākaraśrī, Prabhaśrī, Jyotiśrī, Sarvārthaśrī, Sarvaratnapāṇi, Cūḍāmaṇi, Merudhvajapāṇi, Vairocanagarbha, Ratnagarbha, Jñānagarbha, Sacintyārthagarbha, Acintyārthagarbha, Dharmodgatagarbha, Dhvajaketu, Suketu, Anantaketu, Vimalaketu, Gaganaketu, Ratnaketu, Garjitaghoṣadundubhisvararāja, Anantāvabhāsajñānarāja, Sarvatamo’ndhakāravidhamanarāja, Sarvavikiraṇabodhividhvaṃsanarāja, Sarvacaryātiśayajñānarāja, Lokendrarāja, Atiśayendrarāja, Vidhamanarāja, Nirdhūtarāja, Ādityarāja, Abhāvasamudgatarāja, Svabhāvasamudgatarāja, Abhāvasvabhāvasamudgatarāja, Avivakṣitarāja, Svabhāvapuṇyābha, Lokābha, Amitābha, Mitābha, Sunetrābha, Susambhavābha, Arthabhāvābha, Adhṛṣya, Amṛṣya, Akarṣa, Akaniṣṭha, Amala, Anala, Dyutipati, Mati, Sukha, Mukha, Nemi, Nimi, Ketu, Ṛkṣa, Divideva, Divya, Nābhi, Ravana, Lokaśānti, Upāriṣṭa, Dundubhisiddha, Śiva, Ākhyadivya, Duprasaha, Durgharṣa, Durālabha, Dūraṅgama, Dūrasthita, Ūrdhvadravyatama, Khadyota, Samahadyota, Adyota, Ṛṣabha, Ābha, Sumanāya, Sumana, Mahādeva, Sunirmala, Malānta, Dānta, Sami, Sucihna, Śvetadhvaja, Imi, Kimi, Kaniṣṭha, Nikarṣa, Jīva, Sujāta, Dhūmaketu, Dhvajaketu, Śvetaketu, Suketu, Vasuketu, Vasava, Pitāmaha, Pitara, Niṣkakuru, Lokākhya, Samantākhya, Mahākhya, Śreyasi, Tejasi, Jyotikiraṇa, Samantakara, Lokaṅkara, Divaṅkara, Dīpaṅkara, Bhūtāntakara, Sarvārthaṅkara, Siddhaṅkara, Dyotiṅkara, Avabhāsaṅkara, Dundubhisvara, Rutasvara, Susvara, Anantasvara, Ketusvara, Bhūtamuni, Kanakamuni, Krakucchanda, Kāśyapa, Śikhin, Viśvabhuk, Vipaśyin, and Śākyamuni.

Then, having illuminated that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods with these and many other Blessed Buddhas, and having taken their seats upon lotus thrones, they addressed the assembly of Bodhisattvas and the sons of the gods in this manner: "Such is the form [of this teaching]."

They are as follows: Ratnapāṇi, Vajrapāṇi, Supāṇi, Anantapāṇi, Kṣitipāṇi, Ālokapāṇi, Sunirmala, Sukūpa, Prabhūtakūṭa, Maṇikūṭa, Ratnakūṭa, Ratnahasti, Samantahasti, Gandhahasti, Sugati, Vimalagati, Lokagati, Cārugati, Anantagati, Anantakīrti, Vimalakīrti, Gatikīrti, Amalakīrti, Kīrtikīrti, Nātha, Anātha, Nāthabhūta, Lokanātha, Samantanātha, Ātreya, Anantatreya, Samantatreya, Maitreya, Sunetreya, Namantatreya, Tvaddhatreya, Sarūlātreya, Trirantātreya, Triśaraṇātreya, Triyānātreya, Visphūrja, Sumanodbhavarṇavān, Dharmīśvara, Abhāveśvara, Sammateśvara, Lokeśvara, Avalokiteśvara, Sulokiteśvara, Vilokiteśvara, Lokamaha, Sumaha, Garjiteśvara, Dundubhisvara, Vitateśvara, Vidhvastesvara, Suvakṣas, Sumūrti, Sumahadyaśovat, Ādityaprabhāva, Prabhaviṣṇu, Someśvara, Soma, Saumya, Anantaśrī, Lokaśrī, Gagana, Gaganāḍhya, Gaganāṅgakṣiteśvara, Maheśvara, Kṣiti, Kṣitigarbha, Nīvaraṇa, Sarvāvaraṇa, Sarvāvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Samantanirmathana, Samantabhadra, Bhadrapāṇi, Sudhana, Susaṃhata, Rasapuṣya, Sunabha, Ākāśa, Ākāśagarbha, Sarvārthagarbha, Sarvodbhava, Anivartin, Anivartita, Apāyajaha, Avivartita, and Avaivarttikasarvadharmopaśānti.
Together with these and other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, the Blessed One Śākyamuni was dwelling in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.

There are also other Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who assume the form of women; who, by means of infinite conduct, purposes, and worldly enjoyments, establish all beings upon the non-retrogressive path according to their inclinations; who possess inconceivable vidyā-padas, mantras, dhāraṇīs, and the forms of medicinal herbs; who assume various forms such as flocks of birds, yakṣas, rākṣasas, jewels, mantras, and the kings of gems; who enter into the reckoning of both sentient and non-sentient beings while conforming to the conduct of beings; who imitate beings in accordance with how they are to be disciplined according to their inclinations; who conform to forms more distinguished than those [beings]; who have emerged from the Dharma through the realization of the instructions of the Vidyārājas; who establish the path of speech that cannot be transgressed by the samaya of entering into all mundane and supramundane realms—the lotus and vajra of the Tathāgatas; and who ensure the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels. They are as follows: Uṣṇīṣa, Atyadbhuta, Atyunnata, Sitātapatra, Anantapatra, Śatapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, Lokottara, Vijayoṣṇīṣa, Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Kamalaraśmi, Kanakaraśmi, Sitaraśmi, Vyūḍhoṣṇīṣa, Kanakarāśi, Sitarāśi, Tejorāśi, Maṇirāśi, Samanantarāśi, Vikhyātarāśi, Bhūtarāśi, Satyarāśi, Abhāvasvabhāvarāśi, and Avitatharāśi. Together with these and other Uṣṇīṣa-kings who have entered the infinite dharmadhātu, fulfilling the intentions and desires of beings according to their inclinations, and who have arrived from the hearts of all the Victors—it would not be possible even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons to state the limit of the number of these Uṣṇīṣa-kings, nor to describe the majesty of those whose strength and prowess are inconceivable.
It is explained by way of a concise summary and in brief.
The assembly of the Vidyārājñīs shall now be described.
They are as follows: Ūrṇā, Bhrūlocanā, Padmā, Śravaṇā, Grīvā, Abhayā, Karuṇā, Maitrī, Kṛpā, Prajñā, Raśmi, Cetanā, Prabhā, Nirmalā, and Dhīvarā.
Likewise, there were other Vidyārājñīs emanated from the infinite and boundless forms of the Tathāgatas, namely:

Tathāgatapātra (Tathāgata’s Bowl), Dharmacakra (Wheel of Dharma), Tathāgataśayana (Tathāgata’s Bed), Tathāgatāvabhāsa (Tathāgata’s Radiance), Tathāgata-vacana (Tathāgata’s Speech), Tathāgatoṣṭha (Tathāgata’s Lip), Tathāgatoru (Tathāgata’s Thigh), Tathāgatāmala (Tathāgata’s Stainless One), Tathāgata-dhvaja (Tathāgata’s Banner), Tathāgata-ketu (Tathāgata’s Crest), and Tathāgata-cihna (Tathāgata’s Emblem).

By these and other Vidyārājas, Rājñīs, Kiṅkaras, Ceṭas, Ceṭīs, Dūtas, Dūtīs, Yakṣas, and Yakṣīs— spoken by the Tathāgata, emerged from the Cloud of Dharma adorned with exceptionally sublime arrays, flowing forth as the natural outpouring of specific meditative absorptions, surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of retinues, and moving one above the other within the entire host of Vidyās—
those Vidyārājas also came to preside there in the palace of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, as well as in the Lotus Family.

They are as follows: the Blessed One with twelve arms, with six arms, with four arms; Hālāhala; Amoghapāśa; Śvetahayagrīva; Sugrīva; Anantagrīva; Nīlagrīva; Sugrīva; Sukarṇa; Śvetakarṇa; Nīlakaṇṭha; Lokakaṇṭha; Vilokita; Avalokita; Īśvara; Sahasraraśmi; Manaḥ; Manasaḥ; Vikhyātamanasaḥ; Kamala; Kamalapāṇi; Manoratha; Āśvāsaka; Prahasita; Sukeśa; Keśānta; Nakṣatra; Nakṣatrarāja; Saumya; Sugata; and Damaka.
And by these and other vidyārājas,

headed by Abjoṣṇīṣa, who have become the outflow of the samādhis of the infinite accomplishment of the clouds of Dharma, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps, and by many vidyārājñīs emanated from the samādhi of the form of Lokeśvara.

Desiring to manifest this great maṇḍala of the Great Search and the miraculous transformations of the Great Bodhisattvas, they gathered and sat down.
They were desirous of hearing the Dharma and of illuminating the accomplishment of the purpose of mantra practice.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that entire circle of the assembly with a pure intention, and having understood that the realm of sentient beings is by nature non-existent, has the nature of space, and transcends the three periods of time, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Pay attention, Mañjuśrī, to the conduct for the benefit of sentient beings: cultivate the Bodhisattva-samādhi named *Mārabalābhivardhana*, which brings about the attainment of the purpose of mantra-conduct through the possession of faith in the desired fruits of action according to one's inclinations; which consists of the words of the Dharma, the words of action, the state of peace, and the state of liberation; which is the removal of conceptual construction and the attainment of non-conceptual equanimity; and which possesses the ten powers of the Tathāgatas, universal power, and strength that increases the power over Māra.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta entered the meditative absorption that had just been described by the Blessed One.

As soon as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had entered that absorption, he caused this trichiliocosm—as well as other trichiliocosms equal in number to the atoms in hundreds of thousands of world-systems—to tremble; and having illuminated it with a great radiance, he displayed his own power of purity and spoke his own mantra-words.
Homage to all Buddhas,
who have arisen from the nature of non-existence.
Homage to the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas.
Homage to the Bodhisattvas, the lords established on the ten stages, the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.

Namely: *uṃ*! O subduer of wicked beings, you who hold a sword, a club, an axe, and a noose in your hands; four-armed one, four-faced one, six-legged one, go, go, O destroyer of great obstacles, you of deformed countenance, you who cause terror to all spirits, you who utter the loud laugh of *aṭṭahāsa*, you who wear a tiger skin; perform, perform all rites!
Cut, cut all mantras! Split, split the supreme mudrā!
Summon, summon all mudrās!
Churn, churn all the wicked ones!
Enter, enter into the center of the mandala!
O destroyer of Vaivasvata, accomplish, accomplish my purpose!

Daha daha! Pañca pañca! Do not delay, do not delay! Remember your pledge! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Shatter, shatter! O fulfiller of all hopes! Ho ho, Blessed One, why do you tarry? Accomplish all my aims! Svāhā!
This great wrathful king of the Blessed Mañjuśrī, named Yamāntaka, slays even King Yama; he brings him under his power— how much more so other beings?

As soon as the Great Wrathful King had been spoken, all sentient beings approached the presence of the Blessed One— afflicted, terrified, trembling, agitated in mind, and broken-hearted; they had no other refuge,
no other protection.
There was no other refuge, except for the Buddha, the Blessed One, and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Then, whatever beings there were—whether moving on land, moving in water, or moving through the air; whether stationary or mobile; born from a womb, born from an egg, born from moisture, or born spontaneously—all those included among the class of sentient beings, even as they remained in infinite and boundless world-systems above, below, across, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions, were at that very moment and instant driven forth and led away by the Great Wrathful King himself.

Furthermore, this King of Wrath must not be recited in the presence of one who has not yet abandoned passion; for such a person might die or wither away. Having taken up the pledge (*samaya*), it should be recited before an image of the Buddha or before Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
It should not be recited for the sake of any other ritual action, nor here or there;
for the reason is that such a cause leads to great calamity and great ruin, resulting in self-destruction.

For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, are supremely compassionate; they are solely intent upon establishing the knowledge of omniscience, leading the entire realm of sentient beings to the attainment of nirvāṇa, and have desired that their teaching endure. They possess the three measures, are bound by the three fetters, and illuminate the mantra practice so as not to sever the lineage of the Three Jewels. With a mind that is the natural outflow of the power of great compassion, they overcome the forces of Māra, destroy great obstacles, ward off wicked kings, subdue their own strength, and restrain, strike down, destroy, discipline, dry up, satisfy, and terrify the forces of others. They manifest their own mantra practices and accomplish swift tasks by increasing longevity, health, and sovereignty. Possessing great loving-kindness, great compassion, great equanimity, and great joy, they spoke with a mind free from all conceptualization and discursive thought, based on those causes and conditions.

Then there were those *nāgas* and great *nāgas*, *yakṣas* and great *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas* and great *rākṣasas*, *piśācas* and great *piśācas*, *pūtanās* and great *pūtanās*, *kaṭapūtanās* and great *kaṭapūtanās*, *mārutas* and great *mārutas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas* and great *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *vyāḍas* and great *vyāḍas*, *vetāḍas* and great *vetāḍas*, *kambojas* and great *kambojas*, *bhaginīs* and great *bhaginīs*, *ḍākinīs* and great *ḍākinīs*, *cūṣakas* and great *cūṣakas*, *utsārakas* and great *utsārakas*, *ḍimphikās* and great *ḍimphikās*, *kimpakas* and great *kimpakas*, diseases and great diseases, great diseases and seizures, seizures and great seizures, planetary spirits and great planetary spirits, space-mothers and great space-mothers, *rūpiṇīs* and great *rūpiṇīs*, *krandanās* and great *krandanās*, shadows and great shadows, messengers and great messengers, servants and great servants, *yakṣiṇīs* and great *yakṣiṇīs*, *piśācīs* and great *piśācīs*, fevers and great fevers, quartan fevers and great quartan fevers, constant fevers, irregular fevers, continuous fevers, momentary fevers, those caused by wind, those caused by bile, those caused by phlegm, and those caused by a combination of humors; Together with these and other great yakṣa generals, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of yakṣas, they assembled right there in the great circle of the assembly in the Śuddhāvāsa palace through the empowerment of the Bodhisattva and the application of supernatural power; and having assembled, they sat down to listen to the Dharma.

Together with these and other great nāga kings, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of great nāgas, they assembled and sat down in that great circle of the assembly to hear the Dharma.
There were also those sages and great sages, namely:

Ātreya, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhagīratha, Jahnu, Aṅgiras, Agasti, Pulasti, Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa-Gautama, Agni, Aṅgirasa, Jāmadagni, Āstīka, Muni, Munivara, Aśvara, Vaiśampāyana, Parāśara, Paraśu, Yogeśvara, Pippala, Pippalāda, Vālmīka, and Mārkaṇḍeya.
Together with these and other great sages, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of great sages, they approached that assembly circle.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, they sat down to hear and rejoice in the Bodhisattvapiṭaka concerning the purpose of mantra practice.
Those who were the kings of the mahoragas also entered that circle of the assembly and sat down together;
namely: Bheruṇḍa, Bhūrūṇḍa, Maruṇḍa, Mārīca, Dīpa, and Pradīpa.
Those who were the kings of the *garuḍas* also assembled in that circle of the assembly, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands.

They were as follows: Suparṇa, Śvetaparṇa, Pannaga, Parṇaya, Sujātapakṣa, Ajātapakṣa, Manojava, Pannaganāśana, Vainateya, Vainateya, Bharadvāja, Śakuna, Mahāśakuna, and the kings of birds (*pakṣirāja*).
They too gathered in that circle of the assembly.
Those kings of the kinnaras as well, with their retinues of many hundreds of thousands of kinnaras, also assembled in that circle of the assembly.

They were as follows: Druma, Upadruma, Sudruma, Anantadruma, Lokadruma, Ledruma, Ghanoraska, Mahoraska, Mahojaska, Mahoja, Maharddhika, Viruta, Susvara, Manojña, Cittonmādakara, Unnata, Upekṣaka, Karuṇa, and Aruṇa.
These and other great kings of the kinnaras, with their retinues of many hundreds of thousands of kinnaras, had assembled there to hear the Dharma.

Thus [there were] Brahmā Sahāmpati, Mahābrahmā, Ābhāsvara, Prabhāsvara, Śuddhābha, Puṇyābha, Aṭṭaha, Atapā, Akaniṣṭha, Sukaniṣṭha, Lokaniṣṭha, Ākiñcanya, Naivakiñcanya, Ākāśānantya, Naivākāśānantya, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, the Śuddhāvāsa, Tuṣita, Yāma, Trāyastriṃśa, Cāturmahārājika, Sadāmatta, Mālādhāra, Karoṭapāṇi, Vīṇātṛtīyaka, Parvativāsin, Kūṭavāsin, Śikharavāsin, Alakavāsin, Puravāsin, Vimānavāsin, Antarikṣacara, Bhūmivāsin, Vṛkṣavāsin, and Gṛhavāsin.

Likewise, the lords of the Dānavas— headed by Prahlāda, Bali, Rāhu, Vemacitti, Sucitti, Kṣemacitti, Devacitti, Rāhu, and Bāhu— accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of millions of Dānavas, possessing diverse movements and diverse purposes, those Asuras who fight with the gods— they too gathered in that circle of the assembly to behold, worship, and attend upon the miraculous manifestation of the Bodhisattva through the empowerment of the Buddha.
And those planets and great planets that move through the atmosphere, which act for the benefit of the world;

They are as follows: Āditya, Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, Śanaiścara, Rāhu, Kampa, Ketu, Aśani, Nirghāta, Tāra, Dhvaja, Ghora, Dhūmra, Vajra, Ṛkṣa, Vṛṣṭi, Upavṛṣṭi, Naṣṭārka, Nirnaṣṭa, Haśānta, Māṣṭi, Ṛṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Lokānta, Kṣaya, Vinipāta, Āpāta, Tarka, Mastaka, Yugānta, Śmaśāna, Piśita, Raudra, Śveta, Abhija, Abhijata, Maitra, Śaṅku, Triśaṅku, Lūtha, Raudraka, Kratunāśana, Balavān, Ghora, Aruṇa, Vihasita, Mārṣṭi, Skanda, Sanat, Upasanat, Kumārakrīḍana, Hasana, Prahasana, Nartapaka, Nartaka, Khaja, and Virūpa.
Thus these great grahas, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of followers, through the empowerment of the Buddha, assembled and sat down together in that palace of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
Now, as for those stars that move through the sky, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of stars;

They are as follows: Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśirā, Ārdrā, Punarvasū, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Maghā, both Phalgunīs, Hastā, Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūlā, both Āṣāḍhās, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, both Bhadrapadas, Revatī, Devatī, Prabhijā, Punarṇavā, Jyotī, Aṅgirasā, Nakṣatrikā, both Phalgu and Phalguvatī, Lokapravarā, Pravarāṇikā, Śreyasī, Lokamātā, Īrā, Ūhā, Vahā, Arthavatī, and Asārthā.

Thus these queens of the constellations, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of constellations, gathered through the Buddha’s empowerment and sat down together in that great assembly circle within that palace of the Pure Abodes.

There are thirty-six zodiac signs (*rāśi*), namely: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, Pisces; monkey, sub-aquarius, mongoose, rhinoceros, elephant, buffalo; deity, human, bird, gandharva, conqueror of world-beings, fierce splendor, moonlight, shadow, earth, darkness, passion (*rajas*), secondary passion (*uparajas*); suffering, happiness, liberation, awakening, solitary buddhahood, disciple, hell-being, knowledge-holder (*vidyādhara*), great brilliance, great majesty; animal, hungry ghost (*preta*), asura, flesh-eater, *piśāca*, *yakṣa*, *rākṣasa*; belonging to all stages, elemental, downward-moving, upward-moving, horizontal-moving, blossomed, meditative, established in yoga; superior, middling, and inferior.
Thus these great hosts, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of myriad hosts, approached the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and the circle of the great assembly;
having arrived, they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and sat down in their respective places.
And those great yakṣiṇīs as well, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs.

They are as follows: Sulocanā, Subhrū, Sukeśā, Susvarā, Sumatī, Vasumatī, Citrākṣī, Pūrāṃśā, Guhyakā, Suguh yakā, Mekhalā, Sumekhalā, Padmoccā, Abhayā, Jayā, Vijayā, Revatikā, Keśinī, Keśāntā, Anilā, Manoharā, Manovatī, Kusumāvatī, Kusumapuravāsinī, Piṅgalā, Hārītī, Vīramatī, Vīrā, Suvīrā, Sughorā, Ghoravatī, Surasundarī, Surasā, Guhyottamārī, Vatavāsinī, Aśokā, Andhārasundarī, Ālokasundarī, Prabhāvatī, Atiśayavatī, Rūpavatī, Surūpā, Asitā, Saumyā, Kāṇā, Menā, Nandinī, Upanandinī, and Lokāntarā.
Thus these great yakṣiṇīs, with retinues of many hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs, stood at a distance from that great assembly circle, bowing in homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Those great female piśācīs as well, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of female piśācīs, also gathered there, paying homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

They were as follows: Maṇḍitikā, Pāṃsupiśācī, Ulkāpiśācī, Jvālāpiśācī, Bhasmodgirā, Piśitāśinī, Durdharā, Bhrāmarī, Mohanī, Tarjanī, Rohiṇikā, Govāhiṇikā, Lokāntikā, Bhasmāntikā, Pīluvatī, Bahulavatī, Bahulā, Durdāntā, Dhaṇā, Cihnitikā, Dhūmāntikā, Dhūmā, and Sudhūmā.
These great piśācīs, surrounded by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of piśācīs, also entered that maṇḍala of the great assembly.
There are also those Mothers and Great Mothers who roam the world, causing harm to sentient beings and receiving offerings of oblations and garlands;

namely: Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī, Kaumārī, Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī, Aindrī, Yāmyā, Āgneyā, Vaivasvatī, Lokāntakarī, Vāruṇī, Aiśānī, Vāyavyā, Paraprāṇaharā, Sukhamaṇḍitikā, Śakunī, Mahāśakunī, Pūtanā, Kaṭapūtanā, and Skanda.
Thus these great mothers, with retinues of many hundreds of thousands of mothers, also remained in that great circle of the assembly, uttering the words, "Homage to the Buddha!"
In this way, many hundreds of thousands of humans and non-human beings, from the great Avīci hell up to the pinnacle of existence, filled the entire expanse of space;
yet among the assembly of beings, there was no hostility toward any living creature whatsoever.

And through the Buddha’s empowerment and the adornment of the assembly of Bodhisattvas, every single being beheld the Buddha, the Blessed One, and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta standing before them at the crown of their heads.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire world-system with his Buddha-eye, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Speak, speak, O pure being! Recite the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, which is the detailed exposition of the chapter on the meditative absorption for the definitive determination of the meaning of mantra practice, whenever you deem it to be the right time."

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having been granted permission by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, entered the samādhi called "The Array and Ornament of the Nature of Space" and "The Array and Ornament of the Hardened Continuum of the Vajra-Compaction.

As soon as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had entered that state, he empowered that abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), which extended for many hundreds of thousands of yojanas, so that it became composed of vajra.

There, those many yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, maruts, and piśācas—in short, the entire realm of sentient beings—by means of the bodhisattva’s empowerment, became established and seated within that celestial palace which resembled a diamond-jewel, remaining there without harming one another.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, perceiving that great assembly gathered there, addressed the wrathful king Yamāntaka.
O, O Great King of Wrath, destroyer of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas! Protect, protect this great assembly-circle and all sentient beings; bring them under your control!
Subdue the wicked!
Awaken the gentle!
Pacify her who is not yet pacified.
Until I have spoken the Bodhisattvapiṭaka— the extensive ritual procedures for the maṇḍala of mantra practice according to my own mantra conduct— go outside and protect her.

Thus addressed, the Great Wrathful King, assuming a most hideous form, issued forth; and Yāmāntaka, the wrathful king, surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of wrathful deities, set out in all directions—throughout the entire assembly circle—to protect and govern all sentient beings. Uttering a terrible roar, he stood positioned in the four cardinal directions, above, below, and across.

Then they all became gentle and well-disposed, and they did not transgress his command. And they heard this proclamation: "Whoever should violate this agreement, his head shall split open like a cluster of flowers on an *ajaka* plant.
And that was due to the empowerment of the Bodhisattva.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke these dharma-words concerning the purpose of his own mantra practice:
"The mantras of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is endowed with a single quality shall attain accomplishment.
What is that one quality? Namely, perceiving all phenomena as being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)."
The mantras of a bodhisattva established in two qualities will attain accomplishment.
Which two? Not abandoning the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and equanimity toward all sentient beings.
Through three qualities, they reach the fulfillment of the instruction on the purpose of their own mantra practice.
By which three? By not abandoning any sentient being through the protection of the bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline, and by not abandoning one's own mantra.
For a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of awakening, when endowed with four qualities, his mantras will attain accomplishment.
Which four? Not abandoning one's own mantra; not interrupting the mantras of others; applying loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; and having a mental continuum cultivated by great compassion.
The mantras of a bodhisattva who has first generated the mind of awakening (prathamacittotpādaka) shall attain accomplishment when he is endowed with these four qualities.
Those qualities through which the bodhisattva’s inclusion within the scriptural collection (piṭaka), the realization of mantra practice, and the fulfillment of awakening are achieved—
what are these five?
Frequenting secluded places, not harboring malice toward other beings, not looking to worldly mantras, and establishing oneself in ethical discipline, learning, and proper conduct—
these five qualities lead to the fulfillment of the purpose of mantra practice.
Furthermore, six qualities lead to the fulfillment of the purpose of mantra practice.

What are the six? They are: not severing one's faith in the Three Jewels; not severing one's faith in the Bodhisattvas; not disparaging mundane or supramundane mantras; honoring the non-proliferated realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); not rejecting the profound meanings of the Mahāyāna sūtras; having a tireless mind; and seeking the practice of mantras without falling away from the side of virtue.
These six qualities lead to the convergence of the accomplishment of the practice of knowledge and mantras.
Seven factors lead to the entry into the practice of mantras suitable for the time of accomplishing knowledge (*vidyā*).
What are the seven?

It is the profound method; it is the liberation through the practice of the perfection of wisdom—its cultivation, recitation, teaching, study, and transcription—and the conduct of a bodhisattva; it is the entry into the method of the Mahāyāna Dharma and the equipment of a bodhisattva by means of endurance regarding time and place, the performance of *japa*, fire-offerings (*homa*), silence, and austerities, and by means of unimpeded movement, intelligence, mindfulness, wisdom, and fortitude; it is skill in the activities of one’s own mantras, the summoning of mantras, protection, and accomplishment; it is the cultivation of the perfections of great compassion, great loving-kindness, great equanimity, and great sympathetic joy; it is the convergence upon the realm of sentient beings, the realm of phenomena, and suchness, which are free from conceptual proliferation; it is the thorough seeking of the omniscient knowledge that transcends dualistic forms; and it is the non-abandonment of all sentient beings due to having no longing for the Lesser Vehicle.

These seven factors lead to the complete fulfillment of the accomplishment of knowledge, ignorance, and mantras. What are they? They are: faith in what has not been seen, seeing what has not been seen, faith in the results of what has not been seen, curiosity, the desire for inquiry, and even medical treatment. These eight factors lead to the convergence upon the accomplishment of the purpose of the practice of knowledge and mantras.

Through the manifestation of purity resulting from faith in the Bodhisattvas; through the respectful veneration of the teacher in receiving the mantras without error; through the non-deceptive reception of the instructions of the masters of the mantras and tantras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, accompanied by the renunciation of all one's possessions; through the skillful elucidation of dreams regarding the suitability or unsuitability of sites for the field of accomplishment (*siddhakṣetra*); through being free from the stain of stinginess and all sloth and torpor, and through the constant offering of oneself to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with the arousal of vigor; in short, through being girded with the great armor of insatiable roots of virtue, desiring to strike down all obstacles, possessing a self-nature that aspires to the great enjoyments of treading upon the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and great sovereignty; and through the unceasing association with Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva and spiritual friend, who is encountered by persons of great renown.
These eight factors lead to the accomplishment of the purpose of mantra practice and to its convergence.

In brief, friends, for one who is not devoid of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who is not separated from the Three Jewels, and who—though even of extremely immoral conduct—is tireless in mind and constantly devoted, my extensive array of mantra sections, which has arisen from a mind flowing forth from the infinite and marvelous conduct of a bodhisattva, will be accomplished.
It should not be understood otherwise.
Having become free from conceptual construction in mind, one should practice this even for the sake of inquiry.

Then that entire assembly, empowered by the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas, uttered these words: "Excellent, excellent, O Son of the Conqueror! This teaching of the Dharma has been well-expounded for the benefit of all sentient beings, following the entry into the principles of the Dharma and the performance of the purposeful activities of the various mantra practices. Oh, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, this eloquent speech is well-suited to the mantra practices and follows the diverse teachings of the Dharma!"

O Great King, whoever shall recite, uphold, or attend to this chapter on the Assembly, or shall place it upon the back of an elephant at the head of a battle, or shall honor it with various flowers, incense, perfumes, and ointments—we shall bring his adversaries and enemies under his control;
we shall cause the destruction of the enemy forces and armies.

"Or, having had it written in a book, he will place it in his own home; for that son of good family or daughter of good family, or for the great king or queen, or for the monk or nun, or for the layman or laywoman, I shall provide great protection, great wealth, long life, health and well-being, and the constant increase of prosperity."
When this had been said, that entire assembly became silent.

From the *Mahākalpa* which sets forth the practice of mantras of the Mahāyāna, from the extensive section on the miraculous transformations of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, this is the first chapter, the "Assembly," from the *Mūlakalpa*.
Now begins the second chapter,
"The Ritual for the Mandala.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having surveyed the entire assembly, entered the meditative absorption known as "The Survey that Penetrates the Nature of All Sentient Beings."

And as soon as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had entered [that state], a ray of light issued forth from the region of his navel, accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays; having illuminated the entire realm of sentient beings on all sides, it returned to illuminate that very abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and remained there.

Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Speak, speak, O Son of the Jina! Having entered that which is called 'the entry into the samaya of all beings,' they shall attain your assembly of mantras and the accomplishment of all mantras, both mundane and supramundane.
When this had been said by the Lord of the Guhyakas, the King of Yakṣas, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke the tantra of the supreme secret maṇḍala.
He manifested a miraculous transformation called "The Impelling of All Vidyās.
Raising his right hand, he pointed with the tip of his finger toward the circle of the assembly;
from that fingertip, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of vidyā-kings issued forth.
Having emerged, they illuminated the entire great realm of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven with a vast radiance and remained there.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta [expounded] the heart-mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, which accomplishes all rites, is the solitary hero, and bestows the powers of summoning, dismissal, pacification, enrichment, and malevolent magic; as well as invisibility, traveling through the sky, entering the subterranean realm (pātāla), walking upon trees, attracting, causing hatred, and subjugation; and the offering of all perfumes, garlands, ointments, and lamps within one's own mantra-tantras—in short, however it is applied, this great king of wrath, named Akṣara, of great power, accomplishes all aims.
And what is that?
Oṃ.
Hrūṃ! This is the heart-mantra of the Great Wrathful One.
It is effective for all rites, taught by the Great Being Mañjughoṣa for all mandalas and all mantra practices, and it destroys all obstacles.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, raising his right hand, placed it upon the head of the Wrathful One and spoke thus: "Homage to all the Buddhas!
May the Blessed Buddhas attend to me!"
"Whatever bodhisattvas of great supernatural power, infinite and boundless, are established throughout the world-systems of the ten directions, may they empower this samaya!
Having spoken thus, he whirled that King of Wrath around and hurled him.

As soon as the Great King of Wrath was hurled, within a single moment, he subdued and brought under control all those beings of evil intent and great supernatural power throughout the entire world-system.
He caused that great assembly circle to enter the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods;
having established them in their proper positions, he became enveloped in a garland of flames on all sides and stood upon the heads of the wicked beings.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, looking again toward that circle of the assembly, said: "Listen, all you beings! For this King of Wrath will bring about the subjugation of anyone who transgresses this, my pledge (samaya).

Because the paths of the secret mantra-meanings and the words of the pledges of the Blessed Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are not to be transgressed, I shall speak of them by way of a concise exposition.
Listen to it; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak."
Homage to all Buddhas!
Oṃ ra ra smara, you who possess the form of a youth with unimpeded command, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
Noble ones, this is my root mantra.

The mudrā named Āryamañjuśrī is renowned as the Great Mudrā of the Five Crests (*pañcaśikhā-mahāmudrā*); one should employ it with this root mantra, for it becomes the heart-mantra that accomplishes all rites.
It is the Buddha, the auspicious performer of all deeds.
*Oṃ dhānyada namaḥ*.
And here the mudrā is known as the Triśikhā (Three-Pointed), which increases all enjoyments.
And here there is an upahṛdaya:
HŪṂ at the exterior.
And here the mudrā is known as the "Three-Pointed," which attracts all sentient beings. And here is the supreme heart-mantra:
MUṂ.
And here the mudrā is known as the Mayūrāsana, which brings all sentient beings under control;
it is the heart-essence of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, there is another [mantra] called Mahāvīra, consisting of eight syllables, which is supremely beneficial, most purifying, a severer of the path of the three realms of existence, a preventer of all miserable rebirths, a bringer of all peace, a performer of all rites, secure, leading to the attainment of Nirvāṇa, and present like the Buddha himself before one's eyes.

Mañjuśrī, this Bodhisattva himself has appeared in the form of a mantra as the supreme heart-essence for the benefit of all sentient beings, which fulfills all hopes; by the mere recollection of it, one purifies even the five deeds of immediate retribution—how much more so, then, for other [sins] that arise!
And what is it?
Oṃ āḥ dhīra hūṃ khacaraḥ!
O noble ones, this very one is I; it is the eight-syllable Great Hero, the supreme secret heart-mantra, which, like Buddhahood itself, is established as the means of realization.
In brief, it is capable of bringing all undertakings to their ultimate conclusion.
And here the mudrā is that known as Mahāvīrā, which fulfills all hopes. And here is the invocation mantra:
Oṃ he he, you whose own form has the appearance of a youth, who awakens [all] through the speech of children, come, Blessed One, come!
To the one holding a play-lotus like a youth, stay, stay in the center of the mandala! Remember your vow! O you of unimpeded command, hūṃ!
Do not delay!
*ru ru phaṭ svāhā*!
This, O Blessed One, is the mantra for summoning Mañjuśrī.

Having consecrated sandalwood water seven times with the mantra for all sentient beings, all bodhisattvas, all pratyekabuddhas, noble śrāvakas, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, piśācas, rākṣasas, and all spirits, one should scatter it in the four directions—above, below, across, and everywhere.
Then all the buddhas and bodhisattvas, Mañjuśrī himself along with his retinue, all mundane and supramundane mantras, all hosts of spirits, and all sentient beings will arrive.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Oṃ dhu dhura dhura, you who dwell in incense, you who are the radiance of incense, hūṃ! Abide; remember your pledge! Svāhā!
This is the incense mantra.
Then, having combined sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, one should offer incense.

When the Tathāgatas who have arrived and all the Bodhisattvas have their minds refreshed by the incense, they are summoned. In this regard, there is a mudrā known as the Mālā, which is auspicious and summons all sentient beings.
And for the mantra of invocation, this very auspicious lotus-garland mudrā is used.
Once all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have arrived, as well as all sentient beings who have come, the *arghya* offering should be presented.

Having stirred water with camphor, sandalwood, and saffron, and having mixed it with one or another of these flowers—Jāti, Navamālikā, Vārṣika, Punnāga, Nāgavakula, Piṇḍitagara, or whatever fragrant flower is appropriate for the season—one should present the *arghya* with this mantra.

Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: *He he! O Great Compassionate One, bearer of manifold forms! Accept the offering, cause it to be accepted! Remember the pledge (*samaya*)! Stay, stay in the center of the mandala! Enter, enter! O you who have compassion for all beings! Seize, seize! HŪṂ! To the one who wanders in the sky, svāhā!* And here, the mudrā is renowned as "Full" (*pūrṇā*), which follows in the footsteps of all Buddhas.
The fixed incantation for the fragrance here is as follows:
Homage to all Buddhas! Homage to the Tathāgata Samantagandhāvabhāsaśrī!
Namely: *Gandhe gandhe gandhāḍhye gandhamanorame pratīccha pratīccheyaṃ gandhaṃ samatānusāriṇe svāhā*.
And here there is a mudrā called Pallavā, which fulfills all hopes.
And here is the flower mantra:
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! Homage to the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarāja!
It is as follows: *kusume kusume kusumāḍhye kusumapuravāsini kusumāvati svāhā!*
One should fumigate with the aforementioned incense, using that very same incense-mantra.
Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and wondrous forms,
I shall proclaim the bali-mantra spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded. It is as follows: *He he bhagavan mahāsattva buddhāvalokita mā vilamba!
Accept this offering, accept it! Hūṃ hūṃ sarvaviśva ra ra ṭa ṭa phaṭ svāhā!* With this, one should cause the offering to be presented.
And there is the offering for all spirits (*sarvabhautika*).
Regarding this, there is a mudrā called Śakti, which wards off all malevolent beings.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded and who destroy all blinding darkness; homage to the Tathāgata Samantajyotirgandhāvabhāsaśrī.

It is as follows: "He he, Blessed One, whose body is adorned with hundreds of thousands of light rays! Manifest, manifest! O you whose form is illuminated by the universal flames of the great Bodhisattvas! Leap, leap! Behold, behold all sentient beings! Svāhā! This is the lamp mantra; and with this, one should cause the lamp to be offered.
The mudrā named Vikāsinī, which beholds all sentient beings:
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: *jvala jvala jvālaya jvālaya*.
Hūṃ!
Vivodhaka, Harikṛṣṇapiṅgala, svāhā!
These are the mantras for the fire-ritual.
And here there is a mudrā named Sampuṭa, renowned in the world, which illuminates all sentient beings; it was previously taught by the best of sages for the wise Bodhisattva.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"O Lord of the Guhyakas, these mantra-words, together with their secrets, are supremely secret. They belong to your renowned family and are fierce and always terrible."
This indeed is [the essence] of all mantras being accomplished by the wise.
This vidyā shall be proclaimed for the purpose of utterly destroying him who is renowned as Mūrdhūṭaka, [the enemy] of both the Jina and Kula lineages.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded! Oṃ! Act! Act! Perform! Perform my task! Shatter! Shatter all obstacles!
Even more so, [subdue] all Vajra-Vināyakas!
O you who bring an end to the life of Mūrdhaṭaka, you of great and distorted form, cook, cook all the wicked ones!
O you who bring an end to the life of Mahāgaṇapati, bind, bind all the seizing spirits (grahas)!
O six-faced one, six-armed one, six-legged one, bring Rudra!
Bring Viṣṇu!
Bring the gods beginning with Brahmā!
Do not delay, do not delay! Flash, flash! Cause [him] to enter into the center of the maṇḍala! Remember the pledge!
HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ!
O Lord of the Supreme Guhyakas, this is that supreme secret, the Great Hero Mañjuśrī, the great wrathful king named Ṣaṇmukha, the destroyer of all obstacles.
Merely by reciting this, the bodhisattvas established on the ten stages are put to flight.
How much more so, then, evil obstructors!
By the mere recitation of this, great protection is established.
And here there is a mudrā known as the "Great Spear" (Mahāśūlā), which destroys all obstacles.
This is the heart-mantra of this very King of Wrath:
Oṃ hrīḥṃ jñīḥ vikṛtānana hūṃ!
Destroy all enemies, paralyze them, phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
By means of this mantra, one causes all enemies to be seized by a great piercing disease (*mahāśūlaroga*) or by a quartan fever (*caturthaka*),
either through a hundred recitations or as long as it pleases, until they attain a state of friendliness (*maitratā*) or else conceive a mind of compassion (*karuṇācitta*).
Liberation will not occur at the end of the recitation.
Regarding those who have offended the Three Jewels, it must be performed until death; however, for those with peaceful minds, the *mahāśūla* mudrā alone should be employed.
And here, the *upahṛdaya* mantra is as follows:
Oṃ hrīḥṃ kālarūpa huṃ khaṃ svāhā.
The mudrā of the Great Trident alone should be employed.
It causes whatever one desires to be done by all malevolent beings.
The supreme heart-mantra,
empowered by all the Buddhas, known as the Single Syllable:
HŪṂ.
This is the performer of all rites;
it should be employed with the Great Trident mudrā alone.
It wards off all misfortunes.

This King of Wrath, who brings all beings under his control, is to be employed in brief for all rites. Recitation within the mandala is especially distinguished at the time of accomplishment. [Mantra 78] O
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Jaya, Jaya, Sujaya, O Great Compassionate One, you who possess all forms! Go, go to your own abode, and dismiss all the Buddhas;
cause them, along with their retinues, to enter their own abodes.
Recall the pledge!
May all my purposes be accomplished through these mantra-words; fulfill my heart's desire, svāhā!
This is the dismissal mantra, which should be employed in all rites.

The mudrā is renowned as the Bhadrapīṭha; one should offer a seat with this [mudrā] recited mentally seven times. There is dismissal for all mundane and supramundane maṇḍalas and mantras, and indeed the accomplishment of the mantra.
And it should be employed during the observances of the time for reciting the mantra according to the rules of the samaya.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having again surveyed that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, spoke this extensive chapter on the mantras and the assembly of vidyās for his own great circle of the assembly:
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Oṃ riṭi svāhā!
This is the vidyā named Keśinī, a follower of Mañjuśrī, which performs all rites.
It is to be employed with the great five-crested mudrā in all rites concerning poisons.
Homage to all the Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Oṃ niṭi. This is the vidyā named Upakeśinī, which accomplishes all rites; one should employ it with the Vikāsinī mudrā in all rituals concerning grahas.
Homage to all Buddhas of unimpeded movement!
Oṃ niḥ!
This vidyā, named Balinī, is auspicious and performs all rites.
When joined with the Bhadrapīṭha mudrā, she brings the Yakṣiṇī under control with certainty.
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms;
joined with the seal and the power, she is the slayer of all ḍākinīs.
Oṃ jñaiḥ svāhā!
This knowledge-mantra named Kāpatalinī was spoken by Mañjughoṣa;
it is praised by all the Buddhas everywhere and possesses a divine form.
Homage to all Buddhas who move with unimpeded gait!
It is as follows: Oṃ varade svāhā!
One who seeks prosperity should employ this very three-crested mudrā.
The goddess, assuming many forms, swiftly accomplishes the attainment of enjoyments.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
Oṃ bhūri svāhā!
When joined with the trident mudrā, this destroys all fevers.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
Oṃ nu re svāhā! This knowledge-mantra named Tārāvatī is praised for all rites;
when joined with the mudrā of the spear-staff, it destroys obstacles.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
It is as follows: Oṃ vilokini svāhā!
This vidyā, named Lokavatī, brings all treasuries under control.
When joined with the vajra-mudrā, she bestows all happiness.
Homage to all Buddhas, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms.
It is as follows: Oṃ, O Viśvā, source of the universe, you of universal form! Kaha kaha! Enter, enter! Remember the pledge!
*Ruru tiṣṭha svāhā!* This knowledge-mantra of great power has been revealed by the Leaders of the World; joined with the fang-mudrā, it enters into all beings as a weapon.
She is auspicious, the bestower of boons upon all beings, and is fully revealed as Viśvā.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
It is as follows: Oṃ śvetaśrī vapuḥ svāhā!
When applied with the peacock-throne mudrā, this [mantra] accomplishes all rites.
Renowned as Mahāśvetā, she possesses inconceivable and wondrous form;
she bestows good fortune upon the world and brings men and women under her control.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous.
It is as follows: *Oṃ khikhirikhiri bhaṅguri sarvaśatruṃ stambhaya jambhaya mohaya vaśamānaya svāhā*.
This mantra is proclaimed as a great vidyā, a yoginī.
When joined with the seal of speech (vāk-mudrā), she pacifies wicked beings.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose movement proceeds with unimpeded gait!
It is as follows: Oṃ Śrīḥ!
This vidyā, Mahālakṣmī, was taught by the Lords of the World.
When joined with the sampuṭa mudrā, she bestows great sovereignty.
Homage to all Buddhas, who bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
It is as follows: Oṃ! Ajite!
O you who possess the form of a youth! Come, come hither!
Accomplish my purpose! Svāhā!
The maiden known as Ajitā is born from nectar;
joined with the full mudrā, she is the warder-off of all enemies.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous.
It is as follows: Oṃ jaye svāhā!
Vijaye svāhā!
Svāhā to Ajitā! Svāhā to Aparājitā!
These are known as the Four Sisters, the attendants of the Bodhisattva.
They wander throughout the entire earth, acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
Their brother, known as Stumburu, is their attendant.
Mounted upon a boat, they dwell in the waters;
when invoked with the fist-gesture (muṣṭimudrā), they fulfill all hopes.
Homage to all Buddhas, the sovereign lords of the world.
It is as follows: Oṃ!

O Youth, Great Youth, play, play! O six-faced one authorized by the Bodhisattva, you whose hand is raised with the peacock-throne, red-limbed one, lover of red perfumes and ointments! Kha kha! Eat, eat, eat!
Huṃ! Dance, dance!
O you whose form is worshipped with red flowers, remember the pledge! Wander, wander! Cause to wander, cause to wander, cause to wander!
Quickly, quickly! Do not delay; accomplish all my tasks! O bearer of variegated forms, stay, stay! Hūṃ hūṃ! You who are authorized by all the Buddhas, svāhā!
When these words were spoken by the Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, the leader,
the entire earth shook in six ways on all sides.
For the benefit of all sentient beings and to ward off wicked beings,
the formidable son of Maheśvara has come here for the sake of those to be disciplined.
Skanda and Aṅgāraka, clearly marked by the signs of the planets, were there;
then Mañjubhāṣiṇī spoke with a mind possessed by compassion.
This Great Being is a Bodhisattva who acts for the benefit of the ignorant; since he is said to practice the conduct of a sentient being, he wanders everywhere throughout the world.
Endowed with the staff of the power of the mudrā, that great-souled one causes even those beginning with Brahmā to revolve; how much more so, then, the fruit of human [attainment]?
This mantra of Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī has been proclaimed as a concise summary of the entire Kaumārabhṛtya for the morning.
The Bodhisattva has come here out of a desire to benefit sentient beings;
the three-syllable heart-essence of this mantra has been proclaimed.
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, one who is intent on attracting enjoyments should employ the mudrā of the power-staff; when thus applied, it accomplishes all activities.
Oṃ hūṃ jaḥ!
This mantra, in brief, shall produce human results.
Homage to all Buddhas whose forms are universally radiant!
Oṃ vikṛtagraha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
And when his subsidiary heart-mantra is joined with the power of the mudrā,
it causes all beings— including the grahas and the mātṛs— to revolve [under its control].
When applied to all the sealed mudrās, it becomes fruitful;
it terrifies the spirits and liberates those possessed by evil beings.

This youth named Kārttikeya-Mañjuśrī is the attendant of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; he performs all rites by mere recitation. He terrifies all spirits, draws them forth, brings them under control, withers them, and slays them; or rather, he accomplishes everything according to the desire of the vidyādhara.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is as follows: Oṃ, Brahmā, sublime Brahmā, in the splendor of Brahmā, perform peace, svāhā!
This mantra, the Great Brahma, was spoken by the Bodhisattva;
at that very moment, all beings attained peace and became cool.

The *mudrā* joined with five crests brings swift well-being; it is effective in all rites of sorcery (*ābhicāruka*), or if it is recited [in other contexts]. This has been stated briefly as a summary of its ritual manual (*kalpa*).
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
Namely: Oṃ, you whose vehicle is Garuḍa, wielder of the discus, four-armed one, huṃ huṃ! Remember the pledge!
The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
Commanded by Mañjughoṣa, he who swiftly accomplishes the purpose and brings auspiciousness causes the spirits of embodied beings to flee, appearing in the form of Viṣṇu.

When joined with the three-crested mudrā, it is firm and swiftly accomplishes one's aims. Whatever extensive ritual procedures (*kalpavistara*) have been taught in the Vaiṣṇava tantras were spoken by Mañjughoṣa as skillful means for the sake of training sentient beings.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
Namely: Oṃ, Great Maheśvara, Lord of Beings, Bull-bannered One, wearer of the crown of long matted locks, whose form is grey with white ashes, hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ!
The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
This mantra has been proclaimed by me out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings;
when combined with the trident mudrā, it is the destroyer of all malevolent spirits.

The beings dwelling upon the surface of the earth will say, "It is exactly as I previously described this ancient kalpa," for the various extensive qualities proclaimed by me in the Śaiva Tantra [shall be realized].
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded.
Namely: Oṃ, Śakuna, Great Śakuna, you whose wings are spread like a lotus, destroyer of all serpents, kha kha, devour, devour! Remember your vow!
Hūṃ, stay!
The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
This mantra is of great power, renowned as Vainateya;
it is the supreme tamer of the difficult-to-subdue and the destroyer of the poison of serpents.
When joined with the Mahāmudrā, it destroys most terrible misfortune;
there is no doubt that it neutralizes both stationary and mobile poisons.
By the command of the Bodhisattva, that king of birds of great splendor wandered in the form of a garuḍa to discipline sentient beings through skillful means.
All the extensive ritual manuals (kalpa) that have been taught in the Gāruḍa Tantra have been declared by me alone for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Garuḍa, having come here for the sake of Vainateya,
moved about in the form of a bird to destroy the poison of the serpents.
Whatever worldly mantras there are, they have all been proclaimed in this ritual manual; for the sake of training sentient beings, I move about in various ways accordingly.
However, those Tathāgata mantras belonging to the Vajra and Jewel families have already been taught previously within this extensive ritual manual.
Just as a nurse diligently caresses children in many ways,
so do I move among those of childish intellect in the form of a mantra.
That which was taught by the Ten-Powered Ones in the past has now been spoken by me;
the entire meaning of the mantras and tantras was also declared by the Greatly Radiant Youth.
Those which were sung by the supreme Jinas and sung by the sons of the Ten-Powered One,
those were sung by Mañjusvara, who possesses inconceivable and wondrous forms.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities and that great circle of the assembly, entered the samādhi called "The Exhortation of All Samayas."

In that state, when Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta has entered into meditative absorption—his mind intent on the conduct for the deliverance of all beings without exception, and in which all sentient beings become established—the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities becomes a maṇḍala adorned with various arrays of precious jewels and the inconceivable, marvelous miraculous transformations of a bodhisattva. This maṇḍala cannot be drawn even by bodhisattvas who have entered the conduct of all pratyekabuddhas and noble śrāvakas, nor even by those lords established on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). How much less so by beings who are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*)? Upon seeing Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, who stands established in the state of the accomplishment of the divine and noble maṇḍala-pledge, all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; all the pratyekabuddhas; all the noble śrāvakas; all the bodhisattvas established on the ten stages; the noble ones who have attained the consecration of the crown prince (*yauvarājyābhiṣeka*); and all beings, both with and without outflows (*sāśrava* and *anāśrava*), perceived themselves through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta as having entered a maṇḍala that is inconceivable, produced from the mental excellence of a samādhi, and flowing forth from the conduct of Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
It cannot even be taken as an object of the mind by ordinary beings, let alone be written down or caused to be written.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having entered into the commitment (*samaya*) of that great assembly circle, addressed the beings:
"Listen, worthy ones!
This commitment of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas is not to be transgressed; how much less so for other beings, whether noble or ignoble?"
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas:

"O Son of the Conqueror, you have explained the transcendent human rite arising from the mind; now I shall speak of the human rite for those Tathāgatas who have entered final nirvāṇa, by entering which sentient beings may attain all mundane and supramundane accomplishments."
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Speak, speak, O Son of the Conqueror, whenever you deem it the right time!
For the peerless Lord of the World, the Lion of the Śākyas, has entered final nirvāṇa."
Just as Buddhahood [is for all beings], so is your mandala upon the earth for sentient beings.
For in this world, mere sight [is sufficient], and the mantras attained success;
yet, [this fails] when performed without knowledge of the ritual rules, or by one who is lying down or in a state of mental derangement.
Even for the high-souled Brahmā, mantras would not attain success if one is uninitiated in this tantra and has not perceived the samaya proclaimed therein.
Mantras do not attain accomplishment even with repeated effort if they are devoid of the application of the samaya, even for Śakra himself despite his exertion.
Mantras do not attain accomplishment even on this earth among humans;
however, for one who knows the reality of the commitments (samaya), the scriptures, and the principles, as well as in the practices, rites, and means of achievement,
they are accomplished merely by being recited— both the noble (ārya) and the worldly (laukika) mantras.
Having entered the maṇḍala of Mañjughoṣa, one performs all rites;
the accomplishment of mantra is certain for him within the teaching of the Youthful One himself.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, spoke to that Mahāsattva in the midst [of the assembly]:
"O, O Mahābodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, speak briefly of the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala."
Thus addressed by the Lord of the Guhyakas, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta spoke the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala for the benefit of all sentient beings.

First of all, during the fortnight of the messenger (pratihāraka-pakṣa), in the months of Caitra or Vaiśākha, on an auspicious day of the bright fortnight observed by pure planets and conjoined with a favorable lunar mansion—either on the first day of the waxing moon or the full moon, or at another time excluding the rainy months—in the forenoon, the Maṇḍalācārya should take up residence upon the ground. He should do so either by resorting to a great city where he himself resides, or by resorting to a river flowing to the ocean, or near the seashore; specifically, in the northeastern direction of the great city, neither too far nor too near, the Maṇḍalācārya should dwell for seven days or for a mere fortnight in a secluded hut that he has constructed.

In that place, one should take a very clean area of ground, square on all sides, measuring sixteen or twelve cubits, free from stones, gravel, ash, charcoal, husks, potsherds, and bones; having made that area of ground very clean and well-prepared, one should sprinkle it with water mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or with water scented with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, which has been consecrated eight thousand times by the wrathful king Yamāntaka while joined with the great mudrā of the five crests (*pañcaśikha-mahāmudrā*). One should thus sprinkle that area of ground in the four cardinal directions, as well as above, below, across, and in all intermediate directions.

Then, that area of ground should be square on all sides, measuring sixteen cubits, twelve cubits, or eight cubits; among these, the sixteen-cubit is the superior, the twelve-cubit is the middling, and the eight-cubit is the inferior. This threefold mandala has been proclaimed by the All-Seeing Ones for one who desires sovereignty. Of these, the superior increases enjoyment, the middling increases prosperity, while the inferior, though consisting of mere conventional practice, is auspicious and performs all rites. Thereafter, one should draw whichever mandala is desired by the mind.
There, one should dig that spot of ground to a depth of two cubits.
If stones, charcoal, ashes, bones, hair, or various kinds of living creatures are seen there, one should dig another spot of ground;
it must be free from defects and free from disturbances.

If not, he should carefully examine mountain peaks, river sandbanks, ocean shores, or the sandy banks of great rivers; having made such a place very clean and free of living beings through great effort, he should draw there.

Furthermore, that area of ground should be filled with water free of living beings mixed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or with pure earth from a riverbank, or with earth from an anthill where no living creatures are found.
