Having filled it, one should have it well-compacted, made level, and have a threefold mandala constructed all around as desired.

In the four directions, one should drive in four stakes of *khadira* wood, having consecrated them seven times with the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*). Then, using a five-colored thread consecrated seven times with the Heart-mantra of the Wrathful One, one should encircle that maṇḍala on all sides in a square shape.
In this same way, one should construct a square shape in the central area and likewise within it.

The Maṇḍala Master, standing in the center, should recite the root mantra of the vidyā eight thousand times. Having bound the five-crested Great Seal (mahāmudrā), he should perform protection for his companions and protection for himself using the root mantra.
While reciting, having circumambulated the entire maṇḍala clockwise, he should sit facing east upon a bundle of kuśa grass, keeping all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind.
He should then encircle that maṇḍala on all sides in a square shape.
Having made her stay outside for one night, he should cause her to be banished.

In that regard, the mandala master—having completed the preliminary practices (*puraścaraṇa*), being skilled in the independent mantras, devoted to the Mahāyāna for the sake of sentient beings through skillful means, having stayed for one night, and accompanied by good companions—should, by means of a rite seen in the ritual treatises, place that powder in the center of the mandala; the powder should consist of five colors, be fine and radiant, well-prepared, and have been consecrated with the six-syllable mantra and empowered with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*).

Outside, one should prepare a section of ground adorned with crossroads featuring raised banners, flags, and archways, hung with clusters of fruit-bearing plantain stalks, and made resonant by the sounds of beaten *bherī* drums, *mṛdaṅga* drums, conchs, and lutes.
One should have books of Mahāyāna sūtras being recited in the four directions—sūtras that accord with the fourfold assembly for hearing the Dharma of auspicious sound;
specifically, one should have the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā* recited in the southern direction.
The noble *Candrapradīpa-samādhi* is in the western direction;
the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha* is in the northern direction;
the noble *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* is in the eastern direction.

In this way, one should request a person who has studied the four sūtras—a Dharma-preacher—to listen to the Dharma in the absence of a book. Then, the Maṇḍala Master, having risen, should scatter white fragrant flowers mixed with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron over that entire maṇḍala while reciting the root mantra. Having scattered them, he should go outside.

After seven days, having subsisted on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), two or three highly skilled painters—whose minds have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who observe the *upoṣadha* vows, and who are accustomed to fasting—should be admitted.

Having bound their topknots with the root mantra itself, they should then receive fine powders of gold, silver, various jewels, and five-colored, brilliant, beautiful, and subtle pigments in copper vessels; it should be caused to be painted by beings of great wealth and by righteous great kings.
This leads inevitably to awakening, being directed toward awakening and culminating in awakening.
If such is the case merely by seeing the maṇḍala, how much more so when accomplishing the mantra!
For beings of little merit, now that the Bull of the Śākyas has passed into nirvāṇa.
"How could such enjoyments exist? This must surely be the work of destiny.
Thus did Mañjughoṣa, of great splendor, reflect upon seeing the poverty of the people.
One should proclaim the summary of the ritual procedure and the mandala in brief:
one should delineate it with fine powders of rice flour, radiant with five colors— namely, white, yellow, red, black, and green.
The Maṇḍala Master himself should take the powder previously prepared, form the five-crested Mahāmudrā, and seal that powder while reciting the root mantra.
Meanwhile, another practitioner-master should have a fire-pit constructed outside the maṇḍala in the southeastern direction, according to the ritual procedure.

One should prepare a pit measuring two cubits in circumference and one cubit in depth, shaped like the calyx of a lotus on all sides, with the exterior also shaped like a lotus calyx. Having kindled a fire with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, one should summon the fire by forming the *mudrāmuṣṭi* (fist-gesture) while holding moist fuel-sticks of *bilva* wood, each one span (*vitasti*) in length, smeared with curds, honey, and ghee, while reciting either the root mantra or the six-syllable heart mantra.
Having summoned it, one should again offer oblations one hundred and eight times using that same previously mentioned single-syllable root-heart mantra.
Then the Maṇḍala Master, having bound his uṣṇīṣa and prepared his equipment, should himself or have highly skilled painters execute the work.

Then the Maṇḍala Master, keeping the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in mind, should offer incense with the previously mentioned incense-mantra; having joined his palms in añjali and bowed to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having paid homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, he should take the powder and cause the form to be drawn.
The painters must then complete the forms.

According to this procedure, one should first paint the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, residing in the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, and teaching the Dharma. Once he has been painted, the assistant of the maṇḍala master, having performed the rite of self-protection with the root mantra, should offer a bali-oblation to all spirits and cast it in the four directions, above, below, and outside the maṇḍala.

Then, having bathed and gone near the fire-pit, being pure and clothed in clean garments, and having performed the protective rites, one should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee mixed with saffron using the root mantra.
Then, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and performing the recitation, one should remain right there.
Having consecrated white mustard seeds eight times with the wrathful king Yamāntaka, one should place them in a pair of shallow earthen bowls (*śarāva*).

Upon seeing any kind of obstacle that has arisen—such as a foul day of wind and rain accompanied by various distorted forms and terrible sounds—one should offer seven oblations of mustard seeds with the *huta* fire;
then the obstacles will perish.
Or, in the case of human obstacles, five oblations should be offered.
Men become paralyzed and powerless, or they die;
or else they are seized by non-human beings at that very moment—of this there is no doubt. Even Śakra would somehow die quickly.
How much more so then will humans with evil minds, or other obstructors, flee here and there, utterly destroyed by the fear of the wrathful Yamāntaka?
Then, the assistant practitioner should remain right there, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, reciting the mantra of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath.

Then, the Maṇḍala Master should depict two Pratyekabuddhas seated upon lotus thrones in the full-lotus posture on the right side of the image of the Blessed One Śākyamuni; beneath them, two great Śrāvakas should be depicted listening to the Dharma.

To their right is the Blessed One, the Noble Avalokiteśvara, adorned with all ornaments, white as an autumn reed, seated upon a lotus throne; holding a lotus in his left hand, he displays the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*) with his right hand. To his right is the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī, holding a lotus in her hand, bowing to the Blessed Śākyamuni with her right hand, seated upon a lotus throne; she wears a crown of matted hair, is clothed in white silk garments, has a silken upper robe, and is smeared with black ashes on her three topknots.
In this manner, Tārā and Bhrukuṭī should be depicted well-established in their respective seats and postures.
Above them, the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, Tathāgatalocanā, and Uṣṇīṣarāja should be depicted.
In this way, the sixteen Bodhisattvas are to be fashioned.

They are as follows: Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Maitreya who has abandoned the lower realms, Camaravyagrahasta (holding a yak-tail whisk), gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One; Vimalagati, Vimalaketu, Sudhana, Candraprabha, Vimalakīrti, Sarvavyādhicikitsaka, Sarvadharmīśvararāja, Lokagati, Mahāmati, and Patidhara.
These sixteen great bodhisattvas should be depicted with serene forms, adorned with all ornaments.
The Sovereign King of Knowledge (vidyārāja) and the Queen of Knowledge (vidyārājñī) have their forms and mudrās in the center of the lotus.
He [the practitioner] should draw the remaining deities in their respective places according to his memory and according to the scriptures.
Finally, in that place, he should establish a square-shaped area adorned with lotus flowers.
"By this [mantra], may the deities of the vidyā whom you have remembered remain in this place."
Thus, on the right side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two Pratyekabuddhas, Gandhamādana and Upāriṣṭa, [should be placed].
In this way, the maṇḍala should be made facing east with entrance doors on all sides.
On either side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, two other Pratyekabuddhas, Candana and Siddha, should be painted.

Below them, two great śrāvakas, Mahākāśyapa and Mahākātyāyana, are to be depicted. To their left is the noble Vajrapāṇi, with a complexion dark like a blue lotus, of serene form, adorned with all ornaments, his right hand holding a fly-whisk and his left hand in a wrathful form as a vajra-fist. [He is accompanied by] Vajrāṅkuśī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, Subāhu, and Vajrasena, each with their respective dress, emblems, positions, and seats, together with their retinues of all the vidyārājas and vidyārājñīs; they are to be depicted according to their forms, mudrās, and so forth, as remembered.
To the left of those as well, one should draw a square-shaped double-vajra mudrā.
Having drawn it, one should say: "Those hosts of vidyās who have not been remembered in this place, may those hosts of vidyās who are now remembered by means of this place remain here."
Above them, the Blessed Perfection of Wisdom and the goddess Māmakī are to be depicted, adorned with all ornaments and possessing serene forms.
Above them as well, eight Uṣṇīṣa Kings, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, should be depicted;
their respective seals and forms as Great Universal Monarchs (Mahārāja-cakravartin) should be drawn,
golden-colored, with serene faculties, and adorned with every ornament.
The Tathāgata slightly [perceives] those who have given rise to the view of a personal identity, namely:
Cakravartin, Uṣṇīṣa, Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, Kamaloṣṇīṣa, Tejorāśi, and Unnatoṣṇīṣa.

Therefore, these Uṣṇīṣa Kings should be painted to the left of the Pratyekabuddhas. At the entrance, to the right of the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, one should paint the one named Lokātikrāntagāmin, who wears a crown of matted hair, has a serene form, holds a rosary in his right hand and a water-pot in his left, faces the door, and has a face with a slight frown. To the left, at the entrance, the Great Bodhisattva named Ajitañjaya should be painted.

With a serene form, wearing a crown of matted locks, with a staff and water-pot resting in his left hands, holding a rosary in his right hand and bestowing boons, with a face slightly furrowed by a frown, he should be depicted facing the door.

Beneath the lion throne is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides; beneath that as well is a jeweled celestial palace (*ratnavimāna*). Seated therein is the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, appearing in the form of a youth, with a complexion as fair as saffron, of serene appearance and beautiful form, his face slightly smiling. His left hand holds a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and his right hand, resting upon a *śrīphala* fruit, is in the gesture of granting boons (*varada*). He is adorned with all the ornaments of a child and beautified by five locks of hair (*pañcacīraka*); he has a pearl necklace as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a silken cloth as an upper garment (*uttarīya*), and is dressed in fine silk garments. Radiant in every direction and surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, he sits upon a lotus seat, casting his gaze toward the wrathful king Yamāntaka, facing the entrance for entry into the maṇḍala; he is to be depicted everywhere as one of lovely appearance.

On his right side, beneath the lotus, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be depicted with a greatly distorted form, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, awaiting his command, and gazing toward the Great Bodhisattva; he should be painted everywhere [in this manner].
On the left side, beneath the lotus, five bodhisattvas in the form of sons of gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be depicted.
They are as follows: Sunirmala, Sudānta, Suśānta, Saṃśuddha, Tamodghātana, and Samantāvaloka.

And all of them should be depicted as seated in the abodes of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, appearing like surfaces of rock blazing with many jewels, strewn with various flowers emitting light on all sides, and possessing beautiful forms.

Outside, on all sides, an inner mandala should be constructed, square in shape, with four archways in the four directions, blazing with various five-colored hues, and bound by well-proportioned lines.

In the eastern direction, above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, in the center among the lines, there should be a small-sized image of the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, seated upon a lotus throne, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons, and sitting in the cross-legged posture.
To its right, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin mudrā should be drawn;
to its left, the Tejorāśi mudrā should be drawn;
and above Tathāgatalocanā, the Prajñāpāramitā mudrā should be drawn.

Above the Blessed One Āryāvalokiteśvara and to the right of the Prajñāpāramitā mudrā, the Blessed One Amitābha should be depicted in the form of a Tathāgata, with his hand in the gesture of granting boons (varapradāna), seated upon a lotus throne, and surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides.
To its right as well, the mudrās of the bowl and the robe should be made.
In this same sequence, lotus mudrās should be made at the entrance.
Or, according to the intention of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarāja, the Uṣṇīṣatejorāśi mudrā should be drawn, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides.

To his left, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu should be depicted, seated upon a mountain of jewels, teaching the Dharma; he should be painted with a universal radiance emanating from all sides amidst variegated flames and rays of blue beryl, emerald, and ruby.

To his left as well, the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, should be depicted. To his left as well, the Dharmacakra mudrā, possessing flames on all sides, should be depicted.
To his left as well, the khakharaka, water-pot, rosary, and bhadrāsana mudrā should be depicted.
In due order, at the location of the door, a vajra-needle with flames blazing on both sides should be drawn all around.
Below the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, either the great mudrā named Pañcaśikhā or the utpala-mudrā should be drawn.
These two, blazing all around and joined to one another, should be drawn in the form of a complete mandala.
From the entrance, one should enter facing west and face east.

In all cases, there is an outer maṇḍala, brilliant with the colors of the five hues, variegated and beautiful to behold, divided into four corners, and shaped like four archways; it should be drawn outside the inner maṇḍala, two cubits in width on each side of the four directions.

In the eastern direction is Mahābrahmā, four-faced, clothed in white garments, wearing a white upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), golden-hued, wearing a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), with a staff and water-pot held in his left hand.

To his right, the son of the gods Ābhāsvara is to be depicted, golden in color, his form absorbed in the intermediate dhyāna; he is clothed in silk garments with a silken upper robe, his face is very serene, he wears a crown of matted hair and a white sacred thread, and he sits in the paryanka posture, granting boons with his right hand.
To his right, the god Akaniṣṭha should be depicted, adorned with all ornaments, of serene form, his mind absorbed in meditation, dressed in garments of fine silk, and wearing a silken upper robe.
To his right, seated in the paryanka posture, he bestows boons with his right hand and wears a white sacred thread.

In this manner, in successive order, the sons of the gods—Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, Suyāma, Śakra, and so forth—are to be depicted according to their sequence and as adorned with their respective attire.
Below Śakra, the deities belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings—the Sadāmattas, Mālādhāris, Karoṭapāṇis, and Vīṇādvitīyakas—should be depicted.
Furthermore, the terrestrial sons of the gods (bhauma-devaputras) should be painted in their proper order and according to their respective attire.
Likewise, in the southern direction, the gods Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, Parīttābha, Puṇyaprasava, and so forth, should be depicted according to their respective attire and positions.
In this manner, they should be depicted in two rows below them in the western and northern directions.
Outside the second maṇḍala is the third maṇḍala;
there, the four Great Kings are to be depicted in succession in the four cardinal directions.
As he enters from the northern direction, there is Dhanada to the right; he stands near a treasure, is adorned with all ornaments, wears a slightly bent crown, and has the form of a yakṣa.
To his right, Maṇibhadra and Pūrṇabhadra, the two yakṣa generals, are to be depicted.

In this manner, Hārītī, the great yakṣiṇī, should be painted in succession. The boy Priyaṅkara, seated upon her lap and gazing at the maṇḍala, should be painted; as well as Pañcika, Piṅgala, and Bhīṣaṇa.
And near them, the mudrās of the yakṣas should be drawn.
In this same sequence, Varuṇa, with a noose in his hand, should be drawn in the western direction.
The two nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, as well as the eight great nāga kings beginning with Takṣaka and Vāsuki, should be drawn.

In this manner, those residing in two rows should be depicted in successive order: the yakṣas, rākṣasas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and ṛṣis; the siddhas, pretas, piśācas, garuḍas, kinnaras, and humans; the various medicinal herbs beginning with humans; and the special gems, mountains, rivers, and islands—all these principal figures should be drawn in succession.
In the southern direction, Yama is to be depicted along with his retinue.
The seven Mothers are to be placed in the southeastern direction.

Agni is surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides; his hands are occupied with a staff, a water-pot, and a rosary; he wears a crown of matted hair and is clothed in white garments, with a silk upper robe draped over one shoulder, a white sacred thread, and a golden complexion, marked with three lines of ash.
In this manner, they should be depicted arranged in two rows according to their specific distinctions of weapons, attire, posture, color, and essential nature.

Entering from all sides into the outer maṇḍala, there is Umāpati, whose vehicle is a bull, who holds a trident in his hand; and the goddess Umā, golden-colored and adorned with all ornaments; and Kārtikeya, seated upon a peacock, with a spear raised in his hand, having the form of a youth, six-faced, with a body of reddish luster, and clothed in yellow garments.

Wearing a yellow garment as an upper robe and holding a bell and a red banner in his left hand, Bhṛṅgiriṭi—extremely emaciated in form—should be depicted first, followed by Mahāgaṇapati, Nandikeśvara, Mahākāla, and the Seven Mothers, each drawn according to their respective ornaments, weapons, attire, and postures.
Then the eight Vasus, the seven Ṛṣis, and Viṣṇu, who holds a discus, with four arms bearing a mace, a conch, and a sword, seated upon Garuḍa and adorned with all ornaments.

The eight planets, the twenty-seven lunar mansions, and the eight subordinate deities (upagrahas) who move within the terrestrial mandala should be depicted in successive order; likewise, the fifteen lunar days (tithis) of both the bright and dark fortnights, the twelve zodiac signs (rāśis), the six seasons, the twelve months, and the year.

Furthermore, the four sisters mounted upon a boat, with their brother as the fifth, dwelling in the waters—these deities should be briefly established in their respective seals (mudrās). In brief, they should be arranged in two rows in succession within the three mandalas, based upon the mandala of the ancestors (pitṛ-maṇḍala).
It should be drawn as a square;
this same arrangement applies even to the three mandalas.
In brief, the Buddha, the Blessed One, must certainly be depicted at the forefront of all sentient beings.
In the Lotus family, Āryāvalokiteśvara must necessarily be depicted on the right;
in the Vajra family, Vajrapāṇi must necessarily be depicted on the left;
and at the head of the Bodhisattvas, Ārya Samantabhadra must necessarily be depicted.
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta must certainly be depicted;
he and these others are to be depicted according to their established positions among the mudrās.
Within this inner maṇḍala, in the middle maṇḍala as well, Brahmā Sahāmpati must certainly be depicted in the eastern direction.

Likewise, in the southern direction, the Ābhāsvara gods, the Akaniṣṭha gods, the formless (arūpin) gods, the Maṇḍalākāra gods, the unmanifest (avyakta) gods, and the gods of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and in the northern direction, Śakra, king of the gods, along with Suyāma, Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Paranirmita, Parīttābha, and the other sons of the gods—each one of these kings of the gods must certainly be depicted.
These are to be established among the mudrās.
Likewise, in the third mandala, in the northern direction, Īśāna, the lord of spirits, must certainly be depicted together with Umā.

Near the second gate is Kārttikeya Mañjuśrī, seated upon a peacock, holding a spear, his form radiant red, dressed in yellow lower garments and upper robes; in his right hand he holds a bell and a banner, appearing as a youth, and gazing at the mandala.
In the eastern direction is Vainateya in the form of a bird.
The seer Mārkaṇḍeya must certainly be depicted;
he is to be established among these mudrās.
To the southeast, four maidens accompanied by their princely brothers, situated upon a boat, should be depicted wandering upon the great ocean;
and Agni, the king of the gods, must certainly be drawn there.

Likewise, in the southern direction, the city of Laṅkā and Vibhīṣaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, must be depicted; and stationed there, resting against a *picumanda* tree, the Bodhisattva in the form of a yakṣa named Jambhalajalendra must certainly be painted.
In this manner, proceeding in due order, King Yama, possessing great supernatural power over the hungry ghosts (preta), must certainly be depicted;
likewise, the Piśāca king named Vikarāla must certainly be depicted.
This is how they are to be arranged among the seals (mudrās).
In this manner, in the southwestern direction, the two chief nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, must certainly be depicted.

In the western direction, the chief of planets, Āditya, and the excellent sage named Kapila Muni—the bull among the Nirgrantha Tīrthaṅkaras—should be placed in succession, appearing in the form of a Nirgrantha. These are to be established among the mudrās.
And in the northwestern directions, the Yakṣa king Dhanada, the Gandharva king Pañcaśikha, and the Kinnara king Druma—these must certainly be depicted.
They are to be drawn in their respective positions, following the sequence of the mudrās.

The fourth maṇḍala is outside, consisting of five lines, adorned with mind-seals (mudrā) and garlands, square in shape, having the form of four archways (toraṇa), and decorated by the four Great Kings stationed in their proper order. For instance, as for the seals: in the front region, a blue lotus is to be drawn.

To the right and to the left, one should fashion a square perimeter filled with garlands on all sides, using various hand-gesture symbols (*mudrā*) of weapons such as a lotus, a vajra, an axe, a sword, a spear, a trident, a mace, a discus, a svastika, a vase, a fish, a conch, an earring, a banner, a flag, a noose, a bell, a *kadvāraka*, a bow, and an iron arrow; beyond this, in the four directions, the four great oceans should be established.

Having made a square-shaped mandala in the northern direction, one should make a triangular-shaped mandala with a triple-pronged double-vajra (ubhayavajra) radiating light on all sides and place it there.
In the southern direction, having made a bow-shaped mandala, one should place a bowl emitting flames on all sides.

In the western direction, having made a mandala with a form of universal radiance, one should place a blue lotus complete with its stalk and leaves, emitting flames on all sides. And in the intermediate directions, there are four mudrās.

In the northwestern direction, having made a circular mandala for the noose with flames on all sides; in the southwestern direction, having made an elongated mandala for the staff with flames on all sides; in the southwestern direction, having made a triangular mandala for the axe with flames on all sides; and in the northeastern direction, one should place the sword with flames on all sides.
Having drawn [the mandala] on all sides—above, below, and across—three seals (mudrās) are to be drawn outside the maṇḍala at the time of the gate, using colored powders alone.
Namely: the vajra-fan and the sandals; these, blazing all around, are to be depicted.
This ritual procedure for the mandala has been taught here in brief by the wise Mañjughoṣa, out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings.

Then, the mandala master should first of all favor those disciples who have unimpaired faculties, whose limbs are all beautiful, who belong to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, who have generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), who follow the Mahāyāna, whose nature is to have no longing for other vehicles, who are great beings (*mahāsattva*), endowed with faith and virtuous qualities, who desire great sovereignty, who loathe meager enjoyments, and who delight in great enjoyments; who are auspicious, disciplined, and observant of moral conduct; who are monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen established in their vows and committed to the *upoṣadha* fast and its restraints; who harbor no malice toward the great Bodhisattvas, who are of noble Yakṣa lineage, and who by their very nature practice the Dharma; who have fasted for a day and night, are clothed in clean garments, have fragrant hair, bathe three times a day, and maintain silence.

On that day, those who possess the fragrance of camphor, saffron, and cloves from their mouths, who have constantly performed ritual ablutions (*upaspṛśita*), who sit upon bundles of *kuśa* grass, and who have performed the rites of protection—brahmacārins who are truthful—should be stationed not too close to the maṇḍala.
They must be pure and very clean; from eight down to one, and no others.
And they should be mutually unattached, whether they be Kṣatriyas or great kings who have been consecrated (*mūrdhābhiṣikta*).

And their sons—both boys and girls—who do not yet know the ways of the world, have as their cause the Blessed One Mañjuśrī, the Great Bodhisattva in the form of a youth, who awakens the ignorant and is devoted to the play of children.
Therefore, the youth should be entered first.

For one who desires the increase of great kingship, long life, health, and sovereignty, there will especially be an increase in enjoyments; for children, the accomplishment of mantras is certainly established.

Having established this [image] as previously positioned, accompanied by good companions and remaining vigilant, the mandala master, burning camphor incense, should then go out from behind. Having gone out, he should bathe and perform ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) with water that has been consecrated eight hundred times with the root mantra at the appropriate time, using water marked with the great five-crested mudrā. Then, being pure and dressed in clean garments, he should go to the fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa), sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing northeast, and offer eight thousand oblations mixed with camphor, saffron, and sandalwood.

Having invoked and dismissed [the deities] according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should enter the maṇḍala once again. Having entered, one should offer eight full vases— adorned with clean cloths and decorated with mango sprouts, their interiors filled with gold, silver, jewels, grain, and rice— one to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, and a second to all the Buddhas.
The third is for the entire Saṅgha of Pratyekabuddhas and noble Śrāvakas;
the fourth is for all Mahābodhisattvas;
the fifth is for the Mahābodhisattva, the noble Mañjuśrī.
The sixth [image] is for all the gods.
The seventh and eighth are to be placed in the door-chambers of the second maṇḍala;
they should be adorned with clean garments.
One [portion] is for all beings;
the second, dedicated to all sentient beings, should be set aside as common property.
Then, burning incense according to the very same procedure previously described and forming the great mudrā with five crests (*mahāmudrā-pañcaśikhā*), one should again perform the invocation.

One should invoke all the Buddhas, all the Pratyekabuddhas, the noble Śrāvakas and Mahābodhisattvas, all spirits (*bhūta*), and all sentient beings, as well as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, according to the procedure previously described.
In this manner, one should present flowers, incense, perfumes, lamps, and food offerings according to the very ritual previously specified.
One should perform this for all [deities] in every respect, following the proper sequence.
By the mention of "lamps," one should offer lamps filled with ghee.

Having offered to all—both noble and non-noble—by means of receiving the consecrated food (nivedya), one should present to the Tathāgatas everything including rice cooked with milk (śālyodana) mixed with curd, special preparations of honeyed milk-porridge (madhupāyasa), cakes fried in ghee, aśokavartīs, sugar-candies, and various other delicacies. One should also present to all the Pratyekabuddhas, Noble Śrāvakas, Great Bodhisattvas, and Noble Deities offerings such as clarified butter (havis), śrīveṣṭa, honey-syrup, and various milk-prepared foods.

In this manner, one should offer the aforementioned specific ingredients for the cakes, such as those containing sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*), as well as all the hosts of gods and spirits and all sentient beings, accompanied by mantras according to the ritual procedure.

Likewise, one should offer fragrant flowers—such as jasmine (*jāti*), tagara, nāgapuṣpa, punnāga, and so forth—as previously specified, to all the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, and Great Bodhisattvas, both noble and ordinary.

Specifically, in the Tathāgata family, the *jātī* flower is prescribed; likewise, in the Padma family, the lotus; and for the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi), the blue water-lily. For other mantras, the opposite is used—namely, camphor incense for the Tathāgata family and sandalwood for the Padma family. Guggulu resin is recommended specifically for the Lord of the Guhyakas, Vajrin himself. One should offer incense for all other mantras. For the noble mantras, one should cause clarified butter lamps to be given; for all non-noble mantras, one should cause fragrant oil to be given.
In due order, according to the prescribed method and by means of the previously seen cause,
that which is called "fragrance" is always taught for all mantras.

Whatever was spoken by Avalokita and whatever was spoken by Vajrapāṇi regarding the accomplishment of the purpose of mantra practice within their respective tantras— all those should be seen here in this ritual manual and should always be followed.
Thus it is said.

Then, the mandala master, having performed the rites of invocation, worship, incense offering, and so forth, up to the presentation of the food offering (*naivedya*) according to the previously observed procedure, the skillful assistant, acting with haste, should offer the *sārvabhautika* bali—free from meat—in all directions. Amidst the sounding of drums, conchs, and the resonant proclamation of the *nandī* drum, and adorned with incense, flowers, lamps, and garlands, he should circumambulate the mandala clockwise from the outside, above, below, and across, in all four cardinal and intermediate directions. He should then offer eight thousand oblations of rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.

For one who offers oblations with the heart of the six-syllable root mantra, those great beings previously established within the maṇḍala—having performed the rites of protection, having been accepted as disciples by the maṇḍala-ācārya, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), having observed the *upoṣadha* vows, having surrendered their bodies to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having shared in the enjoyments of sentient beings for the sake of accomplishment, being skilled in ascending to the seat of unsurpassed awakening, and desiring to obtain the omniscient knowledge of a Buddha—are liberated from all sins merely by the sight of the maṇḍala.
"Even those people who have committed the immediate transgressions are liberated at that very moment."

Then the mandala master, having covered the faces of those wishing to enter the mandala with a cloth that is unwashed, drawn from the tantra, free of hair, consecrated seven times with the root mantra, and anointed with fragrant sandalwood and saffron, should first cause a prince who has been consecrated, or a son of a kṣatriya, or another person of great energy desiring a great kingdom, to enter—one who is between the ages of sixteen and three years old, and who is adorned with five locks of hair, or one lock, or a topknot, or is headless.

Having covered the face of the one situated in the second mandala and having formed the utpala mudrā, one should recite the root mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta once. Having had [the disciple] perform this and having offered fragrant flowers, one should have him cast the flowers with both hands, which have been cleansed and mixed with sandalwood and saffron. To whichever [deity] his flower alights, one should give that deity’s mantra to him;
it is proclaimed as "his own mantra."

That very [root of goodness] follows him through his succession of births; that very [root of goodness] acts as his spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for the sake of fulfilling the wisdom of the Great Bodhisattvas as he proceeds toward the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). That very [root of goodness] is what must be accomplished by him, and it brings about for him association with persons of great wealth, great sovereignty, and great renown.
In this very life, without deliberation, success is achieved in all rites;
thus, those desiring accomplishment should proceed in this sequence, focusing on one at a time until all eight are mastered, and not others.

For the sake of others who wish to exhaust their sins, it may be for a mere moment; thus, the Maṇḍala Master, while bestowing the consecration, should first consecrate a portion of ground in the northeastern direction outside the maṇḍala, neither too far nor too near, and purify it with mantras using the root mantra. Then, regarding himself as one receiving a royal consecration, [he should initiate] one who has single-minded faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, who is devout, highly energetic, never separated from the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), a follower of the Mahāyāna, a benefactor of the Three Jewels, whose faculties are unimpaired, who is not blameworthy, and who desires to accomplish the mantras in this very life.

Those who possess a noble disposition, whose minds are intent upon the practice of mantra, who are curious by nature, and who—out of a desire for knowledge—have their minds focused on the meaning of the mantra without conceptualization; from one person upwards, as many as there may be, they are to be consecrated, served, and honored.
Those who are wise and of unerring conduct are, for the most part, to be consecrated.
Nor for others.
Therefore, having gathered all the requisites like those for a royal consecration, or whatever else might please the preceptor, [one should proceed].

Then, with a canopy spread above, a white parasol held over his head, and white yak-tail fans waving on both sides, he was honored with great ceremony amidst the resounding blasts of drums, conchs, and kettledrums, the shouts of "Victory!", and the chanting of auspicious verses and hymns of praise for well-being spoken by the Jinas. Having circumambulated that mandala and bowed down to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Ācārya, he should speak thus: "O Ācārya, I wish to enter the accomplishment of the mantra-practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; I wish to enter the secret mandala of liberation that transcends all worldly things; I wish to attain Buddhahood through the entry into the sovereignty of all Dharmas. In brief, he should say: "May I become a Buddha."
Then, having sat upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing the east, he should have [the practitioner] tie his hair in five tufts (*pañcaśikhā*).
Then, whichever mantra he prefers, it should be written with yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*) on birch bark (*bhūrjapatra*).
Having written it and smeared his hands with sandalwood and saffron, he should place the birch bark inside a pair of earthenware bowls (*śarāvasampuṭa*) and set it at the feet of the Bodhisattva.

Then, having sat down there, one should recite the root-mantras of the vidyā one hundred and eight times. Prior to that, however, he who is to be consecrated should be seated upon a bundle of kuśa grass.

Within the outer maṇḍala, the preceptor, taking the full jar—which was previously placed near the entrance and is common to all sentient beings—should sprinkle him on the head while reciting the root-mantra.
The remainder [of the water] may be used as one pleases.
Then that vessel-cup should be given to him;
and he should be made to recite it by means of a lamp.
If she herself is the mantra, it will be accomplished through effort in due course.
Now, another [practitioner] achieves success through the mere recitation of the mantra.

Furthermore, if the mantra is given with syllables either deficient or redundant, one achieves success at the very first practice; thus, without hesitation, this aforementioned [mantra], when practiced by the teacher through the three methods of accomplishment, achieves success without effort.
Thus, first one should bestow the Knowledge Empowerment (*vidyābhiṣeka*).
For the second, the Mandala Empowerment, one should consecrate [the disciple] with the full vase that was offered to all the deities in the second mandala;
or, as before, by means of that very same rite upon the head, one is liberated from all sins.
And he is authorized by all the Buddhas; he becomes unimpeded in the accomplishment of all worldly and transcendent samaya-maṇḍalas and in the practice of all mantras and mudrās.
Thus, [the master] should bestow the master’s initiation (ācāryābhiṣeka) by means of all the Bodhisattvas.

In the third mandala, one should consecrate [the disciple] on the head with a full water-pot that has been offered to all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, according to that very same rite. It should be said: "You are authorized by all the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power to write, recite, explain the maṇḍala, and teach the mantras, tantras, mudrās, and conduct of all mundane and supramundane mantras; or to practice them yourself or instruct others.
In this very life and in successive lives, until the very end, you shall certainly attain Buddhahood."

Likewise, during the consecration of Jaya and Vijaya, according to the previously prescribed rite, he was consecrated with the full vase offered by the Blessed One Buddha and with the full vase offered by the Bodhisattva;
and with that full vase, he was consecrated in the same manner.
And it should be said: "You have been authorized by all the Blessed Buddhas, by the Great Bodhisattvas, and by the Śrāvakas."
Invincible to all beings, unconquered by all embodied ones, may you be victorious over all mantras; accomplish whatever you desire.
Then, by the mandala master, the five empowerments should be bestowed upon each individual according to their desire; indeed, all [disciples] should receive exactly five.
Then, having led her into the mandala in due order and having offered her to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should circumambulate the mandala three times to the right and dismiss her.
On the day following that, she should be instructed in due order and appointed to the practice of mantras.

At that very moment, taking the full water jar which was previously offered to the Blessed One, the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, one should have those who have entered the mandala drink three handfuls of water while facing the east.
And they should be told: "O, do not transgress this secret pledge (*samaya*) of the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta;
lest you produce much demerit.
Furthermore, no mantras whatsoever should be rejected.
Furthermore, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas must not be deceived,
and the Guru must be propitiated;
otherwise, there would be a transgression of the samaya.
Furthermore, the mantras would not attain accomplishment;
there would be great merit.
Thus should they be dismissed.
Then the mandala master should again offer oblations of rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, using the eight-syllable heart mantra.

Then, having risen and entered the center of the mandala, he should mentally offer the *arghya* to all [the deities] with the flowers previously specified and according to the previously mentioned ritual procedure. He should contemplate them all with his mind.

Having incensed all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas and Noble Śrāvakas, and all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, yogins, siddhas, and ṛṣis, as well as all sentient beings, with the very same incense mentioned previously, and having scattered flowers over them, one should sprinkle them with water scented with sandalwood and saffron.
One should dismiss them according to the very procedure mentioned previously;
for there is liberation from all [obstacles] through the mind alone.
Then the mandala master should cause the offerings, the sacrificial oblations, and all the powders to be cast into a river,
or they should be given to suffering living beings.
Having made the area of the earth well-swept, well-sprinkled, and beautifully adorned, it should be smeared with cow dung.

It should be flooded with water, or smeared with very clean clay, or with sand; this much must be done for it, and one may go wherever one desires. Those who have entered the maṇḍala must subsist on milk-rice or on sacrificial food (haviṣya).

Thus concludes the second chapter, the Instruction on the Ritual for the Maṇḍala, from the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvataṃsaka*, the Great Sovereign of Ritual Manuals (*Mahākalparājendra*), from the *Mañjuśrīkumārabhūtavikurvaṇa*, the Extensive Section on Bodhisattvas.
Now begins the third chapter,

"The Ritual of the Maṇḍala. Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having again surveyed that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas assembled in the great maṇḍala of the assembly, spoke the single-syllable mantra— the supreme secret, the destroyer of all poisons, effective for all rites, the means for accomplishing his own maṇḍala, and applicable to all minor activities.
And what is that?
Homage to all Buddhas!
It is as follows: Jaḥ!
This, together with the sages and all the hosts of beings, is the second mandala-arrangement for this very single-syllable mantra; it should be applied in brief.
Having purified a plot of ground measuring eight cubits or four cubits, one should draw it oneself using powders of five colors, and not by others.
Whether here or there, there is no fault in this;
one should first draw a square mandala, adorned with three circles and five crests, as the Great Mudrā.
Then, one should draw the lotus mudrā, the fang mudrā, the vajra mudrā, and the staff mudrā of the Blessed Mañjuśrī.
These mudrās are to be drawn in the eastern sector of the inner maṇḍala.

Thereafter, at the base of the outer gate, one should draw the lotus, the vajra, the blue lotus, the banner, the flag, the parasol, the archway, the chariot, the elephant, the horse, the bull, the buffalo, the svastika, the peacock, the goat, the ram, the man, and the youth;
they should be drawn in a row according to their proper sequence, situated within the three maṇḍalas, and executed in this manner.
Then, with the single-syllable mantra itself, the fire-ritual (agnikārya) should be performed in the southeastern direction.
One hundred and eight oblations of *apāmārga* fuel-sticks, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, should be offered.
Thereafter, an offering of water (*arghya*) should be presented with flowers.
With the single-syllable mantra alone, one should offer the bali, the food offering, and the lamp as desired;
or one may offer incense, and perform the invocation and dismissal.
Then, one who desires sovereignty should be led into the center of the city and [the mandala] should be drawn.

One who desires wealth [should be placed] near a *vaṭa* tree; one who desires a son near a *putrañjīvaka* tree; one who is childless and desires elephants or horses in an elephant stable or a horse stable; one who has been bitten [by a snake] in a great lake or a temple of the *nāgas*; one suffering from quartan fever, constant fever, or every kind of fever, at a place with a single *liṅga* or to the south of a village; one possessed by a *rākṣasa* in a cremation ground or an empty house; one possessed by a *piśāca* near a *vibhītaka* tree or an *eraṇḍa* tree; those possessed by all the *mātṛs* at crossroads or near a house where there is a death or birth impurity; and one possessed by a *brahmarākṣasa* at a *tāla* tree or a *śleṣmātaka* tree. For one who has administered poison, water should be consecrated seven times with the single-syllable mantra itself and poured right there in the center of the maṇḍala; thus he is liberated.
In this manner, for a woman or a man seeking fame, it should be drawn at a crossroads or in a sacred precinct (*brahmasthala*).

For a woman whose children have died, it should be drawn at a fruit-bearing tree or a milky sap tree; for a woman who is childless, it should be drawn in the middle of a field where *śāli* rice is being cultivated. For women afflicted by various diseases caused by others or by malevolent spirits, or those stricken by great illnesses, it should be inscribed on a raft and so forth; or for the purpose of warding off *rākṣasas*, it should be inscribed on a river sandbank, on a bank, or on a mountain peak.

In all diseases and in all circumstances— even those caused by ḍākinīs— one should perform this at the Brahma-pālikā, in an empty house, in a secluded place, or in a low-lying area. Thus, for all rites, it should be drawn at midnight, at midday, or at any time whatsoever.
Having offered water for honor (*arghya*) with flowers using that very same single-syllable mantra and having performed the dismissal (*visarjana*), the mandala should be flooded with water;
thus, great protection is established for all who are ill.
One is liberated from all diseases and one's desired aims are accomplished;
a sonless man obtains a son, and the unfortunate becomes fortunate.
A poor person obtains wealth merely by seeing the mandala;
whether it be a woman, a man, or even one who is faithful and observant of ritual rules,
they shall always attain various kinds of prosperity according to their desires.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Ritual for the Mandala, from the *Mañjuśrī-kumārabhūta-mūla-kalpa*, an extensive section of the *Bodhisattva-paṭala*.
The Fourth Chapter.
Homage to the Buddha and to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Then Mañjuśrī, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, and having again looked upon that great assembly gathered in the maṇḍala, prostrated at the feet of Śākyamuni, and with a smiling countenance, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

Therefore, O Blessed One, out of compassion for us and for all sentient beings, please explain that extensive chapter on the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), which is the rain from the Dharma-cloud—the natural outflow of the accomplishment and application of the methods for mantra practice—for the benefit of all beings; which produces unsurpassed merit; which brings forth the seed of perfect enlightenment; which brings to completion the entirety of the knowledge of the Omniscient One; which, in brief, fulfills all hopes; which is correctly joined with the fruits of all mantras and makes them fruitful; which renders the practitioner’s efforts never in vain; which fulfills the conduct of all Bodhisattvas; which is donned by the great armor of the Great Bodhisattva; and which overcomes and turns back the forces of all Māras.
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One Śākyamuni said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you have set out for the benefit of many people and out of compassion for the world, thinking it necessary to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter. Listen to it, and attend to it well and thoroughly; I shall speak to you. I will explain to you, in due order, the entry into the practice and the accomplishment for all beings through the detailed ritual of your cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), as previously taught by all the Tathāgatas."
I too shall now speak.
First of all, on a clean spot of ground free from dust, those beings who have entered the samaya should take cotton and purify it.
Having purified it, the mandala master should consecrate it one hundred and eight times with this mantra:
*Namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvānāmapratihatamatigatipraticāriṇām*.
Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the King of Kings who Purifies and Pacifies All Suffering.
It is as follows: Oṃ, purify, purify! O destroyer of all obstacles, Great Compassionate One, you who assume the form of a youth!
Manifest your miraculous power, manifest your miraculous power!
Remember the pledge! Stay, stay! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

Then, having bathed a maiden previously described—one born of a true, rustic family, whether from a Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya lineage; not of excessively dark complexion, nor devoid of the proper caste-mark; with all limbs unimpaired and beautiful; authorized by her parents; observed by the Upoṣadha fast; who has generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta); compassionate; of pure white complexion and free from other colors; in short, one possessing the most excellent marks and characteristics of a woman—on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight, when watched over by white and auspicious planets, in a clean place free from smoke, dust, and wind, and devoid of drafts; and having dressed her well in clean garments, one should perform protection for her using this very mantra together with the Great Seal (mahāmudrā). Then, having mixed white sandalwood and saffron with water free of living organisms, one should sprinkle that girl while she drinks it, using that same purifying mantra.

One should scatter white sandalwood and saffron water in the four directions; thus, having combined white sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, one should first cause them to be offered above, below, and in the intermediate directions,
either by oneself or by the practitioner-teacher.
Thus, one should speak these words three times: "May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Great Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, empower this cloth-thread.
Then those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Great Bodhisattvas will attend to it.
While burning incense at that time, various auspicious birds— peacocks, curlews, swans, cranes, ruddy geese, and others, whether moving on land, in water, or through the air—
should pass by or utter auspicious cries;
this should be known by the practitioner.
Fruitful is this action of mine; it has been empowered for me by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and by the great Bodhisattvas.
That cloth and thread are well-lived for me in this birth; my accomplishment of the mantra is not in vain.
There may arise the sounds of drums, kettledrums, clay drums, conchs, lutes, flutes, cymbals, or mouth-organs.
At that time, they might speak thus out of confusion: "Victory! Success! Siddha! Datta! Dinna! Gr̥hṇa! Śreyasaḥ! Saphalaka! Śakraprabhūta! or other such auspicious words may be uttered;
or there may be the sound of bells or the sound of rejoicing. Then the Vidyādhara should recognize [the situation].
This is the empowerment of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the great Bodhisattvas; it is not otherwise, for its accomplishment is never in vain.

Then, at that time, they utter cruel cries; words such as "Seize!", "Eat!", "Make him eat!", "Lost!", "Perished!", "Wretched!", "Far!", "Very far!", and "He does not exist! issue forth. Sounds like those of monkeys, buffaloes, jackals, donkeys, cats, and other loathsome animals—whether two-legged or four-legged—may also issue forth. Then the practitioner should know, "I have no success," and he must bring [the rite] to an end in this very life.
Or rather, having performed further preliminary service, one should begin;
thus up to seven times.
Even for one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, success is achieved on the seventh application of the rite.
Then the practitioner, having performed the protective rites for that maiden, should have her sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass.
Having established her facing either the east or the north, he himself should consume sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), and he should feed that girl sacrificial food as well.
Upon that very same pre-arranged bundle of *kuśa* grass, he should have her spin the cotton according to this procedure.

Having gathered that well-spun white thread from a girl previously instructed, the knower of mantras should prepare this highly praised collection of eight, five, three, or one, starting from as few as sixteen *mātrās* up to a *pala* or a *karṣa*. For middling rites, he should make it one-eighth of a *gāthā*; for other minor rites to be accomplished, he should make it according to his ability in all ritual actions.
From that time forward, whatever sinful karma was previously committed perishes at that very moment, provided one does not disregard the meaning of this Sūtra.
Having collected this sūtra, one should place it in a clean vessel;
for one should not, having placed it within the threads, fumigate it with camphor incense.
Or [an image] produced from non-living materials, adorned with saffron, sandalwood, and the like,
and worshipped with fragrant flowers such as jasmine and campaka.
Having established [the image] in a clean place, secured with protective coverings,
the knower of mantras, skilled in all rites, having performed his recitation and being well-composed, [should proceed].
Then, having gone to a weaver and given him the desired price,
[one should obtain] one who is free from physical defects, not emaciated, and always devoted to pure dharma.
One who is not afflicted by disease, not aged, and free from cough and asthma;
one who is free from cough and asthma, not impotent, and born of a true womb.
Blameless and not hunchbacked, free from lameness or blindness,
endowed with all auspicious marks, praiseworthy, and beautiful to behold.
One who desires accomplishment should request such a person— one whose conduct is characterized by pure intellect and who follows worldly customs— for the weaving of this supreme cloth.
It is praised if it is of auspicious color, or if it is made by those who are intelligent and well-trained,
and by the most excellent and preeminent weavers for the sake of excellence.
One should perform the highest rites with the best [substances], middling rites with middling means;
with the others, one performs minor and inferior actions in every respect.
Then, having paid the craftsman his due price,
that knower of mantras, at the first word uttered by the craftsman, [should act].
One should then swiftly bestow the merit; this is called "heroic purchase.
And by the mere request of this [mantra], the reciter becomes a partaker of merit.
For this supreme, unsurpassed cloth-painting brings swift accomplishment;
it performs all rites, is worthy of worship, and bestows divine and human happiness. It is for the welfare of all beings and was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Thus it is said.

Then, having given the *poṣadha* vow to the weaver, the *vidyādhara*—at an auspicious lunar mansion during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), on a bright day observed by favorable planets, or at another time in the bright fortnight; during that most excellent season, the springtime when the mango trees are in full bloom with clusters of flowers and other excellent trees are rich with blossoms—at that time, at that moment, when the sun has risen in the forenoon—he should cause the previously designated weaver to consume sacrificial food (*haviṣya*), to be dressed in clean garments, to have a turban bound upon his head, to be well-bathed, well-anointed, with his limbs smeared with either white sandalwood or saffron, his face scented with camphor, joyful in mind, and free from hunger and thirst. Then, having washed all the vessels and tools such as ropes with clay and cow dung, he should wash them repeatedly with fresh *pañcagavya*.
Then, having washed it with water free of living organisms, one should sprinkle it with white sandalwood and saffron.
On a clean spot of earth, free from clamor, devoid of people, in a secluded seat that is serene, protected, and honored with flowers.

Then the practitioner, having consecrated white mustard seeds one hundred and eight times with the purification mantra itself, should scatter them in the four cardinal directions, as well as above, below, and in the intermediate directions.
Then, having struck the weaver with the mustard seeds and having bound the five-crested great mudrā, he should perform the binding of his topknot.
Thus, great protection is established.
If it is the superior cloth, one should have it woven by a weaver to these dimensions: four cubits in width and eight cubits in length.
The middling is two cubits in width and five cubits in length.
The inferior is the measure of a Sugata’s span in width and one cubit in length.
In this context, the span of the Blessed Buddha—measuring one cubit according to the standard of a man from the Middle Country—is proclaimed as "the Sugata’s span.
By means of this measurement, the authoritative standard is declared.
"Arise! The supreme accomplishment has been taught by the leaders of the world."
While the supreme sage was invisible, those desiring sovereignty sought the middle one.

For men who desire great enjoyments, as well as for those possessing the enjoyments of the three classes of gods and asuras, success is declared in the lowest [grade]; in the middle [grade], middling success is attained.
Minor rites are always accomplished on a small cloth;
indeed, all tasks and all ritual substances are always accomplished [therein].
The accomplishment taught in the three paintings is for men who seek the highest good;
if one deviates from the prescribed rules, it will not be achieved even for Śakra, the lord of Śacī.
In this way, all rites are accomplished quickly and without effort,
even for one who has passed away, provided they are performed in accordance with the prescribed ritual.
This path has been fully proclaimed by the Victors and the sons of the Supreme Victors,
for the welfare of all sentient beings who are poor, protectorless, and suffering.
Indeed, the entire path to enlightenment has been shown by those who perceive reality;
this path, which is the cause of enlightenment, is demonstrated through the way of mantra.
Mantras are accomplished without effort, as are all worldly maṇḍalas;
even the supramundane maṇḍalas that have been described are accomplished.
Success shall always belong to those whose minds are intent on the cause of enlightenment;
success is not said to belong to others who are always harmful to the world.
Success is always proclaimed for those beings who have set out for enlightenment,
and especially here for the high-souled Mañjuśrī Kumāra.
In order to accomplish his task swiftly, he should obtain everything required here;
thereafter, the artisan should diligently weave the cloth in the proper sequence.
In sixteen days, or in four days for each of the two [sections],
the completion of the cloth-weaving is swiftly achieved within a single day and night.
Indeed, for those desiring the highest accomplishment, there is excellence within a single day and night;
provided they are endowed with purity and proper conduct, and remain constantly established in their craft.
Having gone a distance of one *āvarta* from the village, one should void urine and excrement;
then, having bathed with one's clothes on and put on other garments, one should proceed.
Wearing white garments and adorned with garlands, having sipped water repeatedly and having smeared his limbs with white sandalwood paste, he rubbed his hands together before the artisan.
One should weave it further with effort, always making it smooth and well-knit;
by means of such applications or others spoken by the Jina.
One who is reflective and diligent, having completed the entire weaving of the cloth as prescribed in the previous ritual procedures, should proceed when the cloth is finished.
One should perform [the rite] equally on an auspicious day when the moon is full and not diminished;
then, one should cause it to descend through the tantra during the most beautiful bright fortnight.
Having taken the painting that is clearly manifest and beautifully adorned with bound fringes,
and having secured the painting by fastening it to a bamboo pole, one should then depart.
Having provided for the welfare of the artisan with extensive gifts and distributions,
the mantra-practitioner, well-conducted and firm in his vows, should depart as he pleases.
Having worshipped it with fragrant flowers, one should place it in a clean location,
having performed protection and sealed it with this very mantra.
With that very same [thread] by which that cotton was previously purified in many ways, one should indeed perform the protection of both oneself and the cloth-painting.
The great hero Mañjuśrī has been proclaimed in the form of mantras by many past [Buddhas], and by me as well, now and again.
He alone wanders among all mantras, taking the form of mantra;
he is of great heroism and great splendor, the accomplisher of the purpose of all mantras.
The beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa, whose conduct and intentions are deluded, perform three kinds of diverse acts that serve as causes for protection.
But those who lack faith, who are the opposite [of faithful], who practice false conduct, and who are full of greed,
do not indeed accomplish mantras nor any ritual substances whatsoever.
For this very reason, they wander in the dark prison of saṃsāra;
whereas he whose mind is always pure, who is faithful, and who is ever intent on auspicious rites and wonders, [is liberated].
They are constantly eager to grasp and retain all mantras;
these great-souled ones desire accomplishment, possessing great energy and great splendor.
For those [who possess faith], the mantras spoken by the Jinas will ultimately succeed;
however, for beings who lack faith, the white dharma does not take root.
Just as a seed sown in saline soil produces no sprout,
so too has it been said by those who perceive all truths that faith is always the root of the Dharma;
for those who practice the Dharma for its true purpose, the accomplishment of mantras is always proclaimed.
Thus it is said.
Then, for the accomplishment [of the rite], an artisan, or a well-trained painter, or one who is himself skilled in drawing should be employed.

Taking pigments that are free from impurities, brilliant in every way, and endowed with color, the painter—endowed with the proper characteristics and following the same procedure as previously described for the weaver—should execute the work in detail according to the extensive method previously set forth for the weaver; by that same means, the cloth (*paṭa*) should be painted, or it should be painted by oneself.
The image should be perfumed with camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and other such substances.

Having recited that same mantra eight hundred times while burning incense, and having scattered over that cloth flowers such as *nāgakesara*, *punnāga*, *vakula*, *campaka*, *vāpīka*, *dhānuṣkārika*, and *mālatī*, he should paint that cloth—facing east, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, with a composed mind, his thoughts directed toward all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, holding a fine brush in his hand, and with a mind free from effort.
First of all, one should draw the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

One should depict the form of the Tathāgata, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, marked by the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, his body adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics, seated upon a jewel-lotus, blazing with light on all sides, beautified for a fathom in every direction, teaching the Dharma, with a serene form, endowed with the excellence of all aspects, standing upon a central lotus with a beryl stalk and a great core below. Two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda, should be depicted holding that lotus stalk; they gaze at the Tathāgata, pay homage with their right hands, are white in color, adorned with all ornaments, and have human forms with the bodies of half-serpents. One should draw them thus.

And all around that lotus-shaft, it should be depicted as completely filled with lotus leaves, flowers, buds, blossoming aquatic plants, and creatures such as birds and fish, arranged in their entirety in a form that is beautiful and enduring.
From the very stalk and branches of the Blessed One’s primary lotus, many other lotus flowers emerge, rising in succession; on the left side, there are eight lotus flowers.
And upon those lotuses, the forms of the eight great bodhisattvas should be depicted seated.

First, Noble Mañjuśrī should be depicted: slightly pale like the filaments of a lotus, or the color of saffron-gold; having the form of a youth, with the appearance of a young boy, his head adorned with five locks of hair, and decorated with the ornaments of a prince. Holding a blue lotus in his left hand, he pays homage to the Tathāgata with his right hand; his form is beautiful, his gaze is fixed upon the Tathāgata, his appearance is gentle, his face is slightly smiling, and he is surrounded by a circle of blazing light on all sides. On another lotus, Noble Candraprabha Kumārabhūta should likewise be painted.
In the third [assembly] was Sudhana; in the fourth, Sarvanīvaraṇa; in the fifth, Gaganagañja; in the sixth, Kṣitigarbha; in the seventh, Anagha; and in the eighth, Sulocana.
All these should be depicted in the form of young boys.

On the right side of the Blessed One are eight great bodhisattvas, adorned with all ornaments and decorated like youths, with the exception of Maitreya. Near the Blessed One is the noble Maitreya, wearing the garb of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*); his head is bound with a crown of matted hair, he is golden-colored, wears saffron-dyed robes, and has a red silk upper garment. He bears the mark of three horizontal lines (*tripuṇḍra*) on his body; his left hand rests upon a staff and a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), while his right hand, holding a rosary, has its palm draped over his left shoulder across a black antelope skin. Paying homage to the Tathāgata, his gaze is directed toward him, and his mental activity is absorbed in the object of meditation.

On the second lotus, Samantabhadra is to be depicted in this manner: dark green in color like the priyaṅgu plant, his body adorned with all ornaments; his left hand holding a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇiratna*), and his right hand holding a *śrīphala* fruit while granting the boon of charity; he is of beautiful form.

In the third [panel], there is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed-stalk, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a crown of matted hair and a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). He bears the image of the Omniscient One upon his head and sits with his matted locks touching the base of the noble Amitābha, who possesses the ten powers. His form is beautiful; he holds a lotus with a fly-whisk in his left hand, while his right hand is in the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*). His mind and conduct are absorbed in the object of meditation, and his body is illuminated on all sides.

In the fourth [panel], there is the noble Vajrapāṇi, golden-colored, adorned with all ornaments, holding a vajra in his left hand and displaying the boon-granting gesture (varada-mudrā) with his right hand grasping a fruit; he is of beautiful form, of gentle appearance, his body draped with necklaces and half-necklaces, wearing a sacred thread of pearl necklaces, a crown radiant and studded with jewels, lower garments of silk, and an upper garment of white silk cloth. Likewise, there are the noble Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra, their bodies clad in lower garments and upper robes of bark-fiber, and in appearance as previously described.
Likewise, on the fifth lotus is the noble Mahāmati; on the sixth, Śāntamati; on the seventh, Vairocanagarbha; and on the eighth, Apāyajaha.
These are the bodhisattvas who are to be depicted.

Their hands hold fruits and books; they are beautifully adorned with all ornaments, wear silk garments as upper robes, are decorated with every kind of ornament, and are clothed in fluttering silken lower garments.
And above them, eight Pratyekabuddhas are to be depicted;

they wear the robes of monks, their bodies possess the marks of a Great Man, they are clothed in saffron-colored garments, seated in the cross-legged posture upon jeweled stones, possessing a peaceful appearance, surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides, and strewn with fragrant flowers.

For example—one should paint a celestial palace (*vimāna-maṇḍala*) fashioned from many jewels, shaped like a very long structure adorned with the king of mountains, appearing like a mountain covered with precious stones; this should be depicted being strewn on all sides with flowers such as *mālatī*, *vārṣikā*, *dhānuṣkārikā*, *puṇṇāga*, and *nāgakesara*, located to the left of the Blessed One Śākyamuni and above the noble Mañjuśrī.
One should draw eight Blessed Buddhas situated therein.

One should depict the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin, who has a radiance extending for a fathom in all directions, shimmering with the light of jewels such as vaidūrya; who is brilliantly illuminated on all sides by various great precious gems, including ruby, sapphire, emerald, vaidūrya, and agate; whose body has the color of the rising sun; who wears a yellow upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and a yellow lower garment (*nivāsita*); who is seated cross-legged and teaching the Dharma; whose body is armored with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*); whose form is adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*); who is serene in appearance and endowed with the excellence of all attributes. Thus one should paint the Tathāgata Ratnaśikhin.

Second, one should depict the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, golden in color; one should depict him as being strewn with flowers such as nāgakesara and bakula, gazing upon the Noble One, possessing universal radiance, and surrounded by a halo shining with the splendor of jewels.
One should depict the third Tathāgata, Śālendrarāja,
with the luster of the filaments of a lotus, teaching the Dharma.
One should paint the fourth, the Tathāgata Sunetra,
just like this Duḥprasaha;
and the sixth, the Victor Vairocana.
The seventh is Bhaiṣajyavaidūryarāja;
the eighth one should depict the Tathāgata Sarvaduḥkhapraśamanarājendra.

All the forms of the Tathāgatas should be depicted as having a golden complexion and granting the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayapradāna*). Above the Tathāgatas, situated within the clouds at both corners of the cloth painting, two divine sons (*devaputra*) belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm should be portrayed, releasing a rain of flowers.
Remaining in the sky, they should be depicted paying homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas.
And to the north of the Pratyekabuddhas, the eight great Śrāvakas are to be depicted, seated in subordinate positions below the heads of the Bodhisattvas.
They are as follows: the Elder Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākāśyapa, Subhūti, Rāhula, Nanda, Bhadrika, and Kaphiṇa.
The Pratyekabuddhas were as follows: Gandhamādana, Candana, Upariṣṭaśveta, Sitaketu, Nemi, and Sunemi;
all of them were exceedingly beautiful, wearing peaceful attire and appearing perfectly self-controlled.
The great Śrāvakas also stood with palms joined, gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni.

And above, close to the Śuddhāvāsa heaven, two other sons of gods should be depicted, holding beautiful long cloth canopies on all sides; these two sons of gods, wearing divine garlands and garments, should be shown supporting [the canopy] above all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas.

Above the head of the Blessed Śākyamuni, one should depict a cluster of jeweled threads woven with pearl necklaces, rubies, emeralds, sapphires, and other gems; this should be well-arranged as a canopy of silk cloth, adorned on all sides by hanging pearl necklaces.

And below the lotus seat of the Blessed Buddha, near the feet of Noble Mañjuśrī and beside the Naga King Upananda, one should depict the Great Wrathful King Yamāntaka. He stands upon a great jewel mountain rising from a lotus lake, which is encircled by jeweled sprouts, caves, ravines, and coral creepers, and is frequented by great ṛṣis and siddhas. On the lofty peak of that mountain, one should paint Yamāntaka, the Great Wrathful King of most terrible form, holding a noose in his right hand and a staff in his left. With a frowning face, he awaits a command, his gaze fixed upon Noble Mañjuśrī. He has a wolf-like belly, hair standing erect, and resembles a black cloud of crushed collyrium. His tawny beard is long and formidable, his nails are long, and his eyes are red. His neck is adorned with snakes, he wears a tiger-skin garment, and he is the destroyer of all obstacles—a most fierce and great Wrathful King, blazing with flames on all sides. Thus one should depict Yamāntaka, the Great Wrathful King.

At the foot of that mountain, one should depict the practitioner seated upon a stone slab on the ground with his knees bent and body bowed; his hands occupied with an incense burner, wearing his prescribed attire and assuming the appropriate physical posture, his gaze fixed upon the noble Mañjuśrī, and his conduct following the prescribed rules.

Near the king of the Nanda nāgas, beneath the Blessed One Śākyamuni, on the right side, one should depict the Great Jewel King of Mountains rising from a lotus lake, as described, with the Tathāgata seated thereon.
One should also depict it free from the wrathful king Yamāntaka, strewn with divine flowers.
One should depict the noble Avalokiteśvara;
one should depict that mountain as being made of ruby stones, lofty and high, with a single peak composed of beryl.

Therein, one should depict the Noble Goddess Tārā, who is the compassion of the Noble Avalokiteśvara; she is adorned with every ornament, wears a jeweled silk upper garment and a lower robe of variegated silk, and is decorated on all her limbs with female ornaments. With her left hand she holds a blue lotus, and she is golden-hued, slender-waisted, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too young nor too old. Her mind is absorbed in meditation as she awaits a command, her body slightly bent forward with her right hand in the gesture of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*). She sits cross-legged, while the Noble Avalokiteśvara gazes at her with a slight turn of his head. She is surrounded by a garland of flames on all sides. Right there, upon that peak of lapis lazuli gem, is a *punnāga* tree encircling her; its branches are everywhere covered with blossoms, fully opened and beautifully flowered, overshadowing the Blessed Lady Tārā. And by that very tree, whose branches are beautifully arrayed and entwined with coral sprouts, radiant with various forms and colors, one should depict the Goddess Tārā looking toward the face of [Avalokiteśvara].
One should draw the auspicious goddess, the destroyer of all obstacles, the supreme dispeller of fear,
and the bestower of boons, for the protection of the practitioner.
The Goddess who assumes a female form, born from the Compassionate One who possesses the ten powers, bestows boons; one should depict her for the welfare of all living beings.
Here, the mother of the youth Mañjughoṣa, who possesses great splendor,
[is present] for the sake of destroying all obstacles for the practitioner from every side.
For the sake of protection and for the welfare of lords of men,
one should place that King of Wrathful Lords, who is stationed upon a mountain peak, upon a cloth-painting.
For the destruction of all obstacles, it has been taught by the sons of the Supreme Victors;
he is most formidable, most venerable, most fierce, and most radiant.
It is intended solely for the subjugation of beings who are hostile toward the Teaching;
furthermore, it serves to protect the practitioner and destroy all obstacles.
Terrible and wrathful by nature, he is the mantra-deity who, when invoked,
is most fearsome and of horrific form, the restrainer of all those devoid of compassion.
He brings under his control those who are otherwise unsubdued and who act with sin and ferocity,
whether they move through the sky, upon the earth, or throughout the netherworld.
It destroys all the wicked ones who are hostile toward the teaching of the Sage;
one should indeed paint a square cloth with four corners on all sides.
And at the bottom edge of the cloth, one should depict the abode of the expansive river,
with the bodies of the nāgas coiled around it on every side.
Born from a body in human form with white, auspicious limbs,
she should always be placed with her head toward the north, with her hands joined in the gesture of reverence.
