Radiant with seven splendors, of great heroism, and renowned as one of great majesty, he was known by the name Ananta;
adorned with precious jewels, he gazed upon the Tathāgata.
One should draw the renowned great lord of nāgas, who is exceedingly beautiful, of lovely form, adorned with jewel ornaments, and garlanded with flames.
One who is intent on the welfare of the entire world and has entered the teaching of the Sage should draw [the deity] situated upon a river for the destruction of all obstacles.
This supreme procedure for the cloth-painting, spoken by the Jina,
has been declared both in brief and in detail, as previously taught by the Tathāgatas; indeed,
the merit of that wise person who paints it is infinite.
Whatever extremely terrible sinful karma has been committed over ten million eons is destroyed at that very moment upon seeing the cloth on the ground.

One should not withhold the painting even from those who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution, those of immoral conduct, those who are loathsome, those engaged in every kind of evil, those wandering in the darkness of saṃsāra, or those of the lowest destinies and births.
The sight of that cloth spoken by the Lord of Sages is fruitful;
merely upon seeing it, they are instantly liberated from that evil.
How much more so, then, would human beings attain accomplishment, being pure in conduct, possessing perfectly purified conduct, embodied, and ever-exerting themselves in the mastery of mantra?
Whatever merit belongs to all sentient beings from making offerings for ten million eons,
that merit a practitioner of mantra obtains on earth by painting a cloth-painting.
As many as are the grains of sand in the Ganges that have been proclaimed, so many would be the Buddhas and the noble sons of the Pratyekajinas.
Practitioners who have repeatedly conquered many [obstacles] in this world shall obtain that fruit in the mortal realm by seeing the drawing on the cloth.
Merely by reciting it, or by honoring it, or even by rejoicing in it,
the accomplishment of mantras for that person is certain, as are all the rites prescribed.
"Whatever worldly mantras have been spoken by the preeminent Jinas,
as well as those by their disciples, the divine sword-wielding ones, and the great-souled Bodhisattvas—
all those mantras indeed attain accomplishment in the presence of the foremost cloth-painting."
From the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, the fourth [chapter],
the first detailed exposition on the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting, is completed.
The Fifth Chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon that entire assembly circle, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, there is yet another medium-sized procedure for your cloth-painting."
I shall speak of that;
listen, and attend well and thoroughly to it in your mind.

First of all, by means of the very same thread previously specified, according to the very same procedure previously described, and having it prepared by artisans previously selected, one should have that central cloth made with the same measurements as before—using a very beautiful, white, well-woven, new cloth, free from stains, animal hair, and refuse such as hair—exactly as was done for the first; however, omitting the measurement and form [of the previous image], that cloth should subsequently be caused to be painted.

First, one should depict the abode of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsabhavana*), which is beautiful in form on all sides, appearing as if fashioned from radiant jewels, and adorned with white pearl necklaces. In its center, the Blessed One Śākyamuni is to be painted, seated upon a jeweled lion-throne, teaching the Dharma, endowed with all the supreme marks. On his right side is the noble Mañjuśrī, with the luster of lotus filaments or the color of saffron and the sun; on the region of his left shoulder he holds a blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), his hands joined in the gesture of reverence (*añjalipuṭa*), gazing at the Blessed One Śākyamuni with a slightly smiling face. He has the form of a youth, his head adorned with five locks of hair, decorated with the ornaments of a young child, and his head is bowed toward the circle of the right knee. And on the left side of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as an autumn reed, is to be depicted exactly as described before.

However, beside the Blessed One with his fly-whisk being waved, Ārya Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Vajrapāṇi, Mahāmati, Śāntamati, Gaganagañja, and Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin should be depicted in succession. Just as with the first, they are all to be painted adorned with every ornament.

And above them, eight Buddha-Bhagavats are to be depicted standing, with their right hands granting the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*), their bodies clad in yellow upper robes (*uttarāsaṅga*), and their left hands holding the corner of the robe; they are well-dressed in saffron-colored lower garments with a slight reddish luster, possessing universal radiance and endowed with all excellent marks.
They are as follows: the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, Ratnaśikhin, Śikhin, Viśvabhuk, Krakucchanda, Bakagrīvin, Kāśyapa, and Sunetra.
These Buddha-Bhagavats are to be thus depicted.

On the right side of the Blessed One, in the vicinity of Noble Mañjuśrī, the great assembly maṇḍala should be depicted. The eight great śrāvakas and the eight pratyekabuddhas should be depicted exactly as they were previously described.
However, Noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra should be painted standing, fanning the Blessed One Śākyamuni with whisks.
In this manner, the sons of the gods belonging to the Śuddhāvāsa realm are to be depicted.

Śakra, the lord of the gods, as well as Suyāma, Santuṣita, Sunirmita, Śuddha, Vimala, Sudṛśa, Atapa, Ābhāsvara, Brahmā Sahāmpati, Akaniṣṭha, and other such sons of the gods of the form and desire realms, are to be depicted in successive order, standing near the noble Mañjuśrī, arranged within the surrounding assembly circle, and painted according to their own natural forms and attire.

Beneath the Bhagavat’s lion throne, a great mountain rising from the great ocean should be painted all around, extending to the edge of the cloth. In one corner of the cloth, the practitioner should be painted according to his actual dress, posture, and appearance, with his knees, elbows, and head bowed, and his hands occupied with an incense burner. And on that jewel-mountain, beneath Ārya Mañjuśrī, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be depicted as previously described.
On the left side, beneath the Blessed One’s lion throne and near the feet of Noble Avalokiteśvara, the goddess Tārā should be depicted seated upon that jewel mountain;
she should be painted exactly as previously described.

Furthermore, the entire cloth [painting] should be strewn all around with loose flowers, scattered everywhere with blossoms such as the campaka, blue lotus, saugandhika, mālatī, varṣikā, dhānuṣkārīka, punnāga, and kesarā.

And above, at both ends of the edge of the cloth's corner, two sons of gods (devaputra) should be depicted, white in color, wearing variegated forms, standing in the intermediate space, hidden within clouds of water, emitting a great shower of flowers, and leaping upward.
This is declared to be the Madhyamaka, the manifestation of the cloth for the sake of prosperity;
the middling accomplishment of human beings on this earth depends upon it.
Whatever evil was committed previously while wandering through cyclic existence,
that is destroyed at that very moment by seeing this cloth-painting here.
Deluded beings, wandering through the wheel of rebirths, do not know [this],
yet those who behold the cloth-painting of Mañjughoṣa in its center [do].
Even one who is a sinner, even one who has committed the five crimes of immediate retribution,
and even one of immoral conduct— such mantras spoken in various ways shall be accomplished for them.
Even one who has performed the recitation shall attain accomplishment more swiftly;
the sick are freed from disease, the poor obtain wealth,
and the childless obtain a son upon seeing the middle-sized cloth painting.
Merely by seeing it at that time, one shall obtain vast and great merit;
that person will certainly become a partaker of the happiness of gods and humans,
and at the end of that birth, Buddhahood will surely be attained.
By writing, by reciting, by worshipping, by drawing it,
as well as by seeing and touching it, one is liberated from all sins.
Indeed, by thus praying and entreating this one of great splendor who wanders [the earth], one makes one's birth fruitful; and likewise, rejoicing [in his deeds] brings swift results.
It is not possible to describe by speech, even in tens of millions of aeons,
the merit that a living being would obtain from the fruitful sight of this cloth-painting.
From the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvataṃsaka*, the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, this is the fifth detailed chapter.
The second section on the ritual for the cloth-painting is completed.
The Sixth Chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta once again:
"Mañjuśrī, there is yet another secret procedure for the cloth-painting, the third one, known as the 'Minor' (kanyasa)."

So that all sentient beings may attain accomplishment without even effort, a cloth-painting should be depicted by skilled artisans according to the previously described procedure: measuring one span of the Sugata in width, and likewise equal and square as before, with the previously specified features.

First of all, the noble Mañjuśrī should be depicted sitting upon a lion throne in the form of a young boy as before, teaching the Dharma, with beautiful forms and rays of light radiating in all directions. On the left side, the noble Samantabhadra should be depicted as before, standing upon a jewel-stone, holding a yak-tail whisk in his hand, with his left hand resting upon a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), and having a complexion dark like the priyaṅgu flower. On the right side of the noble Mañjuśrī, the noble Avalokiteśvara should be depicted as before, standing upon a jewel-stone.
He should be depicted with his hand occupied by a *camara* (fly-whisk), with a lotus placed in his left hand, and his form radiant on all sides.
Below the lion throne, a golden-colored mountain should be painted extending as far as the edge of the cloth.
In the corner of the cloth’s edge, on the right side beneath the lion throne of the noble Mañjuśrī, the wrathful king Yamāntaka should be painted as previously described.
With a censer held in his hand, the practitioner should, just as before,

have the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra depicted above the noble Mañjuśrī, measuring sixteen finger-breadths and nestled within a cave on a mountain of jewels. Ten mountains with precipitous slopes, resembling gabled pavilions, should be depicted.
One should depict that cloth [painting] surrounded on all sides by mountains.

Above, situated at the corners of the cloth and clinging to the mountain slopes, two sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm named Śuddha and Viśuddha should be painted as before, flying upward and scattering a profusion of flowers from their celestial palaces (vimāna).
Furthermore, that cloth should be depicted strewn with various kinds of flowers.
All this has been told regarding the threefold characteristics of the cloth; indeed, by name this is the "inferior" cloth, which is superior for minor rites.
Whatever extremely terrible sinful karma has been committed or caused to be committed,
one is liberated from it by the mere sight of the cloth-painting for thousands of millions of eons.
Indeed, upon merely seeing the cloth, one is liberated at that very moment.
Even a wise person who would honor thousands of millions of Buddhas does not approach even a sixteenth part of the merit gained by seeing this smallest cloth.
Whatever merit is gained by performing worship to all the Buddhas who are ardent in their practice,
a wise person shall obtain that same merit by beholding the cloth painting (paṭa) for even a moment.
Furthermore, one should perform auspicious deeds here for the sake of attaining enjoyments.
Whatever mantras there may be spoken by Brahmā, Indra, and the ṛṣis,
as well as those proclaimed by Vainateya, Varuṇa, Āditya, and Kubera;

All the mantras spoken by Dhanada and the others, by all the Rākṣasas, by the lords of the Dānavas, by the great serpents, by Soma, Vāyu, Amā, and others, and by Hari, Hara, and the rest— have been brought here; they are all accomplished in front of this cloth-painting.
One should always perform rites of pacification and likewise rites of enrichment here;
one should avoid fierce rites, for they are censured by the best of Jinas in this world.
The sixth detailed chapter from the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka;
the third [section], the ritual for the small cloth-painting, is hereby completed.
The Seventh Chapter.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed him thus: "Excellent, excellent! This Dharma-discourse has been well-spoken by the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of those who practice the vows of all vidyās, and out of compassion for the world; it demonstrates the skillful means of the Bodhisattvas. It is a path leading toward Nirvāṇa, a distinguished entryway, a continuity that is certain to culminate in awakening. It shall serve as the means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras and practices, and it will spread this secret of mantras among all people in the future age. When the Teacher of the World has passed away, when the sun of the Tathāgata has set and his lineage is abandoned in all Buddha-fields; when the vessel of the world has become shrouded in darkness by the absence of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas; when the Noble Path is severed, and the realm of sentient beings is devoid of light—lacking all vidyās, mantras, herbs, jewels, and gems, and bereft of virtuous people—the beings there will become indolent, their aspiration lost, faithless, fragmented, taken hold of by non-virtuous friends, deceitful, fraudulent, and of rogue conduct."
Having heard this Dharma-discourse, they will fall into terror;

delighting in indolence and laziness, they will not have faith; seeking after sensual desires, they will not believe; and being devoted to false views, they will produce much demerit. Being adversaries of the True Dharma, they are headed for the Avīci hell, having gone from the terrible to even more terrible states.

For the sake of those suffering beings, for bringing under control those who are not yet controlled, and for instilling fear in those already subdued, may the Blessed One, through the gathering of skillful means, speak the ritual procedure for the mantra-paṭa;
do so now, if you deem it the right time.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata regarding this matter.

Mañjuśrī, there exists your own supreme and most secret expansion of the chapters on the practice of the vidyā-vow and the ritual procedures for the paintings, which contains the meaning of the supreme heart-mantras—most secret, of great significance, and serving as a treasury for all mantras. These six six-syllable supreme heart-mantras attain accomplishment without conceptualization at that time."

For the sake of taming those beings, for their entry into the secret mantras of the equipment of skillful means, and for their certain attainment of perfect awakening—this which was previously spoken by seventy-six billion Buddhas, I too shall now speak at this time.
Out of regard for future generations, listen well and attend to it thoroughly;
I shall speak it to you.
And what is that?
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke this mantra: *oṃ vākyārthe jaya* / *oṃ vākyaśeṣe sva* / *oṃ vākyeyanayaḥ*.
Oṃ, salutation to Vākyaniṣṭhā. Oṃ, salutation to Vākya.
Oṃ, salutation to Vākya.

Thus, Mañjuśrī, these six-syllable mantras of yours possess great power; they are equal in strength, supreme heart-essences, and most highly accomplished. Arisen like the Buddhas themselves for the benefit of all sentient beings, they have been proclaimed by all the Buddhas. Bound by the pledge (*samaya*), thoroughly activated, and effective for all rites, they point the way to enlightenment. As the foremost mantras in the Tathāgata family, they are applied in three ways—superior, middling, and inferior—and being most beautiful, they bestow the ripening of karmic fruits. They shall achieve accomplishment even during the time when the teaching has disappeared.

Those who will accomplish these [practices] for the sake of protecting the eye of the True Dharma during the time of the final convergence, they will accomplish them by means of even a small investment for the sake of great kingdoms, vast enjoyments, and sovereign power.
At that time, in that very moment, they will attain accomplishment most swiftly.

Indeed, these supreme heart-mantras should be accomplished even for the sake of mere investigation; in brief, in whatever manner they are applied, in that same manner they will attain accomplishment. This is the summary.
At that time, at that moment, during the Great Terror—the age of the five corruptions—sentient beings will have little merit;

they will be of little renown, short-lived, possessing few enjoyments, and lacking in vigor, such that they will be unable to undertake rituals such as the extensive procedures for the cloth-painting (*paṭa*).
For their sake, I shall speak in a much more concise manner.

First of all, having purchased thread by means of trade—either a full *pala* or half a *pala*—one should have a cloth woven by a weaver that is one cubit in length and half a cubit in width, complete with its fringe. Alternatively, taking another fresh piece of new cloth that is free of hair, one should take from two cubits up to four cubits, or five, six, ten, or eight cubits in size, and have it painted by a painter according to one's desire, provided it is very white. From this point forward, one may take as much as desired along the way.

Having combined the cloth with sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and white [pigments], and having stirred them together with pure water free of living organisms, one should soak the cloth in a new vessel. After keeping it well-covered for three days, one should place it on the road.

Having performed the protection ritual in a clean location and having purified oneself, on the full moon day of the bright fortnight, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east before the vessel containing the cloth and recite these mantra-words one hundred and eight times.
It is as follows: *Oṃ he he bhagavan bahurūpadhara divyacakṣuṣe avalokaya avalokaya māṃ samayamanusmara kumārarūpadhāriṇe mahābodhisattva kiṃ cirāyasi / hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
Having performed the recitation with this mantra, one should sleep right there.
In a dream, it indicates either success or failure.
Then, having risen and seen a dream that is a sign of unimpeded success, one should have that cloth-painting painted; provided that dreams indicating failure are not seen.
Having removed that cloth from that container, one should dry it in the sun.
After drying it, one should place it again in another new container.
One should keep it well-concealed and protected.
Then, having taken one of those supreme heart-mantras (*paramahṛdaya*), one should recite [it] for one hundred thousand syllables from among the six-syllable [mantras], as much as desired.
Thereupon, that cloth-painting (*paṭa*) will quickly be accomplished.

First, having taken that cloth-painting on the fortnight of miracles, or on another bright day joined with an auspicious constellation, on a favorable lunar date, or on a day of the waxing moon; when there are very auspicious omens and the night is considered auspicious, at the time of midnight, one should have the painter—observing the *upoṣadha* vows—paint that cloth in a clean place while burning camphor incense.

First of all, one should paint Noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a young boy, with his head adorned with five locks of hair and decorated with the ornaments of a child. He is golden in color, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk and an upper robe of blue silk. He is teaching the Dharma, seated on a lion throne in the half-lotus posture with his right foot resting upon a jeweled footstool placed before the throne. He is endowed with all ornaments, beautiful to behold, with a slightly smiling face, and his gaze is directed toward the practitioner. One should thus depict him.

On the right side, one should cause Noble Samantabhadra to be depicted: waving a white chowrie, dark green like the priyaṅgu flower, with a cintāmaṇi jewel placed in his left hand, beautiful in all his limbs, adorned with all ornaments, dressed in a lower garment of blue silk, wearing a pearl necklace as a sacred thread, and seated upon a white lotus throne.

To the left side of Noble Mañjuśrī is Noble Avalokiteśvara, dressed in a garment of blue silk, beautiful in all his limbs, adorned with every ornament, and wearing a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) of pearl necklaces. In his left hand he holds a white lotus, and in his right hand he brandishes a white yak-tail whisk (*camara*) fixed upon a golden handle. He has a serene appearance and his gaze is directed toward Noble Mañjuśrī. Likewise, Noble Samantabhadra is also to be depicted; both of these [bodhisattvas] stand upon a single lotus stalk, seated on white lotus thrones.
There are three lotuses.
Upon the pericarp of the central root-lotus is the lion-throne and jeweled seat of the noble Mañjuśrī;
on the second lotus is the noble Samantabhadra; and on the third lotus is the noble Avalokiteśvara.

And that lotus stalk should be beautiful, shaped like an emerald lotus, with many lotus buds and leaves, rising from the great lake Anavatapta with its blossomed and half-blossomed flowers; its base should be supported by the two Naga kings, Nanda and Upananda. Those two Naga kings should be depicted as white in color, adorned with seven hoods, their bodies beautified by all ornaments, with human torsos and forms marked by serpent coils, gazing at the noble Mañjuśrī, half-submerged in the water, and their heads adorned with precious jewels. One should have this drawn.

And all around the great lake, below it, on the right side in the corner of the cloth, the practitioner should be depicted according to his actual appearance: looking at the foot-mandala of the noble Mañjuśrī, with a censer held in his hand, his head bowed, and his body with elbows and knees bent, dressed in his proper attire.

Above the noble Mañjuśrī, from both corners of the painting, two very beautiful sons of gods should be depicted, bearing garlands and holding flower-garlands, flying upward while hidden within the clouds, emitting a great shower of flowers.
One should depict that cloth [painting] strewn all around with flowers such as *nāgakeśara* and others;

or one may depict it as presided over by three forms as desired. Noble Mañjuśrī teaching the Dharma, Noble Samantabhadra, and Noble Avalokiteśvara—with their hands holding yak-tail whisks—should be caused to be painted.
Alternatively, the practitioner must have three images painted according to his own preference;
they may be of whatever form he desires or arranged in whatever configuration he likes, and they should be painted exactly as it pleases the practitioner.
In the center is Ārya Mañjuśrī; at both ends are Ārya Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra, or whichever others are desired, who must certainly be caused to be painted.

On whatever cloth fragment is available—whether measuring a span or a cubit—it should be caused to be painted either by oneself or by another painter, whether that painter observes the *poṣadha* vows or does not, whether he is faithful or faithless, pure or impure, or possessed of moral conduct or immoral.
The practitioner himself must necessarily have completed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), be endowed with faith, and have generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
In this way, mantras are indeed accomplished; they are not for others who are evildoers.
Having become faithful, one should thus practice the mantra-deities.
The king of mantras is accomplished for that person who possesses faith, and not otherwise;
for faith is the supreme vehicle by which the Vināyakas proceed.
In a person who lacks faith, the pure dharma does not grow,
just as a green sprout does not emerge from seeds scorched by fire.
For a mortal established in faith, the deities succeed through his ritual action when he is a seeker of awakening; for one lacking faith, they do not succeed.
All mantras,
especially those that are worldly deities as well as those that are supramundane—
all these indeed succeed for one who has faith and is free from defilement.
For those whose minds are fixed upon that, awakening and its accomplishment are swift and certain;
for others, accomplishment is not spoken of, as they are excluded from this teaching.
The cloth is proclaimed to be either small, distinguished, or middling;
now, however, I shall explain the means of accomplishment for all ritual actions.

Thus concludes the fourth section on the ritual procedure for cloth-paintings, from the seventh extensive chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
The Eighth Chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, for the sake of those beings whom you have described, this detailed procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) has been proclaimed."
They will achieve [their goals] by means of very little effort.
For their sake, I shall explain the ritual procedures for accomplishment, along with a detailed analysis of the distinctions of qualities and the classification of activities.
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly, and I shall speak.
For the benefit of all sentient beings.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One:

"Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! Well-spoken by you is this description of the conduct of mantra practice, which illuminates our own realization and brings about the manifestation of the perfection of its qualities.
May the Blessed One speak upon that."
Now, do as you deem the time for it,
out of compassion for us.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon the entire circle of the assembly, smiled.
Then, from the gateway of the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s mouth, rays of light—blue, yellow, crystal-colored, and so forth—issued forth.

As soon as those rays had issued forth, they illuminated the entire assembly circle and the great trichiliocosm; having eclipsed all the abodes of Māra, they also eclipsed the light of all the stars, the luminaries, the mountains, and the hosts of celestial bodies—even the moon and sun, though they possess great supernatural power and majesty—were so overwhelmed by that radiance that they no longer shone and became devoid of luster.

They did not shine and were seen to be eclipsed; having rendered the radiance of all jewels, mantras, medicinal herbs, and gems lusterless, they then vanished once more into the mouth of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi was present and seated right there in that assembly circle.

Rising from his seat with a sense of urgency, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition.
What, Blessed One, is the cause; what is the condition for manifesting this smile?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi:
"So it is, Vajrapāṇi; so it is.
It is just as you say."
There is no smiling by the Tathāgatas that occurs without cause or condition;
there is a cause, and there is a condition.

Those who shall enter into and follow this sovereign king of sūtras, the *Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa*—which relies upon the Dharma-clouds that serve as the means for the accomplishment of rites through the practice of vidyās—those who shall uphold it, recite it, have faith in it, and having written it in a book, honor it with salutations, powders, ointments, incense, garlands, parasols, banners, flags, or various kinds of musical instruments and diverse types of percussion and cymbals; [they shall attain the supreme goal].

Even those who obtain at least a mental continuity accompanied by rejoicing, or who experience horripilation, or who rejoice and give their approval upon hearing the power and efficacy of the *vidyā*, or who shall undertake the practice—
they have all been prophesied by me for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they shall all become Buddhas, Blessed Ones.
For this very reason, the Victors manifest a smile, and not otherwise.

First, one who has seen the ritual conventions, performed the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*), and received initiation, having taken hold of the root-mantra, heart-mantra, or sub-heart-mantra of this King of Rituals, or another mantra, or even a single-syllable mantra, or whichever other is desired, should go to a great forest and recite it three million times while subsisting on fruit and water or eating roots and leaves; thus he becomes one who has completed the preliminary service.

Then, having ascended a mountain and installed the senior cloth-painting facing west, one should sit oneself facing east upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass. One should offer one hundred thousand white lotuses, anointed with white saffron, beneath the painting to the Blessed Śākyamuni and to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas. One should also burn camphor incense according to one’s means and perform worship to the sons of gods and the *nāgas*.

With flowers as they are obtained, then at the time of midnight on the full moon of the bright fortnight, when the night is perfectly full during a *prātihāraka*, one should prepare a fire-pit in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) in the shape of a lotus. Having kindled a fire with white sandalwood logs and having combined saffron and camphor, one should offer eight thousand oblations,
having performed the protection rites according to one's means.
Then, rays of light issue forth from the Blessed One Śākyamuni, and the cloth painting becomes a single mass of flame on all sides.

Thereupon, the practitioner, moving with great haste, should circumambulate the cloth three times to the right, prostrate before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas, and take hold of the cloth.
Then, having grasped the hem of the previously described practitioner’s cloth from the past, he flies up as soon as it is taken;
with a mere snap of the fingers, he transcends the Brahma-world and arrives at the Kusumāvatī world-system.

Wherever that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Saṅkusumitarājendra, dwells, remains, and sustains himself, and teaches the Dharma, there one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī in person, hears the Dharma, and sees many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and attends upon them; for a thousand great eons, one lives free from old age and death, sporting in bliss.

The painting remains right there, empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; one perceives their empowerment, traverses hundreds of thousands of realms, or manifests hundreds of thousands of bodies; one becomes endowed with manifold miraculous powers, has the noble Mañjuśrī as a spiritual friend, and is destined for enlightenment without fail.

Thus ends the first [chapter] from the eighth extensive section on the ritual procedures for the supreme means of accomplishment, from the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra, the Ornament of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka.
Now begins the ninth detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed the entire assembly of gods seated within the maṇḍala:

"Listen, O noble sirs, to this most secret heart-mantra, the supreme king of great vidyās spoken by all the Tathāgatas, which serves as the means for accomplishing the practice and maṇḍala-mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, and as protection for the practitioner."
By reciting this, all mantras become recited.
O hosts of gods, this King of Vidyās is not to be transgressed;
even Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta was summoned, brought under control, and made compliant by means of this King of Vidyās.
What need is there to mention other bodhisattvas, or mundane and supramundane mantras?
This one of great heroism destroys all obstacles; possessing singular power, he alone is declared the foremost of all mantras.
He alone is declared the single syllable among all single-syllable [mantras].
And what is that?

It is the single syllable that accomplishes all aims, performs all tasks, cuts through all mantras [of adversaries], destroys the evil deeds of those who act wickedly, annihilates all sins, fulfills all mantras, brings about auspiciousness, and stands superior to all mundane and supramundane mantras; it is the unimpeded heart of all Tathāgatas and the fulfiller of all hopes. And what is that? Namely: *kaḷlhīṃ*.

O worthy ones, this is that most supreme secret, the single-syllable King of Vidyās effective for all rites, which cannot be transgressed by any sentient being; it is unassailable by any spirits, the auspiciousness of all Buddhas, the accomplisher of all mantras, the lord of all worlds, the sovereign of all masters of wealth, friendly toward all who are hostile, compassionate toward all creatures, and the destroyer of all obstacles. In short, however it is employed, it acts accordingly; it performs its activities even when not specifically empowered.
By reciting the mantra over whomsoever one touches, that person becomes submissive. Having consecrated garments with the mantra, if one wears them, one becomes fortunate.
Having consecrated a tooth-stick and chewing it, one removes toothache.
Having consecrated a white karavīra tooth-stick and chewing it, food is obtained without having to ask for it.
For eye pain, one should grind rock salt (*saindhava*) and, having empowered it seven times with mantras, fill the eye; this removes the eye pain.

For earache, one should cook a small ball (*chatrikā*) made from elephant dung that has arisen from a thundering cloud, wrapped in *kedhuka* leaves, over a gentle fire. Once it is well-cooked and comfortably warm, one should strain it with rock salt powder and fill the ear with it after empowering it seven times with mantras.
It pacifies [the pain] at that very moment.

For a woman in labor, or one with a retained fetus, or one overcome by colic, one should grind the root of *āṭaruṣaka* with water free of living organisms and smear it on the region of the navel; she will give birth with ease. Or, for a man with a lost splinter, one should empower old ghee eight hundred times with the mantra and have him drink it, or smear that region; he becomes free of the splinter at that very moment.

In cases of indigestion, colic, or dysentery, one should empower either black salt (*sauvarcala*), rock salt (*saindhava*), or any other salt seven times with mantras and consume it; one is then freed from that disease and becomes healthy on that very day.
In cases of both types of dysentery or acute dysentery, one should squeeze the fruit of a *mātuluṅga* and drink it with water free of living organisms; one is thereby freed from that affliction.

If one desires the birth of a child for a woman who is barren or incapable of bearing offspring, one should cook the root of *aśvagandha* with cow’s ghee, grind it with cow’s milk, and having mixed it with cow’s milk, recite the mantra over it twenty-five times. At the time of her menses, after she has bathed, one should have her drink it; meanwhile, the householder should refrain from the wives of others, avoid sexual misconduct, and approach his own wife.

Whether she has failed to conceive a husband, or has exceeded the natural time for giving birth by fifteen years, or is obstructed for many years; or whether it is caused by the spells, mantras, or herbs of another, or by the supreme seals (*paramudrā*) of others, or by the malevolent acts of enemies, or by the suppression of conception, or by the arising of disease, or any other ailment whatsoever—whether caused by the suppression of others, or by artificial and non-artificial poisons derived from stationary or moving beings, or produced by the application of roots, mantras, herbs, friends, or enemies—one should take twenty-seven times [the aforementioned substances], mix them with aged ghee and the eye of a peacock feather (*mayūracandraka*), and grind them together.
Then, having ground it well and mixed it with sugar, one should consume a dose the size of a *harītakī*.
For seven days, one should cause [the patient] to drink boiled milk combined with sugar, consecrating it repeatedly with mantras.
In the case of a headache, one should rub [the head] with a crow's wing feather that has been consecrated seven times; [the patient] becomes healthy.

In cases of diseases such as menorrhagia, one should grind the root of *ālambuṣā* with milk, combine it with the root of *nīlikā*, empower it one hundred and eight times with mantras, stir it with milk, and have the patient drink it.

Likewise, for quartan, quotidian, tertian, quaternian, continuous, or chronic irregular fevers, one should have the patient eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with ghee, empowered one hundred and eight times with mantras;
thus the person becomes healthy.
Likewise, for those seized by *ḍākinī* spirits, one should empower one's own face with the mantra one hundred and eight times and look upon them;
they will become healthy.

Similarly, for those seized by all non-human, wicked, and terrible entities such as *mātṛ*, *vālaka*, *pūtana*, *vetāla*, and *kumāra* spirits, one should empower one's own hand one hundred and eight times and touch the head of the possessed person.
He becomes established in his own nature.

With one recitation, there is protection for oneself; with two recitations, protection for one's companions; with three recitations, protection for the house; with four recitations, protection for the village; with five recitations, protection extends to those within the range of one’s watch.
In this manner, up to ten recitations, protection for the entire army camp is accomplished.
Furthermore, all these and other minor rites are performed even when the mantra has not yet been mastered through formal consecration.

Now, if one wishes to accomplish minor rites (*kṣudrakarmāṇi*), one should go to a solitary place in a secluded region—either at the source of a river flowing to the ocean, on the shore of the ocean, on the bank of the Ganges River, or resorting to the bank of a great river—and having constructed a hut in a pure location, one should recite [the mantra] three million times for the sake of attaining success (*siddhi*). One should bathe three times a day, change one's clothes three times, observe silence, subsist on alms, and consume either barley-gruel, milk, or fruit. Having seen the signs of success, one may then begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*).

In that very region, at that place, having performed a great worship of the superior cloth-painting (paṭa), one should offer one hundred thousand lamps to the painting. These lamps may be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay, filled with either *turuṣka* oil or cow’s ghee, with wicks fashioned from pieces of fresh cloth.
By means of these lamp-garlands lit simultaneously on all sides, rays of light will issue forth from the painting.
Immediately upon the rays being emitted, the cloth becomes enveloped on all sides by a garland of flames;
and from above, in the sky, drums resound and the sound of "Well done! is heard.

Then, by the Vidyādhara, appearing in a form of great haste, one should offer an *argha* oblation to the previously painted cloth that has emerged from the corner of the practitioner’s cloth, circumambulate it, and prostrate to all the Buddhas before taking hold of it.
As soon as it is taken, one flies up together with all the beings who hold lamps, or they go toward a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) characterized by a single additional [dimension].

That practitioner is then consecrated into the sovereignty of a Vidyādhara Cakravartin, surrounded on all sides by Vidyādharīs accompanied by divine musical instruments, sweet-sounding songs, instrumental music, and dance.
Together with those who carry lamps, he sports like one who is ageless and immortal;
he remains for a great eon (mahākalpa),
resembling the rising sun, adorned with the beauty of divine limbs and arrayed in variegated garments.
These very ones are his servants;
he moves about together with them,
and all the kings of the vidyādharas attend upon him as his slaves.
One becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas;
one becomes long-lived and invincible;
and one becomes supremely fortunate among all the Siddhas.
One gains mastery over the daughters of the *vidyādharas* and worships all ritual substances as well as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
thereafter, in a mere instant, one goes even to the world of Brahmā.
He does not even take Śakra into account, much less other vidyādharas;
and in the end, he attains the state of Buddhahood.
The practice for the noble Mañjuśrī is even more intense than that.

Therefore, having gone to a secluded place, free from people and devoid of attachment or social ties, one should enter a great forest. At a spot where there is a lotus pond provided with a river, situated near a single mountain, one should ascend a mountain peak and take up either the Single-Syllable King of Vidyās spoken in the *Mañjuśrī-kalpa*, or one spoken by the Tathāgatas or other Bodhisattvas, or any other mantra. Subsisting on lotus roots and fruits as desired, or subsisting on milk products, one should recite the vidyā three million six hundred thousand times.

At the conclusion of the recitation, having installed the superior cloth-painting according to that same previously described procedure, one should kindle a fire with *khadira* wood and offer thirty-six thousand previously prepared lotuses smeared with white sandalwood and saffron.

Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering, rays of light issue forth from the cloth painting of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. Having illuminated the practitioner, they vanish into his crown. As soon as he is touched by them, the practitioner becomes possessed of the five superknowledges.
Having attained the stage of a bodhisattva and possessing a divine form, he wanders at will;
he lives for thirty-six kalpas and traverses thirty-six buddha-fields.
He perceives their power,
upholds the teachings of thirty-six Buddhas,
and takes delight in honoring and serving them.
And he becomes one who is destined for awakening; he is taken into the care of the noble Mañjuśrī as a spiritual friend, until reaching the culmination of awakening and the finality of nirvāṇa.

Thus concludes the second section on the ritual procedures for the supreme means of accomplishment, from the ninth chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke again regarding the supreme accomplishment of rites:

"In this King of Rituals, having taken up any one of the mantras, one should descend into the great river Gaṅgā and, staying upon a boat in the middle of the Gaṅgā while subsisting on milk-rice, recite the mantra three million times over as many days as desired."
Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, he sees all the *nāgas*.

Thereupon, one should begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*). Right there in the middle of the boat, one should have a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) constructed in the shape of a lotus. Then, having performed a great worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) with *nāgakesara* flowers, one should install the superior cloth painting facing west and sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east. Having consecrated each individual *nāgakesara* flower seven times with mantras, one should offer them as oblations into a fire kindled with fuel of *khadira* wood.

Up to thirty thousand [beings]—whether they be white sandalwood, saffron, or *nāgakesara* flowers, or other *nāgas*—may appear for the purpose of being seen; and though they may attempt to entice one with perfected substances (*siddhadravya*), these must not be accepted.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire offering, he flies up together with the boat;
he becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas,
and all the kings of the Nāga lords become his attendants.
They remain like servants;
he lives for thirty intermediate kalpas,
and he becomes one who moves according to his own will.
With unimpeded movement, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face;
he touches the crown of one's head, and as soon as touched, one becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā) and will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, there is another method for accomplishing the supreme ritual action:

having descended to the great river Gaṅgā, one should construct a boat from a single piece of wood made of *bilva* wood, ensuring it is well-examined and well-crafted. Having boarded that vessel made of *bilva* wood, the practitioner himself—being clearly manifest, skillful, and highly proficient—should steer that boat, navigating throughout the great river Gaṅgā without leaving it, whether across or along its length.

Therefore, having taken one or another mantra—whether it be the root mantra, the six-syllable, the eight-syllable, or the single-syllable; or the female wrathful messenger (*krodhadūtī*), the male messenger (*dūta*), or any other mantra—one should install the supreme cloth-painting (*paṭa*) right there facing west, while oneself faces east at first, and thereafter as desired. One should subsist on milk, barley-gruel, or fruit; or on water, tubers, roots, and fruits; remaining silent, bathing three times a day, changing clothes three times, practicing pure deeds, and possessing a perfectly pure intellect.
First, one should recite the vidyā six million times before the cloth painting, following the previously taught and observed ritual procedure.
Then, at the conclusion of the recitation, a boat that travels upon the great ocean will appear.
Then the practitioner, having gathered the requisites, should place them right there on that boat as previously arranged.
Then, while traveling across the great ocean, one must not be afraid,
nor should one turn back.
And they cannot be turned back, except by the power of the practitioner.
Then, in just a moment, he enters the great ocean even if it is situated at a distance of a thousand *yojanas*, let alone a short distance.
Having entered there into the abode of the rivers, he should begin the ritual of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood in a previously prepared fire-pit or in an earthen vessel made by a potter, he should offer sixty million oblations of the filaments (*kiñjalka*) of *nāgakesara*, mixed with white sandalwood and camphor, in either very small or very large quantities.

And as they were making offerings, the Rākṣasas dwelling in the city of Laṅkā, assuming many forms, raised a cry of "Alas! Alas! while the Nāga kings dwelling in Bhogavatī, the city of the Nāgas, also rose up, assuming various forms—some more cruel and others more gentle.
Those Nāgas and Rākṣasas spoke thus: "May the Blessed One arise! May the Blessed One arise! Be our lord!"
In this way, asuras, yakṣas, gods, mahoragas, siddhas, and all humans will attempt to entice one;
yet one must neither rise up nor be afraid.
Then, while reciting the mantra, the vidyādhara should threaten them with the index finger of his left hand.
Then they flee, running hither and thither, escaping and perishing.
Then, at the conclusion of the *homa*, she takes that practitioner on her ship and in an instant goes to the Akaniṣṭha realm.

She also travels to and returns from other world-systems; she becomes one who knows the minds of Bodhisattvas, possesses the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), and becomes one of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*).
He constantly beholds the noble Mañjuśrī;
all nāgas, all rākṣasas, all gods, all asuras, and all sentient beings become subject to his will and carry out his commands—
except for all the buddhas, bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, noble śrāvakas, and those here who have attained mantra-siddhi.
And they become friendly toward him and supportive, until he becomes invincible to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is another supreme means for the practice of ritual action:
one should have a large boat constructed from bilva wood,
or one should construct a large dwelling using a collection of logs from a single type of timber.
One should prepare a boat on an island situated in the middle of the Ganges.

On that boat, one should station one hundred and twenty persons wearing white garments, who have performed protective rites (*rakṣā*), whose hands are occupied with lamps, and who are holding flowers; they should be seated within the boat in front of the Great Cloth (*jyeṣṭhapaṭa*) established according to the previously described ritual procedure.

Then, having performed a grand worship of the Cloth, one should offer thirty-six thousand oblations (*āhuti*) of *nāgakesara* powder mixed with saffron, white sandalwood, and camphor, into a fire of *khadira* wood.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, that boat travels to the world of Brahmā in a mere instant and returns;
it moves about as one desires.
One beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face;

upon merely seeing him, one attains the [bodhisattva] stages, possesses the five superknowledges, becomes long-lived, remains for a great eon (*mahākalpa*), and becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) among the great holders of vidyā-mantras.
Furthermore, those who hold lamps for him become accomplished holders of vidyā-mantras.
He roams with them as companions according to his desire and becomes one who moves at will;
he delights in making offerings to other Blessed Buddhas;
and in the end, Buddhahood becomes certain for him.
Furthermore, it also becomes the supreme means for accomplishing ritual actions.
On a riverbank, on a seashore, or likewise on the Himalaya mountain,
or on this king of mountains, Vindhya, one should accomplish the supreme rite.
On Sahya, Malaya, Arbuda, Gandhamādana,
and on this Trikūṭa, the king of mountains, one should accomplish the supreme rite.
In the great ocean, as well as on mountains rich with trees and abounding in flowers—
in these regions, indeed, the mantras spoken by the Jina are accomplished.
In a secluded, pure, and remote place, free from the ways of village life,
as well as in mountain caves, all the kings of mantras are accomplished.
In a delightful and remote lodging, praised by the Supreme Victor,
and free from wicked beings, all the kings of mantras are accomplished.
When the king is righteous, when the people of the land are devoted to purity and proper conduct,
when they are devoted to their mothers and fathers, and when they do not neglect the twice-born castes,
the deities attain success in that place; but it is not otherwise.
On the delightful bank of the Bhāgīrathī, on the most beautiful Yamunā,
on the banks of the Sindhu and Narmadā, and on the pure shore of the Candrabhāgā.
The Kāverī, the Sarasvatī, and the Sitā, the great river of the gods—
these are declared by the sons of the One Possessing Ten Powers to be fields of spiritual accomplishment.
The lands and mountains of the northern region were proclaimed by those possessed of the ten powers;
namely, in Kaśmīra, in the land of China, in Nepāla, and likewise in Kāviśa.
In Mahācīna, indeed, all the fields of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) without exception are found;
as are the mountains and rivers situated in the northern direction.
Those lands which are declared to be meritorious, where the inhabitants eat barley and wheat, and where beings are compassionate— in those places, success will certainly be achieved.
On the great mountain Śrīparvata, known as Dakṣiṇāpatha,
at the shrine of Śrīdhānyakaṭaka on this earth which contains the relics of the Jina.
Indeed, mantras are swiftly accomplished there for all purposes and rites—
at the Vajrāsana, at the great caitya, and at the beautiful Dharmacakra.
The supreme sage has attained peace; there too, perfection is seen at the great shrine of Devāvatāra and at Saṅkāśya, the site of the great miracle.
In the great city named Kapila, in the excellent grove of Lumbinī,
the preeminent place praised by the most eminent of Jinas, the King of Mantras is accomplished.
Likewise, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, always in the Sītavana grove on earth,
in the delightful city named Kusuma, and always in the city of Kāśī;
In Madhura, Kanyakubja, and the city of Ujjayinī on earth;
likewise in Vaiśālī, at the Caitya, and in Mithilā, he is always present on earth.
Whether they be the principal cities and towns or others inhabited by people,
accomplishment is ordained in those places that are praised as meritorious regions.
These and other regions— villages, districts, market towns, cities, excellent and preeminent capitals, as well as holy places situated along rivers— [are all auspicious].
There, following the practice of begging for alms, one should be devoted to recitation and fire-offerings;
and one should always remain in speech, in the open air, and in empty dwellings.
One should perform the preliminary service for mantras in all ritual activities;
the practitioner of mantra should always recite the mantra everywhere in the Middle Country.

Constantly engaged in recitation and ever-disciplined through the practice of renunciation, the knower of mantras is one who is perfectly truthful in conduct and habit, and is devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Faithful in the practice of mantra, the observer of vows should first perform recitation in a pure place, a fertile field, free from barbarians and thieves.
In all [places] such as those inhabited by reptiles, it is considered avoided;
whereas in a place endowed with fruits and flowers, praised, and possessing pure water, it is permitted.
All those who know the mantra should recite the mantra; it is not proclaimed in other places, but rather in a temple, a cremation ground, or a place characterized by solitude.
Likewise, at a solitary linga in a remote place, the knower of mantras,
having performed self-protection and protection for his companions, indeed performs the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa).
The mantra-practitioner, ever joined with the mantra, should practice the supreme mantra in a great forest, amidst a large tree rich in flowers and yielding fruit.
On a mountain peak, at a waterfall, in a pure and clean water-place, or on the excellent bank of a great river.
The knower of mantras should practice the mantra here in these places:
in the eastern region, at Lauhitya, at the great river, and at auspicious rivers.
Likewise, in the region of Kāmarūpa, in that most excellent city called Vardhamāna,
where that most meritorious and foremost of rivers, the Nīmnāgā, flows closely by.
In that place, one who is pure and constantly engaged in recitation should resort to a beautiful cow;
therefore, indeed, one should perform the preliminary service for all ritual acts.
Likewise, at Gaṅgādvāra and constantly at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
one who is pure and observant of vows should indeed recite the mantra during its practical application.
These are the great cremation grounds; there the reciter should always perform his recitation, as well as at rivers with pure water that are free from worms.
Therefore, the reciter should recite the mantra there with a concentrated mind;
for no merit whatsoever is seen there in the activities of worldly people.
However, under the pretext of receiving instruction in the mantras, one should indeed reside there for a short time;
or else, one should depart from there at the proper time, like [the moon] during an eclipse.
Having reached the [proper] time, he should dwell there for some time, and not otherwise;
or else, being capable and a knower of mantras, he should quickly go from there elsewhere.
One should always dwell upon the ground at caityas where Sugatas have resided,
as well as at all the worldly shrines that have fallen into false views.
One who knows the mantras should always avoid other sites of pilgrimage;
the knower of mantras should not dwell there, for they give rise to the path of false causes.
The surface of the earth is traversed by the supreme Victors, by those who possess the individual diamond-scepter,
by the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, and by the Śrāvakas, the sons of the supreme Victors.
The knower of mantras, reciting the mantra, should frequent all those places;
having first prepared with such effort, he should always practice in that location.
One who knows the mantras should recite the mantra again and again according to the prescribed rite;
for through recitation and burnt offerings, he destroys all the sins of embodied beings without exception.
Therefore, with every effort and with a well-composed mind, one should recite the mantra.
These locations have been prescribed for all rites and for the practice of the supreme rites.

If one does not obtain these, then in whatever pure place it may be, one who is free from doubt through faith should perform the preliminary service (*pūrva-sevā*) and carry out the supreme rite suitable for accomplishment.

First, having installed the senior cloth painting facing west and having positioned oneself facing east, one should take earth from the top of an anthill or earth from the bank of the Ganges river, and mixing it with uśīra, white sandalwood, saffron, camphor, and other such substances, one should fashion the form of a peacock.

Having placed that [image] before the cloth painting, and having fashioned a circle out of kuśa grass with uncut tips grown in a pure place, one should hold it with the right hand in front of the cloth painting while holding a peacock with the left hand; on the night of the full moon, having performed a great worship of the cloth painting and burning camphor incense, one should recite the mantra until dawn.
Then, at the time of sunrise, that clay peacock becomes a great king of peacocks;
the wheel becomes ablaze,
and he himself possesses a divine body, adorned with celestial garlands, garments, and ornaments, resembling the rising sun and able to assume any form at will.
Having prostrated to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, circumambulated the cloth painting, and taken hold of the cloth, he sits upon that peacock throne; in a moment, he transcends the Brahma-world.
Surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Vidyādharas, he becomes a Vidyādhara Cakravartin. He lives for sixty Manvantara-kalpas.
He moves at will through all realms of existence;
his gait is unimpeded, and he becomes endowed with divine prosperity.
He beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face—yes, he beholds him face to face.
He alone becomes his virtuous friend,
and in the end, he attains buddhahood.

In this manner, having washed with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and sprinkled all these items—such as staffs, water-pots, sacred threads, realgar, yellow orpiment, swords, iron arrows, slings, axes, and various other specific weapons; clay figures of bipeds, quadrupeds, and specific mounts such as lions, tigers, and bears; or those made of anthill-clay or river-clay, saturated with fragrant scents; as well as seats, vehicles, beds, white parasols, crowns, and various ornaments; all kinds of precious gems; all the specific requisites of renunciants, including rosaries, sandals, wooden clogs, alms-bowls, robes, small bells, needles, and tools, whether made of flower-metal (*puṣpaloha*) or whatever other implements and vessels there may be, made of anthill-clay or river-bank-clay—one should consecrate them one hundred and eight times with a purificatory mantra, or with the single-syllable mantra, or with any other mantra taught in this King of Rituals (*Kalparāja*), excluding those used for the subsidiary practice (*anusādhana*). Then, having performed protection for oneself and having provided defense for one's companions, being skilled in the secret mantras and tantras, one should place the objects facing west in the previously specified locations. Having performed a great worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) as before, while burning camphor incense for the eldest [deity], one should select any one of those previously specified artificial weapons and requisites on the night of the full moon, and recite the mantra throughout that night until the time of sunrise.
In the meantime, a cloth [painting] adorned with a great garland of light is seen.
If a particular vehicle has been taken up by the practitioner, then having mounted it, he goes wherever he desires.
If it is a particular ornament or a particular weapon, by taking that, he becomes a venerable universal monarch among the Vidyādharas.

Possessing a divine form, he travels at will, resembling the rising sun, garlanded with great radiance, his body illuminated like lightning; he becomes the lord of all *vidyādharas*, long-lived, enduring for a great eon (*mahākalpa*), surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of *vidyādharas*, and moving through the sky with divine, great *maṇi* jewels. Whatever vehicle was previously envisioned and seen by him when he attained accomplishment, that very thing becomes his source of great power.

That very [deity] becomes his vehicle; that very one becomes his companion. Having warded off the success of others' mantras and spells, he applies the success of his own mantra, being of a friendly nature, desirous of benefit, and constantly following him. Whatever specific weapons, ornaments, jewels, seats, beds, vehicles, living beings, and so forth he possesses, those very things become his constant attendants for the sake of great protection, shielding, and guarding.
He becomes possessed of great majesty, great heroism, and a great body.
He beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face.
He gives his approval;
by being touched on the crown of his head, he obtains the state of a spiritual friend,
and until he reaches the seat of awakening, he will certainly attain the ten powers.
He becomes worthy of worship;

he is invincible to all sentient beings and unassailable by any spirits; he is one who does not sever the lineage of the *bhūtakoṭi* (the limit of reality) and has attained the [bodhisattva] stages. He follows the certainty of the bodhisattvas possessing the ten powers. In brief, one who delights in supreme worship before the front of the supreme cloth-painting situated in a supreme place should perform only supreme deeds.

One should accomplish this extensive *kalparāja* for the sake of attaining the state of a *vidyādhara*, the power of moving through the sky, entry into the rank of a *bodhisattva*, the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the attainment of the [bodhisattva] stages, the ability to travel between world-systems in this very body, the fulfillment of the lineage of the Ten Powers, the direct vision of the noble Mañjuśrī, the hearing of his teaching of the Dharma which is never fruitless to behold, the non-interruption of the lineage of the Buddhas, the sequential attainment of the knowledge of the Omniscient One, the entry into the spreading cloud of Dharma, the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of those who bear the rain of nectar that does not dry up, the performance of activity for the benefit of the world, the protection of the eye of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, making the word of the Tathāgata fruitful, the manifestation of the methods for the practice and accomplishment of mantras, and the revelation of the majestic qualities of all Buddhas, *bodhisattvas*, *pratyekabuddhas*, and noble *śrāvakas*. This king of banners (*paṭarāja*) is to be accomplished according to the ritual path in all mundane and supramundane mantra-kalpas and all tantras—whether by the primary banner associated with the recitation of mantras or, in brief, even by the rites spoken in other kalpas.
As for what I have stated—that the accomplishment of those mantras occurs swiftly—it will certainly be accomplished.

The tenth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for the supreme cloth-painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, is completed.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, there exists within your tradition a procedure for the medium-sized cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), a method of practice (*sādhanavidhi*) suitable for intermediate rites; I shall speak of it in brief."
Listen to that; attend to it well and thoroughly;
I shall speak.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One, the Teacher who has compassion for the world and delights in the welfare of all beings, speak now, if he deems it the right time;
out of compassion for us and having regard for future generations."

When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to him: "Listen, Mañjuśrī! First of all, hear the procedure for ethical discipline, vows, purity, conduct, observances, recitation, fire-offerings, and meditation, by means of which all mantra practices, accomplishments, and rites become fruitful and not in vain;
and quickly all mantra practices, accomplishments, and rites become fruitful and not in vain;
and quickly all mantra applications attain success."
And what is that?
I shall speak; listen, O youth.
First of all, one should initially undertake the undertaking of the knowledge-vow and the practice of ethical discipline;
first, one should enter the commitment (*samaya*) taught by the maṇḍala master.

Having obtained from you an intelligent person as described in the *Kalparāja*, who has received the initiation of an Ācārya, who is knowledgeable in the teaching, skillful, clear-minded, righteous, truthful, highly energetic, grateful, firm in friendship, neither too old nor too young, free from desire for all gain and honor, celibate, compassionate, one who does not speak falsely out of mere greed, for the sake of enjoyment, or out of favoritism—let alone for trivial forms of greed and delusion—one who is firm in his vows, impartial toward all beings, merciful, generous by nature, one who has performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), a reciter of your secret mantras, one who has mastered the sciences through prior service, one who has entered your maṇḍala in the proper sequence, one who knows the world, knows the ritual procedures, is benevolent, capable of action, discerning, intent on the highest good, fearless, undaunted, unhesitating, firm in vigor, free from disease (by which disease one becomes incapable of performing the rite), and born of a very high lineage.
One endowed with these qualities becomes a master of the maṇḍala.
The practitioner, being either equal to or slightly inferior to him in some respects, should request such a Maṇḍala Master and pray:
"I wish to enter the samaya of the Great Bodhisattva, the Youthful Noble Mañjuśrī.
Therefore, may the Master, out of compassion for us, with a mind intent on our welfare and full of mercy, speak [to grant it]."
Then, that mandala master, having examined the disciples according to the previously described procedure as before, should cause them to enter.
Having bestowed the initiation as before, he should give the mantra.
He should duly demonstrate the commitments (samaya) in their proper sequence.
One should reveal the secret tantras, mudrās, and ritual actions only after a long period of thorough examination and having ascertained the disciple's disposition;
this is the proclaimed rule that such rituals for all tantras, mantras, and so forth are not for others.
Thereafter, the disciple should offer himself and his possessions to the mandala master according to his ability, or whatever else would please the master.
Then, that mandala master should establish the perception of [the disciple] as a son;
he should behave toward him like a son,
and provide for his mother with enjoyments.

Then, having taken up a certain mantra from that practitioner, the practitioner should go to a secluded place and, at the previously designated location, perform the ritual in detail according to the procedure taught for the maṇḍala—beginning with the *peyāla*—using those very mantras for the invocation, dismissal, and the offering of lamps, perfumes, incense, and food-oblations.

Having invoked [the deity] and offered the water for the feet (*argha*) and a seat, he should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) three times daily, bathing three times and changing his clothes three times. In this context, "time of twilight" (*sandhyākāla*) refers to the period starting from the end of the night until the sun has risen to the height of a yoke; the interval within this is called the first twilight.
When the sun is at midday, the solar disc situated in the sky at a distance of one *yuga* (four cubits) from both ends is called the middle *sandhyā*.
And at the time of sunset, when one *yuga* remains, it is called the third *sandhyā*.
One who is endowed with moral conduct and vows, a teacher who is skillful and wise, born of a noble and high lineage, and possessed of firm vigor in every respect.
Diligently engaged in mantra and tantra, possessing an intellect skilled in all activities,
subtle and proficient in the knowledge of mantras, he is always a bearer of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Possessing great energy and brilliance, disregarding worldly dharmas,
and having faith in this dharma of the supreme sages, they have abandoned those of the world.
Having performed the recitation, knowing the distinction [between states], following the preliminary service,
being a knower of the mantra of Mañjughoṣa, and being intent upon having witnessed the signs of efficacy.
One who knows the application of worldly mantras spoken by the Buddha,
having performed protection and possessing firm strength, should always delight in pure conduct and observances.
Following in every respect the path taught by the Buddha,
I am diligently engaged in this mantra-recitation, which is praiseworthy and extolled by the Conquerors.
Always perceiving the fruits of karma in this world as well as in the next,
he should be fearful of all evils even in their most minute forms;
he should be pure, skillful, free from laziness, intelligent, and pleasant to behold.
The mantras taught by those possessing the ten powers, as well as by the sons of the Victors,
and even the worldly mantras belonging to the Vajra and Antaka families—
those who have constantly exerted themselves in these and who uphold the meaning of their texts and treatises, [attain success].
Free from disease, not lacking in power, devoid of both old age and childhood,
having perfected mantras, likewise well-protected, he is swift in action in every respect.
Not procrastinating, likewise modest, and especially skilled in discerning gestures;
a celibate student of great wisdom, wandering alone and free from attachment.
One who has received initiation and is a hero in this Mañjubhāṣita tantra,
who is devoted to the completion of recitation and likewise accomplished in the sciences;
Possessed of great majesty, knowing the world, contemplating the reality of the states of existence,
devoted solely to the highest good, he was a giver delighted in the welfare of all beings.
In that way, a distinguished preceptor must always indeed be requested;
the mandala of mantras written by him attains accomplishment.
When the consecration is thus bestowed by him, it yields great fruit;
and one who desires accomplishment should always worship him like a sage, along with his disciples.
The disciples must diligently carry out his word, which is not to be transgressed;
they should provide him with enjoyments according to their available means.
Whether it be very little or abundant, by whatever means one attains contentment—
for the sake of the body and life— one should regard the mind as the body does for its father.
In the same way, a disciple who knows the Dharma should give wealth to the teacher;
he shall obtain fame, accomplishment, long life, and indeed health.
The disciple who honors his guru attains an abundant state;
moreover, his mantras become effective through the instruction of the path of ritual practice.
Through serving them, honoring them, and even through worshipping them,
all the Buddhas as well as the sons of the supreme Victors are likewise pleased.
All the gods are indeed pleased when there is always proper reverence toward the guru;
all this has been told regarding gurus who perceive the mantras.
For a practitioner who has first or previously entered the commitments,
whether the person [to be initiated] be equal to him, or even superior, or indeed more excellent;
A guru must never be despised, whether he be equal to or even superior to oneself;
for by him alone is instruction always given in this tantra.
The mantra-attainment should be bestowed upon this disciple, as shown according to his capacity; one should not feel envy toward this disciple who has been prepared beforehand.
The eye that follows affection is well-established for embodied beings;
the teacher, for the sake of the disciple, should make that very person his disciple.
Wherever there is a continuous succession of affection that follows one another,
and which maintains a stream of friendliness, one should indeed bestow the mantra there.
In this manner, both the teacher and the disciple should always remain eager upon seeing one another, due to their state of constant reverence.
For them, the path is indeed constant in the observation of mantra-conduct;
both the father and the son are knowers of mantra who follow it with success.
Both the disciple and the teacher always attained steadfastness and contentment;
likewise, a son who is devoted to dharma should always be protected with great effort.
Indeed, for those Buddhas who have severed their bodily parts, such is the true nature (dharmatā) regarding them;
in their absence, one should give the mantra as prescribed to those who are protectorless.
And for poor beings, especially for those who are weak,
the practice of mantra is superior even for all other beings.
One should perform it at all times— whether in inferior, superior, or middling circumstances—
and always, toward all phenomena, for the sake of bestowing grace.

One should bestow [the teaching] even upon those who desire it, for the destiny and birth of one who lacks effort [depends on this]; however, the disciple himself, having received the mantra from him according to the prescribed manner, [should practice].
One who desires accomplishment should strive in that path taught by him alone, and not otherwise, for it is the supreme goal of others.
Having bowed with his head as if to a father, he should depart from there at his pleasure;
then, having gone to a solitary place, he should recite the mantra in brief.
A mendicant who subsists on alms, observing silence and reciting prayers three times a day,
should proceed according to the path as previously described.
Then, following that [instruction], he should be a practitioner of service, frequenting locations and sacred abodes such as the great forest, mountain peaks, and likewise pure riverbanks.
In a cow-pen, or even in a great city, in a secluded place devoid of people, in an empty temple, under a tree, or on a mountain peak.
On the delightful banks of a great body of water, or on a sandy shore, or at a lamp-stand,
and in various other charming locations previously specified.
In these and other locations, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind,
accompanied by friends who possess the proper characteristics and are experts in the meaning of the mantra and in logic.
By those who know the truth of gestures and appearances, who are like themselves and similar to them,
who are brave, victorious in battle, virtuous, and patient;
By those faithful in the practice of mantras within this teaching proclaimed by the Victor,
who are praiseworthy, endowed with the [auspicious] marks, and patient, one should be accompanied by such assistants.
For him, however, all rites are accomplished without even effort;
having risen from bed at dawn and bathed in pure water, he becomes purified.
In water free from living organisms, originating from rivers or great lakes,
the knower of mantras should rub his body with powders of clay and cow dung.
Then, having purified the clean and stainless water with mantras,
the practitioner of recitation, with a disciplined mind, should bathe and not let the proper time pass by.
Then, having risen and stood on the bank, he washed his hands with clay twenty-one times— seven, seven, and again seven times.
Having sat down there, one should then use a tooth-stick;
after discarding the tooth-cleanser, one should then pay homage to the Protector.
Having paid homage to the Lord of the World, one should perform a delightful worship,
praising him again and again with various offerings of hymns of praise.
Having offered argha with fragrant flowers to the Teacher, the reciter should then bow his head to the Buddhas who have arisen as disciples.
In the presence of those Lords of the World,
one should perform confession and offer food there before the central painting.
Seated upon a bundle of kuśa grass, remaining there with a composed mind,
one should perform the recitation continuously with that rosary.
One should indeed recite only the mantra as it was received, and not another mantra at that time;
one should avoid what is excessively inferior or excessively superior.

In rites of middling power, the practitioner of the vow should always recite the mantra with a moderate voice; he should carefully avoid speech that is excessively loud, as well as any other [inappropriate] speech.
The medium [mantra] is praised for medium rites and has been extolled by the Victorious One;
one should always recite the medium [mantra], which is neither too high nor too low.
This instruction was spoken by all the Buddhas of the past:
one should never recite [the mantra] in the presence of others or while engaged in the activities of others;
rather, one should recite the mantra of medium length in a secluded place known to oneself.
Likewise, if someone well-versed in the meaning of mantras should find their recitation to be deficient,
they who desire middling accomplishment should recite that mantra further.
Therefore, in a secluded place free from living beings, where the true meaning of mantras is well-heard and where there is no crowding, the practitioner of recitation should mutter the mantra.
