In the fourth part of the night, at its very midpoint,
when [the sky] is copper-red and the solar disc has risen the height of a yoke.
Thus has the first twilight been described by the foremost of sages;
the middle one is proclaimed to be the measure of a *yuga*, which is four cubits.
Therefore, when the sun has risen into the sky, one should then cease the recitation of the mantra;
having ceased the mantra recitation, the observer of the vow offers the arghya water and performs the ritual dismissal.

Then, during the remaining time, one who is devoted to this wholesome teaching of the Sage should engage in the recitation of the true Dharma and so forth, such as the Prajñāpāramitā and other scriptures.
The books known as the *Daśabhūmika* should always be honored and recited; having arrived at the proper time, one should indeed bow down to those preeminent among the Victors.
Then, having recited his own mantra and that of the Lord of Mantras, he should not go about for the sake of a livelihood;
rather, he should move about at the proper time, eating at the proper time, with his senses conquered.
A practitioner who is righteous and diligent, having faith in the Buddha's teaching,
should enter among the villages observing silence and always devoted to pure conduct.
The practitioner of recitation should always enter the house of a righteous being for alms,
[only] when it has been prepared with water free of living organisms and is considered pure.
In such a family, where the Buddha’s teaching is honored by its devoted wife who possesses right view, one seeking alms should always receive alms.
Just as a warrior, well-equipped and armored, might enter the perils of battle,
constantly crushing his enemies and never being slain by them;
In this way, the practitioner who subsists on alms should always enter a village;
likewise, upon seeing a pleasing form or hearing auspicious sounds, he should remain composed.
For the sake of pacifying passion, one should meditate on the unattractive and the attractive;
having seen a body among women adorned with the conduct and ornaments of youth.
One should meditate upon the body as impure, foul-smelling, and loathsome—
drenched with worms, situated in a cemetery, impermanent, and suffering.
There, the foolish and deluded indeed wander through the five destinies,
bound by the threads of karma that have shone for a long time.
But those deluded beings who are shrouded by ignorance, like those blind from birth, are the cause of their own suffering;
being possessed of perverted intellects, they sink into ruin when attached to that [world].
Adorned with various garments and colored in many ways,
they were seen going back and forth, mounted upon long swings.
But those whose movements and gestures of the feet are joined with dancing itself,
where beings devoted to purity sink for a long time on the path.
For those born from the waters of the ocean of existence, their births— submerged in the water of suffering— do not come to an end, like the buckets of a waterwheel.
For it has been declared by the Buddhas, as well as by the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and Pratyekabuddhas, that woman alone is the root of suffering.
This great ocean, the unshakeable sea of existence, is difficult to dry up;
therein sentient beings, their consciousness deceived, sink because of women.
The hell realm, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts along with that of the asuras,
the human world, and indeed the divine— such are their constant destinies.
Powerless and deceived by women, they indeed wander everywhere;
they sink into the great mire of the prison of the ocean of saṃsāra.
Foolish men attached to women are like jackals drawn by a corpse;
wherever beings are constantly indulgent, they indeed endure intense suffering.
Those who have lost the white dharmas, though they have entered the Buddha's teaching,
do not ward off any of the sufferings within the ocean of existence.
For those who are devoted to the recitation of mantras, who have the eyes of Maheśa, who are wise, radiant,
and have conquered their enemies, no suffering exists.
For those who are self-restrained, who know Brahman and the Truth, who worship their gurus and deities,
and who are devoted to their mothers and fathers, no suffering exists even among women.
To those who pursue the ultimate truth, the female body is impermanent, suffering, and empty; likewise, for those who recite mantras, it is like a tumor or a thorn.
One who is lustful, childish, and of evil intellect, who has not fled from saṃsāra and is constantly attached to women, for him no accomplishment is found.
For a reciter here who is of immoral conduct, there is no superior rebirth, nor a middling rebirth, nor even the lowest attainment or success.
The Lord of Sages has not prescribed the accomplishment of mantras for one who is immoral,
nor has he taught the path that leads to the city of Nirvana.
How indeed could mantras succeed for a fool in this contemptible place?
Furthermore, there is no happy rebirth for that person of immoral conduct in this world.
Nor indeed will one reach the summit of heaven, nor be devoted to happiness;
how much less, then, could one attain the very accomplishment of the mantras spoken by the Jinas?
Furthermore, when a palmyra tree has been cut down at its very summit,
it is impossible for it to become green again or to produce new sprouts.
Thus has the accomplishment of mantra for the deluded person been proclaimed here:
how could the king of mantras be accomplished by one who is immoral, engaged in evil deeds, constantly attached to women, and associated with unwholesome friends?
Therefore, one who is self-controlled, always reciting mantras, and not reflecting upon the faults of women should avoid attachment to them; for success is ordained through them.
Success is not declared for others—for the foolish who are infatuated with women;
rather, it belongs to the wise one who delights in being undistracted, who is pure, skillful, and free from attachment.
One who is of noble birth, firm and brave, friendly, and pleasing to behold,
and who knows how to discern between dharma and adharma— for such persons, spiritual success is not difficult to attain.
Having proceeded in this manner, the knower of mantras should enter a village for the sake of alms; having gone to whatever place he desires, he should go to a spot previously prepared there.
Having gone to a suitable place,
one of pure mind should set down the alms-bowl in a clean spot and then eat what is permissible.
Having washed his feet and gone out from that dwelling,
he should first wash only his shanks in water that is free of living organisms.
Secondly, having embraced and rubbed the shank with the left hand,
one should again perform the rite with the right hand (apasavya) and wash the hands with earth.
Then, using exactly seven pure and clean vessels previously prepared,
one should place the food— purified by mantras and kept spotless— into a clean and stainless vessel.
Having taken excellent cow dung from a tawny cow renowned for its excellence,
one should prepare a circular maṇḍala for the Teacher in water that is free of living organisms.
First, one should especially construct a [stūpa] one cubit in height for the Best of Sages;
second, for the Lord of the Excellent Mantras; and third, for the Family Deity.
Furthermore, whenever the mantra-reciter performs that [practice],
it is proclaimed as the fourth [offering], which is for the enjoyment of all sentient beings.
To the right of the mandala of the Lord of the World, one should always construct here for the Triple Gem a square mandala.
The second belongs to the Pratyekabuddhas, and the third to the sons of those who possess the ten powers;
thus these seven mandalas are square on all sides.
Day by day, the reciter of mantras should perform this in a secluded place for a span of one cubit or half a cubit; thus, every day, it shall destroy all evil.
Then, having risen, the mantra-practitioner should again diligently wash his hands and perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) in water that is clean, pure, and free from living organisms.
In a clean and pure vessel,
carefully brought from a great lake, a spring, a pond, or the flowing current of a river;
Having approached a pure place and having taken [the earth] with the hands of a pure being,
the mantra-practitioner should always perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya) two or three times.
Then he should touch his face, as well as his ears,
his eyes, his nostrils, and his arms.
One should touch the head and the region of the navel with auspicious water;
one should perform this five or seven times, doing everything according to the prescribed rule.
Endowed with purity of conduct and having become clean, the reciter should take his alms-bowl and go to a body of water.
Wherever water is established, whether in a low-lying place or at a source,
one should always wash the alms-food from rivers, springs, and the like.
Then, having risen, he should go again to the monastery or the dwelling where he previously resided;
he should enter that very place over which he has mastery.
Having gone to that place, the reciter should set down the vessel;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśya), he should quickly take up the vessel once again.
One should offer the gift for the Teacher in a vessel made of clay, leaf, silver, gold, copper, or even bark.
The King of Mantras should again offer the food-oblation to the Teacher with his own mantra;
having approached on a single lunar day, he should give according to his ability even to those who are suffering.
One should not offer an excessive amount of the oblation in any respect;
the knower of mantras should act with skillful means in every way and never act to his own detriment.
He always gave the measure to be established as being only the size of his belly;
for one afflicted by hunger and thirst is not capable of accomplishing the purpose of the mantra.
Neither one who eats excessively nor one who eats too little is capable of following the mantras;
for this very reason, it was said by the Lord of Jinas for all embodied beings.
Food is the sustenance of sentient beings, by which humans live,
as well as gods, asuras, gandharvas, nāgas, yakṣas, and kinnaras.
Neither Rākṣasas, Pretas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, Ustārakas, nor the planets—
none of these exist who can look upon one who is intent on the vessel [of the Dharma].
The Tathāgata has declared that coarse food consists of morsels and mouthfuls, while there are indeed sentient beings who subsist on subtle nourishment.
The divine beings of the form realm subsist on meditation and engage in activities characteristic of that realm;
the gods of the formless realm, indeed, enjoy the fruit of meditative concentration.
Beings in the intermediate state are proclaimed to subsist on the food of intention;
likewise, beings in the desire realm consume various kinds of material food.
The gods and asuras are desirous of sensual pleasures and subsist on food consisting of morsels;
for this very reason, it has been taught by the Lords of Jinas through the causes of the Dharma.
It is proclaimed that food is the sustenance for all sentient beings;
however, for one who is constantly disciplined in recitation, the act of eating should be done with moderation alone.
For one who is established in this diet is able to practice the mantras;
being pure in conduct, he is skilled in the life of a celibate student.
And for one who knows the proper measure in eating, success is not difficult to attain,
just as a cartman easily lubricates his cart with axle-oil.
Just as [oxen] are given fodder for the sake of their endurance so that they may carry a burden for a long time,
even so the counselor who knows mantras gave him food for the sake of his stability.
The reciter should always nourish his body for the sake of its maintenance and for the sake of its non-decay,
in order to accomplish the mantras and as a cause for the equipment of enlightenment.
Likewise, one should recite the mantra in the world of mortals for the sake of benefiting the worlds;
for this very reason, the most excellent sage of great splendor spoke thus.
In the past, on this earth, one named Kāśyapa always recited this mantra for the sake of the welfare of all beings.
It was spoken for the sake of all those in the world who suffer, who are wretched and exhausted by poverty, who are weary from toil, and who are afflicted.
For the welfare of beings who have come into this cycle of existence,
one should recite this supreme mantra for the sake of providing sustenance to those beings.
"Listen, all you disciples and those who rely upon the Bodhisattvas;
receive this word of mine, this mantra that destroys disease."
But those beings who are afflicted by the disease of hunger, and those who are thirsty—
listen, you who desire the stages, for the sake of pacifying all suffering!
Having spoken thus, that Kāśyapa of great splendor, who resembled a sage,
with his disciples’ minds filled with joy, entreated that Lord.
Speak the mantra, O Knower of Dharma, King of Dharma, Great Sage!
Compassionate toward sentient beings, you are supreme; the moment has now arrived.
Having spoken thus, the foremost among the sages should recite the mantra in detail—
a sound like the warbling of the kalaviṅka bird, with a resonance like a drum or a thundercloud.
The Conqueror has a voice like Brahmā, possesses great heroism, and is indeed the foremost of the Brahmas;
let all the hosts of beings who have gathered here listen!
Whether they be footless, many-footed, two-footed, or four-footed— in brief, for the sake of all sentient beings, I shall proclaim this mantra that brings about happiness.
Sentient beings of the past and future, and those of the present who have come here—I shall speak of them in brief; listen, you who desire the truth.
Thus it is said.

Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded! It is as follows: Oṃ, in the sky, O Sky-Treasury, bring everything here quickly, quickly! Remember your vow! O summoner, do not delay! Accomplish for me whatever is desired! Svāhā!
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One Kāśyapa became silent.

In that interval, by the Blessed One Kāśyapa, the perfectly enlightened one, the words of the knowledge-mantras were recited in full detail, and the entire sky was seen filled with clouds of most precious food.
The entire great trichiliocosm was seen with the surface of the sky completely covered by clouds of food.
To whatever being desired food according to their disposition, whatever nourishment they wished for, that very thing was provided for them.

And for the purpose of allaying the suffering of hunger, he performed the act of eating with whatever foods were desired; and for the thirsty, there fell right there a stream of water endowed with the eight qualities, exactly as they wished.
And at that time, at that very moment, for all sentient beings, there was the pacification of all hunger and disease and the removal of all thirst.

And that entire assembly, having attained wonder and joy, having delighted in and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and vanished right there.
Both the Blessed One Kāśyapa and the Tathāgata Śākyamuni dwelt in the dwellings of the Tathāgatas; thus it has been spoken and approved by me, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, even now.

In this supreme king of rituals, for the benefit of all sentient beings and for the purpose of removing hunger and thirst—especially for those who recite mantras—the practitioner must first accomplish this mantra.
If one is unable to go out for alms, one should ascend a mountain peak and recite it six hundred thousand times, subsisting on the three white foods or consuming only milk.

Then, at that very same mountain peak, having installed the medium-sized cloth painting (*paṭa*) of Noble Mañjuśrī and having performed a great worship as before, one should present a most magnificent *bali* offering.

Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood fuel-sticks using this very mantra spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One Kāśyapa, one should offer eight thousand oblations of fresh *udumbara* fuel-sticks—measuring a span (*vitasti*) and smeared with curds, honey, and ghee—or alternatively, *bilva* fruit fuel-sticks.
Then, at the time of midnight, a great circle of black clouds and wind will arrive;
one must not be afraid,
nor should one rise and depart.
One should perform self-protection with the eight-syllable heart mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, as well as the binding of the maṇḍala for one's companions, as previously described.
Then that black whirlwind of wind vanishes.
And all the women, adorned with every ornament, garlanded with light, and illuminating the quarters, appear before the practitioner.
"Arise, O Mahāsattva! I have attained success. Having said this, she departs. The practitioner should offer an *argha* oblation with scented water mixed with *jātī* flowers.
Then she vanishes right there;
on that very day, she provides for herself and her twenty-five companions food at will according to their desires,
and she supplies whatever requisites they wish for.

Then the practitioner, having dismissed [the deity] and offered the *argha* water, should circumambulate the cloth painting three times, take up the cloth, and, having prostrated to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, proceed to a place suitable for practice as desired—one previously specified such as a great forest, a mountain peak, or a desolate place devoid of humans.
In that place, one should dwell having constructed a shelter with companions.
While residing in that location, one should perform such rites as traveling through the sky.

Then, the practitioner, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass as before, having installed the central cloth painting, and having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood as previously described, should offer eight thousand oblations of white flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one days.
Then, at the time of midnight, at the conclusion of the fire offering, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī face to face.
He grants the desired boon:

whether it be the power of traveling through the sky, invisibility, the stage of a bodhisattva, the state of a pratyekabuddha, or the state of a śrāvaka; or the possession of the five superknowledges, long life, great sovereignty and great wealth, or being beloved by kings.
While practicing the mantra together with the noble Mañjuśrī, he grants everything that is desired in brief;
whatever one asks for, he bestows that upon them,
or they obtain all the substances required for spiritual accomplishment (*siddhi*).
It effects the summoning of great beings;
in brief, it performs everything exactly as it is commanded.
Furthermore, it purifies past karma or transgressions—so said the Blessed One, Śākyamuni.
There is also another middling sādhana suitable for ritual action.

First of all, in a distinguished place, a pure location, or on the sandy bank of a river, having performed everything as before, one should install the cloth painting facing west and sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass facing east. The details should be carried out extensively as described.
One should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times during the three junctions of the day.
And upon the completion of the recitation, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *karṇikāra* flowers mixed with white sandalwood or saffron.

As before, having likewise kindled the fire and at the conclusion of the *homa* offering: if the cloth (*paṭa*) trembles, one attains the status of a mantra-master; if it emits rays of light, one attains kingship; if the cloth is filled with a garland of flames on all sides, one attains the kingship of the Caturmahārājakāyika gods; if speech issues forth from the cloth, one attains the three-fold sovereignty of the Tridaśa gods, namely the state of Śakra; if the cloth issues forth a teaching of the Dharma, one attains the sovereignty over the three stages of a Bodhisattva; and by touching the arms or the head of the cloth, one attains the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), the realization of the seven stages, and the certain, gradual attainment of the ten powers (*daśabala*).

Then, when the practitioner has accomplished the mantra spoken by the Blessed One Kāśyapa and has attained the means for warding off hunger and thirst, he should practice the dharma conducive to accomplishing the purpose of the mantra-observance according to that very same procedure and with those very same requisites;
success is not achieved otherwise.
In this way, following the gradual practice of mantra-conduct according to the rules must be performed; it will certainly succeed.
This applies to substances, implements, medicinal herbs, and all other precious gems as previously described.
In that place, the mantra-knower who recites the mantra, his mind focused on the prescribed ritual,
should then eat white rice grown from pure seeds.
Having eaten with a satisfied mind and always with well-nourished faculties,
one should secretly take that remainder of the alms-bowl and go to a river of pure water.
Having set it aside in a secluded spot, the observer of the vow gave it to the animals;
and having given it to the animals, he diligently washed the bowl.
Furthermore, one should carefully subject an earthen vessel to firing; as for the remaining vessels, they should be made free of grease and devoid of meat.
Having abandoned even the scent [of food], the best of sages should leave the remainder in his bowl;
in whichever bowl he wanders for alms, he does not eat from that very bowl.
One should never eat solid foods there; however, one may always consume fruits.
One should not eat from a lotus leaf, nor from leaves produced by the *kuvalaya* water-lily.
The mantra-practitioner should avoid fragrant flowers; he does not consume those that grow in autumn, nor leaves originating from the *plakṣa* or *udumbara* trees.
Nor with banyan leaves, nor with the leaves of the karṇaśāka or the gulmin plants, nor with mango leaves, nor likewise with those produced from the palāśa tree.
With śāla leaves and śirīṣa flowers grown from the Bodhi tree,
where that Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, sat.
One should avoid that tree with great effort, nor should one even dig up its wood;
one should not strip off the leaves from *nāgakesara* trees.
Nor does he ever eat at any time; all such things are avoided by the wise.
Nor, out of delusion, should one ever step over the leaf-huts of the sages.
The mantra practitioner falls from his commitment by eating from those leaves;
the practitioner should not eat his meal there with any other leaves.
One should always take up food in vessels made of clay, those specified as being of copper, likewise of silver, of gold, of crystal, or of stone.
He did not eat from the backs of leaves, nor likewise from the palms of his hands—
those leaves that had been offered to the Son of the Ten-Powered One, the Enemy of Māra.
The practitioner of recitation should avoid the leaves of those who are Pratyekabuddhas (Khaḍgins) as well as Śrāvaka individuals, and he should not step over them with his feet.
The mantra-practitioner should carefully refrain from taking various kinds of cakes, as well as drinks and food, even if all of it has been offered.

The practitioner of recitation should always avoid that which has been offered to the Jinas, to those who follow the conduct of the Jinas, as well as to the individuals who are Śrāvakas, and even to the Three Jewels.
Even the slightest [mantra] does not succeed for embodied beings who disregard him; how much less so the divine mantra which brings about the highest good and is esteemed as all-auspicious?
The rites for nourishment and pacification, which fulfill all desires—
these rites for nourishment and pacification that fulfill all desires will not succeed for one who eats the offerings presented there.
The mantras of one who is pure, skillful in character, compassionate, and likewise righteous— indeed, of one who delights in clean conduct— succeed everywhere.
Having first given food to all there, the reciter should not eat;
he should not consume any other food, but should eat only that which has been offered by others.
One who knows the mantra and proceeds with even a very small amount of food that has been given by oneself will have success resting in the palm of his hand.
By this procedure, the practitioner who maintains the vow and performs recitation should take his food;
for it is praised by the sages as the method seen in the rules for all ritual acts involving food within the practice of all mantras.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the mantra for the purification of all things. Having performed the ritual rinsing (*upaspṛśya*), the reciter should always recite this mantra;
then, having recited it seven times, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) effects the purification of the body.
Listen to the detailed explanation of its meaning, O assembly of beings and deities:
having touched the entire body, the Sage spoke this mantra.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!

It is as follows: *Oṃ sarvakilbiṣanāśani nāśaya nāśaya sarvaduṣṭaprayuktāṃ samayamanusmara hūṃ jaḥ svāhā*. With this mantra, whatever food a monk eats—whether it be rice or something else—he should consume it after having consecrated it with the mantra. Having eaten and sipped water for purification, he should rub his entire body starting from the head as before, and then rest.
Having rested for a moment, or for half or even a quarter of a watch (*yāma*), one should then pay homage to the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and recite the books of the True Dharma of all the Buddhas:
the *Ārya-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Ārya-candrapradīpa-samādhi*, the *Ārya-daśabhūmika*, the *Ārya-suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, the *Ārya-mahāmāyūrī*, and the *Ārya-ratnaketu-dhāraṇī*.
One should recite any one of these while maintaining the posture of a palm tree with a height equal to a yoke’s length.

Then, having dedicated [the merit] and recited [the text] according to one's ability, one should set aside the book, or cover it with clean cloth, and pay homage to the True Dharma. Thereafter, having gone to a riverbank or a great lake to bathe, one should take earth free of living organisms, consecrate it seven times with mantras, and sprinkle water with this mantra.
Which one? *Namaḥ samantabuddhānāmapratihataśāsanānām* (Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded).

It is as follows: *Oṃ, paralyze all malevolent ones, hūṃ! O you who hold the blue lotus, you who assume the form of a sporting youth, bind, bind! Remember the pledge! Sphaṭ, sphaṭ, svāhā!* Having performed protection with this mantra, as well as the binding of the directions, the binding of the circle for one’s companions, the binding of the mouth, the summoning of all the wicked and malicious, and the binding of the semen, one may wander everywhere with a thread over which the mantra has been recited seven times tied around the waist.
At all times during recitation and at all times for bathing, one should recite this mantra one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*) for the purpose of destroying and pacifying evil obstacles.
Thereafter, one accomplishes all rites.
One should employ the great mudrā of Pañcaśikha in all rites.
It accomplishes everything; it does not become otherwise.
Then the practitioner, having taken clay, cow dung, powder, and so forth, should bathe as he pleases.
He should bathe with water that is free of living organisms;
indeed, in all rites and in every respect, he should act only with water that is free of living organisms.
Then, having bathed with applications of clay, cow dung, or other various fragrant substances, he should not discharge phlegm, urine, excrement, or the like into the water,

nor should he discharge a stream of spit into the water. Nor should he play about, but rather, feeling compassion for all sentient beings and reflecting upon himself, he should regard them as being overwhelmed by sensations obstructed by suffering, empty, and selfless— like a being distressed by the pain of separation from a mother.

Thus, one who knows the mantra but lacks the means of accomplishment should behold himself situated in the depths of the ocean of saṃsāra, obstructed by such painful conditions as being struck, falling, scattered, and destroyed. Seeing himself without a home, without a mantra, and without refuge, yet with an undepressed mind, he should meditate—
standing in water reaching up to his neck or standing in water reaching up to his navel— establishing one-pointedness of mind right there in the midst of the water.

First of all, one should meditate upon a great lotus stalk, endowed with great lotus flowers, adorned with great lotus petals, beautiful to behold, composed of jewels, with a calyx made of beryl, emerald leaves, and filaments of ruby, with a thousand petals of crystal, fully blossomed, and further adorned with flowers of *jāta*-crystal and rubies. Upon it is a lion throne made of jewels, embellished with many gems, covered with a pair of fine cloths. Seated there, one should meditate on the Blessed Buddha as he teaches the Dharma—pure as gold, garlanded with flames on all sides, adorned with a circle of light, of vast proportions as if scraping the very sky, seated in the full-lotus posture.

And to the right is the noble Mañjuśrī, endowed with all the finest ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne, standing and not sitting, holding a chowrie for the Blessed One; his body is reddish-white or the color of ground saffron. And to the left is the noble Avalokiteśvara, white as the stalk of an autumn reed, with a chowrie held in his hand.

Thus, one should meditate on eight bodhisattvas: Ārya Maitreya, Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Apāyajaha, Ārya Vajrapāṇi, and Sudhana—these ten bodhisattvas [along with the two previously mentioned] on the right side. One should also meditate on eight pratyekabuddhas: Candana, Gandhamādana, Ketu, Suketu, Sitaketu, Ṛṣṭa, Upāriṣṭa, and Nemi. Furthermore, the eight great śrāvakas are in that very same place.
Namely: the noble Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Gavāmpati, Piṇḍola Bharadvāja, Pilindavatsa, the noble Rāhula, Mahākāśyapa, and the noble Ānanda.
One should meditate upon an infinite saṅgha of monks in the presence of these great śrāvakas;
one should meditate upon an infinite number of pratyekabuddhas in the presence of the pratyekabuddhas.
One should meditate upon an infinite assembly of great Bodhisattvas in the eight locations.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the surface of the sky thus adorned, endowed with a great mandala of the assembly.

And oneself, standing in water reaching to the navel, should perform worship to the Blessed One with various kinds of flowers—divine and human—such as *māndārava*, *mahāmāndārava*, *padma*, *mahāpadma*, *dhātu*, *kārika*, and *indīvara* blossoms; with various kinds of large-sized flower-baskets piled high.

One should perform a delightful worship for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas with powders, parasols, banners, and flags, as well as with abundant divine and human offerings, including hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of lamps.
In this manner, all offerings and requisites for worship—such as bali-offerings, incense, and food offerings—whether divine or human, should be presented.

Furthermore, one should meditate upon oneself being illuminated by a ray of light issuing from the *ūrṇā* (the hair-treasure) of the Blessed One Śākyamuni. For the practitioner who recites the mantra immediately upon entering such meditation, there is the attainment of the fruit of Brahma-merit; he will certainly become destined for enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Thus have these meditations been described by the preeminent ones in the world for the sake of the welfare and benefit of all beings and of practitioners of mantra.
Then, for the benefit of all mantra-practitioners, the foremost and most excellent sage, the best of beings, spoke this primary meditation to all sentient beings.
The first was spoken by the Sage concerning the mandala-shape and that aversion;
the second is the mandala, and the third is the doctrine of mantra beyond that.
In the first [case], there is the supreme accomplishment; in the middle, likewise the superior;
and in the lowest, the inferior accomplishment—thus declared the bull among sages.
Likewise, the banner-like meditation is categorized as superior, middling, and inferior;
in brief, that meditation is the destroyer of all defilements.
Beyond this, the wise should not resort to any other form of meditation;
for his mantras, being well-established in this meditation, truly attain accomplishment.
Having meditated upon the meditation as described according to the ritual according to one's desire,
the reciter should indeed dismiss the mantra there, having offered the *argha* offering as he pleases.
Having crossed that flood of water, one should then proceed at ease to the previously specified place, which is prescribed by rule and well-restrained.
Then the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra according to the previously described ritual;
having dismissed the mantra there, the invited deities should also be dismissed.
Then, having likewise performed the protection of his companions,
he— being skilled, knowing the true principles of ritual action, and devoted to the performance of rites— is considered fit.
Having praised the Supreme Person with various offerings of hymns,
as well as his own mantra, the Lord of Mantras, the Śrāvakas, and the Pratyekabuddhas who possess the rhinoceros-like horn, [one should proceed].
Then, rising again from that seat, those mantra-reciters [beheld] the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, who are capable of bestowing grace upon the three worlds.
Having gone far from his dwelling to a place sheltered from the wind,
he should discharge phlegm, snot, urine, and excrement.
During the day one should face north, and at night one should face south;
the reciter of mantras should never contemplate worldly matters while in that state.
One should not recite there a mantra spoken by one's own family for their specific rites;
rather, having sat upon the ground, one should do so when it is auspicious according to the signs of the [proper] course and other such indicators.
Having sipped water that is pure and filtered through the hem of a clean garment,
one should wash both feet with seven applications of clay up to the knees.
One should perform seven [hand-washings] after urination;
thirty when discharging feces; two at both ends of the hand;
and likewise two for spitting and for nasal mucus.
Then, having touched water, they went from afar toward their dwellings on the ground; having reached there, they made a mere sound, as if traveling along a road by means of arrows.
Beyond that, one may go as far as one desires toward the southern direction outside [the city],
even to places such as chasms, fields, arid wastes, and likewise those strewn with sand.

Except for a river, one should avoid the far bank of any water body that is impure due to refuse heaps or filth; rather, one should dwell confidently in a secluded spot at the edge, free from people and free from flavors.
At that time, however, the physician should perform the evacuation of the impurities;
the mantra-reciter, knowing the proper time, should practice the retention of the urges.
Then, having gone to a pure region as desired, according to the rules,
one should construct a hut or a spring in that place at one's ease.
Whether at dawn, in a secluded place, a covered spot, or on the ground,
one who is silent and free from attachment should always perform urination.
Once the urine and feces have been eliminated, the observer of the vow should always perform purification using clay that is soft, pleasant to the touch, well-ground, and free from living organisms.
Having taken three [handfuls] and likewise one, he should always place them at the anus, at both ends, and likewise on the hands;
first, however, as previously instructed by the Mantrin, he should always do so upon the ground.
Having diligently washed his feet, and then specifically the right one,
the practitioner of *japa* should always keep his two feet joined together with one another.
The detailed purification for those who recite mantras was explained previously;
however, the purification consisting of being free from odor and stains was taught by the pure ones of old.
Thus has purity for those who follow the mantras been briefly explained.
Purity through the removal of odor and stains ensures that one is always pure;
this is seen in all these tantras, so said the Lord of Sages.
Having performed the ritual ablution, the ascetic practitioner, devoted to the rites of accomplishment,
should recite [the mantra] according to the previously explained procedure with a mind that is inwardly pure.
Purity is declared to be fivefold for practitioners in all tantras: physical purity, as well as purity through mantra, purity through meditation,
the fourth is purity through truth, and water is said to be the fifth.
Those who possess the true Dharma, have conquered anger, know the tantras, perceive the treatises,
are skilled in the meaning of subtle reality, know the mantras, and are proficient in ritual actions.
For those who are skilled in the causes and in internal [knowledge], accomplishment is not difficult to attain among them;
one should not speak of false worship that is devoid of truth and the Dharma.
Cruel and even more cruel, devoid of all truth,
inciting hatred, full of wrath, harsh, and piercing the vital points.
But she who is devoid of truth and dharma, who oppresses other beings,
who is malicious, whose mind is afflicted, and who has abandoned all dharmas—

One who constantly practices violence, one of immoral conduct, and even one who practices dharma— such a person should always be avoided by a practitioner of mantra-recitation, as should one who engages in vulgar sexual practices.
False speech and anger are indeed censured by one who is extremely fearful of the next world,
as well as by all the Buddhas and the wise Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, in this world, those who desire success and seek their aims on earth must always avoid false speech, both as Pratyekabuddhas and as Śrāvakas.
The speaker of false speech goes to the most terrible hells;
furthermore, he is always reborn among animals, as well as among the hungry ghosts and in the world of Yama.
The evil-minded one who lives by falsehood dwells eternally right there in the terrible and scorching Tapana hell, and in the blazing Kālasūtra.
A living being who speaks falsehood shall dwell for many eons in Sañjīva, in Asipatra, and likewise in the Śālmalī forest.
How indeed could the mantras be accomplished for one who speaks falsely?
Deluded by false speech, he causes living beings to tremble;
therefore, that person of deluded action does not perceive the accomplishment of the mantra.
And thus, for one who speaks such words, there is no accomplishment for practitioners of mantra;
how could there be accomplishment for him even in many millions of kalpas?
He who rejects the teaching of the Buddhas upon this earth will,
because of that, fall into a terrible state of great fear characterized by ignorance.
In the Sañjīva, Kālasūtra, and Pratāpana hells,
he shall dwell for a great eon (mahākalpa) because of his destruction of my True Dharma (saddharma).
Foolish people, having despised the true Dharma and being shrouded in blind darkness, are cooked in the most terrible hell.
Out of ignorance, or due to childishness, fools who possess false pride fall into a terrible hell if they indeed despise the King of Vidyās.
Therefore, one should not commit evil, nor engage in contemptible and false actions;
for indeed, the disparagement of the true Dharma and false views are both censurable.
Therefore, always being faithful and constantly practicing the ritual procedures of the mantra,
speaking the truth, knowing the mantras, and always intent on the welfare of sentient beings—
the knower of mantras should devote himself to the mantra; for him, success is indeed certain.
One performs various actions—superior, inferior, and middling—for it is action that accomplishes the task, not inaction; indeed, action is always beneficial.
For one who is joined with action and its performance, success shall always be theirs.

Because it contains all meanings for the sake of action, action is always meaningful; both that which is not for the sake of action and that which is for the sake of action are appropriately termed "action" and "object. Perform always that action which is fruitful and indeed constitutes true action.

In this way, that which is to be done, the action, and the fruit— this triad of "that which is to be done, the action, and the fruit"— are always such that the fruitless attains fruition, and the fruit itself becomes eternally fruitful.

Both fruitless and fruitful, all indeed arise from fruit; through conjunction the mantra is accomplished, for conjunction is the means of accomplishing the mantra. Disjunction is the absence of conjunction, yet disjunction is the means of accomplishing conjunction.
But the relationship of the probandum and the probans is not established among them;
for substances that are already established are everywhere contradictory causes of establishment.
For those who have mastered the mantras, the mantras—which are the means of accomplishment—are not [previously] established.
That which the agent most desires to reach is the *karman*; it arises from the action of one desiring to perform that *karman*.
One should not perform non-action among all actions, for there are causes for action;
one who is joined with the meaning of mantra and tantra should undertake every rite.
One should undertake the action that has been begun, and likewise not undertake what is not an action;
for those who do not undertake the performance [of action], the mantras do not succeed for any embodied beings.
In the past, this was sung by the most excellent sages who proclaim all the true Dharma;
it reveals the commitment of the sons of the Conquerors regarding the practice of mantra.
The practitioner, who knows all mantras, [should follow] the other path taught here in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja) in the form of mantras as the cause for awakening.
All my mantras are accomplished where there is always proper application;
he shall attain his desired success in a very short time.
For the welfare of all beings, the Fully Awakened Ones have proclaimed [this] by means of their manifested forms for those who are destined for the city of Nirvana.
Likewise, the path to awakening is eternal, fulfilling all actions and purposes;
Buddhahood is the primary state, its ultimate consummation and final resort.
In this state of effortlessness, one shall attain accomplishment here with its fruits;
for those who know the various karmas and dharmas, there shall be the performance of mantras.
This attainment of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and liberation has been briefly described by the foremost of the Victors as the means for accomplishing all goals.
One shall obtain abundant wealth and the basis for the highest state;
likewise, O Lord of Yakṣas, one shall always [attain] even the lowest [state] through the cause of kingship.
All practitioners of mantra shall attain sovereignty over the worlds of humans, gods, and asuras;
likewise, he brings their activities to fruition.
Endowed with purity and proper conduct, always delighting in ethical discipline and meditative concentration,
the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra spoken among all mantras.
He performs various deeds— superior, middling, and even inferior— accordingly,
as he desires the prosperity of his ministers.
For the reciter, there is an increase in enjoyments in the lowest case, and for embodied beings in the middle case;
however, by means of the highest [practice], one attains the most excellent [result].
At the conclusion of the recitation, the mantra-practitioner should rest for as long as he deems necessary;
there, at the appropriate time, the reciter should perform the sādhana.

All rites are accomplished; nevertheless, in that regard, the practitioner of mantras who constantly recites [the mantra] performs the ritual action according to the prescribed rules, and through the destruction of the sins of men, whatever is done is effective throughout the succession of actions.
Success remains for that person until it attains full perfection;
therefore, the reciter of the mantra should again recite the mantra for the sake of destroying evil and, consequently, for the destruction of karma.
May the mantras be successful—those that are supreme, as well as those that are middling or inferior, and those honored by the world;
through their recitation, they destroy without remainder whatever evil has been committed throughout a succession of births.

Thus, the sins of all embodied beings are destroyed; he creates a beautiful woman adorned with various ornaments on her limbs, endowed with all excellent qualities, who dwells constantly as a queen among the Yakṣas. By reciting the mantra of the Tathāgatas, they attain the accomplishment of all aims.

Thus concludes the fourth chapter, the detailed exposition on the procedures for all rites, including the methods of accomplishment, the stations of ritual action, the rules for recitation, fire offerings, meditation, purification, and conduct, from the eleventh section of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī, to [the teaching] for those followers of your vidyā-mantras—those beings who are engaged in the welfare of all sentient beings."

Listen well and attend thoroughly to that method of the rosary (*akṣasūtra*) by which mantras are recited, or by which they are caused to be recited— the method common to all tantras and applicable as a means for accomplishing all mantras. I shall speak.
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"Excellent, Blessed One! Please speak for our sake, out of compassion for us, for the benefit of those beings who have entered the observance of all mantra practices, and for the benefit of all sentient beings.
When Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta had spoken thus, the Blessed One said this to him.

Listen, Mañjuśrī, I shall speak in full detail that by which beings engaged in all mantra practices accomplish all their aims. And what is that? First of all, there is the mantra: [Oṃ] namo ratnatrayāya | namaḥ āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya | tadyathā | oṃ maṇi-padme hūṃ | svāhā || This, Mañjuśrī, is the mantra that accomplishes all purposes for those who apply themselves to the practice of mantras. It is the king of mantras, the supreme among mantras, the great destroyer of all obstacles, the fulfiller of all desires, and the bestower of all success. One should recite it one hundred thousand times at the beginning; thereafter, it will grant all accomplishments. Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, the practitioner should first purify his body, speech, and mind. He should dwell in solitude, free from distraction, and maintain a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings. Having prepared a clean altar, adorned with various flowers and incense, he should visualize the noble Avalokiteśvara before him, seated upon a lotus throne, radiant with a thousand arms and eyes, holding a lotus, a jewel, a sword, and other implements. With a mind focused on the deity, he should recite the mantra until he perceives signs such as visions, sounds, or dreams. Once these signs have appeared, he may perform the rites for pacifying, increasing, subjugating, or destroying, according to his purpose. Thus, through this mantra, all beings devoted to the conduct of mantras shall achieve every goal. This is the secret of the Tathāgatas, the treasury of the Bodhisattvas, and the source of all worldly and transcendent attainments. Listen well, and I shall explain its application in detail.
Homage to all Buddhas, whose forms are inconceivable and marvelous!
It is as follows: *Oṃ kuru kuru sarvārthān sādhaya sādhaya sarvaduṣṭavimohani gaganāvalambe viśodhaya svāhā*.
With this mantra, one should perform rites upon all rosaries.

One should perform the rites of purification, piercing, seizing, purging, and so forth, first upon the rosary beads, and then consecrate the tree with mantras thirty-seven times. Having performed the protection rite, the practitioner, observing his vow, should then sleep there for one night; and in that dream, he sees [the deity].
O son of Sumitrā, whatever non-human being appears before him— whether endowed with beauty, deformed, or long-standing— he should capture it and question it according to the facts.
Then, having risen early in the morning, that practitioner should go to that tree;
moreover, he may see a dream that is either deformed or extremely terrifying.
The mantra-practitioner should avoid that tree, or else go elsewhere;
first is the rudrākṣa, and after that, the indrākṣa.
One seeking a son, or desiring something else that arises from fruit,
should climb a tree well-endowed with climbing aids together with companions.
In the absence of companions, the reciter may ascend by himself,
standing upon the fruit located on the upper branches.
From that [tree], having emerged upon the upper branches,
one should take fruit from the upper branches and employ the upward-directed rite.
The supreme accomplishment is declared by the foremost of persons to be in the upper [state];
the middling accomplishment is in the middle, while the lowest is indeed in the inferior.

Having always taken up the fruit among them, which is freedom from aversion toward living beings, and having attained it upon the trees in the final age, the purposes of the ritual substances are accomplished.
In the north, one should bring together the deities belonging to the yakṣa lineage and others;
this rite known as "attraction" (ākarṣa) is for the purpose of pacifying all beings.
The gods, asuras, gandharvas, kinnaras,
and rākṣasas perform their duties well for the sake of nourishing the welfare of all beings.
It renders fruitful all actions performed upon the earth without exception;
those branches situated in the eastern direction that produce fruit [are likewise effective].
One should always apply effort toward those [places], for they are the causes for the sake of long life;
therein one performs various forms of practice where success is always attained through the fruits.
But that branch which goes toward the south, abounding in leaves and shoots,
the reciter of mantras should avoid it, because it is a taker of the life-force of sentient beings.
Those fruits which have grown high upon the branches extending toward the south should be recited over with the *akṣa* mantras; this destroys the sins of one's enemies.
The reciter should avoid those with effort, for they are causes for much merit;
however, those fruits which are proclaimed to be situated hanging from lower branches [should be avoided].
One should go to Rasātala with those [fruits] belonging to the women of the Dānavas;
indeed, a rosary made from those fruits is proclaimed to be "Gṛhītā."
Whichever lower abodes there may be, by that [mantra] one shall go to Pātāla;
having entered there, the practitioner of recitation indeed attains divine happiness.
If one remains attached to the female spirits of the asuras, he shall stay for an eon;
having grasped all the seeds of the *akṣa* fruit, the reciter should then descend from that state.
Having performed the protection ritual together with his companions, he should then proceed at his ease;
having gone to a distant place, he should always remain in a clean location.

The mantra-practitioner should remain there and purify the beads produced from the *akṣa* tree; taking hold of the *akṣa* fruits, he should be intent on them and thoroughly cleanse them in every respect.
Having purified [the eyes] in every way, one who possesses the mantra should pierce the eyes;
either three, seven, eight, or once—these amount to twenty-one times.
One who knows the mantras and the beings should always purify [the site] with the primary mantra;
when it has been recited seven or eight times, purification is then considered accomplished.
The practitioner observing the vow should prepare a wick using five triple-stranded threads spun by a maiden and made from lotus stalks.
One who knows the reality of mantras should wrap it with a thread that is fine, well-rounded, without holes, always free of insects, unblemished, and not contemptible.
One should likewise take a Rudrākṣa that is beautiful, of lovely color, without holes, and uncracked,
or one with a living seed, or even the fruit of the Indrākṣa.
The mantra-practitioner, as instructed, should always diligently string together a rosary that is auspicious, beautiful, ever-free from defects, and esteemed for its fruit.
It is prescribed that it may be made of gold or silver, or likewise of ruby, crystal,
high-quality conch-shell, or even pearl.
One should fashion various garlands for the rosary from coral;
likewise, one may fashion an auspicious rosary from other divine gems.
With focused concentration, one should string together round earthen beads upon a thread,
or other small beads made from fruits or derived from minerals.
One should diligently prepare a string of *kuśa* grass tips for the reciter who follows the instructions:
one hundred and eight, twenty-five, or fifty [knots] for the middling [recitation].
A mantra-practitioner, being composed, should string together this rosary;
he should make the "eldest" (jyeṣṭhikā) rosary consist of one thousand and eight beads.
This fourfold garland should always be strung by practitioners;
then indeed, the garland should be strung with either three or two *mātrās*.
One should briefly string the garland with bracelets made of flower-metal (puṣpaloha), or likewise with gold, silver, or even copper.
Then, having formed a noose at the end, one should place it in that sequence;
one should encircle it until the end of the three junctions so that it remains bound.
Then, having made the appearance of the mandala clearly manifest,
one should surround it with all enjoyments in their respective forms, fully adorned.
Having bathed in auspicious water or in a pure river, [one should wear] that which has the appearance of a pearl necklace and is fashioned in the form of a short neck-ornament.
Having bathed as before, he should emerge from the water;
then, having sipped water according to the rule, he should take up the domestic [fire] prepared with unhusked grains and thread.
Having washed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise with powdered earth,
and having washed it again in auspicious water with fragrant unguents;
Having carefully washed it with excellent pigments, white sandalwood, and saffron, one should then proceed from there to the sacrificial fire.
Having gone to the proper place where that middle-sized painting is located—
wherein is the best of Jinas, the foremost Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men.
Likewise, one should always [perform this] near the image of the Teacher, or near the excellent relic of the Jina on earth.
Having installed [the image] on that cloth and placed it before him,
one should recite [the mantra] one thousand eight hundred times, and one hundred and eight times in a single session.
Having fasted for a day and night and having previously performed the prescribed number of recitations, he offered the garland to that best of sages in accordance with the same ritual measure.
Then, having consecrated the rosary with recitation, the knower of mantras should deposit it right there at night and sleep on the ground upon a bed of *kuśa* grass in that very place.
If, in a dream, he sees a beautiful vision,
then the success indicated by that dream is ordained for him as fruitful.
If anything is seen in a dream by a Buddha, a Śrāvaka, or a Pratyekabuddha,
the practitioner of mantra will certainly achieve success, and his ritual performance will bear fruit.
If, having seen in a dream a child with the form of a youth, variegated and beautiful to behold, he likewise offers a garland,
then his mantras— accomplishers of all aims— will unfailingly succeed.

Thus ends the twelfth detailed chapter on the ritual for rosaries, from the *Madhyamapaṭavidhānavisara*, which is part of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed once again and yet again upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, there exists for you a specific procedure for the fire-ritual (*homakarma*) when a practitioner of the *vidyā* is engaged in it according to the general and particular rules set forth in your chapter on mantras; this [procedure] consists of the specific ritual for the service of the fire."
That wherein all beings engaged in the practice of all branches of knowledge abide;
and what is that?
It is the secret mantra-words of knowledge.
It is as follows: *Oṃ uttiṣṭha haripiṅgala raktākṣa dehi dāpaya hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ sarvavighnān vināśaya svāhā*.
This, Mañjuśrī, is the supreme heart-mantra of fire; it performs all rites and grants all desires.
First of all, the practitioner, having recited this Heart of Fire once, should offer three oblations of clarified butter into the fire;
thus the fire becomes summoned.
Now, for one who has not yet performed [the preliminary rites], there are three kinds of fuel-wood for the rites of pacification, enrichment, and ferocity.
For the purpose of pacification, aśoka wood that is moist is especially recommended;
it should be one span, one cubit, or three finger-breadths in height.
This procedure is prescribed for that which is glossy in appearance and praised;
it should be without hollows or cavities, and likewise resemble a parrot’s wing.
One should avoid wood that is green, white-colored, or black-colored;
one should also avoid that which has been eaten by worms, and instead select wood that is free from hollows.

One should employ wood that is of any color but excellent in quality, free from defects, and devoid of unrighteousness; it should not be too dry, nor too moist, nor should one begin with wood that is burnt.
One should avoid [wood] that is rotten, crooked, or excessively tall;
likewise, one should construct the fire-pit as being square on all four sides.
Then one should diligently dig downwards with a measurement of four cubits,
or three cubits, two cubits, or likewise even one cubit.
It should always be devoid of living beings and established in the form of a lion;
it is shaped like a lotus, and from that, the altar is circular in shape on all sides.
One should also carefully fashion it as a quadrangle, or likewise in the shape of a bow;
resembling the form of a thunderbolt, with two tips and three prongs.
One should construct this fire-pit, two cubits wide,
in a pure and well-swept place, such as an excellent riverbank.
And one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa), being well-exerted, in a solitary place, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, and likewise on a mountain peak.
Always in an empty temple, and likewise in a great forest—
those places for practice which have been described by the supreme persons.
These places have been described in every respect as the locations for the performance of the fire oblation (homa).
Then, having stood at a distance of one cubit, seated upon a bundle of kuśa grass;
In those places, the knower of mantras should especially perform the rite of fire-oblation (homa);
by means of these, accomplishment is swiftly attained in those very locations—of this there is no doubt.
Facing either east or north, the mantra-practitioner should perform rites for pacification and nourishment;
however, he should avoid performing those fierce rites toward the south.
Success in rites for pacification is attained when facing east, and likewise for rites of enrichment when facing north;
with these [directions], the practitioner of mantras should always begin the recitation of mantras.
One should perform rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika) using wood from the bilva, āmra, plakṣa, and nyagrodha trees;
for malevolent rites (ābhicāruka), one should use wood that is dry, bitter, sour, or pungent.
One should always avoid all those [types of wood] which have been forbidden by the sages;
for rites of pacification and enrichment, moist wood is recommended.
Likewise, such actions as those involving cruelty are always avoided by the sages;
in the absence of such [sacrificial] wood, one should instead prepare wood for them.
One should arrange it on all sides with *kuśa* grass spread out, with both ends pointing outward,
using blades that are green, glossy in appearance, and resembling the neck of a peacock.
One should always perform rites for pacification and nourishment with such *kuśa* grasses,
as well as with dried blades of grass that resemble the color of an emerald or the sky.
One should perform the rites of fire here, which have been prohibited by the Supreme Victors,
only in water that is stainless, pure, and always free from worms.
Then, having sprinkled water all around and performed a circumambulation,
one whose mind is disciplined should kindle the fire after touching water according to the prescribed rule.
With pure grass roots, one should fashion a torch according to its proper measure;
having made it about the size of a fist, one should then carefully ignite it with fire.
Nor should one ever [fan] with the breath of the mouth or with the edge of a garment; one should avoid using one's lower or upper robes for this purpose, nor any other clothing.
Nor should one fan it with the wind from the hands, nor with a fan made of peacock feathers, nor likewise with a clean cloth, nor even with leaves, while being intent on the practice.
When the fire has been kindled and the wind produced by these [means],
the one who knows the mantras and desires to perform the oblation (homa) should, being well-composed, cause it to blaze up.
Then, having sprinkled [water] three times while keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya),
one should indeed offer three oblations there in clarified butter made from cow's milk.
Then one should indeed perform prostration to all the Buddhas, the Protectors, and to one’s own mantra and the Lord of Mantras; thereafter, one should pay homage as desired.
Then, having recited the mantra within the heart of the fire, one whose self is united with the fire should always invoke it with fragrant flowers alone.
The wise knower of mantras should always summon [the deity] and provide a place;
having offered a seat and a location, one should do so with that specific mantra and no other.

For the purpose of worshipping the fire, one should offer three pieces of fuel wood soaked in curd, mixed with clarified butter, and anointed with honey, throughout the entire ritual action accompanied by mantras.
Then one should prepare both types [of oblations]: those mixed with fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and those mixed with substances;
likewise, those combined with clarified butter (*ājya*) and honey, as well as those mixed with curd (*dadhi*).

The practitioner of secret mantras should arrange one thousand, or a hundred thousand, or even one hundred and eight [offerings]; likewise, having recited the mantra once, he should cast them into the fire.

One should offer oblations into a fire with garlands of flames or likewise one with a single flame for rites of pacification (śāntika), and into one that is smokeless for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika).

If, while engaged in the ritual of fire-offerings within a smoke-filled fire that is fierce in its activity, censurable, yet praised by the Best of Victors, the color of the fire should appear as follows:
For pacification rites, a white color is always praised by the supreme Victors;
indeed, mantras are accomplished there for one who offers oblations into a white fire.
Likewise, a red color is always desired for the accomplishment of nourishment (pauṣṭika);
while black, smoke-colored, or even tawny colors are for the accomplishment of subjugation (pāyika).
Thus, this threefold accomplishment is set forth in three ways:
as having other colors, or cloud-like colors, or described in various forms.
Furthermore, there is no accomplishment of mantras upon this earth for those who possess such a complexion or are described as having various forms and colors.
But having seen the fire blazing, one should again commence the ritual;
if, after performing the recitation once more, the accomplishment of the mantra does not occur, [one should proceed as follows].
One should again perform the oblation according to the ritual procedure;
having performed the dismissal and the invocation, one should utter the mantra to the fire.
In this very mandala prepared as before,
one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the rules for the rites of dismissal and invocation.
One should perform all rites with that very [mantra] in that very rite;
one should likewise begin the fire-ritual (agnicaryā) in front of the cloth painting (paṭa).
Mantras indeed attain accomplishment there, as previously stated by the Tathāgatas;
one should perform the rites praised by the Victors there, and not [perform them] anywhere else at all.
One should not perform other actions, especially sinful ones,
which are censured by the supreme Victors and are contrary to what is esteemed by the world.
Arise! You shall become either a universal monarch, a bodhisattva, or a sovereign of the earth;
likewise, upon attaining this, you will achieve the five superknowledges or even the state of divinity.
On this cloth, one who is constantly disciplined and skilled in the rite of homa may attain lordship over the underworld or the power to move through the atmosphere.
One always attains the state of a terrestrial deity or a yakṣa in the summoning of yakṣīs,
whether in a kingdom, a lordship, a district, or even a village.
One attains the state of a Vidyādhara and an Asura, bringing all sentient beings under one's control,
and the power to summon spirits and great-souled Mahāsattvas.
By means of the rite of homa, one can summon even the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas who abide on the ten stages; how much more so a human being on this earth?
Likewise, he attains the command of an army, as well as sovereignty in the world especially,
the mastery over all beings, and even the status of a king.
For the purpose of bringing all beings or even a king under one's control on this earth,
one should likewise constantly perform all rites everywhere by means of fire-oblation (homa).
One whose self is entirely disciplined in every way should undertake all actions;
for him, action performed with constancy leads to the attainment of the highest welfare.
Furthermore, middling and even inferior rites are accomplished;
all substances therein are said to achieve success in three ways.
When the rite of fire-oblation (homa) has been undertaken, success is seen to be fruitful,
provided one forms the five-crested mudrā and recites the Keśinī mantra.
One who possesses the wisdom of self-protection should perform all ritual actions;
when engaged in the rite of *homa*, one should then recite this mantra.
In this rite, it should always be recited seven or eight times.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded.
It is as follows: *Oṃ jvala tiṣṭha hūṃ ru ru viśvasambhava sambhave svāhā*.
By means of this application of the mantra, one who knows the mantra should repeatedly recite it over a piece of wood and then offer it into the fire, having recited it twice or seven times.
Or with flowers, incense, and perfumes, or indeed with everything on all sides,
one should sprinkle [the area] with water over which this mantra has been recited.
Then one should undertake all ritual actions according to the prescribed method;
indeed, in all rites, they must be performed by means of the preliminary practice itself.
Having bound the glorious Great Seal (mahāmudrā) with the five locks of hair tied forward,
and having then established his protection, he should always be a reciter of the mantra of Keśinī.
Those who are confident should undertake all actions for the sake of success,
provided that auspicious omens are seen and sounds are always favorable.
His mantras are indeed fruitful in granting boons as desired;
when applied in the initial rites, they proceed by means of the mantra.
Complete success, both fruitful and total, is ordained for them;
there shall be the sound of the word "Victory! and the resonance of kettledrums and drums.
Success is indeed said to be everywhere for one who relies upon the rite of fire-offering (homa),
as well as when there are other excellent omens or the auspicious cries of birds.
The meanings of sounds consisting of various types of resonance have been praised by the Victors;
they are excellent, divine, auspicious, celestial, delightful, and manifold in their tones.
Parasols, banners, and flags, as well as adorned women,
a full water-pot, and likewise the sight of half-moons, are causes for success.
Alternatively, those who possess many excellent forms and colors, who are praiseworthy and honored by the world—
for them, the mantras of various domains are accomplished upon being seen.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Then follows the fourteenth chapter.
Now, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, there exists [this teaching] which is authorized for all mantras that serve as the means for accomplishing the secret vidyās of your own [family]; it is the master and the most senior of all mantras—both mundane and supramundane—which have issued from the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgatas, which have entered the cloud of Dharma, and whose nature is like space, just as a prince is among all beings."
In this regard, the Tathāgata is declared to be the most senior, the most excellent among gods and humans, a bull among men, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

For thus, O youth, this King of Vidyās among all mantras is declared to be the foremost, the most excellent, as previously designated by the Tathāgatas—those Blessed Buddhas whose merit is equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā and whose wisdom is inexpressible. It is the supreme heart-essence (*paramahṛdaya*) and supreme secret (*paramaguhya*) of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu; it is esteemed as the most auspicious of all, praised and extolled by all Buddhas, the source of consolation for all Buddha-beings, the destroyer of all sins, the granter of all desires, and the fulfiller of all hopes.
And what is that?
In that interval, from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, there issued forth a ray of light named "Exhorter of All Buddhas.

Having illuminated all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, above and below, and having gladdened the minds of all sentient beings, it vanished into the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Blessed One Śākyamuni above.

And from the uṣṇīṣa of the Blessed One, there issued forth the Vidyārāja named Ekākṣara, whose form was adorned with flames on all sides, who was unobservable by any sentient beings, invincible, arisen from great majestic power, his body adorned with a halo of light, possessing various forms and the form of a great universal monarch.

Having emerged, he illuminated the entire expanse of the sky; surrounded by all the kings of vidyās and preceded by many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of vidyās, he was honored by all the supramundane sovereigns of the vidyā-wheel and praised by all mantras. Being empowered by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—great beings who have attained the ten stages—he filled the entire vault of the sky. His body was adorned with great maṇi-jewels and embellished with divine gems; possessing a beautiful form and being exceedingly radiant, he emitted hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of emanations in various forms. Uttering the sound of the single syllable and releasing a great net of light rays, he stood in the atmosphere above the Blessed One Śākyamuni, looking directly at him, illuminating the entire realm of the Pure Abodes and the great assembly circle.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [taught] the single-syllable sovereign of knowledge (*vidyācakravartin*), the heart of all Tathāgatas, named Ratnaketu—the supreme heart and most profound secret of the Tathāgata Ratnaketu—which had been established by all the Blessed Tathāgatas: Sālendrarāja, Amitābha, Duḥprasaha, Sunetra, Suketu, Puṣpendra, Supināntalokamuni, Kanaka, and other Tathāgatas; which was spoken and rejoiced in by them, and uttered and approved by all the Perfectly Awakened Ones of the past.
And what is that?
It is as follows: *Bhrūṃ*.

This, Mañjuśrī, is the supreme heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas, the single-syllable great purifier known as the Vidyā-Cakravartin who possesses all virtues. When this is practiced, all mantras are accomplished.

O Youth, those who follow all the mantras in this supreme king of manuals of yours—the supreme secret, the foremost authorized one that purifies all karmic obscurations—must certainly accomplish their rites among all mantras. O Youth, within this king of your manuals, all mundane and supramundane mantra-tantras are to be accomplished. By means of this, one who has performed the protection becomes unassailable by all spirits and is not overcome by any obstacles, whether mundane or supramundane.
And when this was spoken by the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lord of Universal Jewels, the entire trichiliocosm shook in six ways;
all the Buddha-fields were illuminated, and all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, became assembled together.

In that assembly circle, all those seated in the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens—bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages and are irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, as well as all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and beings of great supernatural power—shall come, brought under control by the rays of light impelled by the King of Vidyās.

And many other beings, established in infinite and boundless world-systems and dwelling in the miserable states of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, being touched and illuminated by that great radiance of light, their sensations of suffering which had been fully awakened were stilled; with minds gladdened by happiness, they would certainly become established in the three vehicles.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that great circle of the assembly, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta: "Listen, Mañjuśrī, to this King of Vidyās, who possesses great supernatural power, the solitary hero, the performer of all rites, the universal sovereign of all vidyā-kings, the fulfiller of the hopes of all sentient beings. He has entered into the detailed ritual manuals of all *kalpas*, including your own mantra-tantra ritual manuals. He is the common ground for the practitioners of all mantras, a being of great authority and great energy, the means for purifying the path to all enlightenment through the skillful means and wisdom of the practitioner, and the sequence for establishing [beings] in nirvāṇa. He is skilled in the approach to the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and he constitutes the equipment for that approach. In brief, I shall explain his extensive ritual manual, the procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*), the mandala, and the methods for accomplishment, following the conduct of the former mantra-practices, wherein established beings shall accomplish the Great Universal Sovereign, the King of Vidyās, the great being, the supreme lord of all mantras, the light-maker, the fulfiller of all hopes, the leader, the benefactor of the entire world, the self-existent one present in person like a Buddha himself—the supreme, middling, and inferior performer of all rites."
He who leads to security, who is auspicious, peaceful, and the destroyer of all evils;
the god even among gods, the bull among sages among sages.
The Buddha is bound to the sun, pure, renowned throughout the world,
knowing the intrinsic nature of all actions, the stainless limit of reality;
I shall proclaim his supreme ritual manual— listen, you who desire prosperity!
First of all, one should paint upon a divine cloth that is free of hair, devoid of adhesions, new, white, and especially provided with fringes;
it should be two cubits in length and one cubit in width.
On such an auspicious, pure, and beautiful day,
when the moon is bright, white, and full, during a favorable lunar mansion, and free from the *pica* constellation;
On a white cloth that removes impurities, whether it be fine silk (*dukūlaka*),
raw cotton (*ātasya*), or even one made of bark fibers, provided it is pure and free from loose threads.
It should not be produced by worms or wind, nor should it cause harm to living beings;
likewise, it should not be made of silk, nor anything else that has been disparaged by the virtuous.
And upon such an excellent cloth, one should have a temple painted;
having depicted the image of the Teacher, adorned with a garland of light-maṇḍalas.
Then, having drawn him of golden hue, encircled by a garland of flames,
solitary, hidden in secret, situated upon a mountain, and made of great iron;
One should indeed construct a canopy of silk bound with garlands of jewels;
above it, one should depict the two deities as being supported.
Indeed, one should construct a garland of jewels upon the mountain,
and the canopy all around should be adorned with strings of pearls and half-strands of pearls.
Having carefully drawn everything above the king of mountains,
one should likewise draw below the mountain the great ocean that floods it.
And on the edge of the cloth, one should likewise draw flowers all around:
*nāgakesara*, *puṇṇāga*, *vakula*, and *yūthikā*.
The *mālatī* flower, as well as the *priyaṅgu*, the *kurabaka*, the blue lotus (*indīvara*), the *saugandhī*, and thereafter the white lotus (*puṇḍarīka*).
Various species of flowers as well as others that possess fragrance;
these indeed are the flowers.
And for the sake of worship, they should offer something pleasing to the Teacher upon the supreme cloth-painting,
according to the previously prescribed ritual.
The sūtra, the weaver, and likewise the painter are considered [to be the three requisites];
one should have it painted on the most pure day during the fortnight of miracles.
When the time for such engagement has arrived, and likewise during the recitation (jāpa),
everything that was previously taught for him should be performed in its entirety.
One should paint the universal form of the Teacher, radiant with color, richly adorned with various ornaments,
endowed with many aspects, and possessing a luster like that of the *karṇikāra* flower.
One should draw [the Buddha] with a radiance like that of the campaka flower, depicted in the color of gold;
