having thus drawn the Sage, who is endowed with these features and born from jewels.
One should paint that jewel of a Buddha, the highly fortunate Ratnaketu, the most excellent bull among sages, who has attained mastery over all phenomena.
Seated upon a mountain of jewels, adorned with jewel-caves, he sat cross-legged, imparting instructions on the Dharma.
Having drawn the hero with a slightly smiling face outside the cave, with his mind fixed in meditation, one should likewise draw him all around below.
The practitioner is seated at the corner of the edge of the cloth, with his knees covered in camphor,
his hands occupied with incense, and his body slightly bent forward.
One should arrange him wearing the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), according to his dress and characteristics,
beneath the Blessed One on the right, even below the surface of the great ocean.
One whose self is ever-disciplined and who seeks the highest good should have the mantra-master painted;
this procedure for the cloth-painting has been taught by those honored by the world.
Now the maṇḍala of that deity shall be explained;
at that time, the mantra-practitioner, skilled in mantras, should be properly equipped with the mantra.
Having always performed service to the mantra and practiced it for the sake of attaining mastery in recitation,
one is then consecrated into this mantra-ritual spoken by Mañjughoṣa.
One who is perfected in the conduct of the mandala and is constantly consecrated is himself consecrated for all mantras and is confident within this mandala.

The one of great splendor should always consider those who possess reason as beneficial for self-protection in the tantra; likewise, he should thoroughly examine his companions by means of those things that destroy obstacles.
The teacher is highly diligent toward those who have undertaken the practice of the vows;
he is possessed of great wisdom, ever affectionate, illustrious, and compassionate.
One should likewise indicate the characteristics of all the assistants:
one, two, three, or even eight, as well as others.
One should accept disciples who are well-endowed, and one should avoid those who are numerous;
furthermore, one should always perform the previously seen ritual procedures within this mandala.
Those maṇḍalas first described by the One Endowed with the Ten Powers belong to Mañjughoṣa; they are not for others, nor through other rites.
I shall now declare the measurement of the mandala of great splendor:
it may be four cubits, two cubits, or likewise eight cubits and beyond.
In a pure place, on the bank of a river, and especially on a mountain peak,
one should [draw the mandala] with five-colored powders according to the ritual previously observed.
It was square, with four gates, adorned with four archways,
having four corners, level, divine, and possessing a splendor equal to divine conduct.
One who has good companions should undertake [the work] that is brilliant with color, variegated, beautiful in hue, very lovely, fragrant, and well-formed.
Observing the vow of silence, practicing the eightfold observances, with an unafflicted mind, knowing the proper measure, righteous, and always engaged in recitation.
Having undertaken actions free from evil, performing rites for pacification and nourishment,
one should then enter into a state of neutrality and draw the forms of the Teacher with colored pigments.
First, all of that should be drawn: the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, of great splendor, seated in a cave and adorned with various jewels.
One should paint upon the cloth everything exactly as it is: [the Buddha] seated in the paryanka posture, turning the Wheel of Dharma, and worshipped by the śāstṛs.
One should decorate it with lines in three rows and also with mudrās,
covering every row on all sides.
One should place the Great Lord Cakravartin in their midst, both individually and collectively, without confusing his specific attributes.
Exerting effort, one should draw the one who follows the great wheel, who has the form of a youth, is radiant with light, and resembles the rising sun.
Having the appearance of a great king, adorned with a crown as an ornament,
wearing a diadem, the Great Being is decorated with every kind of finery.
He is wrapped in a beautiful half-silk cloth and wears a variegated silk garment;
he bears a garland, possesses a gentle complexion, and is adorned with flower wreaths and fine raiment.
Smelling the *vakula* garland with his right hand,
he beheld the Lord of great heroism and sovereign power, whose face was graced with a slight smile.
He is indeed of beautiful and lovely form, devoid of both children and the elderly;
he always holds a wheel in his left hand, wears a blazing garland, and is touching [the wheel].
One should paint that image, seated comfortably in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka) with one arm resting [on the knee],
possessing a divine complexion, beautiful in form, and endowed with exquisite beauty.
Seated upon this fragment of jewels, the Great Radiance, the Source of All Beings,
the Bestower of Boons, has always been engaged in the welfare of all mantras.
Blazing with the form of fire, beautified by a mandala,
and encircled by a garland of flames on all sides, it blazes forth when impelled by the wind.
Thus, by means of these mantra applications, human beings on earth are ignited;
such is that which possesses great heroism and accomplishes all mantras.
For whoever beholds it is a righteous soul who is liberated from all sins—
even one who has committed the five acts of immediate retribution, is of immoral conduct, or is dull-witted.
Indeed, all sins are pacified and one is liberated by the mere sight of the Lord;
merely by seeing the mandala of the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus.
At that very moment, one is liberated from those other sins that have been enumerated;
then, having purified the eastern gate with the mantra of the Lord himself.
Having completely encircled it with archways and adorned it all around with plantain trees,
one should fashion the mandala so that it is entirely radiant and beautiful in form.
One should respectfully perform the offering of bali, incense, lamps, and pure perfumes and garlands, according to the very same procedure as before.
One should place a full water-pot in the center, directly in front of the practitioner of the wheel-mantra; that pot is called Vijaya, and the knower of mantras must not move it.
Likewise, the fire-pit should first be prepared according to the rite prescribed by rule;
the commencement of the fire-offering (homa) must be performed with the *vibhu-mantra* and not with any other.
One should perform eight thousand oblations with a fire fueled by *khadira* wood,
as well as with *pālāśa*, *śrīkaṇṭha*, *bilva*, *udumbara*, and *akṣa* wood.
Likewise, one should diligently offer apāmārga in all rites,
or sesame seeds mixed with clarified butter and saturated with the fragrance of burnt offerings.

In all rites, one should always perform the oblation one thousand and eight times at the three junctions of the day; the previously described bathing and the wearing of the garment [should also be performed].
The wise have declared the Triśūla to be an auspicious lunar mansion;
it is suitable for the previously mentioned rites, as well as for recitation (japa), fire-offerings (homa), and other such activities.
One should perform all rites for all purposes using either a family of mantras associated with a universal monarch or indeed with a single-syllable mantra.
Endowed with great power and purpose, this solitary hero, ever supreme,
should always practice the ritual manual of all mantras while constantly reciting them.

All ritual manuals— those pertaining to the mundane world and those esteemed by the world, as well as those supramundane ones— are accomplished through great heroism, along with the Vidyārājas of great ascetic power.
Indeed, all mantras are accomplished through this ritual manual;
for it was taught by the sages as well as by the sons of those who possess the ten powers.
By Śakra and the other world-protectors, by Viṣṇu, Īśāna, and Brahmā,
as well as by the Moon and Sun, and by others such as the lords of the Yakṣas and the Rākṣasas.
By the mahoragas and the kinnaras, as well as by the best of sages on earth,
by the garuḍas, the mātṛs, the worlds, and likewise by others who are designated as sentient beings.
Those mantras which have indeed been spoken attain accomplishment here;
they are the attractors of all mantras and the leaders of all ritual actions.
He possesses mastery over all mantras, he is the director of all ritual actions,
and he holds sovereignty over all spirits through the extensive tantras and mantras.
This single-syllable mantra makes the recitation of all practitioners fruitful;
merely by being recited, it attracts all the deities.
This Great One-Syllable [Mantra] possesses mastery over all ritual procedures (kalpa) and produces various forms that are manifold and well-described by the virtuous.
One who applies himself correctly shall accomplish worldly mantras;
having made the cloth-painting perfectly clear and beautiful to behold in its entirety.
One should place it in a pure location, on a riverbank, or on a mountain peak; following the previously described ritual application, one should always face westward.
The practitioner, facing the east and seated upon a bundle of *darbha* grass, should perform the recitation with an undistracted mind according to the ritual procedure prescribed by rule.
Neither too loud nor too soft, and not with a mind intent on anything else,
one who does not revile any living beings will attain swift success in this world.

With a mind of loving-kindness, he always regards those in the world who are suffering, miserable, and ever-woe-begone; those who are protectorless, dejected in spirit, afflicted by calamity, and extremely weak.
Then, filled with compassion for those fallen into this terrible saṃsāra, one attains accomplishment;
one should always diligently perform great worship before the cloth painting.
One should contemplate or indeed perform the mental, human, and divine [rites] arising from the heart of the Universal Cloth of the Lord of Jinas.
Right there, the practitioner, knowing the ritual procedure for the principles (tattva), should construct a fire-pit;
indeed, he should offer oblations into that well-provided fire.
Having worshipped with white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron mixed together,
the knower of mantras, blazing with the six [perfections], should offer one hundred and eight oblations.
One should constantly kindle a powerful fire using wood produced from the Khadira, Plakṣa, Nyagrodha, or Pālāśa trees.
In the absence of these woods, one should procure another wood—
such as that of the *picumarda*, the *kadvama*, the sour wood, or likewise that produced from the *madana* tree.
Those described as engaged in sinful deeds, who possess every kind of thorn-like flaw, should be avoided;
one should perform rites for pacification and nourishment using the single-syllable mantra alone. For such a person, success will come swiftly even if they were to commit a sinful act.
For here, all mantra-holders, together with their ritual actions and extensive manuals, should be employed by one free from conceptual construction; they will always attain accomplishment.
Then the mantras are drawn forth and indeed become bestowers of boons.
Of fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, *udumbara*, or indeed *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha*,
anointed with clarified butter, mixed with curd, and combined with honey, he should offer them with a concentrated mind.
On this earth, a mantra-practitioner desiring sovereignty should offer oblations on all sides;
one longing for a kingdom should offer saffron and sandalwood to the Goddess.
Desiring sovereignty over the Vidyādharas and the gods,
one should offer thirty-six hundred thousand lotuses together with their filaments.
At the conclusion of the fire offering, one should indeed present the water of honor (*arghya*) there as an offering to the Teacher;
then the supreme cloth, marked by the Victor, blazes forth on all sides.
And as soon as it is touched, one shall fly up to the abode of Brahmā,
reaching as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven and down as far as the depths of the netherworlds.
In this interval, he always becomes the king of all the siddhas;
possessed of great heroism and firm vows, he puts all malevolent beings to flight.
He shall always be the king of the Vidyādharas in the accomplishment of his tasks;
furthermore, he shall live for the duration of an entire kalpa, traversing the long path of existence.
Having passed away at that great time, he is destined for enlightenment;
this other karma, which is constant, has thus been explained both in brief and in detail.
Having gathered white lotuses combined with white sandalwood, one should perform a hundred lakhs of oblations; he shall behold Ratnaketu.
Having seen that supreme Jina, one shall then possess the five superknowledges;
one shall live for a long time, a great kalpa, and become an attendant of the Buddha.
And then he beholds the Buddhas residing throughout the infinite directions;
he should constantly worship them and dwell together with them.
There is a single realm named Ratnāvatī where that Blessed One dwells—
the supreme sage, the most excellent and foremost Tathāgata, Ratnaketu.
There he dwells eternally, purified by mantra; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, another desired rite has been taught by the foremost of persons.
The mantra practitioner, having combined equal parts of nāgakesara, camphor, sandalwood, and saffron, should then perform seventy-eight hundred thousand oblations.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, O God, you then arrive here with the Discus;
ever pleased and granting boons, you touch the practitioner upon the head.
As soon as he is touched by that, the practitioner becomes the sovereign of the seven stages;
he is called a Bodhisattva, the legitimate son of the Victors.
He will certainly be prophesied as destined for the culmination of enlightenment;
from that point onward, whatever knowledge and object of knowledge belongs to the Son of the Conqueror [is attained].
I know the course, majesty, and power of all mantras;
by merely seeing this King of Mantras, one shall possess the five supernormal knowledges.
When he is always devoted to the practice of worship, he constantly assumes a physical form endowed with the excellence of all aspects in its various manifestations.
At that very moment, he becomes diligent in the work of awakening;
in a mere instant, he then goes to the world-systems of the Buddha-fields.
Thousands of world-systems, like cosmic eggs, wander everywhere;
at that time, they behold the conduct of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
One hears the Dharma and is intent upon the ritual of worship for them;
furthermore, there is another rite here concerning the appearance of a Cakravartin Jina.
One should offer a lamp characterized by a clean wick and ghee,
in a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay.
When the lamps were ignited by men numbering in the hundreds of thousands,
they were placed there by groups of hundreds of thousands of sailors.
Men, excluding women, with lamps in their hands on all sides,
should present the cloth painting known as the *bimba* of the Teacher during the rite of worship.
When all have proceeded equally and are consecrated with the single mantra, one should offer [the oblation] with the mantras of the Teacher; at that very moment, one should declare success.
A roar resounded everywhere like the sound of kettledrums, and indeed, many hosts of gods let out cries of "Excellent! (sādhukāra).
Then the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, stationed in the sky, said:
"Excellent, excellent! O wise one, you have performed a well-done deed."
Do you not see again the suffering submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra?
You have taken refuge in Buddhahood—secure, auspicious, and fearless in nirvāṇa.
You have entered upon the auspicious, stainless Eightfold Path practiced by the virtuous,
O you who are protected by the single-syllable mantra-form of the Wheel-turner.
Furthermore, there is karma alone which is based upon the supreme destination;
it is understood as having great power and purpose, and has been fully revealed by all the Buddhas.
Taking wood from a *nimba* tree, one should fashion a three-pronged vajra;
both its tips and its middle side should be fashioned according to the characteristics of the thunderbolt.
Then, having purified it with mantras before the cloth painting in the lower [position],
the mantra-practitioner, having touched it, should recite the mantras with a concentrated mind.
When sixteen hundred thousand [recitations] are completed, success is desired;
then that vajra becomes a single flame and blazes forth on all sides.
From there he rises up, for he ascends to the inconceivable;
from there he goes to the world of Brahmā or to another realm equal to the gods.
Then, one shall travel through the sky as the foremost among all accomplished ones;
indeed, one exercises sovereignty over the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others.
Then, in the presence of the deity, that king becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) and performs various kinds of physical movements.
Remaining for ten intermediate eons, he shall not be shaken;
he will always partake in happiness, worthy of worship, and always beautiful and handsome in form.
One whose conduct is rooted in the thought of awakening becomes free from the suffering of birth;
indeed, such a person becomes a divine being or a siddha, entirely devoid of all evil.
Having passed away from there, that mortal shall be devoted to great happiness;
traversing all states of existence, he becomes intent upon awakening.
In this king of mantras, infinite and diverse rites, honored for the sake of the welfare of many worlds, are recited according to the detailed prescriptions and their variations.
Furthermore, it brings about sovereignty over the earth, the state of Śakra, or the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
likewise, it effects the superior mastery of the Vidyādharas and the gods.
Or if that which is described here as having manifold forms is well-employed by the mantra-practitioner, he shall attain all accomplishments.

Having ascended to the cross-legged posture at night and reciting the inconceivable mantra as one observing the vow, the practitioner attains accomplishment at dawn; the reciter shall become possessed of the five supernormal knowledges.
Having stepped upon a corpse in a cremation ground, the practitioner, remaining motionless, should recite that single-syllable mantra of great significance; success is desired at dawn.
If one dwelling in a cremation ground recites this King of Vidyās of great supernatural power,
they will attain accomplishment within six months and achieve whatever result they desire.
Whether in this place or that, when recited, it is of great supernatural power; staying there, one attains accomplishment when well-employed by practitioners of mantra.
A white parasol, as well as a sword, a jewel, sandals, earrings, necklaces,
armlets, a cloth, and a finger-ring.
A waist-thread, as well as a garment, a staff, a water-pot,
a sacred thread, a turban, armor, and even a shield;
The deerskin, the lotus, the rosary, and the sandals—all these are the most excellent ornaments; in this world, both are equal.
Indeed, by means of ornaments, all— whether gods, mortals, or others—
attain success for the reciter in front of the cloth painting.
All kinds of objects, as well as minerals, ornaments, and even jewels—
all these various weapons were arranged before the cloth painting.
Chanted once, it is then completely purified; when consecrated eight hundred thousand times, it blazes forth when combined with all [the rites]. By the mere touch of it, the reciter rises up.
Furthermore, the natures of sentient beings, appearing in various forms,
may be ornaments or weapons, either made of clay or existing by their own inherent nature.
Those beings who are renowned— whether artificial or natural— who possess beautiful forms, movements, and dispositions, even among the various flocks of birds.
Whether they possess the notion of a sentient being or are devoid of such a notion, they are accomplished when honored with mantras;
they are arranged with various substances and fashioned from various elements.
Or else, she who is highly honored among the destinies and wombs,
having been placed before this cloth according to the previously seen ritual procedure.
Having touched it, the mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra six hundred thousand and seven hundred thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, when those [bones] blaze forth, one attains abundant accomplishment.
As soon as they are touched by those [rays], they shall rise up in the four directions;
they shall live long and obtain the long-lasting happiness of the dwellers of heaven in this world.
In whatever manner this King of Vidyās of great supernatural power is applied,
in that very manner he shall be pleased and shall always become a granter of boons.
But those engaged in other activities are swiftly perfected by those very actions, even over the course of many eons, as are the Vidyārājas of great supernatural power.
One who is pure, whose mind is pure, and who always delights in pure actions—
the knower of mantras who dwells in a pure place— attains pure accomplishment.
One should understand that action and its fruit correspond; from superior [action] there arises the superior, from middling action the middling, and what follows is considered inferior.
A rite that is not extensive bestows great wealth and produces the activity of a spirit;
yet, if it is unaccomplished, even if the rite is successful, it will yield only a very small result.
And by the mere constant recitation, he always brings about great enjoyment, great strength, being dear to the king, and the status of a minister for the practitioner.
His evil is destroyed when this king of mantras is recited even once;
when recited twice or seven times, it becomes a great protection for oneself.
Chanted eight times, it provides protection for companions from all sides;
furthermore, the mantra-practitioner should then consecrate both garments with the mantra.
Both garments, when consecrated with these mantras, liberate one from all diseases;
by touching them while reciting those mantras, the fever of embodied beings is destroyed.
Or, if one carefully consecrates water with a mantra and sprinkles it upon the eyes of an angry person,
that angry person will be destroyed as soon as he is seen by the practitioners of mantra.
And as for those hosts of spirits who are wicked, harmful, and performers of evil deeds—
the King of Mantras, recited thirty times, should gaze upon their faces.
And one should consecrate one's own hand again and again;
by directing a blow with those [mantras], one is liberated from all embodied beings.
One should always perform the bathing, drinking, and feeding of children with this supreme,
excellent mantra, which has been recited sixty times and is worshipped by the gods.
All the wicked ones— the flesh-eaters, the mothers,
and the planetary spirits— being terrified by the mantra, perish and always abandon the foolish.
In this manner, he performed many such deeds upon the surface of the earth for human beings; likewise, he always established them swiftly.
Whatever beings there are that have crawled forth, both various kinds of stationary and moving creatures,
whether poisonous or non-poisonous, they are destroyed when addressed with the mantra.
Whatever various sufferings there may be, and whatever sensations experienced by sentient beings,
when applied by the King of Mantras, they quickly bestow peace.
Various sufferings of exhaustion and the calamities of great pestilence are destroyed very quickly by thus reciting the mantra six hundred times.
One should perform the fire-offering rites with blue lotuses that are fragrant, mixed with honey, liquor, and clarified butter; eight thousand of them should be offered while being worshipped.
Through the sesame seeds, the spirits attained peace and the people regained their composure;
such were the many kinds of events that had arisen over many eons.
When properly employed by practitioners, it indeed swiftly accomplishes everything;
merely by recitation, one may effect the destruction of the anger of enemies.
For those who possess many mantras and meanings, and for the extensive ritual manuals (kalpas),
the accomplishment (siddhi) pertaining to them is here said to be attained through the prescribed rites.
One certainly accomplishes minor rites through the recitation of mantras;
indeed, by means of such recitation, one always swiftly brings about all goals.
For the purpose of subjugating all beings, it is desired that one recite [the mantra] at the three junctions of the day;
and one should always perform the rite of fire-oblation with *mālatī* flowers.
When prepared with white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron,
the mantra always brings fruit for the excellent reciter.
One who recites the mantra shall accomplish their desired aims through daily fire-offerings;
indeed, the daily offering is prescribed when performed with camphor and other such substances.
One should accomplish various rites as they are conceived according to one's desire;
from even a very small rite, a vast abundance of prosperity arises.
Success is always declared to come from intermediate rites performed at the midpoint;
therefore, one should especially perform the fire-oblation (homa) in all ritual actions.
Thus [it is said].

Thus concludes the fourteenth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the mandala and the means of accomplishment for the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi was present, having assembled right there in the midst of the assembly.

Having sat down, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! Well-taught, well-proclaimed, and most excellently spoken is this great Dharma-cloud issued forth from the application of vidyā-mantras; it is the heart of all Tathāgatas, the sovereign wheel-turning king of great vidyās, the extensive great kalpa that fulfills everything in every way. It is fruitful, the unsurpassed path for those who follow the practice of ritual distinctions, twilight recitations, burnt offerings, and the conduct of vidyās; it is the cause and sign produced by the conditions of karma with visible results, the source of great wonders, the skillful approach to the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa), and the certain final goal."

Therefore, may the Blessed One, the Teacher, please speak of the signs of the time for perceiving dreams that are conducive to the accomplishment of mantras, so that beings who follow the practitioners of *vidyā* may undertake the rites for the sake of the signs of success, and so that all *vidyās* may become fruitful through those ritual signs.

When this had been said, the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi: "Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Yakṣas! You have set out for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings, and for the sake of all practitioners of vidyā-mantras. Listen to that; attend well and thoroughly to it, and I shall speak it to you."

First, having gone to a place free from attachment for all activities—whether at the start of a previous rite or for any other purpose—and having constructed a hut in a pure location such as a mountain peak, a riverbank, or a cave courtyard, one should install the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and perform a great worship. Then, according to that same procedure as before for all rites, during the bright fortnight or the fortnight of miracles, on a necessarily auspicious day, in the first watch of the night, one should mix white sandalwood, camphor, and saffron together. Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations (*āhuti*) in front of the cloth painting, using fuel sticks four cubits in length, while the fire is smokeless and devoid of flames. At the conclusion of that homa, one should offer eight thousand lotus flowers.

Anointed with white sandalwood paste, at the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), one should form the mudrā and offer a seat upon an auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha) for one’s own mantra, using that very mantra.
One should perform the fire offering with this mantra: "Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded."

It is as follows: *Oṃ kumārarūpiṇa darśaya darśaya ātmano bhūtiṃ samudbhāvaya svapnaṃ me nivedaya yathābhūtam | hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā |* With this mantra, having performed the protection, one should perform the fire-offering (*homakarma*) and all other rites.

Then, having spread out *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing toward the north, one should lie down not too far from and not too close to the front of the painting, using a bundle of *kuśa* grass as a pillow for the head. Devoted to the practice of wakefulness during the first watch of the night, one should bow to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, confess one's misdeeds, and offer oneself to all the Buddhas.
Then, one may succumb to sleep at one's ease.
Dreams that occur during the first watch of the night are known to arise from phlegm; those in the second watch, arising from bile, are considered contemptible and worldly in origin.
In the third [dream] one should recognize it as being caused by wind (vātika); in the fourth, as arising from truth;
but in the case of a dream dominated by phlegm (śleṣmika), one should always see such [visions].
He sees himself surrounded on all sides by heaps of jewels, strings of pearls,
and abundant masses of water, and he sees himself immersed within them.
Surrounded on all sides by flowing rivers and submerged in the great ocean—
standing there, one sees indeed that very place where my own body resides.
There, that region was filled on all sides with lotus ponds,
as well as water-lifting machines, drinking saloons, and dwellings.
And one should see the Himalaya mountain or likewise the great river, situated as if made of crystal, being carried away on all sides by floods of water.
He sees a mountain, a rock, and a king all piled together with crystal,
covered by nets of pearls, and he sees a heap of pearls.
That bearer of the *kahā* sees a great rain and a flood of water,
as well as a white, bright umbrella or even a pale ornament.
An elephant of white form is said to be a dream for one with a phlegmatic constitution,
as is the sight of a white yak-tail whisk, a man, or even a garment.
The touching of rock salt and other salts on all sides,
as well as cotton, linen cloth, iron, silver, and likewise agallochum;
In dreams characterized by phlegm (śleṣman), touching or swallowing [substances] is desired;
likewise, beans that have swollen, sesame paste, and rice with molasses.
Various kinds of bean dishes are desired as dreams for one with an excess of phlegm (kapha),
as are svastika cakes, other types of cakes, kṛsara, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
For one with a phlegmatic constitution, the consumption of these in a dream is prescribed;
likewise, *śaṅkulī*, *parpaṭa*, various types of snacks, and diverse kinds of soups.
Through touching and eating [these substances] in a dream, there is an increase of phlegm and impurities;
for such things have previously been considered as various kinds of food and drink.
From eating or touching those [substances], there occurs in one of phlegmatic temperament (kaphin) the behavior seen in dreams:
the consumption of food, bedding, vehicles, or mounts originating from sentient beings.
If dreams involving touching, ascending, or seeing [the deity] are seen during the first watch of the night, all of this is said to pertain to one with a predominance of phlegm (kapha).
Dreams of this kind involving activities arising from water,
or various sights of foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as those related to phlegm (śleṣman), [are indicative of rain].
Having indeed seen the activities of those afflicted by phlegm in their dreams,
other inconceivable dreams have been described by the Leaders of the World.

Furthermore, for those embodied beings with a predominance of bile (*pittika*), dreams during the second watch of the night consist of the form of a blazing fire, or [visions] arising from various jewels.
If a person sees in a dream a firebrand or a great meteor blazing in every direction, it is because that individual is indeed overwhelmed by bile (pitta).
One should recognize that seeing a ruby, or another gem born of jewels,
in a dream pertains to a person of bilious temperament (paittika).
In dreams, those overwhelmed by bile see various yellow-colored things due to contact with fire, touching it, or even consuming it.
One who, fainting with the body overcome by bile, sees in a dream the sun constantly scorching and its heat always pungent.
If one sees the sky as gold-colored and the surface of the earth as yellow in a dream, it arises from a disorder of bile.
For at this time of dreaming, a person overcome by bile sees fire blazing on all sides, illuminating the vault of the sky.
At that time, the earth, the mountains, or the mass of rocks will be gold-colored;
likewise, the great elephants and the vehicles will all be made entirely of gold.
Constantly remaining in a state of sleep, one who is overwhelmed by the activity of bile perceives everything as consisting of golden vessels, vehicles, ornaments, and mounts.
Furthermore, sitting upon or lying down on a seat or bed made of gold,
as well as touching or ascending them, results in a dream-vision characterized by bile (paittika).
Clad in yellow garlands and garments, adorned with yellow cloth,
rich with the fragrance of yellow light, and wearing a yellow sacred thread.
And he who perceives himself as having a yellow appearance in a dream does so because of the onset of a bile-induced fainting spell, seen during the second watch of the night.
Various dreams of such kinds as those described,
which appear with various yellowish lusters, arise from bile.
In the middle course, they are not specifically designated for embodied beings who favor bile;
rather, they possess many forms and arise with a yellowish luster.
The dreams arising from bile have been described by the foremost of the world;
now those dreams arising from wind are indeed told during the third watch:
all directions are seen as radiant on every side.
And there is also the ability to travel through space, even horizontally across the vault of the sky.
For it wanders constantly all around in the sky and the vault of heaven; such a dream is said to be caused by wind (vātika), and it is described as being of this nature.
Jumping, leaping, and climbing trees;
the recitation of all the scriptures, and especially of the mantras.
Excessive talking and chatter also occur in one with a predominance of wind (vātika),
as does the climbing of thorny trees and the eating of extremely bitter things.
In cases of Vāta disorders, one should consume pungent and sour foods among all types of edibles,
as well as fruits that primarily cause the obstruction of Vāta and aggravate it.
In dreams, the consumption of those [substances] is indicated as arising from wind (vāta);
likewise, specific foods and substances that increase wind are [indicated].
Likewise, a living being whose mind is deranged by the mere touch or even the eating of [the flesh of] all beings becomes a servant to them simply by the sight of their own selves.
Indeed, those who see such things in a dream are known to have a wind disorder (vātika);
they exhibit various forms of movements and speak with various signs.
Various terrible utterances occur in a dream-vision characterized by wind;
such dreams as these have been described by the foremost among men.
The applications and so forth are joined with passion, hatred, and delusion in three ways;
one should know that for those possessed by passion it arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*), and that which arises from hatred is of the bile (*pittika*) type.
That which arises from delusion is the windy [type], while that which is mixed is the combined [type];
the affliction caused by dreams is called passion, which is the perception of vulgar conduct.
In a dream arising from phlegm (śleṣman), there would be a count of women therein;
in a dream arising from bile (pitta), there is that which is called quarreling with those who are hostile.
Born of delusion, having a stupefied appearance when mindfulness is lost from sight,
dreams are indeed always seen as being joined with a state of confusion.
Therefore, in every respect, that which is called a dream is devoid of sentient beings;
it has been taught by the seers of reality to be equal to the time of ritual action.
Those of a phlegmatic temperament are said to be endowed with a fine complexion, pleasant in speech,
long-lived, dull-witted, possessing a glossy appearance, and self-confident.
They are fair-complexioned, tall, and well-proportioned; they are always devoted to the company of women, steadfast in dharma, eternally brave, and ever-delighted in great honor.
One born under the lunar mansion designated for birth becomes envious and unmarked;
likewise, others become rulers of the earth or established as army commanders.
Those born under Bhogavatī become those who subsist according to their past actions.
The mantra is taught as being produced by the fruit of one's own karma, not devoid of action;
yet the leaders of the world have declared that action is not the primary factor of the mantra.
Therefore, success on this earth is said to belong to a being of phlegmatic temperament.
May sovereignty over the earth and great wealth come to him as his accomplishment;
however, the reciter should not excessively consume any foods that increase phlegm.
For these dreams, when practiced excessively, arise from the occurrence of impurity;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should not indulge in them, as they are described as having the purpose of causing division.
At that time, one who is logical and discerning should not sleep;
rather, the conduct of a person of bilious temperament (paittika) is always described as follows.
One who is angry with a form of hatred is dark-complexioned and weak;
he is cruel, performs cruel deeds, and is always crooked in disposition.
He is always heroic and daring, endowed with strength and intelligence;
he speaks much, possesses many friends, and has attained mastery over many scriptures.
One characterized by hatred is born righteous, firm in his undertakings, praised for his rising resolve,
high-minded, and possessed of great power.
He is heroic, yet free from hatred; possessed of great wealth, he knows the world and is pleasant to behold. He is liberated and without desire, steadfast, and always difficult to overcome.
He will always be proud, envious, and angry toward women;
yet he becomes one who possesses great energy, firm counsel, and great enjoyment.
Having stepped upon sentient beings according to their acquired karma,
his mantras that obstruct life-breath always achieve success.
For such a person, the sage swiftly accomplishes even fierce and powerful objectives;
indeed, those actions involving the injury of living beings succeed for that embodied being.

Whatever various ritual applications (prayoga) have been performed by all mantra-practitioners, they are accomplished through respect; they are not accomplished through other sentient beings' rituals.
Those mantras which are indeed hostile and afflict other beings, as well as the mantras of others— one who possesses the nature of wrath succeeds in cutting them off.
Krodha mantras are effective for the purpose of seizing the property of others and for obstructing the lives of others; however, one should not employ them in other types of mantras.
Furthermore, this being born of hatred exercises sovereignty;
it is black in color, or dark, or fair, or a mixture of these.
A mortal is born prone to anger and deprived of a golden complexion;
such a man is born with a rough, smoky, or tawny hue.
One born in the zodiac sign of Scorpio is brave, cruel, and likewise greedy;
being situated in the domain of the planet Mars, such a person possesses phlegm (kapha) due to Jupiter.
For one who eats little and partakes of pungent and sour flavors, long life arises; moreover, memory and mantras are born within him.
I shall now describe the conduct and the behavior of one afflicted by wind (vātika):
he is discolored and has a parched complexion, yet his physical stature is not excessively weak.
The wise man’s intellect is constantly lost; his heart is indeed unstable and unsettled;
there is trembling of the limbs, dizziness, vomiting, and excessive discharge.
He indeed becomes one who eats much, eats constantly, and speaks excessively;
he is opposed by all the world and is born with many enemies.
Born upon the surface of the earth both ill-behaved and miserable, for such a person,
the secret mantras of invisibility are said to bring success.
Those foods which provoke the wind humor follow after him;
therefore, the practitioner of recitation who desires the accomplishment of his rites should never consume them.
But for these beings whose wind-humors are provoked, [the mantras] arise from delusion;
indeed, these are said to be born of delusion and accomplished through deluded mantras.
The accomplishment of the delusions of the deluded is always desired in those [constellations] when a water-born sign is present among the constellations and is aspected by a true planet.
One should not perform auspicious rites when a person afflicted by wind (vātika) is in a state of fainting;
likewise, one should avoid rites for subjugation, summoning, deluding, or paralyzing spirits.
Even among beings dominated by wind, these characteristics of dreams— which arise from the sins born of delusion— are declared as the vision of truth.
Indeed, these were described by the sages of old as the accomplishers of all goals: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo.
Libra, Virgo, and likewise Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn,
Aquarius, Pisces, the elephant, the divine monkey, and the asura.
The Siddhas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others who have been proclaimed among men—
these are the zodiacal signs (rāśis) of many beings, as described by the foremost of teachers.
There are many kinds, with diverse meanings and various descriptions of karma;
in all those karmas, the extensive qualities bear fruit.
Indeed, it is taught that for embodied beings there is nothing free from karma and its qualities;
and when joined with qualities and karma, one brings about rebirth once again.
A quality joined with Dharma and Artha arises within efficacious mantras;
the reciter who knows the reality of qualities perceives the merit and demerit of the bonds of karma.
One does not perform beneficial action if there is no proper treatment even toward the qualities;
for it is action that accomplishes the task, not action devoid of qualities.
Endowed with the qualities of ritual action and its performance, he shall accomplish it;
for ritual action preceded by the prescribed method was taught of old by the Ones Possessing the Ten Powers.
For these actions, objects, and qualities are indeed the observer's own mental constructions;
they appear as various dream-forms arising from karma.
Therefore, by means of the dream-sign, extensive ritual activities should be performed—
those which are manifold in form, variegated, delightful, and pleasing to behold.
Those men who possess great enthusiasm and great heroism, and who desire accomplishment, see both forms that appear as obstacles and those that are formless, which serve as the causes for dreams.
Success is ordained for those among the superior, inferior, and middling;
however, dreams that are fierce and involve cruel deeds always yield immediate results.
The supreme worldly rites, which are capable of producing virtues for the leaders of the world, lead to success in steadfast actions over a long period of time.
Various dreams are seen by those who recite mantras for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi; however, for the sake of failing to attain mantras, sleep and lethargy are produced.
At that time, the mantra for destroying obstacles is prescribed;
the practitioner should employ those mantras, which take the form of logical reasoning, at that moment.
Then, the great wrathful one with six arms and six faces was manifested;
the four-syllable great mantra issued forth from the form of Kumāra.
Of terrible form and most fearsome, born in the likeness of a boar,
that very King Kālarātri exists for the purpose of destroying all obstacles.
Clad in a tiger skin, with a serpent’s hood hanging down, the great being of immense power held a sword in his hand, possessing the form of Kṛtānta.
Compassionless toward all obstacles, the destroyer of the lives of the Vināyakas—
let all beings indeed hear this most terrible mantra in the tantra.
The destroyer of beings who have been seen, the remover of all obstacles,
and the accomplisher of all mantras— O hosts of gods, listen to me!
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
It is thus: *He he!* O Great Wrathful One, six-faced, six-legged, destroyer of all obstacles, *hūṃ hūṃ*!
Why do you delay, O Leader, ender of life? Destroy my bad dreams!
Leap, leap! Remember the pledge! Phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!

As soon as this Great Wrathful King was spoken, all obstructors and leaders of obstacles— afflicted, terrified, with broken hearts and trembling minds— paid homage to the Blessed One Śākyamuni and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
and they remained steadfast in their commitment.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire abode of the Pure Abodes and that great maṇḍala of the assembly, spoke thus: "O hosts of gods! This King of Wrath shall subdue and wither, along with their entire clans, any wicked being who might harass a practitioner of recitation while any worldly or transcendent mantras are being accomplished;
yet he shall not cause the obstruction of life."
Having scorched and dried it up, he will establish it in its proper state;
he will remain for the protection, preservation, and guarding of the reciter,
and he will cause him to flourish.
For whoever should thus transgress this samaya and harass the practitioner who has been protected by the King of Wrath—
"His head shall split into seven pieces like the cluster of an arjaka flower.
Having spoken thus, the best of sages then addressed Mañjughoṣa.
O Youth, [I shall explain] the extensive exposition of all the purposes of your mantras,
specifically for those practitioners who have been liberated through the meaning of the mantra-tantras.
The King of Wrath, who destroys all obstacles, has been taught in the tantra;
indeed, this was likewise employed in the past by the Lords of the World.
For the destruction of wicked obstacles and the subduing of the anger of enemies,
this should always be recited at night by those who constantly engage in mantra-recitation.
This is for the protection of sentient beings and the destruction of bad dreams;
it has been taught by the leaders of the world as the means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of men,
among whom mantras— whether superior, inferior, or middling— are brought to accomplishment.
He was radiant and high-minded, with a golden complexion and a large belly;
he had wide eyes, was very gentle, free from passion, and devoid of anger.
One with reddish-cornered eyes who speaks kindly to others achieves the highest success;
he has thin skin, a dark complexion, slender limbs, and is not excessively tall.
Possessing great energy and great majesty, contented and auspicious in every respect,
he is preeminent by birth, pure, having few desires, and free from weakness.
His success is seen to be certain and supreme in all rites;
he is complete in his limbs, dark-complexioned from the front, and possessed of great majesty.
With an unafflicted mind and being wise, he is a celibate practitioner, always pure,
constantly delighting in dwelling [in solitude], knowing the world, and virtuous in his conduct.
He always has many friends, is ever-generous, and always acts with moderation; he is pure, possesses skillful conduct, and is always devoted to cleanliness and proper behavior.
For one who speaks the truth and is compassionate, the highest success is achieved;
he is always of noble birth, righteous, and possessed of the full expansion of all excellent qualities.
Devoted to his mother and father, honoring brahmins and guests, and being exceedingly compassionate and steadfast— for him too, the highest accomplishment is attained.
He is dark-complexioned yet fair, affectionate, speaks little, and is always pure;
he desires delicious food and approaches a pure wife.
One who knows the world, is highly esteemed by beings, and possesses supreme accomplishment—
neither too short nor too tall, with hair like crushed collyrium.
With eyes of a gentle hue, pure, and always delighting in bathing, he was devoted to the Three Jewels; for him too, the supreme accomplishment was attained.
Engaged in supreme activity, knowing the intentions of sentient beings,
patient, pleasant in speech, and full of joy toward the Son of the Victor—
then his supramundane accomplishment remains fruitful.
He is a great being, possessed of great heroism, great splendor, and great vows;
he is one of great wealth, a knower of mantras, and a perceiver of reality in all tantras.
By caste, he is a preeminent Kṣatriya or a wise Brāhmaṇa;
he is always devoted to women, full of passion, and golden-hued in appearance.
He is seen to be tall and fair-complexioned, with a prominent nose and mighty arms;
he has long-reaching limbs, is heroic, and desires a great kingdom.
He is devoted to the sons of the Victors, a worshiper of the goddesses known as women, and full of faith in the Three Jewels; he is adorned with the thought of awakening,
exceedingly compassionate, and steadfast, yet occasionally wrathful and possessed of great power.
Possessing great wealth, great generosity, and great splendor, he is difficult to overcome;
being beloved by women and heroic, for him too there is supreme accomplishment.
Delighting in pride, brave, and always attached to women;
with a golden complexion, eating little, broad-chested, firm, and pure.
Compassionate, merciful, skillful, and knowledgeable of the world, highly esteemed for his virtues, a reciter of mantras, and always devoted to the Lords of Jinas, he [attains] the Radiant One.
Among them, in the second auspicious [kalpa], there will always be sons of the Śrāvakas and Khaḍgins, as well as powerful leaders of the world, distinguished by their appearance.
He was free from physical defects in all his limbs, yet always cruel and impetuous;
he was generous by nature, had conquered his enemies, and was a judge of both dharma and adharma.
One who is neither too stout nor too thin, neither too tall nor too short—a person of medium build is the best; for such a person, the highest accomplishment is attained.
His nails were coppery and very glossy, his palms were red and pure;
from the tips of his feet they were red and lustrous, adorned with wheels and svastikas.
A person endowed with hundreds of thousands of auspicious marks sees on their hands and feet banners, arches, fish, flags, lotuses, and blue water-lilies.
Such a person is considered the most excellent, destined for supreme accomplishment;
his teeth are white, without gaps, prominent, and even like mountain peaks.
A prominent nose, large eyes, well-knit eyebrows and chin—these are auspicious; likewise are eyelashes like those of a cowherd, dark pupils, and eyes adorned with stars.
He whose forehead is broad, whose head is auspicious and shaped like a parasol,
and whose head is further characterized by a protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), and whose ears are beautiful and auspicious;
His jaw is always shaped like a lion's, his two lower lips have the luster of a ripe bimba fruit, his tongue is seen to have the reddish glow of a lotus petal, and his palate is likewise very red.
The neck is like a conch shell, and broad shoulders arise [therefrom];
the armpits and chest are auspicious and excellent, and likewise the breast is wide.
The region of the navel is slightly small, broad, firm, and auspicious;
the navel is deep and clockwise, free from a network of veins.
His arms hang down long and his biceps are great; his waist is marked with the signs of a lion;
his thighs are rounded, and his elbows are free from deformity.
His shanks are like those of the eneya antelope, celebrated as being well-proportioned and rounded;
his feet are fleshy and elevated with well-formed toes.
The two [feet] are reddish, with red nails, glossy, elevated, and adorned with flesh; moreover,
the two heads [of the feet] are beautiful and pleasing to behold, matching the color of the earth's surface, unjoined, pure in hue, praiseworthy, and marked by the signs of the world.
Above those, indeed, the network of veins is not elevated.
The two channels for the discharge of feces and urine should have deep, clockwise-rotating folds;
they are praised when they are very small and the two testicles are always round and auspicious.
It is proclaimed as both indivisible and manifold within the limit;
when it is purified in the arising of the limbs, it rests at the end of passion.
And during the time of sleep, if semen is seen to be discharged due to the consumption of aphrodisiac foods and drinks,
it appears blue or red in color.
One who has abundant secretions and is unctuous, marked with auspicious characteristics—
such a being is said to be fit for the highest accomplishment.
Passing urine three times and excrement six times, being pure and devoted to the practice of purification,
that person who indeed sleeps at the end of the watch and rises in the morning— O living beings!— [attains purity].
Its purification is always seen as most excellent, effective for all rites,
yielding various kinds of fruits or even abundant prosperity.
One who is characterized by middling marks will become an enjoyer [of pleasures],
as will one born under the constellations Puṣya, Revatī, or Phalgunī.
In the asterisms of Maghā, Anurādhā, Citrā, Rohiṇī, and Kṛttikā,
a father is seen standing [in the horoscope], capable and marked by planets.
Success is seen for those born at dawn;
likewise, at midday, in the forenoon, and at the end of the day, the planets are pure.
The Moon and Venus are white, and Mercury and Jupiter are yellow;
they gaze upon all living beings for the sake of accomplishing their capacity and purpose.
And in this interval, those humans who have been born as performers of auspicious deeds—
for them, mantras succeed without effort in accomplishing all aims.
At midday, and always at sunset,
during this interval, cruel planets always behold embodied beings.
The Sun, Mars, the cruel planets, Ketu, Rāhu, and Saturn;
and those who are the chief among the grahas, such as Kampana, Nirghāta, and Ulkin; [all these are to be worshipped].
Tārā, Ghoratama, Kṛṣṇa, Ariṣṭa, as well as Kālamārakuru and Raudra— these are seen at that time due to the influence of the age.
At the time of sunrise, Mercury beholds the earth;
Bṛhaspati beholds it when it is raised to the height of a chariot-pole, at a distance of one yuga.
When the sun is in the Yuga [constellation], Śukra, the lord of wealth, gazes from beyond;
from midday onwards, the moon becomes full, and there is the appearance of those who possess a lunar body.
During the period of Mercury, there shall be sovereignty; during that of Jupiter, it brings wealth and enjoyment;
during that of Venus, there is the attainment of riches, great kingship, and an abundance of enjoyments.
O long-lived one, likewise, sovereignty under the Moon is fruitful;
and at midday, under the Sun, it is said to be equal to a middling aspect.
When midday has passed, the sun always gazes toward the direction;
at a distance of one *yuga* (four cubits), it is not high—thus is the *ketu* described.
Rāhu and Śanaiścara, as well as Tama, Kāla, and Yugāntaka;
thereafter, when the lifespan is further diminished, there will be Niṣṭa, Ariṣṭa, Ulka, and Kampa.
When the sun, copper-red and resembling a mass of vermilion, has set,
that chief of planets appears in the form of a young child.
With a spear in hand, he was exceedingly cruel, appearing like glowing embers;
then, as the sun reached the end of the eon, the sources of the auspicious planets [were eclipsed].
One born under Ādityadarśana will be cruel and impulsive;
one born under Satyakaṅgāraka will be wrathful, greedy, and arrogant.
When Ketu appears with smoke-colored halos, it produces the outbreak of diseases;
people will always be impoverished, afflicted by illness, greedy, and arrogant.
[He sees] Kāla, Tamaka, and Āpāta; Ulkika and the reviled Graha;
Kampana, Nirghāta, and Tāraka; and the scorching Aśani.
Likewise, for the bears and other such creatures, it is ordained that there be another [lunar day] called Vajra-ariṣṭa;
however, the terrible appearance of Rāhu is seen by all living beings.

Human beings are always born as the poor, the helpless, and the immoral; they are men who are sinful and thievish, mortals who are perpetually suffering, afflicted by disease and death, lepers, and those with many ailments— such as the one-eyed, the lame, and those with skin diseases.
Eunuchs, impotent men, those childless, the unfortunate, and those despised among women; likewise, men, women, and others who are loathsome in appearance and grasping—[these are the ones excluded].
Worlds are born in many ways from the very birth-charts (jātaka);
among them, white and yellow planets are the best, for they bring about the auspiciousness of one's birth.
In terms of color, those with white and yellow lusters are praised and extolled by the Victors;
these are the four chief planets: Venus, the Moon, Jupiter, and Mercury.
For the sake of accomplishing the vision of those [deities] in all rites by the reciter,
and for the sake of foolish beings, birth itself is always auspicious.
All forms of prosperity are always said by the foremost of men to be as fleeting as a moment, or even the blink of an eye, or the snap of a finger.
This brief account of their birth has been told by the leaders of the world;
this alone is the measure of the planets as conceived by those who contemplate the world.
Thus they arise constantly at this very time according to reality;
for these [beings], through merit and evil, always wander like a wheel.
Those who perform both auspicious and inauspicious deeds here always employ the mantra as one;
they have indeed resorted to the world of the gods.
Among these, in some cases, a certain evil intention arises;
furthermore, due to their lack of attachment to the fruits of good and evil, they are born again in many ways.
They say that this is the "vision" of these planets who consume karma;
because they move swiftly, they approach beings with great speed.
The movement of a flash of lightning is swift, lasting for a visible moment or an invisible one;
from these, time is calculated.
This measure of time has been demonstrated by those of supreme intelligence.

Henceforth, I shall always declare the twelve Muhūrtas that occur during a fixed birth, which are the causes for each respective time; and I shall also describe those who are unfit vessels, whether they are causes for success or not.
Furthermore, by observing the omens of the world again and again through both sight and non-sight,
one discerns the ruin of the kingdom, famine, and the prosperity of the king.
Then, O people, Māriṣa constantly brought about auspiciousness, even when there was an improper time;
likewise, he caused the trembling of comets, thunderclaps, and meteors accompanied by smoke.
The movement of the constellations, days of the week, and stars, both auspicious and inauspicious; the conduct of all beings, and the various activities of Śiva and Śivā.
I shall likewise describe the conduct of the flesh-eating mothers, those of fierce nature who cause harm, and other wicked beings who subsist on raw meat.
There, the deities are gracious toward those whose intellects are supreme in the jewel-like Dharma,
who are ever engaged in virtuous deeds, and who possess hearts of loving-kindness and compassion.
For those whose actions, objects, and intellects are virtuous and who rely on the fulfillment of others,
they are drawn in by the utterances of mantras, which serve as the cause for medicinal herbs and nourishment.
I shall describe in detail their conduct, upon which the characteristics depend;
having entered the bodies of others, they remain there as those who have passed into human existence.
The gods spoke thus to him, while the asuras did so out of pride;
both these classes of gods and asuras were present there among the assembly.
They also go there in two ways, being either cruel or common;
they also go there in two ways, according to the five destinies of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Abiding there, they proceed through three types [of rebirths] for twenty,
thirty, or incalculable [eons], reaching as far as the lords of the Akaniṣṭha heaven, the Yāma gods, and the incalculable Abhūpaka gods.
As far as the realms and worlds are infinite, so too are the pure and impure;
as many as there are worldly beings, and as many as there are noble disciples.
Of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as their legitimate sons,
the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas established upon the ten stages;
All sentient beings are likewise eternally dependent upon the womb of existence; all foolish creatures are dependent upon the wombs of their various destinies;
while for the Buddhas—who are liberated from the serpent of saṃsāra—and for all the noble ones, [there is no such dependence].
I shall explain in detail their characteristics, conduct, and the truth regarding their speech and gestures at all times and in every way.
All beings are drawn forth by means of mantras, tantras, and proper methods;
one who knows the mantras for summoning and drawing in perceives them as having entered and taken refuge within another body.
By those who are virtuous, knowledgeable in wholesome actions, heedful,
practitioners of mantra-recitation, all of whom are free from deluded conduct and capable of both restraint and favor, the earth was drawn forth for the world of humans by those reciting mantras.
I shall explain everything regarding the signs of their accomplishment according to the truth,
for the sake of conforming to the bodies of those humans who are always afflicted by disease.
It is always intended for the sake of the ultimate Dharma and for the sake of liberation;
therein lies the restraint of the wicked and the honoring of those who are pure.
In this way, the mantra and tantra are prescribed for both restraint and favor;
here, the threefold action is applied in three ways to wind, phlegm, and bile.
For them, one should prescribe pacification; indeed, a threefold sequence is recognized.
In that regard, one should always perform the medical treatment for humans by means of mantras.

The conceptualization of the great elements (mahābhūta-vikalpa), however, is traditionally held to be "the element" (bhūta) and "that which exceeds the elements" (bhūtādhika). That which is overcome by the elements is called "that which exceeds the elements" (adhibhūta).
When a living being produces ill-health through a spirit (*bhūta*),
then that spirit is classified into two types according to its nature.
Likewise, that which is sentient is conceived as being eternal, and that which is insentient is likewise conceived;
so too are bile, phlegm, vitality, and whatever else [is considered].
The four great elements and the fifth, space, are recognized;
water conjoined with fire, and earth conjoined with wind.
The wise always say that he is reckoned among non-beings;
indeed, the one of great splendor declared him to be the foremost lord of the world's summit.
For that which is not reckoned among sentient beings is non-human;
yet the one of supreme intelligence, the best among speakers, calls it "human" and "sentient."
Whether it be non-human or human, including all beings counted among sentient beings as well as the gods,
the speech of the Omniscient One is intended once again for the welfare and excellence of all beings.
Thus has karma, which gives rise to the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, been taught by the Buddhas of the past, the future, and likewise those of the present.
The mere word of the Buddhas necessarily brings about the result;
for that reason, through the commonality of their spiritual lineage, accomplishment is indeed clearly perceived.
They call it omniscient knowledge—secure, peaceful, and eternally pure;
it is held to be liberation, the ultimate reality, characterized by the purity of selflessness.
That very path among sentient beings is proclaimed as this Sūtra;
therein, he spoke the entire teaching on the mantras, the seats, and the medicinal herbs.
It is the reality of the past and the future, supremely honored by all scriptures;
it is the foremost state in the world, the selflessness of phenomena, the ever-peaceful and auspicious ground.
This word of the Omniscient One is the ultimate; it is his supreme state.
However, both [the omniscient being and] the arising of the omniscient knowledge are merely conceptualized.
The power of all the Buddhas and the wise Bodhisattvas,
as well as the accomplishment of mantras in all rites, has been demonstrated everywhere;
for this very reason, the Lord of Sages has proclaimed this King of Rituals.
Traveling by this path in the form of mantra for embodied beings,
one reaches the city of Nirvāṇa, which possesses the wealth of peace and freedom from decay—
free from sorrow, stainless, secure, culminating in awakening, and eternally auspicious.
This tantra, which is the teaching of all the Buddhas for those who recite mantras,
has been told on the surface of the earth in its entirety for those who recite mantras.
All that is knowledge and the object of knowledge is bound by the cause of karma;
all this, however, is the meaning of mantra, which flows toward the threefold awakening.
The complete knowledge of the Buddhas has been revealed here in this eon,
and for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, it has been set in motion throughout all worlds.
Whatever is found in this *Kalparāja* is not seen in other *kalpas*; and whatever has been taught in other *kalpas* by the sons of the Sage, those best of sages, [is likewise contained herein].
Indeed, this is the extensive ritual manual (kalpa) for all mantras;
for this very reason, it was taught by the Lord of Jinas for the sake of all embodied beings.
And upon the surface of the earth and within these three worlds,
there is no one who has not been brought under control or subjugated by this sovereign king of rituals.
When the Moon of Sages has set and the circle of the earth is empty,
he will act for the sake of the teaching while this world remains in this eon.
The Youth Mañjughoṣa, ever auspicious among all beings,
shall likewise perform the Buddha-activities in this world and in this teaching.
Having heard the power of this King of Rituals (kalparāja), those who have long desired it will gain faith in it upon hearing it even once; for them, accomplishment shall always be attained.
This auspicious speech is always unfailing for all beings,
for those mantra-practitioners who are constantly devoted to recitation and fire-offerings among all creatures.
In whichever of the three types of knowledge a particular cognition operates,
that very same cognition operates within this supreme king of rituals.
The teaching of the Buddhas here is declared to be the consecration of mantras;
yet that mantra is free from conceptual construction, even though it is spoken here within this realm of conceptual construction.
It effects the welfare or misfortune, the auspicious or inauspicious, for all sentient beings;
likewise, it determines the destinies, the intellects, the nature of beings, and the prosperity or adversity of the worlds.
This very [reality] is elaborated upon in the Kalpa; yet the Tathāgatas are beyond elaboration.
Though they have transcended the world and are self-awakened Buddhas, they speak here for the sake of the world.
Surpassing all phenomena, for he transcends worldly conditions;
the agent performs various and manifold deeds that are honored by the world.
The King of Mantras, engaged in ritual activities for the benefit of the multitude of beings, he,
the youth Mañjughoṣa, performs the work of a Buddha.
Its purpose is the accomplishment of qualities and the support of the world; it is both auspicious and inauspicious.
I am indeed the requester and the speaker; one who does not request is not said to be a teacher of the Dharma.
For the sole benefit of all sentient beings, I shall now proclaim that which was spoken by the Buddhas and which was indeed spoken by all the Buddhas of the past.
They will have faith that the lineage of the Buddhas shall remain unbroken,
and they will possess the arising of the knowledge of the Omniscient One for all the rites of the mantra-practitioners.
However, only that action which proceeds from the wisdom of omniscience is praised;
one's own past karma in this world is what is being experienced now.
Therefore, one should perform difficult deeds here in these births;
thus, mantras are accomplished without effort, and the bondage of karma is severed even in this world.
Success may be attained here even through action;
therefore, all the Buddhas have praised action alone.
But that rite performed according to the rules brings success quickly even in this world;
however, foolish beings, being utterly deluded, wander about deprived of the proper method.
Therefore, in every respect, action alone is praised;
one who is disciplined shall accomplish that which is joined with the ritual procedure when it is conjoined with action.
Likewise, action devoid of the ritual procedure does not succeed even after a very long time.
For there is no liberation without meditative absorptions, nor is there liberation devoid of meditative absorptions;
therefore, the union of meditative absorption and liberation is called awakening.
Thus [it is said].
Thus concludes the thirteenth chapter, the section on the purpose of all ritual actions, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Then, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again surveyed the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Listen, Mañjuśrī! I shall explain in detail, within the midst of this assembly, the extensive section on the ritual procedures for accomplishing all aims that was previously taught. This has been requested by the wise Vajrahasta, the King of Yakṣas, concerning the auspicious and inauspicious nature of dreams associated with the purpose of all mantras.
Thus, by way of this incidental discussion, all this has been told for those who recite mantras; the King of Yakṣas, with a pleased mind, placed his joined palms upon his head.
Having bowed his head to the Teacher, he joyfully addressed him with these words:
"Indeed, for the sake of favoring the worlds, this has been taught by the one of supreme intelligence."
For the sake of my compassion for them and for the arising of happiness for all beings,
[I shall explain] the auspicious and inauspicious dreams of those who recite all mantras.
The conduct and the expansion of qualities of those beings who were most debased,
their supreme destinies from various wombs, and the activity of their knowledge of causes.
Knowledge of the past and the future, knowledge of the present, and knowledge of the auspicious and inauspicious—
all-pervading knowledge of all things is the activity of the omniscient one’s wisdom.
Unmanifest, without an object of perception, free from conceptual proliferation yet described through proliferation,
endowed with the supreme form of mantra, Śiva is proclaimed as peace.
The power of all the Buddhas has indeed been described by the one of supreme intelligence,
especially for those who recite mantras and are endowed with the meaning of all mantras.
All karma and the fruit of karma, as well as the time of action,
the recipient, the place, and the attire, were explained in the context of dreams.
O Yakṣa King, the best of sages, the supreme one, the seventh Tathāgata of the seven mantras—
among those who are the Buddhas in this Fortunate Aeon, this Śākyapuṅgava is the seventh.
This seventh one is designated as the Lion of the Śākyas, the Conqueror of Enemies;
in this degenerate age, he has attained perfect awakening as the Lord of the World, the Maker of Light.
The Sage of great heroism and great wisdom, Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
and the Yakṣa Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, paid homage to him.
Then the wise Mañjuśrī, possessed of great insight, remained silent upon his own seat; he was then questioned by the Sage.
He entreats that Buddha, the youngest and best of sages:
"Excellent, Blessed One, perfectly awakened one! [Please explain] the knowledge of karma in full detail."
The Jātaka is ever auspicious;
it is the life-story of many beings, together with the causes of their karma and knowledge.
For those who are intent upon their desired activities, who are devoted to the pursuit of the means for attaining the highest good,
and who recite mantras, there appear signs of accomplishment regarding what is to be achieved or not achieved.
Likewise, for those in the world who desire prosperity, who long for the enjoyment of sovereignty,
who are preeminent in their pursuit of the causes of kingship, and who desire the attainment of siddhis and dhāraṇīs;
"May all-pervading knowledge be revealed in its entirety in brief!
Thus spoke the supreme Sage when he was entreated by the Son of the Victor.
The wise one has the voice of the kalaviṅka bird and the resonance of a divine drum;
he possesses the Brahma-voice and the thunderous sound of a mighty rain-cloud.
Urged by the Buddha’s word, the pure seventh Sage spoke this verse:
"O youth, for those who have set out for the sake of others and have achieved success for the benefit of the world—
those leaders who guide the entire world toward the highest good and all welfare— may they remain pure and abide in the splendor of liberation."

For those who possess inexhaustible vigor through truth, whose minds are fixed on that [truth], who delight in joy and loving-kindness, and who are devoted to that [practice]—for such people there is always success in their endeavors; no one else shall ever attain accomplishment in any way whatsoever.

Those who are always delighted by and devoted to this supreme mantra within the teaching of Cakradhara, or likewise Mañjudhara, shall subdue Māra and set the wheel in motion; such a person here is indeed fit to be a Cakradhara.
His speech is divine and enchanting, forever devoid of anything childish;
it is celestial and delightful, pleasing to the ear, lovely, sweet, and agreeable.
The Buddhas proclaim that it is "Mañju" because it bestows the bliss of mental refreshment;
its non-existence cannot even be known by those [others] through the specific wisdoms of the Tathāgatas.
Among them, there were sons who had entered the stages [of bodhisattvas], numbering as many as ten times the number of the most excellent divine Tathāgatas;
even they, though distinguished in the world by their lordship over the gods, were unable to comprehend his divine power.
Those belonging to the form realm, the formless realm, as well as those of the non-earthly, the divine, or those born of humans—
whether they be yogins who have attained accomplishment or the most distinguished leaders among men in this world— all are [included].
There is no being whatsoever to be found who can truly claim my glory;
the Buddhas declare that Mañjuśrī is like a mere conceptual construction of glory.
This name Mañjuśrī, which is equivalent to the "imagined," was likewise given by former Victors;
it was established for you in the Saṃjñita eon by divine Buddhas of the past and the future.

If one hears this name and remains pure, and if their mind does not become distracted but becomes one-pointed, for them there shall be this auspicious peace; they shall attain supreme, foremost, and distinguished enlightenment.
May all mantras be accomplished without exception; may one attain birth in a supreme womb;
may one always rely upon the supreme Dharma and be free from obstacles, so that success may be achieved.
Having accomplished all his desired mantras, he will swiftly go to that Mañju-bodhi;
having reached it, that foremost of sages, seated for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, shall attain awakening.
He awakened and set in motion the wheel of enlightenment; this virtue has been proclaimed by the foremost of Jinas.
Remembering the name "Mañjuśrī" within you, inconceivable virtues have been proclaimed by the foremost of Jinas.

O Youthful One, pure one, let your eternal power be revealed— that which cannot be told even in hundreds of mantras throughout incalculable eons by the foremost Jinas of the past who have gone everywhere.
O Mañjuśrī, this mantra practice of yours has been spoken by all the Buddhas without exception;
O Youth, this teaching of yours is indeed all-pervading, the supreme delight for heroes.
Indeed, those beings seated in the Pure Abodes seek after every single sentient being;
yet they never at any time, nor in any way here, employ my own mantra, nor even your mantra.
Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the fourteenth chapter, the detailed exposition of the section on verses, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the meditative absorption named "The Miraculous Manifestation of All Tathāgatas."
Immediately upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni entering [meditative absorption], rays of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows—
blue, yellow, white, crimson, and crystal-colored.
Having illuminated this entire buddha-field and lit up the intervals between all world-systems, they eclipsed all planets and constellations in a mere moment and drew them toward themselves.

Having drawn them from their respective places and having summoned that assembly by the Buddha’s empowerment, [the light] vanished back into the *ūrṇā-kośa* (the hair-treasure) of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Then all the planets, lunar mansions, and stars, being overwhelmed by the great light, distressed and terrified, approached the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
With palms joined in reverence, they stood trembling, falling repeatedly to the surface of the earth.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, for the sake of benefiting all the planets, lunar mansions, stars, and luminaries, as well as embodied beings whose intellects are produced by ignorance, uttered these words:
"Listen, O worthy ones, you hosts of gods and humans! Karma alone divides the manifold variety of the world for sentient beings."
