those called Kalaśas, the Carmaraṅgas, the Samotadyas, and the Vaṅgakas.
During a terrifying planetary conjunction, if there is noise, it shall slay various kings;
if the sound comes from the eastern or southern quarter, there will be great danger.
The Kaliṅgas, the Kosalas, the Sāmudras, and the Mleccha inhabitants are slain by cruel weapon-wielders, as are their governors, kings, and spies.
When a great and cruel sound arises in the eastern and western quarters,
like the roar of clouds from a massive storm by day or night;
"O hosts of gods, know that I perceive this as a thunderbolt;
at that time, O best of men, it brought both good and evil upon humanity."
When the asterism was auspicious, the lunar mansion most excellent,
the lunar day preeminent, and the moon was bright, he heard a sound from the earth.
Auspiciousness, abundance of food, health, prosperity, and the means for play shall be accomplished;
and the mantra, having been mastered, will always grant boons to those who recite it.
At that time, success shall be achieved when applied to all rites;
one should know that results arise from both malefic and benefic planets.
Therein, the accomplishment of karma becomes joined with all ritual actions;
listen now as the various types of *nirghāta* (calamities) are explained on this earth.
Some words instantly take away life, some bring about the fruit of truth,
and some deep-sounding words accomplish all goals.
And let the hosts of gods quickly listen to that sound;
understand it as the roar of one who is steadfast, profound, and endowed with wisdom.
Just as the sound from long drums brings [the result] directly before one,
so too that sound— terrible and cruel— is the producer of the effects as previously described.
At a time equal to the falling of meteors, an earthquake does not arise;
one should also indicate and apply a sound that is a cruel roar.

At that time, one should know that there will be great danger and this confusion of all instructions; from that, one should know the destruction of beings, as well as the occurrence of famine and disease.
Then he wrought superhuman illusions and calamities;
within twenty-three days, death then overtook the kings.
All those who performed the prescribed rites heard sounds resounding with fierce roars.
Now I shall describe the earthquakes; listen as they are being told, specifically those earthquakes that occur among the lunar mansions.
The lunar day (tithi) should be joined with everything everywhere, and the asterism (nakṣatra) should also be joined accordingly;
just as in the case of a thunderous crash (nirghāta), one should apply this to all ritual actions (karmas).
If the earth trembles under Aśvinī, one should predict famine;
under both Bharaṇī and Kṛttikā, the two types of tremors bring about the arising of happiness; and under Rohiṇī and Mṛgaśiras, an earthquake brings about the attainment of wealth.
Ārdrā and Punarvasu are the two constellations thus characterized;
if the earth should quake during these, there will be great danger in that region.
The Middle Country and its rulers will perish if the earth together with its inhabitants trembles during the asterism Puṣya;
however, one should predict prosperity, peace, abundance, and health for that region.
When [the moon] moves through Āśleṣā, the entire earth quickly trembles;
that region will be overrun by barbarians, thieves, and fierce men.
When the earth trembles under the asterism Maghā, it does not happen everywhere, but in all places;
in the land of Aṅga, the Māgadha king shall perish,
and all the people of the Māgadha region will be afflicted by disease and thieves.
If an earthquake occurs under both Phalgunī constellations,
then the Gaṅgā situated within the womb of the Himālaya mountains will flow northward.
The inhabitants of Vṛji and Mithilā will quickly be slain by diseases; then all the rulers of Vaiśālī will likewise be struck down by afflictions.
Various chiefs of the Mlecchas, originating from the ridges of the Himalayas,
dwell indeed within its belly and on its slopes;
these foremost leaders of the Mlecchas are constantly slain by means of weapons.
When the *hastacitra* nakṣatra is present and the earth trembles during the two twilights,
the Mlecchas, thieves, and royal officials are always slain by weapons.
When conjoined with the constellations Svāti, Viśākhā, and Yuktī,
the entire earth trembles, and other merchants are seen [perishing].
The best and foremost among merchants, the preeminent and the pure,
as well as those who move upon the waters, perish through diseases and the falling of weapons whenever the constellation Jyeṣṭhā— also known as Anurādhā— is always present among the lunar mansions.
The entire earth trembles and even the formidable mountains—
those excellent peaks situated on high ground and in low valleys— bow down.
When both armies have met, the surface of the earth trembles cruelly;
then there will quickly be fear and a censured famine.
Then, within six days, the death of the great king shall occur;
those people in the central regions will quickly perish, and their excellent cities will be destroyed.
When Anurādhā is present, the earth shakes slightly, resulting in auspicious outcomes; crops will ripen everywhere, though their yield may be only moderate.
It should be known that when [the earth] trembles specifically during the asterisms of Mūla or Āṣāḍhā— namely,
Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā— it portends the arising of threefold suffering.
If an earthquake should occur during the day, it should be known that the earth will be afflicted on all sides by disease, famine, thieves, and other such calamities.
When the earth trembles under the asterism Śravaṇā, or indeed throughout Dhaniṣṭhā,
there will be abundance of food, long life, and health, and the land will be free from famine.
If the earth, abundant with crops,
should tremble at night during the asterisms of Śatabhiṣaj or Bhadrapada, [it portends a great calamity].
Famine and the destruction of the kingdom are indeed seen there in that place;
mortals are slain by thieves, and there is also loathsome famine.
Mortals on the surface of the earth tremble at midnight;
this is proclaimed to occur under all the *uttarā* constellations and under Revatī.
Both constellations, Revatī and Bhadrapadā, are auspicious in every respect; for it was during these very constellations that the earthquake occurred everywhere.
An earthquake observed among the constellations as previously described brings happiness;
these earthquakes have been fully explained, as well as the portents marked by thunderclaps.
At the time of a falling meteor, the affliction of living beings arises from the three humors;
and when it has passed, that which was previously described in detail shall come to pass.
The caves should be constructed right there, as well as everything in the direction called Diśā;
it is described as having sound, vibration, light, and being endowed with happiness.
At the time of accomplishment, all [these] are seen by those who recite mantras;
likewise, for yogins, accomplishment arises without fail.

Thus, for the sake of attaining the enlightenment of a Buddha, the powers of the Bodhisattvas and the foremost sages arise through their supernormal faculties, even as their minds are free from attachment.
At that time, the best of gods shall also proclaim the arrival;
with its light, its waters, its earth, and the thundering roar of its sounds,
an earthquake will quickly arise due to these very causes.
When the earth trembles, silent and devoid of light,
one should point out that the beings of the hells, being shaken,
are afflicted by many kinds of suffering; their bodies are most terrifying, worn out by me.
And as they behold the suffering born of their own karma, O best of sages, that which was proclaimed by the sound of karma is seen by those people in its recurrence.
Understand all of this in its entirety and retain it with the desire for happiness;
everything situated in the sky is perceived by means of the banner, and thus one should proclaim it.
By night and by day, the northern stars are seen in the sky;
at midday, Dhruva is seen everywhere at its greatest height.
Smoke-colored and possessing great rays of light, it emits smoke as a sign of great danger;
having taken hold of whatever region, it causes the vault of the sky to smolder.
Indeed, in that very region, the foremost king will certainly be slain by diseases,
corresponding to whichever planet, day, and radiant lunar mansion [the comet] has resorted to.
A bright streak of smoke is seen even in the sky;
one should clearly observe that very constellation, lunar mansion, and planet.
At that time, the living being is slain by weapons and diseases;
for a smoke-colored line is seen, portending great fear.
A cruel planet will undoubtedly destroy that region quickly;
moreover, a smooth, blue-colored line resembling smoke has appeared.
One should know that such [a flame] is auspicious and pacifying, increasing longevity and health;
however, one that is dry-colored, discolored, or smoky in hue is censured.
Praiseworthy, white in appearance, and arising from four rays,
she is always proclaimed as gentle and bestowing the fruits of auspicious colors.
One should know that place to possess the splendor of flowers where she is celebrated; do not go there. She is white like a mass of snow, pure, and resembles smooth crystal.
That which is known as Soma-Saumya has a luster equal to a dry color;
it brings about auspiciousness, the accomplishment of goals, and a vision of suffering and nirvana.
In whatever region she has arisen,
or in whichever constellation she is joined at the foremost point in the circle of stars;
When that renowned one has departed into the sky, he is seen upon the surface of the earth;
all those who take refuge in the stars have attained longevity and health on every side.
In that case, one becomes powerful, happy, a master who practices dharma, and is born as the most excellent of mortals; one should therefore take refuge in that lunar mansion.
It is said that when a planet is pure, it wards off all suffering;
wherever a line is seen [in such a state], one should know that person to be endowed with happiness.
Endowed with a joyful form and adorned with a gentle appearance,
a line of smoke-like vapor rose into the sky, portending great terror.
Furthermore, when another [planet] is joined with a benefic or is auspiciously situated in the sky,
the wise know that region to possess prosperity, abundance, and health.
In that situation, for the most part, auspicious signs arise from the comet;
white rays of light, resembling crystal, gather from all sides.
One by one, they became renowned as the glorious Tārakas in this vault of the sky;
thereafter, there were also those born from forms consisting of rays resembling crystal.
Prabhava is known as the source of the illustrious one; one should take refuge in that lunar mansion.
Many types of comets are mentioned, numbering two thousand or even three thousand.
And thirty-one [beings] arise in many ways through the emergence of various fruits of karma;
some are superior, some are middling, and some are turned away from the Dharma.
Then some [omens] arising are known to be extremely terrible and fearsome;
others are to be understood as having a smooth appearance and a radiance like the color of crystal.
One that is glossy and beautiful should be known as having a luster equal to the appearance of crystal;
one that is glossy and beautiful should be known as having a lovely color for those with little enjoyment.
Some of these cruel beings move horizontally, while others go north, south, or in other directions;
possessing a radiance equal to the moon, they arise for the welfare of all living beings.
These great-souled, yet deformed and exceedingly long ones, who bring about the destruction of kings,
have indeed arisen in the middle [of the sky], with their rays extending toward the east.
If it moves from east to west, it will kill the ruler of the eastern region;
if it moves from west to east, it will kill the king of the western region.
If rays arise from all sides, one should predict famine everywhere; for these, when risen in the intermediate directions, portend the increase of barbarian tribes and border-dwellers.
One should command that they be slain everywhere and stationed at that place;
they are smoke-colored, discolored, rough-hued, and bringers of great terror.

The source [of light] has gone everywhere; one should indicate its presence among all living beings. If it is seen constantly from all sides during the day at midday, then great suffering and a great portent shall enter upon kings.
Wherever a horizontal line arises from a fixed point,
it destroys the king situated there, in whichever region that line has arrived.
One should predict the onset of major diseases, the harassment of thieves, and death in that location, as indicated by the intermediate directions during the day.
When one sees a blue-colored comet in the sky during the day,
O rulers of the earth, there will be various sufferings of exhaustion and diverse calamities.
Indeed, these have been described in their entirety as terrifying with great suffering;
some are said to be fierce and burning, while others bring auspicious results at night.
When one sees the comet, red in color, situated near the moon,
then the earth will soon be drenched in blood and struck down by the falling of weapons.
Swiftly he cast his blood upon the earth, which was like a night-roaming female demon,
causing harm to many beings and providing no refuge from manifold sufferings.
In whatever place one may designate, there the countries arise;
and she is seen in the sky in embodied form, yellow and radiant with yellow light.
When comets arise in the sky resembling turmeric in appearance, with a luster like yellow orpiment, or the color of gold,
one should know that it is a sign of great suffering for all living beings.
The presiding deity of the Mahāmārī class, having been alerted among the people,
likewise brings destruction for twelve years through calamities such as drought and the like.

They say that one which is excessively black is "fierce" (raudra), while those that are excessively smoky are to be avoided; likewise, one resembling the color of an *atasī* flower is devoid of the "remnants of fire" (*pāvakocchiṣṭa*).
Appearing like great clouds, colored like blue collyrium,
some with the form of boars and others with the radiance of cuckoos—
when such terrible beings are seen in the sky, one should depart from that place.
Likewise, those who perform cruel deeds are seen to be extremely fierce and terrible;
there is great suffering, great horror, or even the onset of pestilence; they say that in that region there is a terrifying and great famine.
When one sees the comet risen in the sky, having the appearance of an *oḍra* flower, resembling a red sun, and possessing the color of blood;
At that time, one should predict the death of kings at that very moment, as there will be a universal panic caused by disease and the obstruction of many living beings.
If a man or a woman suddenly sees [such a vision],
his death is ordained to occur within seven days.
He is slain by weapons within two nights or even three days;
then he may suddenly see [the signs] either by day or indeed at night.
His death is ordained upon the earth at that very moment;
the creature will be killed by poison or by weapons, without a doubt.
White and of glossy color, it brings forth happiness like the cool season;
otherwise, the sight of those possessing various forms and shapes is not desired.
Whether in one's own body or another's, if they are dependent on a comet—
whether by night or by day— they are known to take life instantly.
When one sees [the deity] white in color, with a radiance like that of the moon or cow's milk,
having an appearance like snow or a jasmine flower, and possessing a luster like various jewels—
for such a person, sovereignty is proclaimed, or else the accomplishment of the mantra-reciter.
These desired banners, whether in the body or in a temple,
or in one's own army or in the enemy's army— wherever they are situated, there they bestow their fruit.
They say that this is the most excellent among those celebrated [omens], possessing a luster equal to various wonders.
They are seen everywhere by mortals as being remembered as bringing many misfortunes;
they are described by mortals as occurring everywhere, whether in a conflict or even within one's own home.
The *ketus* of those belonging to the bodies of the Siddhas are remembered as being desirable in every way and fruitful;
otherwise, they are all contemptible, bestowing much suffering and fear.
All these comets marked by planets have indeed been described;
everything arising from lunar days, asterisms, and zodiac signs has been explained as before.

Through various *vāra*-yogas and also by means of the planets, those of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) are [to be understood] as before; thus has everything regarding them been explained throughout the world.
Then all of them were conscious; some possessed beautiful and uniform radiance, while others were variegated, and in some places bright, glossy, and auspicious in color.
He has beautiful eyes, is named Netra, and possesses a radiance equal to a white kunda flower; he has lovely brows and fine eyes, a golden complexion, and is adorned with gold.
All of them are white and variegated, arisen with various names; understand that these comets belong to the six classes of colors.
One should employ the respective designations for those of various colors and forms,
as well as for those who are deformed, terrible, and extremely cruel.
Those which were previously described by me, along with their names in every respect—
these and others like them have been declared as the many-formed comets.
At that time, for human beings, there arose the emergence of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds;
and the conflicts of the principal planets were seen on all sides.
In the war between the gods and the asuras, those of great power and great majesty— divine beings of celestial origin— reveal their own selves.

All those white ones, who bring about auspicious results, have resorted to the assembly of the gods; whereas those of deformed or undeformed appearance, who are contemptible and possess distorted complexions,
all belong to the faction of the asuras and practice cruel ends of action.
When a great terror prevails during the war between the gods and the asuras,
and the asuras are defeated by the gods, those banners indicate this;
they shall show mortals upon the surface of the earth and the entire sky.
White [planets] always yield auspicious results; they are beloved and dear to the gods.
Taking refuge in the side of the gods, they reveal themselves at that time.
For mortals, one should then predict an immediate abundance of food and good health.
When the gods are indeed defeated by the asuras at that time,
then comets of distorted color, impelled toward cruel deeds,
truly rise on the side of the asuras.
Then, cruel winds blow from all sides for living beings;
there are great rains, droughts, and likewise cruel serpents.
He released water filled with poison and many diseases;
he then brought upon men the affliction of poisonous eruptions and fainting.
Various Rākṣasas, as well as those inhabited by Daityas and Yakṣas,
indeed cause harm to human beings, desiring most terrible obstacles.
Causing suffering that obstructs the vital breaths here upon the surface of the earth,
a rain of stones will then fall from the sky onto the ground.
At that time, terrifying great winds blow;
fierce winds blow, causing harm to many living beings.
Various animals and many hosts of cruel beings brought about the destruction of crops on this earth;
they then created obstacles for human beings, obstructing their very lives.
For there are many such types of beings, abounding in numerous obstacles,
belonging to various animal realms— fierce beasts of prey and serpents.
Various beings dwelling in the womb of the *nāgas* cause harm to living creatures;
likewise, various barbarians and thieves bring about the obstruction of life.
When the gods are defeated, various winds born of fire— terrible and of tawny hue— blow throughout the world.
At that time, the mortals dwelling in Jambudvīpa will always be most unrighteous;
then those on the side of the gods will decline before those born of the Daitya lineage.
When beings endowed with Dharma have gathered here upon this earth—
excellent ones who delight in the Buddha’s Dharma and always preeminent within the Saṅgha.
Devoted to their mothers and fathers, possessing true courage, and intent on the recitation of mantras,
those gods then completely conquered the one born from the womb of the Daityas.
At that time, the earth will be abundant with crops and fruits, and completely full.
Mortals will have long lifespans and will be devoted to great numbers.
All kings will be righteous, bestowing happiness and devoted to the welfare of others;
at that time, the Daityas in those lands will be joyful and destroyers of disease,
and they shall all become cool causes of happiness for the world.
The seasons were always pleasant, being neither too cold nor too hot;
and flocks of various birds would constantly warble sweetly.
The trees were auspicious on all sides, rich with many flowers and fruits;
and all living beings dwelling upon the earth were entirely free from disease.
At that time, the righteous king felt no agitation;
there was abundance of grain and happiness, as well as various jewels and palaces.
The men dwelling in Jambūdvīpa behold all types of wombs; there the trees are always rich in fruit, and the cows yield much milk.
And all the people dwelling in Jambudvīpa, like wells and hollows everywhere, act as enemies to the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana).
Abiding in delight for the dharma of living beings, they exist in many ways and of many kinds;
by them, the earth is filled everywhere and on all sides.
In that lowest age, the time of the Kali Yuga, their conduct deviates from the established norms; one should declare the results of their actions to be otherwise than what is prescribed.
One should desire action that is both fruitless and fruitful, as well as modified, cause-born, and indeed inauspicious within the realm of desire.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Great Chapter on the Arising of the Knowledge of Signs, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka*.
Now begins the twenty-first detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, within your ritual manual (*kalpavisara*), for one intent on the practice of mantras during the time of accomplishment—which serves as the means for all accomplishments—there appears the designation of *graha* (planetary/possessing spirits) for Rāhu, the lord of the gods and leader of all *grahas*, throughout the extensive details of all mantras and rituals; he is perceived through his conjunction with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) among the moon, the sun, and other celestial bodies."
Listen to that well and properly; take it to heart, and I shall speak to you.

When the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Perfectly Awakened One, had spoken thus, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, circumambulated the Blessed One three times, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined toward the Blessed One, prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet. Rising once more, he gazed at the Blessed One with unblinking eyes, his eyes wide with joy, and being filled with delight and satisfaction, he addressed the Blessed One in this way: "It would be well, Blessed One, if you would explain the arrival of Rāhu; for therein lies the time of accomplishment for those beings devoted to the practice of mantras, as well as the arising of happiness for all beings, or the signs of the auspicious and inauspicious. May the Blessed One explain that."
Do now whatever you deem to be the right time.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you question the Tathāgata on this matter, being so intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen; I shall speak."
And he taught it for the sake of all sentient beings.
First, one should understand according to the scriptures the time when the cruel planets [enter] the lunar orb of Rāhu, as it has been taught.
When a great battle between the gods and asuras occurred and there was great fear,
then that king of the Daityas, the lord of the Dānavas, possessed of great supernatural power, [appeared].
Indeed, that great and terrifying mountain, rising high on all sides, would even exceed Mount Sumeru in size.
Of immense stature, cruel, and exceedingly arrogant with pride,
that preeminent and powerful graha entered the abode of the gods.
Then, having touched Sumeru, which is equal to the gods, with his hand,
the Daitya looked toward the celestial vault where the Apsarases dwell; at that time,
the king of the Daityas held the full moon in his left hand.
When various jewels upon his hand have become bracelets,
he is then called a "planet" (graha) in this world on earth.
When a red radiance appears in this ruby,
then the speculative thinkers say that it is the fiery mandala of the Lord.
But when, within this blue or red [object], the radiance attains blueness,
then it should be known as "blue," whether in the moon or even in the sun.
On earth, those who are logicians call it the realm of Mahendra;
at that time, those very same logicians also say it is the mandala of Vāyu.

Various [beings arise] from various garlands of jewels; various [beings arise] from various precious gems; various [beings arise] in the treatises of logicians; and various [beings arise] from the wombs of their respective modes of rebirth.
The activities of those who lack correct knowledge are indeed manifold, and their attainment of results is likewise manifold; such is the activity of the foolish.
Therefore, one should properly apply oneself to the knowledge of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the vision of the Asura was fixed solely upon the ignorance of the celestial dwellers;
he brought the chariot of the high-souled Śaśin to a standstill,
at which time Rāhu’s arrival upon the earth among mortals occurred.
When that planet stands having traversed the lunar disc, one should know that there will be great fear; understand this specifically regarding the lunar mansions.
When both the solar and lunar discs are eclipsed while conjoined with the asterism Aśvinī—
occurring either by day or by night— the wise know that constant conjunction with Aśvinī portends famine.
When the moon or the sun enters the lunar mansion Bharaṇī,
one should predict a diverse harvest of crops as well as an abundance of food.
When the moon is certainly eclipsed by Rāhu while in the Kṛttikās,
whether at night or at dawn, it is harmful at the end of the watch (yāma).
At that time, one should know there will be great suffering or even the outbreak of diseases;
this shall occur in the Middle Countries and not elsewhere due to the first lunar mansion (Aśvinī) and the others.
This should be declared regarding the various types of calamities arising for kings throughout the inhabited lands.
When the moon or the sun, possessed of great supernatural power, have both previously been eclipsed by Rāhu and then set while in the constellation Mṛgaśiras in the vault of the sky;
At that time, men in the eastern region will be struck down by diseases;
one should predict that the kings and officials in that land have reached the end of their lives.
When the Moon and the Sun are eclipsed while the moon is in Ārdrā or Punarvasu,
one should proclaim that the entire earth, including the lands of the Mlecchas, will be drenched in blood.
Struck down and shattered by one another, their lives destroyed and their lifespans ended,
those of base and evil deeds were previously designated for this region and the two northern regions; they have now become Mlecchas and thieves.
When the conjunctions of Puṇya and Āśleṣā occur with the Moon or the Sun in the sky,
and their disks are eclipsed by Rāhu at midday or midnight, then one should know there is a great calamity; thereafter, another sovereign of men will arise.
If, under the asterism Maghā, the orbs of the moon and the sun are eclipsed by Rāhu, and these two supreme planets set while being overwhelmed,
then one should know that [the calamity] will perish throughout all of Jambūdvīpa.
One should predict famine, the destruction of the kingdom, and a great plague;
when both [asterisms] are conjoined with Phalgunī, there will be the arrival of Rāhu.
At midday or at night, one is liberated again in an instant;
thereafter, an abundance of food is seen throughout Jambūdvīpa.
When Rāhu swallows both the moon and the sun during the Hasta constellation, they are released together after being eclipsed; yet when they set, they bring suffering.
There will be fear of great pestilence and of thieves on all sides;
then kings, excellent monarchs, and preeminent leaders will be struck down by diseases,
and one should predict famine everywhere in all directions.
When Viśākhā and Svātī are conjoined— these two most excellent and honored constellations—
one should know that Rāhu’s arrival brings about affliction for livestock;
at that time, various leaders of families are slain by weapons.
When the two constellations Jyeṣṭhā and Anurādhā are joined together,
the arrival of Rāhu therein should be declared as bringing about an abundance of food.
If Rāhu, situated in the Moon, is seen on the earth by means of the Mūla constellation, then the rising Moon is eclipsed,
or it is eclipsed as soon as it has risen in every respect.
If that very Rāhu were always to cause the moon to set,
the governors of the east and the dwellings of the people of the eastern regions would perish.
One should predict a great falling of weapons and also famine;
the people of Gauḍa will be divided and terrified by fear of a foreign army,
and the king there will indeed perish, overwhelmed by disease.
When Rāhu eclipses both the Āṣāḍha months at that improper time,
there will be suffering and great disease seen upon the earth;
then all the chief kings will become malicious toward one another.
Under Dhaniṣṭhā and Śravaṇā, it was foretold that which is censured by the world:
indeed, the various leaders of the Gaṇas will become divided from one another.
If the arrival of Rāhu is observed during the lunar mansions of Pūrvabhādrapadā as well as Śatabhiṣaj, one should likewise predict an abundance of food.
When Rāhu’s arrival occurs while the moon is conjoined with the Uttarā Bhādrapadā constellation, it is most auspicious by day, but censured at night.
When the moon is eclipsed on all sides by Rāhu while in the constellation Revatī, or likewise when the sun rises or sets within the lunar disc;
When Rāhu sets with the foremost and most excellent of the planets,
the central regions are afflicted, and there is the death of the Māgadha king.
This is the knowledge of calculation for humans on the surface of the earth;
this is also proclaimed as the measure of the lunar mansions.
It is impossible for other humans to determine the measure arising from the origins of the planets.
Indeed, the variegated garland of constellations revolves in the vault of the sky;
this is the calculation for humans, and beyond that is the calculation for those born of divine origin.
Whichever planet is the primary ruler of one's [ascendant], or whichever is situated in one's natal sign or constellation— as previously described— that [planet] renders that [person] otherwise.
There is no fault in a slight deviation from the measure; rather, there is censure in excessive speech.
Indeed, at the time of measurement, this chief planet is traditionally held to be the one that effects the result.
The time should be known as it has been described, and the rule is likewise proclaimed:
earthquakes, thunderclaps, and meteors occurring in conjunction with specific lunar mansions and zodiac signs [are significant].
If the Sun and the Moon are seen situated there along with the planets,
then his birth-nakṣatra is adorned by both ends.
Otherwise, one should know that it is fruitless, or its power may even be censured;
therefore, at that time, one should perform the recitation for the attainment of mantra-siddhi.
When the sky is seen everywhere as always smoke-colored, then one should know there is great danger; at that time, there will be fear from an enemy army.
When the moon and the sun also become smoke-colored,
one should know that there will be great danger within two or three days.
When there is mist at all times during a terrifying [period],
one should know that it is inauspicious in every respect and that there will be an outbreak of diseases therein.
If a mist arises during the summer or the autumn season for seven nights on all sides, one should know that there will be great danger there.
Whether by day or by night, if a mist arises,
[it may be known] by the stars, the signs of the planets, or by the lunar day and the interval between the days of the week.
Everything has been explained as before, just as in the case of the portents of thunderclaps and meteors;
one should apply the same [interpretations] to the appearance of mist during those very days as previously stated.
If at midnight or at midday smoke constantly arises,
one should know that there will be great distress for kings and for the preeminent city.
Whether in autumn, winter, summer, or even the rainy season, a mist is to be recognized everywhere; it is likewise proclaimed by the constellations.
Likewise, one should know whether it is auspicious or inauspicious by day or by night;
indeed, a spell may be proclaimed as fruitless or even as fruitful.
If there is an earthquake everywhere, or likewise a solar eclipse in one place,
and if smoke should arise from all sides in the sky,
then that kingdom will soon be constantly struck down by the sword.
Power is proclaimed everywhere in every region, as is death itself;
within seven days, the winds on earth, which are the source of all living beings, shall be overcome by the foremost victory.
Constantly slaughtered on all sides by those bearing weapons, they fall under the power of death;
with hearts devoid of compassion, they seize one another's kingdoms.
These men born of royal lineage are swiftly torn apart by weapon-wielders, like merchants [slaughtered] for their wealth.
In summer, where the sky appears white in color, there is fear of a great disease; however, if it is blue, there is the arising of auspiciousness.
When the sun is seen rising with a yellow radiance during the summer, death is declared; however, in the autumn season, it is considered inauspicious.
In both winter and spring, it appears copper-colored;
otherwise, if it has a yellowish luster, it is censured and avoided by the world.
In autumn, one should know that a patient with measured speech is praised;
likewise in the bright rainy season, one who is yellow or not [otherwise discolored] is favorable.
To him who resembles great majesty, whose radiance is equal to the great blue sapphire,
who is to be known at all times, and who bestows the fruit of all happiness— homage to him!
Conversely, one should know that there will be affliction from the region and the dwelling place;
furthermore, there will be destruction of crops, pestilence, and even famine.
"O gods, this is most grievous; indeed, this terrifying danger has been brought about by the corruption of the essence (rasa) within the sky, amidst the loud and horrific roar of Śukra."
At that very moment, he should arrange for all the kings something other than that which threatens their lives, ensuring it is joined with auspiciousness and leads to their ultimate welfare.
When the sun and the moon are eclipsed by Rāhu during a time of great terror,
the various populations there, born of their diverse karmic origins, perish; thereafter,
another sound arises, auspicious and honored by the world.
O best of gods, O most excellent of planets, you shall be appointed for the sake of the highest good;
various mantras will be perfected, yielding diverse roots and fruits.
Whether they were all diverse or not, all those born from the vital breaths were endowed with many forms; their own natures were then transformed.
There are various weapons indeed, arising from various arms;
for all these supreme mentalities, adorned with the root mantra,
shall surely attain accomplishment along with the planetary deities when they are being practiced.
When the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu while the sun is also eclipsed by a planet,
at that time the practitioner of recitation should constantly repeat the mantra.
They all indeed become bestowers of boons;
for this is the fruit of benefiting sentient beings, and therein is seen their firm foundation.
The King of Mantras is swiftly accomplished when recited during the planet Rāhu.
When the planets, including the moon and the sun, are well-honored for seven days,
months, or even fortnights, the accomplishment of mantras is declared;
likewise, the Tathāgatas have stated that accomplishment occurs at the end of a watch or indeed at midnight.
Mantras joined with the proper ritual procedure certainly succeed, whereas those devoid of it are not desired to work;
this is true even for a high-souled Brahmā, let alone for humans on earth.

Success shall not be attained even by the god Śakra, nor by Rudra the wielder of the trident, nor by Viṣṇu who holds the discus and mace in his hands, nor even by the high-souled Tārkṣya, through rites performed devoid of the prescribed rules.
When a mantra is well-recited and joined with the causes prescribed in the tantras,
it succeeds even for another person.
Released by humans according to the ritual procedure, adorned with the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva),
they— along with the planets— attain success when cast [into the fire], recited, and applied at the proper times.
Knowledge applied everywhere bestows its fruit;
knowledge consists of causes, actions, and fruits, and it is the subduer of [false] causes.
One should know that action is accompanied by its cause; one should understand that the arising of cause and fruit is through knowledge.
One should apply knowledge to the fruit of action and likewise join other causes to it.
Likewise, when the fourth Vidyā is applied to the four types of ritual actions,
that Vidyā, being joined with the appropriate cause, will swiftly bestow the fruit of the action.
That vidyā should be known by its fruit as being highly honored even by the Buddhas;
it is endowed with all purposes, preeminent, and efficacious for all rites.
When that vidyā is applied to ritual actions, it bestows success through those actions;
it shall lead one toward the highest good, for it is beyond the scope of ordinary mantras.
Understand the power, the accomplishment of mantras, and the reality of the world;
as well as how action may be fruitless, or how both fruit and action exist therein.
Whether as the cause or the fruit, mantras applied to the principles of the world are seen and have been praised by the Buddhas.
Fruit does not destroy action nor sequence; nor does fruitless action constitute a higher ritual act.
Success in mantras arises from the undertaking of action for the sake of its fruit.

Because the sequence of qualities is not joined with substances, and because the sequence of substances is not joined with action, the King of Mantras is accomplished therein; thus the fruit is applied to the rituals.
One who is endowed with the prescribed materials, established in right conduct, and engaged in ritual action—
his status is not to be known by birth alone, for he is one who is constantly joined to the fruit through his actions.
They do not attain the state of great power nor the perfection of the syllables of the mantra at all times;
therefore, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra while relying upon the source of the ritual procedure.
The sequence of time, the qualities, the ritual procedure, the source, the state of existence, and the Sugata—
all these kings of mantras are accomplished when they effect the purpose of the ritual and the time.
A quality is not to be known as a substance, nor is a quality said to be non-substantial;
through the union of quality and substance, and by means of their conjunction, one should worship the mantra.
One should employ all the deities who have been worshipped by means of the very face [of the mantra]; one shall quickly accomplish the measurement, the quality, and the substance within the mantras.
The sequence endowed with the qualities of time, the activity of the sequence of qualities and time,
and accomplishment well-applied within mantras itself are seen to be fourfold.
When applied specifically to virtuous qualities, mantras bestow power, an expansion of virtues, and the arising of happiness through the conduct of sentient beings in every respect.
The origin of all things is established as action, quality, and substance;
nor do these qualities exist apart from substances, nor do they exist devoid of substances and actions.
Those mantras prescribed for the mind do not bestow accomplishment quickly through mere mental intent alone; nor do they arise from speech without the mind.
Nor is it known through mantras by another means, nor is it other than the mind;
nor is there any other action—success is held to arise from the conjunction of the mind alone.
It is not inferior due to its view or its action; it is not desired as being devoid of action.
Right view, as well as action, speech, and mind, are thus properly applied.
The deities are swiftly accomplished through the application of right view and the engagement in right action, as declared by the syllables of the mantra and tantra.
Mantras always succeed perfectly when they are endowed with the excellence of the conclusion of the ritual action and speech, and are properly joined with right view.
Mantras are accomplished in every way when correctly applied to their respective ritual actions;
yet there is no mantra without the mind, nor is there mind without mindfulness. These two exist together.
Through right mindfulness, the mind is seen for the sake of mantra-siddhi;
indeed, the Tathāgatas have stated that a mantra is not effective when it is devoid of mindfulness.
When properly applied through mindfulness and the state of meditative concentration,
they are seen to be empowered by the mantras and are brought to accomplishment by means of samādhi.
The cultivation of right concentration consists of mantras highly honored by the world;
these mantras are thoroughly permeated by that very concentration through their application.
There, the king of mantras is accomplished, as is the most abundant yoga;
one should meditate upon the supreme mantra through perfect samādhis, beginning with meditation.
The mantras of the yogins are accomplished; success is not said to come from non-yoga.
That which was previously spoken by me is correctly explained and well-applied.

The sages, who are compassionate toward living beings, have declared that success is not achieved otherwise; a mantra correctly applied to the meaning of reality does not come to fruition without intentional resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
Mantras are accomplished through right resolve when they are properly applied according to the ritual rules;
however, all kings of mantras do not succeed when they are devoid of right resolve, even if worshipped.
Mantras are accomplished in every way when employed with a correct livelihood;
it should be understood that the arising of happiness within mantras itself results from right intention.
When correctly employed, mantras attain purity in one's livelihood;
those foremost mantras, when well-applied as prescribed on earth, bring about accomplishment.
Indeed, one who is disciplined should properly apply his livelihood as its fruit;
the mantra-practitioner, delighting in right livelihood, should always be pure in mind and clean.
For one who is pure, whose actions are pure, and who conducts himself with purity in all his deeds,
the pure mantras always succeed, whether the circumstances be foul or stainless.

The other mantras, as well as those others that have been proclaimed, are the mantras of practitioners; the mantras spoken specifically for the *kravyāda* [flesh-eating] deities are those by which they achieve success.
Chants sung by Rudras, Viṣṇus, grahas, thieves, and even Garuḍas of great supernatural power, as well as those by yakṣas and rākṣasas, bring success to those whose mantras are otherwise obstructed.
Even when recited by various hosts of spirits and piśācas,
mantras do not succeed on their own if they are deficient in the prescribed ritual procedure, nor among those who delight in impure conduct.
When employed according to the prescribed rite, it swiftly bestows success even amidst impurities;
therefore, one should not perform a mantra-rite devoid of the proper procedure.
Mantras accompanied by outflows (*sāśrava*) are accomplished when properly applied through ritual actions;
likewise, the noble mantras spoken by the Buddhas are to be realized.
Their accomplishment is declared to be well-established within the paths themselves—
the Noble Eightfold Path, which is perfectly integrated with the Four Truths.
This [practice] always consists of the four dhyānas and relies upon the four bases of psychic power;
however, the preeminent mantras taught by the Buddha are distinguished as superior.
Indeed, the nature of mantras, as taught by the ritual rules, is an ineffable essence, possessing the nature of the voidness of space; so too is that of the Noble Ones of great majesty.
O dwellers of heaven, I shall explain the methods for the vidyās as prescribed for those on the stages, which are devoid of the path to supernatural powers; listen to that.
Divine mantras are accomplished through the path of the ten courses of action, through virtue, and through well-spoken words, by means of ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.

Thus ends the fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction for the ritual application of mantras and the signs for the determination of the arising of [the deity], from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra which is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, from the nineteenth detailed section.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, within your *mūlakalpa* chapter-series, there exists a teaching titled 'The Exposition on the Section Concerning the Knowledge of the Signs and Sounds of All Beings.'"
I shall speak of that,
knowing which all sentient beings engaged in the application of the practice of all mantras will understand the proper and improper time for all mantras;
listen to that.
Pay close and careful attention;
I shall speak.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground. Bowing with palms joined toward the lion throne of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, he circumambulated him three times, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and addressed the Blessed One as follows: “It would be well, Blessed One, if you would explain that teaching on the knowledge of the cries of all beings for the benefit of all sentient beings.”
That shall serve as the requisite for the observance of all times for the sake of attaining the signs of accomplishment for all those who have entered the practice of mantras;
now, O Blessed One, do as you deem fit.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you consider it necessary to question the Tathāgata on this matter.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen; I shall explain."
When this had been said, Mañjuśrī prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, rose up, and sat down to listen to the Dharma.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the entire assembly, entered the meditative absorption named "The Incitement by the Sounds of All Beings.

As soon as the Blessed One had entered that absorption, all those beings whatsoever who were situated in infinite and boundless world-systems were illuminated by the Buddha’s rays; and having bowed their heads to all those Blessed Buddhas and paid homage to them while remaining in those infinite and boundless world-systems, they approached the lion throne situated above the Śuddhāvāsa palace of the Blessed Śākyamuni.
And he established himself in the Sahā world-system;
standing there, all the hosts of beings, through the Buddha’s majestic power, manifested their respective voices and approached the presence of the Blessed One’s feet to hear the Dharma.
Having bowed to and honored the Blessed One, they sat down in their respective places to hear the Dharma.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Son of the King of the Śākyas, instructed, inspired, and gladdened those beings with a discourse on the Dharma; he gave such a teaching of the Dharma to all those lords of spirits and gods that some among them all conceived the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Some were established in the state of a *pratyekabuddha*, some in the state of a *śrāvaka*; some had seen the truths, and some had realized arhatship. Some, abiding in the ten paths of wholesome action, made this vow:

"May we serve infinite Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, throughout infinite millions of eons, providing them with attendance, medicine for the sick, robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, and requisites; and may we become destined for the enlightenment of a Buddha."

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, knowing the disposition of those beings, spoke this mantra called "Supernatural Knowledge of the Cries of All Beings," by the accomplishment of which all bodhisattvas and all beings would understand the cries of all beings in a single instant, according to their respective spheres of experience as they abide.
And what is that?
Homage to all Buddhas, whose teachings are unimpeded, who abide everywhere without limit, and who possess great compassion.
Oṃ, homage to the All-Knowing One, svāhā!

The ritual procedure for this is as follows: first, having gone to a great forest, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on milk and barley-gruel, or on roots, fruits, and vegetables.
Bathing three times a day and wearing garments of bark, everything else should be performed according to the previously prescribed rules.
Just as it is in the mantra-tantras arising from the Tathāgata family, so too,
having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) until the end of one hundred thousand syllables, one should then begin the practice (*sādhana*) in that very place,
even without a painted cloth (*paṭa*).

Having prepared a fire-pit measuring two cubits in depth and four cubits in width, square on all sides, and having offered water for honor (*arghya*) with all kinds of flowers and fruits, one should sit facing east upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass. Having kindled a new fire and set it ablaze with wood from milk-exuding trees, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* fruits smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter. This should be done three times a day for twenty-one days.
Then, having created a great radiance in the eastern direction, the Buddha, the Blessed One, approaches.
He then touches the crown of the practitioner's head.
If the practitioner has not been touched, at that very moment the voice of the Blessed One issues forth: "You are accomplished; go as you wish," and having said this, he vanishes.

From that time forth, the practitioner becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), endowed with a divine form of great power, following the conduct of a bodhisattva, appearing as one sixteen years of age, moving according to his will, and knowing the cries of all beings; in a single moment he understands the speech of all beings and becomes powerful, able to go wherever he desires.
He lives for five thousand years and becomes an irreversible (*avaivarttika*) bodhisattva.

One will certainly attain success through twenty entries into the practice; therefore, no doubt should be entertained in this matter. Even for one who has already achieved success, one should not recite the mantra [without care]; listen now to what must be understood regarding the beginning, the middle, and the end.
The knowledge of sounds, their power, and their very nature are proclaimed among the dwellers of heaven— at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
That which was spoken is recited in the world and proclaimed in the Middle Country;
it is spoken in Māgadha and the Maṅga regions, and by the best of men in the city of Kāśi.
Just as it was among the people in the middle of Vṛji, Kośala,
and Malla, so did all those kings of the gods choose their mantras according to their own nature.
O Vatsa, behold how Tridaśa is in Madhyadeśa and Daśārṇava;
as it is in speech, so it arises in various regions.
Likewise, such speech was uttered everywhere among all the Tridaśas;
and the Yāmas, the chief gods, as well as the Nirmāṇas and those created by Nirmāṇa.
Then the speech uttered by the speaker moved toward the meaning of the Middle Country;
indeed, all those in Akaniṣṭha were likewise endowed with great supernatural power.
All those excellent deities, dwelling in the realm of form, subsisting on the food of meditative absorption and being serene, at one time spoke these words.
She possesses the intellect of Brahmā and Īśvara; her voice is like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, with a resonance of sweet syllables and a sound like that of the intoxicated cuckoo.
Whatever speech may be meaningful, endowed with steadfastness and profundity,
and likewise entirely free from crookedness, it is highly honored by the vision [of the wise].
Those gods always reside in the Middle Country; they are eloquent, endowed with sweet syllables, and possess smooth, deep voices.
Their speech is like the roar of clouds; one should observe it as such, just as people from the Middle Country are honored even among those in Avanti.
One should know the Mistress of the Gods (Sureśvarī) as being endowed with speech and sound;
she is produced by speech for those who are formless, arising from the sphere of the unconscious (asaṃjñāyatana).
Due to the absence of those [words] and because of their basis, the gods did not resort to speech;
all the most excellent gods were speakers only in the Middle Country.
This speech proceeds as the sign of wealth for those in the Middle Country;
then indeed the gods, and then the earth-dwellers, and the yakṣas of great supernatural power.
Likewise, there are hosts of many beings who have entered the divine womb,
as well as the Karoṭapāṇi gods and those always considered to be the Vīṇakas.
The four great kings also rely upon the four modes of birth;
the thirty gods, the leaders of the deities, likewise rely [upon them] together with Śakra.
Furthermore, Suyāma and all those who are above him,
as well as the most excellent hosts of all the gods— this speech is indeed proclaimed by them.
Just as mortals in the Middle Country are of low, superior, or middling [status],
so too is speech endowed with divinity of low, superior, or middling [quality].
Speech should be known as threefold: inferior, superior, and intermediate;
it should be known as threefold according to its action: inferior, superior, and intermediate.
Likewise, in a temple, speech should be sweet and composed of well-spoken verses; one should understand that such sounds and thoughts are intended for employment in ritual acts alone.
The speech of the Asuras shall always be that which originates from Gauḍa and Pauṇḍra;
just as the cry of the best among the Gauḍa people is adorned with refined sounds,
so too should the leaders of the hosts of Daityas employ such a cry.
As they were wandering about on all sides, the foremost leaders of the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pretas, as well as the nāgas together with the pūtanas—
all those belonging to the faction of the asuras— resorted to the banks of the Vaṅgā and Sāmataṭa.
One should likewise arrange [the worship] for Harikeśa, Kalaśamukhya, and Carmaraṅga in their entirety,
or indeed for all those regions.
One should never separate those three types as they have been described;
one should likewise always proclaim them for the gods and for those who walk before them.
The lords of the hosts of pretas and yakṣas, Skanda, the mātṛs, and the kinnaras,
as well as the nāgas— listen at all times to what has been spoken.
Just as it is in Lāḍa, Odra, Sindh, and likewise in Uttara,
so indeed among all people everywhere should one employ that [method] for them.
Just as the speech of the Nāgas is said to be charming and wise,
so too is the speech of the Yakṣas for those men who dwell in the northern direction.
Just as [the glory] of the Garuḍas is proclaimed by Indra, and that of the Kinnaras is celebrated, so too is it spoken everywhere in Nepāla; let one understand it as it truly is.
Likewise, there is the speech of *pūtanās*, of women dwelling in the womb of the Vindhya mountains,
of men born in the Vindhyas, and of the *mlecchas*.
That speech which was proclaimed for the Pūtanas is known as theirs;
the best of gods chose that very speech which belongs to the Rākṣasas.
The southern regions were created and are celebrated among the Andhras and Lāṭas;
however, for all the Draviḍas, [the speech] always abounds in the letter *ḍa*.
One should identify her by her speech and assign her to the Rākṣasa class;
thus, the family origins of the Rākṣasas should be known to be of three types.
This speech is indeed of three kinds, and one should employ it in a threefold manner;
it should be known as threefold in every respect, and those regional dialects are likewise threefold.
Likewise, one should apply the threefold action to the three regions;
it is to be known as threefold in every respect, for action is traditionally said to be threefold in its sound.
One should appoint another officiant there for all [the rites] equally;
various hosts of spirits are proclaimed as those who dwell upon various parts of the earth.
And humans, who possess knowledge of many diverse languages and are adorned with various sciences,
[teach] human lore expressed through various modes of speech.

The doctrines of various scriptures are to be known; they possess the meanings of various mantras, they have various presentations of ritual actions, and various accomplishments are thereby liberated.
When mortals who are possessed have gathered at the place of the vessel,
they are properly joined by means of mantras applied according to the ritual rules.
One should clearly visualize the deities who have arrived upon the ground through mere speech;
one should then assign the linga, the meaning, the vessel, and the deity themselves.
One should observe the manifestations of those possessed [by deities], both for the sake of the superior and for the sake of the auspicious;
they exhibit the customs of various lands and the emergence of various languages.
One should characterize those who possess various occupations, purposes, and associations by their diverse marks;
those whose speech becomes unstable outside of the Middle Country.
Those men should clearly be known as Mlecchas, for they are devoted to the Mleccha tongue;
they are cruel and terrible Rākṣasas who practice the most fierce of deeds.
Speech abounding in the sound "ḍa" and indistinct with the sound "la" is characteristic of the Mārṣas;
like the speech of those from the South, it is fickle and censured.
And likewise, among these, this speech is proclaimed for the Rākṣasas;
it is manifold in its resonance, and the eldest [speech] belongs to those possessed by the three supreme ones.
Quickly summoned by mantra-practitioners, or having come here of their own accord,
the Mothers and the gods accompanied by grahas seize sentient beings in many ways.
Garudas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras,
piśācas, uragas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and pūtanas— [of these...]
Now, listen as the characteristics of those possessed by them are described:
they speak like barbarians, are flesh-eaters, are Piśācas, and speak indistinctly.
Speech abounding in the letter *la* and ending in the letter *ḍa* belongs to the Pūtanās;
their gaze directed upwards is employed in these rites.
Those who are stingy, cruel-natured, false-spoken, and delighting in impurity—their vision does not go upward; for they possess only half-vision and do not ascend.
Likewise, the speech of the Mothers is endowed with auspicious meaning;
the speech of the Planets and the chief Kumāras is purely [beneficial].
With speech endowed with beautiful limbs and joined with meanings suitable for children,
he was more excellent than all the inhabitants of heaven in every respect through his power.
One should observe the speech of the Garuḍas when they are possessed;
it should be known as being equal to the sound "ga," appearing like the language of the Mlecchas.
"Unmanifest, yet appearing clearly, endowed with fame, and the source of auspiciousness—
this [mantra] beginning with 'suparṇine pāyava' is the destroyer of poison and pride."
For their arrivals are manifold, and their gatherings are of various kinds;
they are to be known by their diverse colors and characterized by their various signs.
O Śubhākara, O Abhākara, you who shine forth, the Naga King Bhakṣaya stands at your feet;
Vāsuki and the other Nagas are righteous upon the surface of the earth,
dwelling there as lords of serpents, endowed with swift speech.
One should designate each being according to its respective body and according to the specific characteristic by which it may be identified.
All these are said to be degrading, for they are indeed characterized by downward vision;
they should be known as belonging to various classes of beings through their various sectarian marks,
and one should understand that they assume various bodies due to actions performed while in various bodies.

Indeed, these various kinds of numerous signs have always been described for mortals on earth who are possessed by [spirits] through various actions performed with diverse intentions and who have resorted to various wombs, as spoken by the one who speaks with many characteristics.
Just as the speech of the gods and the asuras indicates their respective purposes,
so too should one quickly apply that [knowledge] when the earth has attained the state of humanity;
then one should know it to belong to the gods with a well-pleased mind.
They gazed upward and in all directions,
undaunted in mind and free from agitation, joyful and endowed with beautiful forms.
One should observe that all these foremost of gods have pure eyes and unblinking eyes, they are smooth-skinned and have smooth faces, and likewise, they all possess a serene gait.
It should be known that some are seated upon a cross-legged posture on pure ground,
while others, having emerged from the sky, are seated as sky-goers.
The gods beginning with Brahmā are said to be absorbed in the joy of meditative concentration;
above them, in the abode of the most excellent, are those with form and those with manifold forms.
Drawn by the mantras of the mantra-practitioners and dependent upon them,
their radiant form and splendor— those very supports— I shall transform.
Always absorbed in the joy of meditative concentration, with faces of gentle smiles,
they possess pure and wide eyes, and are endowed with many excellent forms.
Then those gods, endowed with splendor, beauty, and form,
who were knowers of supreme wisdom, should instruct him.
Seated cross-legged and constantly meditating like a seer,
they understand through their intellect that possession brings about the accomplishment of desired goals.
One should employ this for the welfare of all mantras as the most excellent means;
O lords of the gods, understand that everything has been thus explained.
For these have been described by the Ṛṣi; they are self-controlled and established as sages. I have thus described the characteristics of the Ṛṣis when they are possessed.
The gods have their gaze directed upward; the *kaśmala* beings have their feet turned upward;
the *vikṛta* and those of fierce form have their hair standing erect, as do the *rākṣasa*s.
Thus, among the Mothers, for whom indeed is this seen?
The flesh-eaters stand naked, yet having been with clothing, they have become unclothed.
With their feet turned upwards, known as the "Deformed," and with hair standing erect,
other seizing spirits roamed everywhere across the entire earth, including its riverbanks.
In a solitary tree, in a cremation ground, at a single linga, on a riverbank,
in temples, on roads, in the valleys of the Vindhyas, and on mountain peaks.
And from the peak of the Snowy Mountain, those of deformed appearance, who dwell in the abodes of barbarians and thieves, were drawn there by mantras and arrived.
They quickly seize those living beings who are averse to purity and proper conduct;
out of fear, they go throughout the entire earth, deluded by the search for food.
In the world, they seize [beings] in many ways, afflicting them with many diseases;
they possess various distorted forms and assume various supreme guises.
They quickly seize the corpses and the urine-sleeping [victims] of living beings;
their signs have been described and their conduct has been clearly explained.
Speech has been previously described on this earth as the first sign;
likewise, the signs of those possessed among human beings have been observed.
O best of gods, understand that these stable types are found everywhere;
likewise, the signs of those possessed by spirits among men on this earth have been described.
He gazes constantly with affection and, moreover, with an unblinking gaze,
toward the most excellent of gods upon this earth, even amidst human beings who are afflicted by passions.
He chose the earth, speech adorned with a multitude of sounds and meanings,
and the dharma conducive to the highest good within the human state, having gone beyond all attachments.
The foremost among the gods has departed; he should be known as the chief accomplisher of all aims.
That which was intended by the reciter has gone into the abode of the awakened mind.
One should quickly inform the mantra-practitioner of all that has been thought;
this is correctly explained as the divine possession upon the earth.
Even those who are without consciousness are always drawn to this earth by mantras;
O gods, do not speak sweet words nor perform sacrifices with haste.
Deprived of their excellence and rendered helpless, they remained resorting to silence;
there was nothing from them in speech, nor in thought, nor even in pride.
Therefore, the practitioner of recitation should not draw him [the mantra] toward oneself, but should cause it to revolve;
for even that which is impossible for others is not so for those mantras born from the Victor.
Nothing exists that cannot be drawn forth by those who are devoted to the meaning of the recited mantras;
likewise, the noble ones are drawn forth by the noble mantras when applied with proper method.
The marks belonging to the noble ones, which arise from the disciples of Khaḍgi,
as well as those of the great-souled Bodhisattvas who abide on the ten stages—
Likewise, they are drawn forth by means of mantras and well-adorned with pledges (samaya),
as well as by the great female messengers (mahādūtī) and the uṣṇīṣas, which are properly joined with the colors of the Sage.
By the wise sons of the Buddha, born from the families of the Lotus and the Vajra,
who are the foremost of mantras called *kuliśa* and possess the great supernatural powers of the Kings of Wrath;
Neither other worldly kings of mantras possessing great supernatural powers, nor those who know the *samaya*, are capable [of this], nor is the supreme Lord of Mantras [capable] among them.
To describe it, to calculate it, or to go to that place where they always dwell— their cause, which is established by karma, is set in motion by time.
Indeed, their cause, which is concentrated in karma, is drawn forth;
and their tantra is drawn forth by means of the commitments spoken by the Buddhas.
Therefore, one should not disturb them with effort, nor should one vainly engage them for some purpose;
those great-souled ones possess great supernatural power and are established upon the ten stages.
Indeed, all the mantras were then unable to go where those Tathāgatas were; likewise, O you who are honored by the immortals, remember my command.
Then all those who know the mantras for the purpose of reciting them shall come;
there will be signs of those who have been summoned, whether they be human or non-human.
Steadfast, with a glossy complexion, and a skillful teacher of profound meaning;
having attained steadfastness and profundity, he would then have few tears.
The eminent knower of mantras, whose mind was unwavering, being questioned,
bound his own mudrā in the sky toward the well-known direction.
For he is the foremost knower of other beings, the teacher of the true meaning of the nature of phenomena;
his conduct is permeated by joy and happiness, and his mind is filled with compassion.
Possessing great zeal and firm resolve, and teaching the meaning of the Buddha’s Dharma,
he may enter a human body for even a moment or a brief instant.
Possessing many forms and beautiful form, may you stand above in the vault of the sky;
may your vision be directed toward the Buddha and the Dharma, and may there be reverence for the Saṅgha as well.
At that time, she remained for only a moment, having assumed a human body—
truthful, high-souled, having conquered anger, and the destroyer of the three humors.
First, the spell was employed, and afterwards it was withdrawn by humans; then they were released again and went wherever they pleased.
Stiff, with motionless eyes and likewise white in complexion,
one possessed by Aṅgaketu becomes firm, deep, and possesses a beautiful voice.
Extremely serene and possessing a great body, he stands upon the surface of the earth,
seated in the paryanka posture, his mind filled with compassion.
Endowed with the lotus seal, that Great Being entered;
he is the Sage Avalokita, the most excellent Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
He has come to the worlds by his own will for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings;
he is the cause of the foremost state of fearlessness.
Holding the supreme *abhaya* mudrā with their hands, standing with their gazes directed upward,
they look upon the practitioner with a compassionate mind.
Some gods had faces with gentle smiles; the Great Being, the Great-Souled One, was adorned with creeper-like eyebrows and acted for the welfare of sentient beings.
One should know him as Avalokita by his serene form in every aspect;
he is the fierce Vajradhara, the foremost Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
Every cruel person is possessed [by this spirit], whose eyes are long and red at the corners;
one should observe that her form has the luster of a blue lotus, appearing slightly upon the body.
Then, while touching the vajra, he binds the mudrā of his own self;
being pleased, the bestower of boons always grants mortals their enjoyments.
At that very moment, a great-souled being of dark complexion appeared;
having spoken with smooth and deep words, he then addressed them.
"For what purpose do you ask this? We shall grant you an excellent boon upon the earth.
They say that the sight of the wielder of the thunderbolt, the lotus-born one, the Invincible, and the Victor is never in vain."
Then and there, the radiant mantras, being granters of boons, shall bestow their fruit;
and the arrival of the Jina there on earth shall be a manifestation for the sake of humanity.
Indeed, these castes have been declared according to the *samaya* and explained as such;
for they arise from the Tathāgata as their basis, or rather, from the emergence of cause and fruit.
The emanation is said to be the image, yet the image does not depend upon the emanation;
for just as there is no reflected image [independent] of both the original object and its emanation.
He has the color of the filaments of a lotus, the color of gold, and great splendor; he possesses the luster of refined yellow orpiment and shines like saffron.
Like the rising sun, with a radiance equal to that of the *karṇikāra* flower—
such is the form found within the reflection that is conjoined with the reflection of the Buddha.
Possessing the resonant sound of Brahmā and the melodic cry of the kalaviṅka bird,
it is employed through the application of logic for the welfare of all beings.
Having seen such characteristics, living beings call him a Buddha;
their lineage and ritual procedure are then those of the Vajra and Lotus families.
But for worldly mantras, one should employ the Lord of Mantras;
everything that was previously explained is adorned with many introductory contexts.
Then the minister, having appointed him to all the mantras,
was instructed in the single abode of the sages and the garuḍas.
One should employ that [mantra] of the ministers through its own characteristic and by means of speech;
then, this [mantra], possessing many characteristics as well as its own characteristic, shall bring success.
For these are indeed sealed by their own mudrās; others are known as *vyantara*.
Thus has been explained the entire process of possession (*āveśa*), which is supreme yet brings suffering to one's own mouth.
This is the sequence of time; one should apply it both in yoga and in the state of possession.
One should also ward it off with mudrās of great power and with mantras as well.
The mantra-practitioner should employ [the mantra] in every way as soon as it has been recited; otherwise, he who acts differently will always be treated like other ordinary practitioners.
Then, one should always protect that vessel with mantras of great supernatural power,
as well as with the hosts of female and male messengers, and the groups of male and female servants.
I also invoke the other worldly deities of great supernatural power, as well as all the various kings of the yakṣas and the yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power.
At that very moment, the mantra-practitioner should summon whatever is desired by the mind;
however, other mantras should never be summoned, nor any other hosts of deities.
But those who have come of their own accord at the proper time, one should employ them;
for all these mantras bring about every success and accomplish all goals.
Therefore, one should not perform other rites, nor should one avoid the ritual invocations (*āveśa*).
When gods of great supernatural power— whether celestial, noble, or earth-born—
are summoned for a trivial purpose, a violation of the sacred pledge (*samaya*) occurs.
Takṣaka gazes fixedly, and Vāsuki dances;
so too do the great nāgas Karkoṭaka and Mucilinda, who is renowned for his glory.
The lords of serpents, difficult to distinguish from Śaṅkhapāla, dance;
namely, Śaṅkhapāla, Śaṅkha, Maṇināga, and Kṛṣṇila.
They wander swiftly through the ocean and fall down again and again;
like serpents, they hiss, their pride of poison fully aroused.
Indeed, these various excellent nāgas—learn of their different ends among them:
some are thrilled as one meditates, while others remain motionless.
Some fall quickly with their limbs restored to health and their hair standing erect; others fall in various forms, and indeed some perform leaping movements.
Ananta wanders swiftly like a lotus in tremulous water;
those born from the womb of the Nāgas are infinite, as are those designated by their marks and dress.
As previously stated,
one who possesses skillful means should liberate those bitten by the great poisons of possession by means of the mantra called Vajra, which belongs to the King of Wrath.
One should join them, ending with the word *kuñjarī*, by means of the mantra itself;
for the mantras specified here as being made of leaves (*parṇin*) are destroyers of poison.
Those mantras, however, should always be employed in all cases involving those bitten by venomous creatures;
likewise, one should apply the remaining ones joined with the obstructors (vighnas), the planets (grahas), and the mothers (mātṛs).
One should perform the ritual for the Grahas, Mātṛs, and Pūtanas by that very same method;
for these symptoms are indeed innumerable among living beings who have been bitten or possessed.
One should employ those very worldly mantras for each respective rite;
indeed, all this has been explained, as well as the characteristics of one who is bitten by a venomous creature.
Now I shall explain the speech of animals as well as that of humans;
listen also to the speech of those in the hells as it is being told.
When all the flocks of birds had gathered together from all sides,
they then established their village dwelling at midday in that human habitation.
Then they shall speak words joined with the sound *repha*, which are terrifying;
those who speak cruelly are called crows (*kāka*), and they say that *kraka* is the letter *ka*.
Then, at dawn, peacocks and cuckoos gather together and cry out, manifesting both fear and hunger.
One should display a fierce appearance and communicate fear therein;
one should speak of hunger and likewise provide food.
I am always seen by all people in the villages;
then they speak these words, terrifying and fearsome.
Within six months, the excellent food known as *grāmyaktā* will perish in that land;
to those [people], water equal to milk should be given, which brings about happiness.
Led by śārikās and parrots, as well as pigeons, green birds, ruddy geese, hawks, and crows— all have come and gathered together.
For when these, having gone into the midst of the village, perform the *mālaya* rite,
they then proclaim this as the cause of a great famine.
Likewise, drought, disease, the onset of many illnesses,
spiders, boils, and the presence of great thieves.
"May you understand, indeed, that in six months it shall come to pass,
when all the flocks of birds have acted with extreme cruelty and great ferocity."
Then, while weeping, he informed all the beings;
as things stood and according to the time, he applied himself to that very task at that moment.
When those who speak the human tongue come to this village dwelling and speak words abounding in the sound "da," just as they do,
one should perform a rite for well-being at night and depart from that place.
When the birds sang together with sweet-sounding notes,
they thus announced that there would be abundance of food and good health.
When one goes toward the south, if deer should go ahead of one,
those deer indicate success that is truly abundant.
Those who dwell constantly among dogs and jackals show you death;
a wise person should not go there when warned by the jackals.
He should quickly enter his own abode; thus he spoke to them then.
Those extremely fierce [beings] shall roar;
the mantra-practitioner should then cause them to run ahead and proceed at that very moment if he desires his own accomplishment.
If a jackal goes from the left to the right as one is traveling,
