one should understand that this success in the journey has been announced by the jackal.
The blue jays and all other birds, as well as the wild animals including jackals, deer, rabbits, and various species of the animal kingdom.
And when they performed circumambulations, he told them all: "Go; you shall become worthy of worship and possess abundant great siddhi."
For all these—snakes, beasts of prey, and the like—are indeed inauspicious;
if they are seen on the path, where or to what place should one go?
They all said this: "There is no success;
turn back! Go to your own abodes; remain healthy in your own homes."
One who knows the mantras should not go there when it has been announced by the serpents;
if he should go, then at that time there will be either agitation or death.
Various living beings belonging to the animal realm— those dwelling in water, those moving on land,
both stationary and mobile— proclaim what is auspicious and inauspicious.
One should know fear from those who are perverted; those who are healthy have attained a state of well-being.
At that time, some among the animals became divine, and humans spoke the language of the gods.
Whatever this [deity] announces through speech, one should apply that very thing accordingly;
by its own signs, it always indicates well-being, and by fierce ones, even great terror.
Then, for the sake of certain determination, the knower of mantras should apply his intellect to the signs,
which are manifold and observed as residing in various wombs.
Likewise, among humans, those who speak with speech that expresses moderate meaning employ the language of the Middle Country,
which is articulated through clear words and meanings.

They say that speech which is human is [Sanskrit], while any other is the speech of barbarians (mleccha); this should be understood as the standard for all regions, as it is established in the Middle Country (madhyadeśa).
It is composed of sweet syllables, heart-pleasing, and brings delight to the ears;
it is not diffuse, arises from the mind, and speaks with an undistracted meaning.
That which is known by human speech and its natural sounds is [meaningful];
all others, being devoid of purpose and consisting of barbarian (mleccha) syllables, are merely speech.
Having spoken of the human [sacrifice] or another, the sacrifice of animals is now described here:
even a lion, having entered a region, would always go toward a preeminent city.
One should swiftly and thoroughly uproot that most dreadful tree;
indeed, the king of beasts will cry out piteously and report it in distress.
One should then know that there is great danger and a deluge affecting the entire country, when the sound "O King of Beasts! is heard within the great city.
One should know there is great danger in the west; in the south, a desire for peace;
and in the east, there will be a wheel [of fortune], which the wise understand as the arrival of a foreign kingdom.
If it occurs in the north, there will be a terrible deluge due to excessive rain;
and if it occurs in all the intermediate directions, it shall announce danger everywhere.
By two or three roars it should be known that there is great danger in the cardinal directions; security is indicated on the right by the lion itself, as thus announced.
Four, five, or seven [syllables] are known as the sixth;
they say that beyond eight, one should employ them as being fruitless.
One who stands to the south is auspicious for the attainment of prosperity both below and above; however,
at the crossroads of a temple or in a place where there is a constant clamor,
one should avoid that vicinity and depart from such a location.
Just as it is with the lion, so should one apply this to all [beings] among all living creatures;
understand now how it is likewise with the *śarabhas* known as *śārdūlas*.
Indeed, due to the absence of humans, the Śarabha always dwells in human habitation out of fear;
however, that most excellent of goddesses is described as possessing pleasing knowledge,
and one should likewise employ her everywhere among the jackals.
When an elephant cries out violently in the eastern or western part [of the city],
one should know that there will be great danger for living beings in those regions.
Crows from the cremation grounds indeed cry out with their beaks upturned;
one should know that great terror is signaled there by these crows.
If a crow cries out most dreadfully from the left side of a minister who has set out and desires to reach a particular place,
a wise person should not go there, as it has been indicated by the crow.
If it cries to the right, it portends excellence; but if it cries in front, one should ward it off.
A knower of mantras should not go there; going thither, he would fall under the power of death.
When a bird cries while eating cow dung, one should know it portends the arising of happiness;
one should predict the eating of delicious food and even the acquisition of cattle.
When that crow, having ascended a temple and remaining there constantly,
cries out at the time of midnight, one should predict the ruin of the house.
When that crow, perched upon a heap of grain, cries out,
it warbles very auspiciously and speaks with sweet speech;
one should know that before long there will be the acquisition of much grain and wealth as its fruit.
When one sees a crow crying loudly at the door of a house,
there will be an attack by thieves with weapons upon that place during the night.

When [the omen occurs] at a milk-tree, it is excellent; at a thorny tree, one fond of strife; and it is auspicious when [the bird] is mounted upon the shoulder of an elephant or on the back of a horse.
Sovereignty rests upon the heads of the wealthy, and prosperity dwells within lotus flowers;
there are various kinds of riches, accompanied by the sweet warbling of syllables.
That which was previously described as beneficial for all signs and meanings should be applied equally to all [cases], whether the sound is harsh or mild.
Śivā is to be known as bestowing fruit from the south in every respect;
all that should be known from Siṃha, and always after Śiva.
Cruel, with inauspicious sounds, miserable, and intent upon death,
[such omens] bring about the non-attainment of happiness from all sides and the failure of the fruit arising from crops.
All these auspicious Śiva-gaṇas are said to be present at evening and at dawn; if they are situated in the southern direction, they are known as the Ekārās.
The first [howl] is declared to be auspicious and most propitious; the second is proclaimed during the night;
likewise, the third should be known as bringing wealth to the king.
In the fourth [house], there is great gain; in the fifth, she is said to bestow sons;
in the sixth, there is the acquisition of wealth; but in the seventh, it is not auspicious for one's existence.
One should know that the eighth is fruitless; beyond that, she is afflicted by fear.
Śivā acts thus there, and those [others] are also countless and bestow what is undesirable.
In the west, a jackal is to be known as a sign of fear from an enemy army;
when there is a second one in a wilderness of famine, it is a howl of cruelty.
In the third [note], there is loss of wealth; in the fourth, the obstruction of life-breath;
and when the fifth note is uttered, the ministers are afflicted by disease.
In the sixth [case], one should know there is the arrival of thieves; however, that [sixth] is auspicious in every respect.
In the seventh, there is a great disease, and in the eighth, it is censured. Beyond that, she speaks while afflicted by fear and distress, or being hungry.
Furthermore, if the howling of a jackal is constantly heard to the north,
one should predict a most terrible disease in that place.
If there is a harsh cry in the second [watch], it will then bring suffering;
in the third, the loss of wealth; and in the fourth, the occurrence of fire.
In the fifth [case], there is a great rain; in the sixth, the king is deposed;
in the seventh, one should predict a great war with a clash of weapons;
in the eighth, one should know it to be fruitless; and beyond that, whatever weeps is of no consequence.

When a jackal howls in the eastern direction during the final watch of the night, one should know that it portends the arrival of a king; however, at the second howl, it portends the arrival of messengers.
In the third [month], death comes from a king, or if it is heard that one has been imprisoned;
in the fourth, suffering arises from thieves; in the fifth, there is the loss of life.
In the sixth [year], illness occurs; in the seventh, there is fear from fire;
in the eighth, one should know it to be fruitless; the remainder is always as previously described.
When the jackal howls in the intermediate direction between the south and the east,
there will be happiness at first, and in the second [watch], it brings prosperity to all people.
In the third [year], there is the production of wealth; in the fourth, an abundance of crops;
in the fifth, a good harvest is predicted; in the sixth, security is ordained;
in the seventh, it should be known that [prosperity] comes from all sides; and in the eighth, it is always fruitless.
When it is always indicated from the southern part toward the middle of the west, it should be known as Dhruvā; it is remembered as both auspicious and most cruel.
By the first [mark], death occurs; by the second, a Brāhmaṇa is slain;
they say that by the third, a Kṣatriya is slain; by the fourth, a Vaiśya;
and by the fifth, those of Śūdra birth.
In the sixth [case], it kills barbarians; in the seventh, thieves;
in the eighth, one should know the learning to be fruitless and there is extreme suffering for those who cry out cruelly;
however, for those beyond counting, it is seen [to prevail].
When she cries out intensely in the northwestern quarter,
it portends a great disease for the king or indicates that a disease will soon befall him.
By the second [mark], the king’s chief elephant, the best of tuskers, is slain;
by the third, death indeed occurs as ordained therein;
and by the fourth, death comes to the chief lords of wealth.
In the fifth year there is loss of wealth; in the sixth, disease may arise;
in the seventh, there will be suffering and danger from all sides;
and in the eighth, one should know that all previous efforts have been entirely fruitless.
One should observe [the jackals] in the north, between the east and north, and indeed in the intermediate directions;
when a jackal howls very fiercely and swiftly,
one should observe it in the north, from the east, in the middle, and in the intermediate directions.
When a jackal howls very harshly and swiftly,
then a living being is slain by death— the chief of the city, a lord of wealth.
With the second [syllable], the practitioner should strike; with the third, he should command the elephant;
and with the fourth, those born of various wombs who live as barbarians or thieves.
In the fourth [period], there will be disease for all people at that time;
in the fifth, the king's son or minister will certainly perish.
In the sixth [year], O lord of men, death has been ordained by Mahādevī;
in the seventh, she shall destroy the kingdom, even if it be liberated, so it is indicated;
in the eighth, one should know it to be fruitless, as has always been explained before.
Thereafter, when such a howling of jackals occurs,
mortals know it to be non-human and a cause of great calamity;
one should depart from that place or provide protection through mantras.
One should perform fire-offering rites (homa-karma) with those renowned for their great power, born from the lotus-family of the Jinas; therein, one should prescribe the rite of pacification (śānti).
For there are many such animal births described in great detail; likewise, understand the various flocks of birds and their cries as well.
Some among those born as animals are of various kinds; some are born from the forms of goats and sheep, while others have deformed bodies, being fierce and harmful to living beings.
Some roam the surface of the earth killing living beings;
some, delighting in drinking blood, wander across the world;
others roam the surface of the earth by the scent of blood.
For these various mothers are indeed the chief of the grahas, yet they are childish;
the grahas are said to be of various other kinds in the forms of boys and girls. They roam throughout the entire earth in every direction in a mere instant.
Some wandered for a thousand yojanas like the wind;
others were disguised as cattle; and some were destroyed by the mere sight of them among living beings.
They all perform various [rites] everywhere upon the surface of the earth,
among beings who are dead or deceased, as well as those who are asleep or afflicted.
Some seize humans for the sake of offerings and garlands;
some traverse the entire world of humans from the surface of the sky.
Those who know all forms should be known as possessing many shapes and subject to transformation;
they should be known everywhere by their signs as being both auspicious and inauspicious in sound.
All results, whether auspicious or inauspicious, as well as all transformations and meritorious deeds,
are to be known through various types of scriptures marked by the true meaning of worldly reality.
It is always inhabited by sages, sons of the Conquerors, those who possess the sword of wisdom, the most excellent Victors,
and disciples of great supernatural power, all of whom have taken refuge in various types of births.

The reality [of the planets] should be known from the scriptures, or through the realization of the traditional teachings, by means of the planets— the most excellent and renowned ones that are marked as signs for the world.
Through the application of various signs and by discerning the destinies and wombs [of beings],
all that is auspicious and inauspicious is to be known by means of both malefic and benefic sign-possessors.
An umbrella, a white banner, my own flesh, and raw meat; then the earth was lifted up, and lotuses, mechanical devices, and cow dung were likewise scattered.
One should recognize curd, flowers, fruit, a woman adorned with garments,
white cloth, and likewise a twice-born man speaking of what is beneficial for one's welfare [as auspicious].
One should recognize [the signs] as a bull, an elephant, and likewise a horse adorned with chowries;
and a lamp placed upon a vessel, filled with grain and yielding the fruit of success.
Or an image of a deity or a twice-born being, always being worshipped by kings;
or the image of a king, or of ministers, intended for the purpose of consecration.
The sound of conchs, kettledrums, and paṭaha drums, as well as the great dundubhi drum;
the ringing of bells and the joyful proclamation of the cry of victory.
Having announced these omens— which bestow the fruits of victory and success— whether uttered by humans or otherwise, as well as the desired [object] that has been presented.
It brings about all prosperity, is secure, desired, and highly honored;
one shall obtain all goals arising from the mind, made fruitful.
Then, one who desires accomplishment should proceed with the recitation of mantras;
one should prescribe success for all sentient beings who have set out upon their path.
This one who is the overseer of the deities, the beloved, born of the lineage, and the supreme—
whosoever should constantly seek his instruction, for him there is the fruit of beholding the Liṅgin.
The gods are always said to possess various forms and signs;
likewise, those who bear their emblems are described as having various dress and insignia.
Whichever one a person perceives as most beloved, from that very one the arising of the fruit occurs.
When those humans on earth engaged in conversation with one another, they uttered many kinds of auspicious speech.
And when others, being full of confidence on all sides,
made their choice, they spoke thus, always reciting auspicious and beneficial prayers:
"May there indeed be security, health, well-being, peace, and the arising of happiness for all."
Dhanin, Devatāmukhya, Sura, Dharmarāja,
and likewise Bhāskara on all sides [are the presiding deities] of the umbrella, the banner, and the flag.
One should always [take refuge in] the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, as well as the Mantra, Tārā,
and the Youthful One (Kumāra), who is golden, radiant, like a mass of fire, and a great festival.
The Jina, Padma, Vajra, Lokeśa, and supreme enlightenment;
likewise the Bodhisattvas, the worlds, Brahmā, and the highest of gods.
For he heard many kinds of words— praiseworthy and well-described— just as one who is about to go forth would hear them so as to attain all of them.
Then others [heard] that sound which is loathed by the world and censured;
for these auspicious birds were intent on chanting as they set forth.
For all of us, yoga is the means for the attainment of the goals of exertion;
everything other than that is censured, as it does not yield the fruit of action.
One should go everywhere only where it is auspicious, and one should not travel where it is inauspicious;
having bowed down to the Buddhas in every direction and performed three circumambulations.

Having prostrated to one's own mantra, the Lord of Mantras, and to one's mother and father— even if they have performed difficult deeds— one should go forth everywhere and point out the auspiciousness therein.
Having diligently honored the preceptors, the chief gurus, and the upādhyāyas,
as well as the excellent preachers of the Dharma and those who are praiseworthy and devoted to their vows,
one should then worship the chosen deity according to what is appropriate.
Then, having bathed and eaten, being confident, at dawn, with his senses subdued,
the practitioner devoted to purity and right conduct should go in all directions; he shall obtain auspicious results from every quarter, in accordance with the fruits of each specific direction.
It is indeed peace and prosperity, increasing longevity and health;
it is declared to be the foremost of fortunes and wealth, fulfilling whatever is desired by the mind.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction of omens, signs, and the knowledge of the cries of all beings, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which is an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avaṃsaka*.
Now begins the twenty-third detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, within the extensive ritual manual of your [teachings], there is a section named 'The Exposition of the Enumeration of Sounds'."
Listen well and attend thoroughly;
I shall speak.

When this had been said, the Blessed One Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he circumambulated him three times. Prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, he rose and spoke thus: "It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would explain it."

Having heard this Dharma discourse titled "The Enumeration and Designation of Sound and Knowledge," there shall arise for all beings who have entered into the practice of mantras a knowledge of the enumeration of all sounds; may the Blessed One, desiring their welfare and seeking their benefit, speak for the sake of all beings this knowledge that transcends the enumeration of all sounds, which brings about the arising of benefit and bestows happiness upon all beings who have entered into the practice of mantras.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! It is well that you consider this matter—the perfection of the welfare of all beings—to be something that ought to be undertaken before the Tathāgata.
Therefore, listen, Mañjuśrī, and I shall explain it to you."
Then Mañjuśrī, having been granted permission by the Blessed One, rose from there and sat down upon his own seat to hear the Dharma, gazing intently at the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire realm of the Śuddhāvāsa deities with his Buddha-eye, entered the samādhi called "The Immovable Beyond the Calculation of All Sounds.
Immediately upon the Blessed One’s entry into that samādhi, great nets of light rays and circles of radiance issued forth in colors such as blue, yellow, white, crimson, and crystal.

Having emerged and illuminated all world systems with a great radiance for the sake of all sentient beings, and having illuminated the abodes of all sentient beings—including those in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, the world of Yama, and the abodes of the asuras—they alleviated the experience of great suffering and then vanished once again into the body of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Having fully awakened all sentient beings, the Blessed One spoke thus:
"Now, this knowledge of sounds is to be mastered, honored for its meaning and its dharma;
and the Knower of the World spoke sweet words regarding calculation itself."
The word should be understood from its base form, adorned with its suffix;
by means of that [base], the word is extensively expanded through the addition of suffixes arising from verbal action.
The indicative mark (liṅga) is to be known through words; there is no indicative mark devoid of words.
Through the manifestation of both word and indicative mark, the purposes of dharma and artha are accomplished.
This is not a case where the word is led by the cognition, nor is the cognition joined with the word;
rather, that entity which arises from the word and the cognition is the word that joins with the true meaning.
Conditionality should be understood as causality; a condition is the arising of a cause.
When there is a condition, that is the cause, which manifests through the application of activity.
Indeed, that which is called *dhāraṇā* (retention) is the basis (*āśraya*) and the condition (*pratyaya*) for knowledge;
through the conjunction of root and suffix, a word becomes the uniter of both the phenomenon (*dharma*) and its meaning (*artha*).
A word is not to be known through its meaning, nor is the meaning intended to be derived from the word;
rather, that word is designated as such by those who know the rules of grammar through its connection with the cognition of the meaning.
The elements were proclaimed in many ways, and the conditions are dependent upon them;
depending on those excellent supports, the sounds then manifested.
That knowledge of words by which mantras are spoken according to their true meaning—
one should not understand that [meaning] merely through the sounds of the words, without the underlying realizations of the mantras.
In the same way, mantras do not arise without a causal condition or a basis;
therefore, one should not seek everywhere for auspicious mantras that lack such a condition.
Know that to be neither a conjunction nor the intended meaning of a word or sentence, which is empty of the cognition of objects and devoid of the [eight] elements.
The movement indicated by the *liṅga* is not born from causes, conditions, or elements;
likewise, accomplishment is joined with the horse, while the *liṅga* is joined with the purpose of the Dharma.

A sentence is a word-unit culminating in an action directed toward a specific goal and location; beyond this, there is a state of manifoldness in speech, for one who would constantly emit such utterance.

The accomplishment of the goal does not arise from mere sound; rather, it is applied to the signs (*liṅga*). The word "mūrdhaja" (born from the head) is said to be sound adorned with the meaning of the syllable *huṃ*.
Everything depends upon conditions and is without a substratum; the palate, lips, and so forth are merely the manifestation of a substratum for speech, according to others.
The object of knowledge is approached through tranquility; there is the unerring method, the intellect, and likewise the reality of the elements, which is adorned with extensive meaning.
The *dhātu* (verbal root) effects the conjunction [of sounds], marked by the meaning of the suffix;
thus, the dental and palatal [sounds] follow, and after that, the labial sound according to the doctrine of Śabda.
O Ṛjikṣu, understand through the power of the mantra how all worlds, along with their emanations and the activities of the elements, reach their final end within the physical basis.
The suffixes (pratyaya) born from verbal roots (dhātu) are always considered to have movement (gati) as their meaning;
both of these are traditionally held to be the basis for the production of the word.
Having analyzed in many ways the mantras that rely upon the scriptures of true reality,
one sees that these sounds and mantras arise everywhere from the source of grammatical inflection.
It should be known that [the power] distinguishes the objects of knowledge; likewise, it is honored through the combination of one and two, resulting in the seventh meaning of the number three.
It should be understood that for human beings, the number is taught as eight more than the incalculable.
They say that the support (ādhāra) is to be known in the worship of the meaning of mantra and tantra;
it is prescribed by rule in the seventh [chapter] regarding the attainment of mantra for those who recite.

The seventh [chapter] should be understood according to its seven meanings; one should apply the various explanations of sequence to the meanings of the seventh chapter, just as the sequence of the seventh is presented.
Sixty-six groups of mantras are proclaimed, as well as their constituent parts;
indeed, due to the connection between the mantras, two indicative marks (liṅgas) are assigned.
Its transformation is said to be manifold, consisting of six types;
one should apply the sixth, which possesses a female sign, among women and the eight mantras.
The five types of mantras are the striving for the sake of the fivefold meaning;
the meaning of the neuter gender mantra is said to be devoid of the purpose of the Dharma.
Those mantras that have issued forth there, applied for the purpose of seizing,
are all known to be life-takers;
they issue from the head through the conjunction of sounds [produced] by the lips and teeth.
Those for whom the tongue is pressed down here, who have obstructed the life-force of sound,
and who are stilled by equal cognition— they are joined with the element of tranquility.
One should apply this very method for those who have reached the end of the suffixes;
however, those verbal roots whose purpose is nourishment (puṣṭi) are words beautifully adorned by the meanings of suffixes.

Those others who have been proclaimed as distinct locations are known to be employed in rites for prosperity (puṣṭi) and in cases of withdrawal (apādāna). Having divided them according to their respective places, they are thus described.
Nourished by words and syllables, O Dhātu, they blossom clearly;
likewise, mantras in the masculine gender are endowed with great power and purpose.

The syllable adorned with the vowel *mātrā*, belonging to the fourth position of the two divisions, is indeed declared at the beginning of the *pavarga*; it is the most excellent and accomplishes all rites.
Born from the combination of the letter *ra* and the suffix, then the beautiful letter *u*,
the central mark which is the *visarga*, and the letter *bha* adorned with the vowel *i*.
They know that speech is the most excellent means for accomplishing all actions and purposes when it is applied to a bodhisattva established on the certain and ultimate path.
They call this the unsurpassed sound, the path of the way of great enlightenment;
by reciting which, a human being will swiftly accomplish all mantras.

Therefore, the meaning of the fifth [vowel] is declared to be marked by a single syllable; those who know always recognize that which is born from the end as belonging to the *pavarga* class and ending with the letter *ma*.
But humans say that the second [type] is the "word" (śabda), which is the foremost in the world;
it is not merely a conjunction of sounds, nor is it adorned by the final release [of breath].
He was born as the preeminent mantra, the most excellent, born from the source of sound— the Buddha, the supreme teacher of the world, characterized as the *chatra-uṣṇīṣa*.
O Teacher of the World, the triad has been taught at the beginning of the group of *ta*-letters;
for these mantras are everywhere foremost, accompanied by sound, and honored by the world.
The first part ends in the vowel *a* and signifies the case endings; the second part is understood to end in a *visarga*.
The middle part ends with the word *liṅ*, and the final part is adorned with the word *śabda*.
They know that word to be the supreme mantra worshipped by the gods,
which is applied to the meaning of "five" in the context of calculation arising from enumeration.
For these, having the fifth [vowel] as their division, possess the meaning of the case-ending *sup* and end in the fifth vowel;
these mantras are said to be infinite, spoken by the infinite Victors.
The mantras are the *uṣṇīṣas*, the hair of the Victor’s head;

they should be known as infinite, the knowers of sound, and sounds that bring about the fulfillment of all aims. One should employ the mantra endowed with sixty-four supreme qualities, joined with sound.
That sound is the most excellent of all; it is the fourfold word-group in which the four combinations of the letter *m* are applied at the end.
Those primary mantras accompanied by sound, which accomplish the purpose known as the parasol, are declared to be the fourth category; they are the divisions born from the source of sound.
The mantras for the purpose of giving have attained a dual gender as their basis;
these mantras are taught by the Lotus-Born One for the sake of nourishment and the attainment of wealth and purpose.
The fourth [chapter] describes the mantras employed in four ways:
the sounds of the four syllables are the head-consonants (mūrdhan), the sibilants (ūṣman), and the palatals (tālu).
It has been explained in the third [chapter] on the designation of sounds;
one should apply it for the sake of expansion regarding the clear elements, and then apply it to the suffix and the gender.
The sound that exists at the beginning and at the end—that sound is honored by the world;
it is the excellent mantra known as the primary, properly applied.
That sound is indeed said to belong to Puṣṭin, arising from the conjunction of the letter A and the Ketu of the year;
it ends with the letter TRA, is the union of the three, and its middle portion is highly praised.
That sound is the foremost of the world's leaders, always preeminent in its meaning; one should employ it for the sake of the true goal, endowed with the elements and possessing the constant form.
And then he chose Uṣas as his wife;
learn of her who was endowed with sweet syllables and joined with the letter *u* in the masculine form.
That sound, the foremost in the world, is called the preeminent mantra;
that syllable is to be avoided in the fourth [vowel], while it is proclaimed [to be present] in the second.
This supreme [mantra] spoken by the Buddha should be known for the purpose of pacification;
it is the third labial, the aspirate, devoid of any other causal object.
Always engaged with the signs of nourishment, joined at the end with the earth element (bhū),
and likewise having an upward-pointing mark that moves— this is the mantra spoken by the Buddha.
Regarding the third [category], based on the case ending, the meaning of the words *bhūti* and *saśabda*:
the first is to be grasped by its phonetic form; it is ungraspable, brings about pacification (*śāntika*), and gives rise to nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
The second [case] is prescribed for the object (karman), and likewise the third for the instrument (karaṇa);
it should be known that the king of mantras is traditionally remembered as being accompanied by both of these case-endings.

They say that the first [member] is the *karma* (object) when there is an agent who is independent; likewise, the Victors, the Lotus and Vajra families, the mantra, and the Lords of Mantra are beneficial.
All those ending in case-terminations (*vibhakti*) and those ending in suffixes (*pratyaya*) born from verbal roots (*dhātu*) should be understood as being for the sake of benefit.
The meaning should be understood through its characteristic signs; it arises from the sentence and from the words.
The mantras are said to be primarily those born from the Victorious One, the Lord of the gods.
The mantras of the Jina and Padma families, as well as those of the Vajrin and the worldly ones,
grasp the transition into the meaningful realm.

The mantras, indicated by the acute (udātta) and grave (anudātta) accents as the means for accomplishing the objects of knowledge, should be understood; they are contained within their characteristic marks, and having offered oblations in the middle, they are likewise raised.
One should apply the sound that is without beginning or end, as well as its mantras;
these are extensive, ending in *n* or *m*, and joined with the letter *r*.
Between the word denoting the object to be bound and the word [denoting the binder], that which is heard with its gender and case-ending,
provided it is accompanied by a svarita accent, one should quickly apply that as the *liṅga* (the binding element) in the mantras.
The capacity for the passing away of preceding words is joined with [the subsequent ones];
that meaning which arises from between the two words is what is known as "sound" (śabda).

Therefore, for the sake of thorough knowledge, that mantra spoken by the Buddha— which is well-formed, described as beautiful, and which brings about the highest good through its fruit— is the supreme means for attaining the goal.
Time is proclaimed as being by nature non-existent, and [the world] as being by nature [conditioned].
The cessation of these two is the peaceful state, adorned with the meaning of the Dharma.
This speech is supreme among others; it is peaceful, meaningful, syllabic, and auspicious.
That which is to be known by practitioners as the mantra spoken by the Buddha is praised;
this is the single-syllable Brahman, adorned with the meaning of the word "Oṃ."
He should be known as embodied, pure, praiseworthy, and bringing auspiciousness;
indeed, he is said to be the accomplisher of welfare, laudable, and endowed with blessings.
That mantra has been declared by the Lords of the World as being preeminent;
it possesses various meanings and primary words, and likewise consists of supreme terms beyond others.
That sound is the excellence of the substratum; those mantras, arising in the sequence of action and time, have issued from the Solar Lineage and are adorned with radiant words and meanings.
The mantras, whether designated as gentle or fierce, blaze within the fire when properly applied;
they are always beautiful in form, possess a gentle mind, and are characterized by the names of the lunar mansions.
The mantras have arisen in this moon, through sounds uttered by the lunar syllables;
they are declared to be well-arranged, stainless, single-syllabled, and supreme.
Renowned for being beyond measure, of beautiful complexion, and possessed of great supernatural power,
these Uṣṇīṣa mantras are declared by the sons of the Victors to be the most excellent.
The applications of various forms remain like the satisfaction of yoga;
they are always serene and pure, as taught by the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
The mantra of the two Pratyekabuddhas is praised for rites of pacification;
these mantras, honored by the meaning of the syllable Oṃ, end with the word Svāhā.
That mantra, which arises from the Pratyekabuddhas, is designated as "one" or "two" for all rites; it should always be employed for the sake of excellence alone.
The end should be known as being joined with *nanta*; the beginning and the middle should likewise be [joined] with *dāśca*.
Mantras possess many *liṅgas*, and their syllables consist of the meaning of many mantras.
Indeed, these elements are known to be manifold and ending in the letter *ṣa*;
the accomplishment of those mantras lies in the first letter of the *ta*-group.
Those born from the mantra-lotus should first strike the end of the letter *ra*; [then recite]:
"O Avalokiteśvara, out of compassion for these, deliver the suffering beings!"
That indeed is the foremost Tārā, while the mantras are truly infinite;
between the sounds *tvaryāccha*, the letter-group *pavarga* is remembered as Māmakī.
In the labial class (pavarga) is the goddess renowned as Kulamātā, the accomplisher of goals;
she is the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī, whose white insignia is well-known for its purpose.
Tārā was indeed described previously; one should employ her for the sake of protection.
A warrior [mantra] abounding in the letter *la* and ending with the word *yodha* arises from those three.
The sound produced from the limbs of the Victor is called the goddess Locanā;
one should apply this sound, which is the syllable of meaning, as the accomplishment in all mantras.
This [practice], renowned throughout the families of the Victors, Vajras,
and Lotuses, should be employed at the very beginning of all mantras for the sake of pacification.
Locanā is renowned on earth; there, the foremost mantra is to be accomplished.
Since everything is to be known as such, one should apply it to the initial mantras.
For the sake of the success of mantras and for the purpose of self-protection,
one should know that the goddess Jinalocanā is everywhere fully accomplished.
Mantras, possessing manifold forms, always resound within the letters from beginning to end, throughout the sixty-four syllables.
One should employ mantras and tantras everywhere among all the classes [of beings];
and in all initial positions, the *tavarga* consonants belong to those two classes.
One should apply all the peaceful [mantras] in three ways as they have been taught;
from the letter *ta* among the natural letters (*prakṛtivarṇa*), those ending in *la* are born from all sources (*sarvayoni*).
Those are the colors for nourishing rites (pauṣṭika), while others are for malevolent rites (abhicāruka);
furthermore, they should be known as threefold: cruel, pacifying (śāntika), and nourishing.
Thus they are of three kinds, for they have been described as threefold and threefold;
those infinite measures of yoga are again threefold.
Know that the gentle syllable is for the sake of peace; one should separate it from that [state].
For some syllables are granters of boons, while others are middling and serve as causes for nourishment.
One should know that the supreme syllable ending in *ha* is fierce and a performer of evil;
thus it is well-adorned by its application and by words as well.
Know that the syllables are indeed infinite, and the deities of the mantras are infinite;
in this way, through this yoga, one should apply the infinite mantras.
They know that mantra-king to be masculine, which accomplishes all aims;
that syllable which is joined with the letter *e* is a sound adorned by a mantra,
and they know that mantra to be neuter— one should employ it in intermediate rites.
That syllable which is accompanied by the letter *i* is known as a mantra;
it is celebrated as being effective for women and other mantras used in minor rites.
All these [mantras] are again threefold here, adorned with various sounds;
one should employ all of them—threefold and of three types—in all ritual actions.
That which is known as the masculine, the person (*puruṣa*), is considered the meaning in every respect; one should know that as the *puruṣa-mantra* and employ it in all ritual actions.
Know that a mantra which possesses a neuter gender-sign is neuter;
it should be employed in all rites for the arising of all happiness and well-being.
Know that a mantra which has a feminine designation is always a woman;
though they perform all rites, one should constantly employ them for protection.
These mantras perform infinite actions, possess infinite purposes, and are the source of all sounds.
Indeed, various sounds and principal mantras combined with diverse tantras—
by practicing in this very way, the mantras will quickly be accomplished without effort.
The cognition of sound, which accomplishes the purpose of all mantras, has been explained;
its enumeration is now proclaimed by the wise.
O gods, know that this was spoken for the sake of the welfare of those who recite mantras;
through the combination of these [factors], it is said to last for up to a hundred [years].
Ten times five thousand is twenty thousand; understand that.
Ten thousand is the number proclaimed as "ayuta."
Ten times ten thousand is always called an ayuta; a hundred thousand is called a lakṣa;
a thousand lakṣas is a koṭi; and the place beyond that is remembered as an arbuda.
Ten arbudas are known as nirbuda, and beyond that is samudra;
ten times that other [number] is known as sāgara, which is applied to the meaning of "ten."
One should know that *akṣobhya* follows, and after that, *niḥkṣobhya*;
the wise proclaim that *devarāja* and *sarva* are celebrated as the *vivāha* [nitya].
Merchants say that when it exceeds ten fingers in width, it is called a *khaḍga*;
the minister knows that as *nikhaḍga*, and also a *khaḍgin* as *nikhaḍga*.
Beyond that is indeed the Śaṅkha; beyond that, however, its number is to be known by me as the final Mahāmāyā in calculation.
Those mortals who know the incalculable [number], and others born of divine origin—
all these are multiplied by five and increased by ten and a half.
Beyond that, what is possible and even what is impossible or difficult to conquer can indeed be accomplished;
when honored and cultivated in the proper place, the wise know this to be the "place of vision."
Then there is the superior and the inferior [knowledge] born from infinite and boundless wombs;
beyond that is the knowledge of the Buddhas, as well as that of the Śrāvakas and the Pratyekabuddhas (Khaḍgins).
The sons of the Buddha are great-souled, and even those gods who know reality have infinite destinies; their reckoning is in the highest station.
The abode of those with infinite knowledge is not for those who dwell upon the surface of the earth;
this has been declared by the ministers who know calculation as the place established in calculation.
For those engaged in the accomplishment of mantras,
the application [of the mantra] at the time of recitation should be known as the authoritative measure for calculation, for the purpose of the recitation of the mantra.
For those who recite the meaning according to the prescribed rule, the measurement of the number of recitations is the means of accomplishment;
one whose mantra is perfected may enter the Vindhya mountains, while one who has not yet achieved perfection should remain in the cow-pen for their own benefit.
Likewise, one who has perfected the mantra may always go to the Himavat mountain;
for that embodied being who has perfected the mantra, movement is as he desires.
If the minister were to go to the Himalayas for the sake of recitation,
he would not withstand the unbearable army nor the coolness of all dualities.
The attainment of value is declared to be achieved with little effort and little exertion;
[this occurs] on the slopes and ridges of the Vindhya mountains, which abound in many flowers and fruits.
He sent him to the Vindhya mountain for the purpose of properly reciting the mantra;
therefore, the Vindhya was always designated as the place to be resorted to for the sake of japa.
Therefore, one should know that success is found in the mountain caves of the Vindhya range;
on the southern side of the Gaṅgā, one should apply everything within the Vindhyas.
One should point out the Himavat mountain in the northern region;
from there, one should accomplish mantras as they have been declared for those who are pure according to their desire.
The Siddha goes to the Himavat, the Siddha goes to the slopes of the Vindhya;
he dwells in mountain caves and along their banks, in the abodes and mansions of the caves.
Whether on the bank of the lord of rivers or constantly upon its shores,
one should accomplish mantras everywhere in a manner that is pleasing and beneficial.

Thus concludes the twenty-first chapter, the detailed exposition on the teaching of the names and the calculation of the knowledge of sounds, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which is an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avaṃtamsaka*.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed all the constellations, planets, stars, and luminaries included within all world-systems, situated in every direction, who were possessed of great supernatural power and most excellent, summoning them with mantras.
"Listen, O noble friends! In order to demonstrate the power and the words of your own authority over all planets and constellations, may you accomplish the purpose of all mantra-activities.

In this King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*) within the teaching of Mañjughoṣa, and in other King of Ritual Manuals hereafter, may you apply yourselves with zeal. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni [spoke]:
'The entire conduct of the planets shall be carried out for the sake of sentient beings and for the sake of a single purpose.'"
I, the All-Knowing One, shall explain everything regarding the meaning of the mantras for all those who recite them, as it has been fully established.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and Kṛttikā—
these three lunar mansions are indeed marked by the planet Aṅgāraka (Mars).
In those [months] declared for the sign of Aries, success does not arise;
rather, only superior, middling, or inferior success is seen.
One who is obstructed by malefic planets should not travel on any path whatsoever.
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, and Ārdrā are declared to be the lunar mansions; Punarvasu, Puṣya, and Aśleṣā are likewise proclaimed.
Both Maghā and Phalgunī, as well as Hasta and Citrā;
likewise Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla.
The two Āṣāḍhas are auspicious and highly praised, beneficial for those who recite mantras;
the constellations Śravaṇa and Dhaniṣṭhā are for cruel rites.
Both the constellations Śatabhiṣaj and Bhadrapadā are causes for success;
one born under Revatī becomes illustrious, skilled in battle, and wise.
But the remaining principal constellations are not born in this lowest age;
Abhijit and Sucarita alone are proclaimed as meritorious for the attainment of success.
Tiṣya, Upapada, Kaniṣṭha, Niṣṭha, Bhūta, Satya, Loka, and Āloka are likewise proclaimed.

Aniruddha is indeed the bestower of enjoyment and the giver of auspiciousness, while he is also the one who restrains. He is the king who bestows fame, the sovereign of splendor, and likewise the ruler of the world.
The constellations are said to be manifold, numbering sixty-four thousand;
yet their power does not manifest in this time, this most debased age.
It was taught solely for the sake of knowledge in the *Kalparāja* that brings about happiness;
indeed, during that time, in the Kṛta Yuga, sentient beings possessed the power of self-origination.

All were capable of traveling through the sky and were free from old age and death. At that time, in the first age, the most excellent of yugas, there were no constellations, no sun or moon, no stars, no gods, and no asuras in the world.
There is indeed no name, nor lineage, nor lunar day, nor birth;
there is no fasting, nor mantras, nor any action, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
These beings wander according to their own will; there is neither food nor eater.
Indeed, these sentient beings are pure, free from affliction, and equal in many ways. It is only within this [world-system] that the designation "receptacle world" functions.
Then, drawn by their previous karma, they go to the earth,
where there are divine palaces situated upon the ground, along with gods and asuras.
From that, they arise in the intermediate [age];
when the intermediate age has arrived, they have taken recourse to human bodies.
For those greedy for food and drink, that radiance is destroyed;
indeed, there is a harshness in their limbs, and their conduct becomes a mixture of auspicious and inauspicious.
From that time on, the days and months were indeed obscured by the light of the planets;
from then onwards, whatever knowledge of the luminaries exists,
all of that was created by me, capable of bestowing grace upon sentient beings.
In ancient times, this wise one indeed assumed the guise of a rishi, then the guise of Brahmā; moreover, having resorted to the body of Maheśvara, he then took on the guise of Viṣṇu,
and further, having assumed the form of Garuḍa, [he acted] against the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Vāris.
"Whichever body one is born into, that very body shall be a *paiśācī* form; this I declare.
Yet, Bodhisattvas are skilled in those various births."
By the power of rebirth, for the sake of the purpose of the bodhisattva conduct,
I myself was that very bodhisattva in that former age.
Enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, I was indeed a fool in the past;
for whatever skills, crafts, or activities exist in this world, [I knew them not].
In the treatises, as well as in ethics and the Purāṇas, there are the Vedas and grammar,
prosody, astronomy, mathematics, and the ritual manuals (kalpa).
False knowledge, as well as true knowledge, and likewise false conduct—
all such things have been sung by me in the world for a long time through all the scriptures.
Yet, I did not attain that knowledge by which this sage has indeed become so tranquil.
For the sake of the cause of awakening and for the purpose of liberation, and likewise for the cause of release,
I am imprisoned in the jail of saṃsāra and am not yet freed from my karmas.
Buddhahood is stainless, peaceful, the state of nirvāṇa, the immovable ground;
it has been rightly attained by me, that which was desired for a long time.
By means of the proper methods and through my own actions, I have now personally reached it with full justification.
The primordial wisdom of Svayambhū, previously revealed by the Victors, has been attained;
I do not see any such state that can be obtained through an external path.
Wandering in the wilderness of saṃsāra, I failed to obtain the knowledge such as this of the Self-Existent One, which is so difficult to find even for the sake of awakening.
Now I have attained Nirvana, devoted to what is auspicious and engaged in my duties;
however, this compendium of treatises shall indeed be spoken by me alone.
And no causes for accomplishment are found apart from karma;
this long thread of saṃsāra is bound and constrained by karma.
This is the greatness of its power: it ripens both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
these [planets] merely indicate the results of the stars, planets, and celestial bodies.
No such sign is seen among other humans who are unrighteous;
for this very reason, she is joined with the planets and so forth, and is to be favored in matters both auspicious and inauspicious.
The four world-protectors are proclaimed to have become water, earth, wind, and fire as their luminous sparks;
these great elements are the causes for the gathering of all beings.
When they are indeed impelled by the mantra for the sake of gathering sentient beings,
the accomplishment of the mantra arises through the regulation of their timing.
In those recitations, one must indeed strive to protect [the mantra] from both auspicious and inauspicious influences;
it is held in high esteem by the leaders of the world, including Śakra and the other lords of the gods.
At that time, at the end of the age,
those mantras conceived for that period will achieve accomplishment through effort, even in the lowest of ages.

For this very reason, Mañjughoṣa, the great wise one, who was conceived as a youth by the Lords of Jinas, wanders through this entire world in the form of a young boy, capable of bestowing grace upon sentient beings.
At that time, the accomplishment of Mañjughoṣa will be seen;
at that time, there will be knowledge of the stars and astrology.
In that lowest of ages (yuga), twenty-seven lunar mansions, the muhūrtas, and the twelve zodiac signs are proclaimed to exist at that time.
Those planets, having indeed divided the constellation-masses among themselves,
resort to all their various broad domains individually.
Beings are established in the [three] heaps; those born of delusion are indeed perverted, giving rise to the fruits of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Therefore, those zodiac signs, which express karma, repeatedly determine the auspicious and inauspicious journey toward accomplishment for sentient beings.
In the Jātaka stories, however, the asterism Rohiṇī is assigned [to this birth]:
one who is illustrious, endowed with patience, having many sons, and long-lived.
Likewise, he who is born in the sign of Taurus always holds the office of commander-in-chief;
such a person is crushed under the weight of his own prosperity.

One born under Mṛgaśiras will be a knower of the world, righteous, and pleasing to behold; likewise, one born under the portion of Kṛttikā will always rule the earth as a sovereign of the three oceans, provided he relies upon a clearly manifest horoscope.
Furthermore, if the birth [chart] is complete and the planet is marked by Jupiter, the person will become a king over a limited territory, a fortress, or a single region.
He will enjoy the entire earth on all sides;
his sovereignty is ordained for fifteen years.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, and a portion of Kṛttikā are prescribed;
this lunar mansion is indeed capable of providing profit through trade and the attainment of wealth.
If one is endowed with a favorable birth-chart, there will be an abundance of power and enjoyments;
his birth occurred under a lunar mansion when the solar disc was red.
When it has set, as is constant, a transformation occurs within him;
he becomes cruel, impulsive, and a speaker of untruth.
Then, he appears on the surface of the earth with thin skin and a reddish hue;
his lifespan is declared to be the duration of a blink of an eye.
And for that which is born in this interval, these are the details of its qualities; yet the birth of these is proclaimed to last for no more than the duration of a finger-snap.
Therefore, when birth is mixed and confused, various kinds of beings are born who have fallen from their proper caste and are devoid of the influence of the planets.
The accomplishment of their rebirth is mixed, as is the excellence of their enjoyments;
for this very reason, they are not born among those [beings] described as being of the same class.
Thirty Jātaka stories have been told, which bring about the arising of both auspicious and inauspicious fruits;
for among these, there is indeed a cruel birth marked by the planet Aṅgāraka (Mars).
Furthermore, when one is aspected by the planet Jupiter, he is born with a large belly, a pleasant appearance, wide eyes, and is always sweet-spoken and steadfast.
When the sun has risen to the height of a yoke, and the two deities, the moon and the sun, have both appeared,
a birth occurring at such a time is always considered a perfectly auspicious *jātaka*.

But when other birth-charts are constructed with errors, the results derived from the observation of planets will be erroneous; thus, the auspicious and inauspicious outcomes of a false birth-chart are likewise false.

The production of false fruits and the arising of right knowledge and virtue depend upon the realms of existence and the modes of birth; they are established within the field of birth according to the specific destiny and womb.
The pure Mahāsattva, Bhārgava, is marked by the planets;
Ārdrā and Punarvasu are said to be the portion of Āśleṣā.
This man who has been born is a great renouncer, yet he is deceitful and impulsive;
he is always attached to women, greedy, and a hater of wealth and misfortune.
One who approaches the wife of another is born dark-complexioned or even black in hue;
he is born smoky-colored, fierce, and indeed fond of sexual intercourse.
This Śanīśvarī is born depending upon the zodiac sign of Maithuna;
she moves there as Śani, day and night, again and again.
This Jātaka, which arises from the manifestation of power at midday,
is declared to have the same duration as that which was born at that time.
In the asterism of Puṣya, as well as in Āśleṣā, the attainment of wealth and the manifestation of sovereignty upon the earth are ordained.
This Kaṭaka constellation is a heap joined with Jupiter, possessing great supernatural power;
yellow in color, it is proclaimed as the foremost among those born under its influence.
Likewise, one born at midnight is always declared to be a *jātaka*;
however, if a being is considered to have been born at that specific time according to the measure [of the moment], [the result is as follows].
For this indeed accomplishes all aims by means of causes seen in the ritual rules;
it brings about the attainment of sovereignty and wealth from childhood onwards.
Then, one who appears with a yellowish or dark complexion, endowed with excellent color,
devoted to purity and right conduct, illustrious, and confident, is born.
Maghā, Phalgunī, and a portion of Uttaraphalgunī constitute that solar field;
it is ordained as the zodiac sign of Leo.
Those born there will be great heroes, devoted to eating meat;
taking refuge in mountain strongholds, they will indeed exercise royal sovereignty.
If the birth [ascendant] is perfected, situated in a field, and fixed, they rise just as the sun does; thus is the "birth" (jātaka) proclaimed among these.
A man born under the constellations Uttarā-phalgunī, Hasta, or Citrā will be brave and a thief.
If one who lacks self-restraint commits adultery with another's wife, he may hold the office of commander-in-chief;
yet if he is endowed with the qualities of his birth, he will certainly become the cause of a kingdom.
For this [constellation] is indeed the sign of Virgo (Kanyārāśi), wherein these stars are situated;
both of these shall be its lord, or perhaps another may be its lord here at some time.
Among these, Tārakā is the most excellent; a fierce planet guards her, while Saumya, Punarvasu, and Bhadra always protect her with joy.
Birth is determined by the completion of midday; among these, the birth-chart is observed in the portion of Citrā, Svātī, and more than half of Viśākhā.
The zodiac sign of Libra is the moon that moves through the bodies of embodied beings for the sake of supreme goals;
this is the field of Aruṇa, where Saturn and Venus have their abode.
Indeed, for those born under the Jātaka [constellation] situated in these [lunar mansions], at the end of the watches of the night,
mortals born therein will always be devoted to much drinking;
they will be modest, possessed of shame, and honored by the great assembly.
In some cases they obtain a kingdom, in some cases enjoyments, and in some cases stability;
in the *jātaka* it is seen that they are uncertain, devoid of motherly care, and lacking childhood.
If endowed with a favorable *jātaka*, they have many offspring and the arising of happiness.
One born under the lunar mansion Anurādhā is preeminent in accomplishing tasks;
he is friendly by nature, possesses many friends, and is always brave and courageous.
It is said that a person born under Jyeṣṭhā is indeed fierce in this world;
such a person becomes one who endures much suffering and is cruel by nature.
They say that Scorpio is a zodiac sign; one born under it is always sharp and impetuous.
It is declared that birth and the *jātaka* (astrological horoscope) pertain to these very signs.
Likewise, if a creature is born when the sun is at midday,
he will certainly become a king, fierce and victorious in battle.
At that very moment, he assumes the form of a young boy;
he who is called Aṅgāraka is the auspicious deity of the earth.
For this very reason, he enjoys the earth, and his own son likewise protects it;
however, for others, it is the opposite. Birth itself is auspicious or inauspicious:
one is born long-lived, radiant, and high-minded.
For one born under Anurādhā is indeed highly wise and affectionate toward friends.
This is the domain of Aṅgāraka (Mars), which is always interspersed with other planets.
One born under the Mūla constellation, as well as under Pūrvāṣāḍhā, is likewise [of such nature].
In the northern portion of Āṣāḍhā, the zodiac sign of Sagittarius (Dhanu) is proclaimed;
this is the field of Jupiter, and one born therein becomes his [Jupiter's] progeny.
Whether at midday when the sun is shining, or indeed during the nights of the moon,
they say that for one who is born for the sake of sovereignty, this is his *jātaka*.
One might destroy one's own family at its very root; therefore, it is said that effort is auspicious. One born in the middle position will undoubtedly obtain enjoyments.
But when his youth has passed away, like the orb of the sun,
the king becomes old in age, yet possesses great enjoyments and vast wealth.
One who possesses power is renowned in low-lying regions, but not in other lands;
however, various other Jinas are seen to be the opposite of that.
Likewise, Uttarāṣāḍhā would be [the constellation], and Śravaṇa is proclaimed;
Dhaniṣṭhā is the most excellent nakṣatra, and its zodiacal sign would be Capricorn (makara).
This is the domain of Saturn, marked by other planets as well;
it is seen constantly present on the surface of the earth in the rites of birth and so forth.
Those born during the first, last, or middle portions of the night as it passes away are seen everywhere to possess great enjoyments.
Those who dwell in low-born families become protectors of the earth;
they are fierce, with a dark complexion, or they possess a swarthy hue.
Those with eyes red at the corners, who are gentle yet brave and always daring,
indeed exercise sovereignty over a region abounding in water.
For those who are long-lived are childless, enduring much suffering;
others, however, are the opposite—people who are poor and afflicted by disease.
Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and likewise Pūrvabhādrapadā—
this portion constitutes the zodiac sign known as Aquarius (Kumbha).
This field is always inhabited by the chief of planets,
as well as by mixed lunar mansions and by the wise Śukra alone.
Birth among these occurs at night and is seen at dawn;
this birth is excellent and constant, due to the purity of conduct in the world.
In the matter of cruel deeds, he is declared to be wise;
he shall experience various riches and enjoyments upon the surface of the earth.
But others different from those are the opposite: people who are poor and afflicted by disease;
and the lunar mansion Bhadrapadā as well as Revatī are likewise proclaimed [to be unfavorable].
In the portion of Pūrvabhādrapadā, established in the sign of Pisces,
she is constantly present in birth ceremonies and is seen everywhere.
During the middle watch of the night, or when the sun has risen during the day,
or when half a watch has passed and the sun has slightly risen at midday.
When only a small portion has emerged and one hand's length remains, it is born at a single time;
it is pure, exceedingly white, and its whiteness is perfectly joined.
The gods who observe the vow of celibacy know that as the field of Śukra;
it is presided over by planets that are yellowish-white in luster. That field is eternally conducive to the highest good, righteous, and supremely auspicious.
Those mortals born under these [asterisms] shall have all their limbs exceedingly beautiful;
they will desire sovereignty, possess great heroism, and be firm in their affection for kinsmen.
Long-lived and possessing great wealth, they will dwell in low-lying regions;
relying upon the eastern direction, they shall always attain prosperity.
In that forest region, no growth occurs for them, nor does it cease;
fish are never seen at all moving about the roots,
yet the floods of water increase where the dwellings of the sages are situated in the midst of the waters.
Among them, the birth [signs] are proclaimed, and the zodiacal signs (rāśi) themselves are proclaimed;
for mortals born under those [signs] indeed thrive exceedingly in low-lying regions.
The rulers of the earth, possessing great enjoyments, are always established in the eastern quarter;
the most excellent planets, beginning with Jupiter and ending with Saturn, are observed there.
Those born in these [signs] undoubtedly exercise sovereignty over the east;
the zodiacal signs have been described in many ways, and the lunar mansions in numerous ways.
The chief planets are indeed of three kinds, but not so at present after a long time;
therefore, humans possess knowledge [only] of the fifteen lunar days (tithis).
Thirty days are proclaimed to be a month;
fifteen days and nights constitute a fortnight (pakṣa), and two fortnights are called a month.
Then, twelve months are proclaimed to constitute one year;
this is the measure of time determined for the end of the age (yugānta).
In the time when the Kali Yuga has arrived, this number has been proclaimed;
likewise, the lifespan of human beings is declared to be one hundred years.
Within their year, the seasons have been proclaimed;
they are declared to be of three kinds—at the beginning, at the end, and likewise in the middle.
In this world of humans, the lifespan may be high or low in between;
for them in this human world, portents have been proclaimed.
The lifespan of human beings is proclaimed to be one hundred years; however,
the non-human beings in this world of living creatures run hither and thither,
wandering here and there, truly terrified and afraid.
Whenever war breaks out between the leaders of the gods and the asuras,
they then cause the outbreak of diseases in this world of men, as well as comets, earthquakes, meteors, thunderbolts, and lightning.
The quarters of the sky are indeed smoky on all sides, and a comet is visible;
the orbs of the moon and the sun appear like headless trunks and stakes.
A hole is seen in the sun and even in the moon of great supernatural power;
indeed, in this way, various forms are seen again in many ways.
There will be famine, loss of longevity, and likewise the destruction of the kingdom;
there will be the death of the king and great danger for ascetics.
And for all the worlds, there was a terrifying event in that region when the earth shook under the asterisms of Maghā, Aśvinī, and Punarvasu.
At that time, the Middle Country will be oppressed by thieves and violent men,
and the great kingdom will be plundered by those residing in the Deccan.
When a terrifying earthquake occurs during the asterisms of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, or Mṛgaśiras, fear arises among the people.
When kings die resorting to the western direction,
then even those living in border regions who subsist as barbarians or thieves [will perish].
Likewise, O Lord of Men, those who dwell upon the slopes and in the valleys of the Vindhya mountains were also afflicted at that time, overwhelmed by disease.
O people, the arising of enemies for those [kings] occurs through mutual superiority when the moon is in the moist Puṣya nakṣatra, or in Āśleṣā, or in Phalgunī.
Both [of these] are preceded by Uttara;
when these asterisms are in motion, kings of men [suffer].
And another, by obstructing the sunlight, causes all things to become disordered;
slaughter, imprisonment, and afflictions arise, and famine occurs among the people.
If an earthquake occurs when the moon is in Hasta, Citrā, Svātī, Anurādhā, or Jyeṣṭhā,
it will be a great calamity for this world-receptacle.
The Mlecchas dwelling in the Himalayas and the bandits from all directions,
as well as those residing in the valleys of the Khaśas under the ruler of Nepal, [were subdued].
All the kings there will be mutually antagonistic;
they will all be inclined toward war, of this there is no doubt.
This earthquake occurs in the Mūla constellation, as well as in the two Āṣāḍhas—the Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā;
indeed, such tremors of the earth are observed specifically within these constellations.
Previously, the regions and people of Pauṇḍra and Odra were capable of changing their forms at will;
the king who is the lord of Vaṅgāla shall die—of this there is no doubt.
The illustrious lord of the Gauḍas will be besieged by foreign kingdoms;
he will either suddenly fall ill or, in some cases, death will occur.
Likewise, the worlds as far as the ocean's edge, situated along the banks of the Gaṅgā,
will all be submerged in water and tormented by many diseases.
If [a child] is born when Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣā, the two Bhadrapadas, Pūrvā or Uttarā [Āṣāḍhā], or Revatī are in the ascendant;
At midday, there was a great earthquake; the entire earth, along with its mountains and forests, trembled, causing the world-receptacle to shake.
All of them, scattered and distributed, are always seen in the sky,
as well as the regions of the northern path and those situated in the western region.
Throughout the southern region, in every direction,
there dwell excellent kings, abounding in prosperity, who obstruct one another.

During great plagues of sentient beings, during famine, and during the division of kingdoms; at dawn, during auspicious peace, and during the trembling of the earth for embodied beings—[in these times, one should practice].
Then, at the time of the ultimate limit, a violent trembling arises;
and even more extreme than that, there will be those intent on the slaughter of the people of Magadha.
The lands of Aṅga will be afflicted, as will the king of Magadha;
thereafter, when the sun has reached its zenith at midday and is in the afternoon.
If this earthquake were to occur throughout the entire surface of the earth,
all renunciants would constantly encounter the onset of disease.
They are constantly afflicted by diseases such as fever, illness, colic, and eruptions;
however, for seven royal reigns thereafter, they will experience prosperity.
If an earthquake occurs when the sun’s darkness has diminished,
the Brāhmaṇas— who drink the Soma juice and are the most excellent among the four castes— will perish.
The mantra-practitioner suffers and is even destroyed, as is the king— of this there is no doubt—
as well as the most virtuous domestic priest, the minister, or any servant of the king.
Or another who is preeminent among those observing the vow, skilled in the mantras and the meaning of the mantras—
whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or likewise a Śūdra.
Though he be skillful, learned, and possessed of knowledge regarding the principles, meanings, and ethics of the scriptures,
he is struck down, perishes, or is even tormented by disease.
One who possesses mindfulness, knows the truth of the scriptures, and reflects upon the *itihāsas*,
is swiftly struck down by disease, like a tree by a thunderbolt. Then, when the sun has set, he is asked even more excellent questions.
If an earthquake occurs in the afternoon or at the end of a cosmic age (yugānta),
sentient beings will become confused and resort to animal births,
whereas humans, who are the leaders of the world, will become supreme lords during that earthquake.
If an earthquake occurs during the first watch of the night,
a great rain is seen that results in the falling of stones.
Then, indeed, when the night had diminished and the earth began to tremble,
having seen that sign, a great wind and rain occurred.
Then, at the end of the night-watch, a terrible deed is seen;
one should know that there will be the arrival of a foreign army and a western king.
Then, when a second tremor arises,
there will be death, disease, foreign invasion, and severe abdominal ailments.
He agitates the diseases arising from bile and phlegm in living beings;
he terrifies the spirits and likewise causes them to migrate from one region to another.
Then, during the second watch of the night, an earthquake occurs;
from that one should know a great wind will arise, which will shatter trees and temples.
There is no doubt that it causes the towers and peaks of mountains to fall;
it swiftly brings down delightful monasteries, dwellings, and palaces with their arched gateways, as well as the abodes of spirits and those belonging to the animal realm.
If an earthquake occurs at the time of midnight,
the foremost and preeminent kings will be slain; then the sovereign of the eastern regions will perish,
or his son will be destroyed, or one should predict a famine.
Then, during the final watch in the middle of the waning phase, a tremor arises throughout the entire surface of the earth; this indicates peace and health.
Then, at the end, when an earthquake occurs at midnight,
the coastal regions and the Middle Country will be afflicted by disease under the king;
they shall die from terrible sufferings, being mutually antagonistic.
When the third month arrives, which brings happiness to the simple-minded,
mosquitoes, gadflies, moths, and all thieves shall perish.
If there is an earthquake at dawn, it shall bring long life, health, and abundance;
however, one should recognize that there will be conflagrations throughout all the cities.
When an earthquake occurs at sunrise in the sun, then,
whether in the Middle Country or everywhere else, there will be a sudden onslaught by thieves;
at that time, the death of the king is seen to occur after seven days.
In whatever place and at whatever time a powerful earthquake is observed,
the auspicious and inauspicious activities are seen to manifest in that very place at that time.
One should predict a meteor, a thunderous crash, and an earthquake occurring at the same time;
when a white meteor blazes, it shall destroy that which is crooked.
A white color is always auspicious and bestows good fortune;
a red color is most terrible and indicates a conflagration.
A smoke-colored or black [bird] portends the death of the king;
likewise, one that is yellow, tawny, or of mixed colors [indicates the same].
Then one should indicate a mixed earthquake as well as a portent; and when a thunderous crash occurs, one should predict its effects in whichever direction it is proclaimed.
If it is the middle [note], then it is proclaimed to belong specifically to the Middle Country;
being accompanied by its own tone and sweet, it indicates security and health.
In this world, the sound of the drum is exceedingly cruel and terrible, yet it brings auspiciousness;
though it is fearsome and most terrifying, one should predict famine therein.
These and other such applications of the planets should always be performed;
one should then carry out rites for accomplishment under these auspicious lunar mansions.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Puṣyā, both Bhadrapadās,
Revatī, and Anurādhā are praised for the time of recitation;
indeed, mantras are perfected during these [asterisms] and they grant the fulfillment of one's purpose.
And the mandala itself should be drawn with these very stars,
which possess a yellowish-white luster and are the foremost among the planets and lunar days.
Indeed, these lunar days are auspicious; likewise, on the fifteenth day, known as Pūrṇimā, one should not go on a journey, but rather should draw the maṇḍala.
The first, third, fifth, tenth, seventh,
and thirteenth days— on these, O lords of men, let the journey be undertaken; for travel by vehicle on these days is praised as bringing auspiciousness to all living beings.
One should not draw the mandalas of all mantras, nor those of the tantras and mantras;
for in such cases, the mantras will certainly not be accomplished, as they are declared to be causes of obstacles.
Success in the journey comes from the fire oblation; the lunar day is determined by the conjunction of the most excellent planets:
Jupiter, Venus, the Moon, and Mercury are the best for all rites.
These four excellent planets, when conjoined with the lunar days, always bring about success and auspicious journeys in this world upon the surface of the earth.
Free from malignant *ariṣṭa* signs, and devoid of cutting, breaking, or stretching,
one should calculate the days only when [the body] is entirely free from these defects.
One should employ exactly twelve muhūrtas at that time;
Śveta and Maitra would be thus, and they are proclaimed as having red eyes.
Raudra, Mahendra, Śuddha, and Abhijit which is very auspicious;
Bhramaṇa and Bhrāmaṇa are likewise proclaimed as bestowers of welfare.
Then there are Saumya, Varada, and he who is celebrated as Śubhaprada;
Soma and Varada as well—these are the twelve moments (kṣaṇas).
The characteristics of the thirty muhūrtas have been declared in many ways;
likewise, rain may fall on the tenth lunar day, as well as during the night of the fourteenth.
The eighth and twelfth days are indeed to be avoided;
one engaged in calculation should begin from night during the dark fortnight.
But the cause of obstacles for these is Vināyaka, who is the fourth;
this is the proper calculation, and this is proclaimed to be the [correct] time.
The opening and closing of the eyes, a finger-snap, and a swift movement—
this is the measure of time, which will be explained in detail once again.
A hundred snaps of the fingers are proclaimed to be one *nāḍikā*;
four *nāḍikās* are called a *ghaṭī*, and four *ghaṭīs* are known as a *prahara*.
A day consists of four watches, and nights are likewise proclaimed by these [same measures].
Thus, when joined with eight of these, a full day and night (ahorātra) is defined.
Ten openings and closings of the eyes are reckoned as a mere moment (kṣaṇa);
ten tālas in measure are likewise said to be a mere moment.
Ten *kṣaṇas* are said to constitute a *muhūrta*, as determined by the sages;
four *muhūrtas*, however, are reckoned as a *prahara* by those who know the mantras.
One should determine this measure of time for the three junctions;
likewise, one should apply it during the time of fire-offerings, recitation, and the attainment of accomplishment.
Whether during sleep or while awake, whether at the time of bathing or drinking throughout the day,
or indeed throughout the day and night— the term "day" (divasa) is proclaimed to apply to all of this.
Fifteen days are proclaimed to be one fortnight;
those expert in calculation say that two fortnights constitute a month.
In the same way, the moon is swallowed by Rāhu again after six months;
therefore, the term "year" (varṣa) is proclaimed [to consist of] twelve months.
Then, for twelve years, that is called the "Great Rain" (*mahāvarṣa*).
The planets, lunar mansions, and the lords of the *dānavas* are proclaimed to be adverse;
thus, during that twelfth year, they bring about both auspicious and inauspicious results here on earth.
When Rāhu, the lord of the asuras, is seen on one side of both the lunar and solar discs— whether entirely covering them, partially obscuring them, or casting them in various positions—
a great falling of weapons is seen upon the surface of the earth.
One should always and constantly employ these and other [mantras] at the appropriate times;
for many terrible obstacles are seen to arise in manifold ways.
When the time of the end of the age had arrived, and the world-vessel was most unrighteous,
the moon was entirely eclipsed, having entered the constellation Mūla.
If that moon sets during the night while it is still in conjunction,
or if it sets during the day while afflicted by the sun, [it portends misfortune].
When the sun and the moon set at midnight during an eclipse,
they do so out of fear of the shadow of the lord of the Dānavas.
