The wicked king staying in his own territory will be slain, without a doubt;
he will either face the danger of death from his own side or be destroyed by his enemies.
The lord of the Mlecchas will plunder the eastern region;
likewise, all the Udra districts and the lord of the Udras [will do so].
If the two planets, the Moon and the Sun, should be seen in Aśvinī, or likewise in Rohiṇī,
or when they are seen in Bharaṇī or Kṛttikā;
Various diseases arising from phlegm, bile, and wind,
as well as others that are combinations of these, arise in all embodied beings.
Various outbreaks of disease are seen among all the foolish when the moon is in Maghā, Phalgunī, Uttarā, or Pūrvā.
Likewise in Hastā, Citrā, Svātī, and Viśākhā—
whenever the moon or the sun is eclipsed in these, there is no doubt.
Just as the moon and the sun are first swallowed by Rāhu,
so too is the ruler of the eastern region.
The king of Vaṅga, Aṅga, or Magadha will be seized by pain in the eye;
either his son will die, or there will be danger from the death of his wife,
or else there will be a gathering of enemies with malicious intent.
In Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, and likewise Aśleṣā—
indeed, in these, Rāhu is seen eclipsing both the sun and the moon.
Then the King of Magadha will be afflicted, as will the people of the Magadha countryside;
his ministers shall experience the fear of disease, along with the suffering of imprisonment for the citizens.
During the asterisms of Anurādhā and Jyeṣṭhā, all the lords of the Dānavas shall be visible;
at that time, they will produce disease throughout all inhabited lands, pervading everywhere.

In Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Śravaṇa, and likewise in Uttarāṣāḍhā, there will be killings, imprisonments, afflictions, and various kinds of exhaustion; moreover, people will be bound and confined by the leaders of men, and [the population] will increase therein.
The orb of the sun becomes distorted, and the moon assumes a reddish hue;
there is the constant arrival of planets, and famine arises.
When the moon or the sun is eclipsed during the lunar mansions of Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Pūrvabhādrapadā, or Śatabhiṣaj;
Knowing that the planet has arrived assuming a black appearance,
one should recognize great sorrow, exhaustion, and famine on all sides;
one should know that all the districts will face great danger from kings and thieves.
Now, when the moon and the solar disc are eclipsed by Rāhu under the constellation Revatī or Uttarā-bhadrapadā,
and the sun is subsequently seen for one fortnight as it has been positioned [there].
The entire Magadhan king, the lord, is deprived of his kingdom;
these are the signs said to appear when Rāhu approaches.
In whichever directions one perceives the lunar or solar disc,
in those respective regions, auspicious or inauspicious events then arise.
Whatever tremors of the earth have been described as marked by worldly signs,
one should understand that the auspicious or inauspicious results of those [tremors] apply specifically during a planetary eclipse.
If there is smoke for five days at the end of the day, it will be the cause of rain;
thereafter, for half that duration, there will be anxiety among the people centered on Tīrabhukti.
All the inhabited lands, which are the abodes where diseases arise, will perish;
and even the king on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā shall perish.
Likewise, Himavanta was placed in the womb; Durbhagajvara was situated there, and the kings were also stationed all around as guardians of the quarters.
Then, on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, that lord of the Tīrabhukti region,
the ruler of men, shall die from various sorrows and agonies.
That lord of men perishes together with his sons and wife;
indeed, one should predict smoke during those lunar mansions in which an earthquake occurs.
In all directions, terrible clouds devoid of rain have arisen;
five days have passed, and it has always been excessively cloudy.
Mortals born of human lineage would perish through one another's gaze;
there, the sight of humans does not function toward one another.
One should know that there will be great danger therein; it shall destroy the king along with his kingdom, wherever such a trembling occurs accompanied by the falling of meteors on all sides.
Furthermore, if there is a terrifying appearance of two or three [omens] placed among the seekers,
or if there is a rainbow at night, or a crow with white wings;
Then white-colored [beings] appear as black, and black ones as white;
the colors of the birds are reversed, and the sounds of the seasons are inverted.
Wherever birds appear in reverse order, there is great danger;
this applies to all bipeds, quadrupeds, and even those with many feet or no feet at all.
If birds fly sideways, it is an omen for animals; if they do so in reverse, there is great danger.
Likewise, if dogs howl repeatedly with their muzzles pointed upward, whether by day or by night, there will be great danger wherever that occurs.
Wherever such various and manifold portents as these are manifested,
there shall be drought and the king's wheel of sovereignty shall perish.
Just as the auspicious and inauspicious [omens] of living beings are declared in the *jātakarma* rites,
so too do portents born from that [same source] produce good and evil results here in this world.
No sign whatsoever is seen to arise otherwise than from a prior cause; obstacles and the occurrence of portents do not manifest without a cause.

Thus concludes the twenty-second detailed chapter on the light of knowledge regarding omens from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed the hosts of planets, constellations, stars, and luminaries:
"Listen, all of you!"

This king of manuals of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, consisting of the procedures for mantras, tantras, consecrations, and mandalas, as well as the rules for recitation, fire-offerings, and the practice of the accomplishment of vidyās, is not to be transgressed. O you who possess the superknowledges regarding the lunar days, constellations, conduct, and calculations, you must not create obstacles for the holders of vidyā engaged in this supreme manual. And all you hosts of gods must provide protection there for those engaged in this teaching.
And all wicked beings must be restrained, obstructed, and disciplined; none of them at all must be killed, but they must be established in the rules of this teaching of the Ten-Powered Ones.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the samādhi called "The Exalted Uṣṇīṣa of All Tathāgatas" for the purpose of warding off all malevolent beings among all sentient beings.

As soon as the Blessed One Śākyamuni had entered that state, all those Tathāgatas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions beheld the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, in the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa), and approached him.
Having approached, through the inconceivable empowerment of their own buddha-nature, they addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero, for the arising of the welfare of the worlds,
as all mantras and their tantras proceed according to the ritual rules!
This King of Vidyās of great supernatural power, the single-syllable supreme and foremost, was taught by all the Buddhas for the degenerate age of the Kali Yuga.
The most excellent of all mantras, spoken by all the Buddhas,
is the Uṣṇīṣarāja of great heroism, which wards off all malevolent spirits.
He is the restrainer of the planets, the constellations, and the malevolent mātṛs; likewise, he is the subduer of all obstacles in the world and whatever others there may be who are evil-minded.
For the sake of favoring sentient beings and for the arising of happiness for those who recite [mantras],
he is indeed the foremost in this entire teaching— the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) of great supernatural power,
the King of the Uṣṇīṣa, possessed of great heroism, the supreme lord over all.
"Speak now, O Tathāgata, regarding the time for this.
Thus addressed, those Buddhas remained silent.

Then, through the gathering of those Buddhas, the entire great trichiliocosm and the world-receptacles of all sentient beings became a single mass of flame, yet not even a single sentient being experienced any suffering;
by the empowerment of the Buddhas, great radiances were seen.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed that entire realm of the Pure Abodes, addressed those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, the sons of the gods residing there, and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas gathered in the great assembly of the Blessed One.

May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, all the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Noble Śrāvakas attend to me! I shall now once again proclaim the ritual manual (*kalpa*) for this time, in this degenerate age (*kaliyuga*), concerning the Blessed One, the Uṣṇīṣarāja Cakravartin—whose single-syllable spell is a universal monarch of vidyās, who dwells above and beyond all the Uṣṇīṣas of the Tathāgatas, whose teaching is unimpeded, and whose strength and prowess are immeasurable.

Now, I shall speak again of the mantra of the Blessed One, whose teaching is difficult to transgress, the Teacher of the three worlds, honored by all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas, and the accomplisher of the purpose of all rites. In the Kali age, at the time when the teaching is on the verge of disappearing, the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣacakravartin will become the protector of the teaching; he shall attain accomplishment and, at all times—even during the period when the teachings of all Buddhas are vanishing—this Blessed Buddha will act for the benefit of sentient beings.
This Blessed One is the protector, thoroughly imbued with the Dharma-treasury of all the Tathāgatas.
Listen, O hosts of gods and all sentient beings! BHRŪM!
This Blessed One, the omniscient one, established by the Buddhas in the form of mantra,
is the Great Compassionate Teacher who wanders among all embodied beings.
The glorious Lord of Mantras, renowned and honored as Uṣṇīṣa,
having arisen from the essence of compassion, remains as this imperishable syllable;
having emerged from the Dharmadhātu, he stands here in manifold forms.
For just as the relics that have issued from the bodies of the Buddhas are honored by the world when accompanied by material offerings, they are especially so when free from material offerings.

The spheres of the True Dharma are said to be free from worldly attachment and are the causes for the world; those with worldly attachment are said to reside within the bodies of the Greatly Powerful Lords of Jinas.
The Moon-like Sages have proclaimed various elements (dhātu) that are free from outflows (anāsrava),
as well as those with worldly attachment (sāmiṣa) and those without it, which have spread forth for the sake of the world.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, the Lord of the World, the Maker of Light, remains in the form of mantra, perfectly blended with the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Possessing all forms and omniscient, he is indeed seen upon the surface of the earth;
this mantra, which accomplishes all aims, was spoken by all the Buddhas.
This is the mantra in brief; when recited by oneself according to the ritual procedure, it indeed always accomplishes every action that is desired, making it fruitful.
Furthermore, his ritual procedure shall be explained briefly at a later time:
when the world’s best of sages, the Tathāgata, has passed away at the end of the age,
the accomplishment of the ritual and the accomplishment of the mantra will be proclaimed for that time.

Now, the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of the single-syllable [mantra] of the Blessed One, the Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*), the Tathāgata-Uṣṇīṣa, the destroyer of the applications of others' rites, the Unconquered Victor (*ajitañjaya*), the sovereign of all mantras, who is authorized by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin—is here set forth, having been previously taught in detail, but now in brief.

First of all, in whatever place this is recited, within a distance of one *yojana* around that site, all malevolent grahas flee; even all accomplished mantras have no power there; and all gods abandon their presence. Except by the will of the practitioner, it robs other practitioners—whether worldly or supramundane—of their accomplishments, and it releases the mantras employed by others from being severed, split, or uprooted.

Desiring to sever the spell (*vidyā*) oneself, one should take a handful of green *kuśa* grass, empower it with eight hundred recitations of the mantra, and cut it with a weapon while aiming at that spell; thus, the spell is severed.
Having fashioned an image (*pratikṛti*) by this means, one should strike its heart with a wedge (*kīlaka*);
it becomes pinned down.
One should tie a knot with a thread dyed with safflower and consecrated by seven recitations;
thus it becomes bound.
One should seal [the object] with a shallow bowl over which one hundred and eight recitations have been performed; thus it becomes obstructed.
If one cuts the heart in two with a weapon, it becomes split;
if one colors it with mustard seeds stained with poison and blood, it becomes smeared;
if one strikes it with a *karavīra* creeper, it becomes crushed.
One performs all desired magical rites (*abhicāruka*) according to one's wish.

Having bathed [the image] with milk and pearls, one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*); thus there is peace. By a fire-oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), peace and nourishment are brought about for all.

By clenching the fist, one paralyzes all mantras; by [releasing] it with the mind, one liberates them. One who desires to accomplish a mantra should accomplish it after first restraining it with this very [mudrā]. If one wishes to accomplish another ritual procedure (*kalpa*), one should accomplish that with this very [mudrā];
it succeeds.
With this very mantra, the invocation (*āvāhana*) takes place.
Furthermore, by this very [mantra] the dismissal is performed;
by this very [mantra], he for whose protection it is done also becomes invisible.
If a mantra does not succeed or does not grant a response, one should recite it together with this very [mantra].
It is quickly accomplished, or it gives a response;
if it is not accomplished, it provides a response [of refusal],
and he dies.

One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day for seven days, directed toward whichever mantra; that person will come under one's control and will perform whatever task is commanded. Or, I shall provide an instruction: if one desires to bring the gods under control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *devadāru* wood; within seven nights, they will become submissive.
One desiring to bring the *nāgas* under control should offer the three sweets (*trimadhura*) as an oblation;
they will become submissive.
One desiring to bring the *yakṣas* under control should offer curd-rice as an oblation; they will become submissive.
One who desires to bring a *yakṣiṇī* under control should offer oblations of curd-rice (*dadhibhakta*).

One brings a *gandharva* under control with all types of perfumes. With fuel-sticks or flowers of *aśoka* and *priyaṅgu*, one subdues *yakṣiṇīs*, *nāgas*, and *nāga-grahas*. With *rājikā* seeds, one subdues kings; with *siddhārthaka* (white mustard), Brahmā; with a flower-oblation, a Vaiśya; with curd, milk, and ghee, a Śūdra; with chaff and dust, a woman; with an oblation of salt, a widow; with an oblation of beans and *jambūlika*, a maiden; and with an oblation of ghee and oil, one brings everyone under control. In all these cases, one should perform this at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
Having spoken thus, the supreme Victor remained silent;
then that seventh bull among sages, the knower of worldly dharmas, laughed at the assembly of gods and, his mind having attained liberation, he became free.
Then the supreme sage addressed his eldest son;
he then chose Mañjughoṣa, the bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
This ritual procedure has been declared by me as but a single portion for the wielder of the discus—
the wise Lord, the God of gods, whose extent is vast.
The measure of which cannot be expressed even by the Victors throughout eons—
I shall describe it to you in brief for the sake of the arising of welfare for human beings.
When this had been said, the glorious Mañjughoṣa, possessed of great supernatural power,
then made a formal request to that Buddha who was stationed above the Pure Abodes.
Speak, speak, O Great Hero, Perfectly Awakened One, Supreme among Humans! For the sake of the arising of happiness for human beings in this lost time at the end of the age.

How is it that the king of mantras of this one of great majesty and great heroism is seen to grant success through the cloth-painting? And how is the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting performed so as to bring swift results?

Thus concludes the twenty-third chapter, the detailed exposition on the emergence of the One-Syllable Universal Monarch, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the brief procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) of the one-syllable sovereign (*ekākṣaracakravartin*), who possesses great majesty."
This has been explained in detail previously;
now, in brief: in this degenerate age, sentient beings possess little vigor, little wisdom, and dull minds;
they are unable to accomplish the practice of the proportions of the cloth in its detailed form.
Out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I shall speak in brief so that those practitioners of recitation may attain the accomplishment of the supreme goal.
One who desires to perform the supreme sādhana should have the Blessed One painted on an unbleached cloth that has its fringe intact and is free of hair, using non-adhesive pigments.

He is the King of Dharma, the Turner of the Wheel of Dharma, the Lord of all worlds, the Supreme Person, the Foremost of bipeds, the Jewel of the Tathāgatas, the Victor named Ratnaketu, teaching the Dharma, surrounded by a halo of blazing light.
Below him are Brahmā and the noble Vajrapāṇi; above him are two sons of gods bearing garlands; and below is the practitioner.
In front of it, burning agalloch incense at the three junctions of the day, one should recite the mantra one million times;
thereafter, the ritual activities will succeed.

Desiring to perform the first wheel-sādhana, one should fashion a twelve-spoked wheel made of flower-metal (*puṣpaloha*). During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), one should recite [the mantra] ten hundred thousand times before the Blessed One at the three junctions of the day while burning agarwood incense. At the end, on the full moon day, having performed a grand worship and grasping it with the hand, one should recite until it blazes.
Having taken hold of it, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the vidyādharas.
He flies up together with those by whom he is seen and those whom he sees.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the parasol (*chattra*) should have a new, variegated white parasol made, marked with the sign of a golden wheel and draped with silk cloth; having placed it upon his head according to this very procedure, he should recite [the mantra], and the Vidyā will manifest of its own accord.
Furthermore, in front of the Blessed One, he should recite it three times a day for one million times while burning *agaru* incense.
At the conclusion, on the full moon day, having performed a grand worship, he should grasp it with his hand and recite until it blazes forth.
Having taken it, one becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas.
It is accomplished every month on the full moon day during the five fortnights of the *prātihārika* period. Then, as soon as it is accomplished, all dharmas become manifest before one.
One attains all supernormal knowledges (*sarvābhijñā*).
Delighted by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one becomes perfected in penetrating into the midst of all sentient beings.
Even in other world-systems, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) with a retinue of a thousand followers.
Then, one desiring to accomplish the uṣṇīṣa should fashion a staff one cubit in length made of gold, silver, copper, or gemstone, and recite the mantra until it blazes.
Having grasped it, one wanders at will and teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.
He lives for a great eon (mahākalpa).

Now, one desiring to accomplish the auspicious jar (*bhadraghaṭa*) should fashion a golden auspicious jar, fill it with all kinds of seeds, jewels, and medicinal herbs, and wrap it in white cloth; one should accomplish it by means of this [mantra]. One should begin the rite during one fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*); it is perfected during the other. Having placed it in one's hand, whatever one desires, that one obtains.
It becomes inexhaustible.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the *cintāmaṇi* jewel should fashion a golden staff with a genuine gem and a crystal gem, or a golden [staff] adorned with hanging cloth, and accomplish it according to this very procedure; whatever one thinks of, all that is accomplished.
By holding this, among gods and humans, one becomes possessed of unimpeded strength and prowess.
Then, if one recites the mantra of the Blessed One ten million times, one flies up into the air with one's own body.
He lives for many great divine *kalpas*.
Furthermore, other rites such as those known as the "Black Parasol" (*asitātapatra*) and so forth are accomplished by this [mantra] when recited one million times for the Blessed One.
Thus, the Tathāgata’s Uṣṇīṣa is unimpeded; in whatever manner it is employed according to the ritual procedures of other systems, in that very manner it is accomplished.
If recited one million times, this sovereign of all vidyā-mantras, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin of the Blessed One, accomplishes everything in no time at all.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the vajra should fashion a single-pronged vajra made of red sandalwood, or alternatively, one made of flower-metal (puṣpaloha). Having washed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, having performed a grand worship before the cloth painting, and having lit lamps of ghee, he should wash it with scented water; then the yakṣas become submissive.

Having dedicated oneself to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and having performed protection by means of this Uṣṇīṣarāja together with its retinue—specifically the Tejorāśi and Sitātapatra—and having performed the binding of the maṇḍala and the protection of one’s companions, one should take a vajra in the right hand, sit down when the first watch has passed during the second watch, and recite with a one-pointed mind until [the deity] blazes forth.
In the meantime, all the Vidyādharas, as well as all the gods, Nāgas, and Yakṣas, assemble;
and all the kings of the Vidyādharas arrive.
Being praised by them, he goes to the city of the Vidyādharas and becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas.
With a body like that of Vajrapāṇi and strength equal to Vajrapāṇi, he goes to the Akaniṣṭha celestial realm in a mere instant, a moment, or a brief duration.
Abiding for a great eon, he beholds the Blessed One, the noble Maitreya,
and hears the Dharma;
upon death, he is reborn wherever he desires.
Whatever he desires arises from the presence of Vajrapāṇi.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the sword-rite should take a flawless sword, fast for a day and night, and perform a grand worship of the Blessed One; he should then recite the mantra until, once it has blazed and been perfected, he flies up together with his retinue.
With curled, ringlet-like hair and the appearance of a sixteen-year-old, he does not yield the path and is inaccessible to all Vidyādharas; he lives for an intermediate kalpa.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the practice of realgar (manaḥśilā) should purchase it through "heroic purchase" (vīrakraya). Having fasted for three nights with an offering of flowers, he should feed alms designated for the Saṅgha and cause them to grant his authorization.
Once authorized, he should enter the place of practice.
Having performed a magnificent worship, he should light a thousand lamps of ghee.

Having fasted for three nights, having generated a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, and having offered oneself [in sacrifice], one should take realgar and recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained.
One must first contemplate the stages of heat, smoke, and flame.

If the accomplishment is not yet released, by applying a tilaka-mark that is emitting heat, all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, bhūtas, piśācas, and so forth, as well as the sentient beings dwelling in Jambudvīpa, become one’s servants.
They become his servants;
he lives for a thousand years.
Having made a *tilaka* while [the fire] is smoking, he becomes invisible.
If he so desires, he becomes invisible even to the gods;
in a moment, a brief instant, or a muhūrta, he becomes visible again, and then disappears once more.
He becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility;
he lives for three thousand years and, blazing with light, becomes a vidyādhara; together with his retinue, he flies up into the air.
He becomes a king of the Vidyādharas,
possessing a body like that of a celestial youth, invincible to all gods, let alone to the Vidyādharas;
he remains for an eon, and upon his death, he is reborn in the Tuṣita realm of the gods.
Now, one desiring to accomplish the trident (*triśūla*) should fashion a trident made of *puṣpaloha* (flower-metal) and recite the mantra for one year.

Then, having fashioned a stupa (*caitya*) out of sand measuring one cubit in height, having performed a great worship of it and offered a magnificent sacrificial oblation (*bali*), one should grasp the trident with the right hand and recite the mantra until—having assumed the cross-legged posture—it quivers, blazes, and emits thousands of rays of light.
In the meantime, the gods headed by Maheśvara arrive.
All the vidyādharas shower a rain of flowers.
Then, surrounded by them, he flies up together with all those whom he sees and who see him.
Having three eyes like a second Maheśvara, honored by all the vidyādharas, and remaining for a great kalpa, he strikes down those of evil intent merely by his gaze.
He becomes unassailable by anyone in the world including the gods, let alone by the *vidyādharas*; upon passing away, he is reborn in Sukhāvatī.
Now, one who seeks to accomplish the Vetāla:
having taken a man with uninjured limbs and seated himself upon his chest—which has been secured with four stakes of khadira wood—one should offer oblations of powdered jewels.
Then, the Cintāmaṇi jewel will appear at the tip of his tongue.
Having taken it, one becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas;
whatever weapons one thinks of appear by mere thought,
and one illuminates a hundred yojanas with one's radiance.
He passes away at will;
he goes wherever he desires;
and even in other world-systems, he becomes a universal monarch of the vidyādharas.
Having passed away, one is reborn in the world-system Vimalā.
The second is the accomplishment of the vetāla:
having seized a vetāla with its limbs unimpaired, and having pinned it down with stakes of jujube wood, one should offer iron filings into its mouth;
its tongue will then protrude.
Having cut that [cord], he flies up with a retinue of a hundred;
he lives for an intermediate kalpa and sports and delights upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
When he dies, he becomes a regional king.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the goad (*aṅkuśa*) should fashion a goad out of *kuśa* grass. Having washed it with the five products of a cow (*pañcagavya*) from either of the two black [goats], one should remain for one night. The handle of the goad should be made to the measure of a cubit (*hasta*). Having performed a grand worship, one should cause a hundred ghee-lamps to be lit for Vajrapāṇi.
One should likewise fashion a vajra, and protection must be performed for oneself by means of the White Parasol (*Sitātapatra*).
Having performed the binding of the maṇḍala with a mass of light and having consecrated seven stakes with mantras, they should be driven into the ground in the four directions;
thus the place becomes bound and protected.

Then, during the second watch, with a one-pointed mind, having sat in the cross-legged posture and worshipped the hook with perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having performed the protection and paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should take the hook in hand and recite the mantra until, in the meantime, the sufferings of the hell-beings and the gods are pacified.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, he flies up as a king of the Vidyādharas with unimpeded movement, his hand grasping a goad. Upon seeing him from afar, all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and others prostrate themselves.
When one who remains for an eon dies, he goes to the Vajra-abode and beholds Vajrapāṇi.
If he accomplishes the cloth-painting, by means of its blazing, he becomes a vidyādhara.

Having grasped the name of that mantra by which one wishes to accomplish a rite, one should recite it one hundred thousand times. At the conclusion, having fasted for one night and performed a grand worship, one should kindle a fire with *arka* wood and offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
At the end of the homa, [the deity] arrives and grants whatever wealth one desires.
He remains under control, subject to the power of his servants.
Then, desiring to become Maheśvara, one should perform a great worship of Maheśvara, kindle a fire with *arka* wood at the southern image, and offer eight thousand oblations.
A sound of "hā hā" will arise.
One must not be afraid; he will then arrive and say, "What should be done? May all the *vidyās* of Maheśvara be accomplished for me."
Whatever boon he desires, that he grants;
having said, "So be it," he vanishes.
In this way, one draws in Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others.
This same procedure should also be performed for whomever one chooses;
the rite must be carried out by one who has established protection.

Now, one who desires to summon a yakṣiṇī should take her name and offer oblations of aśoka flowers for seven days. She comes and grants a boon; on the seventh week she will certainly arrive, whether as a mother, a sister, or a wife, according to whatever one requests.
If he does not go,
his head shall split apart.
For one desiring to attract a *nāgī*, this same procedure applies using *nāga* flowers.
For one desiring to attract a *yakṣa*, one should offer curd-rice as an oblation for three months.

At the conclusion, having fasted for one night, performed worship of the Blessed One, and presented the *yakṣa*-bali offerings and incitements, one should resolve in mind, "I shall perform the attraction of the *yakṣa*," and offer eight thousand fuel-sticks of the *vaṭa* tree smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
In the meantime, the yakṣas headed by Kubera arrive;
an offering (argha) is presented to them with red flowers.
They will say, "What should be done for you?"
They should be told: "On each day, send a yakṣa who carries out your commands. Then they provide one yakṣa at a time, and his command must be given.
They bring a woman even from a hundred yojanas away;
at dawn, they lead her back to that very same place;
and they provide food for him surrounded by a hundred attendants.
Having mounted its back, one goes wherever one desires;
it carries one there and bestows an elixir of rejuvenation.
When commanded, he performs everything.

Now, one who desires to accomplish the practice of Vajrapāṇi should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) fourfold or sevenfold. During the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), having performed a complete and most magnificent worship until the full moon, and having performed worship on the full moon day itself, he should feed the monks designated for the Saṅgha. Then, the Noble Vajradhara himself should be thanked with a recitation of appreciation (*anumodana*). After performing a magnificent worship, when the first watch of the night has passed, he should sit in the lotus posture during the second watch and, with a one-pointed mind, form the resolve: "I shall behold Vajradhara. He should then offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) of balls of *guggulu* resin, the size of jujube seeds, for one watch of the night.
Then the garland of flowers on the Blessed One’s head begins to sway;
the earth trembles;
and the clouds rumble.

All the vidyādharas rained down a shower of flowers. In the meantime, the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi arrived, surrounded by all the vidyās, encompassed by the vidyārājas headed by Vidyottama, and surrounded by all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and bodhisattvas.
At that very moment, the intense sufferings of the beings in the hells were brought to an end.
An offering of water with fragrance (arghya) should be presented;
having prostrated, one should stand [before him], whereupon Vajradhara will say, "What boon shall I grant you?

Whether it be the status of a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas, entry into a subterranean cave, sovereignty over a kingdom, or invisibility—whatever is desired is obtained from the presence of that very Blessed One.

Alternatively, if he desires the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*— becoming a universal monarch of all *vidyādharas*, possessing a vajra-body like Vajrapāṇi, with all weapons produced by mere thought,
and remaining for a great eon (*mahākalpa*)—
then when he dies, he goes to the Vajra-abode.

This same procedure applies in brief to other Vidyādharas as well—those in the *Vajrapāṇi-kalpa*, those in the *Avalokiteśvara-kalpa*, and those taught by the Blessed One in various *kalpas*, as well as those in the *Brahma-kalpa* and the *Maheśvara-kalpa*. In short, whatever practices are to be accomplished within worldly and transcendent *kalpas* are all perfected through this very means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Great mantras that do not succeed when practiced otherwise will certainly grant a vision [of the deity] if recited together with this for seven nights.
If he does not grant it, [the practitioner] perishes.
If one recites [the mantra] in the presence of the gods headed by Maheśvara, he will grant a vision within seven nights;
if he does not grant it, his head shall split into twenty-one pieces.

During an eclipse of the moon or an eclipse of the sun, one should accomplish the preparation of ghee, vacā, collyrium, purifying materials, wooden staffs, sacrificial threads, yellow orpiment, red arsenic, and so forth.

Now, for one desiring to accomplish the ritual substance (*dravya*), one should take realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and grind it with human milk to make five pills. Having placed them in a casket of agarwood, one should perform the rite together with white *siddhārtha* mustard seeds. During a lunar or solar eclipse, having performed the offering of oblations (*balividhāna*), when the mustard seeds begin to crackle, then the first [pills] are accomplished; by means of that which subjugates all people, everyone belonging to the worldly realm becomes subject to one's will.
Whatever is commanded, he performs it all.
Then, when he emits smoke, he becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility;
he lives for an intermediate kalpa.
When it blazes, one becomes a king of the Vidyādharas with a body like that of a divine youth and the brilliance of the rising sun;
he lives for a great eon (mahākalpa).
In this same manner, yellow orpiment, green vitriol, and other such substances are to be accomplished.

Then, desiring to accomplish the ointment, one should take *śrotāñjana*, blue lotus, *kuṣṭha*, and sandalwood, place them together in a copper vessel, and recite the mantra during a lunar eclipse until it emits smoke. With eyes anointed by that, one becomes invisible, able to assume any form at will, and becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the sword [sādhana] should take a flawless sword and, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed an extensive worship of the cloth painting (paṭa) and the offering of oblations (bali), and having established protection, should grasp the sword with the right hand and recite the mantra until it vibrates.
When it blazes and vibrates, one becomes a solitary Vidyādhara;
by means of its blazing, one becomes the king of all Vidyādharas.
Possessing unimpeded strength and prowess, he flies up together with those by whom he is seen and those whom he beholds.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the vajra should fashion a vajra out of flower-metal (*puṣpaloha*), sixteen finger-breadths long, with three points on each end; having anointed it with red sandalwood (*raktacandana*), beginning from the first day of the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), one should perform grand worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and recite the mantra daily, while feeding an increasing number of monks.

Having fasted for three nights, having installed the cloth-painting in a shrine containing relics, having performed a grand worship, and having lit a hundred lamps of ghee, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, grasp the *vajra* with both hands, and recite the mantra until it blazes forth. Taking hold of it, one flies up together with a retinue of seven and becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*.
Possessing prowess equal to that of Vajrapāṇi, he lives for a great eon;
when his body is dissolved, he goes to the abode of Vajrapāṇi.

In this way, all weapons such as the spear, the discus, the arrow, and the javelin, as well as the cloth, the sandals, the staff, the wooden [staff], the sacrificial thread, and so forth, are to be accomplished according to the procedures prescribed in other ritual manuals.
For all of these, there are three kinds of accomplishment.

Desiring to perform a rite for pacification (*śāntika*), one should construct an altar in the shape of a lotus, kindle the fire with sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*), and offer eight thousand oblations of the finest cooked rice mixed with curd, honey, and ghee using a *sruva* ladle.
Through three nights, peace is attained for oneself or another;
through seven nights, for a village or a city.
During a great plague, one should offer oblations of *śamī* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
During a drought, one should offer oblations of *udumbara* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one should offer the "three sweets" (*trimadhu*).
There is supreme peace everywhere.
One who subsists on alms should recite [the mantra] three million times.

During the fortnight of miracles, on the full moon of the bright half of the month, having fasted for three nights, one should drink black cow’s milk that has been consecrated eight hundred times during a lunar eclipse; it becomes a medicinal elixir endowed with excellent qualities.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of young durvā shoots smeared with curd, honey, and ghee for ten nights; untimely death is pacified,
and one becomes long-lived.
One should consecrate banners, conchs, and other such items with mantras;
by seeing or hearing them, one paralyzes the enemy army.

Having prepared a new jar filled with all kinds of grain and scented water, one should touch and bathe a person afflicted by Vināyakas with that water over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times.
One who is consecrated becomes possessed of fortune;
by this consecration, one is liberated from all sins and performs the rites of the maṇḍala.
By reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, one destroys all poisons with a peacock feather;
by that same [recitation], one destroys fevers, eye-pains, diseases, and so forth.
With a thread, when joined with the mudrā and the mantra, one destroys the mechanical devices of the asuras.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of khadira wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
it bestows a great treasure.
Having descended into a river flowing to the ocean, one should cause a hundred thousand lotuses smeared with red sandalwood to float away.
One obtains a treasure equal to that heap of lotuses;
when it is given away, it becomes inexhaustible.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of bilva fruits smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
one obtains enjoyments.

Desiring to bring the gods under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *agaru* wood fuel sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, at the three junctions of the day for twenty-one nights. Having combined rice grains smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, one should offer them as a single oblation;
then food becomes inexhaustible.

For the subjugation of yakṣas, one should offer oblations of guggulu pills smeared with curd, honey, and ghee. With aśoka wood fuel-sticks for yakṣiṇīs; for nāgas, with nāgapuṣpa flowers; for the noble Vajrapāṇi, with agarwood fuel-sticks; for vidyādharas, with damanaka fuel-sticks; for gandharvas, with agarwood fuel-sticks smeared with turuṣka oil; for pretas, by offering kunduru incense; for kinnaras, by offering sarjarasa resin; and for vināyakas, by offering the same. For all of these, the oblation consists of eight hundred offerings. For seven days, for a king, one should offer eight hundred oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with oil.
If one recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times facing the sun for seven nights at the three junctions of the day, one is liberated from all sins.

Desiring to master all branches of knowledge, one should subsist on cow’s urine and barley gruel, fashion an image out of uśīra root, worship it with white flowers, offer eight hundred oblations of milk, bathe the image with milk,
and offer incense of agaru wood consecrated by eight hundred recitations.
One becomes nourished;

by reciting it twice, protection for oneself is accomplished; by reciting it thrice, protection for another is accomplished; and by reciting it thrice, protection for the ritual substance is accomplished.

Desiring to perform the restoration of those [mantras] that are severed, split, destroyed, or pinned down, one should fashion an image out of uśīra root, worship it with white flowers, and before the cloth painting, recite this Uṣṇīṣarāja and offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Directed toward the vidyā, it becomes unpinned.

Having ascertained that the knowledge [of the dream] is free from defects caused by wicked people, one should write it on birch bark with *gorocanā* pigment. Then, having consecrated one's own mantra eight hundred times and having performed a magnificent worship of the Blessed One, one should recite it eight thousand times together with this Blessed One and sleep right there upon a bed of *kuśa* grass.
The Blessed One, appearing in the dream, will speak whether the [knowledge] is deficient or excessive.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the lotus should fashion a lotus out of red sandalwood, perform an extensive worship, and fast for three nights. Taking that lotus with the right hand, he should recite the mantra until it blazes.
Then, accompanied by a retinue of twenty, he flies up and becomes a universal monarch of the Vidyādharas.
Possessing unimpeded movement,
when he dies, he is reborn in Sukhāvatī.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the vajra should fashion a vajra from clay mixed with anthill earth and sand. Subsisting on alms, observing silence, and not giving way to anger, he should take the vajra and recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.
A single-pointed vajra should be made. At the conclusion, that vajra should be placed in the midst of white mustard seeds and kept there during a lunar eclipse.
One should recite the mantra as long as mustard seeds crackle;
then the vajra becomes accomplished.
With that vajra held in hand, one performs all rites.
He pulverizes mountain peaks,
dries up dragon lakes,
and causes rivers to flow upstream.
It puts the nāgas to flight,
renders poisons harmless,
and paralyzes all living beings.
He deludes,
he causes to fall,
and he pulverizes mechanical devices.
It also paralyzes carts and the like, crushes them,
and performs all such actions.
This is the sādhana of the single-pronged vajra.
For one who accomplishes the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, no one whatsoever is able to create an obstacle;
for even Mūrdhaṭaka himself [cannot do so] when the rite is performed according to the rule, and not otherwise.
And during the time of reciting this, one should constantly recite the Buddha-locanā mantra both before and after.
In this way, gentleness arises,
and accomplishment becomes manifest.
Then, having descended to a river that flows to the ocean, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses; Śrī,
having arrived, bestows a boon and grants a kingdom.
Then, if one should offer three hundred thousand [mantras],
one becomes a universal monarch;
one becomes the sovereign lord of Jambūdvīpa.
Having installed the cloth painting (paṭa) in front of the opening, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times;
all magical devices (yantra) will fall away.
One should enter without hesitation.
Having entered, it extracts the essence and elixir;
then, if it remains right there, the fear of Viṣṇu’s discus arises.
But if one enters [the mantra], by the mere act of recollection, it is reduced to ashes.
He rouses [them] by means of the mind;
he never enters into that [state].
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should strike the big toe of the Blessed One’s foot with *jātī* flowers at the three times of day, after the mantra has been recited once;
this should continue until a ray of light issues forth from the big toe and dissolves into the body of the practitioner.
At that very moment, his hair becomes curled like a ringlet;
he flies up together with his retinue and becomes a king of the Vidyādharas, remaining for an eon.
Then, having installed the cloth painting facing west on the seashore and kindled a fire with *nāga* wood, one should offer one hundred thousand *nāgapuṣpa* flowers dedicated to the ocean.
Waves will come from the ocean;
one must not be afraid, as this is a sign of success.
This shall continue until the ocean arrives in the guise of a brahmin and asks,
"What should I do?
To which he should say:
"Be subject to me!
Then he does everything that is commanded.
Having drawn a thousand-petaled lotus on the ground and sat upon it, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
It pierces the earth and rises up;
surrounded by a thousand followers, one flies up and becomes a king of the vidyādharas who remains for a great eon.
One who gives without expectation illuminates five yojanas with splendor.
During the fortnight of miracles, one should offer one hundred thousand jasmine flowers above the Uṣṇīṣarāja of the Blessed One; each flower should be consecrated with a single recitation,
continuing until a ray of light issues forth from the uṣṇīṣa.
It dissolves into the body of the practitioner;
at that very moment, he becomes possessed of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijña*).
When recited one million times, in whatever way it is employed, if the vidyā is recited together with this very Blessed One, she will certainly come.
If she does not come in person while this is being recited, his head will split or wither.

And this Single-Syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin is the Tathāgata himself in person; who else in the world with its gods could be the king of all mantra-vidyās? It is the Tathāgata alone, whose retinue consists of the White Parasol, the Mass of Splendor, and so forth—[the foremost] of all the Uṣṇīṣa kings.
The entire procedure for accomplishment (*sādhanavidhāna*) is to be applied right here;
all the Uṣṇīṣa Kings are to be accomplished by means of this.
For one desiring the supreme accomplishment, it should be applied without hesitation.
If the supreme accomplishment is not attained through application,
in brief, all the gods are drawn in by this [mantra].
Then, one opens the treasure-chest:

having gone to where the treasure is located, one takes the Unseasonable Jar (*akālakalaśa*), anoints it with all kinds of perfumes, pours white sandalwood water into the jar, consecrates it eight thousand times with mantras, and places it over the treasure.
If the treasure is present, then that ground will burst open.
If the treasure lies at a man's height, it should be touched with water;
having dug a hole one cubit deep, it should be taken.

Now, one desiring to accomplish the lion [sādhana] should fashion an image from the clay of an anthill, smear it with *gorocanā*, and install it upon a pedestal. Having performed a grand worship, one should recite the mantra until it moves. Once it has moved, success is attained;
having mounted its back, with hair curled like a ringlet, one flies up into the air as the fifth person including oneself.
Having attained [this state], he lives for nine thousand years with the lifespan of Brahmā,
having come into the presence of all the vidyādharas.
In this same way, elephants, horses, and buffaloes are to be accomplished;
when one utters the lion’s roar, then the gods tremble on their seats.
Having gone to a lotus pond, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses;
one obtains the sovereignty of a neighboring kingdom.
One should perform a fire-oblation of a hundred thousand buds of red karavīra flowers.
One obtains a princess.
By casting one hundred thousand *jāti* flowers into a river flowing to the ocean, one obtains whatever maiden one desires.
All these supreme accomplishments (*sādhana*) are perfected.
Wherever that Uṣṇīṣacakravartin goes, even Indra offers him his own seat;
and all the kings of the gods, upon seeing him from afar, become afraid and terrified;
moreover, he eclipses the radiance of all those kings of the gods.
He performs it within a range of one hundred yojanas.

"This Tathāgata Cakravartin—in the world of the gods and throughout the entire eon—all [deities] remain under the power of the Blessed One, the Single-Syllable Uṣṇīṣacakravartin. All mantra-tantras, along with their ritual manuals and extensive details, are inclined toward him. Thus spoke the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Lion, the Supreme among Men.

Thus concludes the twenty-fourth chapter, the detailed exposition of the ritual procedures for the Single-Syllable Universal Monarch, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta once more, as well as the hosts of gods dwelling there, and all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas.

Mañjuśrī, this treasury of Dharma, which is the very essence of all the Tathāgatas and resembles a wish-fulfilling gem, has been taught for the purpose of fulfilling the aspirations of the world. At that time, during that period of the lowest age when the Buddha-fields are empty and the guidance of the True Dharma of the Tathāgatas who have entered parinirvāṇa is disappearing, it shall serve as a hidden storehouse within this King of Ritual Manuals (*kalparāja*) of your own boy-mantras and tantras, for the sake of protecting the treasury of mantras of all the Tathāgatas at that time and at that moment.

When recited according to the prescribed rite, this Mañjuśrī, the very essence of all the mantra-tantras of the Tathāgatas, shall become the foremost in your *Kumāra-kalparāja*; this One-Syllable Universal Monarch (*ekākṣara-cakravartin*), when recited, causes all the Vidyārājas of the Tathāgatas to be recited as well.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, in your own King of Rituals (Kalparāja), there was previously a single-syllable [mantra] that was a treasure, the very essence, the foremost, and the eldest.

In a past time, in a past age, sixty-two eons ago—resembling the sands of the river Gaṅgā—there appeared a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

By the mere recollection of whom, or by the mere utterance of his name, the five deeds of immediate retribution are destroyed. Many beings who merely hear his name will certainly be destined for enlightenment;
what need is there to mention those who [practice] for the sake of mantra-siddhi?

Furthermore, those who recite all mantras must necessarily first bring to mind this Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarāja, and speak these words: "Homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra!"
Then, having paid homage to Amitābha, Ratnaketu, and all the Buddhas, the mantras should be recited according to one's desire;
they will swiftly bestow accomplishment.

For what reason? Because the proclamation of the names and the homage to the Tathāgatas and all the Tathāgatas for the sake of increasing great merit is the standard measure; he certainly becomes one who is intent upon enlightenment and has fulfilled the accumulation of wholesome qualities.

One enters the ranks of the Bodhisattvas, and the mantras grant him swift accomplishment. This single-syllable mantra, which is the heart of all Tathāgatas, favored by all mantra-tantras, and the accomplisher of all rites, was taught by the Tathāgata Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One. O Mañjughoṣa, it is the supreme secret, the most profound mystery within your Royal Compendium of Rituals (*kalparāja*); it should be employed for the benefit of oneself and the world.
And also toward one who is not a disciple, one who is unrighteous,
and likewise toward one who has no faith in this teaching of the Teacher proclaimed by the Victor.
It should never be employed against one who is wicked, arrogant, a violator of the Teacher’s instruction, or lacking faith in the sons of the Jina.

To those disciples and even to those who possess the rhinoceros-like [solitary] vehicle, if they are incapable of honoring and following [the teachings], one must certainly not give them the mantra; for no accomplishment (siddhi) is seen for them.
Faithful, gentle-minded, and serene in the teaching of the Jina,
the Bodhisattva is likewise always intent upon worship and bestowing grace.
Success in this mantra shall be achieved here in this greatly exalted ritual manual,
within the great one-syllable mantra dedicated to Mañjughoṣa.
Therefore, that Lord of the World bestowed this mantra which brings happiness;
it is the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the source of all mantras.
In the past, seventy-six crores of mantras were sung by Svayambhū for the sake of the welfare of embodied beings who are deluded by sin.
All mantras have set, having taken refuge in the image of the Teacher;
among them, this King of Vidyās, possessed of great supernatural power,
is the very essence, and it proceeds as this single, eternally established syllable.
This limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi) remains established for the Buddhas who act for the welfare of the world;
by relying upon the guide of the Dharma, this single syllable stands firm.
This mantra accomplishes all aims and wards off wicked kings;
it performs a variety of rites and brings all activities to fulfillment.
And likewise, it certainly performs eight thousand rites;
through the ritual procedure as prescribed, it bestows manifold prosperity.
This syllable *ma*, conjoined with the mantra, is the heart of Mañjuśrī;
it is the eternal knowledge residing in the syllable *u*, set forth in the world by the virtuous one.
The King of Infinite Life and Wisdom has revealed the definitive meaning;
this was set in motion by the Buddha for Mañjughoṣa through the cause of his mastery.
Therefore, at the end of this age, when the Teacher has passed into parinirvāṇa,
one shall swiftly attain accomplishment through ritual action as prescribed by the rules.
There is a buddha-field named Amitāyus;
there, that Blessed One, the Buddha, turns the wheel of Dharma.
He remains for immeasurable eons, having empowered his lifespan;
for this very reason, his name became Amitāyurjñānaviniścaya (The Determination of Infinite Life and Wisdom).
This Tathāgata, the lord of kings of all worlds and possessed of great supernatural power,
shall bestow the foremost and supreme mantra upon the wise son of the Buddha.
The eldest [son] of that preeminent son [was established] in a great station of vast supernatural power;
thereafter, this was applied by that son to Samantabhadra.
Then that son of the Buddha indeed gave it to Mañjughoṣa;
now I, the Tathāgata, shall proclaim its foremost ritual manual.
This indeed is that foremost of mantras spoken by Dharmarāja;
for the sake of the welfare of all beings, he recited this mantra.
Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra; homage to all Buddhas, beginning with Śālendrarāja, Rāma, Amitāyus, and Ratnaketu.
Having paid homage to these, the single-syllable mantra should be recited three times.
And what is that?
Release!
This, O worthy ones, is what was spoken by the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra.

Remaining in the world-system Amitavyūhavatī for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all beings, out of compassion for the world, for the sake of the great multitude, and having regard for future generations, he—recognizing that the time had come for the disappearance of the teaching—bestowed [this teaching] upon his eldest legitimate son, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in order to ward off wicked kings who would harm the Three Jewels during the final age.
By the empowerment of the Buddha, he bestowed it upon Samantabhadra.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra gave it to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Then, for the sake of favoring all sentient beings and by the power of great compassion, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta established it within his own form, residing in his heart. Looking toward future times, [he thought]: "In the lowest of ages, at the time when the teaching is about to vanish, I, the final Tathāgata, shall cause this supreme mantra to act for the protection of my teaching during that wicked time, the Kali Yuga."
I shall explain its ritual manual (kalpa) in brief.
Listen, O Youth Mañjusvara of beautiful voice, to this greatness and the detailed expansion of the manual;
I shall explain it in even greater detail for this sovereign king of manuals.
First, having ascended a mountain peak, one should recite [the mantra] two million times;
thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished.

One should recite while subsisting on milk, observing silence, with the mind focused nowhere else but on the mantra, having taken refuge in the Three Jewels, having generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and having undertaken and embraced the vows of the *moṣadha* discipline and the bodhisattva vows.
Then the ritual actions are performed.
First of all, a cloth painting (paṭa) must be commissioned.

By a painter who has observed the *upoṣadha* fast, using non-adhesive pigments and a clean piece of cloth or a wooden board treated with sandalwood, camphor, and saffron, it should be painted by a pure artist in a clean place. The artist, wearing clean garments and eating the three white foods, should paint from sunrise until midday on the fifteenth day of the lunar month when the moon is full, under an auspicious constellation.
One should avoid [these] from others;
thus, day by day, until it is completed.
First of all, one should paint the world-system of Amitāyus upon the cloth.

On a cloth measuring one cubit, or on a rectangular panel of four Sugata-spans, one should have [the following] depicted: the world-system of Amitāyurvati, adorned on all sides below by mountains of ruby, sapphire, crystal, and emerald, and above by the appearance of great jeweled celestial palaces adorned with raised banners and flags. In its center, the Tathāgata Amitāyurviniścayarājendra is seated upon a lion-throne made of jewels, teaching the Dharma, garlanded with a halo of light radiating in all directions, and slightly reddish-white in complexion. On his left side is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta, seated upon a jeweled stone, holding a fly-whisk in his hand and gazing at the Tathāgata; his left hand rests upon a citron fruit, he is dark-green like a priyaṅgu flower, his body is adorned with all ornaments, and he is surrounded by a halo of flames. On the right side is the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, standing upon a jeweled stone, holding a fly-whisk with his hand raised and waving it; his left hand holds a jewel, his body is adorned with all ornaments and a jeweled crown, he is dark-green like a priyaṅgu flower, dressed in a blue silk garment, wearing a pearl necklace and a jeweled sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), and bound by a halo of flames radiating in all directions. To his right is the noble Mañjuśrī, standing upon a jeweled stone, in the form of a youth, his head adorned with five locks of hair and decorated with the ornaments of a young boy; he is golden-colored, dressed in a blue silk garment, wears a sacred thread interspersed with strings of pearls and jewels, gazes at the Tathāgata, has a slightly smiling face, a gentle appearance, and a beautiful form; with palms joined in reverence, he is endowed with the excellence of all marks and should be caused to be painted.

Below that, the practitioner, wearing his characteristic marks and attire, holding a lotus garland, with knees and elbows resting on the ground and head bowed, should be caused to be painted in the corner of the cloth.
Above the Blessed One, four Blessed Buddhas should be caused to be painted:
in the southern direction, two—Amitābha and Puṇyābha.
On the upper left side, two Tathāgatas should be caused to be depicted: Sālendrarāja and Ratnaketu.

They are all-pervadingly radiant, with flames on all sides, golden-colored, endowed with the excellence of all marks, strewn with all kinds of flowers, and seated upon lotus-thrones alone, not on any other seats. Teaching the Dharma, they are seated cross-legged with gentle countenances. Above the Blessed One, one should cause to be depicted the Tathāgata named Sunetra, emerging from within a cloud, rising up while raining down a shower of flowers.
Endowed with the excellence of all aspects, garlanded with a blaze of universal light, he grants a boon with his right hand and holds the corner of his robe with his left hand.
This is the procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra.
This is the single-syllable mantra (*ekākṣaramantra*) of that very Blessed One.
He is the King of the Uṣṇīṣas, the Uṣṇīṣa-Cakravartin, who rivals [the Buddha], possessing equal heroism and equal power.
The extent of its qualities and its power are inconceivable; it possesses great supernatural efficacy and great majesty.
In brief, it performs all those extensive ritual procedures that have been taught for the One-Syllable [Mantra], the Great Universal Monarch who is the Uṣṇīṣa King of all Tathāgatas.
Even when not yet fully accomplished, it performs its activities merely by being recited.
How much more so, then, when it has been accomplished;
it bestows the perfection of fruits according to one's desire, and that which is sought becomes attained.
Whatever is desired by the mind, from the mere sight of this painting, one will certainly become destined for enlightenment.
By the empowerment of that very Blessed One, Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, he is called the Heart of All Tathāgatas; he is called the Uṣṇīṣarāja of All Tathāgatas;
he is called the Cakravartin;
he is called the Mahācakravartirāja.
It is called the heart-essence of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta;
it is called the "Single Syllable. In brief, its power is inconceivable.
For the empowerment of the Buddhas is indeed inconceivable;
the miraculous display of the Buddhas is inconceivable.

Even one who has not accomplished [the practice], even one who has not performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), even one established in all domestic undertakings, and even one who indulges in all kinds of food, intoxicants, meat, and worldly sexual conduct—[may succeed], with the exception of those who lack faith and have not generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
For these, there is no success— namely, for those who have harmed the benefactors of the Three Jewels and for those who have damaged efforts directed toward them.
Even minor rites do not succeed for such people.
What need is there to mention middling or supreme accomplishment?
For one who practices the conduct of enjoying all desires and engaging in all activities, eight thousand rites—along with the minor rites—will be accomplished when applied.
And what are they? First of all, protection of oneself is achieved by reciting [the mantra] once.
Recited twice, it provides protection against others; recited thrice, it becomes great protection (*mahārakṣā*).
Even by a Great Bodhisattva established on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it cannot be disturbed.
What need is there to mention other beings?
If one wraps [the waist] with a five-colored thread that has been recited four times,
the retention of semen is accomplished.
Furthermore, he shall not suffer any harm from dreams;
however, except by his own will, if he so desires, this should be performed alone during the night on that very day, or daily.
But if he does not desire it, he should empower ashes with the mantra seven times and touch the region of his navel.
The binding of semen (*śukrabandha*) is accomplished after three weeks.
Having meditated upon the Buddha, the Blessed One, and recited the mantra five times, whoever one touches becomes submissive.

During an eclipse of the moon—the seizing of the hare-marked one—one should kindle a fire with *arka* wood and, even without a painted cloth (*paṭa*), offer ten thousand oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) while facing the east.

Near a royal palace, either separated by a river or in a divine abode that is not separated [from it]—in whatever place the king resides, one should perform the fire-oblation (homakarma) in its vicinity.
At dawn, the king becomes submissive;
he does everything that is commanded.
When he does not see [the object], then his mind becomes withdrawn, or it becomes dull,
or it falls into a state of mental distraction.
One should perform a further propitiation;
one should offer eight thousand oblations of milk at whatever time or place.
From that time forward, he becomes healthy.
This rite must not be performed for those who possess faith, who have serene confidence in the Three Jewels, and who have generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta);
if one performs it for them, they would accumulate a much greater mass of demerit.
One should perform this for others who have caused harm;
furthermore, those with malicious or violent minds should be granted a vision [of the deity] day after day,
so that they become gentle-minded.
If they do not exist, they are deprived of great wealth and their lives are reduced to a mere remnant.
Furthermore, there is another ritual:
during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *palāśa* wood fuel-sticks, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter.
At dawn, one becomes the king and lord of the land; one may issue commands and deliberate on matters of counsel.
He demonstrates his true nature;
within six months, he bestows a village with a thousand households as the object of instruction.
If one performs the homa at midnight, he does so within three months.
If one performs the oblation throughout the entire night, one obtains [the fruit] within one month;
if one performs the oblation for a month, every single night, one obtains a kingdom,
or a village equal to a kingdom, or any other kind of wealth.
Enemies do not prevail;
even if they should prevail, it is again karma that comes to pass.

During a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with *apāmārga* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *palāśa* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee into the fire of a Brahmin enemy.
At the conclusion, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *picumanda* leaves smeared with pungent oil.
At dawn, the gentle Brahmins [will prevail], and the king will become hostile.
There is another rite as well:
during a lunar eclipse, having kindled a fire with whatever wood is available, one should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee.
At the conclusion of the homa, one should cast that ash in the direction where the lord resides.
He becomes submissive;
at whatever time he chooses, whether it be this or that, he provides extensive wealth and assistance,
and he bestows a very small or even a large village, or a province.
And accomplishment becomes unfailing within six months, certainly.

Then, with a mind full of anger, a member of any of the four castes may go to some place of transformation, or by means of a distinct and preeminent sign, he approaches one who is devoted to another deity among worldly beings; in whichever direction they stand, that very house he causes him to depart for another land,
and he becomes agitated, or he flees at night.
If his family is divided,
eight thousand oblations of milk should be offered for its reconciliation;
he will then become well.
There is yet another ritual procedure:

during a lunar eclipse, according to that same method, one who is pure and dressed in clean garments, having fasted for a day and night, should perform the rite with water free from living organisms before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva on a cloth, or a book of the True Dharma, or a stupa containing relics.
He should prepare that place with fragrant dry flowers and fill it with sandalwood and saffron, and fumigate it with camphor incense.

Where this ritual is employed, one should kindle the fire with *palāśa* wood for the enemy of a Brāhmaṇa, *aśvattha* wood for the enemy of a Kṣatriya, *khadira* wood for the enemy of a Vaiśya, and other woods for the enemy of a Śūdra; having thus ignited the fire, one should perform that very same ritual.

At the conclusion of the *rājyahoma*, one should employ *palāśa* fuel-sticks for a Brāhmaṇa, *aśvattha* fuel-sticks for a Kṣatriya, *khadira* fuel-sticks for a Vaiśya, and *apāmārga* fuel-sticks—or whatever else is available—for a Śūdra. Likewise, the Great King should likewise perform the ritual and offer fuel-sticks from the root of the *aparājita* plant.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of ghee, and at the end of that, one should cast that very same ash in whichever direction the Great King resides,
or toward where an evil-minded person approaches; having formed the single-syllable mudrā of Uṣṇīṣacakravartin, one should cast it.
Or he turns back in terror at the sight of the *utpala* mudrā;
or his wheels break,
or some other great portent occurs.
A great affliction and instability of mind, by which his speech is brought to a halt.
These or other rites may be performed as desired.
Having consecrated a garment with mantras, one should wear it;
one becomes fortunate.
Having consecrated the eyes with mantras, one should apply collyrium;
one becomes beloved by all people.
One should perform this seven times consecrated.
Having placed his eyes and mouth everywhere, he should gaze at the face of one who is angry;
that person will become submissive.
Furthermore, having consecrated seven times a gentle flower, fruit, or anything else fragrant, he should present it to the king.
Merely by smelling it, one becomes submissive;
or any other being whatsoever becomes submissive merely by seeing it.
For all types of bodily pain, having consecrated [the water] one hundred and eight times, one should bathe with warm water.
He becomes healthy;
he should perform these actions, but not for the sake of suffering beings.
One who has faith in the Three Jewels may perform such an act for one who is destitute, fallen, impotent, or even for one who observes vows here in this teaching.
One should certainly not perform ritual work for women, nor for children, the elderly, or the sick; nor for the poor, the suffering, those of little strength, or those born of improper wombs.

One should not perform such an action; rather, one should employ it against a *mahāsattva* (great being), a hero, one who is reckless, one who is greedy, one who has a great following, one who possesses great wealth, one who is excessively proud, and one who is fierce. Such an action should be performed against these.
For one who hates the teaching, for one who is angry, for one who steals the property of others,
for one lacking faith, and for all mantras, medicinal herbs, and yogins [these are ineffective].
One should employ ritual action against those who are arrogant, evil-minded, unrighteous kings, and those despised by the world; one must avoid employing it against those who are righteous.
They say that another rite is devoid of mental focus;
indeed, the reciter, when enraged, casts that very ash toward whichever direction he desires.
The enemies stationed there become enraged, and even the king perishes;
those people also certainly fall into a state of long-lasting exhaustion.
Furthermore, if a great pestilence and calamity are seen in that country,
one should not perform the rite even if one has fallen into dire straits.
Within three weeks, all those rulers of men there shall perish;
however, when that karma is fully exhausted, he shall withdraw them after two weeks.
In the first [week] there is distraction of mind; in the second week, illness;
likewise, in the third week, death; therefore, one should avoid him.
In the first [week] they flee; in the second, there is confusion of the region;
likewise, in the third week, there is destruction. One should not perform such a rite.

The leaders of the world have taught that these beings are to be disciplined solely through their own spiritual strength; for these Buddhas, whose minds are pure, do not bestow [their] abundant success upon them.
All Buddhas have condemned any action that obstructs the vital breath;
therefore, one who recites mantras and desires supreme accomplishment should not perform such an act.
Rebirth in the hells is seen only within these very realms of desire;
however, this alone has been declared as the arising of the fruit of black and white karma.

The majesty of the diversity of karma, as it has been seen by the best of bipeds, is capable of constantly producing auspicious results; even that which is dark brings about what is auspicious for him.
Likewise, mixed karma is taught as being indeed mixed;
thus has this variety of karma been demonstrated by those who perceive reality.
The reciter should avoid that which is black or mixed action;
he should resort to the white, auspicious [action], which brings about the arising of the fruit of virtuous deeds.
But by obstructing the breath, the reciter goes again and again to hell;
therefore, the dharma that turns it away—non-violence—is the supreme action.
Heaven, as well as the accomplishment of mantras and an auspicious destiny, are attained through virtuous deeds; conversely, that which is contrary is said to result from contrary actions.
I have proclaimed dharma and adharma, and the conduct that leads to omniscience; one who constantly recites auspicious mantras should undertake [this practice] with the desire for accomplishment.
The mantras of that reciter shall be accomplished when he abides in auspiciousness;
for him who is devoted to white karma, liberation is indeed irreversible.
The Tathāgatas declare that for a minister, success comes through what is beneficial;
however, the diversity of karma is taught for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
One thousand rites, or even slightly more than eight hundred, will be accomplished as desired;
however, one may perform minor rites, but the supreme one will not be obtained.
The middling [attainment] is accomplished somewhat through effort consisting of recitation and fire-offerings;
the inferior [attainment] is accomplished quickly by means of ritual action as prescribed by rule.
Three kinds of action have been taught: superior, inferior, and middling;
likewise, one who possesses an excellent form and is an ascetic attains the superior [result].
Likewise, one who performs moderate recitation shall obtain moderate success in their actions;
likewise, one who constantly performs few recitations shall be occupied with few actions.
One obtains only a minor accomplishment (kṣudrasiddhi), but does not attain any other accomplishment;
furthermore, the measurement of time for recitation (japa) in the fire-oblation (homa) is seen to be threefold.
Success that is superior to the superior is seen among those of middling capacity; for those of lesser capacity, only a small or even smaller degree of action is obtained, resulting in minor success.

Thus concludes the twenty-fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for the cloth-painting and the heart-mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, consisting of the single-syllable root mantra, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, there is another procedure for your cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) which serves as a means for accomplishment and achieves the purpose of all rites."

By means of this very single-syllable heart-mantra, or the six-syllable mantra ending with *vāmakara*, or by your own root-mantra consisting of six syllables, or the heart-mantra beginning with *oṃ* and consisting of one syllable, this very ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is to be performed before the cloth-painting.

In the future time, in the final age, when I, the Tathāgata, have passed into parinirvāṇa, when the Buddha-field is empty, when the lowest of ages has arrived, and when the world is without protection, without refuge, and without resort— this very king of rituals shall become a protector, a refuge, a shelter, and a final resort.
And what is that?

First of all, one should have the Blessed Buddha Śākyamuni painted beforehand on a new, hairless cloth, seven cubits long and three cubits wide, with its fringes intact, and treated with saffron and sandalwood paste.
He should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma, and looking toward Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
