On the right side, one should have Sudhana, Subhūmi, the noble Akṣayamati, and Mañjuśrī depicted paying homage to the Blessed One; Mañjuśrī should be in the form of a youth, his limbs adorned with all ornaments. On the left side, one should have Samantabhadra, the noble Avalokiteśvara, Bhadrapāla, and Suśobhana depicted.
The image of the Blessed One should be drawn somewhat shorter [than the others].
The noble Avalokiteśvara and Sudhana should be portrayed with chowries held in their hands.
And below,
the Earth should be depicted with her hands holding jewel-caskets, emerging from the front part of the body;
and above, two young Vidyādharas bearing garlands and clouds raining down along with lightning should be painted.
And all the bodhisattvas should be depicted as scattering flowers while gazing at the face of the Blessed One;
they should be adorned, with serene gazes, and drawn as if seated with their upper bodies slightly bowed forward.
Having placed such a painting in a reliquary shrine (caitya), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while facing west.

Regarding this Mañjuśrī, one should observe silence like wood, bathe three times a day, change into three sets of robes, constantly maintain the *poṣadha* vows, and subsist on a diet of vegetables, barley-gruel, or whatever alms-food is obtained. Having divided the food into four parts, one should offer one part to the Three Jewels, another to Mañjuśrī, and the remainder to all sentient beings; then one should consume what is left for oneself.

With body unperturbed, having brought the Blessed One to mind and with a mind that takes all sentient beings as its object, one should perform the recitation after reflecting: "I do nothing, nor shall I do anything, for my own sake, but solely for the sake of all sentient beings.
One should offer bathing water, incense, flowers, incense smoke, sacrificial offerings, and lamps.
One should constantly offer the bathing water upon the shadow of the cloth-painting, and below it, the incense, flowers, and sacrificial offerings.
In that very place, one should first offer to them;

after the Three Jewels, then to Maitreya, immediately thereafter to Avalokiteśvara, Ārya Samantabhadra, Ārya Ākāśagarbha, Ārya Akṣayamati Kumārabhūta, Candraprabha, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Ārya Vajradhara, Ārya Tārā, Ārya Mahāmāyūrī, Ārya Parājitā, and the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā. Having first offered all these—perfume, flowers, incense, and food offerings—to each of them, one should afterwards offer them to the cloth painting (paṭa).

Afterwards, in a certain spot outside, one should fashion effigies (*vināyaka*) in the forms of camels, donkeys, horses, and elephants out of the earth from an anthill, and offer them everything [without exception].
Without forgetting, one should avoid oil-cakes, flour, sesame preparations, horse-gram (*kulattha*), fish, meat, radishes, eggplant (*vārttāka*), lotus leaves, and bronze vessels.
Seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, weary from that very exertion, one should cultivate the recollection of all the Buddhas (*sarvabuddhānusmṛti*).
One should perform the recitation mentally.
Elsewhere, in a secluded place, one should prepare a bed upon a layer of *kuśa* grass.
One should avoid excessive drinking, excessive eating, excessive wandering, excessive sightseeing, and excessive sleeping.
One should practice the recollection of the Buddha three times a day, maintain the retention of the vital essence,
and not disclose auspicious dreams to anyone else.
One should inform the Blessed One.
Thus, proceeding in due order with haste, one should recite one hundred thousand syllables.
At the conclusion, one should recite the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā.
During the time of recitation, one should perform the recitation while gazing at the face of the Blessed One or of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
With syllables and words free from confusion,
one should offer salutations at the end of the rosary and make the announcement.
Having performed the preliminary service according to this rite, one should place the cloth-painting in some stable location and perform the ritual action.
Wherever there is complete satisfaction of the mind, the procedure for the cloth painting is finished.

Thereafter, one should have an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made of white sandalwood, seated upon a lotus throne, holding the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā in one hand and holding a fruit in his right hand.
Having placed it facing west in a clean location, one should construct a fire-pit before it.
For all rites, it should be square, measuring two spans in size, and one should cast fragrances and all kinds of grains beneath it.
One should construct it upon that.

Having generated the new fire according to this procedure, one should take fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *aśvattha* wood—or alternatively, of *aśoka*—and having brought together clarified butter, rice, boiled rice, milk, curd, and honey, place them all in a copper vessel. Having recited the mantra eight thousand times, one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*).

Afterwards, on another day beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should perform the rite: having kindled the fire with *aśvattha* fuel-sticks and seeing that it is free of smoke, one should invoke the fire:
"Come, O tawny-hued one, with flaming tongue and red eyes; O tawny-hued one, give and cause to be given! Svāhā!"

With this mantra, one should offer three oblations. Afterwards, one should invoke the Blessed One: "Come, come, O Kumārabhūta! I am intent upon the welfare of all sentient beings; provide me with assistance. Accept this incense, flowers, and perfumes, svāhā!"
Whatever one gives, that should be given by this [method].
To the one who has arrived, an *argha* offering should be presented with fragrant flowers and water; thereafter, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Having recited [the mantra] seven times, one should cast a single oblation.
In this manner, for seven days, one should effect nourishment with ghee, rice, sesame, and barley gruel.
Furthermore, one will certainly see the noble Mañjuśrī in the form of a youth.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks, each measuring two finger-breadths in length;
day by day, this brings one hundred lords of the earth under one's control.
One should offer one hundred thousand *jātī* flowers;
the king becomes submissive.
One should offer one thousand lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains wealth.
Having kindled a fire with *śamī* wood fuel, one should offer sesame seeds as oblation;
one becomes a lord of riches.
One should constantly offer water into water;
having risen in the morning, one becomes beloved by all people.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains a village consisting of a thousand households.
One should offer oblations with the *bahuputrikā* mantra;
one obtains whatever maiden one desires.
One should offer oblations of *apāmārga*; this pacifies disease.
Having kindled a fire with wood from milk-producing trees, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds.
Whatever one performs while contemplating a particular object, that one obtains.
One who desires a kingdom should offer a hundred thousand lotuses;
he obtains a kingdom.
By offering a hundred thousand barley grains, inexhaustible food is produced.
One should offer guggulu and priyaṅgu together with clarified butter into the fire;
one will obtain a son.
In the absence of kākoli, one should offer jasmine flowers into water as an oblation.
Within seven days, one obtains a village.
Taking each flower of the *jātī* jasmine one by one, one should offer them as oblations into water.
Whomever is given the remaining fragment for smelling becomes submissive merely by the act of smelling it.
Having placed saffron, musk, clove, and flowers in one's mouth, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).
Whomever one converses with thereby becomes submissive.
Having consecrated black pepper (*marīca*) eight thousand times and placed it in one's mouth, even if one is angry, one becomes beloved through one's speech.
One should bind the topknot with this very [mantra];
one becomes invisible.
Upon seeing Śakra, if one recollects [the mantra] mentally, one becomes free from anger.
By constant recitation, one becomes beloved by all people.
Rising at the great dawn, one should offer water together with *jāti* flowers upon the ground in a clean place;
thus one becomes a master of mantras.
His word is not to be transgressed;
when fear arises, one should bring him to mind,
and fear will no longer exist.
Even toward another who is angry, one should cultivate loving-kindness and, having recollected it, look upon their face;
thus, the other becomes free from anger.
One should perform a fire offering (*homa*) with all kinds of fragrant flowers; whoever is the object of this rite shall become submissive.
One should drink water consecrated seven times at dawn;
it exhausts karma that is destined to be experienced.
By washing one's face with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, one becomes beloved by all people.
Having consecrated flowers with mantras, whoever one gives them to becomes submissive.
Through a single hundred-thousand-fold homa of rice grains, one attains the status of a teacher;
through sesame seeds, the status of a provincial governor; and one should offer a thousand lotuses.
One obtains a thousand dīnāras.
Having combined together vīrakrayakrītā, guggulu, sarjarasa, gandharasa, and śrīvāsaka, one should perform oblations.
On every fifth day for six months, when that period is complete, one obtains a thousandfold.
Having fashioned an image with all kinds of perfumes, one should cut it repeatedly with a sharp, single-edged weapon and offer it as an oblation.
By using the right foot of a man or the left foot of a woman, whomever one desires becomes submissive.
For seven days, at the three junctions of the day, one should offer *dhuttūraka* flowers as an oblation.
One obtains cattle;
with *arka* wood one obtains grain; with *śirīṣa* flowers, horses; with *aśoka* flowers, gold; and with *vyādhighātaka* flowers, one obtains garments.
Whatever one desires, all that is accomplished by means of an oblation of *jātī* flowers.
Whatever the color of the flowers one offers into the water at sunrise,
one obtains garments of that same color.
Having consecrated a vessel with seven recitations, if one goes for alms, one obtains inexhaustible alms.
Having risen during the night and recited [the mantra] over himself, he sees auspicious dreams.
Then, desiring to bring a king under one's control, one should take the dust from his feet, mix it with mustard seeds and oils, and offer it as an oblation;
after seven days, performed at the three junctions of the day, he becomes submissive.

Desiring to bring a queen under one's control, one should combine *sauvarcala* salt, *śatapuṣpā*, and *vārāhī* together and offer them as oblations for seven nights at the three junctions of the day; she will become submissive. Desiring to bring a royal minister under one's control, one should fashion an image out of *bhallātaka* nuts, sesame seeds, and *vacā*, and offer it as oblations.
For seven days and seven nights, he becomes submissive.
One who desires to bring a domestic priest under control should combine *brahmadaṇḍī* and *śatapuṣpā* together and offer them as oblations;
for seven nights, at the three junctions of the day, he becomes submissive.
Desiring to bring Brahmins under one's control, one should offer oblations of milk-rice mixed with ghee;
all will become submissive.
Then, desiring to bring a Kṣatriya under one's control, one should offer oblations of boiled rice mixed with ghee.
For seven days,
for the purpose of subjugating Vaiśyas, one should offer oblations of barley-gruel mixed with molasses;
they will become submissive.
One should offer oil-cake as an oblation;
Śūdras become submissive.
Having gathered all [of them] together, one should offer [the oblation]; then all become submissive.
Having offered a bali-oblation at a crossroads, in a solitary place, or in an empty house, whoever is afflicted by illness shall be liberated from it.
If one touches the face while reciting [the mantra], the fever departs.
By binding the topknot with [the mantra] recited eight hundred times, one is liberated from all diseases.
Having bound the *mūśraka* against all illnesses and performed the binding of the topknot, one should go to sleep.
All diseases depart;
one seized by illness is liberated by mere recitation.
In the case of throat-obstruction, one should apply an ointment after reciting over earth from an anthill.
The disease departs.
In the case of eye disease, one should offer oblations of blue indigo buds;
it will be pacified. This is the rite for the affliction related to the procedure of the cloth painting.
According to the previously described procedure, on an unbleached cloth free of hair, the noble Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta is to be depicted, adorned with all ornaments, red in color,
having the form of a youth, and seated upon a lotus throne;
to his right side is Āryāvalokiteśvara, and to his left side is Samantabhadra.
Slightly smaller than that of Noble Mañjuśrī;
having placed that cloth painting [in a shrine], one should recite the mantra ten million times,
and one becomes a king.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sandalwood fuel-sticks smeared with saffron;
one becomes a king.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of agalloch wood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One becomes a king.
One should offer ten million *jātī* flowers soaked in ghee;
one becomes a king.
One obtains a heap of dināras equal in number to the heap of lotuses that one offers as an oblation.
As long as he does not accept the [lotuses] while they are being recited, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*.
One should offer a hundred thousand *bhallātaka* fruits; he gives a thousand dināras.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of fruits that destroy disease; one becomes a great lord of wealth. By offering eight thousand oblations of *guggulu* fuel-sticks, one obtains grain.
By constantly offering oblations of sesame seeds, one obtains an uninterrupted supply of grain.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *gotaṇḍula* rice grains together with curd; one obtains a thousand cows.
One should offer *bahuputrikā* fruits and *śamī* fruits combined together.
Whichever girl he desires, he obtains her;
he should offer oblations of *śamī* leaves,
and he becomes a granter of all desires.
One should offer agasti flowers soaked in milk for the subjugation of brahmins;
one should offer white karavīra flowers.
For the subjugation of Kṣatriyas,
one should offer karṇikāra flowers; for the subjugation of a king,
one should offer dhuttūraka flowers.
For the subjugation of a Śūdra,
one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of Arka flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
[the practitioner] is liberated from all diseases.
By this very method, one should offer one hundred thousand fragrant flowers at the base of the feet;
one will become eternally happy.
Having kindled a fire with *aśvattha* wood, one should offer a thousand *śamī* flowers as an oblation.
The affliction caused by the stars is pacified.
Having written the mantra with *gorocanā* and bound it upon one's head, if one enters into battle,
one will not be touched by weapons.

Having placed Mañjuśrī at the head of the army upon the neck of an elephant, the enemy force is broken by his mere sight. Having fashioned the image of a youth seated upon a golden peacock-throne at the top of a banner, one should enter the battle;
by the mere sight of it, the enemy force is broken.
One should offer a hundred thousand jasmine flowers at the base of the feet;
there, one should prepare a bed upon a layer of kusha grass.
In a dream, [the deity] will speak according to one's desire.

Having offered a thousand lamps, one should prepare a single lamp with a wick made of lotus fiber, wrap it with licorice (madhuyaṣṭi), and light it; by looking [into it], one sees Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta exactly as he truly is. The second procedure for the cloth-painting (paṭavidhāna) is completed. Alternatively, having fashioned an image of the Youth (Kumāra) out of gold or silver, with his right hand in the gesture of granting boons (varada) and his left hand holding the Blessed Lady Prajñāpāramitā, and having placed such an image before him along with a casket containing relics, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should perform worship during the day;
young boys and girls should be fed in his presence;
and one should engage in singing, instrumental music, and the recitation of scriptures.
Upon the completion of the recitation, one should offer an *argha* with three flowers and dismiss [the deity].
Having performed the invocation and dismissal according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should perform the recitation while forming the lotus mudrā.

One should perform the turning of the banner mudrā, the seat with the svastika mudrā, the *argha* with the full (pūrṇa) mudrā, flowers with the single-linga mudrā, the lamp with the wish-fulfilling (manoratha) mudrā, incense with the twin (yamala) mudrā, perfume with the peacock-seat mudrā, and the offering (bali) with the staff (yaṣṭi) mudrā. According to this procedure, one should perform these rites day after day at night until the completion of the recitation.
Thereafter, one should perform the ritual actions.
One should float a hundred thousand *jātī* flowers upon a river flowing to the ocean;
one will obtain a kingdom.
Having made a heap of *jātī* flowers at night, one should sleep before the Blessed One.

One sees the Blessed One teaching the Dharma, surrounded by bodhisattvas; one should perform exactly that rite intended for him and not perform any other. Beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, one who observes the *upoṣadha* vows should offer incense of *śrīvāsaka* mixed with honey; thus one obtains a kingdom.
If one recites [the mantra] ten million times, one sees Mañjuśrī himself; he then delivers a teaching of the Dharma.
If one converses with him, he speaks face-to-face, and one becomes an irreversible Bodhisattva. This is the third procedure.
One should have an image of a youth made of red sandalwood, with Priyaṅkara on one side and Vīramatī on the other, both leaning against an aśoka tree.

Having placed it on one side, one should fashion an effigy of red sandalwood mixed with salt and *sarvaparājikā* plants; cutting it up again and again, one should offer it as an oblation in the name of whomever—that person becomes submissive.
If one offers *udumbara* fruits in the name of someone, that person becomes submissive.
One should offer the fruits of the *kākodumbarikā* while reciting the name of the person [desired]; that person will become submissive.

One should offer *śṛṅgāṭaka* for the subjugation of a Brāhmaṇa; for the subjugation of a Kṣatriya, one should offer lotus roots (*padmamūla*); for the subjugation of a Vaśya, one should offer *kaśeruka*; and for the subjugation of a Śūdra, one should offer *śālūka*.
To subjugate a Śūdra, one should offer eight thousand oblations of salt and sugar.
If one performs this at the three junctions of the day for seven days while reciting the name of a person, that person becomes submissive.

One should offer eight thousand oblations of neem leaves smeared with pungent oil at the three junctions of the day for seven days; by means of such an offering, whoever’s name is recited becomes submissive.
Subjugation is achieved through every oblation.
One should offer one hundred thousand flowers of the *bṛhatī*; one obtains gold.
One should offer eight thousand flowers of the *kālāñjanikā*; one obtains a large village.
One should offer *pāṭala* flowers; one obtains inexhaustible grain.
One should offer *śrīparṇī* flowers; one obtains gold.
One should offer *vacā* root smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one becomes a superior debater in all discussions.
Having placed *brāhmī* juice mixed with ghee in a copper vessel, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times; thereafter, one should drink it and will defeat all disputants.
If one takes a clod of earth and, having empowered it eight thousand times, throws it before an angry person, that person will release their anger. This is the fourth procedure.
On an unbleached cloth, free of hair, an artist who has observed the *upoṣadha* fast should paint the noble Mañjuśrī using pigments that do not require glue.

He is seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) and teaching the Dharma; on his right side is the noble Mahāmekhalā, and on his left side is the noble Prajñāpāramitā, engaged in recitation, adorned with all ornaments, and dressed in white garments.

Below that is a lotus lake, strewn with many kinds of flowers. From the two bodies of the Naga kings emerge two figures holding lotus stalks in their hands; on one side is the Noble Aparājitā, destroying obstacles and impediments, her mouth a blaze of fire and her eyes knit in a frown; on the other side is the Noble Parṇaśabarī, her hands busily grasping a noose and an axe, her eyes black and red, mounted upon the back of a peacock, protecting the practitioner.

The practitioner, with hands occupied by a lotus garland, should gaze at the face of the Blessed Mañjuśrī; and above him, two sons of gods should be depicted holding chowries, flower garlands, and drums.
Having placed that cloth painting facing west in a reliquary shrine (*caitya*) containing relics, one should recite [the mantra] ten million times.

At the conclusion of the recitation, having performed a great worship and having caused the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā to be recited, one should recite it ten thousand times while gazing at the face of Mañjuśrī.
Afterwards, the cloth vibrates;
one obtains a kingdom and obtains sight.
By reciting it, one becomes a vidyādhara; by laughing, one becomes a cakravartin;
by speaking it, one becomes a bodhisattva who has attained the first bhūmi.
And he hears his teaching of the Dharma.
In front of that very same cloth, having taken cow-ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color and placed it in a copper vessel, one should recite the mantra until it becomes warm,
emits smoke,
and bursts into flames.

By drinking it while it is steaming, one becomes supremely intelligent and possesses a retentive memory; when it is smoking, one gains invisibility; and when it is flaming, one gains the power of traveling through the sky. Having placed *vacā* root inside a hollowed-out earthenware cup and wrapped it with *jātī* flowers, one should recite the mantra until it sprouts.
Having consumed it, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara).
If one recites another ten million times, one sees Mañjuśrī face to face and hears his teaching of the Dharma.
And he resolves upon that.
Having had a hundred-petaled golden lotus fashioned and having placed the right knee upon the ground, one should recite the mantra until it blazes.
As soon as it is grasped by him, he becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) among the *vidyādharas*, invincible by others.
Alternatively, having placed realgar, yellow orpiment, or collyrium inside a casket made of *śrīparṇī* wood, one should recite the mantra until it makes a "khuṭ-khuṭ" sound.
Merely by taking hold of it, one becomes the invincible lord of the *rākṣasas* and *piśācas* who roam the earth.
Having taken a sword that is free of blemishes and endowed with auspicious marks, one should recite the mantra until it stands up like a serpent spreading its hood.
By seizing it, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) of the *vidyādharas*, possessing a lifespan of an eon and remaining invincible.
Having encased realgar in the three metals and placed it in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra until it makes a "culu-culu" sound;
then one becomes invisible.
As an invisible wielder of the sword, one performs all deeds associated with virtue.
Excluding anything connected with sensual desire,
one should take the heartwood of an *aśvattha* tree growing from a *śamī* tree, encase it in three metals, place it in the mouth, and recite the mantra until it makes a *culuculu* sound.
One becomes invincible and lives for a thousand years.
Having fashioned a silver wheel, one should recite [the mantra] before the entrance of the asura cave until the wheel pierces the asura-machines and enters. At that very moment, asura maidens emerge;
having entered together with them, one becomes a resident for an eon.

Having fashioned an iron trident, one performs the recitation at that entrance to the opening; there, all magical devices (yantras) shatter. One enters together with as many [companions] as one desires, and remains for the duration of a kalpa.
And he beholds the Blessed One Maitreya. This is the fifth procedure for the cloth painting.
Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī made of white *arka* wood and the size of a thumb, one should offer one hundred thousand *arka* flowers;
one will obtain the sovereignty of a neighboring kingdom.
Having fashioned [an image] from the root of white *karavīra* wood and likewise the size of a thumb, one should offer ten million of those flowers; one becomes a master of mantras (*mantrin*).
Having had an image made of *karahāṭa* wood measuring exactly one span (*vitasti*), one should offer a hundred thousand of its flowers;
one will obtain the rank of general.
Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Mañjuśrī out of white sandalwood measuring exactly one span, one should offer a hundred thousand *jāti* flowers.
One obtains the office of family priest.
Having fashioned an image of the Blessed Lord Mañjuśrī made of aśvattha wood and measuring one finger-breadth in size, one should offer a water-pot at a place where no crows dwell;
one will then become esteemed by many people.

Having fashioned [an image] out of all kinds of perfumes and having offered all kinds of fragrant flowers, one obtains whatever one desires. If the practitioner of mantras continuously offers oblations of *agaru* (aloe) fuel sticks, he becomes honored by many people.
By constant recitation, he dispels even the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).
At the time of death, one beholds Mañjuśrī,
who delivers a teaching of the Dharma to them.
Rising up again and again, if one recites [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one becomes invincible to all beings.
Having recited the mantra over one's eyes, one should look at the master;
he will become well-disposed.

For whomever one performs this rite, it accomplishes every task—except for those connected with sensual desire—within seven days if the person is on the spot, twenty-one days if they are in another village, four months if they are in another district, and six months if they are separated by a river, whether performed according to the procedure of one's own lineage or the procedure of another mantra.
And the rite of sorcery (*ābhicāruka*); this is the sixth procedure.
Thus was it spoken by the Sage of old for the benefit of beings of little merit at the end of the age.
When the teaching of the Teacher, the ascetic Śākyasiṃha, has disappeared,
one will attain accomplishment during that fierce and most terrifying time.
Indeed, the seventh [chapter] will be spoken here in this auspicious ritual manual (kalparāja);
I have taught this ritual manual at that most terrible time.
Indeed, this path has been set forth for sentient beings of little merit,
serving as the cause for the equipment of enlightenment and flowing toward the way of the three vehicles.
At that time, in that age, I display skillful means to sentient beings;
for indeed, sentient beings are deluded by craving and agitated by passion and hatred.
To them, who follow the influence of craving, I show this path;
yet they remain bound by the fetters of craving, though their actions may be wholesome due to the cause of karma.
Likewise, the substances to be accomplished for the sake of *siddhi*, as well as the mantras and tantras,
were taught by the Leaders of the World for the purpose of disciplining sentient beings;
such is the majesty of this ritual for practitioners who recite [mantras].
Having spoken thus, the supreme sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men,
explained in detail the power and efficacy of the mantras and tantras.
At that time, in this degenerate age, the Supreme Victor revealed unfailing accomplishment; then the hosts of gods chose Śuddhāvāsa.
O worthy ones, this which has been proclaimed as the extensive King of Rituals (Kalparāja), the teaching of Mañjughoṣa, is for the sake of the welfare of all the world.

Thus concludes the twenty-sixth chapter, the detailed section on the ritual procedures for Noble Mañjuśrī, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the twenty-ninth detailed section.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Mañjuśrī, there exists in your section on ritual procedures the seventh chapter, the "Ritual for the Cloth-Work," which those who shall accomplish at that time, at that moment, during the end of the age, will find their accomplishment to be unfailing.

Fruitful, bringing about happiness and resulting in happiness, to be experienced in this very life, warding off all miserable rebirths, their accomplishment will certainly be directed toward awakening.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke the heart-mantra of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta—
the six-syllabled mantra which consists of the liberation from the six realms of existence, which is inconceivable, peerless, and incomparable, possessing great supernatural power,
and which delivers one from the ocean of all existences and from the bonds of the fetters of existence and the suffering of the three types of suffering.
Unbearable to all beings, it is anointed by all the worlds;
unassailable by all beings, it is the purifier of the path to existence.
It brings about the attainment of the qualities of a Buddha, wards off all that is evil,
is rejoiced in by all the Buddhas, and produces every kind of prosperity;
it is the most excellent among all mantras in the teaching of Mañjughoṣa.
And what is that?
Om, obeisance to Vākyeda.
The ritual procedure for this is as follows:
subsisting on a diet of vegetables, barley gruel, or alms-food, bathing three times a day and changing one's garments three times, one should recite the syllables one hundred thousand times;
thus the preliminary service is accomplished.

Then, on a cloth with its fringe intact, a painter who observes the *poṣadha* vows should paint Noble Mañjuśrī using non-sticky pigments. He should be depicted seated upon a lotus throne, teaching the Dharma, adorned with all ornaments, in the form of a youth, and wearing a loose upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*). To his left, Noble Avalokiteśvara should be painted, holding a lotus in one hand and a fly-whisk (*cāmara*) in the other; to his right, Noble Samantabhadra. Above them, two Vidyādharas emerging from the midst of clouds, bearing garlands, should be caused to be painted. Below, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), holding an incense burner in his hand, should be depicted, and mountain peaks should be painted all around.
Below is a lotus pond.

Having installed the cloth painting facing west at a reliquary containing relics, having performed extensive worship and lit lamps of ghee, one should empower eight thousand *jātī* flowers one by one with mantras and strike Mañjuśrī’s face with them.
Then, a great and profound sound of "Hūṃ" will be heard,
or the cloth painting will tremble.

By the sound of the syllable *huṃ*, one becomes a sovereign king; by the shaking of the cloth, one becomes the superior debater among all disputants and the sole knower of the scriptures of all the world.
If it is not accomplished, one becomes capable of performing all rites. This is the first ritual procedure (*kalpa*).
One should offer as oblations throughout the entire night sticks of *agaru* wood, measuring one and a half finger-breadths in length, soaked in *turuṣka* oil, upon smokeless coals of *khadira* wood.
At the rising of the dawn, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī.
He grants him whatever boon he desires,
with the exception of that which is connected to sensual pleasures.
In front of that very cloth painting, burning sandalwood incense continuously throughout the entire night, one should recite the mantra.
Then, the noble Mañjuśrī will appear in person and teach the profound Dharma;
one will gain resolute faith in it.
Having resolved with faith, one becomes liberated from all diseases and attains mastery.

Having fashioned a lotus made of red sandalwood, six finger-breadths in circumference and with a stalk, and having smeared it with red sandalwood paste, one should perform a thousand oblations of *sampāta* and consecrate it a thousand times with mantras. On the full moon day, having placed it upon a lotus leaf in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and grasping it with the hand, one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth. By taking hold of it, one becomes a divine youth (*devakumāra*) with the form of a sixteen-year-old, possessing the luster of molten gold and a brilliance exceeding even that of the sun; he is honored by all the Vidyādharas and lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*). When the body perishes, he is reborn in the Abhirati world-system.

During a lunar eclipse, one should take white *vacā* root, wash it with the five products of a cow (*pañcagavya*), and support it with *aśvattha* leaves. One should recite the mantra until it emits heat, smoke, or blazes.
When it smokes, it brings all people under one's control and grants victory over all disputants; when it blazes, one attains invisibility and lives for thirty thousand years;
when it blazes [with fire], one attains the power of traveling through the sky and lives for a great eon (*mahākalpa*).

Having taken the ghee from a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, and having placed it in a copper vessel over seven *aśvattha* leaves, one should recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment is attained.
Having drunk that, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (*śrutidhara*), achieves invisibility, and gains the ability to travel through the sky.
Having placed a lotus seed in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra during a lunar eclipse until it makes a "culuculu" sound.
Having encased it in the three metals and placed it in the mouth, one becomes invisible;
when it is spat out, one becomes visible again.

Having placed the scent of cloves in one's mouth, one should recite the mantra six hundred thousand times; whoever he speaks to becomes submissive to him. Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should recite it one hundred thousand times, and one becomes a Vidyādhara.
Subsisting on alms and observing silence like a log, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; one becomes invisible.
If one recites it ten million times, Noble Mañjuśrī teaches the Dharma in such a way that one becomes a bodhisattva in his final existence.
Through constant recitation, there is an increase in all aims.
Having made an image of someone with all kinds of perfumes and having cut it up, one who offers it as an oblation becomes subject to their will within seven nights.
One should offer one hundred thousand pills of guggulu resin, the size of jujube seeds and smeared with clarified butter; one obtains one hundred thousand dīnāras.
Having descended into a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses;
one will see a great treasure equal in size to a heap of lotuses,
which never comes to an end.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds anointed with saffron;
the king will become submissive.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter.
One becomes a great householder who gives everything.
Having made a mandala with fallen cow dung and having scattered loose flowers upon it, one should recite the mantra eight hundred times.
Then, one should have a volume of the True Dharma read aloud.
Within one month, one becomes supremely intelligent.
Having performed the recitation eight hundred times over *rocanā*, one should apply it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*);
one will become beloved by all people.
Having consecrated one's topknot by reciting [the mantra] seven times, one becomes invulnerable to all beings.
One should offer ten thousand oblations of *kirimāla*;
one is then liberated from all diseases.

If one recites this seven times every day, it exhausts karma that is destined to be experienced. Furthermore, by reciting it one hundred and eight times at the time of death, one beholds the noble Mañjuśrī in his entirety before one's eyes.

Thus concludes the twenty-seventh chapter, the seventh detailed section on the ritual procedures for the Mañjuśrī cloth-painting, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, in your mantra-tantra, there are places for the accomplishment of all mantras, headed by the Universal Monarchs among the Vidyārājas and the Uṣṇīṣas of all the Tathāgatas."
In that regard, throughout the northern region, the vidyārājas of the Tathāgatas attain accomplishment in brief.
In China and indeed in Mahācīna, Mañjughoṣa himself will be terrified;
and those mantras of his which exist there will surely attain accomplishment.
Indeed, the accomplishment of the Uṣṇīṣa Kings shall be seen everywhere there, in Kāpiśī,
Vakhala, and likewise throughout Udīyāna.
In Kaśmīra, in the land of Sindh, and at the junctions of the Himalayan mountains,
having gone forth toward the northern direction, mantras lead to the attainment of the highest welfare.
Those songs which were sung by the Buddhas of the past, those now being set forth,
and those yet to be uttered by the future Perfectly Awakened Ones— all are for the sake of peace.
All indeed attain success there in this auspicious and blessed land situated in the valley of the Himalayas; therefore, I shall begin to perform rites for peace for the welfare of the people.
Likewise, these mantras born of Padma attain accomplishment in the Middle Country;
furthermore, accomplishment is seen there in the Gaja and Umā families as well.
The success of the mantra of the yakṣa Pañcika, of Hārītī who was born from the yakṣa womb, and of those mantras belonging to the gandharvas is likewise declared.
Then [he dwelt] constantly in the city of Kāśī, throughout Magadha,
as well as in the land of Aṅga, in the east, and throughout Kāmarūpa.
On the delightful bank of the Lauhityā, throughout the regions of Vaṅga,
there shall be the accomplishment of Jambhala, as well as that which arises from the Maṇikula.
On the shores of the ocean, on islands, and everywhere where there is water, the delightful city of the Siṃhalas exists; there the mantra-deities are accomplished.
Bhṛkuṭī, Mahāśrī, Yaśasvinī,
and Sitā— these four maidens are all mantras within the great ocean.
They indeed attain success in that region, throughout the eastern country,
as well as those situated within the womb of the Vindhya mountains and all around Agra and Indraprastha.
Then Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī attain accomplishment everywhere—
in the depths of Śṛṅgāra, on Mount Kukṣi, in its caves, and in its forests.
There, the Vināyakas who create obstacles for those engaged in recitation [are present];
they possess the form of an elephant, have many tusks, and are endowed with great majesty.
Likewise, she who had assumed the form of a horse, possessing many shapes,
was the divine daughter of Īśāna, appearing in various forms and creating obstacles.
There, the mantras as they were taught and the field of accomplishment (siddhikṣetra) are seen,
along with Mothers of various forms and most terrible planetary spirits (grahas).
The realm of the preta-yoni, inhabited by those who subsist on human food and belong to the Nairṛtas,
is declared to be the field of accomplishment (siddhi-kṣetra) ordained by the King of Pretas.
One should designate that as the field of accomplishment for all beings from the very beginning;
indeed, the Vajrakrauñca of great heroism attains accomplishment in that direction.
The foremost mantras of the Asuras, as well as others that are worldly,
indeed attain accomplishment there, having taken recourse to the southern direction.
Likewise, one should always assign [the rites] to Yama, the King of the Pretas;
for then the mantras of the various castes, as well as those of Śiva and Viṣṇu, will attain success.
Cruel mantras, commanded by Vajrapāṇi and others, are ineffective when applied to non-cruel rites or to fields and other such locations.
Having gone to the southern region, those who have committed evil deeds achieve success;
indeed, the ripening of their inauspicious fruits is seen in that very direction.
The mantras spoken by Āditya and those proclaimed as belonging to Soma,
as well as the mantras of Indra, are successfully accomplished in the beautiful western direction.
There, the lord of yakṣas himself, the giver of wealth to all beings, possessing great supernatural power, will achieve accomplishment for those who are foolish and deluded.
By means of the causes prescribed by the ritual rules, he bestows his heart upon living beings;
in the western region, he becomes one who possesses enjoyments and accomplishes all aims.
Renowned here on this earth by the name Dhanada,
he is the Yakṣa Vajrapāṇi himself, a Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
The foremost of mantras, the most excellent of boons, himself the sovereign of the ten stages— indeed,
all mantras born of the Vajra and Lotus families are accomplished through him.
Likewise, the mantras of the eight families are based upon the eight directions;
indeed, the mantras born of the Jina are accomplished in the northern direction.
Likewise, in the eastern region, there is accomplishment through mantras born of the Lotus family;
relying on the southern path, those belonging to the Vajra abode are accomplished.
In the west, Gaja is proclaimed, and likewise Maṇikula in the intermediate direction;
in the junction of the west and north, Siddhi is assigned among them.
Likewise, at the junction of the west and the south is the family of yakṣas;
and in the southeastern quarter is the place of the śrāvakas of great majesty.
Among them, that which is called the "clan" is indeed seen; in those locations, success is achieved.
In the northeastern direction, there is the origin of the Pratyekabuddhas from the Jina.
That which is called the Kula is highly esteemed in the world; indeed, accomplishment (siddhi) resides within them.
Furthermore, in the downward direction, all worldly accomplishments are attained.
The mantras that enter the netherworld are indeed accomplished within the eight families;
likewise, the supramundane mantras, such as the Uṣṇīṣas and others, are proclaimed.
Those [attainments] proclaimed by the Cakravartin Jina lead to success above;
however, for the Vajrin, success is achieved everywhere in all directions.
Likewise, all other kings of mantras originating from the Lotus-Born,
as well as all mantras that bestow enjoyments, are always successful in every respect.
Success is achieved at all times in this [place] for both the Vajra and Lotus families;
this is designated as the field, and now that time is proclaimed.
At the beginning of the emergence of all Buddhas, there was the mantra-siddhi proclaimed by the Jina;
but in the intermediate period of the Buddhas, it arose from the lotus and the vajra.
The accomplishment of these mantras, as well as that of other mantra-holders, is declared to occur at this specific time; it is not proclaimed to occur at any other time.
Through austerity, one may attain supreme accomplishment within three human births;
[this applies to] those who constantly recite the mantra, are devoted to it, and have their minds fixed upon it.
For the sons of the Victors who are serene, success is achieved even in this very life—
for those devoted to the Three Jewels and adorned with the mind of awakening.
For one who abides in the vow, possesses great wisdom, and is skilled in the tantras and mantras,
the mantras are accomplished without effort because she is established in the vow of awakening.
The accomplishment of beings' karma is declared to be the accomplishment of the self;
mantras are always already accomplished, but they appear unaccomplished when beings are deluded.
For this very reason, the Lord of Jinas has proclaimed this King of Rituals; for the seventh [chapter] is the most excellent of Buddhas, having made the mantra extensive.
Then that chief of sages, the Moon of the Buddha possessed of great supernatural power,
chose Mañjughoṣa, the eldest son of the Buddha, who is endowed with great majesty.
Listen, O Youth, to the ultimate course of power of the mantras,
at which time the Buddhas, the leaders of the world, always remain present.
At that time, the accomplishment (siddhi) of the Uṣṇīṣa and others is proclaimed;
likewise, the Wheel-turning King (cakravartin) is proclaimed as a mass of splendor (tejorāśi).
Many [deities] such as Sitātapatrā and Uṣṇīṣā have been described by the Jinas;
likewise, such uṣṇīṣas will be accomplished at that time.
When a universal monarch shall appear in Jambudvīpa at that time,
and when the Perfectly Awakened One, the King of Dharma and supreme among bipeds, remains [in the world],
at that time there shall be the accomplishment of all mantras as they have been spoken.

Thus concludes the twenty-eighth chapter, the detailed exposition on the rules for the determination of fields and times, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-first chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī! I shall speak of the previously described state of those possessed by spirits, their conduct, and the auspicious and inauspicious signs."
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, placed his joined palms to his head, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would speak of the mental activities of beings who have entered the bodies of other beings—such as noble ones, gods, *etis*, *siddhas*, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, mahoragas, and so forth—whose bodies are produced by diverse karma, who reside in various destinies, who possess many marks of various forms, and who are human or non-human. It is the right time, O Blessed One; it is the right time, O Sugata."
"Now, do as you deem the time is right.
Having been addressed thus, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta remained silent on his own seat, having requested the supreme Victor, the Leader of the World, Gautama, the best of Conquerors.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni spoke concerning the knowledge of the signs of the mental conduct of sentient beings, their characteristics, and the [appropriate] time.
A being who has gone to another world, drawn by the application of mantras,
or some [spirits] out of greed for food, seize a human on earth.
Others, indeed with minds full of rage, and others because of former enmity—
these most dreadful beings seize humans in this world upon the surface of the earth.
Likewise, those who are eternally free from passion, out of compassion and in accordance with their commitment,
take on human form in this mortal world.
A woman who is praiseworthy, auspicious, free from physical defects, and superior in complexion to men—
when she is thus rising like the sun, her possession [by a spirit] is said to occur.
Their incarnations occur at this time when the sun has set and night has fallen;
they are seen during the first watch of the night in the bright fortnights.
An incarnation is seen among those men who are always righteous, whose deeds are auspicious, and who are endowed with purity and skill; such people are highly praised.
Then, mortals are possessed by those who are free from passion and possess great supernatural powers;
this occurs in a pure place and among virtuous people, under auspicious lunar mansions and stars, on a praiseworthy day and weekday, during the bright fortnight, on a fortunate day.
When the lunar day is conjoined with a bright planet and fully completed,
and the moon is likewise full, their descent is seen among them.
A sign of one who has entered existence yet is free from passion and possesses great supernatural power is that,
having leaped up from the earth, he stands in the sky at the height of a palm tree.
He is seen seated in the paryanka posture within a fixed abode;
likewise, there are various divine and incomparable sounds, such as those of Brahma, which are pleasant to the ear.
That great being speaks wherever he stands with an intent to cause pain;
drawn by the Uṣṇīṣa mudrās, he falls upon the surface of the earth.
While standing without touching the ground, one should immediately offer the *arghya* consisting of white sandalwood and saffron mixed with *jātī* flowers.

The practitioner of mantra, having prostrated himself upon the ground, should immediately offer water mixed [with ingredients], as well as the arghya and pādya, and make this request out of a desire for their welfare.
For when that being, whose mind is free from envy, is requested,
he utters divine speech that is flawless and pleasant to the ear.
Then, being confident and skilled in the knowledge of mantras, one may ask whatever one desires;
at that time, one must not be afraid, but should instead call Mañjughoṣa to mind.
Having bound the five-crested mudrā and another born from the uṣṇīṣa,
one should then perform the binding of the directions— above, below, and across.
Then he will relate the entire account from beginning to end—
the beginning, the middle, and likewise the time— exactly as it occurred in the past and what is yet to come.
That one of great splendor describes the present exactly as it is;
with unblinking eyes and motionless, he gazes upon those who are terrified and their enemies.
The word uttered by him shall not become otherwise than true;
likewise, he [knows] the accomplishment of success, the substance, the womb, the collection, and the destination.
It is certain for the awakening of a pratyekabuddha, for arhatship, and for great awakening;
it is certain for the lineage of Buddhahood.
Marked by the samaya, that yogi shall speak the truth regarding everything— the absence of lineage, the time, and the sentient being of great power who is destined for liberation;
he shall speak merely according to the characteristics [of the situation] and shall not wait for another time.
Whatever one may pray for with a well-disposed mind at this very moment,
all that one obtains quickly, as well as the complete perfection of the mantra;
one shall attain every prosperity exactly as desired and sought after.

Having quickly dismissed them and offered the appropriate *argha* water, the mantra-practitioner should perform the protection of the vessel according to the ritual procedure as seen in the scriptures.
Having considered the fallen body lying upon the great earth,
one should employ the mantra appropriate for the Victor, conjoined with the uṣṇīṣa mudrā.
With that very [substance], or with the five-crested mudrā, one should perform protection;
then, while his body is healthy, the being [should eat] on the ground from the leftovers.
This protection has been devised for all beings who are possessed;
indeed, malevolent beings are powerless to harm those who have taken refuge in a worthy vessel.
Indeed, this is a great protection for living beings arising from the vessel;
his speech is declared to be neutral in the Middle Country.
Having resorted to the divine womb, these and other signs arising from form are seen among the gods of the Form Realm, beginning with Akaniṣṭha.
Those who are lords of the desire realm and among the celestial dwellers of the desire realm possess a gait and appearance inferior to those, yet their speech is very sweet.
Then, having emerged from the earth and standing in their celestial palaces,
those inhabitants of heaven addressed the city of Kāśī and those yakṣas with words full of joy.
Likewise, the speech of the Aṅgas is proclaimed as that of the Mahoragas;
the eastern speech belongs to those Garuḍas of great splendor.
Likewise, that speech which arises as even in Vaṅga,
and the speech of the Kinnaras— that speech is considered [to be of the same nature].
The speech of those possessing swords shall always be in the Yaudheya dialect; however, that speech of the Vidyādharas is [in the] Siddhavidyā dialect.
But for the sages who possess all forms through speech, that speech is conceived as having five superknowledges (pañcābhijñā) and being capable of assuming any form at will.
That which is the *sāmā* riverbank speech and that which is the *harikelikā* speech—
both the indistinct and the distinct— are indeed dependent upon the letter *ḍa*.
Speech that abounds in the letter *la* is called the Paiśācī language;
it arises in the islands known as Karmaraṅga, which are produced from the filaments of the *nāḍikā*.
In Dvīpavāruṣaka, born of Nagna and Vālī,
among the beings of Yavadvīpa and those born in other islands as well;
Speech that abounds in the letter *ra*, speech that has become indistinct,
unclear, harsh, and full of anger leads to birth among the *preta* realm.
The speech of the southern region consists of Andhra, Karṇāṭa, and Drāviḍa;
it also arises among the beings of Kosala, Aḍavi, and on the island of Siṃhala.
Speech in which the syllable *ḍa* is joined with the letter *ra* is known as Rākṣasī;
it is also spoken by humans dwelling in other continents.
Having spoken these words, he designated the fifth speech among the highly powerful Mothers as belonging to Vaidiśī and Mālavī.
The Vatsamatsārṇavī is fashioned by speech; the Śūrasenī, the Daśārṇavī, the Pārvatī, the Śrīkaṇṭhī, and the Gaurjarī as well.
By speech, the supreme planet Āditya and others were designated;
however, the other principal planet was conceived as Pāriyātrī.
In Arbuda, Sahma, and Malaya, among those dwelling in the mountains,
and among the people born in the Khaṣa valley— such is their speech.
Such speech is designated as born from the womb of the Kūṣmāṇḍas; it arises from the letters śa, ra, ṣa, sa, and is produced from ya, ra, la, va, ka, and ma.
The speech proclaimed with the syllable "gha" should be identified as belonging to the Dānavas;
it originates from the land of Kaśmīra and the people's abode in Kāpiśī.
All those born of noble families are born from the family of Vajrapāṇi;
the speech of all these foremost mantra-holders is thus intended.
Likewise, those situated in the center of the lotus, having resorted to the *kula-yoni*,
are seen to be born from the lotus, characterized by speech and their respective movements.
Thus it should be as previously described: the mantras of the Jinas are conceptualized;
however, those signs belonging to those free from passion are the signs born of the Jinas.
In whatever place a voice may arise, one should point out the being situated there according to its movement and behavior, identifying it by all those signs.
Dwelling within the womb of the Himalaya on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā,
Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Ṛṣis appear among people through their speech.
Those creatures born in the valleys of the Vindhya mountains, on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā,
as well as those born on the Śrīparvata mountain;
The Rākṣasas, Tārakas, Pretas, the deformed ones, and likewise the Mātṛs;
those of terrible form, the great obstacles, and the most dreadful planetary spirits (grahas).
Greedy for taking the lives of others, she arises from the speech of those people;
whatever signs exist in that region, such are her movements and behaviors in that land.
The speech and the utterances of those possessed by the wicked,
as well as their various movements— these and many others are the manifestations of their actions and gestures.
And having forms of various shapes and marked with diverse signs,
various wombs are intended for the foremost among the various classes of beings.
One should perform this rite, characterized by these signs and marked by the [proper] course of conduct,
for all human beings so as to bring them happiness.
For the sake of protection, one should employ the youth born of the universe;
the reciter should perform this by means of the six-syllable mantra itself.
When conjoined with the Mahāmudrā and placed upon the five strips of cloth, it will become a great protection.

Thus concludes the twenty-ninth chapter, the detailed exposition of the ritual for manifesting the activities of those possessed [by spirits], from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-second chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, I shall explain according to their measure the causes of accomplishment for your mantras—which enter into all tantras, which contain the secrets of all vidyās, and which yield results through various qualities and times—as well as the signs of their connection."
For example:
accomplishment [attained] in another birth is not an accomplishment resulting from time or causes;
rather, the application of its measure arises from what was previously connected.
Success comes from being attentive to what is beneficial;
it is through rational inquiry that the principle of taking refuge in your son is seen by all embodied beings.
In this context, previously performed karma is designated as "reasoning" (yukti).
Through its application, the wise person shall attain supreme accomplishment by means of reasoning.
An unaccomplished action is accomplished, yet there is no accomplishment without action;
when joined with both the object and the agent, accomplishment is conceived through their union.
He attained the supreme state through causes joined with ritual procedure;
he did not choose a mantra from the counselor, for one who lacks a mantra cannot be a counselor.
By practicing the conduct of silent ritual action, one attains abundant accomplishment;
the reciter, through the accumulation of seed-syllables, brings forth the supreme intellect.
One who is free from attachment shall attain the first goal, the most excellent state of space;
through the absence of attachment to space, being established in one's own self, one shall attain the wealth of the immortals.
In brief, for one who desires success at an improper time, there is no success in the mantras even for Śakra himself, regardless of the signs.
Furthermore, for one who acts harmfully toward living beings and proceeds at an improper time,
no success is seen, even for a high-souled Brahmin.
Endowed with lassitude and thirst, possessed of intoxication and pride, characterized by laxity and arrogance, he is constantly delighted in the company of women.
If he is indolent and joined with a wife, how can he achieve success? For if he were the preceptor of both the gods and the asuras, then [he would have no need for such things].
They too are unable to accomplish the mantra if it is devoid of the prescribed ritual;
likewise, a rite performed without the proper procedure causes confusion of the mind.
Therefore, one should not mutter that mantra improperly or without the prescribed ritual;
such [practices] produce a delusion of vision in the foolish.
But the foolish, being utterly deluded, fall thereafter into a most miserable state;
then those holders of mantras rescue them from that once again.
Then, in due order, they bestow accomplishment and a fortunate rebirth; thereafter, those mantras establish that reciter upon the immovable mountain of Śiva.
Thus, the Tathāgatas have declared that the recitation of mantras is unfailing;
even when the mind is deluded by wrong views, it is employed solely for the sake of bringing about spiritual benefit.
These indeed are the spiritual friends; these are those who cherish sentient beings.
For them, the auspicious equality of the three vehicles is taught as the accomplishment.
Therefore, with all effort and with a concentrated mind, one should recite the mantra;
for mantras, when employed by mantra-reciters through improper application, [fail].
Liberation from saṃsāra is held to be achieved only after a long time;
it is seen that the accomplishment of mantras is attained only after a very long period has passed.
For mantras employed according to the prescribed rules indeed attain success quickly;
one perceives the accomplishment of their fruit, for a mantra is not said to be fruitless.
In this very life, the mantras are perfected, arising with their fruits;
there is no accomplishment without the action that bears fruit, nor is an action desired that is without fruit.
The fruit arises from the conjunction with action; thus action is said to be fruitful. That which is born from recitation is produced in the sky as a manifestation of non-existence.
Those of peaceful disposition are liberated through that auspiciousness designated by the world;
such is the greatness of the destination attained by one who follows the path of the Buddhas.
Even in this age of Kali, which is characterized by perversion, success is seen for him as well;
success may be attained in this very life, or it may manifest at the end of the birth.
Until there is the ultimate peace, the unconditioned path of Śiva—
that most stainless state of Śiva which is proclaimed by the World-Honored One.
Buddhahood is indeed luminous and revealed in every way by all people;
the attainment of mantra-siddhi is said to be its very limit, for that is truly its end.
The non-existence that is unmanifest, which arises within each individual,
has been described in the world by the Moon-like Sages of great supernatural power as being the mantra.
Manifest accomplishment is ordained for embodied beings even in this very life;
when the mantra enters one who knows reality in the field of the Void, it brings about Buddhahood.
At the time of the onset of the Kali age, when the Knower of Reality has attained peace,
mantras will not quickly grant success to those who desire their goals.
At that time, one who knows the mantras and tantras should accomplish [the goal] through application and ritual action as prescribed by the rules, according to the teaching spoken by the Sage.
When a Tathāgata is present, supreme accomplishment is swiftly attained;
likewise, during the intermediate period, middling accomplishment is proclaimed.
When the time of the end of the age has arrived, it is called the lowest accomplishment;
whereas in a beautiful age and at an auspicious time, there is likewise the power of flying through the sky.
The accomplishment of all mantras has been taught by the leaders of the world;
at that time, the foremost family of the Lords of Jinas will be successfully accomplished.
In the middle [age], accomplishment belongs to the Lotus family; at the end of the age, however, it belongs to the Vajra family.
By the power of their former vows, certain mantras always bring about accomplishment.
Avalokiteśvara, Mañjuśrī, Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, and the King of Yakṣas—
all the yakṣas who move among māṇicaras— attain accomplishment at all times.
Those mantras and others, including worldly ones marked with clear signs, which were employed by all the deities, attain accomplishment in the time of the Kali age for those who possess passion.
It was proclaimed by gods and humans, by lords of the Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas,
as well as by Ṛṣis, Garuḍas, Piśācas, hosts of Bhūtas, and Grahas.
Both human and non-human beings, belonging to the realm of desire—
those possessing great supernatural powers and merit, as well as those of cruel deeds and extreme ferocity.
These mantras of great supernatural power were proclaimed by Śakra, Brahmā, and Rudra, as well as by Īśāna and others, by Viṣṇu, and by all the spirits.
Even they attain accomplishment for those who recite mantras at that end of the eon;
likewise, success in fierce rites is achieved at that time of great terror.
On this earth, the accomplishment of subjugating, attracting, or [dealing with] flesh-eating spirits is seen to be fruitless and condemned even in the next world.
Therefore, at that time of great terror, the Lord of Jinas,
intent upon benefiting sentient beings, was instructed by Mañjughoṣa.
Then those beings who are devoted to this teaching and are worshippers of the Three Jewels will perish by means of the mantra-forms of those who recite it.

Thus concludes the thirtieth chapter, the detailed section on the rules for rituals and the proper times, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-third chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having surveyed the entire abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

In your *Mañjuśrī-kalparāja*, which is fully proclaimed, in this extensive section of the supreme jewel-chapter of the Great Sūtra—which follows the outflow of the *dharmadhātu* and the *tathāgatagarbha* that is the treasury of the *dharmadhātu*—and which is authorized as the supreme secret of the Tathāgata, when the mantra-slayings are being accomplished, there arise all the various cries of beings, which are sounds expressing the notions of both non-sentient and sentient entities; these serve as the means for accomplishment, mediated by signs, knowledge, marks, and the measurement of time.
It is said that there is verbal knowledge, as well as what is called non-verbal knowledge; likewise, there is mixed [knowledge]. Thus, the practice of logic and mantras is threefold.
Endowed with divine sounds, it is employed for the sake of impermanence; it is eternally free from corrupt words and adorned with the meaning of refined linguistic usage.
In all established doctrines, the noble mantras are proclaimed to be eternally devoid of referential objects; they are divided into three types.
Adorned with heavy, light, and medium syllables,
that mantra-goddess shall be further embellished by vowels and meters.
The discourse on the conditioned and the unconditioned, as well as the meaningful and the meaningless, according to others;
likewise, the meaning of the elements (dhātu), the logical reasoning, and that which is adorned with the meaning of the mantras of the states of existence (gati).
The speech of all worldly mantras is characterized by a profusion of conceptual constructions;
it consists of one or two syllables, follows metrical rules, and possesses the *āścarita* and *ālaya* accents.
The accomplishment of the phonemes is held to occur at the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, as well as the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth [day].
These syllables, which are the causes of all letters, are joined with ten vowels;
indeed, these syllables are seen on the surface of the earth as being tenfold.
From one hundred syllables down to twenty, and even unto a single syllable—
mantric perfection is composed of such measures of phonemes.
The mantras spoken by the Jinas, which accomplish all aims, are endowed with four lines; they are indeed the eldest, the most excellent, and the noblest of mantras.
But those which were then middling or inferior were spoken by their sons, the sons of the Conqueror; those indeed are the middling ones.
Those mantras which are indeed spoken as mundane are inferior;
those mantras spoken by the Nairṛtas are said to be base.
The measure of these mantras spoken by the Noble Ones and the Victors is ten, eighteen, twenty-eight, or even up to more than a hundred.
The number of syllables in these mantras, as proclaimed by the Bodhisattvas, ranges from one or two syllables up to five hundred syllables.
The application of mantras is declared to be arranged within those syllables;
the meters are joined with vowels and adorned with the meanings of verbal roots and their objects.
Speech that is well-employed and endowed with the principles of tantra may sometimes achieve success, even if it is devoid of the proper sounds and accents.

Accompanied by mudrās and sounds, [the practice] proceeds from the head down to the *ūṣman* [consonants], the palate, the teeth, the lips, and the throat; the sound thus emitted is the ritual of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
But that which is well-employed is declared to be free from the unmanifest;
one who employs it correctly will accomplish the word as a complete sentence.
A mantra that deviates from the prescribed rules, is devoid of ritual action, and is separated from its proper words and meanings, will not achieve success quickly; it requires a long period of time.
For such a reciter, success is never fruitless; his recitation is not performed in vain. Even in another birth, the granting of boons through mantra-siddhi is seen.
Through the power of that mantra, and because of its long duration for those who recite it,
the mantra makes the ritual action unfailing for people who know the mantra and possess the mantra.
All worldly mantras, whether belonging to humans or proclaimed by all the bhūtas, as well as those mantras characterized by envy, are inferior to [this].
Their syllables are said to be one, two, or three in number,
expressed through various Mleccha languages as well as those proclaimed in the divine language.
They are strung together, arranged in rows, and always intermingled by way of sound;
they range from one thousand, eight hundred, and eight, down to even a single syllable.

That which has four feet or half a foot is declared to be prose (gadya) and verse (padya); a *śloka* consists of [eight] *daṇḍaka* measures, while the *gāthā*, *skandhaka*, and *pañcika* are composed of those same measures.
The reasoning of the counter-argument, adorned with a thousand meanings,
conceptualizes words in both Apabhraṃśa and Saṃskṛta as being devoid of meaning.
When the unmanifested, devoid of manifestation, is joined with that which is devoid of measures (mātrā),
the accomplishment of mantra is said to occur through the dissociation from the destination and location.
This is the characteristic of all mantras:

those mantras that abound in the letter *śa*, are adorned with the meaning of the syllable *oṃ*, and abide within the tantra characterized by the letter *ta*— in them, accomplishment (*siddhi*) will certainly occur.

Those mantras which begin with the syllable *oṃ* and end with the letter *ma*, when joined with a thousand *śa*s, are likewise fruitful and auspicious; those beginning with the letter *ta* and having a square form (*caturasra*) are devoid of any final elision (*pratyāhāra*).
The syllable *takāra* joined with the letter *repha*, together with the mantra, is the rite of accomplishment;
it is the first, abounding in two *rephas*, arising from the quality of the syllable *huṃ*.
Within the square enclosure of the letter *va*, the syllables are capable of accomplishment:
the letter *ka* joined with *ra*, ending with *ma* and mixed with a vowel;
beginning with *ma* and *na*—this is said to be the most excellent mantra.
That mantra which is seen in all tantras to abound in the letter *ta* is said to be "gentle" (*saumya*); that which is adorned with the syllable *huṃ* is "southern" (*yāmya*);
and that which abounds in the letter *bha* is said to be "northeastern" (*aindrāvāyavya*).
They say that the letter *ca* belongs to Varuṇa and is beneficial for prosperity in the world;
while a mantra in which the letter *va* predominates is seen to belong to Mahendra.
The first mantra is the going for refuge to the Three Jewels; by performing this salutation, it becomes a cause for peace and brings about happiness.
That other [mantra] is employed for the purpose of paying homage to all the deities;
that mantra, together with its own mantra and the Lord of Mantras, is effective for all rites.
Any mantra that abounds in the syllable *ḍa*, or is uttered with *phaṭ* and *huṃ*,
these mantras are extremely fierce, radiant, and possessed of great power.
Since [death] is brought about by the immediate obstruction of breath through the application of cruel means,
one should therefore not perform sinful deeds, especially those that are particularly harmful.
The reciter should avoid that [place], because it has always been avoided by the sages;
for even in both matters, the mantras for pacification and enrichment will be accomplished.
In an instant, they accomplish all whatever rites have been spoken; for these mantras, when well-recited, are powerful and possess great supernatural efficacy.
One should perform pacifying rites with those spoken by the Jina;
however, one should perform all nourishing rites within the Kokanada family.
All evil deeds are employed in sorcery (*ābhicāra*);
one should perform all acts of sorcery by means of the Vajra family.
Though forbidden by the Protectors of the World, they were revealed by the Lord of Yakṣas.
For the sake of disciplining sentient beings, the arising of the majesty of mantra has been explained in three ways throughout all the three families.
Regarding those eight foremost families which were proclaimed by the Sage himself, within them threefold accomplishment has occurred; they are declared to be of three types:
superior, middling, and inferior, and thus they are divided into these three.
Pacifying (śāntika), enriching (pauṣṭika), and even the malevolent (ābhicāruka) are intended;
the application of mantra alone is declared to be the application of tantra (tantrayukti).
The great power of the movement of mantras is employed for malevolent rites;
however, this action is inferior and is censured by the Omniscient Ones.
One should not perform an action that obstructs life even when fallen into hardship;
however, this has been described briefly merely for the sake of illustrating the greatness of karma.
The procedure for the application of tantras through mantras, with its extensive elaboration of ritual actions,
is taught here in this King of Rituals (Karmarāja), though it is also seen in other tantras.
One who is proficient in the application of all mantras should not employ that which is devoid of ritual action;
this applies to as many worldly mantras as there are, whether they be with form (sakala) or without form (niṣkala).
All these are indeed supramundane, and their qualities are always immeasurable; the accomplishment of mantra is likewise proclaimed to be immeasurable.
Although it was previously stated that they begin from the number one up to twenty,
there are likewise thirty in brief, and another forty as well.
Then, they say there are sixty-three, seventy, and likewise eighty; and another ten, and yet another number, eighty.
They say that ten times ten is ninety; a full hundred is ten times more than that.
The number "hundred" is thus reckoned, and ten times that is a thousand.
Ten thousand is an ayuta; ten ayutas are a lakṣa;
ten lakṣas are a vilakṣa; and ten vilakṣas are a koṭi.
Ten times ten million (daśakoṭi) is indeed an arbuda;
ten arbudas are said to be a nirbuda, and ten times that is held to be a khaḍga.
Ten *khaḍga* is a *nikhaḍga*; ten *nikhaḍga* is considered a *kharva*. Ten *nikharva* is likewise a *padma*, and ten *padma* is a *mahāpadma*.

Ten padmas constitute a vāha; likewise, ten vivāhas constitute another unit; ten mahāvivāhas are seen to be a māya. Ten māyas are called a mahāmāya. Ten mahāmāyas are said to be a śaṅku. Ten śaṅkus are known as a mahāśaṅku. Ten mahāśaṅkus are declared to be a samudra. Ten samudras are said to be a madhya. Ten madhyas are called a mahāmadhya. Ten mahāmadhyas are declared to be an anta. Ten antas are known as a mahānta. Ten mahāntas are said to be a parārdha. Ten parārdhas are declared to be a mahāparārdha. Thus, O best of the twice-born, the enumeration of numbers has been explained to you. One should know that the number of atoms in a single finger-breadth (aṅgula) is twenty-one thousand, two hundred and sixty-four. Know that the number of atoms in a single finger-joint is three times that. The number of atoms in a single finger is one hundred and twenty-three thousand, eight hundred and sixty-four. The number of atoms in a single cubit is five hundred and seventy-two thousand, nine hundred and twenty-one. The number of atoms in a single bow is twenty-three crores, thirty-six million, two hundred and eighty-eight thousand. The number of atoms in a single krośa is ninety-three crores, four million, eleven hundred and fifty-two thousand. The number of atoms in a yojana is three hundred and seventy-two crores, sixteen million, forty-four hundred and eighty thousand.
