The tenth power of that is *mahāmāyā*; the tenth power of *mahāmāyā* is designated as *samudra* by the leaders of the world in the science of calculation.
Thereafter, the Mahāsamudra is twenty-five [yojanas] in circumference;
thus indeed is the Mahāsamudra described, and then the Sāgara is ten [yojanas].
They say that twenty-five [mahāsāgaras] constitute one *prayujyate*;
ten *mahāsāgaras* multiplied tenfold is indeed called a *pragharā*.
Ten *pragharas* are said to be one *ghara*; that is what is proclaimed. Ten *gharas* are also called by the name *nāma*, and all of that is described as *aśeṣa*.
The measure known as *mahāśeṣa*, which is the remainder when all [preceding numbers] are exhausted, multiplied by twenty-five—
that is declared by the Leaders of the World to be the measure of the *asaṃkhya*.
They say that ten times the number "saṅkhya" is "asaṅkhya";
when that is multiplied, it is likewise beyond that.
That world is proclaimed to be a thousandfold greater than Amitā;
beyond that world is Mahāloka, which is multiplied by the same factor as Mahāloka.

Then that which is called "total darkness" is described by means of *tamas*; light is described by means of *tamas*. Having multiplied the light by the great luminosity, that is called the "great mass."
From a great heap comes what is called a "great heap"; from a heap, it is said to become profound.
They say that the profound is stable; from stability, one should proceed to greater stability.
Beyond that, by means of great deliberation, the highly esteemed position is declared;
those who are diligent in the knowledge of calculation say that it is a position superior to all other positions.
One should then go to Mahāsthāna; Mahāsthāna is considered to be "the measured. Having made the measured equal to the immeasurable, it is proclaimed as being of great significance.
From Mahārtha, one should go to Suśrutasthāna, and from there to Mahārṇava;
they say that [Suśrutasthāna] is the first after Mahārṇava, for it is indeed more primary than the first.
In the first [state], they call it "the best" (*śreṣṭha*); from the "best," it is said to extend to the "eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*).
Beyond the "eldest" is that which is named *mandirasas*, which is proclaimed to be inconceivable.

The inconceivable is the most excellent among those seeking the inconceivable; from the terrible, the kingdom is desired as more terrible. Beyond the kingdom is the hidden; beyond the hidden is the auspicious.
Beyond the auspicious, the Great Mind (mahācetas) will perceive as the Great Mind;
that which is called "mind" (cetas) is described as the mental distraction of thought (citta-vikṣepa).
The expressible and the inexpressible are indeed called "sound" (svara);
beyond the universal (viśva) is the Great Universal (mahāviśva), which is called "soundless" (asvara).

From that comes the Great Bold One, then the Bold One; this is here called Odaka.
Odaka is the state of mental distraction, and another supreme stage follows.
Beyond the highest [level], the Buddhas do not perceive the objects of lower stages;
however, for humans, it is impossible to calculate the conception of the world.
Beyond that, the range of the Buddhas is considered to be nothing else;
it is described as being like the sands of the river Ganges in number within a Buddha-field.
The Leaders explained by means of splitting atoms;
for this is made into an illustration, as it is within the scope of knowledge derived from reasoning.
A substance is established by its cause; it cannot be grasped by those who rely on mere enumeration.
This is the measure [of reality] which I formerly attended upon as the Fully Awakened Ones.
Having propitiated them during this thoughtless eon for such an immeasurable length of time, I was formerly a bodhisattva.
Having fully awakened for the sake of sentient beings, one should enter into Buddhahood;
in various places, I have taught tantras with extensive ritual procedures.
This is the supreme and most excellent kalpa, spoken by the Buddhas;
this is the authoritative standard taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones as my ancient [teaching].
Now, O Kumāra, at this final time of birth, I have proclaimed all the worldly mantras and the beautiful kings of rituals (kalparāja).
Whether supramundane, divine, or human— including those of the gods and asuras—
the application of the tantras for all mantras has been thus proclaimed.
This King of Rituals, possessed of great supernatural power, is indeed authorized in all respects;
through the performance of its ritual procedures, Mañjughoṣa brings about accomplishment for them.
By this very method, through this Mañjubhānin,
success for all of them has been declared by the powerful one.
How much more so in the human world, as well as for other mantra-deities—
all supramundane mantras and mundane ones possessed of great supernatural power?
By this application of the ritual according to the King of Rituals, one attains success;
it is proclaimed that mastery over all mantras is achieved through every ritual manual.
But Mañjuśrī, this one is authorized here in this supreme King of Rituals (kalparāja):
whatever worldly arts and sciences there are that are esteemed by the world.
The omens of knowledge of signs are characterized by the knowledge of astrology;
through the practice of the knowledge of signs, auspicious and inauspicious results are found in sounds alone.
And indeed, the cries of all beings, their conduct marked by the mind,
the element, the most extensive, and the substance.
They say that bodily gestures and omens, as well as mining, metallurgy, and ritual action;
arithmetic, grammar, the sciences, weaponry, sequence, and procedure [are all included therein].
The inner science, medicine— which brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings— and likewise logic, as well as others, and the science of grammar were set forth.
The classification of perfumes, the art of music, and the compounding of fragrances have been proclaimed by me, a Bodhisattva, for the benefit of sentient beings.
In the past, when I was a bodhisattva for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
I previously spoke these words to those dwelling in the ocean of saṃsāra.
I have indeed dwelt for a long time in the dense wilderness of saṃsāra;
there, I act in accordance with the needs of those beings who are to be disciplined.
In whatever way sentient beings indeed undertake beneficial action,
in that very way I perform for their benefit action that is a source of purity.
The various states of beings, which are the sources of their welfare, are made manifold by their diverse karma;
they are fashioned in diverse ways, corrupted by the source of their diverse objects.
Just as they are described in the treatises— with their various purposes and joined with diverse karmas—
I shall likewise bring about for them that same variety of excellence of form.
I shall likewise assume various guises with diverse limbs, both my own and those of others;
out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, I manifest manifold forms.
In the past, I likewise created Maheśvara, Śakra, Brahmā, and the others, as well as Viṣṇu, Dhanada, and Nairṛta, along with the various planets in their celestial forms.
With my mind permeated by great compassion, I shall gradually establish those beings, who range within the sphere of their own dispositions, in the state of auspiciousness.
I have wandered through saṃsāra for a long time observing it;
the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings has been taught in the form of mantras.
The sequential knowledge of the mind and the ritual manual of mantras have been set forth;
after wandering for a long time through births, I have now taken my place within the lineage of the Buddhas.
I have no creator, nor even a master;
having relied upon the fixed lineage, I am the Buddha who has attained supreme enlightenment.
I have attained security—ageless, peaceful, sorrowless, stainless, and auspicious;
I have reached extinction and tranquility, and I am liberated from the bondage of birth.
Now that the wheel has been set in motion, resting upon the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi),
I shall indeed show this ritual manual for the discourse on mantras in full detail.
The reciter should not perform the ritual procedures in detail in vain;
for as many worldly mantras as have been proclaimed, their rituals are likewise described.

All of them are to be honored and revered; indeed, contempt for them must be avoided. Therefore, the mantra-practitioner should not despise them, even regarding their extensive ritual manuals (*kalpa*).

One should not perform these omens, the application of knowledge, and the astrological calculations proclaimed by those who know the stars in vain; they have been declared for the sake of auspiciousness.

In this way, however, the attainment of substances for success and so forth in this very life is accompanied by worldly gain and is a source of attachment; therefore, such success is called a mere "auspicious sign."
It is praised with verses of the Jina and adorned with verses of auspiciousness;
it is performed on excellent, primary days of the bright fortnight, clearly marked by favorable signs.
One should begin the practice of mantra when joined with the best of the bright planets;
likewise, one should employ such auspicious conjunctions and avoid those that are inauspicious.
This was previously taught by me alone; therefore, it should be accepted by those who recite mantras.
Whatever skill in the knowledge of astrology exists in this world, [it all originates from this].
Or others who are experts in that regard, possessing the principles of policy along with their underlying reasons, well-connected to the treatises on logic, acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
All that has been spoken by me alone is to be grasped by those who recite mantras;
this path, which is the cause of accomplishment, has been shown by the seers of reality.
For whatever has been taught as the complete and exhaustive doctrine that causes liberation,
by that very means one should establish the path of mantras, which are the causes of accomplishment.
The reciter should not perform the application of mantras in vain;
for all worldly mantras as well as those proclaimed as supreme are included therein in their entirety.
One should employ all those that are supramundane as well as divine;
one should never cause the mind to be false, nor should one ever corrupt the mental faculty therein.
All mantras are indeed to be honored; they are proclaimed as those who know the samaya.
In this teaching of the Tathāgata, for the sake of the equality and welfare of the Buddhas, let it be so.
The sons of the Victors have settled here, drawn in and introduced into the mandala of the Moon-like Sages; they are declared here to be knowers of the samaya.
Those mantras brought forth with the desire for universal destruction are always unfailing;
one should not bow down to the mantras of others, nor should one act with contempt toward them.
Those mantras which are indeed ignoble are proclaimed to be unfailing.

However many worldly mantras there are— those that are inferior, produced by recitation, associated with afflictions, and ending within the path of vision— they are nonetheless fruitful for those who perform the recitation.

One should not pointlessly direct the mind toward one who is prone to anger or filled with resentment; nor should one offer pleasing words or devotion to such a person, for their actions bear no fruit. Since the mind is dependent on that [anger], one should never yield to it.
But one who employs a single mantra, remaining established in reason and constantly reciting it with a concentrated mind,
obtains the entire fruit exactly as described by the rules of the ritual procedure.
Having made the mind steady, one should recite that single mantra;
for one whose mind is focused on a single object, mantras that accomplish all aims become effective.
For one whose mind is distracted and whose self is deluded, success is not seen; however, one who possesses a focused mind shall attain the complete production of fruit and reach the vast state.
For one whose mind is eternally pure, who possesses faith in the very teaching [of the Buddha],
and who has serene confidence in the Three Jewels, the desired accomplishment is proclaimed.
Thus [it is said].

Thus concludes the thirty-first chapter, the detailed exposition on the instruction of the knowledge of signs for the ritual procedures of action, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-fourth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon that abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Listen, Mañjuśrī, to your *mudrā-tantra*, which contains the secrets and is most supremely hidden; it is not to be revealed to beings who lack faith, who have no devotion to the teaching of the Tathāgata, who lack the authorization of the *samaya*, who do not ensure the non-interruption of the lineage of the Three Jewels, who are under the influence of non-virtuous friends, who desire merit [only for themselves], who are mixed with wicked people, who are under the influence of evil friends, who have become distant from the Buddha-dharmas, and who have become fruitless in this age, lacking the instruction of a master and having been uninitiated. O Youth, it must not be revealed to those who have not seen the most supremely secret maṇḍala, who do not possess the *samaya* within the family of the Tathāgata, or to any common person, even among all those beings who follow your mantras.
One who lacks faith in the Buddha's teachings is indeed far removed from enlightenment;
one should not cause such a person to receive the mudrās, nor should one show them the tantra.
If one who is deluded by confusion through negligence should cause [the rites] to be given out of greed and so forth,
the tantras and mantras will certainly not succeed for that practitioner who recites them perversely.
If one forms the mudrā and recites the mantra otherwise when [the deity] is not present,
one will not quickly attain accomplishment and will even suffer physical decline.
One should reveal the Tantra of Mudrās to those who are gentle, whose minds are intent on the śrāddha rite, who perceive reality at the proper time, and who are engaged in the Tantras and mantras.
One should reveal the mudrās to those who worship the Three Jewels, who have faith in the teaching of the Jina, and who have observed the prescribed applications.
One should reveal the mudrā to those who know the ritual of bodhicitta, who are adorned with bodhicitta, and who always abide on the path to enlightenment.
One should reveal the mudrā to those who have applied themselves to the tantras and mantras, who have perceived the higher and lower within the samaya, and who are intent upon great awakening.
One should reveal the seal to those who are devoted to the Sons of the Victors— the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— for whom there is the fruit visible in this very life.

One should reveal the seal of those who possess faith in dharmas free from conceptual construction, who are free from stinginess regarding their destination, and who understand the logic of the Teacher’s words.
For these mudrās are indeed sealed; they stand at the measure of one hundred and eight, neither more nor less, as revealed directly by the Buddhas.
In the ritual manual (*kalpa*) of Mañjuśrī, there are indeed mantras equal to that;
it is said that there are one hundred and eight mantras proclaimed as being equal to him.
Furthermore, one hundred and eight mudrās were taught by the best of sages in the past.
This is the measure of the eon for the emergence of mudrās and mantras;
it is declared to be the treasury of all Buddhas, the treasury of mantras.
When combined with the appropriate mudrās and mantras, the ritual action is swift;
for without a wheel, no movement can arise in a chariot, even if it is joined [with other parts].
In the same way, among all mantras, those devoid of mudrās do not perform the ritual action;
mantras when joined with and accompanied by mudrās are effective in swiftly accomplishing the task.
For these indeed cause all of the three worlds, including the gods and asuras, to revolve;
how much more so in the human world, regarding other conditioned activities?
For the fruit of these is seen in this very life within the mudrās and mantras;
when combined, they are shown to be pure in both respects through the application of the prescribed ritual.
They cause the beings to turn toward the state of being sons of the supreme Victors;
the mantra, the mudrā, and the austerity—these three types of action reside in the hand.
Just as the practitioner of recitation shall obtain all perfections according to their wish,
so too are the mudrās sealed by the mantras, and the mantras are also sealed by the mudrās.
A mantra devoid of mudrā is ineffective, and a mudrā bereft of mantra is likewise powerless;
however, when mudrā and mantra are joined together, they are fully empowered for all ritual actions.
For these are mutually the fruits of one another, arising as mutual fruits;
when the practitioner applies the method, no action exists alongside them.
Indeed, all mantras of those possessing form are accomplished when joined with mudrās;
for a mantra accompanied by a mudrā, when applied according to the prescribed rite, is successful.
There is no place to be found where one who is drawn [to this practice] does not achieve success;
from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, one traverses the world-systems without obstruction.
There is no being whatsoever to be found who, once possessed by this [power], could not be drawn forth or rendered incurable; indeed, there is no one at all who can turn back from it.
Even Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are drawn in by the chanting of the ritual;
even Bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages are rendered powerless.
Whether to break through protective rites or to obstruct the accomplishment of ritual acts,
those who rely upon mantras and mudrās are invincible to all beings.
For whoever among all beings relies upon the mantra,
these applications of mudrās indeed arise as protection.
The manifestation of all mantras is seen within all mantras; from mantra arise all mudrās, as they are mutually dependent upon one another.
The ritual procedure for the recitation of forms is employed in the path during the rite of fire-offering;
therefore, such accomplishment as has arisen is seen within the mantras through the mudrās.
For one who recites constantly, remains ever diligent, and is always established in those [practices], all mantras are indeed accomplished; the word of the Munis is never in vain.
The speech of all the Buddhas, who act for the benefit of others,
has been established through reasoning within the mantra-tantras.
"O Youthful Mañjuśrī, I declare this again and again: by those who have performed the rite through the entirety of mantra and mudrā, liberation is attained."
The liberation from all mantras without exception is found in the mudrā; therein lies the arising of benefit.
I pay homage to that which brings about deliverance and the production of fruit in this King of Ritual Manuals.
The most secret and beneficial *mudrā-tantra* has been extracted from that;
therefore, he is the one who possesses skillful means, the glorious one, the patient one, appearing in the form of a child.
With a face adorned with a gentle smile, the Youth, the source of the universe,
the Bodhisattva of great heroism, has attained the equality of the ten stages.
O Blessed One, bestow upon me that supreme sage, the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun,
who has been described in this world as the cause of mantras.
"In the past, that was also taught to me by previous perfectly awakened ones;
for what reason has it now been revealed by the Lion of the Śākyas?"
This doubt has arisen within me; explain it, O best of sages, you who possess the voice of a kalaviṅka bird and the majesty of the roar of Brahmā.
But he spoke to the Bodhisattva established on the ten stages:
"In former times, for many eons, I wandered through saṃsāra."
This sovereign king of rituals was obtained from the Sage named Saṅkusumita;
there, in various places, I have performed much benefit for sentient beings.
Having come under the power of compassion, I then made this vow:
"When I indeed arise as the supreme Buddha in this most degenerate age."
Having indeed accomplished the purpose of the teaching and set the wheel of Dharma in motion,
when I enter final nirvāṇa upon this earth in the very last age,
I shall then reveal this King of Rituals before you.
When I have passed away, when the world has become empty,
when the Teacher’s treasury of Dharma has receded far away in the Kali age,
this King of Kalpas shall act for the sake of protecting sentient beings.
This king of manuals, in its full detail, is bestowed upon you alone;
at that time, you shall be intent upon the welfare of sentient beings.
At that time, during that terrifying period, sentient beings will be most unrighteous;
kings will be constantly unstable and possessed of wicked minds.
Both humans and non-humans, all those who are hostile to my teaching,
will destroy the entire treasury of Dharma proclaimed by me.
For the sake of their discipline, this treasury of mantras has been proclaimed;
O Youth, this is your vow from inconceivable past eons.
For as many Buddhas as there may be who have entered nirvāṇa, those kinsmen of the world, for the sake of their teaching, I shall act in age after age.
Taking the form of a young boy, I shall wander everywhere;
through the form of mantra, I will discipline sentient beings from time to time.
O youth, this very vow was made by you in the past;
O child, it has now been attained, and for that very reason I shall explain it to you.
When the buddha-field is empty and the people have no refuge,
you, though appearing as a fool, shall instruct sentient beings by means of mantra-forms.
You will discipline many beings as the bestower of all prosperity;
you are the granter of boons to all sentient beings at that time, in this most degenerate age.
For when I have passed into nirvāṇa and the surface of the earth has become empty,
you yourself, in the form of a child, will perform the work of a Buddha.
"Then, in that delightful great forest born from the lap of the Himalayas,
on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī, my final liberation shall take place."

The thirty-second chapter, the detailed section on the ritual for the invocation of mudrās as taught in response to Mañjuśrī’s inquiry, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, is hereby completed.
Now begins the thirty-fifth detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, entered the samādhi called "The Exhortation of the Treasury of the Tathāgata’s Great Mudrās.
Immediately upon the Blessed One Śākyamuni’s entry into that state, a great ray of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows.

Accompanied by a retinue numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays, that net of light rays illuminated many Buddha-fields and exhorted all the Buddhas; then it vanished back into the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Immediately upon being exhorted, all those Blessed Buddhas entered the samādhi whose nature is space and stationed themselves in the sky above the Pure Abodes.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having honored all the Buddhas, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
Listen, Mañjuśrī, to the ritual procedure for the chapter on the treasury of mudrās, which is empowered by all the Buddhas of the future.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and bowed to all the Buddhas, addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni:

"It would be well, Blessed One, if you would explain the chapter on the treasury of the mudrās of all the Tathāgatas, which is most supremely secret; if you deem it now the right time, let that come to pass."

It will lead to the welfare of many, the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of the great mass of people, both gods and humans; it will result in the arising of happiness and the ripening of happiness for all sentient beings.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having been requested by the Blessed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, looked upon all the Buddhas, took hold of all sentient beings, gladdened all the Bodhisattvas, pacified all the Pratyekabuddhas and noble Śrāvakas, incited all those whose minds were intent on the purpose of mantras, warded off all the wicked, comforted all who were afraid, and established all who were in distress in the security, auspiciousness, and Nirvāṇa; for the sake of the happiness of all who suffer, he spoke this ritual procedure for the chapter on mudrās:
Listen, O Mañjuśrī Kumāra; I shall explain the chapter that is sealed [with the mudrās]. First, there is the five-crested [mudrā], which is considered the Great Mudrā (mahāmudrā).
One should know the second to be the Triśikha and the third the Ekacīraka;
the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds, call the fourth the Utpala.
The fifth is seen as the Svastika; the sixth is called the Dhvaja;
those well-adorned with the knowledge of mantras say that the seventh is the Pūrṇa.
The eighth is designated as the staff by the Lords of the World who have conquered their enemies;
the ninth is designated as the parasol, and the tenth is called the spear.
The eleventh, however, the Fully Awakened Ones should designate as *sampuṭa*;
the twelfth is said to be *phara*, and the thirteenth is likewise *gada*.
The fourteenth is designated as the sword, and the fifteenth likewise as the jar;
the sixteenth is said to be the noose, and the seventeenth is remembered as the goad.
The eighteenth is indeed the Bhadrapīṭha, while the nineteenth is the Pīṭhaka;
the twentieth is said to be Mayūrāsana, and the twenty-first is Paṭṭiśa.
The *ekaliṅga* consists of twenty-two; the *dviliṅga*, twenty-three;
the *mālā*, twenty-four; and the *dhanus*, twenty-five.
It is declared that sixty and twenty [verses] are prescribed for the *nārāca* meter;
they say there are twenty-seven [syllables] employed in the *sama-liṅga* meter.
Likewise, the twenty-eighth is the trident (śūla), the twenty-ninth is the mallet (mudgara),
they say the thirtieth is the javelin (tomara), and the thirty-first is the right [hand].
The thirty-second is the Face (Vaktra), the thirty-third is said to be the Cloth (Paṭa),
the thirty-fourth is the Pitcher (Kumbha), and the thirty-fifth is the Khakhara.
The *kalaśa* is prescribed for the thirty-sixth [day], while the *mauśala* occurs on the thirty-seventh;
the *paryaṅka* is on the thirty-eighth, and the *paṭaha* on the thirty-ninth.
They say that forty [bones] are cited as the *dharma-śaṅkha*;
that fortieth one is proclaimed as the *śaṅkalā*.
The second is said to be highly esteemed; the third fulfills all desires;
the fourth is seen as the Mother, the measured Perfection of Wisdom.
The perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds, call the fifth the "bowl";
the sixth is called the "archway," while the seventh is the "excellent archway."
The eighth is that designated by sound, while the ninth is the sound of recitation;
the fifty are said to be the drum, but the Dharma-drum is superior to them.

They say that "dvipañcāśat" (fifty-two) refers to the elephant; likewise, "varahastatrika" (the three excellent trunks) refers to fifty-four. That mudrā which moves within them should be known as such.
They say the fifth is Ketu, and the sixth is likewise Aśaśara;
the seventh is designated as Paraśu, and the eighth is Lokapūjitā.
In brief, the *bhiṇḍipāla* should be known as fifty-nine [in length],
while the *lāṅgala* should be sixty in length in brief.
Then, sixty-one is called Padma; sixty-two is called Vajra;
and sixty-three is said in the world to be when the Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion.
The Puṇḍarīka [mudrā] should be known briefly as sixty-four;
likewise, one should know the supreme Varada mudrā as sixty-five.
Likewise, the sixty-sixth is proclaimed as the Vajra-mudrā;
and the sixty-seventh is called the Kunta by the wise in the world.
Likewise, one should construct sixty-eight [squares], which is declared to be the Vajra-maṇḍala;
similarly, sixty-nine would be that which is celebrated as the Śataghnī.
Then, one should know the seventy-first [mudrā] in brief as Nādāmudrā;
they call the seventy-first the auspicious Vimānamudrā, the most excellent of mudrās.
In brief, this chariot is said here to consist of seventy-two [factors];
the bed of the Lords of the World consists, in brief, of another seventy-three.
The seventy-fifth is proclaimed, as well as the seventy-fourth;
both the half-moon and the lute are declared to be mudrās.
In the world, the seventy-sixth mudrā is Padmālayā;
the seventy-seventh, the most excellent, is the mudrā Kuvalayodbhavā.
The seventy-eighth is declared to be the mudrā of salutation;
the ninety-ninth and the ninetieth are both most auspicious mudrās.
The *sampuṭa* and the *yamala* mudrās make the number ninety;
they say that the *puṣpa* mudrā is declared as the ninety-first.
The second is the bracelet mudrā; the third always performs the incense offering;
the fourth is the fragrance mudrā, while the fifth is known as the lamp offering.
One should know that the sixth [case] is the means of accomplishment; the seventh is traditionally taught as the seat;
the eighth is declared to be the invocation; and the ninth is the dismissal.
One should likewise know that a hundred [mudrās] complete constitute the "all-acting" (sarvakarmikā) mudrā;
they say that more than a hundred are known as the "great mudrās" (mahāmudrā).
The Uṣṇīṣa of the Lords of the World and the Cakravartin are always for the Guru;
that mudrā is declared first, while the second arises from the White One.
The third is seen as the root mudrā of Mañjughoṣa;
the fourth is characterized as the Dharma mudrā, abiding in the treasury of the Dharma.
The fifth is called the Saṅgha, and it may also be the Mahāmudrā;
the sixth, however, is the Bhūtaśamanī, which arises from the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
The seventh belongs to the Bodhisattvas, while the tenth belongs to those who have entered [the stages];
it is the seal known as the Lotus Garland, which the wise know as the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā).
The bestower of boons among all mudrās and mantras, including those of the worldly realm;
she of great power, most excellent, the eldest, and worshipped by the three worlds.
One should employ the eighth mudrā, which is the abode of the three worlds;
the number of mudrās taught in this great and powerful tantra is [as follows].
One hundred and eight is the number established for the mudrās;
this measure was sung of old by the Perfectly Awakened Ones on the surface of the earth,
and it shall circulate among embodied beings when the Teacher’s doctrine has vanished.
First, having placed the two hands together with their tips joined,
one should then interlace the fingers so they are well-mingled;
then both hands are joined together, marked by five crests.
Then, with those fingers reversed,
the five-crested mudrā is to be known at their tips, as well as the five-tufted one.
Renowned as Mahāmudrā, it is likewise the crest-jewel of the Bodhisattvas; this seal of great power, when applied, is effective for all rites.
One should always employ the mantra of Mañjuśrī, or his heart-mantras, or indeed the mantra of Keśinī, or her root-mantra.
Or again, one should apply [this] according to the prescribed rule among all mantras;
one may perform all ritual actions, for this word of the Sage is never in vain.
In that same manner, one should place the two hands together to form a hollowed palm-cup;
therein, with the fingers interlaced, one should form the three-pronged gesture.
When both thumbs are held in the form of emptiness and supported [by the fingers], and the middle and ring fingers are likewise intertwined in a reversed manner;
This is to be known as the Three-Pointed [Mudrā], and furthermore as the "Form of the Triple Robe";
this is the Mahāmudrā of the wise Mañjughoṣa.
One should perform all rites indeed as prescribed by the rules;
one should apply these to all the mantras of Mañjuśrī.
For those who recite them, their goals desired in this life will be swiftly accomplished.
One should place the hands exactly as described and likewise form the single crest (*ekaśikha*);
with the middle fingers joined together, it will certainly become the Single Crest.
This seal (*mudrā*), the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), has been proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*sambuddha*).
Mantras entrusted to Kumāra, as well as others belonging to the mundane world,
when joined with this [practice], are accomplished and swiftly bring about the fulfillment of one's tasks.
By this, the supreme mantras spoken by the Victors are likewise accomplished;
for one quickly achieves all aims through ritual action performed according to the prescribed rules.
Those same hands joined together, with the fingers arranged and slightly bent,
both index fingers contracted, resembling a needle within an añjali-mudrā.
With the pair of thumbs placed together and the two middle fingers extended,
having encircled the ring fingers, it is declared to be the *utpala* [mudrā].
This is observed to be the root mantra of the Bodhisattva;
indeed, it is everything that has been taught as ritual action in the *Pañcacīraka*.
One should perform all that quickly; one should accomplish it with the utpala [mudrā].
This is the boon-granting mudrā, which swiftly brings about enjoyments.
When joined with the root mantra, it will swiftly accomplish one's purpose.
One should always join both hands together and keep them turned upward;
having formed that very same hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*) with the fingers on all sides.
It is arranged in a beautiful form, arising from the shape of a svastika.
When the little fingers are placed evenly in the middle of the middle fingers,
with the pair of thumbs positioned [on top], this mudrā is called the Svastika.
This mudrā, which accomplishes all aims, is employed in rites of pacification;
when joined with the six-syllable heart-mantras, it indeed performs all activities.
When those very hands are joined together with the fingers interlaced,
those who have attained the excellence of knowledge regarding the destinies call it the *pūrṇamudrā*.
Having formed the añjali gesture from the hollow of the palms with the fingers slightly spread apart on all sides,
the Perfectly Awakened Ones have declared this to be the "Full Mudrā" for those who recite mantras.
This [mantra], which pacifies everything, when impelled by the root mantra, swiftly makes one who is afflicted by the suffering of poverty rich in wealth.
Those who are well-versed in worldly knowledge and pure conduct call this another mudrā:
having positioned both hands in that manner, one rests upon the left index finger.
Having placed the right hand with the fingers positioned [as follows]:
when the index finger and the middle finger are extended, it is called the *dhvaja* (banner).
Known as the *dhvajamudrā*, when raised upward, it is the bearer of Śakra.
With this mudrā, one should perform the sequence of rites such as the bali offering and the homa;
for this [mudrā], when impelled by the root mantra, performs all activities.
When those same hands are placed together with the fingers joined in a hollowed shape,
that becomes the *sampuṭā* mudrā, which destroys all obstacles;
when combined with mantra and knowledge, it performs its activity in due order.
Indeed, when employed according to the prescribed rites, the mantras of Mañjughoṣa, which arise from the location of his heart, swiftly accomplish their purpose.
Joined together, it performs all actions marked by worldly convention;
that same [mudrā] is formed when the hands are placed such that the left hand rests upon the right.
Holding the right index finger and raising the left index finger—
this is known as the *yaṣṭi* mudrā, which wards off Śakra.
It subdues all obstacles, even those that are harsh and most terrifying;
for the purpose of slaying all the wicked, it has been prescribed for those who recite mantras.
When accompanied by the root mantra, it will swiftly accomplish one's aims.
That same hand, placed and raised in the form of a staff,
when the right hand is extended, is called the *chatra* (parasol) mudrā.
With this mudrā, one should perform self-protection starting from the head.
With all mantras, one should perform the rite called protection;
one may conceal the faces of enemies or paralyze them as desired.
One may cause even a wicked person to act according to one's desire;
indeed, all obstacles perish upon seeing the mudrā together with the parasol.
One should form that very [mudrā] with the hands, beautiful in its arranged form:
the tips of the thumbs joined and extended along the middle fingers.
The ring finger, with its tip bent at the middle joint, is designated as the *śakti*; it wards off all malevolent beings.
This protection, which destroys the malevolent planets, was proclaimed by the Lords of the World and deposited by the wrathful King Yamāntaka.
One might very quickly commit a terrible and arising evil in this world—
an act that obstructs life and is shunned by all the Buddhas.
One should not perform such an action that is forbidden by the highest people in the world;
therefore, one should employ the supreme power through mantras that are all-pervading.
Whatever worldly mantras there may be, as well as those spoken by the Jinas—
one should employ them within this mudrā, empowered and with a well-composed mind.
Upon seeing the formidable and supreme mudrā, all the nairṛtas,
piśācas, tārakas, pretas, pūtanas, and mātṛs perish.
O Bālāgra, Virūpākṣa, and oppressors of children!
May all the wicked ones who perform cruel deeds indeed perish.
That very hand, when placed so as to take the form of a spear,
with the fingers interlaced in a reversed casket-shape—
this, the perfectly awakened ones who are free from hatred, call the "casket" (sampuṭa).
One should perform this rite with the single-syllable mantra;
one should seal all directions and intermediate points—this is called the binding of the directions.
This mudrā, acting as a great protection, remains in a state of enclosure;
indeed, all malevolent beings and whatever other harmful things there may be are destroyed.
It protects the entire body and even the retinue within its range;
it protects the entire circle wherever the practitioner of recitation always dwells.
For him, no sin whatsoever nor any misfortune can arise;
there will be security, abundance, and health—whence could there be fear of a foreign army?
Having joined both hands together, one should perform them in reverse;
placing the right hand below and always keeping the left hand facing upward,
these two interlaced with one another are called *pharaṃ* by the Supreme Victors.
Having offered [this], the power joined with syllables wards off the arising of evil from wicked enemies.
Endowed with these mantras of a single color, this [practice] indeed swiftly accomplishes one's purpose;
it performs various meaningful rites that eliminate the evils arising from enemies.
When applied as a root mantra, it destroys the poison of those who possess it,
and it eradicates any other defects produced by [malevolent] applications in embodied beings.
This supreme mudrā has been proclaimed by the perfectly awakened ones, the best of bipeds;
it is formed by placing the two hands together with the fingers interlaced.
Then one should form the shape of a mace (gadā), encircled by the root [fingers];
it is well-encircled by the two little fingers in the middle of the two thumbs.
One should form a beautiful void-shape with six fingers;
this mudrā is called the mace (gada), which destroys all dānavas.
Even the Daityas who possess evil minds become gentle-minded at the mere sight [of it];
they are destroyed when the mudrā is raised, or even when the mace is well-worshipped.
When employed with the root mantra, this auspicious mudrā quickly accomplishes one's purpose;
likewise, it is designated as the "sword" when the tips of the ring fingers are well-contracted.
In that same way, one should form the hands with the tips extended and slightly curved;
having made them equal in shape to a shallow bowl by means of the fingers on all sides,
the Buddhas know this to be the Bell mudrā, which they revealed for the sake of embodied beings.
Having joined both hands together to form a hollow casket,
and having interlaced them with the middle fingers,
one should make it into the shape of a mandala; that shall indeed take the form of a noose.
Then, with the index fingers placed upon the middle joints and well-joined together, this is known as the *pāśa* (noose); this is the mudrā manifested by the Buddhas.
However, for the sake of those to be trained, he is released from the most terrible bondage by all beings,
as well as by those wicked and cruel grahas and all the rākṣasas.
For when this [noose] is even slightly impelled, it binds a mother here;
when commanded, "Bind! Bind!", it binds even Śakra himself here—how much more so the flesh-eating, meat-consuming carnivores in the world of men?
Having placed both hands together so that they are equal,
one should likewise place the right hand upon the left hand.
That very same [mudrā] takes the form of a hook: having pressed the middle joint of the middle finger against the index finger, one should form the hook with the index finger.
This goad, empowered by the root mantra and thus impelled,
swiftly causes the rites desired by the reciters to be accomplished within a single lifetime. It can quickly summon even the lords of the gods, such as Brahmā and others, together with Śakra.
The excellent and supreme mudrā, auspicious for drawing with a hook,
is formed by joining the two hands together in a reversed manner so that they form a single mass.
Having bent the middle and ring fingers drawn into the left hand,
[one should likewise bend] both the index and little fingers, as well as the right index finger.
Indicated by the right hand, the middle and ring fingers are bent;
they are then placed reversed, joined together, and made into a thumb-gesture.
That very auspicious seat is declared to be the excellent and beautiful mudrā;
it is the throne of all Buddhas, which wards off even the enraged Śakra.
It is joined with all the mantras arising from the families of the foremost Jinas;
it establishes all the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power;
indeed, it renders the entire world, including the gods, completely immovable.
That very same *bhadrapīṭha* rests upon the middle fingers; with the middle and ring fingers placed on top and extended,
it is thus described as the *pīṭha* by the lions among sages who have conquered their enemies.
Then, with both hands joined together, one should intertwine the fingers;
thereafter, one should form the needle of the little finger like a braid.
Having quickly contracted the [fingers] from the middle, one should always place the stationary [mudrā], which arises with the span of a lotus petal, by joining the two thumbs together.
This is declared by the Fully Awakened Ones, free from all enmity, to be the peacock posture;
it belongs to the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa.
This mudrā, which is always like a child’s plaything for the best of sages, possesses great power; it was indeed taught of old by the Self-Arisen Ones.
Impelled by the charming mantra, she performs a variety of actions;
she destroys the wicked flesh-eaters and those who devour raw meat.
Thus, beyond this, twenty mudrās are considered complete;
they were taught by the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds and the leaders of the world.
Henceforth, I shall explain the origin of the ritual procedure for the mudrās,
performed with hands that are auspicious, pure, stainless, and cleansed by water.
Having sipped water mixed with white sandalwood, camphor, saffron,
and many varieties of fragrant substances, which has been dried by the wind;
With pure hands, using ointments and even firm goads,
one should likewise form the mudrā to be bound, which belongs to the Best of Bipeds.
Śāla, Saṅkusuma, Amitābha, Ratnaketu,
Amitāyurjñānaviniścayendra, Lokanātha, and Divaṅkara.
To Kṣema, Lokanātha, Sunetra, Dharmaketu,
and the one renowned as Prabhāmālī— the eldest, the most excellent, the peerless, and the supreme.
Having paid homage to one of these Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds,
and having become pure, one should bind the mudrā in a clean place at the conclusion of the recitation.
But having seen the teacher from whom one is released from doubt regarding the meaning,
one who is perfected in such conduct should bind the mudrā as is appropriate.
Having thoroughly cleansed it and made it secluded, one should consecrate the site with mantras;
neither angry, nor impure from eating leftovers, nor reviled by another.
One should never bind the mudrā upon charcoal or in the midst of ashes;
nor, at that time, should one be attached to the wives or the property of others.
Neither standing nor sitting, one should bind the mudrā that brings about bliss;
nor should one do so while facing south, nor while rising with one's back turned to the west.
One should not perform the binding of the mudrās above or below;
rather, one should do so facing north or east, or indeed in those intermediate directions.
One who knows the mudrās and mantras should bind the mudrā while recollecting the Mantra of the Holder of the Discus; this is the most excellent method among all mudrās for binding.
Hereafter, I shall explain the mudrā consisting of more than twenty [fingers]:
one should join both hands together, with the fingers interlaced.
Then, one should indicate the middle void with the fingers:
the tips of the voids placed upon the middle joints, joined by the little fingers.
The knower of mantras should always perform [this mudrā], with the two thumbs resting on the curved [fingers] and joined in the shape of a trident; the wise know this as the *paṭṭiśa*.
This supreme mudrā swiftly cuts through the mantras of others;
likewise, it shatters the supreme mudrās employed by wicked beings.
It shall terrify all spirits, including the grahas, mātṛs, and pūtanās;
it performs a variety of rites and swiftly brings about auspiciousness.
Those mantras which were spoken by Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā himself—
the knower of mantras shattered them through a rite prescribed by the rules.
When joined with this very mudrā and the great *paṭṭiśa* weapon,
and established in the mantra born from the mouth of the Jina;
It performs a variety of actions as well as acts of cutting and splitting;
it utterly destroys, without exception, that evil wrought by other beings.

Having thus folded the hands together, with the middle and ring fingers raised, both hands joined so as to take the form of a *liṅga*, and measuring four finger-breadths in height— this is considered the *liṅgamudrā*.
The divine son Maheśvara indeed proclaimed his own mantra and mudrā within the tantra for the purpose of summoning, as previously taught by the Sage.
And having been drawn forth during this supreme ritual manual (*kalpa*), he revealed in full detail the mantras and mudrās of others as well as his own;
for this most excellent and foremost mudrā is proclaimed among worldly practices.
Whatever mantras have been proclaimed by Rudra upon the surface of the earth,
this single-linga mudrā is indeed their sovereign and foremost.
By the power of the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa,
we have been brought into the maṇḍala as the accomplishers of the ritual action.
Whatever wicked beings roam upon the surface of the earth—
whether they be seizing spirits (*graha*), flesh-eaters, meat-devourers, mothers (*mātṛ*), or *kaṭapūtana* demons— [all these are subdued].
For the purpose of warding them off from the obstacles created by Rudra,
this supreme mudrā has indeed been taught for the rites of bali during the night.
Or, by means of the miraculous power of the Buddha’s empowerment, one performs all activities;
likewise, having performed that in such a manner, it is designated as possessing two characteristics. Similarly, when [the mantra] is placed upon the finger, it is proclaimed as a *mālā*.
Having contracted that very same *mālā* mudrā so as to form a hollowed-out shape (*sampuṭa*),
one should join both index fingers and make them resemble a bow;
pressing the two thumbs within the fists, that is recognized as the *dhanur-mudrā*.
In this manner, one should form the *aṅkuśī* mudrā:
with the right hand extended, the left index finger is pressed against the joint within the fist.
The *nārāca-mudrā* has been described; now I shall speak again of the *samaliṅga*.
Having then placed both hands together, with the fingers interlaced and joined.
Those who are proficient in this teaching and ritual manual know that the raised thumb of the right hand, arising from the *liṅga*, constitutes the "equal *liṅga*."
Having joined both hands together with the fingers interlaced,
one should join both index fingers and form the shape of a trident;
this is called the "Trident," which is for the instruction of wicked beings.
Having extended both hands and formed fists again, one should place the two thumbs in the upright position; this is declared to be the *mudgara* [mudrā].
That same mudrā, when slightly moved within the hollowed palms, is called the Tomara;
it is the foremost mudrā that destroys Śakra.
Then, having formed the *utpala* [mudrā] with the ring fingers,
it is placed between the two thumbs below and kept unshown;
this is called the *daṃṣṭra* (fang), and when opened, it is called the *vaktra* (mouth).
Then, having made the fingers equal on all sides and placing them against the chest, one should cast [the hand] to the left; this is called the *paṭa* [mudrā].
Having joined both hands together in the hollowed *sampuṭa* gesture, they should be beautifully positioned with the fingers interlaced, each tip pressed against the other.
Having raised [the hands] and contracted them, it is called the *kumbha-mudrā*;
joining those very same [hands] into fists and then raising the two index fingers [is another].
One should form the shape of *khakharā*, arising in the form of a braid;
this mudrā is declared as *khakhara* by the Destroyer of Enemies.
That very same *khakhara*, when slightly bent, is beautiful;
when the thumbs are placed [upon it], it is here called the *kalaśa*.
Having raised it again,
one should form the shape of a mallet with the four fingers, originating from the index and middle fingers.
Those endowed with the knowledge of mantras call this mudrā the *muśala* (pestle);
it is that very same [mudrā] with the middle and ring fingers placed downward upon the hands.
Above those, it is always placed, wrapped with a cord slanting from right to left;
having wound it around, the little finger and the index finger are placed upon the two thumbs.
The Tathāgatas call the form of the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka) the mudrā; this is known throughout the world as the "cross-legged mudrā" (paryaṅkamudrā).
Endowed with this mudrā and likewise joined with the mantra—
these mantras taught by all the Victors, arising from the Vajra and Lotus families— one who employs them performs all rites auspiciously.
And those mudrās likewise described, such as the mace and others originating from the trident—
all these indeed belong to the Wrathful King Yamāntaka in this teaching;
for they are fierce weapons manifested for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
Then, through the power and supernatural might of the Bodhisattva,
Kumbha and the others performed everything that was spoken by means of seals for the sake of those who were to be disciplined and the wicked.
That very hand, positioned so as to take the form of a drum,
should be bound together with all the fingers joined and held like a quill.
Having formed a braid with the thumbs and then placing them again upon the hand,
one should position the forefinger in the middle with its tip raised;
this is the mudrā designated as the *paṭaha*, which wards off evil beings.
In that very same way, the two hands are placed together in a well-applied *añjali* gesture;
both index fingers are bent inward, beautiful in the shape of a coil.
Having placed the thumbs downward and bent both thumbs inward so that they enter within the middle cavity, it becomes the beautiful Śaṅkha mudrā;
this indeed is proclaimed as the excellent Dharmasaṅkha mudrā.
When joined with the mantras spoken by the best of sages, it accomplishes all types of rites and performs a variety of actions against all fanged venomous serpents.
When employed with the root mantra, it destroys them all.
One should fill a conch shell that has been consecrated by recitation with the highly powerful kings of vidyās;
any creature who is fainted by poison will quickly become free from poison.
Forty excellent mudrās of great supernatural power have been fully described;
hereafter, I shall explain the origin of the characteristics of the mudrās.
Placing the hands exactly thus with the tips of the fingers interlaced, one should again press them together with effort and turn the left hand downward;
having performed this on all sides below, it is declared to be the *śaṅkalā* [mudrā].
This most excellent and supreme mudrā binds all wicked beings; when joined with these mantras spoken by the foremost of sages, it binds all spirits, grahas, mātṛs, and kaśmalas.
Having contracted the hands in that same manner and released them, one should raise the braid;
having bound it according to that same rule, [one should place it] with another [hand] between the thumb and the middle finger.
Again, having joined both hands at the middle joints with the tips facing each other,
and having positioned them directly toward the fire while properly employing the fire-mantra,
one should always invoke the crested deity (Agni) during fire-rites and oblations.
When joined with this mudrā, the fire-god is summoned quickly;
one should dismiss him with this very mantra, using the tips of the index fingers interlaced.
When the thumb is constantly pressed [against the ring finger], one should release the fire-deity;
this mudrā is highly esteemed as it accomplishes rites involving fire.
For one who recites the mantra, this mudrā— which is highly esteemed by the gods— summoned them at will; when bound and characterized by empowerment,
it performs a variety of rites when joined with the supreme mantras.
One should place the two hands together with all the fingers fully extended, forming a loose, rounded hollow by joining them in the añjali gesture.
Then, having brought the lotus-born bud to full bloom,
one should know that very desire-granting mudrā to be the accomplisher of all aims.
This mudrā is excellent and supreme; it was sung of old by the Tathāgatas and has been entrusted to Mañjughoṣa for the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings.
Whatever mental aspiration a sentient being desires for the sake of their own welfare,
that is swiftly and quickly accomplished by means of mantras endowed with great supernatural power (*maharddhika*).
This supreme and most excellent mudrā is called "The Mental Aspiration" (*manoratha*).
This supreme and most excellent mudrā accomplishes all rites;
it swiftly brings to fruition mantras as well as ritual substances in their full detail.
This moon-like radiance was well-expounded by Municandra;
therefore, this mantra belonging to the Moon family within the Lotus family has been effectively employed.
Born from the white-colored nectar, it performs a variety of ritual actions.
Those very two hands, thoroughly purified, with both fingers joined together,
the six fingers pressed close so as to take the form of a book,
raised up and made circular, with the little fingers and thumbs properly tucked in.
This mudrā is declared to be the supreme, the immeasurable Perfection of Wisdom;
she is the mother of all Buddhas, employed for the sake of liberation.
When applied for the purposes of pacification and nourishment, she shall indeed accomplish all rites.
Placing the two hands thus, with the right hand over the left,
and positioning them at the region of the navel in the manner of a hollowed bowl,
then embracing both hands together— that mudrā is called Pātra.
The bowl, the mother, and the two mudrās, when well-joined with the mantras of the Jinas,
perform a variety of activities as desired by those skilled in mantra.
Raising those same hands, one should extend the index fingers upward;
the tips of the middle fingers, however, should be slightly bent like an archway.
Having raised those very [fingers] upward, he described the "beautiful arch" (sutoraṇa);
having bound those same [fingers] together with one another, it is designated as the eighth by Ghoṣa.
The wise know that the sound of recitation occurs when the two thumbs are raised;
it is the same when both hands are raised with the tips of the fingers well-curved.
The Buddhas know that drum, from which hair grows in sparse strands released by all the fingers, as the raised Dharma-drum.
That very palm of the hand, with the right side raised and the left side elevated,
should be positioned below in a well-composed form resembling an elephant.
One should form the shape of an elephant with the middle finger of the right hand;
this is designated as the Elephant Mudrā by those who have gone to the further shore of saṃsāra.
This is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones;
honored by the world, it performs all those various activities without exception.
Raising the right hand, one should form the gesture of granting fearlessness;
having grasped it at the wrist with the raised left hand.
Touching the middle finger with the index finger, and placing the thumb so that it rests upon the middle joint, this is called the Varahasta mudrā.
This supreme and most excellent mudrā was proclaimed by the primordial Buddhas;
having bound this mudrā which grants fearlessness to all sentient beings, the reciter,
joined with the mantras approved by the Munis, swiftly accomplishes his purpose.
Those same hands joined together, beautiful in the form of a hollowed casket,
with the middle fingers raised— this is the mudrā known as Tadgatacāriṇī.
Thus, having encircled [the thumbs] with the fingers and placed the two thumbs on top, resting upon the surface of the joints— this they call the Mudrā known as Ketu.
That same [mudrā], when at the point of being fainted (mūrcchita), is designated as the auspicious Mudrin. Both index fingers are joined together, their tips intermingled with one another;
the thumbs are bent at the joints, and the little fingers are raised.
That very same mudrā, when pointed with the axe [gesture], accomplishes all aims;
when all [fingers] are again contracted, that mudrā is indeed honored by the world.
Thus, one should raise it so that the tip of the index finger forms a needle;
from that, the *bhiṇḍipāla* mudrā is formed, followed by the *lāṅgala* and the *cakra*.
Having bent the two index fingers, this is the supreme *lāṅgala* mudrā;
thus has the sixty mudrās been described again according to the ritual rule.
All those weapons, when joined with mudrās and impelled by mantras,
[overcome] all faults caused by obstacles, as well as grahas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and mātṛs.
It utterly destroys all those mudrās arising from weapons, which belong to all the chief rākṣasas who terrify everyone with their childishness.
This characteristic of sixty mudrās has been fully proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall explain the origin of the ritual procedures for the mudrās.
When those very hands are placed together and raised in the shape of a lotus,
with all the fingers extended, it is known as the Padma Mudrā.
This is known as the supreme mudrā, arising from the family of the placed lotus;
joined with as many mantras as exist in the lotus family, it brings about auspicious results.
Renowned for performing swift actions and arising from the empowerment of the Buddha,
this lotus mudrā among all mudrās is declared to be the most excellent; it accomplishes all mantras whatsoever that originate from the Lotus Family.
Both hands joined together,
with the index fingers raised and joined by the middle fingers, it arises from a specific arrangement of form.
Placing the two thumbs there upon the joints of the middle fingers—
that very same is declared to be the Vajra, the most excellent Kanyasa mudrā.
As many mantras as there are in the Vajra family, they are sealed by this [mudrā] to be accomplished;
when applied according to the prescribed rite, they are quickly brought to success.
For one who always accomplishes the rite to be achieved by means of the combined [practices],
there shall be constant success— whether superior, inferior, or middling—
and indeed all worldly mantras are accomplished without conceptualization.
Both hands joined together, with the middle fingers raised,
the ring fingers and thumbs contracted, and the little fingers resting upon the needle.
Both index fingers are joined together with their tips bent at the middle joint;
the two middle fingers are placed like needles, giving rise to the form of a wheel.
This indeed is the Wheel of Dharma, proclaimed here as the King of Mudrās;
for it was spoken by the Kings of Dharma in order to set the Wheel of Dharma in motion.
Then the seventh moon-like sage chose the Wheel of Peace;
by means of the recitation that severs the three stains, it was joined with the King of Mudrās.
Those who are Cakriṇīs and Uṣṇīṣās, Locanā and the supreme Vidyā, Bhrukuṭī and Padyakulā, Tārā and Māmakī, as well as the Vajrinī;
All worldly mantras spoken by Viṣṇu and Īśāna are accomplished when joined with the King of Mudrās, the Dharmacakra.
Having seen that [seal] of the reciters, conjoined with the mudrās,
one should know this supreme and most excellent mudrā, which has issued forth from the dharmadhātu.
It indeed performs all actions according to the desires of sentient beings;
this mudrā was proclaimed by the King of Dharma for the sake of peace.
In this most excellent and supreme eon, this mudrā known as the Dharmacakra is the accomplisher of all rites within the teaching of Mañjughoṣa.
One should employ all the foremost mudrās in rites of pacification; this Śivacakra is constantly perceived by practitioners of mantra as the source of all manifestation.
Those same hands, placed together in the form of a hollowed casket (*sampuṭa*),
with fingers slightly extended and both [thumbs] contracted and auspicious,
should be known as the *Puṇḍarīka* mudrā, which accomplishes all aims.
Placing that same hand with the fingers extended and then releasing them from the fist,
the shape of the outstretched hand is called the Varada (boon-granting) mudrā.
Again, having joined both hands together with the fingers on all sides and forming the shape of a braid, this mudrā is called the Rope.
Again, extending that same excellent right hand,
one should form the shape of a needle with the middle finger and the index finger.
With the tips of the fingers slightly contracted and the top [of the hand] bent, one should form the *sthitikā* mudrā there, with the index finger well-positioned upon it.
When they are joined together there, resting upon the ring finger joint,
this is the mudrā designated as the spear by the many leaders of the world.
In that same manner, both hands are placed [together], with both index fingers pointing;
having made both [hands] equal like fists, and again making the fingers even—
that very one is designated as the Vajradaṇḍa mudrā by the wise.
Joining the two hands together in the form of a hollowed casket,
the fingers are placed in the añjali gesture, resting upon one another in close embrace.
Relying on both thumbs, it is called the *śataghnī* mudrā;
then, having placed both hands so that they are hollowed out all around.
Then, having formed the añjali gesture and placed it upon the nose, this mudrā is known as the Bherī by those who seek the welfare of the three worlds;
it delivers all beings from the great ocean of saṃsāra.
Having released that very añjali gesture with both palms displayed in various patterns,
those who follow the path of the upward-moving beings call it the vimāna-mudrā.
By contracting those very hands, it is here called the chariot;
this is the most excellent movement of the three vehicles, for it has been praised by those who seek liberation.
It leads all beings who recite it to the perfection of mantra;
by relying on the supreme vehicle, they go indeed to that state of a Buddha.
Then, having released both hands and joined them together once more,
one should form the pure *citratala* mudrā, which arises in the shape of a pedestal (*vedikā*).
This supreme and most excellent mudrā is well-honored by the Lords of the World;
it is proclaimed by the Sons of the Victors as the bed of all Buddhas.
That wherein the Perfect Buddhas of the past, having relied upon it, attained peace;
wherein they were established in the realm of nirvāṇa, following their ascended intention—
that is known as the Mudrā, the resting place of the Leader of the World.
Placing the two hands together with the fingers joined evenly,
one should position them in a hollowed casket-like form; then, making the single right index finger curved at the tip, it is called the "Half-Moon" (ardhacandra).
Then, having again formed both hands— with the right hand closed into a fist and all the fingers of the left hand extended and properly aligned—
one should form a fist at the tip of the hand, with the right thumb inserted within it.
With the right hands joined together and formed into a hollowed cup, having extended the little fingers, this is declared to be the vīṇā mudrā.
Again, having made both hands hollow with the fingers spread apart,
with both middle fingers between the two thumbs and both index fingers resting [upon them]—
this is the Padmālayā mudrā, as taught by the Perfectly Awakened Ones in the world.
Furthermore, O Kuvalayodbhava, with the thumbs always raised,
this mudrā has been taught in the world by the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds.
Thus, having joined the palms in this manner toward the Teacher of the World who appears in the form of prostration—
this is the renowned "mudrā of salutation" throughout all worlds.
Having fixed those very hands together in the *yamala* (twin) position, this is the *yamala-mudrā*,
renowned throughout the three worlds.
With the hands slightly raised from the base and the two thumbs firmly pressed together,
that shall be the *sampuṭā* mudrā, which destroys grief, fatigue, and fever.
These mudrās have been described, all of which arise from weapons;
those called "flower," those of "reclining," those beginning with "instrumental music," and those named after the planets—
all of them are capable of performing every action when employed with all the mantras as spoken.
Neither a specific lunar day nor a constellation is required, nor is fasting prescribed;
when combined with the appropriate gestures and mantras, they swiftly accomplish all rites.
The wise reciter, endowed with austerity, by merely reciting [the mantra],
and through the application of mudrās and mantras, finds nothing that cannot be accomplished.
Then, having joined both hands together in the *añjali* gesture with the fingers interlaced,
the little fingers, ring fingers, and thumbs placed on the sides is declared to be the incense mudrā (*dhūpamudrā*).
By joining the palms in the *ādhāra-añjali* gesture, one should slightly bend the two index fingers;
this is the general *bali-mudrā*, which was brought forth by the Protectors of the World.
In the center, flowers should be arranged according to what is available;
this is offered for all the bali rituals of the mantras.
Having formed the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with the right hand,
one should grasp the right hand by means of the left hand using the wrist-binding technique (*maṇibandhana-yoga*).
This is declared to you as the fragrance mudrā for all mantras:
always [form it] with the two thumbs and the two middle fingers within the right fist.
Then, having formed the shape of a needle, it is declared to be the lamp mudrā;
it is established from the ring finger and the thumb as if it were a rosary.
Constantly extending the little finger, placing the middle finger behind it, and setting the index finger in a curved position— this is called the *akṣamudrā*.
Then, having placed the *garbhāñjali* mudrā and the rosary,
that knower of mantras should recite the mantra as desired, which swiftly bestows the boon of accomplishment.
This is always the prescribed method for all beautiful mudrās:
one should form the tip of the "fearless" gesture with the right hand of the deity Agni.
Having placed [the hand] facing forward, one should always bend the index finger;
having placed the thumb upon the hand, it should remain bent in the middle.
This is specified as the invocation mudrā for Jātavedas:
the tips of the two index fingers are bent inward and joined together with the two thumbs.
The dismissal (*visarjana*) is observed in all rites within the blazing fire;
one skilled in the ritual of *homa* should perform it for all mantras.
When fully joined with these mudrās and properly applied to the fire-mantra,
it is accompanied by a prostration with palms joined, the fingers being interlaced on all sides.
One should perform it in the reverse manner, however, with the two thumbs joined together,
the index fingers bent outward, and resting upon the middle fingers.
This supreme mudrā has indeed been described as employed in the rites of worship;
it is the salutation to all mantras, to the Lord of Mantras, the Son of the Victors.
One should cause the purification of all mantras and the offering of a seat;
even in the absence of flowers, one should apply them by forming the mudrā.
For these mantras, when worshipped according to the prescribed rite, accomplish all purposes;
by performing worship with the binding of mudrās, it becomes truly auspicious.
The second is the mental worship, which is like that arising from flowers;
this method of worship has been proclaimed by the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds.
In the absence of flowers, however, a two-fold worship is prescribed;
for the sake of accomplishing all mantras, one should employ it in all rites.
This mudrā, which performs all actions, was taught by all the Buddhas.
In sitting, lying down, bathing, drinking, and eating; in beautifying, illuminating, reciting mantras, establishing the site, and constructing the mandala.
This mudrā, which performs all rites, has been taught by the Lords of the World for the sake of empowering all mantras for practitioners;
this rule regarding the mudrās is said to consist of a full hundred.
Hereafter, I shall explain the mudrā that has attained the status of the eighth:
having placed both hands in that very same manner, one should then perform it again.
Having formed the index finger with that same [thumb], the middle finger is joined like a needle;
they are made to touch at the third part below the nail.
Having encircled the sheath and caused it to take the form of a needle,
this is the mudrā of the Great-Souled Śakrin, the Lord of Mantras.
These very same fingers, with the index fingers moved together and the middle fingers level, with the needle-like [thumb] placed upon the nail and the ring fingers joined—
this is indeed the Uṣṇīṣa mudrā proclaimed by the Lords of Jinas.
With the hands placed in that same manner,
the middle fingers entwined and joined with the little fingers— this is the mudrā arising from Bhīma.
Having made the middle fingers equal and the fingertips joined together, with the hands released in a circular form— this is called the Mahāmudrā.
Placing that very [ring finger] at the tip of the index finger with a slight gap between them, one should then place it upon the middle needle with the hands joined below.
The two thumbs placed on the third joints of the ring fingers and pressed by the nails—
this is declared to be the excellent mudrā of the wise Mañjughoṣa.
In that same manner, the two hands are placed in the gesture of *añjali*;
the middle fingers are positioned so that their tips are joined like needles,
and the two thumbs touch the three joints of the middle fingers.
Having formed a needle with the little fingers, they are extended and raised;
this is the excellent and supreme mudrā, which has attained the state of being established within the treasury of the Dharma.
Those very hands, placed according to the prescribed method and joined together,
with all the fingers thus fully drawn in, are established in the form of a sheath.
One should open both hands, covered by eight fingers;
[it represents] the eightfold knowledge of the reality of the person, having reached the fourfold union.
The perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds, call that very thing the Saṅgha;
that alone is proclaimed as the Mudrā-Saṅgha within this abode of existence.
This is the most excellent, supreme Mudrā, which accomplishes all activities.
Having joined both hands together in the form of a hollowed cup (añjali),
one should extend a single index finger, emerging from the right hand.
This very mudrā, which pacifies all beings, has been taught by those who perceive reality; it is known as the supreme mudrā, the accomplisher of the purpose of all ritual actions.
Those very hands, marked at the tips by the braided-finger gesture,
joined together in the form of a hollowed casket, with the thumbs raised and extended—
this is the Lotus Garland, as proclaimed by the Primordial Buddhas.
Those same hands, with palms turned upward, have their fingers on all sides formed into the shape of a full-blown flower,
with the thumbs and fingers joined together.
In the second [mudrā], both the thumbs and the index fingers are placed upon the mountain;
this is known as the supreme mudrā by the perfectly awakened ones who dwell in the abode of the thirty-three gods.
These eight mudrās are the Great Mudrās;
they perform the same functions and possess equal radiance and great power, as proclaimed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones.
Sixty crores and eighty million, along with those that have arisen in the past from countless supreme sages— these indeed are the mudrās revealed;
one hundred and eight mudrās are said to originate from the ritual procedures.
With all of these, one should accomplish all mantra-rites;
likewise, one shall successfully achieve all mantras as well as all activities.
This is declared by all the Buddhas of great supernatural power to be the doctrine of the mudrās;
for when these are applied according to the ritual procedure, they swiftly accomplish one's purpose.
Having spoken thus, the Lion of the Śākyas, the foremost of sages and supreme among men,
endowed with great supernatural power, then chose Mañjughoṣa as a bodhisattva.
This origin of the mudrās in the Mañjuśrī-kalpa has been bestowed by you yourself for the sake of protecting the teaching on earth,
when the end of the age has arrived and I have indeed entered final nirvāṇa.
For the sake of protecting my teaching, all of this has been told by me:
the characteristics of the mudrās have been declared, as well as the mantras in full detail;
the secret of all the worlds and the hidden mystery have also been proclaimed.
In this Sūtra, the sovereign of this eon, the expansion of qualities is extensively detailed,
and the manifold arising of the praise of the qualities of mantras is set forth.
The application of mantras and the application of tantras have been extracted from that;
it is the source of causes for the power, qualities, and established tenets of those who recite [mantras].
For the auspicious arising of the fruit— the destinies and wombs of sentient beings— has been declared,
O Youth, to be joined with the cause for the accomplishment of your mantras.
Thus addressed, the youth Mañjuśrī, stationed in the sky,
bowed his head to the Fully Awakened One, the Lord of the World, the Light-Maker; sighing deeply, moistened with compassion, he then wept again and again.
Having requested a boon from the Buddha, the Giver of Boons, they stood near him and asked:
"When the Blessed One has passed away and the treasury of mantras has vanished from the surface of the earth,
how will there be a greatness of refuge for sentient beings?"
Thus addressed, the Perfectly Awakened One then spoke to Mañjughoṣa:
"Listen, child Mañjuśrī, O youth, if you have a question."
For when I have passed away, when the world has become empty and the surface of the earth is desolate,
and when the treasury of the Dharma has perished along with the disciples who have long since entered nirvana;
Having fashioned an image of the Teacher, the supreme among bipeds,
one should perform worship and honor with incense, perfumes, and ointments.
Having prepared various offerings consisting of diverse excellent garments, other ornaments such as jeweled earrings, and various kinds of foods and edibles,
[he offered them] to the one who can assume any form at will, [endowed with] manifold forms.

Likewise, having repeated the mantra, he attained an auspicious rebirth among the wombs of sentient beings; he entered the most excellent city for the sake of the highest state of existence, and finally,
being inclined toward awakening, he attained peace in his last life.
Thus addressed and urged by the Perfectly Awakened One, the wise Mañjuśrī, a Bodhisattva of great supernatural power, was satisfied and greatly rejoiced;
he then [revealed] all this which had been sung of old while dwelling above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
In the presence of the Buddhas, he who sets in motion the wheel of the Buddha's Dharma then chose the wheel of mantras that has been followed for a long time.
Thus [it is said].
Thus concludes the thirty-third chapter, the detailed section on the ritual of mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-sixth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"Mañjuśrī, there exists your most supreme secret, accompanied by the root mudrā and its retinue—the characteristics of the mudrās which are to be employed in all rites, bestowing all success, fruitful, following after all mantras, and accomplishing the purpose of all activities."
Listen briefly, Mañjuśrī.
First, with the palms extended in *añjali*, the index and ring fingers are each inserted into the middle joints of [the thumbs].
This is your root mudrā, O Mañjuśrī, renowned as being effective for all rites (*sarvakarmika*).

Likewise, having joined the hands together, the ring fingers are held close, as are the index and middle fingers; the little fingers are likewise positioned, and the tips of the thumbs rest upon the upward-facing lines.
This other seal of yours, Mañjuśrī, has been taught:

having formed a fist with the fingers joined to one another, releasing the middle fingers and making them like needles, one should place the pair of index fingers, bent at their sides, at the ends; this, Mañjuśrī, is your seal known as Daṃṣṭrā (The Fangs).
One should place the pair of thumbs at the sides of the seal.
