This mudrā is you, Mañjuśrī, in person; by means of this samaya, you preside with your presence in that place and within those hollowed palms.

Having joined the fingers of two fists so they touch one another, but leaving out the index fingers, with the pair of thumbs positioned in the middle—this, O Mañjuśrī, is your other mudrā, the *cīraka* mudrā.
Having extended the joints of the palms with the ring fingers [joined], and having placed the tips of the index fingers within the space between the middle fingers—
this other [mudrā], Mañjuśrī, is declared to be the very root-mudrā of you yourself. Having made the index finger of this same mudrā extended...

Mañjuśrī, this is that Eye Mudrā of yours: the little fingers and ring fingers are joined like braids and placed in the middle of the hollowed palms; the middle fingers are on the outside; the tips of the index fingers are bent over them; and the tips of the thumbs are joined to the [tips of the] index fingers. This other one, Mañjuśrī, is your Face Mudrā, which performs all rites.

In this manner, by this sequence, one should release each finger one by one; then, with all the fingers joined together including both thumbs, one should extend them one by one, with the right thumb raised high—this, Mañjuśrī, is your Uṣṇīṣa-mudrā. Having contracted the right [hand] and raised the left, this becomes your Lalāṭa-mudrā, Mañjuśrī, upon seeing which all malevolent grahas flee away.

Thus, the ears, neck, arms, heart, hands, throat, waist, navel, thighs, shanks, feet, eyes, face, and tongue—likewise, with the ten fingers raised in successive order, there arises the characteristic of the mudrās in successive order;
and he performs his activities in successive order.

By the mouth-mudrā, there is the binding of the mouth; by the fang-mudrā, the release from evil grahas; by the tongue-mudrā, the warding off of evil speech; by the heart-mudrā, the destruction of a king’s anger; or else, for other beings—whether gods, asuras, humans, non-humans, or those belonging to various other states of existence—it becomes the destroyer of the wrath of those possessing form.
In this manner, by such a sequence, one performs all rites everywhere.
In this way, there are incalculable mudrās according to this order;
and you, Mañjuśrī, perform incalculable rites, for in every respect, all rites exist within all mudrās.
That Mahāmudrā was bound by those innumerable great heroes, the Tathāgatas, as well as by the great heroes who have attained the great stages.
Therein are groves of *nimbaraka* trees numbering thirty-six, eighty-four, nine, and five;
sixty, and those counted in the millions (*nayuta*), all progressively increasing beyond the rest of the world.
All those who are included within all mudrās, as well as all other worldly activities— one should accomplish every purpose by means of any one of these mudrās.
With both hands bound [in the mudrā], during the time of practice in the maṇḍala,
or again during the fire-oblations and recitations by one intent on the preliminary service (pūrvasevā),
the observer of the vow should recite as long as he desires, whether seated or standing.
By means of the great rite of protection, one should perform all rites for oneself or for others at all times among all mudrās.
Thus it is said.

Thus concludes the thirty-fourth chapter, the second detailed section on the ritual of mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna vaipulya sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.

(At the end of this work, after the completion of the fifty-third final chapter, another chapter titled "The Chapter on the Great Seal" (*Mahāmudrāpaṭalavisara*), numbered thirty-four, is found written [there].
Since it ought to be a sub-division of the very same thirty-fourth chapter that has already passed, for that reason it is incorporated here.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

"May all the Bodhisattvas, all sentient beings gathered in this assembly, and all the hosts of spirits and sons of gods possessing great supernatural power, listen! Within the detailed exposition of the ritual manual (*kalpavisara*) of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, there exists a method for the practice of the *mudrā* chapter, which serves as a cause for the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment for those beings who have entered into the conduct of all mantra-tantras.
By means of this, all mantras are accomplished; all activities are most swiftly drawn forth from every side for everyone; and the *mudrās* come into being."
Listen, sirs, to that by which those who are sealed become very quickly submissive;
I shall speak for the benefit of all sentient beings.
These are the mudrās of all mantras.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni entered the samādhi called the Ocean-Seal of the Tathāgata’s Majesty and Qualities, which is the Ornament of Seals for all Buddha-dharmas. Immediately upon his entering it, all the Tathāgatas proclaimed the pledge of all seals.
Rising from that samādhi, he proclaimed the extensive chapter on the Great Seal, sealed with the seal of all Tathāgatas, for all mantras.
First of all, there are heart-mantras for all the mantra families; one should recite them twice, seven times, or once. Thereafter, the mudrās must be bound, and not otherwise.
And what is that? It is the heart of all Tathāgatas:
*jinajik*.
"O noble ones, this is the heart-mantra of all Tathāgatas, effective for all rites.
Within the family of the Tathāgata, all mudrās are to be bound;
thereafter, one should commence the ritual action."
ĀROLIKU.
This Heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara, which accomplishes all rites, should be recited by one who binds all mudrās in the Lotus Family; it is suitable for all practices and for all activities.
VAJRADHRK.
This, friends, is the heart-mantra of Vajrapāṇi. When reciting it among all the vajra families, the mudrā should be bound: *surārak*.
This [mantra] is to be employed in all rites by those who bind all mudrās for all the gods;
it is the heart of all the gods, and the essence of the Yakṣas.
The heart of all yakṣas;
the wielder of the Pināka bow;
the heart of Rudra.
Ṣṭhoṃ!
O noble ones, this is that heart-mantra named Ekākṣara (The Single Syllable).

For the sake of all sentient beings—including all worldly and supramundane beings, all *bhūtas*, *kūṣmāṇḍas*, *pūtanās*, *kravyādas*, and so forth; the constellations, planets, mothers (*mātṛs*), boys, and girls; humans, non-humans, and all those enumerated as *vidyādharas*, sages (*ṛṣis*), and the like; all beings bound by the threads of karma across all realms of existence; and even those beings who have been liberated, who are free from passion, who possess great supernatural powers (*maharddhika*), who have pacified the three faults, and those still submerged in the three muds—this single-syllable mantra serves as the heart-essence for them all.
It performs all ritual actions.
All mudrās should be bound;
while performing the recitation, the recitation must be performed with this very heart-mantra.
One will then be constantly sustained by the empowerment of the Buddha.

This [practice], which possesses great power and great benefits, should be applied gradually to sentient beings in all rites, including those involving mudrās, ritual vessels, the procedures for maṇḍalas, and the means for accomplishing the paṭa.
It accomplishes everything that the practitioner desires in his mind.
From that, there are one hundred and eight mudrās.
First, one should perform the Uṣṇīṣa mudrā for the Victor who wields the wheel;
after that, in this world, it is called the Padma mudrā.
The third is the Vajra-mudrā, which belongs to Vajrapāṇi;
the fourth is the Deity-mudrā, which one should designate as the Svastika.
The fifth is said here to be the sword mudrā of the rākṣasas;
the sixth is proclaimed by me to be the club mudrā of the yakṣas.
The seventh [mudrā] for the mantras of the asuras is proclaimed as the vajramuṣṭi;
the eighth is the śūlamudrā, which is recited for all the krodhas.
The ninth is proclaimed as the Puṣpa-mudrā among the yakṣas and yakṣīs;
one should know the tenth to be Mudgara, and the eleventh is the supreme Phara.
The twelfth is designated as the power (śakti) of the child Kārttikeya;
for the renowned Mañjughoṣa, one should employ the lotus.
This number thirteen has been designated by the sages who teach the way of sentient beings.
The fourteenth is the conch (śaṅkha), while the fifteenth is known as the kettle-drum (bherī);
the sixteenth should be understood as the hand-drum (paṭaha), and the seventeenth is the great drum (dundubhi).
Eighteen is likewise called "bound" (baddha), nineteen is called "instrument" (karaṇa),
and twenty is designated as "axe" (paraśu) according to their numerical measure.
Likewise, the white lotus is proclaimed as the parasol for the uṣṇīṣas;
the robe is designated as the bowl, and the mendicant’s staff is considered to be the supreme one.
Compassion, loving-kindness, as well as wisdom, meditative concentration, and likewise ethical discipline—
the sixfold set beginning with patience and generosity— has been taught by the Leaders of the World.
For these six perfections have been proclaimed by the Buddhas through the hearing of the Dharma;
and thirty mudrās for the Wheel-turner have been proclaimed by the Foremost Men of the World.
Of the single-syllable Hero, the Lord of Mantras, the Sovereign,
the Lord of the World, and the Vidyās, twenty-eight [mantras] have been taught.
She who is called Sitā, Mahāśvetā, as well as Paṇḍaravāsinī and the goddess Bhṛkuṭī— these are born from the hearts of the Buddhas.
The mudrā of Tārā is said to be the lotus;
the mudrā of the formidable Hayagrīva is known as the mouth.
O Vajrapāṇi, likewise there are thirty-one mudrās;
all of them are his weapons, standing in various forms for battle.
The four great mudrās are also proclaimed within the maṇḍala of Māra; they are designated as the tridents of Rudra.
The rosary belongs to Brahmā, the discus to Viṣṇu,
and beyond that, the staff of Yama.
All this— the mudrās of all the gods, of all the lords of yakṣas and men, and likewise of all spirits— is based upon all sentient beings.
The supreme realm exists in three ways for those with passion and those free from passion;
it exists in three ways as the universal manifestation throughout all worlds, consisting of both the stationary and the moving.
For all those beings who speak of reality throughout the innumerable realms known as *dhātus*,
it is said that there is but one mudrā for them all, everywhere.
Thus, one hundred and eight [mantras] have been declared;
their qualities, extent, and power are now described here.
Just as for humans there may be accomplishment joined with the application of mantras,
so too does it act through other applications, adorned by the fingers.
Placed between the two hands, this supreme [mudrā] swiftly grants wealth;
I shall first explain it for you, so listen, O you who desire prosperity!
First of all, in a clean place, wearing white garments and pure clothing,
with conduct consistent with purity, one should, together with one's wife, stand facing east in front of a stūpa in a clean location and perform the binding.
It must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who engages in fierce activities,
nor to one who has not granted fearlessness, but only to one who has entered into the samaya.
For one who is devoted to the sons of the Victors and to the teaching of the Buddhas,
there is nothing that cannot be received from the perfection of the mudrā, even if they have not yet generated the [awakening] mind.
One should always offer it to the devoted sons of the Conquerors, to the wise Bodhisattvas, and to the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who have been honored.
The preceptor, always highly esteemed, is firmly established in the conduct of awakening;
he is always preeminent in the application of all mantras.
Therefore, the mudrā should then be given to the disciple who is free from doubt.
Likewise, the preceptor should be one who knows the application of mantras, pure, skillful, and of noble lineage; he should be righteous, wise, consecrated, and have beheld the maṇḍala.
The mantras have thus been shown; the disciple who knows the tantra should be accepted.
The disciple should likewise maintain love for the guru as if for the Buddha;
otherwise, there will never be success with the mantras or with any of the mudrās.
First, having become pure and facing east, one should rub the hands with white sandalwood and first bind the Samaya-mudrā of the Blessed One Uṣṇīṣa:
both hands joined in the hollow of the palms, not hollowed out, slightly bent, shaped like buds, and not opened like the faces of lotuses.
This is the *samayamudrā* of the Blessed Buddha.
With the hands extended in that same manner and joined together in the shape of a blooming lotus, it is the *mudrā* of Avalokita.
Having encircled both hands as before, one should press down with the little fingers from above the index fingers, using the inner-positioned fingers.

This is the utpala-mudrā of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. By contracting those same little fingers as before, one should display the two index fingers joined with the thumbs, standing upright in the shape of an utpala bud.
This is the mudrā of Tārā for all her limbs.
Contracting that very same [hand] and forming the shape of an eye, this is the mudrā of the noble Bhṛkuṭī.
One should apply that same [hand] to the forehead;
this is the Eye-mudrā of the Goddess Devī.
Again, contracting those same [fingers] with both middle fingers and forming the shape of a pair of tongs, one should place it above the head;
this is the single-syllable great mudrā of the Blessed One, the Wheel-Turning King, which performs all rites.
Placing that very same [mudrā] on the forehead is the heart mudrā of the Blessed Buddha.
One should place it upon the eyes;
that itself is the eye-mudrā of the Cakravartin. One should place that same [mudrā] upon the mouth.
That indeed is the face-seal (vaktramudrā) of the Lord of Knowledge, the Universal Monarch (cakravartin), who is the Single Syllable (ekākṣara).
In this manner, up to the mantra-practitioner, there are twenty types of seals (mudrā) for the arms, knees, shanks, feet, and so forth; eight of these become the great seals (mahāmudrā).
They are to be employed in all ritual actions.

Forming that same hollowed palms gesture (*karasaṃpuṭa*), one should encircle it with the middle fingers and point the little fingers like needles. Both thumbs should be positioned at their tips like barley grains, while the two index fingers are extended and formed into a needle, encased within [the other fingers], free of flesh, with their ends bent and well-placed. This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) of the Blessed Ones. Bending those same thumbs and extending them toward the center, this is the seal for the defeat of the four Māras by the Buddhas.
Placing that very same mudrā over the head, one should display it;
this is the Great Mudrā named "The Destroyer of All Defilements of All Buddhas.
One should place that same [mudrā] upon the forehead.
That which is called Great Compassion is the seal (mudrā) of all Buddhas.
Placing that very [seal] upon the heart is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) called "The Uprooting of the Arrows of All Views.
One should place both hands in that same seal.
The Great Seal named "Accomplishment of All Vidyās" is this very seal; one should place it upon the neck. It is the Great Seal named "Pacifier of All Misfortunes."
One should rotate that very mudrā in every direction;
this is the Great Mudrā named "The Attainment of the Purpose of Great Protection.
In this manner, there are eight great mudrās that accomplish all purposes.
The mudrās of Jayoṣṇīṣa are as follows:
with the hands like young shoots, the two left hands are extended and placed obliquely toward the right;
this is the parasol mudrā of Sitātapatra.
That same pair of hands, when placed thus upon the head, is the mudrā of the Blessed One’s Jayoṣṇīṣa.
Having joined both palms together and placed them on the crown of the head in the shape of an uṣṇīṣa, this is the mudrā of the Blessed One’s Abhyudgatoṣṇīṣa.
One should then open that same mudrā.

This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Flaming-Crested One (Jvālāmālinoṣṇīṣa), effective for all rites and to be employed in all fears and in all activities. One should place that very same seal upon the chest;
this is the Great Seal of all the Uṣṇīṣas.
Those same hands, held firmly with the fingers interlaced, constitute the Great Armor Seal (*mahākavacamudrā*) of all Tathāgatas; it should be employed against all obstacles.
Those same hands, with both tips positioned so as to form the shape of a book, should be placed at the center of the chest.
This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), the mother of all Buddhas.
One should show it to all sentient beings;
it pacifies all obstacles and all misfortunes,
and accomplishes all goals.
It produces the arousal of mindfulness.
One should place those very hands upon the forehead;
this is the Dharma Mahāmudrā, the consecration of all Buddhas.
It should be employed in all consecrations for all sentient beings.
One should place those very hands in a variegated form upon the forehead.
This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) named "The Dispeller of All Māras."

Those very hands, with fingers contracted and joined to one another, arranged in the shape of a needle, with the middle fingers extended to form the mark of a needle, and the two thumbs pressed together— this is the great mudrā of the Blessed One Tejorāśi. Placing that same mudrā above the head, this is the other great mudrā of the Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣa Tejorāśi.

Placing those very hands upon the forehead in that same manner, this is the third eye-mudrā of the Blessed One. With those same hands, both made distinct and positioned one above the other for the sake of the right, or else remaining in the form of a hollowed cup with the left, the thumbs and little fingers being interlaced—
this is the root-mudrā of the Great Vajra-Throne of all Buddhas.

That same [mudrā], with both hands shown above the head, is the Mahābodhivṛkṣamūla-mudrā (Mudrā of the Root of the Great Bodhi Tree). That same [mudrā], with both hands joined and turned back, is the mudrā named Sarvabuddhānāṃ Sarvamāravidhvaṃsanakarī (The Destroyer of All Māras of All Buddhas).
That same [mudrā], with both hands interlaced, one should place them upon the neck.
The mudrā named Sarvabhūtavaśīkarī (Subduer of All Beings): one should wear that very same [mudrā] on the neck. The mahāmudrā named Sarvabhūtavilokanī (Beholder of All Beings).
One should place that very same [hand] upon the knees;
this is the Great Mudrā named Purifier of All Evil Destinies.
One should then throw that very same [hand] upward.
The great mudrā named Sarvadevotpattisannicaya is as follows:
both hands in the gesture of fearlessness (abhayākāra) is the great mudrā named Śani, which represents the sphere of all enjoyments.
That same [gesture] should be placed at the crown of the head in the form of a joined palm (añjali).
The Great Seal named "Treading upon All Buddha-fields":
one should place both hands at the ears in that same manner.
With the palms clearly opened, it is the Great Seal named "Subduing All Nāgas."
Having joined both hands together in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭa*), it should be held at the tip of the nose;
this is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) named "The Support of All Buddhas.
One should place that same seal above the head.
The great seal named Sarvabuddhābhyudgatoṣṇīṣa.
In this manner, there are incalculable mudrās of all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas.

By means of the incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, there is an incalculable lineage of Cakravartins and incalculable Cakravartins. Their sovereign is the Single-Syllable Cakravartin, the Lord of Mantras; and there are incalculable Kings of the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas and incalculable extensive ritual manuals (*kalpavisara*) among all mantras.
Their mudrās will be described in brief here: for all of them, there is but one heart-mantra, the single-syllable Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).
Its root-mudrā is now stated right here among the mantras that have been taught, which possess great power and immeasurable majesty;
by the mere binding of which, all mantras become manifest.

All the Blessed Buddhas bestow accomplishment and grant their empowerment to the practitioner of the vidyā-mantra through the mere recollection of the Lord of Mantras, the peerless single-syllable [mantra]. One becomes one who has acquired the roots of merit of ten billion Buddhas.

Even for one who has committed the four root downfalls, that karma which would otherwise result in birth in the great hells goes to exhaustion through the mere recollection [of him], just as for a monk.
What need is there to mention the recitation?
Even the five deeds of immediate retribution go to destruction;

what need is there to mention other unwholesome acts? Therefore, with every effort, this sovereign King of Vidyās, the Single Syllable, should be remembered, recited, meditated upon, brought to mind, worshipped, and constantly propitiated.
Homage to all Buddhas!
Bhrūṃ!
O worthy ones, this is the root mantra of all the uṣṇīṣas spoken by the Tathāgata.

By means of this very Lord of Mantras, the Uṣṇīṣacakravartin born from the crown of the Tathāgata’s head, one should perform all rites. When accompanied by the mudrā, it is certain that success is achieved in all mantras, both mundane and supramundane, throughout the extensive ritual manuals.
And here is the mudrā:

With the hands joined in the hollowed-cup shape (*sampuṭākāra*), the middle fingers extended, with the tips of all the fingers positioned inward and forming the curve of a coil, slightly tilted upward and downward, one should hold this above the head in the form of a *uṣṇīṣa*.
This is the Great Root Mudrā of the One-Syllable Universal Monarch (*Ekākṣaracakravartin*). With this, one should perform all ritual actions.
One should employ [this] in the highest sādhanas and so forth;
it should also be applied for the sake of all protection, shielding, and concealment.
One who employs it in minor sādhanas and the like becomes one who does not know the samaya.

The mantras of the mantra-teacher do not succeed, except for the rites of protection. For the sake of pacification and for the sake of destroying evil, it should be recited constantly in a pure place—on mountains, at rivers, streams, or the banks of oceans—and it should not be recited in other places; for this reason, this King of Vidyās possesses great power and must not be recited in other locations.
One should recite [the mantra] with a mind exalted by spiritual power, pervading all sentient beings with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
And here is the mudrā:

having formed the two hands in the shape of a hollowed cup (*karasaṃpuṭa*), one should make the fingers distinct and slightly bend the third joint of the middle fingers; one should form it in the shape of a *uṣṇīṣa*.
This is the great mudrā of the Blessed One’s Uṣṇīṣarāja.
Having joined the two hands in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭa*), one should slightly incline them downward; this is the third great mudrā of the Blessed One’s Uṣṇīṣa.
Oṃ godare vīra svāhā.

This is the heart-mantra of all the Tathāgatas; it accomplishes all activities, achieves all aims, and wards off all misfortunes. By the mere act of recollecting it, one becomes empowered by all the Buddhas and is liberated from all sins.
It stands above all mantras;
the Buddha himself should be regarded as being directly present.
It should be employed together with this mudrā.
It performs all rites even more swiftly.
While this is being recited, all mantras become as if recited.
In whatever manner it is employed, in that very manner it accomplishes its tasks.
By the will of the reciter, it becomes effective for all rites.
One should hold those very hands, positioned as hollowed palms, at the head in the shape of a three-pronged needle.
This is the second heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*) of all the Blessed Buddhas.
And here is the mantra:
Oṃ gerure vīra svāhā.
This is the heart-seal (hṛdayamudrā) of all the Blessed Buddhas.
It accomplishes all rites, wards off all misfortunes, brings about all goals, and possesses great power; it is to be accomplished in all mantra rituals.
No doubt should be entertained here:
in whatever way it is applied, in that very way it succeeds.

Again, with those same hands positioned in the hollowed-cup (sampuṭa) gesture, one should firmly encircle them with the inner fingers, extend both index fingers, slightly bend them, place them above the head, and display them.
This is the great mudrā of all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas. And here is the mantra for this occasion:
Oṃ ṭrāṃ bandha svāhā!
This is the root mantra of all uṣṇīṣas; it accomplishes all rites and should be employed in all bindings, [uttering] "diśa diśa" for every binding.
It performs all activities.

At the time of performing the sādhana and recitation, during fire offerings (homa) and so forth, whether for one’s own protection or the protection of others—in all ritual substances and in all mantra manuals, both mundane and supramundane—whatever protections have been taught, they should all be performed by means of this alone.
Thus, a great protection is established;
it should be employed in the context of all mantras.
It succeeds in all rites.

All the chapters on the vehicles and means of accomplishment (*yānasādhana*), the detailed sections (*visarapaṭala*), the seals (*mudrā*), and the mantras of all the Tathāgata-uṣṇīṣas—the great wheel-turning lords of vidyās such as Tejorāśi, Sitātapatra, Jayoṣṇīṣa, and so forth—should be applied in their entirety and in detail. This includes all the extensive chapters on the detailed sections of the mantras and tantras, both mundane and supramundane, as well as infinite seals.
And herein are the mantras:

*Oṃ jvalitogradeha vibhinda hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!* This is the supreme heart-mantra (*paramahṛdaya*) of the Blessed One, the Buddha Tejorāśi; it is to be employed in all mantras, in every respect, and for all ritual actions (*sarvakarmika*).

As for the mudrā: the two hands are joined in the form of a *yamala*, with the middle fingers extended and the index fingers encircling them in the shape of a bracelet, both forming the expanse of a circle like a noose.
And this is the *khaṅkhara* mudrā of the Blessed Buddha; and the mantra for this is:
oṃ dhuna jitāraṇa hūṃ.
This is the *khaṅkharaka* seal-mantra of the Blessed Buddhas, which should be employed in all rites.
It awakens all mantras as desired, brings all spirits under control, provides consolation to all beings, invigorates all substances, accomplishes [all goals], and dries up all evils.
In whatever manner this eight-syllable Tathāgata mantra is employed, in that very manner it accomplishes all activities.
Having likewise joined the two hands together and formed them into the shape of a bowl, this is the bowl-mudrā of all the Tathāgatas; it should be understood as the "Tathāgata Bowl.
One should hold it at the region of the navel; it becomes capable of performing all ritual actions.
And there is a mantra for this:
Oṃ, empowered by the world-protectors, hold, hold, maintain it, O you of great majesty, bowl of the Buddhas, svāhā!
This is the Tathāgata-bowl-seal-mantra of the Blessed Buddhas; when joined with this, it becomes capable of performing all rites.
It performs a variety of actions honored by the greatness of their destination;
it accomplishes all rites spoken of in all mantras.
By the will of the practitioner, it acts swiftly in this world—of this there is no doubt.
Whatever mantras belong to the Tathāgatas, and those of Avalokiteśvara,
as well as the foremost mantras called Vajra that are worshipped by various deities—
all of these attain accomplishment when joined with the vessel of the Buddha.
Indeed, there were various preeminent groups of female messengers, as well as groups of male and female servants;
and there were the leaders of various attendants, including yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kaśmalas.
Likewise, there were female messengers who carried out all commands and performed every task for the various eminent kings born of divine and Gandharva lineages.
The mantras were [revealed] by the accomplished vidyādharas, as well as by the world-protectors of great supernatural power,
and by the foremost gods, such as Śakra and others headed by Brahmā, who are wise.
Whatever mantras there may be that are spoken by Kinnaras and Garuḍas of great supernatural power, which always accomplish all activities—
all of them attain success when uttered from the vessel of a Buddha.
He has drawn forth all mantras, which are based upon his movement and form;
he is the King of Mantras, the Master, the Lord, the most excellent, and of great splendor.
He is designated as the foremost of all mantras by those who perceive reality.
That mantra, residing within a worthy vessel, is like a wish-fulfilling gem in three ways;
it performs a variety of activities according to the desired wish of the practitioner.

It produces a greatness of diverse qualities and a supreme excellence of power; it performs a supernatural feat difficult for all mantra-practitioners to surpass. Even one who is unworthy becomes worthy when abiding by the mantra described by the best of sages.
The vessel, when empowered by mantras and endowed with mudrās,
brings about a manifold expansion of qualities arising from ritual action.

It shall destroy all diseases from every side and bestow abundant enjoyments upon the beings existing throughout the three births— the gods, the daityas, and the lords of men. When employed in all rites, it shall swiftly bring about prosperity.
Thus [it is said].
One should place those very hands, formed into the shape of hollowed palms and bound with various beautiful braids, against the region of the forehead.
This is the Citrahasta [mudrā]. It is also the Cintāmaṇiratna Great Mudrā of the Blessed Buddhas. And here is the mantra:
Homage to all Buddhas! Oṃ, blazing splendor, accomplisher of all aims, succeed, succeed! O wish-fulfilling jewel, *siddhicintāmaṇiratna*, hūṃ!
This mantra of the wish-fulfilling jewel accomplishes all aims;
it shall accomplish one's desired objects as well as the mantras in their full detail.
It brings about the greatness of one's virtues and accomplishes even that which is contemplated;
it also renders fruitful all attainments as well as the well-spoken instructions of mantra and tantra.
He should accomplish the ultimate goal, which is fixed upon Buddhahood;
thus, by his own will, he performed the application of karma and was born as Karo.

I shall accomplish for all [practitioners] the various forms of prosperity, which yield immediate fruit and manifest through their own efforts, as well as that which has been mastered through the mantras and tantras.
Furthermore, he [beheld] the form of divinity, or the state of Śakra, or even the embodied state of Brahmā,
as well as the Sudarśanas who resemble the forms of the Ābhāsvara gods.
"Through this practice, one attains a physical form consisting mostly of gods, reaching the highest of the gods, the foremost of the gods— the Bṛhatphala and Akaniṣṭha heavens."

For contemplation is said to be the foremost of mental activities; it is the extensive expansion of the meaning of mantras, abundant among the mudrās, and the accomplisher of the goals of the dharma regarding one's destiny.
The accomplishment of the purpose of all phenomena, the realization of the purpose of all mantras,
for the sake of all qualities and awakening, having its basis in the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
This which is worshipped as the jewel and the tip of thought has been taught in the form of mantra;
through it, one will especially attain heaven and its various supports.
By means of this practice, one shall attain heaven and the extensive meaning of the path of mantra.
Both hands are placed over the shoulders, with the right and left held half-way up, interlocked and joined at the bases of the palms;
this is the *cīvara-mudrā* of all Buddhas. And here is the mantra for it:
Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa! May all the Buddhas empower this robe for me; svāhā!
This is the mantra of the robe.
Having empowered one's own robe with this, one should put it on.
One becomes invincible to all beings.
A consecrated Kṣatriya Great King, acting as a source of reassurance for all, should empower his own garment with this mantra seven times and enter the battle;
upon seeing him, all enemies will be paralyzed.
Or they turn back;
all beings become submissive upon merely seeing him;
his pride and arrogance are gone, and no weapon falls upon his body.
Furthermore, he has no fear of humans or non-humans;
neither poison nor fire falls upon his body,
and he has no fear of disease.
Furthermore, he has no fear of untimely death;

nor is he slain by a foreign army, nor by *ḍākinīs*, *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, or *gandharvas*; nor can he be harmed or injured by various hosts of spirits that steal vitality, those with fierce minds, flesh-eaters, all types of carnivorous and violent beings, those who harass other sentient beings, or by kings who practice evil deeds.
How much less, without protection, could one break through it in all ritual actions and with all substances, or deprive one of life?

Indeed, there exists no being, nor any class of beings, nor mantra, nor mudrā, nor poison—whether stationary or mobile—nor weapon, nor various implements of attack; nor a rākṣasa, nor a rākṣasī, nor a yakṣa, nor a yakṣī, nor a male elder yakṣa, nor a female elder yakṣa, nor a yakṣa attendant, nor a female yakṣa attendant—who could do so among all sentient beings. This is impossible. This situation does not exist.

Therefore, by means of the protection rite performed with the Tathāgata’s seal, robe-mantra, and either through mere recitation or through its mere remembrance, no one else is capable of breaking it—not even by the mantras of the Tathāgatas or by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—except by the will of that very practitioner himself. Thus, this mantra possesses great power; it accomplishes all rites, achieves all aims, destroys all malevolent beings, is endowed with all auspiciousness, fulfills all purposes, purifies all miserable rebirths, eradicates all afflictions, and brings to perfection the qualities of a Buddha.

In that same manner, as before, one should form the hands with the middle fingers bent downward, the tips of the ring fingers resting [upon them], the thumbs bent around [the middle fingers] so that they do not separate from the third joint, and the little fingers bent; having formed these in the shape of wheels, complete with spokes and hubs, one should place them at the position of the head.
This is the Dharma-wheel mudrā of all the Buddhas. And here is the mantra:
Oṃ chinda chinda hana hana daha daha dīptacakra hūṃ!
This is the dharmacakra mantra of all the Buddhas;
it destroys all afflictions and cuts through all the miserable rebirths and downfalls caused by evil means.
It kindles all the qualities of a Buddha;
it illuminates the darkness of all afflictions;
and it dispels all suffering.
It accomplishes all activities,
liberates one from all sufferings,
and illuminates all substances.

This Blessed One Dharmacakra cuts, tears apart, cooks, dries up, and eradicates the spells of those who have instructed wicked beings in supreme mantras that take life, as well as those spells that are harmful, fierce, and deformed; by the will of the practitioner, he uproots them, liberates them, and establishes them in their proper state.
In whatever way this Blessed One is employed, in that same way he performs the rites, with the exception of malevolent magic (*abhicāruka*) and those connected with sensual desire.
He should be employed in all rites of pacification (*śāntika*).
The great protection (*mahārakṣā*) and other rites should be employed in every respect solely for the benefit of all sentient beings.

In all mundane and supramundane accomplishments, in mantras and mudrās, in all rites described in the *kalpas*, and in all activities such as pacifying (*śāntika*) and enriching (*pauṣṭika*), this very great protection should be employed.

That very [mudrā] consists of the two hands: the right hand is raised for striking, while the left hand, with its index finger extended, is threatening; the corners of the mouth are slightly compressed by the application of the knuckles, the lips are parted, the left foot is placed upon the knee, and the right foot is cast out and slightly lowered as one sits.
This is the Great Mudrā of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā.
The mantra of Aparājitā is the destroyer of all Māras of all Buddhas;
it pacifies all obstacles and increases longevity and health.
It is the most excellent among all mantras for the performance of protective rites,
and it is supreme for generating good fortune in men, women, and youths.
Humans and non-humans, and whatever other beings with malicious intent there may be—
rākṣasas, uṣṭārakas, pretas, skandas, apasmāras, and guhyakas.
The hosts of Mātṛs, Bhūtas, and Grahas, as well as those produced by yoga and mantras; pains, afflictions, and diseases arising from various humors (dhātus).
Snakes, mice, spiders, insects,
and boils shall not afflict their bodies, except as a result of past karma.
In disputes regarding travel, and in the face of kings, thieves, water, or fire, one shall obtain victory, security, auspiciousness, and peace; of this there is no doubt.
Having written it on birch bark, or on cloth, or elsewhere,
one should carry it on the head, or on the neck, or on the waist, or on the arm, or in the hand.
Whoever constantly wears this garland of knots, having performed the binding of the garment and the binding of the topknot, for him there shall be well-being.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, recites this while sleeping,
shall pass away in happiness and remember seven lifetimes.
Possessing beauty, endowed with moral virtue, and having a mouth with the fragrance of a blue lotus,
he will be beloved and his words will be accepted in birth after birth.
And here are the perfected mantra-words known as mantras, which accomplish their stated purposes:

namely— bhañjane stambhane dhā dhā dhā dhatsa yā yā yā yate hā hā hā hate parakaraṇi vīrye vīrye guṇatejabhūtakari bhadrakari raudrakari kumbhavati viṣakumbhavati sarvabale bhūtabale rakṣa rakṣa māṃ sarvaviṣebhyaḥ sarvavighnebhyaḥ!

Namely: Siddhakari, Siddhārthe, Siddhamanorathe, Siddhakārye, Phuru, Nurūpe, Svaste, Praśaste, Siddhi, Siddhārthe, Dhairyavati, Samane, Tapane, Śaraṇe, Bhadre, Bhavati, Śānte, Dānte, Śive, Hununu, Pari, Paritrāṇaṃ kuru, Parigrahaṃ kuru, Paripālanaṃ kuru, Śāntiṃ kuru, Svastyayanaṃ kuru, Rakṣāṃ kuru mama sarvasattvānāṃ ca svāhā!
This is the heart-mantra of Aparājitā;
the preceding is the root-vidyā.
The practitioner must necessarily be intent upon the side of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*).
It should be recited three times a day.
Even before that, one should recite it once from a book or by oral transmission; this itself constitutes the side of wholesome qualities.
And here there is a subsidiary heart-mantra: Homage to the seven perfectly awakened Buddhas together with their assemblies of disciples, who have transcended all enmity and fear:
through the splendor and supernatural power of Vipaśyin; likewise through the wisdom of Śikhin; and through the strength of Viśvabhū and Krakucchanda.
Through the training of Kanakamuni, the virtues of Kāśyapa,
and the heroic power of Śākyasiṃha, may there always be auspiciousness for me.
Namely: *Jaye vijaye aparājite mārasainyapramardanīye svāhā!
Sarvārthasādhanīye svāhā!* This Blessed Lady, the accomplisher of all aims, performs various deeds exactly according to how she is employed.
It should be employed in all protective rites;
it must certainly be kept in mind by the practitioner.
It destroys all obstacles.
He disperses all the deeds of Māra,
brings all mantras to manifestation,
and fulfills all the qualities of a Buddha.
It draws forth all mundane and supramundane mantras;
it fulfills what is deficient and removes what is excessive; and it accomplishes all aspirations.
It wards off all malevolent beings;
in brief, it accomplishes everything according to the practitioner's wish.
Furthermore, at the time of death, it reveals its face directly before him.
It dries up all miserable states and evil destinies;
through constant recitation, it exhausts the five deeds of immediate retribution;
and it attenuates even the four root transgressions.
By mere recollection and by the recitation itself,
it uproots [all obstacles] and establishes one in rebirth among all the gods and rebirth among humans;
it engages one in all the practices of a bodhisattva.

It fulfills all the qualities of a Buddha. Thus, O Blessed Lady, you possess immeasurable virtues and benefits and great power; you have been proclaimed from the mouths of all Buddhas by all the Tathāgatas for the destruction of all Māras. You dry up all afflictions and are unimpeded in all activities. You should be employed for the sake of all protection, shielding, and guarding.
This is the majestic display of all Buddhas.
This is the great lion’s roar;
this is the basis for all conduct;
this is the awakening of all Buddhas.
This is the outflow of the great samādhi;
this is the supernatural power of the great miracle;
this is the preeminent excellence of all.
This is the state of universal peace;
this is the abode of all Buddhas;
this is the state of nirvana.
This is the word for auspiciousness; this is the word for the ineffable;
this is the word for the limit of reality.
This is the phrase of the nature of non-existence;
that is to say, it is the mantra-phrase, the phrase of the empowerment of all Buddhas.
One should place those very hands, joined in the *karasampuṭa* gesture with the middle fingers of both hands pointing upward, against the region of the forehead.
This is the second seal of Aparājitā, which performs all rites when applied together with the root mantra; it fulfills all aspirations.
When placed at the location of the heart and conjoined with the heart mantra, it destroys all demons and eliminates all states of woe and miserable rebirths.
This is the third, the heart-seal of the Blessed One Aparājitā.
Those same hands, hanging down from the region of the navel with the arms bent downward—
this is the fourth subsidiary-heart mudrā of the Blessed Lady Aparājitā.
By means of the heart mantra, it performs all rites.

Consecrating water with mantras that are considered auspicious for all purposes, which bring about all peace and well-being, bathing with it brings about supreme good fortune, removes misfortune, generates prosperity, and bestows glory and success. One should place those very hands upon the region of the face.
This is another great seal (mahāmudrā); it is the fifth great seal of the Blessed One Aparājitā. In this manner, there are innumerable seals, and they should be employed in all the Aparājita mantras.
That same hand is thrown to the right and slightly clenched into a fist, while the left hand forms a firm fist pressed against it.
This is the Mahāśakti mudrā of all the Buddhas.
And the mantra for this is: Oṃ vijaye mahāśakti durdhari hūṃ phaṭ vijayine phaṭ maṅgale phaṭ svāhā.
The Tathāgata’s power-mantras should be employed against all malevolent beings. When great dangers have arisen, they should be employed in villages or in conjunction with mudrās for all rites.

In cases of affliction by planets and constellations, and for those seized by all types of *vetāḍa* spirits, as well as those possessed by all *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, *piśācas*, *marut-grahas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, and so forth, the mantras should be employed after forming the mudrā.
At that very moment, one is liberated.
This [mantra] should be employed during entries into all great cremation grounds;
all obstacles flee, they run away, and they cease to exist in every way, entirely.
In this manner, it accomplishes various and manifold purposes for all rites through the majesty of the mantra-tantra;
it provides complete protection, shielding, and concealment;
and it is a purifier that destroys all demons, increasing longevity and health.

That same [mudrā], with the hands joined in a hollowed cup, the middle fingers slightly bent, the little fingers encircled by the ring fingers, and both thumbs pressed against the eyes in the shape of eyes—this is the Tathāgata-locana-mahāmudrā of the Blessed Buddhas.

In the portion of the eye, she is shown as the measure of the supreme qualities of all Tathāgatas; the mother of all Tathāgatas; the illuminator of all vidyās; the fulfiller of all aims; the purifier of all false views; the producer of right view in all sentient beings; the mother of the family of all Tathāgatas; the sustainer of the families of all mantra lineages; the fulfiller of all worldly and supramundane mantras; the fulfiller of all purposes; the consoler. And here is the mantra: Oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha Siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā!
The Great Vidyā of the Tathāgata’s Eye:
*vacana vacana vacana oṃ buddhalocane svāhā*.
This is that Vidyā of Vajrapāṇi, which performs all rites for him alone.

In that same manner, having formed the hands in the shape of a hollowed casket as before, one should bend the middle fingers, extend the tips of the little fingers slightly downward, encircle the two thumbs with the index fingers, and join the ring fingers so they are slightly curved.
This is the *ūrṇā-mudrā* of the Blessed One and of all the Buddhas. In that same manner, one should place both fingertips at the region of the forehead.

This is the Ūrṇā-mudrā of all the Tathāgatas. With those same hands, having formed the tips of both fingers into a braid, one should place them in the region of the forehead in the shape of a mandala.
This is the third, the Ūrṇā-maṇi-ratna-mudrā.

Those same hands, with both [fingers] bent inward, the little fingers entwined, and the two thumbs joined together—this is the fourth, the Ūrṇā mudrā. Those same hands, with the thumbs bent down, should be displayed in the shape of a tuft at the forehead; this is the Tathāgata-ūrṇā of all the Tathāgatas.

These five great mudrās are equal in potency, equal in power, and effective for all rites. And here is the mantra for them all: *Namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo ’rhadbhyaḥ samyaksambuddhebhyaḥ / he he bandha bandha tiṣṭha tiṣṭha dhāraya dhāraya nirundha nirundhorṇāmaṇi svāhā*.
The *bhaga* mantras of all the *ūrṇā* and *maṇi* mudrās are effective for all rites.
This *tathāgatorṇā* mudrā is unimpeded in all activities and should be employed in all [ritual] applications.
Having made a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with *gorocana*, one should enter battle while reciting the *tathāgatorṇā* mantra.
All enemies become paralyzed;
upon seeing him, they flee,
and their anger vanishes.
With minds of loving-kindness and minds of benefit, all sentient beings become fully comforted.
Upon seeing him, having applied that *rocanā* tilaka, no carnivorous beasts or the like are able [to harm them].
Seeing him, they perceive that great king, that great being of great renown and great energy, as if he were blazing with light.
All those who are wicked and malicious— whether yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, all grahas, bhūtas, or kaśmalas with fierce minds— become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness;
they depart from that place,
and one is liberated from all calamities and harmful practices.

For those seized by all types of planetary spirits (*graha*), for all *mātṛkā* and child-seizing spirits, and for *brahmarākṣasa*s and the like, one should empower yellow pigment (*gorocana*) with mantras and, having applied it as a mark (*tilaka*) on the forehead, show it [to them].
As soon as they see it, they all release their hold, flee, and run away.
In every way, they no longer exist for him, nor do they seize him again.
If they seize them, they will perish entirely.

This same method should be applied to all planetary seizures (*sarvagraha*). Whatever various [practices] are taught in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of all mantras and tantras—whether mundane or supramundane—such as the procedures for the maṇḍala and the cloth-painting (*paṭa-sādhana*), these are to be accomplished by this very [method]; they are accomplished even more swiftly.
Having consecrated *gorocana* with the mantra and applied it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*), one may enter into the midst of enemies.
They become free from anger and cannot be overcome;
one should enter into the midst of a great multitude while reciting this mantra.
All become adorned with loving-kindness;
their speech becomes authoritative;
and they are invincible and unassailable by others among all beings everywhere.
Having consecrated yellow orpiment seven times with this mantra and applied it as a *tilaka*, one should enter the great cremation ground;
all flesh-eaters will flee,
and all planetary spirits (*graha*) and mother-goddesses (*mātṛkā*) will perish.
He becomes unassailable by all humans; seeing him as if blazing with splendor, those who steal vitality (ojas) flee from that place,
not even granting him a sight of themselves.
What need is there to mention taking away their vital energy?
They do not remain for even a moment;
having abandoned the great cemetery, all the hosts of spirits who dwell there depart.
They cannot even be looked upon from this side or that,
let alone having their vital energy taken away or being harmed.
Nevertheless, this Great Vidyā named Tathāgatorṇā— which possesses great majesty and all vidyās, and is endowed with great supernatural power— remains present.
It has been spoken by incalculable Blessed Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and it has been spoken and approved;
it is now being spoken and approved by the Perfectly Awakened Śākyamuni;
and those who will be the Perfectly Awakened Ones in the future time will also speak it.

Thus, it has been praised, extolled, and rejoiced in by the past and future Blessed Buddhas; and now, by me, Śākyamuni, it is likewise praised, extolled, and authorized, so that it shall accomplish all rites for all sentient beings according to their respective methods.
In whatever way one applies it, in that very way it performs all activities—except for malevolent magic (*abhicāruka*) and that which is associated with sensual desire (*kāma*).
Having formed the two hands into the shape of a hollowed casket and interlaced them so as to be variegated, one should place them at the center of one's chest.
This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Blessed One Samādhivajra;
by binding which, one becomes irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and is established in certainty.
And here is the mantra for this: *Namaḥ samantabuddhānām / oṃ vibhide cūrṇaya cūrṇaya vajradhika vajradhika hūṃ hūṃ jaḥ jaḥ samādhijaḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Even if it is brief, all of it should be applied in detail.
And this Samādhi-vajra of the Blessed One, which possesses immeasurable benefits for all Buddhas,
one should place that very mudrā at the region of the throat.
This is the lotus-lotus mudrā of all the Buddhas. One should place this very same [mudrā] on the left side;
it is the utpala mudrā.
One should place this very [mudrā] on the right arm;
this is the Blessed Buddha’s mudrā of compassionate objective loving-kindness (*kṛpālambanamaitrīmudrā*).
With both hands joined in this same way, with the fingers interlaced and the middle fingers extended, forming the shape of a full circle, it is placed in the center of the heart.
This is the second mudrā of loving-kindness;
it performs all activities for all Tathāgatas and is unimpeded.

In this same manner, by this very procedure, the third [mudrā] is on the forehead; the fourth is placed above; and the fifth becomes the Maitrīmudrā when rotated all around. It should be employed at the time of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) upon an object, and then no humans will cause harm.

Neither humans nor non-humans— neither all yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, piśācas, kaṭapūtanas, and so forth— can produce any affliction in his body; and all Māras, though they perform their demonic deeds,
and all obstacles, become non-obstacles.
And there is a mantra for this: *Oṃ prasphura prasphura kṛtālambanamantrātmaka hāṃ*.
This loving-kindness (*maitrī*) of the Blessed One should be employed.
Then, having interlaced the two hands and formed them into the shape of a braid, one should place them upon the mandala.
One should place the two index fingers upright in the region of the forehead;
this is the Mahākaruṇā mudrā of the Blessed Buddha. And the mantra for this is: oṃ viśve svāhā.
It is effective for all rites;
it should be applied to sentient beings,
and they become compassionate in nature.

With those same hands, having performed the *buddheṣṭi* and positioned them in the *citrīkṛta-avabhaya* (the "wondrously displayed fearlessness") gesture, this is the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Blessed Buddha.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ munimuni gagana svāhā*.
This Blessed Lady accomplishes all rites; she fulfills them all when applied with a joyful mind.
She performs everything;
whatever rites exist in all the manuals of mantra, whether mundane or supramundane, she accomplishes them all without exception.

Placing the thumbs of both hands upon them and making them variegated, one should display them at the forehead; this is the Blessed One’s Tathāgata-prekṣā mudrā, which performs all rites and accomplishes all aims.
And here is the mantra: *oṃ mahadgate upekṣaya sarvadharmān viśvātmane viśvamūrti jvala jvalaya sarvabuddhadharmān hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Furthermore, there are six mudrās for the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).
Those same hands, with the gesture of granting boons,
constitute this Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Giving (*dānapāramitā*). Those same hands, slightly bent toward each other, are placed at the region of the navel.
This is the Mahāmudrā of the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā).
Keeping the hands in that same position but lowered and placed against the sides of the armpits—this is the Mahāmudrā of the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
One should place the hands in that same manner above the upper arms.
Being perceived through a distorted form,
this is the Mahāmudrā of the Perfection of Vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).

Having formed the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*) with those very hands and placing them above, having bound the left and right together over the top, one gazes toward the object of meditation (*dhyānālambana*) out of compassion for all sentient beings while seated in the cross-legged posture.
This is the great mudrā of the Blessed Lady’s perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyānapāramitā*).
That same seal of the perfection of meditative concentration, without breaking the cross-legged posture, takes the form of teaching the Dharma;
this is the great mudrā of the Blessed Lady’s perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
One should break that very cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*):
having placed the left hand upon the lap, one should touch the ground with the right hand in the form of the Vajra-seat (*vajrāsana*).
This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of all Buddhas for their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; this indeed is the Great Seal of all the Buddha-qualities.
The mantras for all [the perfections] are as follows: Oṃ dāne dada dada dadāpaya jvala jvala sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite huṃ huṃ jaḥ svāhā.
This is the great mudrā of the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā).
Oṃ śīla śīlāḍhye śāntikaraṇi śive praśaste sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā.
The Great Seal of the Perfection of Ethical Discipline (śīlapāramitā)—Oṃ śānte śrīkari kṣānte kṣāntikari svāhā!
This is [the seal] of the Perfection of Patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Oṃ vīrye vīryam iti sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā!
*Abhāvasvabhāve svāhā* / *Vajrākramaṇi svāhā*.
This is [the mantra] of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
Oṃ śāntikari dhūdhūdhūrdhari dhairye vīrye gagane ramaṇe dhyānavati svāhā!
This is [the mantra] of the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā).
Oṃ dhīḥ dhūḥ! This is the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).

Oṃ! Protect me, O Blessed One, you who are honored by all Buddhas, you who are without objective support, whose nature is space, who have entered the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and who bring forth light! Dispel, dispel the darkness of all afflictions!
Dry them up! Deliver me!
O you who are formless! Huṃ huṃ! Destroy all karmic actions! Huṃ phaṭ svāhā!

This Blessed Lady is the mantra of the great enlightenment of the Blessed Buddhas; she accomplishes all rites, fulfills all purposes, and repels all misfortunes. She brings to completion all the qualities of a Buddha, destroys all afflictions, and annihilates all mantras performed by others. She puts to flight all Māras, effects the mastery of all worldly and transcendent mantras, dispels all evil, dries up all miserable rebirths, and establishes one in all the Buddha-qualities among all gods and humans.
In brief, in whatever way she is applied, in that very way she performs her activities.

It is not possible, even in ten million eons, for incalculable Buddhas, Blessed Ones, to fully describe or praise the greatness of her qualities, nor to speak of the empowerment of her miraculous manifestations, conduct, and the power of her supernatural abilities.
Such is the manifestation of the limitless expansion of the greatness of this Bhagavatī’s qualities, such that she can also extensively manifest the six perfections.

In brief, the power of teaching, conduct, and supernatural power, as well as the lineage of qualities and the conduct established by empowerment, should be known in their entirety, as should the attainment of excellence.
Having the nature of space, they proclaim the Dharma, investigating existence and non-existence;
they employ every kalpa and syllable for the accomplishment of activities.
The wise have declared it to be abundant, arising swiftly from the manifestation of its fruit;
it is the meaning of the mantra whose nature is space, adorned by the clarity of the syllables.
When properly applied and well-examined, they bear fruit in many ways at the right time;
thus has the mudrā-tantra been explained in detail by those who practice according to reality.
The course of mantra and tantra, as well as time and its regulation, are well-applied;
one should know that recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, lead to the fruit arising from reality.
The movement of substances for the sake of their support is clearly characterized by its defining marks;
it is the awakening to the mantra and one's own mantra, arising from the common source of the family.
For the time of accomplishment is indeed perceived through the emergence of the signs of the mudrās.
The mantra-practitioner, established in the ultimate reality and composed in meditation, should recite the mantra;
he shall manifest the accomplishments, the cause of accomplishment, and the family deity.
These mudrās have been declared as excellent, as have the highly renowned mantras;
when practiced according to the prescribed rule, they are accomplished according to one's desires arising from the mind.
Thus [it is said].

That same [gesture], with the fingers interlaced, the right thumbs bent down and resting beneath the left thumbs—this is the heart-mudrā of all Buddhas, spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and it accomplishes all rites. And here is the mantra: Oṃ trailokyapūjitāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
They perform all rites and should be employed in all mandala rituals for the great protection and other purposes of all sentient beings.
In that same manner, both hands are joined with the tips [of the fingers] contracted upward, and these are the middle-finger rings.
This is the root mudrā of all the Blessed Buddhas. And here is the mantra for this: oṃ da dadātu daṇḍa hūṃ.
Oṃ sarvasattvāmṛtapradeśikamkarāya svāhā. Both the staff and the water-pot are root mantras; by means of these, one should perform all rites.

It should be employed everywhere among all mantras as the bestower of all accomplishments; it should be applied in all rites of protection. Those same two hands, with the palms pressed together, should be placed at the position of the head with the fingers interlaced like a braid.
It should be employed for specific purposes.
And there is a mantra for this: *oṃ jvala jvala sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite svāhā*.
By means of this, one should perform all rites within the Tathāgata family.
The stimulation of the substance should be performed with the mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī, using either red oleander (*karavīra*) or jasmine (*mālatī*) flowers.
It should be applied everywhere with the root mantra of Mañjuśrī;
indeed, it is to be employed in all rites in every respect.
One should place those same two hands in the form of double-fists at the position of the head;
this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Uṣṇīṣa of all Buddhas.
And the mantra here is: jrīṃ.
This Uṣṇīṣarāja is effective for all rites. Having formed the two hands into the shape of a lotus, one should place them at the heart;
this is the Avalokita-mahāmudrā of the Lotus Family, effective for all rites.
And the mantra for this is: *jrīḥ*.
One should place those very hands, shaped like a closed lotus bud, at the center of the navel.
This is another great mudrā of Avalokita called "The Pacifier of All Obstacles."
And the mantra for this is: *jiḥ*.

This, which performs all rites, should be employed against all fears by Avalokita. Having formed the two hands in the shape of a beautiful conch (*suśirākāra*) with the fingers interlocked, one should place them upon the forehead; this is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of all Buddhas, named "Arisen from the Mind of Radiance" (*prabhāvamānasodbhava*).
And the mantras to be employed here are these four single-syllable ones: *tāḥ*,
*vāḥ*.
Droḥ / Hāḥ /

These one-syllable mantras were spoken by four koṭis of Buddhas; they are the Uṣṇīṣa-kings of all Buddhas, the power of all vidyās of great supernatural might, and the refuge of all dharmas. They possess the four bases of psychic power and the five limbs, are established in the four noble truths, and have their heads inclined toward enlightenment. They are to be cultivated by all through the four liberations, the four dhyānas, and the samādhis; they are unshakable by any worldly or supramundane mantra-tantras. They are the supreme lords of all vidyā-rājas and universal monarchs (cakravartins), the eldest among all mantras, and inconceivable among all the distinctions of samādhis. Having attained enlightenment, they are the sovereigns of the three worlds and are inaccessible to all families of mantra-tantras, as well as to all bodhisattvas, noble śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas.

Thus, these [mantras] are inconceivable, devoid of intrinsic nature, insurmountable, and established in the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which are of the nature of space and untroubled; in brief, they should be employed in all rites.
By means of these alone, one should perform all rites, especially those according to the ritual procedures of the *Mūlakalpa* of the noble Mañjuśrī.
One should display those very hands in the shape of a hollowed casket at the position of the head.
This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) called "Destroyer of All Poisons" within the family of all Tathāgatas; it should be employed in all rites concerning poison. *ṭroṃ*.
This mantra, spoken by the Buddha, when joined with this mudrā,
quickly renders all beings— both stationary and moving— free from poison.
It renders non-venomous even those serpents that are active and arrogant with poison;
likewise, it destroys all defects born of passion and hatred.
This mantra, joined with the mudrā, overcomes even those born of delusion;
it performs various rites arising from poisons and venomous beings.
In brief, this mudrā,
when applied according to the Mantrayāna, performs various rites arising from poison; it brings his poison under control at will.
Thus, with [the mantra] recited one hundred thousand times;

that very [mudrā], with both hands in the form of the *samayavajra*, having three prongs on each side—with the left hand positioned below and the right hand above, inverted—should be placed at the location of the head.
That same [mudrā] is the heart-mudrā of the Lord of Vajras, effective for all rites.
And here is the mantra: HŪṂ.
This is effective for all rites and accomplishes all aims; it should be employed against all cruel grahas, and no doubt should be entertained otherwise.
OṂ BHADRE BHADRAVATI KARAṬE RATNA VIRATNA SVĀHĀ.
First, one hundred and eight recitations of this [mantra] should be performed;
then Mañjuśrī will be accomplished.
Placing both hands with the fingertips slightly curled over the crown of the head—this is the great mudrā of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

It should be employed in all rites, applied in all protections, and is the accomplisher of all goals; one should first begin with the sādhanas of Mañjuśrī and afterwards perform the ritual action, as it is common to the three families.
One should place that very mudrā on the forehead of the noble Samantabhadra;
it is the great mudrā of Ākāśagarbha.
And here is the mantra for all rites: *svaṃ*.
One should place that very same mudrā at the region of the throat;
this is the great mudrā (*mahāmudrā*) of Vimatela-gate.
And here is the mantra for all rites: *laṃ*.
One should place that very same mudrā upon the middle of the sheep;
this is the great mudrā of Maitreya.
And the mantra for this is: *maṃ*.
One should place the two hands at the region of the navel as before;
this is the great mudrā of Kṣitigarbha.
And here is the mantra for all rites: *KṢIṂ*.
One should apply that same mudrā at the region of the waist and cast it upward;
this is the mudrā of Gaganagañja.
And here is the mantra for all rites: *gaṃ*.
Having placed that very mudrā on both arms, one should whirl it over the head by means of the dance-yoga.
This belongs to all Bodhisattvas, Noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas.
And there is a mantra for this: *Ghruḥ*.
This [mudrā] possesses an expansion of the power of actions with immeasurable benefits; it should be viewed from all sides through its connection with the greatness of qualities worthy of being seen.
Then, having looked upward at that very mudrā and lowered it, one should cast it upward by means of the yoga of dance.

This Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), named Sarvatratalalyā, belongs to all the gods dwelling in the three realms, encompassing infinite world-systems—above, below, across, and in every direction—and to all beings, including yakṣas, yakṣīs, rākṣasas, and rākṣasīs; it should be employed in all rites.
It should also be employed in all practices such as summoning, dismissal, the construction of maṇḍalas, and the performance of sādhanas.
And here is the mantra: *oṣṭrai*.
Placing those very hands in the form of the *añjali* gesture upon the head is the Great Mudrā of the Inner Barrier for Binding All Mantras.
It should also be rotated at the region of the waist.
And here is the mantra for this: *gyaṃ jaye kumāri śuklabandhani svāhā*.
One should bind a thread spun by a maiden, over which the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times, around the waist;
thus the binding of semen is accomplished.
One should then gaze out toward all directions.
All obstacles become paralyzed;
therefore, the practitioner should perform this mudrā-binding for protection in all matters from every side.
This is the first application that must be performed.
Afterwards, the ritual actions (karmāṇi) are to be performed.
In this way, there are one hundred and twenty-eight mudrās.
The practitioner should employ whichever one he desires among them for all rites, or indeed all of them.
In this manner, by means of this application, there are incalculable mudrās and incalculable mantras.

In that same way, the two hands, held in the form of hollowed palms with the fingers interlaced both together and separately and adorned by both thumbs, are made into two fists in the shape of five prongs; one should place them at the position of the head upon the crown.

This is the great mudrā of Noble Mañjuśrī called the Five-Crested; it performs all rites. By the thrusting and withdrawing of the thumbs, with them contracted, there is summoning; with them extended, there is dismissal.
Thus, through all applications performed mentally, it accomplishes all rites.

Whether joined with the root mantra, the heart-mantra, or the subsidiary mantra (upahṛdaya) of Mañjuśrī, or indeed with all mantras, it accomplishes all purposes. That very mudrā, shaped like a three-pronged pin,
is called the "Three-Crested" (triśikhā) of Mañjuśrī.
That same [mudrā], with the little fingers shaped like needles, is to be understood as the *ekacīra*.
Both hands are placed in a hollowed cup, bent inward on all sides, with the fingers well-arranged and set, firmly joined and placed upon the head.
This is the Great Mudrā of Mañjuśrī named *Sarvaśirobhyudgata* (Emerging from All Heads).

Then, placing those same hands with the tips raised and palms facing upward within the middle of the face— this is the Great Face Mudrā of Mañjuśrī. Lowering those same hands and placing them in the middle of the heart—
this is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Heart Mudrā.
That same [mudrā], with the hands positioned half-way down and the forehead slightly bent forward,

is another heart-mudrā (*hṛdayamudrā*). That same [mudrā], having raised the hands with the middle fingers bent downward and the ring fingers shown with their tips bent, the index fingers encircled [around them], and the thumbs extended along their sides.
This other great root-mudrā of Vakradaṃṣṭra is to be employed in all great fears; the two hands are likewise [joined] very gently. This is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Utpala (Blue Lotus) mudrā.
Bending those same [fingers] at the joints and winding them around,
this is Mañjuśrī’s Peacock Throne mudrā. With those same [fingers], the index fingers are held by the little fingers on both sides, slanting across in the shape of a seat.
This is another mudrā, the Bhadrapīṭha-mudrā:
with the fingers thus formed into fists, only one index finger is raised.
This is another mudrā, the Yaṣṭi-mudrā.
Raised twice, it is the banner mudrā;
raised thrice, it is the flag mudrā; raised four times, it is the bell.
That same hand, with the index finger placed on top, is the *chatra* (parasol) mudrā. When all [fingers] are bent downward, it is the *phala* (fruit) mudrā. Hūṃ.
The *aṅkuśa-mudrā* consists of the index finger positioned at the tip of the hook-like finger.
That same [hand], with the index finger held firmly in a fist, is the *muṣṭi-mudrā*. That same [hand], with the fingers positioned like the point of a needle across [the palm], is the *śūla-mudrā*.
The Mahāśūla mudrā consists of both index fingers joined together;
the Ekaliṅga mudrā has one thumb raised upward.
One should place that same mudrā at the heart.
The *manorathamudrā* is formed as follows:

having joined the two hands together in the shape of a hollowed casket (*sampuṭa*), one places them one above the other; this is the *yamalamudrā*. Opening that same [mudrā] into the shape of a bud and casting it toward the head constitutes the *utpalamudrā*.
That very same [hand], full and having the form of space, is the *pūrṇamudrā*. That same [hand] placed at the head and formed with a fist below is Mañjuśrī’s staff-mudrā (*yaṣṭimudrā*).
Furthermore, when the two hands are made variegated, they form the upward-pointing *svastika* of Mañjuśrī; it should all be bound with red *mālatī* flowers.
In that same manner, having crossed the hands in reverse and extended the tips of the middle fingers,
this is another *śakti-mudrā* of Kārttikeya and Mañjuśrī.
The bell and the banner are to be understood as before.
Then, having joined the two hands together in a hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*), one should open them;
this is another *padma-mudrā* of Mañjuśrī.
With those same hands positioned crosswise and well-aligned, one should form the shape of a swastika.
With the four fingers extended in the four directions and well-positioned in the middle,
this is another *svastika* mudrā of Mañjuśrī.
Those same hands, shaped like sprouts, are joined together with the fingers interlaced.
This is another *pallavamudrā*. Those same two hands are made into fists;
this is another *sarvabuddhāspadamudrā*.
This is the Dharma-drum mudrā of Mañjuśrī:

the hands are joined in the hollowed-cup gesture (*sampuṭīkṛta*), with a cavity in the middle; the index fingers encircle [the thumbs], which are placed upon the surface of the base thumbs and bent inward, marked by the shape of a conch.
This is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Dharma-conch mudrā.
The wheel is as before;
having the form of a wheel of Dharma, this is another mudrā of Mañjuśrī, the Dharmacakra-mudrā.
Placing that same mudrā upon the forehead and performing the yoga of dance, one should cast it with the movement of the left side.

This is another seal for the great miraculous play (*mahākrīḍāvikurvāṇamudrā*). It should be employed against great fears by means of the root mantra itself; they perish without exception. In this way, through this application, there are innumerable seals.
And there are incalculable mudrās, kalpas, mantras, and tantras;
and incalculable things are to be seen,
which have arisen from the self-existent one who has emerged with great power.
And all of these should be employed;
in this ritual manual (*kalpavisara*), they should all be used while wrapped within clean garments,
so that they are not seen by beings who do not know the secret convention (*asamayajña*).

Thus, these hand-gestures (*kara-mudrā*) employed as means for accomplishment possess great power; otherwise, there would be a transgression of the *samaya*. These are numerous, involving the application of dance and song with the hands positioned in various ways.
Having thus explained in sequence the specific cries of sentient beings, [the author] now describes the great mudrās suitable for the practice of the maṇḍala:
for all Buddhas it is likewise a stūpa; on the ground, the supreme [symbol] is the relic (dhātu);
on a cloth, it is the same for Bodhisattvas, while for Śrāvakas it is a circle.
The square [mandala] of the Pratyekabuddhas is said to have three circles;
it is adorned with various vehicles and diverse ornaments.
The weapon of the gods, yakṣas, and grahas is the *aparā*;
that of kings is the sword; and that of the sages is the staff and the water-pot.
In this context, within the maṇḍalas, one should briefly perform the mudrās corresponding to whatever is the constant weapon of a deity, or whatever constitutes its vehicle or ornament.
Then one should place the sun and the moon as mandalas above the mandala;
in brief, whatever is the ground for whom, that very thing one should invoke with the mind.
Various living beings have been described; at that time, one should assign them to each of those [beings].
Many types of beings and many mudrās have been proclaimed;
one should perform their rites within the maṇḍala according to the prescribed rule.

The lotus of Brahmā, the thunderbolt of Śakra, the noose of Varuṇa, the trident of Rudra, the sharp-edged spear of Durga, the water-pot of the Ṛṣis, the staff of Yama, the mace of Dhana-da, the sword of Kubera, the fire-pit of Hutāśana, the jar of Pṛthivī—these and others, whatever weapons and ornaments are seen in the world today, should all be employed in all maṇḍalas according to the prescribed rule by one who recollects them everywhere, or they should be drawn according to the procedure declared in the Kalpa. All maṇḍalas should be drawn with a mind intent on the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, with compassion for all beings, having generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), and out of pity for all beings; this should be done by those who have been consecrated in all maṇḍalas, or specifically consecrated in the Great Maṇḍala.
One who has seen the maṇḍala and received initiation from the noble Mañjuśrī must necessarily paint all the maṇḍalas;
the noble Mañjuśrī should be kept in mind.

For this reason: "I, along with all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have consecrated you so that, appearing in the form of a youth and in the form of mantra, you shall perform the welfare of sentient beings by teaching the Dharma through the profound method of the true meaning of all mantras."
One should not perform that which is joined with mantra and mudrā unless it is focused on the Dharma;
herein one should not do what is harmful, nor should one do what is beneficial if it is not desired as wholesome.
Combined with mudrās and mantras, one should ward off what is harmful;
indeed, all that is beneficial and harmful, as well as the warding off of the harmful, [is accomplished] always.
Every mantra should be performed as beneficial when sealed by the mudrā;
one should not perform a mudrā without a mantra, nor likewise a mantra without being sealed by a mudrā.
Joined with the meaning of the mudrā, it will accomplish its purpose;
joined with the mudrā, the mantra becomes fruitful, resulting in the attainment of the fruit of the mudrā.
One should accomplish the extensive ritual actions through meditation equal to the mudrās;
those mudrās which belong to pacification, as well as the mantras for pacification.
Through the union of mantra and mudrā, one should begin the rite of pacification (śāntika);
and for the mantras of enrichment (pauṣṭika), one should bind the arising of the mudrās.
They say that when joined with mantras as described, this is the *mudrā* for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*).
For pacification (*śāntika*), one should perform the pacifying rite using the *mudrās* and mantras proclaimed here.
By means of the Victors, the principal mantras of the Victors, and also the mudrās according to their divisions,
one should accomplish all rites in all seasons during the cool times.
The mantras originating from the Lotus family have been taught for the sake of nourishment;
likewise, the mantra-tantras [are to be practiced] with the fierce mudrās proclaimed by you.
By means of well-known recited mantras and highly efficacious mudrās,
which have been prescribed for the Lotus Family and are pure and radiant.
With auspicious rites that are highly praised and fully conducive to health and prosperity,
as well as with mantras and mudrās described as being joined with wrath.
With those [mantras] prescribed for the attainment of enjoyments and wealth— stainless, beautiful, white, marked with white seals, and conjoined with the appropriate mudrās of the mantra.
One should accomplish the mantras that bring about prosperity and enjoyment in this life;
when accomplished with such mantras and mudrās, they yield fruitful results.
Likewise, the wrathful mantras, as well as the mantras beginning with "mantra" that obstruct the vital breaths,
were taught in the Vajrin-tantra and in the Samudbhava-tantra of the Jina-lotus.
The fierce Tejins, who subdue wicked beings, are appointed to the slaughter of living creatures; a wise person should not perform that act.
The mudrās are the staff, the taming [mudrā], the vajra, the trident, and the battle-axe;
