likewise, there are various weapons and great spears in the case of Yamāntaka.
A wise person should not quickly join with ministers who, having certainly brought about the destruction of life, would obstruct all one's vital breaths.
One who knows the mantras and tantras should employ a fierce [rite] marked by fierceness;
the mudrā employed in fierce mantras is said to be even fiercer than the fierce [rite].
Just as by those of cruel nature who practice cruel deeds,
that evil-minded person here attains various kinds of hellish suffering.
One should not perform malevolent rites against those of evil conduct using cruel mantras;
likewise, people should never bestow cruel mantras or mudrās upon anyone.
Since one must repeatedly experience undesirable results,
the practitioner of mantra then finds no happiness at all, O Krūraka.
It is proclaimed that accomplishment is seen to be threefold.
The *iṣṭa* sacrifice is dependent on the desired fruit;
therefore, one should avoid performing the *iṣṭa* in the case of cruel rites.
That best of sages is a yogi;
the song of the Conqueror is devoid of cruel deeds.
The songs and mantras in the Vajra family are proclaimed to be of three kinds:
inferior, middling, and superior.
"The extensive exposition of mudrās and the detailed meaning of many mantras were previously taught by the supreme Victors; those which are now proclaimed here [are likewise so]."
Thus concludes the thirty-fourth chapter, the extensive section on the Great Mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, which is included within the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-seventh chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, in your *Mūlakalpa*, there is yet another mudrā that is most supremely secret."

This is the ritual procedure for the *mudrā* tantras of all [deities], esteemed by all mantras; when combined with all mantras, it accomplishes all activities, purifies the path to perfect enlightenment, destroys the paths of all worldly existence, and serves as the livelihood for all sentient beings. It fulfills longevity, health, sovereignty, and all aspirations; it completes all factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); it brings satisfaction to all sentient beings; it makes fruitful the hopes and desires of all sentient beings; it performs all actions; it facilitates the success of all mantras; and it is accompanied by all *mudrās* and mantras.

Listen, Kumāra Mañjuśrī! First of all, there is the characteristic of the *uṣṇīṣa*. With both hands extended and palms joined, place the ring fingers within the palms so that each nail rests upon the other; the little fingers are concealed by the tips of the thumbs and joined at their points like needles; likewise, the middle fingers have their nails and tips touching at the middle; and the index fingers are shaped like needles, radiating light on all sides. This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) named the *Uṣṇīṣa-mahālakṣaṇa*.
And there is a mantra for this: ĀḤ MAḤ HAṂ.
Having moved those same index fingers, one should touch nail to nail.
This is the Great Dharma-Wheel Mudrā called "the Burning Away of the Arrows of Evil Views and Perversions" by means of needle-like [finger-tips] in the form of a circle.

And here the mantra is: *Oṃ dhuna pātaya chinda cakre vajriṇi hūṃ samayiravo*. This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) named Vajravīrā, who rests upon the four Māras as her seat, shaking the great earth and the afflictions (*kleśa*), with the forefinger and ring finger extended. And here the mantra is: *Oṃ vajrānani hūṃ phaṭ*.
But when the mudrās and mantras are joined together in all ritual actions,
all obstacles are indeed destroyed, just as clouds are by autumn.
Whatever obstacles created by the four Māras, as well as those involving gods and asuras,
are indeed destroyed the moment this supreme mudrā is seen.
Aiming at an equal distance from the side, with the third finger extended and the tips of the fingers slightly contracted, this auspicious fist is known as the Tathāgatī.
The great mudrā for the three worlds is named Mahāmaheśvaragabhastimālinī;
and the mantra for this is: oṃ vijaye haḥ.
There is also the Tathāgatamuṣṭi mudrā.

Having bound any one of these mudrās with both hands, whether at the time of practice or during the preliminary service, one should recite it once and then chant as much as desired while either seated or standing.
In this way, all obstacles and impediments find no opportunity to enter,
and accomplishment becomes manifest.
Having moved those same index fingers so that their tips are joined above the middle fingers, one forms the Udgatoṣṇīṣa mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ jvalojjvala dīptodgatoṣṇīṣa dhuna dhuna hūṃ.
Moving those same index fingers so that they are always touching the tips of the nails of the middle fingers, this mudrā, shaped like a ring with bent ankles, is the White Parasol Uṣṇīṣa.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ ma ma ma ma hūṃ niḥ.
Raising those same two index fingers equally upward from there and joining them with the middle fingers forming a needle, this is the Tejorāśi mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ tathāgatoṣṇīṣa anavalokitamūrdhni tejorāśi hūṃ jvala jvala eka eka dara vidara cchinda bhinda hūṃ hūṃ sphaṭ sphaṭ svāhā.
Those same [fingers], with the middle fingers joined at their tips like a needle and the index fingers forming a circle, constitute the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: Oṃ jayoṣṇīṣa jvala jvala bandha bandha dama dama ṅraṃ ṅraṃ ṅraṃ haḥ hana hūṃ; these are the Jayoṣṇīṣa mantras.
By moving that same index finger so that its tip is joined with the third part above the nail of the middle finger, this is the *cakravartin* mudrā.

Oṃ, homage to the invincible Tathāgata Uṣṇīṣa, whose crown is unobservable; O Cakravartin, hūṃ! Blaze, blaze! Burn, burn! Shake, shake! Tremble! Terrify! Slay! Destroy! Strike, strike! Aṃ aṃ aḥ aḥ kaḥ kaḥ! Proṃkhini proṃkhini! Kuṇḍalini! Wielder of the unconquerable weapon, hūṃ phaṭ!

Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they are joined at the third part below the nail of the middle finger-tips is the mudrā for the Cakravartin of the Lord of Mantras. Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they are joined below the nail of the [middle] finger-tips is the mudrā for the Lord of Mantras.
Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they are joined between the nail and the joint of the middle finger-tips is the mudrā for the Mahācakravartin.
Moving the tips of those very index fingers so that they are joined below the third joint of the needle-like middle fingers in a circular shape is the mudrā for the Great Cakravartin.

Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they are joined between the two joints of the needle-like middle fingers at the third joint is the mudrā for the Great Cakravartin, the Lord of Mantras.

Moving the tips of those same index fingers so that they are bent at the three joints like a hook and joined below the middle joint of the needle-like middle fingers by means of the third joint is the heart-mudrā of Aparājita-uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin.
And the mantra for this occasion is: oṃ aparājitā dhik.

One should perform all rites by means of the Uṣṇīṣamūla-mudrā or any other [mudrā], arranged with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*). One should effect the invocation (*āvāhana*) by moving the tips of the thumbs and stroking the ring fingers upward.

And the mantra for this is: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya ehi ehi bhagavan dharmarāja pratīccha idam arghyaṃ gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ dhūpaṃ balyaṃ dīpaṃ ca / māṃ cābhirakṣa apratihatabalaparākramāya svāhā //*

The invocation is performed with white flowers; then, in one's own form, the offerings of arghya, pādya, ācamanīya, and the seating upon the throne are presented. Thereafter, with this very [mantra], one should bind [the deity] in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, below, and above.
One should wipe those same two ring fingers with the tips of the thumbs, then bend them;
touching the middle joint, one should lift them up.
With the water for dismissal (*visarjanārghya*), one should rotate [the vessel] counter-clockwise for one's own deity.
The mudrās for binding the directions become released.

And here is the mantra: "Homage to the Unassailable Uṣṇīṣa! Go, go, Blessed One, King of Dharma! Accept from me this water for honor, perfume, flower, and incense, and protect me, O you of unassailable strength and prowess!
This is the mudrā for the dismissal with the offering of the mantra.

Those same two index fingers, joined at their third joints below the needle-like middle fingers, with the thumbs together with the little fingers forming a tightly clenched fist, constitute the "needle-like middle fingers" (*madhyamasūcyau*).

And here is the mantra for this: *namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya om om hrauṃ bandha hūṃ phaṭ / apratihatoṣṇīṣa tejorāśe* (Homage to the Blessed One, the Unconquerable Uṣṇīṣa! Om Om Hrauṃ! Bind! Hūṃ Phaṭ! O Unconquerable Uṣṇīṣa, Mass of Splendor!).
The mudrās and mantras are employed for all bindings and so forth; they are effective for all ritual actions.
Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent, slightly touching the third joint of the needle-like middle finger, form the *vikaraṇoṣṇīṣa* mudrā.

And here is the mantra for it: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya vikaraṇa dhuna dhuna hūṃ vikaraṇoṣṇīṣaḥ*. This *vikaraṇoṣṇīṣa*, the Great King of Vidyās belonging to the Blessed One, the Lord of Vidyās, is employed in all rites within the *Uṣṇīṣa-tantra*: in the destruction of all obstacles and *vināyakas*, in consecrations, self-protection, the binding of the directions, the binding of the maṇḍala, and so forth.

Those same two index fingers, with their tips opened and slightly bent, moved and drawn back, constitute the invocation of Agni; subsequently, one performs the oblation. This very same gesture constitutes the dismissal when the index fingers are spread apart; it is the Jvālāmālinī-uṣṇīṣa-mudrā.
It is unimpeded in all ritual actions.
And the mantra for this is: Homage to the Blessed One, the Unconquerable Uṣṇīṣa! Come, come, O Tejomaṇḍala, to Agni, svāhā!
Those same two index fingers, with their tips bent, are joined at the third joint of the middle finger—between the joints of the middle finger—to form the *balotkaṭoṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
And here is the mantra for this: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya, imaṃ gandhaṃ puṣpaṃ dhūpaṃ baliṃ dīpaṃ ca pratīccha hara hara sarvabuddhādhiṣṭhite dharmarājāpratihātāya svāhā*.

Regarding the mantra for perfumes and so forth: with the ring fingers reversed, the third fingers joined, and the index fingers in the shape of a needle upon the thumbs—this is the Vajratejoṣṇīṣa mudrā.
It is unassailable by all Vināyakas. With this, one should effect the subjugation of companions as well as of directions and times.
Thus, by means of these mantras and mudrās, protection should be performed during the time of recitation, during the time of practice, and also within the maṇḍala; all rites should be carried out.
And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvavighnavidhvaṃsanakarāya troṭaya svāhā*.

The *Aparājitoṣṇīṣa-mudrā* is formed by placing the thumbs at the base of the two ring fingers in a circular shape, while the two index fingers are likewise shaped like needles; it is unimpeded everywhere.
The mantra for this is: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya sarvatrāparājitāya samaye śānte dānte dharmarājabhāṣite mahāvidye sarvārthasādhani svāhā*.
With this, one should perform rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and prosperity (*pauṣṭika*), such as oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta-homa*).
When the two index fingers are bent at their tips and pressed against the ring finger and the two little fingers, this is the *Aparājitā-uṣṇīṣa* mudrā.
And here is the mantra for it: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣa oṃ śaṅkare svāhā*.
It provides protection in all rites.

The tips of the two thumbs are pressed against the third joints of the two ring fingers; likewise, the two index fingers [are joined] as a needle. This is the Vajrāpratihatasaṃmayoṣṇīṣa mudrā, which is common to all samayas.
And the mantra for this is: *namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya / oṃ saṅkare samayaṃ svāhā*.

The two thumbs are placed between the middle joints of the ring fingers; the index fingers are bent at their tips and joined to the middle joints of the middle fingers like needles. This is the Unobstructed Great Samaya Uṣṇīṣa Mudrā, which is employed among gods and asuras when established in the samaya.
And here is the mantra: *Namo bhagavate apratihatoṣṇīṣāya om śaṅkare mahāsamayaṃ svāhā*.
Having performed the binding of the maṇḍala with this, one should recite [the mantra] over even a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), saying: "Abide, abide in the samaya!"
One also surpasses other wheel-turning kings;
by performing the recitation in that very place, one can unimpededly and mutually cause the destruction of the power and strength of all mundane and supramundane mantras.
This applies to all reciters in a single location.
There are thus innumerable such Uṣṇīṣa Kings;
the entire family of all Tathāgatas should be described in detail.
For here, Mañjuśrī, in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), there are immeasurable mantras and various forms of mudrās;
I shall speak of them in brief.
If I were to explain it in detail, it would be impossible for all humans and non-humans to grasp or retain it, even in the span of a thousand eons.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, I shall speak in brief; listen attentively to this summary.
First, O Sage, the preeminent mudrā of the Heart is taught here;
thereafter, indeed, is the mudrā of the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), the God beyond gods.
Then the mudrās of the wise Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvaracandra and of Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the yakṣas, are proclaimed.
Then [he taught] the other great mudrās of immeasurable power,
as well as all the hosts of male and female messengers (dūta-dūtī), and likewise the supreme male and female servants (ceṭa-ceṭī).
Yakṣas and yakṣīs, as well as gods and goddesses, likewise nāgas and nāgīs, and others; and kiṅkaras and kiṅkarīs, and piśācas and piśācīs.
[She is] the one of great supernatural power among the rākṣasīs, as well as among other celestial women,
the wives of the daityas, and all the siddhas and vidyādharas.
The mudrās for all non-human beings, as well as for all humans, have been taught individually— those that emerge from birth within the three worlds for all living creatures.
The mantras, moreover, are of various forms and are effective for diverse rites;
in royal lineages as well as in noble lineages, their mudrās are each distinct.
For Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, both mudrās bring about auspicious results;
for all Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages, [the same applies].
The mudrā and the heart-mantra are each proclaimed for the divine yakṣa family, which is worshipped by ṛṣis and gandharvas.
In the seventh family, it is said that the mudrā relies upon the Gandharvas;
likewise, in the eighth family, the mudrā is proclaimed from the families.
All mudrās have been fully explained, as well as others called by the name of the Sugata,
each belonging to their respective mantras, both worldly and Buddhist.
A mantra accompanied by a mudrā becomes radiant in ritual activities;
the Vināyakas do not follow after one who is skilled in the casting of mudrās and other such rites.
Now, indeed, follows the definition of these [mudrās], beginning with the Mahāmudrā.
It is the definition of the Heart-mudrā of the Blessed Buddhas:
having interlaced the fingers of both hands with one another, one should show the two thumbs.

This is the heart-seal (*hṛdayamudrā*) of the Tathāgatas. This very same seal becomes the seal of Padmadhara when the right thumb is shown individually. Having first formed a fist with the left hand, one should release the pair of middle fingers and extend them together on one side in the shape of a vajra.
This is the mudrā of Vajradhara.
Having lowered a single finger, this is the mudrā of the Bodhisattva Gandhahastin; raising it once again, one should form the shape of a mandala—this is the mudrā of Gajagandha.
One should bend one joint of both [fingers];
this is the mudrā for the Maṇikula.
One should employ it with the very mantras of all the jewel-walkers (maṇicarāḥ), such as Jambhala, Jalendra, and others.
The two index fingers, with their two joints bent and their nails joined to one another—
this is the mudrā for the Yakṣa family, for the five [classes] and other Yakṣas of great supernatural power.
One should hold the thumbs with their nails joined to one another above the [other] nails.

In the same manner, having formed the hands as before, one should raise the pair of middle fingers and form them into the shape of a needle; this is the mudrā of all the gods, the celestial dwellers of the divine family beginning with Akaniṣṭha. Again, in the same way, having restrained the hands and formed a fist, one should show the two thumbs;
this is the mudrā of the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas.
Thus, these eight mudrās are encompassed by the eight families;
however, a single mudrā for all the sons of the Victors shall now be described.
With the palms joined and extended, then slightly contracted again—
this is declared to be the mudrā of the most exalted Bodhisattvas.
The wish-fulfilling gem, the staff, the monastic robe, the alms bowl,
and the hand holding the fangs and the gesture of fearlessness— these seven are the mudrās of the Sage.
The Sugata’s abiding state is the web of light-rays of the loving-kindness of vision, adorned with teeth and a tuft of hair;
this too is that supreme seal of the Jina, born from his own body.
These two groups of seven and these five mudrās have been remembered by me;
together with the heart-mantra of the Sage, they are said to be twenty by the self-arisen ones and others.
Indeed, these mudrās were previously taught by the primordial Jinas;
the retinue of the Cakravartin was declared to consist of twenty,
and the supreme mudrās and mantras are established according to that number.
Having raised [the hands] and coiled them, this is the *cintāmaṇi-mudrā*.
Holding the fists at the shoulder region on the left and right while in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*),
it becomes the *khakharaka-mudrā*.
With the two hands joined together facing each other, it becomes the *saṅghāṭī-mudrā*.
The bowl is held with the hands joined as a support; the robe is held by the left hand. For the *daṃṣṭrā* (fang) heart-mudrā, one left thumb is raised.

The *abhaya-hasta* (fearless hand) is inclined in the gesture of fearlessness, with the robe hanging from the left side. In the *abhaya-hasta*, within the joined palms, one should place the two middle fingers and the two thumbs outside, with the index fingers bent inward.

This is the Buddha-locana mudrā. This same [mudrā], when the index fingers are bent at the first joint and joined together on one side, is the Buddha-maitrī. Having formed the añjali with the fingers spread apart, one should conceal the index and ring fingers by means of the three needles.
The *māmakī* mudrā is as follows:

having formed the *añjali*, one should bend the third joints of the index and middle fingers outward and join them; the two thumbs are held separately in the shape of fingers—this is the *bhogavatī* mudrā.
With the left hand, the index and middle fingers constitute *vijayā*.
With the right [hand], one should hold a three-finger-width vajra at the region of the waist.
In the same way, having personally bound the Vidyārāja-mudrā upon one's own head, one should perform all rites with the eight great mudrās;
or one should scatter flowers at the time of the samaya or within the maṇḍala;
or one should act according to the previously prescribed rule or by this [present] method.
One may cause all rites to be performed according to one's desire.
The pledges (samaya) expressed by the vidyās and mantras become empowered by the mudrās; they possess the power of the mudrās.
If one should suddenly bind a mudrā in an inappropriate place, that itself constitutes a breach of his pledge.
That which is a vajra is a trident;
there is no difference between a trident and a vajra.
That which is positioned upward becomes the mudrā of Vajradhara.

And below that of Maheśvara is the middle [level], which is for the preceptor, the teacher, those worthy of offerings, and all human beings. When one finger is raised, it is the mudrā for all human beings—beings established in the various states of bipeds, quadrupeds, many-legged creatures, and legless beings. When two fingers are raised, it is the mudrā for all yakṣas and yakṣīs.

With the hands raised three finger-widths apart, it is the mudrā of all the vidyādharas and vidyādharīs. With the hands raised four finger-widths apart and placed with palms level, it is the mudrā of the women of the gods and asuras. With the hands joined in the gesture of añjali and positioned in a beautiful form, it is the mudrā of all the gods who dwell in the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Those same hands [held] as they are constitute the mudrā for the gods who dwell in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Those same hands, formed into hollow cupped palms with the fists clenched, constitute the mudrā for all beings dwelling in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), beginning with the Lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātveśvara*) and including humans, animals, hungry ghosts (*preta*), and those belonging to the world of Yama.
Releasing a single finger from that very same mudrā constitutes the mudrā for all *piśācas* and *piśācīs*.

With two fingers extended, it is for the *rākṣasa*s and *rākṣasī*s; with three fingers extended, it is for all the flesh-eaters (*kravyāda*) and so forth, including the *graha*s, *mātṛ*s, and *kūṣmāṇḍa*s, as well as for all the *piśitāśina*s and *ḍākinī*s, and the *vyantara*s and others. With all four fingers contracted, it is the *sarvakaśmalā* mudrā.
With the mudrās drawn in, there is attraction; with the mudrās raised up, there is dismissal.
One should perform all actions with one's own mind.
With these very mudrās, one should employ each respective mantra according to one's desire;
one should not employ others nor perform other rites. One should apply each [mantra] to that specific purpose for which it was intended.
For these mudrās are not to be transgressed, being empowered by all the Buddhas;
indeed, no sentient beings whatsoever are able to provoke them even upon seeing the mudrās.
By transgressing the mudrās, they meet with destruction;

from the destruction of the mudrās comes the violation of the *samaya* and the neglect of all vidyās, resulting ultimately in rebirth in the Raurava hell or the great Avīci hell—those who create obstacles experience this most intensely. However, for those who abide by the *mudrā-samaya*, there is long-lasting and abundant happiness, rebirth among the great gods, and at the end of their course, they will certainly be destined for awakening.
In brief, many varieties of mudrās have been revealed by the primordial Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power;
it is impossible to reach their limit, to calculate their number,
or for all sentient beings to master them.
In brief, within the family of the Victors, there is a single-syllable sovereign king of vidyās; for the sake of protection, it possesses its own mudrā.
First, having formed fists with both the left and right hands, one should extend the pair of middle fingers together;
then, one should bend one joint of both [middle fingers].
The pair of index fingers, bent at two joints and with their nails joined to one another, should be held above the nails of the thumbs.
This Cakravartin mudrā, the most excellent of all mantras, has been taught by the Protectors of the World as being effective for all rites.

When joined with the previously mentioned One-Syllable Cakravartin, it becomes effective for all rites. Once this has been accomplished, the entire Tathāgata family and all mundane and supramundane mantras become perfected.
By the recitation of this, all mantras become recited.
Furthermore, the practitioner must necessarily first perform eight thousand recitations of this supreme mantra proclaimed in this King of Rituals (*kalparāja*).
In this way, all these vidyās become manifest before one, swiftly bestow accomplishment,
and quickly grant boons.
One who is destined for enlightenment certainly performs all rites when joined with the single-syllable heart-mantra of Avalokiteśvara and the lotus-holding mudrā.

Or, joined with the vidyā or mudrā of Pāṇḍaravāsinī, one likewise performs all rites. Joined with the mudrā of Vajradhara and his very same single-syllable heart-mantra, one likewise performs all rites.
Or by means of the Mahāvidyā of Māmakī.

Thus, in the Royal Family, one should perform all rites with the single-syllable heart-mantra of the Bodhisattva Rājagandha and with its corresponding mudrā. Likewise, in the Jewel Family, the Yakṣa Family, the Divine, and the Noble families, all rites should be performed here with their respective single-syllable heart-mantras and those very mudrās.
In this manner, everywhere, all rites should be performed with all mudrās and all mantras.
One should apply the empowerment of the power of the vidyā-mantras according to the appropriate method.
Ritual duties should not be performed by anyone other than [the prescribed person].

Thus, the *svasti* gesture raised with the right hand is for the Brāhmaṇa Sahāmpati; the *ekaliṅga-mudrā* is for Maheśvara; the *cakra-mudrā* is for Viṣṇu; the *añjali* with fingers slightly spread apart is for Garuḍa; likewise, the hand gesture raised as if to cast a curse is for the Ṛṣis; likewise, for the Gandharvas, along with the Suras and Asuras, the gesture is showing the left hand with the thumb placed inside the palm and resting on the hip—this is the *catuḥkumārya-mudrā*, performed with that same mantra. Likewise, the *śakti-mudrā* is for Kārttikeya. In this manner, the mudrās have been prescribed for all beings residing in the three worlds, included within all realms of existence, and dependent upon the realm of sentient beings—including Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Mahoragas, and so forth, as well as all the planets, Mātṛs, Kravyādas, Kaśmalas, and others.
And the mantras should be applied from all sides in proper sequence and order; everything comes about from this way alone, and not otherwise.

First of all, the practitioner, relying upon the auspicious Tathāgata-gati Mahāmudrā and its associated mantras from this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), as well as the mudrās of the Noble Samantabhadra, Mahāsthānaprāpta, Vimalagati, and yours, Mañjuśrī—the Utpala-mudrā—and the mudrās of these other Bodhisattvas, must, having risen at dawn, being pure, standing in a clean place, facing east toward the sun, bind one of these mudrās and cast it upward above his own head.
One should recite any one of these mantras one hundred and eight times;
one will become completely freed from all diseases,
attain long life, and will not be overcome by any obstacles.
One becomes invincible to all beings;
all mantras appear before one,
and they swiftly bestow accomplishment.
He becomes empowered by all the Buddhas;
he becomes destined for enlightenment with certainty;
and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta becomes his spiritual friend until he reaches the seat of awakening.
And what are those mudrās and mantras?
First, the Mahāvīra-mudrā will be explained.

Having joined the two hands in a hollowed gesture (*sampuṭa*), with the fingers interlaced and the thumbs raised, bent at the third joint like a mountain peak—this is the Mahāvīra-mudrā as proclaimed by all the Tathāgatas.
And here is the mantra: ĀḤ VĪRAṂ HŪṂ KHAṂ.
Combined with this mantra, this mudrā performs all rites.

Having formed those same two hands into a hollowed cup (*sampuṭa*), one should again open them with the fingers so that they are fully expanded all around in the form of a vajra; this is the supreme mudrā called *Vikāsinī*, revealed by the primordial Buddhas.
And here is the mantra: *oṃ gaganasambhave dīpta dīpta jvālaya jvālaya buddhādhiṣṭhite vikāśaya vikāśaya sarvabuddhān | hūṃ hūṃ vikāsini phaṭ phaṭ svāhā*.
This is the Vikāsinī mudrā.
When joined with this mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites;
it brings about understanding for those possessed by planetary spirits.

It causes one seized by a planetary spirit to speak; it accomplishes everything exactly as it is employed for those seized by the defilement of carnivorous spirits or those who have fainted from poison.
This is, in brief, the vidyā that accomplishes all aims; when joined with the vidyā-expanding mudrā, even if not yet perfected, it swiftly effects the desired purpose.
Having formed a hollowed cavity with both hands, making the fingers level within, this is the heart-mudrā.
Having consecrated the heart [of the image] seven times with the heart-mantra, it should be released;
this applies in all cases.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ godare vīra svāhā*.
The Heart of the Tathāgata.
That same hand-cupped gesture, with the fingers interlaced so that there is a hollow space between all the tips and middle joints of the fingers, is the uṣṇīṣa mudrā.
And here is the mantra: oṃ droṃ bandha svāhā. This is effective for all rites.
Having formed a fist with the right hand while leaving the thumb free, this is the *khakharaka* mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ dhunājitaraṇa hūṃ*.
This *khakharaka* mantra is effective for all rites.
Having joined this very mudrā and placed the left hand holding the robe [in it], this is the robe-mudrā.
And here is the mantra: Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa, O my robe empowered by all the Buddhas, svāhā!
This is the Tathāgata-robe.
By means of this very mudrā, one performs all rites. Having consecrated his robe with this mantra, he should wear it; he becomes fortunate, and great protection is established for him.
All the grahas, mātṛs, flesh-eaters, carnivores, and malevolent spirits, as well as all obstacles, flee upon merely being seen.
Having joined the left thumb and the right little finger together, holding them below as a support for the hollowed palms is the bowl mudrā (*pātramudrā*).
The mantra for this is: *oṃ lokapālādhiṣṭhita dhara dhāraya mahānubhāva buddhapātra svāhā*.
This mantra, when conjoined with this very mudrā, performs all rites; it should be recollected at the time of eating.
All poisons, even those of the *garuḍa*, have no power over them.
With the two hands joined in fists, the two index fingers are bent at the middle joints;
this is the Cintāmaṇi mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ tejo jvala sarvārthasādhaka sidhya sidhya cintāmaṇiratna hūṃ.
The wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇiratna*).
When conjoined with this very mudrā, it performs all auspicious rites.
Having empowered various excellent ornaments and decorations with this, one should bind them upon oneself; thus, great protection is established.
He becomes supremely fortunate;
having adorned himself and empowered the Dharma with mantras, he may enter into battle, and no weapon shall fall upon his body.
He becomes invincible to all enemies.
He protects his own army and attacks the enemy's army.
One performs these and other such immeasurable rites even while remaining unaccomplished.

Having taken any one of the precious gems, such as a ruby or an emerald, and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with mantras, one should fasten it to the top of a banner, upon one's own head, or on the neck of an elephant when entering the front lines of battle;
then, surely, upon merely seeing it, the enemy army will break without even fighting.
Either great paralysis occurs,
or their armies are broken and their leaders flee in retreat.

Having formed fists with the fingers interlocked, and having bent the two index fingers at their middle joints so that they rest upon the position of the middle fingers, this is the Dharmacakra mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: *oṃ chinda bhinda hana daha dīpta cakra hūṃ dharmacakra*.
With the left foot extended and the right knee placed on the ground, the left hand is stretched back while the right hand, with a *huṃ* sound, strikes with force;
this is the Aparājita mudrā.
And here is the mantra: *oṃ hulu hulu caṇḍāli mātaṅgi svāhā*.
The Aparājitā Dharmacakra is the Aparājitā mantra.
When joined with these very mudrās, it becomes effective for all rites.
In brief, it cuts through all sufferings.
In whatever manner they are employed, in that very manner they perform all activities.
Placing the hand likewise upon the lap of the braid with the right hand in the gesture of teaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanāhasta*), there is the *tathāgataśaktimudrā*.
And here is the mantra: *oṃ vijaye mahāśakti durdhari hūṃ phaṭ vijayini phaṭ maṅgale phaṭ*.
This is the *tathāgataśakti*.
When joined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites;
it paralyzes all obstacles, all malevolent beings, all enemies, and even all gods.
This [mudrā] possesses boundless qualities; in whatever way it is employed, in that same way it accomplishes all activities.

In the same manner, with both hands turned upward, the fingers interlaced, and the tips of the two index fingers joined in the shape of a needle, one should place them inverted and facing downward upon the forehead.
This is the Ūrṇā-mudrā, revealed by the primordial Buddhas for the Blessed Buddhas.
And the mantra for this is: *namaḥ sarvatathāgatebhyo ’rhadbhyaḥ samyaksaṃbuddhebhyaḥ*.
He he! Bind, bind! Stay, stay! Hold, hold! Restrain, restrain! *ūrṇāmaṇi* svāhā!
This is the mantra of the Tathāgata’s *ūrṇā*.
When joined with this very mudrā, it becomes effective for all rites.
Having made a tilaka on the forehead with gorocanā, one should enter into the midst of enemies while reciting the mantra;
one becomes unassailable and is not harmed by any wicked beings.
Or he may enter the midst of battle;
having seen the breaking of the enemy army, he acts,
but not without seeing it— he performs immeasurable deeds.
And it has been spoken by immeasurable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Having formed a continuous añjali with the fingers interlocked, one should bend the two index fingers toward each other at their middle joints, and likewise the two thumbs.
This is the Tathāgatalocanā mudrā.
And the mantra for this is: oṃ ru ru sphuru jvala tiṣṭha siddhalocane sarvārthasādhani svāhā.
This *tathāgatalocanā* mantra, when joined with this very mudrā, becomes effective for all rites. Having consecrated one's eyes with it, one may enter into the midst of enemies;
upon merely being seen, they become free from anger.

Those with a mind of loving-kindness become seekers of welfare and attain friendship. Or, having consecrated one's eyes at the front of a battle, if one gazes upon the enemy army, they will become peaceful-minded.
Being unable to strike back, they retreat without even fighting;
at least, they provide assistance.
Both hands are likewise formed with the fingers shaped like a book, their tips joined together and held horizontally.
This is the *mudrā* of Prajñāpāramitā.
And here is the mantra: *namo bhagavati cārudarśane oṃ tha*.
This Blessed Prajñāpāramitā, when conjoined with this very mudrā, becomes effective for all rites.
While reciting the mantra, one should touch the heart; one will then become possessed of mindfulness.
Reciting it in the midst of wicked enemies, one steals away their minds.
In the midst of battle, she deludes two-legged and four-legged beings, as well as adversaries,
or causes their minds to become distracted; in short,
this Blessed Lady performs all activities exactly according to how she is employed.
In brief, his qualities are boundless and his eon is likewise boundless.
The seals (*mudrā*) and mantras of the Tathāgatas are also boundless; as stated in the *Sannipātaparivarta*, all the retinues of the Tathāgatas should be employed here as seals and mantras.
Furthermore, there are incalculable eons;
the mudrās and mantras should be employed in this King of Ritual Manuals (kalparāja).
Thus, in the Lotus family, she is accompanied by the lotus mudrā.
The mantra is: Oṃ jiḥ jiḥ jināṅgabhṛdbhayabhedine svāhā.
This mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, when joined with the lotus mudrā, is effective for all rites.
By the recitation of this, the entire Lotus Family is recited;
by the accomplishment of this, the entire Lotus Family is accomplished—
whether by means of Pāṇḍaravāsinī or the Great Vidyā.
And here is the mantra: *Oṃ kaṭe vikaṭe nikaṭe kaṭaṅkaṭe kaṭavikaṭakaṭaṅkaṭe svāhā*. One should employ it with the mudrā alone, or with the lotus-mudrā; it becomes effective for all rites.
Furthermore, protection must be performed by one who has gone to any cremation ground.

Thus, one should employ all the innumerable [deities] of the Lotus Family—such as Tārā, Bhrukuṭī, Candrā, and Hayagrīva—as described in the chapter on the Assembly of the Vidyārājas, together with their mudrās, mantras, and extensive ritual manuals.
Thus, the Dhvaja family is accompanied by both [the hand gesture and] the vajra-mudrā;
and the mantra here is: HŪṂ. This is Vajrapāṇi himself; when this is accomplished, the entire Vajra family becomes accomplished.
By reciting this, everything becomes recited.
When joined with the previously described double-vajra mudrā, it performs all rites according to the practitioner’s wish—
even those that are contradictory to the supreme Victors— by virtue of the necessity of training sentient beings.
This great yakṣī is exceedingly fierce; she performs all rites through the great vidyā of Māmakī or Kulandharī.
And here is the mantra: *Oṃ kulandhari bandha bandha hūṃ phaṭ*.

This great vidyā named Māmakī, which accomplishes all rites, has been taught by all the Buddhas; when joined with the previously prescribed mudrā of the great vidyā of Māmakī, it becomes effective for all rites.

In this introductory chapter on the practitioner’s desire, as previously described, the entire Vajra family, without exception, along with its retinue headed by Vajrapāṇi, should be employed here through the conjunctions of mudrās and mantras.
Thus, the mantra of the Bodhisattva Gajagandha of the Elephant Family is: *oṃ gajāhvaye hūṃ khacare svāhā*.
When joined with the previously described mudrā, it is effective for all rites.
In this manner, as before, the entire Elephant Family becomes accomplished.
Thus is the mantra of Samantabhadra: oṃ samāsamajinasuta mā vilamba hūṃ phaṭ.
The mantra for one who has attained the Great Station: Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha mahāsthāne gatabodhaḥ samayamanusmara hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
The mantra for Vimalagati is: oṃ vimale vimale vimala muhūrtaṃ dhaka dhaka samayamanusmara svāhā //
The mantra of Gaganagañja, when combined with the mudrā of all bodhisattvas, becomes effective for all rites.

There are also innumerable mudrās and mantras belonging to these countless great bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages, such as Apāyajaha, Sadāprarudita, Kṣitigarbha, Ratnapāṇi, Maitreya, and others;
they are to be employed in this King of Rituals (Kalparāja).

The extensive nature, the state of being superior to all worldly and transcendent realms, the detailed ritual manuals for all worldly mantras and mudrās, and all conceptualizations that have entered into the great samaya and non-samaya—all these have been explained here, as well as all those mantras to be accomplished here.
In this same way, they should also be applied within the Jewel family, the Yakṣa family, and the divine Noble family.
All the mantras and mudrās of all tantras, though based upon the three times, constitute only one single family and no other; that is to say, the Tathāgata family.
And you, Mañjuśrī Kumāra, are to be seen as belonging to the Tathāgata family.

"Understand, Mañjuśrī, that all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, as well as all mundane and supramundane mantras—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—and all mudrās and conceptualizations have entered the Tathāgata family.
There exists nothing, Mañjuśrī, among the secrets of all mudrā-tantras and mantras that has not entered the Tathāgata family and the Tathāgata’s samaya.
Understand, O Youthful Mañjuśrī, that it has indeed been entered."
Because the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme, therefore the family of the Tathāgata is declared to be supreme.

"In that case, Mañjuśrī, this King of Rituals and this Supreme Jewel of the Family was revealed, taught, established, and elucidated by the primordial Buddhas: by the Blessed One Saṃkusumitarāja, the Blessed One Śālarājendra, the Blessed One Saṅkusumitagandhottamarāja, the Blessed One Ratnaketu, the Blessed One Amitābha, the Blessed One Puṇyābha, Kusumottama, Saṅkusuma, Supuṣpa, Amitāyurjñānaviniścayarājendra, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, Krakutsanda, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, and the Blessed One Konākamuni."
I too have now revealed it, as was revealed by Śākyamuni, and they shall be revealed [by others] in the future.

Thus it is that this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), O Mañjuśrī Kumāra, has come down through the succession of Buddhas; it is the foremost jewel of the Tathāgata family, possessing great benefits, certain, and based upon the Dharmadhātu. It is impossible to describe its benefits even in a thousand eons, nor can its vast expansion of great qualities be told in detail, whether by all sentient beings or to hear them. For those like you, such immeasurable results arise from the vast expansion of its great qualities, pertaining both to the present life and to future lives.

Whoever, being free from doubt regarding the *śrāddha*, should uphold or recite this tantra with application and without conceptualization— whether they practice the mantra, chant it, or even bind the mudrā— and remains constantly devoted to it,
will, in this very life, obtain eight qualities and benefits.
He shall become unassailable by all adversaries.
Moreover, no fear arises within him;
poison does not affect his body,
and weapons do not fall upon his body.
He becomes blessed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he becomes long-lived, happy, and wise; and Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta becomes his virtuous friend.
At night, they grant him a sign through a vision in a dream;
all mantras protect him,
and they reveal the mudrās to him in his dreams.
He becomes invulnerable to Duṣṭarāṣṭra and to those wicked beings who seek his harm;
he is certain to have enlightenment as his ultimate goal.

These eight benefits are to be seen for one who has faith, is free from doubt, and is diligent—whether they be a householder or one who has gone forth, a woman or a man, and those great beings who assist in the teaching. They do not belong to others who are engaged in evil deeds; for such as these, there is a perverted state below in the Raurava hell and other such places.
As it was stated previously— that the binding of mudrās in the forenoon brings long life and victory—
one should honor the mudrās such as the Heart-Uṣṇīṣa and the Ālocanā with the retinue of the Tathāgata mantras.
O Mañjuśrī Kumāra, for these are indeed equal in potency and equal in power to your own mudrās and mantras.
Regarding what was said— that one who is pure should stand in a pure place—
the place is a central area of ground, free from thorns or obstacles, smeared with fallen cow dung, and strewn with fragrant white flowers;
standing there, one should recite the mantra.
One should form the mudrā; one should recite [the mantra] together with the mudrā, neither elsewhere nor for others, but for one [deity] alone.

As for what was said regarding "being pure": when the sun has set, one should bathe with pure water that is free of living organisms; wearing fresh garments, having performed protection by means of a turban, avoiding sexual intercourse, and being devoted to purity, cleanliness, and guarding [the senses], one is auspicious.
Having performed protection with the *uṣṇīṣa* and following the binding of the wheel,
one should meditate there upon the Tathāgatas during the watch of the night that has passed in a dream.

Taking a thread spun by a maiden or by a Brahmin woman who has not yet experienced sexual intercourse, one should empower it one hundred and eight times with this mantra: *oṃ hara hara bandha bandha śukradhāraṇi siddhārthe svāhā*. One should recite the mantra while employing the Māmakī mudrā. Then, having wound the thread three times around the waist, one binds it; thus the retention of semen is accomplished.

Even the Lord of the Desire Realm is capable of producing mental distress in a dream; how much more so, then, the obstructors of dreams? Even the daughters of a seer who is the Lord of the Desire Realm—whether he possesses passion or is free from passion—are unable to produce mental distress through improper means, even for those who have passion, though they may assume various forms. It is only through the proper ritual that this occurs, not otherwise. Furthermore, the daughters of a seer are incapable of producing mental distress in one who is free from passion, even if they assume diverse appearances.
How much more so, then, other women, whether born of humans or non-humans?

Having thus risen at dawn according to the ritual procedure, having discarded the tooth-stick and rinsed the mouth, and having bathed with pure, living-water-free, stainless water while facing east as before, one should form the mudrā and recite the mantras. One will then become long-lived and capable of performing all rites.
One is liberated from great diseases;
one becomes beloved by all people;
and one becomes like a counter-spell (*pratyaṅgira*) to one's enemies.
As soon as it is seen, all malevolent planets, flesh-eating spirits, impurities, and the like flee away;
it paralyzes the enemy forces.
By the mere sight of it, one accomplishes all rites, whether performed with purity or impurity, according to the prescribed rules or without them.
Thus, this king of rituals is surrounded by an incalculable multitude of mudrās and mantras;
it has been spoken and will be spoken by incalculable Blessed Buddhas,
and it is now likewise spoken by me, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, in the midst of a great assembly circle.

Furthermore, Prince Mañjuśrī, you have been appointed for the sake of protecting the teaching and for the sake of long-term preservation of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). After I have passed into parinirvāṇa—when I have rested at the limit of reality (*dharmakoṭi*), reached the culmination of the limit of existence (*bhūtakoṭi*), and become stilled—you, with a mind moved by great compassion, shall speak this for the benefit of sentient beings. This King of Rituals (*kalparāja*) has been spoken by me in detail and in its various divisions for the sake of all beings, in order to restrain and discipline wicked kings and evil beings who harm the Three Jewels during the most terrifying time at the end of the age.

Thus concludes the thirty-fifth chapter, the detailed exposition on the rules and rituals for mantras and mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the thirty-eighth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsabhavana), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Listen, Mañjuśrī!"
In brief, the characteristics of the mudrās and the mantras in detail;
and in brief, the ritual procedure for the maṇḍalas and the observance of the samayas.
And among them, indeed, is the place of the mudrās;
it is the secret of all mantras, the mandala within all mantras.
All of this was previously taught by all the Buddhas of great supernatural power;
the majesty of the course of mantras has been declared across all families as well.
In the past, the primordial Buddhas, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings,
set in motion the wheel of mantras and the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Following the wheel of peace, they departed and took refuge in the limit of reality;
all those Buddhas, possessing great supernatural power in the world, attained peace.
All of this was previously proclaimed by the Tathāgatas of the past;
I too, O Mañjuśrī of noble wisdom, shall teach it in this final age.
Having performed this, Mañjughoṣa Kumāra, with palms joined in reverence before him, then spoke these words to the Buddha of great splendor:
He spoke to the Perfectly Awakened One, the best among speakers and the supreme among bipeds:
"O one of great wisdom, teach the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of the worlds."
"Thus, having been addressed regarding the concise meaning, without elaboration, concerning the arising of the fruit of the greatness of qualities, Mañjuśrī remained silent."
Then the glorious Brahmeśvara, whose voice was like the song of the kalaviṅka bird,
explained all that which is established within the mudrās and the maṇḍala.
At that time, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men, standing above the Pure Abodes, proclaimed the mantra and the tantra.
Listen, O youth Mañjuśrī, to the origin of the ritual procedures for the mudrās,
and to the extensive greatness and qualities of the mantras and their tantric applications.
First, one should [observe] the signs of all Tathāgatas, as well as the sentient and non-sentient,
their forms, conduct, gestures, and all their bodily movements and speech.
With both hands and feet, the head, and the joining of the fingers of one hand—
all that was declared to be *mudrā* by the ancient primordial Buddhas.
The water-pot, the parasol, as well as the lotus, the banner, and likewise the flag;
the fish, the thunderbolt, as well as the conch, the jar, and likewise the wheel.
Whatever various weapons are renowned in the world,
they all take the form of the utpala-lotus seal within this mandala of seals.
Standing here in successive order, these are likewise declared according to the prescribed rule;
one should always draw all of them with forms and essential natures that are identical.
Having stated that "the mudrā is in the maṇḍala," those mudrās are proclaimed as being properly arranged in their respective places throughout all the common [maṇḍalas].
In all mandalas indeed, one should apply one's own form;
likewise, the Wheel-turner [should apply] the wheel in the white emergence at the uṣṇīṣa.
One should draw the white parasol as the primary [symbol] in the mandala;
likewise, the wheel of Dharma for the Buddhas and the lotus for the Lotus family.
The vajra is prescribed for the Vajra family, the elephant for those born of the Gaja family,
and likewise, one should employ the pitcher in the Maṇi family throughout the entire mandala.
One should draw the two preeminent divine and noble families, Śrīvatsa and Svastika;
and in the most excellent Yakṣa family, one should draw the fruit arising from the fruit-bearing tree.
Having drawn a swan for Mahābrahmā, one should also draw Śakra with his vajra;
for Maheśvara, one should draw a trident and likewise draw a bull.
Having drawn the trident and the sharp-edged spear (paṭṭiśa), as well as the spear (śakti) of Skanda,
and having drawn the discus (cakra) and maces of Viṣṇu, along with the Dānavas.
One should always depict in their midst the gods with various weapons, seated upon diverse thrones, and possessing various types of vehicles.
One should draw one or another of these, appearing as a reflection with its form transferred exactly as it is, in every mandala.
The maṇḍalas taught by the supreme Victors consist of one, two, or three, and so on up to an incalculable number; they are equal in measure to the rows of their respective altars (vedikās).
One should place in the center that person for whose sake the mandala was proclaimed;
or else, one should draw a Buddha in the womb of the Jina-family, right in the very middle.
Then one should also paint the image of the Teacher situated within;
the second should be placed in the Lotus family, and the third one should paint as belonging to the Vajra family.
Having thus drawn all of them in succession— the gods and asuras,
and thereafter all beings on earth, including yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans.
Then, having drawn the heretics in their proper sequence as they are situated,
one should likewise draw the guardians of the directions and all those of various origins.
In brief, one should draw a single dot, and then from two onwards up to an incalculable number, extending the maṇḍala as far as the upper limit and pervading all directions.
Then, the surface of the earth within this mandala is indeed said to be immeasurable,
extending from a single point to the infinite reaches of the terrestrial plane.
The ritual procedure for the mandala has been proclaimed; indeed, the threefold [classification] has been specified:
namely, the superior, the middling, and the inferior have been celebrated.
In the highest [degree], the highest accomplishment is attained; in the middling, the middling is declared;
and in the lowest, the minor accomplishment—thus was it taught by the supreme Victors of old.
The supreme Victors have declared that success is threefold according to the minds [of practitioners]:
great success for those of great capacity, and middling success for those of middling capacity.
The third is for small creatures; it is taught as a minor rite.
When the mind is serene, Buddhahood arises with its supreme and fruitful manifestation.
A being who possesses a middling state of mind will certainly attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha at that time simply by beholding the maṇḍala.
The others are declared to be fixed in the state of a Śrāvaka due to their lack of respect;
yet the greatness of their fruit is not in vain, for their destiny is described as peace.
He will certainly attain heaven by not seeing the mandala;
likewise, he shall obtain all the excellent mudrās and the mantras in their full detail.
The mudrās and maṇḍalas are said to be of three kinds and three types, bringing happiness; now the benefit of the mantras is being told.
Beginning with a single syllable and extending according to the measure of the number of syllables,
as many words as are spoken in a mantra are thus proclaimed.
Idle chatter, weeping, laughter, and likewise crying,
as well as all talk and gossip, shall become beneficial for all mantras.
Those mantras are of three kinds and are declared to be of three types;
just as they are known in the mandala, so indeed are they among the mudrās and mantras.
This ritual procedure, joined together, has been taught by the leaders of the world;
in that very way, it proceeds in three ways, as well as in many ways and even in a thousand ways.
It is threefold, of three kinds, and likewise three times innumerable;
for the mantra is indeed dependent upon the mind, and there is no mantra devoid of the mind.
One who is joined with the mind-mantra and properly united will accomplish [the goal]—
those mantras which belong to the Tathāgata family as well as those which belong to the Lotus family.
And those songs which are sung in the Lotus family and in the other families by others—
all worldly mantras indeed have emerged here from them all.
The mantra which was spoken by the Jina and his sons for the sake of sentient beings— whosoever, being diligent, recites it, shall certainly become a Buddha.
Those mantras which are indeed neutral, he who recites them is declared to be a Pratyekabuddha, for he is certainly of that lineage.
Those who are indeed engaged in other mantras spoken by Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats,
as well as those worldly beings intent upon the recitation of mantras;
He will certainly be established in the lineage of the Śrāvakas of great supernatural power;
even there, one should apply effort toward the superior, the inferior, and the middling [levels].

In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), there shall be the enlightenment of a Buddha; likewise in rites for enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), the enlightenment of those who possess the sword [the Pratyekabuddhas].
By other minor mantras, however, the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka is declared.
Therein, the mind is to be observed; it is divided into three ways, and it is further divided into many ways, even into an incalculable number of divisions.

Thus concludes the thirty-sixth chapter, the detailed exposition on the ritual procedures for all activities concerning the mudrās and maṇḍala-tantra, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and having surveyed all world-systems with his Buddha-eye, beholding all sentient beings, once more addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Mañjuśrī, there exists within the extensive exposition of your mantra-tantras and mudrās that which has entered into all mundane and supramundane samaya-maṇḍalas; it is the basis for beings who have entered into the accomplishment of the general ritual procedures. Listen as I briefly explain the practice of the instruction on the treasury of all mantras, all mudrās, all maṇḍalas, and all sentient beings who have entered into all mantras, whose activities are inconceivable.
Then Mañjuśrī, the youthful prince, the bodhisattva mahāsattva, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and made this request:
"May the Sugata grant me his favor for our sake and for the benefit of the world;
that will be for the welfare, the benefit, and the happiness of a great multitude of people, and out of compassion for the world."

Therefore, O Sugata, please explain to me the procedure for entering the commitments (*samaya*), the subsequent instructions, and the methods conducive to accomplishment regarding the recitation (*japa*), fire-offerings (*homa*), nourishment (*āpyāyana*), worship (*pūjana*), and the rules (*niyama*) for all mantras, as well as for all tantric mudrās; and the detailed collection of chapters (*paṭalavisara*) concerning the specific methods, both mundane and supramundane, applicable to all maṇḍalas.
When this had been said, the Blessed One, Mañjubhāṇī, the Omniscient One, remained silent for that interval.
The wise Mañjurava, pleased and knowing the Sugata, accepted this;
and all the Buddhas, assembled everywhere throughout all realms, were present.
Indeed, all Bodhisattvas, all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
and all sentient beings of the three kinds within the beginningless wheel of existence— [all these abide] therein.
Those born of the womb who are bound and joined to the five states of existence,
as well as the presiding lords of all hosts of beings— rākṣasas, uragas, and humans.
Daityas, dānavas, and yakṣas; kūṣmāṇḍas, kaṭapūtanas, chief gods, leaders of the gaṇas, and the highly powerful mātṛs;
All the hosts of planets in the world, as well as the moon, the sun, and others;
Brahmā, Indra, Kubera, the Rudras, Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Virūḍhaka.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Kubera, all the Vasus as well,
and all beings everywhere who are dependent upon the realm of sentient beings.

Bound by the threads of their destinies through actions that yield auspicious and inauspicious fruits, they are both liberated and unliberated everywhere; having arrived at the proper time, they remain established therein.

Through the power of the Buddha’s empowerment and by means of supernatural transformation, those born from auspicious wombs and those born from inauspicious ones, established here in three ways, hear [the teaching].
Then all the Buddhas indeed heard that noble Dharma of the Sugata, which brings about the arising of supreme and auspicious qualities, in the city of Śuddhāvāsa.
It is proclaimed as being invariably endowed with the three— mantra, mudrā, and samādhi—
and it is the path of the Noble Eightfold Way, secure and most auspicious.
The threefold path of action, excellent and leading to the city of Nirvana—
generosity, ethical discipline, and meditative concentration— is thus taught as the threefold path.
The Blessed One, the All-Knowing, spoke on the setting forth of the limbs of the path of mantra;
with a slight smile upon his face, O steadfast one, look toward Mañjughoṣa.
And then, all the hosts of beings, standing there gentle and confident, heard this speech endowed with auspiciousness, which was like the sound of Brahmā.
Lest there be for you a fall from the agreement, which would be useless,
harmful, and detrimental to you for a long time, O you who do not understand the word of the Buddha.
"O child, you will fall into blind darkness and become far removed [from the goal].
These mantras and mudrās have been proclaimed for your spiritual welfare; apply them with diligence."
O worlds, you shall always perform favor and restraint;
you should consider this as being joined with my own action, for my wrath is indeed the Ender of Yama.
He will undoubtedly always exercise restraint in this age;
first, indeed, in a secluded and solitary place strewn with flowers.
Having mentally and through meditation drawn in [the deities] from all sides onto the mandala to be constructed,
the wise one should first meditate upon the lotus of all the Buddhas.
A second lotus rises, possessing the great splendor of the sun;
stationed there is the glorious Mañjuvara, marked by the form of a youth.
With five tufts of hair on his head, knees, ears, and elbows prominent,
his body covered in hair, and with palms joined in reverence, the boy questioned the Sugata, the Knower.
Speaking auspicious words in the abode of the Sugata,
one indeed [attains] the great lotus of all the Buddhas, which is made of crystal.
A lotus made of beryl, with filaments arising from gold,
a stalk of great emerald, and a pericarp together with gold.
It possessed a great mass of branches and was adorned with great jewels,
featuring buds made of rubies that were beautifully decorated in many forms.
Having meditated upon a vast lotus resting in the sky, adorned with divine sprouts made of emerald, for the sake of the best of sages.

Therefore, the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats by concentrating the mind on a lotus that is smaller than that, perfectly symmetrical in its marks, and most beautiful.
Therefore, one who possesses the intellect resulting from effort should make the third lotus slightly smaller by means of the mind;
they know the fourth lotus, which is the "turning" (āvarta), to be the smallest of all.
One should always meditate upon the fifth lotus, which is shorter than the shortest,
equal in form and radiance, and situated within the all-pervading void.
One who knows [this] should fashion for him a lotus situated on the seventh [finger] by means of the mind;
likewise, the lotus of Vajrapāṇi should be like the rising sun.
To the right of Vighnāntaka is Mañjughoṣa, always upon a lotus;
beyond that is a smaller lotus belonging to the great-souled Lokīśa.
The third is indeed the "Lotus" for one who has attained universal illumination;
the fourth is indeed the "Lotus" for the state of inexhaustible eloquence.
O you of slightly pure gait, the lotus is short and consists of five principles;
from that, the sixth is the lotus known as the Noble and the Unrighteous.
One should also visualize the ocean below and all around;
and from the great nāga Ananta, who emerges halfway out, [arise] Nanda and Upanandaka.
All-white great elephants, adorned with every ornament,
born from the ocean, with smiling faces and gazes fixed upon the sky.
With seven heads and great coils, adorned with jeweled earrings,
they are divine in human form, yet possessing the bodies of serpents for half their length.
The seven folds of skin are gentle, and the eyelashes curve upward like half-moons; to the left are the excellent sages, and five [Buddhas] are situated upon a lotus in the uṣṇīṣa.
The wheel-turning [mantra] is thus both beginning and end; it is sharpened by the son of Śakra’s weapon. The single-syllable wheel-turner is a mass of splendor, white and lofty.
One should clearly visualize above Jayoṣṇīṣa, the King of Vidyās of great supernatural power,
and below him, Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Yakṣas.

The wise one, skilled in mantra and the king of mantras, should always and at all times concentrate his mind upon these embodied forms, as well as upon his own intellect, while engaged in the practice.
One should meditate upon him as staying there, established in his observances, seated indeed upon a lotus leaf, and likewise seated below in the paryanka posture.
Always confess all misdeeds in the presence of the sages;
remaining there, the sage born of discipline, having entreated the most excellent of sages, [should practice].
May those born of the Sugata remain and continue to turn the wheel of Dharma;
with a mind intent on recitation, one should rejoice in their incomparable merit.
White mālatī flowers, punnāga, nāgakesara,
campaka, aśoka, tilaka, tagara, and likewise mallikā;
One should cast a divine handful of flowers,
beautiful and auspicious, whether they be real or imagined, endowed with a mind that is most excellent.
They should perform various excellent offerings, enchanting like a vidyā-mantra,
as well as various excellent incenses, perfumes, and ointments.
One should perform that with the mind alone, being truly established in the middle state;
having offered the bali with mantras, one should then place the lamps.
Endowed with various forms, with diverse and variegated foods,
and possessing many kinds of excellence, there was curd-rice and non-glutinous rice.
Having offered barley, wheat, and mung beans, well-adorned with various kinds of food and edibles,
to the Sugata through you, one should indeed offer even one's own self.
That mind by which one is instructed in accordance with reality and not otherwise—
this faith is taught by me as the worship among all forms of worship.
By meditating upon me, all practitioners of recitation will certainly attain awakening;
the accomplishment of the mantra will become fruitful, of this there is no doubt.
In this very life, those lacking in strength succeed with the mantra-deities;
or else, some human beings achieve success in another future birth.
In the past, there was a manifold abundance of enjoyments and various plenteous distinctions, as well as the threefold meditation of body, mind, and speech.
By means of the Buddhas, hundreds of Buddhas, and likewise the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas,
those renowned ones attain the threefold enlightenment.
The accomplishment of mantra in this world is said to be of these three types,
according to the three kinds of beings known as superior, inferior, and middling.
Action is taught to be of three kinds:
that which is sublime is said to consist of meditative absorption; the middling is known as born of ethical discipline.
The gift born of giving is the lowest; that same [gift] is again threefold:
the gift of Dharma is the most excellent, while the gift of material things is the middling.
But the gift of the word is said to be the lowest;
and morality is also declared to be threefold—thus spoke the Sage in the past.
That which is called the transformation into Buddhahood is known as the supreme morality;
individual enlightenment is the middling, while that arising from the state of a Śrāvaka is the lowest.
This is supramundane ethical discipline; now the mundane is being explained.
That too should be known as threefold, and it is the cause for the arising of the outflows.
Through devotion and higher knowledge by those seeking liberation, she arises as one possessing superknowledge;
she is always described by the best of sages as the most excellent and the eldest in the world.
The wise say that this [first kind] is the foremost morality in the world;
O son of a god, the middle should be known as such, while the lowest is for the best among men.
And that [action] is also threefold; when applied to the three types of karma, it is further divided into three ways and three kinds, and is again released in groups of three, two, seven, and five.
That [number] is twenty-one, and it is also divided threefold;
thus the sprout arises from the sprout, and likewise that which is born of meditation is likewise.
Furthermore, the two lords of the gods [should be visualized] with three [faces] and adorned with eight times eight;
this is described as being exactly as previously specified within the meditations themselves.
Thus, it is divided like waves, yet it moves again like a flame;
it should be known as being like the form of a bubble, perishing at the very moment of its arising.
In this very way, through the initial application, it is further divided a hundredfold, and indeed a thousandfold; it should always be known as uncountable and beyond all definition.
The supreme action born of meditation, arising from the mind, is accomplished;
therefore, one possessing meditative concentration should direct the mind toward awakening through mantra.
By this very method, they shall attain accomplishment in the deity of the mantra;
therefore, those who desire accomplishment and recite [the mantra] should apply every effort.
One should always perform mental worship of the Buddhas in every respect; for one who is constantly devoted to meditation, accomplishment is attained even in this very life.
For this restraint of ethical discipline born of meditative concentration is indeed unimpeded everywhere;
from generosity comes the wealth of the Dharma, and from ethical discipline comes birth among the best of gods.
This has been taught in brief for the sake of mantra-siddhi for those who recite mantras, beginning from the meditations on origination up to the state of being without outflows (anāśrava).
Having understood this, all practitioners of mantra will undoubtedly swiftly attain accomplishment in their mantras and quickly reach unsurpassed enlightenment.

Thus concludes the first chapter on meditation, from the *Mahākalparāja-paṭalavisara*, the thirty-seventh [chapter] of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, concerning the reality of accomplishing all ritual purposes through the means of the supreme practice.
Now begins the fortieth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Mañjuśrī, there exists within the detailed exposition of your Great Kalparāja a section concerning that which is born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), free from outflows (*anāśrava*), supremely auspicious and peaceful, having entered the ultimate limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), following the guiding principle of the Dharma of all Tathāgatas, having entered the path of supreme nirvāṇa, having become the security and peace of the noble path, having entered the intrinsic nature of the emptiness and selflessness of all phenomena, having entered the meditative absorption that follows the entry into the truth of all worldly and transcendent matters, and which follows the conduct of sentient beings—satisfying them through the playful drama and the display of childish conduct that summarizes the procedures for accomplishing all mantra practices.
And what is that?
Listen, O illustrious Mañjurava, to this meditation that conforms to all sentient beings;
it should be known as leading to omniscience and accomplishing the purpose of all mantras.
It is the fulfillment of all mantras and the purification of those who have committed evil deeds; by meditating upon which, all people shall attain unclouded accomplishment,
endowed with the excellence of all forms and inconceivable bliss of meditation.
Having attained the three types of enlightenment— superior, inferior, and middling— and having achieved incomparable mantra-siddhi, people shall praise him;
he becomes the accomplisher of all aims in the world, bringing about fame, renown, and the arising of happiness.
They will swiftly attain long life in this world, the exalted state of the gods, and the fulfillment of all their hopes; of this there is no doubt.
Those who contemplate meditation shall attain the supreme enlightenment free from the two-fold conceptual proliferation;
it is proclaimed among all mantras as the foremost for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, through the mere recollection of the mantras and all the tantras,
the accomplishments (siddhis) of those who seek accomplishment quickly bind their hopes [to fruition].
Mortals on earth who have made aspirations go again to those deities;
here, they bring that divine city into the abodes of the gods.
All the kings of mantras abide for one who meditates upon their faces;
and having returned, they all [bestow] everything belonging to those whose forms are the deities and mantras.
They speak truthfully of the arising of the fruits of the auspicious and inauspicious for the practitioner who is awakened to speech, whether in a dream or through direct perception.

Whether it be the fruit arising from auspicious karma or even a deity, all those who have entered the state of sleep perceive it, or else they see it within that interval by means of the mantra-practitioner.
Furthermore, practitioners of worldly mantras who engage in recitation do not perceive the other [the subtle].
Evil is destroyed by meditation, and also when the recitation is abundant.
All the kings of mantras are accomplished without delay for that practitioner,
through the power of the yoga of meditation, which possesses inconceivable and marvelous activities.
Thus addressed by the steadfast Śākyasiṃha, the ascetic,
Mañjughoṣa then remained silent in the city of the Śuddhāvāsa gods.
All the principal hosts of gods, residing in the three realms,
addressed these excellent, pure words to the Guru, the Lord of all Mantras.
Excellent, excellent, O Great Hero! Excellent, O Lord of Dharma, O All-pervading One! For you, indeed, act for the benefit of all sentient beings who recite these mantras.
The meditations have been explained according to their true nature as previously described;
now, however, O Great Hero—
Thus addressed, those gods— the foremost among the foremost, who are devoted to his welfare—
became silent then in that city of the Śuddhāvāsa realm.
Thus spoke the great sage Tejas, most steadfast,
with auspicious words that reveal the divine reality of the principles of the world.
The Fully Awakened One spoke with a voice produced by sweet syllables:
"Listen, all you hosts of beings, you who abide in the threefold abodes."
And being composed in meditation, they speak of the explanation of existence,
which has manifold meanings yet is non-dual, being selflessness and the vision of reality.
For the sake of the power and purpose of all mantras, and for various worldly purposes,
by which those who are well-considered lords of all dharmas in the world arrive,
may they all quickly come for the swift accomplishment of the purpose of the mantras for those who recite them.
First, one should meditate upon the Great Hero, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu,
seated upon a mountain of jewels within a cave radiant with gems,
upon a divine, lofty, great lotus made of ruby.
The Blessed One sat there upon his cross-legged seat, teaching the Dharma—
the Great Hero, meditating, who is indeed born from a lotus.
One should meditate upon the Perfectly Awakened Padmottara, the wise Padmābha, the five excellent sages, and likewise the Tathāgata Ratnābha.
It should be known as well-proportioned and firmly established within the five secret places;
it may be made entirely of stone along with its mountain, or in some cases, made of ruby (*padmarāga*).
In some places it has the luster of a split sapphire, in others it resembles crystal;
its height has the brilliance of emerald, and its measurement is eight hundred [yojanas].
It is one thousand yojanas in height and sixteen hundred thousand yojanas in width;
above it dwell the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme among men, who are infinite in number.
Thus, above, below, in all directions and intermediate directions, and everywhere,
all this has been attained by the excellent sages, the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds.
And it shines with the luster of the moon, with white lotus seats,
with the brilliance of swans, cow’s milk, conch shells, jasmine, the moon, and snow.
"All this is pervaded by the Perfectly Awakened Ones— above, below, and across the seven directions"—
thus [it was proclaimed] in the true void by the foremost of gods from all sides with showers of flowers and other offerings.
One should always contemplate oneself seated cross-legged below, while those who have come from above, equal to space, possess invisible bodies.
He constantly beheld his own principal body, stainless and resting upon a lotus petal, being consecrated from all sides by streams of water.
By incalculable sages, the foremost of sages, the perfectly awakened ones, the supreme among bipeds,
who always extend their right hands with fingers pointing upward on all sides;
With white water flowing in many streams from above,
and indeed on all sides and everywhere, he is the very embodiment of the Self itself.
With streams of water possessing eight qualities— fragrant, tranquil and cool,
clear and unpolluted, and likewise capable of removing all diseases.
One should also contemplate oneself as being drenched by such streams of water, which resemble split crystal and possess the power to destroy old age and death.
Having consecrated oneself with these [mantras] and having one's mind nourished by them,
the meditator shall then become happy through streams of water from all sides.
With a contented mind, the wise one should perceive that knowledge as his seat;
desiring concentration within the mind, he whose intellect is focused should contemplate the five superknowledges.
Thus constantly disciplined, the yogi shall then personally perceive phenomena:
the divine ear, as well as the knowledge that recollects former births.
He is the one who sports with supernatural powers, possesses divine light, and has unobstructed vision; he knows the movements of others' minds and the thoughts of all sentient beings.
Then the Lord of Yogis, concentrated through yoga, will know everything;
his awakening in the unsurpassed state is irreversible forever—of this there is no doubt.

By means of non-conceptualization, this practitioner of constant recitation shall attain, from the very first stage, those dharmas pertaining to the level of a Buddha; he shall become irreversible from the state of immortality.
Without any effort at all, the mantras are correctly accomplished in every respect—
both those that are supramundane and all those spoken by the Abhimukhis.
But by the Bodhisattvas, all those mantras originating from the lotus and those originating from the vajra, as well as the worldly mantras spoken by Brahmā, Rudra, and Indra, [are mastered].
By all the hosts of the chief yakṣas,
by the hosts of mātṛs, bhūtas, and grahas, and by the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras.
Then, by the gods, nāgas, and garuḍas, as well as by the siddhas, vidyādharas, kūṣmāṇḍas, vyantaras, and the dejected flesh-eaters.
And also by Rākṣasas who take the lives of others, by Pretas and evil dreams,
by Piśācas, Bhūtas, and Yakṣas, born of many different species.
Whatever mantras have been spoken in the world, they go toward his slight awakening when awakened by that yogin.
The mantras that accomplish all aims quickly attain success;
indeed, the very word of one who perceives the reality of things becomes a mantra that swiftly bears fruit.
