The sages, the gods, and those born of human origin— whether they be of forceful conduct, prominent, female, male, or neuter.
All those of great supernatural power, whether superior, inferior, or middling,
and all worldly mantras honored by the world—
Furthermore, by means of those very minds and those mantras born of mind,
all that was spoken by the foremost of sages brings accomplishment to the yogin.
Furthermore, the medicinal herbs belonging to the tantras and mantras, as well as the jewel ornaments—
all the excellent mantras, whether superior, inferior, or middling— belong to him.

Or even for the attainment of all hopes, when that which is imperishable flows forth, it is accomplished for that practitioner who is thus disciplined; indeed, for the practitioner who is thus disciplined.
For one who has thus spoken this mantra, especially for the wise one,
first there are the signs and marks which are the causes for the accomplishment of mantras.
An excellent body is born, radiant like a lotus and a source of happiness;
moreover, there is coolness of the limbs and a fragrance like sandalwood and blue lotuses.
The fragrance of camphor, agallochum, and jasmine issues forth from his mouth and the pores of his skin, possessing the color of lotus filaments.
The *jātī*, *yūthikā*, *puṇnāga*, *nāgakeśara*, and *vākula*; the *dhānuṣkārī* along with the *saugandhī*; and that which is produced from the *jāti*, *mallikā*, and *kola*.
Various excellent incenses, or various species of flowers;
various excellent perfumes and various kinds of substances;
and various all-pervading fragrances appropriate for auspicious rites.
Surpassing their excellent, heart-pleasing fragrance, there prevails the divine scent of the *māndārava* flower, along with its filaments and its pollen; together with the scent of musk,
it blows through the world, overwhelming all others.
Then, having recognized these signs— the coolness in the body, one-pointedness of mind, and the face born of discernment— [one knows that the fire has been kindled].
Having thus known the mind born of the first dhyāna as it has been determined—
whether in pleasure, pain, equanimity, or even in the state of cessation— he attains detachment.
In the second [dhyāna], the reciter impels equanimity and purity of mindfulness;
in the third, the practitioner [impels] dhyāna from the perspective of the mind; and in the fourth, from the perspective of the basis.
Just as the meditation taught by the best of sages is auspicious in every respect,
so too should the practitioner engaged in mantra recitation meditate with a one-pointed mind.
Those which have been taught by the Buddhas of the past, those of the present and the future, as well as the sūtras proclaimed by the perfectly enlightened ones and their disciples.
In those yogas, the knowers of mantra should practice meditation in successive order,
having brought to completion the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and that which arises from the Pratyekabuddhas.
Having brought forth great compassion and likewise great loving-kindness with diligence,
one should cultivate the mind in whatever way it accords with its spiritual lineage.

Loving-kindness is the mind intent on the welfare of others; compassion is tenderness toward the suffering of others; sympathetic joy is rejoicing in the happiness of others; and equanimity is the overlooking of the faults of others.
Thus spoke the highly fortunate, perfectly awakened one, the supreme among bipeds: "Impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and emptiness are the reality; this is the auspicious state."
The leaders of the world have pointed out the secure, auspicious, and supreme state;
all conditioned phenomena are momentary, and the three types [of existence] are inactive within the ultimate realities.
Those very unconditioned phenomena are established as threefold in enlightenment;
they alone are declared by those intent on awakening to be the most auspicious in the world.
The selflessness of persons and phenomena, described as a sharp descent [into emptiness],
does not exist on the auspicious, secure path taught by the Buddha.
In this dharma that is ultimately final and rests upon the limit of reality,
you are equal to the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), free from both existence and non-existence.
Awakening occurs within the auspicious source of phenomena (dharmodaya), which is endowed with three modes,
reaches the ultimate goal, and relies upon manifold divisions in liberation.
When the path— well-applied, well-expounded by all the Buddhas, well-taught, auspicious, and the remover of all sins— is established, then the knower of mantras [should proceed].
All phenomena, whether auspicious or inauspicious, which have arisen dependently according to all the supreme sages—
these should all be meditated upon through the application of births by means of the causes taught by the sages.
But as for the training of the śrāvakas, it consists of that which proceeds from higher ethics (adhiśīla),
and that knowledge of higher mind (adhicitta) which is the cause for the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Those who recite [mantras] should always personally understand that which is without sound as being with sound;
the rhinoceros-like [pratyekabuddha] should know the training that arises for the pratyekabuddhas and arhats.
Thus, the one known as Sarvasattva uttered a beautiful voice proclaimed from the third heaven,
in accordance with the reality of the path as taught by the Victors.
Meditative absorption is both with-outflows and without-outflows, as is restraint which brings about the arising of the wholesome;
it is established within the trainings according to its mode of activity and according to its characteristic mark.
By practicing those dharmas, the reciter attains the accomplishment of mantra;
and he gains the merit born of meditation, a merit that arises from the auspiciousness of Brahman.
His success should always be known to arise from meditations and augmented merits;
the mantra-practitioner, observing his vows and devoted to recitation and fire-offerings, should gather [the necessary materials] from all sides.
One should meditate upon the foremost son of the Victors, possessed of great supernatural power,
Mañjughoṣa, the great hero, whose radiance is equal to the appearance of saffron.
The deity has a face with a slight smile, possesses a full left mandala,
is of serene form, stands upon a lotus, and is illuminated by rays of light emanating from his body.
In the previously described place, consecrated by one's own form,
above the stars of water, in the midst of the abode of the supreme Jinas.
One should meditate upon that auspicious Lord Mañjurava, seated there in comfort, absorbed in meditation,
with all the Buddhas above him, his gaze directed upward, and offering salutations.
In her left hand she holds an auspicious blue lotus;
in her right hand, it is said, she holds [a vessel] in a pure and ever-auspicious place.

The mantra practitioner should always meditate again and again upon that son of the Sage, who is ever accompanied by reverence, who possesses a slight degree of ethical discipline, and who is not foolish.
Remaining there, the wise one born of meditative concentration beholds those who are afflicted;
by the mere sight of the mantra-practitioner, they are all liberated from their disease.
And looking downward, he sees the netherworld (pātāla) and all treasures hidden beneath the earth;
he becomes a master of all mantras and a constant uprooter of those who employ mantras against him.
Whatever one may see above, following after the sky-dwellers who have attained perfection,
one shall bring all under control in the world and acquire perfected substances from every quarter.
Then one should always look toward the northern direction [and behold] the lords of the yakṣas,
the kūṣmāṇḍas who bestow wealth, and the Lord of Wealth (Vaiśravaṇa) of great supernatural power.
Īśāna and Bhūtapati,
all these herbs that spring up, and Rudra himself together with Umā.
The kinnaras, gods, gandharvas, sages, and likewise the garuḍas—
those who are the refuge of all beings, as well as those in the northern intermediate directions.
And everywhere in all directions, both the stationary and the moving beings—
all shall come under the control of the reciter merely by his being seen.
Thus it should be known regarding the west: Varuṇa, possessed of great supernatural power, always sees everything with the great nāgas, and they go forth in a state of intense rapture.
In this way, Yama himself, possessed of great supernatural power, [governs] the worlds of Vaivasvata,
as do all those wicked rākṣasas who are of terrible form and great supernatural power.
Accompanied by their offspring and hosts of servants, these birds— devourers of others' lives, flesh-eaters in human form, and always followed by those of terrifying appearance— [approached].
The Vyantaras and the Kaśmalas, as well as the Pretas of great supernatural power, the Piśācas, the Bhūtas, the Kravyādas, and the Vyālas of great supernatural power.
Possessing forms of many kinds and born from wombs of many kinds,
beings with forms as swift as thought indeed roam the earth.
Fierce, drawn by the scent of blood, they always follow the Sun-god for a hundred yojanas all around and even a thousand;
harassing human beings, they roam across the surface of the earth.
Some seek food, while others follow for sport;
all come under the control of the reciter merely by being seen.
Thus it is in the eastern direction, and likewise in the south, following the presiding deities of the quarters.
Savitar, along with all the constellations, the luminaries, the planets, and the moon; the great portents and secondary omens; the beings, the radiant ones, and the lords of the directions.
Whether it be with his sons and retinue, or even an armed enemy from all sides,
they all come under one's control when subdued and conquered through meditative concentration.
And he saw everywhere in all directions,
on the earth, the best of gods, the gods themselves, and women, men, and so forth.
All beings in the world, whether human or born of non-human origins— indeed,
all those beings who are stable in the three realms— come under one's control.
But those who are born from the elements— whether they be primary, middling, or inferior—
all of them come under the power of the meditator, whether they are invisible or visible.
The karma born of meditative concentration is threefold—superior, middling, and inferior.
Having attained supreme enlightenment through the superior [karma], the meditator turns back from cyclic existence.
The unsurpassed, peaceful state is attained individually by those who possess the rhinoceros-like path; the inferior awakening of the śrāvakas is attained in dependence upon others.
The Supreme among Men speaks thus regarding those phenomena that arise dependently, characterized by their origination from causes, and which likewise possess the nature of cessation.
The realization of Arhatship arising from the four chapters,
the knowledge of those who understand fallacious reasons, and emptiness arising from suffering.
The state of arhatship, which is established in the selflessness of phenomena, is ultimately born from the limit of reality;
it should be known as being like cessation and the path, and is the most inferior [of the fruits].

It is the uprooting of the *ālaya*, the cutting off of the path, the speaking of non-selfhood, the quenching of thirst, the drying up of the counter-path, and the severance of the path for embodied beings.
In this beneficial path born of meditation, the arrow of grief for embodied beings, along with thirst, is blocked on all sides within the river of desire by means of meditative absorption.
Likewise, action is of three kinds, marked by manifold forms;
and for those who are preeminent, awakening is proclaimed to be of three types.

In the past, the supreme Victors taught that for Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats who possess the rhinoceros-like [solitary] nature, enlightenment is always designated as the lowest in this world; yet it is also designated as middling.
But the supreme goal is always awakening, the state of perfect buddhahood;
through such preliminary practice, the sequence of ritual action is threefold.
There it is divided a hundredfold, then a thousandfold, and even incalculably;
it should be understood as being like the sprout of rice, and always like the sprout of a field.
Then, like a seed and its sprout, action is proclaimed to exist eternally through a continuous succession; one endowed with pure dharmas is like a medicinal plant produced from a seed.
Furthermore, through the continuity of the consciousness of sentient beings, it becomes like a boat upon the water;
the wise person should again meditate upon the phenomena born of meditation.
Just as a yogi absorbed in meditation perceives purity everywhere—
threefold, of three kinds, and arising in manifold forms.
Accomplishment, the application of mantras, and meditative concentration are proclaimed;
for Bodhisattvas, the dhāraṇīs are said to be of exactly three kinds.
Mantras endowed with many excellent forms are well-honored,
both those that are worldly and foremost in the world, as well as those that are always supramundane.
Having followed the path of the Sugatas, through meditation and a succession of meditations,
all mantras are indeed accomplished for the sake of perceiving the welfare of all sentient beings.
All people who meditate upon him, who is beneficial in every respect,
shall attain glory, fame, long life, and the destruction of all diseases.
O best of men, being constantly composed in meditation, may you attain the knowledge that reveals the true meaning of the path, as well as a most abundant life.
This yoga was previously taught in brief by the best of sages;
now, this composed method of yoga has been declared by me.
When I too have attained unsurpassed awakening in the state of immortality,
they shall be well-honored by these very same applications and mantras.
The Blessed One has declared that unsurpassed gnosis, which is Buddhahood, is attained through meditative concentrations that are divine, auspicious, and engaged in the activity of dhyāna.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another [method]; listen as I speak it:
that which arises from the hundred rites of play for the purpose of playing with all mantras.

Listen, O Mañjurava and people! By the very practice born of meditative concentration, the practitioners of mantra must always know what is beneficial and what is harmful, as well as their miraculous transformations.
By means of the yoga born of meditative concentration alone, one should first always visualize for those of dull intellect the towering form of the Great Naga within the water.
Indeed, the great ocean surrounds it on all sides; it is adorned by the king of mountains, possessing lofty jeweled peaks, extending to the four quarters, and auspicious.
There he saw the Great-Souled One, the Buddha renowned throughout the three worlds,
the Well-Eyed One, who abounds in Dharma, Amitābha, the Supreme Victor.
The son of the Jina, ever white, the illustrious Lokeśa,
the great being Padmaketu, who has arisen from great compassion.
In that place where the excellent sage Sunetra resides, one should find the youth in the form of a child,
always possessing a charming voice and endowed with various auspicious marks of prosperity.
In his left hand he holds a blue lotus, and in his right he holds an image of the Sugata;
there, in the water, dwells the great Naga known by the name Ananta.
The reciter, having meditated upon him as being entirely white and eternally adorned with seven radiant heads, should contemplate him as decorated with various ornaments.
One should also contemplate his face as receiving [the teaching] from the Sugata;
likewise for the two nāga kings, Nanda and Upananda, who possess great supernatural power.
Rising to that same height and increasing twofold on all sides,
there are the nāgas Ananta, Karkoṭaka, and the highly powerful Padma, who are equal [in stature].
Kulika, Śaṅkhapāla, and Kapila according to their colors;
then Mahāpadma, the lord of nāgas, and Padmābha, who are always like creepers.
Vāsuki and Takṣaka should be known as having the color of a slightly opened lotus filament; they both possess the luster of a lotus and are adorned with various types of ornaments.
And Śaṅkha, the great nāga, is auspicious, white in color;
Śaṅkhapāla, the Maṇi-nāga, is slightly white in color;
and there is the great nāga Sāgara and the renowned Mucilinda.
Furthermore, the Kṛṣṇa-nāga is proclaimed to be entirely black in color;
all of them are equal in size, and Nanda and Upananda are likewise well-elevated.
Then there was Elapatra, the lord of nāgas, possessed of great coils and world-renowned;
indeed, Sāgara, the sovereign of uragas, whose deeds were inconceivable and marvelous.
Understand that he performs various white (auspicious) rites;
however, one should never perform them for a corpse or one who has died from poison while asleep at sea.
Having indeed enveloped it with a garland and performed meditative yoga with a wise mind,
one who has died will quickly rise up when placed in the ocean.
One should always step upon a snake that is asleep from poison with one's foot and move it;
by placing it in the ocean, it becomes free of poison at that very moment.
In this same way, one treats fevers, piśācas, carnivorous beings, and auspicious *vyantara* spirits.
[He saw] the Rākṣasas, Pretas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, Piśācas, Uragas, and Mātṛs,
as well as the Grahas who always seize the lives of men in this world.
Resorting to various forms of exertion,
they remain on earth as humans, having assumed human bodies.

One should contemplate with this meditation those beings who have seized the foolish; one should meditate on the Naga kings of the ocean as rising up before them from their thoughts. By contemplating the being as the Mother, the fool is quickly released.
Thus, for those people afflicted by insect or spider bites,
as well as those suffering from ringworm, skin spots, leprosy, scabies, itching, eczema, and other similar eruptions, including fistula-in-ano and Rohita, [this should be applied] constantly.
And likewise Plīhameda and Udara, as well as Padma and Supadmaka;
and for the Yakṣas, Sapadmaka, as well as Padmottara and Kṛśa.
All those afflicted by the disease of fever, including humans,
monkeys, and bears, you should all place within the ocean, O best of serpents.
One should cast away all various miseries and sufferings, and the pains of every disease and affliction,
into the ocean-like locus, by means of that which is established through the contemplation of meditative absorption; then the Naga, receiving the command of the Sugata, will swiftly liberate one.
And thus, by all the auspicious serpents who perform every task,
and by the lords of serpents, the entire aquatic realm was then pervaded.
Excelling everywhere and on all sides, these lords of serpents possess great supernatural power; they are knowers of the *samaya* of Mañjughoṣa, intent upon his command and initiation,
and as divine yakṣas, they are ever-present for the arising of auspiciousness for human beings.
But through mixed actions and knowledge, there arises a mixed result;
those who always support the rain [the clouds] at the proper time adhere to a righteous way of life.
With streams of water on all sides,
when the crops, medicinal herbs, and rice have thus come to fruition, it bears fruit according to its cause.
Embraced by the form of clouds, they wander upon the surface of the earth;
possessing great supernatural power and great majesty, they endure for an eon and enjoy great prosperity. Their city, named Bhogavatī, is situated within the ocean.
When mortals everywhere in Jambudvīpa are devoted to the Dharma,
then the great Nāgas and their retinues indeed abide within them.
Then, having experienced the war between the gods and asuras, those desiring victory remained at the Jambū tree in the center of Jambūdvīpa.
Again and again they frequented men, remaining beyond the range of perception everywhere;
they should apply all virtuous deeds toward those nāgas.
Those nāgas who dwell in the water, having fallen from their observance,
brought affliction like insects; the nāgas, relying on the faction of the asuras, released all kinds of poison, both stationary and mobile, in every direction.
Pramāthin, Jhalujhala, Kapardin, Mahodadhi,
Bhīma, Bhīṣaṇa, Durmukha, and likewise Bahumukha.
These and other great nāgas are exceedingly arrogant and conceited;
they are constantly established in black karma, or others in mixed karma.
When the mortals dwelling in Jambudvīpa become most unrighteous, they will be of great power yet terrifying in form, and their people will be addicted to poison.
Then they shall cause great fear, most terrible poison-induced fainting,
vomiting, and dizziness, as well as many afflictions such as great pestilence.
In this world, they release wicked serpents that bring about misfortune;
likewise, those great nāgas cause many kinds of calamities and inauspiciousness.
Those who delight in what is harmful and release drought after drought—
against them, for the destruction of their pride, one should undertake this meditation.
Mañjughoṣa, the greatly wise Bodhisattva of great supernatural power,
holding a blue lotus in his left hand and bestowing the boon with his right;
possessing a luster like refined gorocana, he is more radiant than gold and saffron.
One should meditate upon the Son of the Sugata mounted upon Garuḍa, the king of birds,
at the heads of those fanged creatures, [destroying] all their virulent poison.
Then, with their hearts pierced and their minds terrified and agitated,
they turned back again and went, entering their own abode in a state of rage.
Having seen various kinds of portents, as well as inauspicious ones accompanied by sounds,
the knower of mantras, being composed, should meditate thus upon Mañjughoṣa.
O knower of mantras, one should fashion snake-fangs of many kinds;
indeed, those that bite have various forms and shapes, as do those born from eggs.
I shall speak correctly, according to the wisdom of the scriptures and through ritual action;
for those born of that lineage, the serpents indeed bite humans upon the earth.
O Garuḍa, one should perform all the rites for embodied beings by means of that very scripture prescribed by the King of Birds according to the rules.
The black, white, and other nāgas who dwell upon the circle of the earth roam the entire world in the form of the sun for embodied beings.
Then, having understood what is curable and incurable, as well as the four beneficial [treatments] for poison,
and [the conditions] involving pitta, śleṣman, and those mixed with vāyu;
They say that due to phlegm (śleṣman), it is called Vāruṇī, being white in color and circular in shape;
whereas that which arises from bile (pitta) is named Ajñeyajā, appearing triangular in form.
Always fire-colored and slightly reddish-brown with tawny arms,
it is square, well-proportioned, and variegated like a family lineage reaching its end.
That which is black in color and very large is to be known as Māhendra;
they say that elephants are born of phlegm (kapha), while those born of bile (pitta) arise from hatred.
That which is born of wind should be known as delusion (moha), variegated and black in color;
that very same [state] when characterized by phlegm (kapha) should be understood as sattvic, white in color.
That which appears silver-like should be known as pertaining to bile (paittika), shining with yellow and red hues;
that which is dark should be known as pertaining to wind (vātika), characterized by a variegated and uneven appearance.
One should observe that among all the intermediate beings, including insects, pustules, and so forth,
as well as among reptiles everywhere, the gender-signs are seen to be mixed.
One should clearly contemplate Mañjughoṣa there, appearing black, rising up,
seated comfortably upon Garuḍa, in the form of a youth, the source of happiness;
one should contemplate him among the Vyantaras and at the joints of humans where they are wicked.
Then one should contemplate the divine youth in the form of a child,
the great-souled one of universal form, seated upon Garuḍa.

Then the wise man should meditate upon that illustrious one seated there, whose enemies are like autumnal reeds, situated between the thighs and reaching up to the navel, extending into the space above.

The meditator should visualize Mañjughoṣa, who possesses great heroism, has a yellowish luster, resides in the region of the chest during deep sleep, and is mounted upon the foremost of birds as his vehicle.
Likewise, one should meditate upon the inconceivable one who has Garuda as his banner in the place of the head;
one should then contemplate him as white-complexioned, seated upon Vainateya, and situated outside.
In the case of a bite by a *sāttvika* snake, however, the victim faints from poison,
vomits phlegm from all sides, saliva flows incessantly, and he sinks down again and again;
one should know that such a person has been bitten by a *sāttvika* snake, and his welfare will depend on the bright fortnight.
When the Lord of All is in a state of paralysis or agitation, one wanders and trembles;
furthermore, when there is a poison born of bile, fainting occurs and a terrible burning sensation arises.
In the rajasic state, there arises this activity of biting for one who possesses fangs;
in the tamasic state, delusion, fainting, and sleep are born from darkness.
When mixed [elements] are present, the activity is indeed mixed and becomes terrible;
when the *sattva* element is present, there is a white luster, and in the case of fangs, it occurs in humans.
The rājasic type should be known as somewhat yellowish in complexion;
furthermore, the one whose nature is delusion (moha) becomes black in complexion.
When mixed, it is smoke-colored, and sometimes pale white;
these arise from the white fortnight and from those born of the twice-born, being characterized by both the *sattva* and *rajas* qualities.

Those born of snakes who are dark-complexioned are of a tamasic and mixed nature; for these belong to families that are both noble and ignoble. Indeed, they are the lords and masters over the serpents, and having embraced the demonic faction, they roam upon the surface of the earth.
In this world of humans, there are species of nāgas who are most unrighteous;
they are cruel and even more cruel in the world, always intent upon the pursuit of food.
Some are for the purpose of causing affliction, others are fanged and life-taking; [others are] for the purpose of destroying poison for those who subsist on all kinds of venomous creatures.
This supreme and primary meditation, which follows the characteristics [of the poison], should be applied to living beings; when contemplated, it quickly releases that poison.
One should employ it at all times and on every occasion for all diseases;
established in meditative absorptions, it destroys all calamities.
Just as with the *nāgas*, so it is with sentient beings, *rākṣasas*, *grahas*, and *mātṛs*,
as well as humans of evil intent who take the lives of others;
one should apply these [remedies] specifically to the symptoms of all those afflicted by diseases in the world.
One should always place meditation, the object of meditation, as well as liberation and action;
[he who is] of youthful form, auspicious, pure, and the destroyer of sin.
Mañjughoṣa, the great hero, the son of the Victorious One, possessed of great supernatural power,
is seated comfortably upon Garuḍa within the rising solar disc.
One should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord, the Master of Mantras, who faces in every direction;
when contemplated everywhere, he destroys all diseases through meditation.
One should perform all rites at all times toward all sentient beings;
for this [mantra] paralyzes everything and beautifies everything auspicious.
All mantras of the worlds, when understood within this meditation, quickly attain accomplishment; even those proclaimed in other kalpas do so here.
And those mantras belonging to the Tathāgatas, as well as those of the Vajra and Lotus families, and those of Śakra, Indra, Brahmā, and Rudra;

For one who meditates upon this ritual manual (*kalpa*), all mantras pertaining to the Ādityas, Vasus, Indras, the constellations, planets, and luminaries, as well as those of Garuḍas, Uragas, Yakṣas, and the foremost Ṛṣis together with the Pūtanas, shall be accomplished.
Even when performing rites according to the dependent [tantra], one should accomplish the success of the ritual quickly through the independent or internal [method] while established in meditation;
having meditated upon the rising [deity] of universal form within the solar disc.
Then [he saw] the Youth, appearing as a child, adorned with the ornaments of infancy,
blazing upon the orb of the sun, mounted upon Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā.
Having seen such an unmanifest form, even when well-visualized within the *mūrjā*, the paralysis of the enemy's forces occurs and one’s intention is fulfilled.
And all those who are bitten become paralyzed and dance with one another; all embodied beings, afflicted by the grahas, laugh while suffering.
Those afflicted by fever and those who have fainted then rise up quickly;
crying out in various ways of distress, they indeed let forth a terrifying roar.
A practitioner of mantra, being composed, should then recognize those humans on earth who have been seized by the *grahas*, the *mātṛs*, and the *kūṣmāṇḍas* by these signs.
By his will, he can swiftly release the transmission of poison;
then, with a desire to sport, the yogi causes the spirits to play.
In one who has fainted from poison, the solar channel (nāḍī) should be employed;
by the application of the solar channel, he shall move all living beings [from their stupor].
While asleep, one becomes free from all poisons, whether stationary or mobile; thereafter, one who was poisoned and rendered unconscious quickly awakens—of this there is no doubt.
And another on the surface of the earth quickly prospers while afflicted by poison;
yet another again, and yet another besides him as well.
In this manner, by means of hundreds and thousands of such methods everywhere,
one should ripen the elements through the application of the channels until [the goal] is reached.
Likewise, in a cloth, a wall, a jar, our water, or fire, one may in an instant move the channel; therein resides the poison within the venom.
Indeed, all those who are afflicted shall become healthy at that very moment upon the earth. By means of this initial application, one should perform eight hundred rites,
or one may perform an incalculable number of rituals using the blood of a supreme mantrin.
This is the practice in brief that has been taught for those who recite mantras;
it should be employed by Garuḍa, who is entirely dependent on ritual application and meditation.
The Mata is said to be born of conceptualization (saṅkalpa), and the Śaiva system especially so;
furthermore, all worldly mantras should be employed within the detailed practice of meditation.
In this Mañjurava Kalpa, which is especially distinguished by meditation and well-honored by the applications of all tantras as well as by mantras,
those mental conceptions that constitute the purpose of the Kalpa should always be employed here.
In this yoga, which is divine meditation proclaimed here in the King of Ritual Manuals (Kalparāja),
all [practitioners] should be engaged through meditation that is stainless by virtue of its logical application.

For one who constantly recites and meditates upon this subtle, pure teaching concerning the object of the mind— the basis for the accomplishment of mantras proclaimed by the Son of the Sage and rejoiced in by all Buddhas— all perfections will become abundantly abundant.

Thus ends the chapter containing the instructions on the meditation for all rites, which serves as a manual for the practice of the ritual procedures for the play of Tārā according to the reality of all worlds; it is the thirty-eighth [chapter] from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a section of the *Mahākalparāja* from the *Bodhisattvapiṭakāvatamsaka*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra.
Now begins the forty-first chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

"O Mañjuśrī! In this great expansion of your own Great King of Ritual Manuals (*mahākalparāja*), which is approved by all Buddhas, follows the practice of the Great Mantras, and has entered into all samayas; which serves as the foundation for entering the Great Root Manual (*mūlakalpa*); and which possesses the superknowledge of knowing the cries of all beings in the fifth [section]—this Garuḍa, the king of birds, shall speak to you concerning the inconceivable domain of the knowledge of the cries of all beings, the superknowledge of the knowledge of cries through following the practice of his own mantras, and the conduct and the knowledge of the cries within the domain of all mantras, all ritual manuals, and all worldly [practices] that have entered their respective samayas, as well as those of all who belong to the animal realm and all Garuḍas, the kings of birds."

Then, indeed, from that assembly circle, Vainateya Garuḍa—surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of garuḍas through the empowerment of the Bodhisattva—rose from his seat, circumambulated the assembly circle, approached Mañjuśrī, and with palms joined in reverence at the feet of the Great Bodhisattva, spoke thus to Mañjuśrī: "O Great Bodhisattva, for the sake, welfare, and happiness of sentient beings, I shall proclaim one hundred varieties of rites, together with their secret instructions, within this Great King of Rituals (*mahākalparāja*).
Therefore, it would be well if the Great Bodhisattva would grant his approval."
Then Mañjuśrī said this to Vainateya: "Speak, speak, O Mahāsattva, out of compassion for sentient beings!
Then Vainateya, through the empowerment of the Buddha, sat upon his own seat and, with a joyful mind, spoke the hundred supreme rites together with their secret instructions:
"Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!"
It was as follows: "Oṃ! O Śakuna, Great Śakuna, you of outspread wings, destroyer of all serpents! Kha kha! Eat, eat! Remember the pledge! Hūṃ! Stay! The Bodhisattva commands: svāhā!
He spoke this hundredfold supreme rite.

[It includes] the summoning of nāgas, the subduing of nāgas, the restraint of nāgas, the causing of possession by those who have been bitten or not yet bitten, the invocation of a serpent by means of speech, the performance of the restraint of serpents, and the playing with poison; [it effects] the expulsion of all poisons, whether by speech, mind, or intellect. One who observes the *poṣadha* vow and has fasted for three nights, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, having prepared an eight-cubit mandala on a clean spot at a riverbank using five-colored thread, established upon eight lotuses, should thereupon draw the Blessed One in the center teaching the Dharma.
To his right, one should depict the noble Mañjuśrī with palms joined in reverence, gazing at the face of the Blessed One;
to the left of the Blessed Buddha, one should depict Nārāyaṇa with four arms, holding all manner of weapons in his hands;
and near him, a Garuḍa of deformed appearance.
Immediately after that, one should draw Vinatābharaṇa. Behind Āryamañjuśrī, one should draw Āryākṣayamati, Sudhana, and Subhūti, with their palms joined in reverence.
Thus should the inner maṇḍala be drawn. Outside at the eastern gate, one should draw a vajra with white ash; to the south, a sword with black pigment; and to the north, a mace with yellow pigment.
To the west, one should draw a noose of red color.

Thus, having summoned all the deities from the outer maṇḍalas with the root mantra, having worshipped them with all kinds of flowers and perfumes, having offered incense of *guggulu* and a sacrificial offering (*bali*) consisting of the three sweets, and having established a fire with fuel-sticks of *khadira* wood in front of them, one should seat oneself upon a serpent-throne, cultivate a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings, and offer eight thousand oblations of *sarpakaṇṭaka* seeds smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter. Then, as a sign of success, serpents will appear;
an offering of water (*arghya*) should be given to them.
In this way, success is achieved.
Having recited one's own mantra, one should say: "Depart after having bestowed success upon me.
Then they depart.
Then, having performed the dismissal with the root mantra itself, one should sprinkle [the area] thoroughly;
thereafter, one should commence the ritual action.
And all the offering substances for the *bali* should be cast into the water.
Afterwards, by mere speech alone, one performs all rites involving poisons.
One who desires to create enmity should offer twenty-one oblations of serpent bones smeared with poison;
enmity will arise.
Desiring to destroy [an enemy], one should offer twenty-one oblations of fragments of a snake’s slough; he is destroyed.
One should offer twenty-one oblations of crow feathers; immediately he wanders about like a crow.
For the subjugation of women and men, one should offer twenty-one oblations of mustard seeds smeared with ghee; they become submissive.
To subjugate a king or a high official, one should offer twenty-one oblations of excellent food smeared with ghee; he becomes submissive.
Having consecrated a clod of earth with mantras, one should throw it into the fire; it will not burn.
With a blade of grass, there is release.
By what has been said, fish are not caught;
one attracts a being, whether conscious or unconscious, by snapping the fingers.
For every disease, one becomes healthy through the sprinkling of water.
Having consecrated a staff with mantras, one should bring it to the door; it becomes opened.
Taking that very same staff, covered with a blue cloth, one should go into battle; the enemy army will break apart at the mere sight of it.
By tying a knot in one's own garment, all mantras are paralyzed.
When [the mantra] is released, liberation occurs.
One should fill the mouth of a snake with ashes;
by uttering the name of whomever one performs this rite, that person becomes mute.
One should destroy the poison of a tumor with water over which the mantra has been recited once; the tumor shrivels and falls away, and the rival spell is destroyed.
With this, one binds;
likewise, it releases.
Having consecrated a brick and turned it around, one should recite the mantra.
It loosens even a firmly tied knot.

Likewise, one who desires to cause rain to fall should draw the previously mentioned mandala, perform worship, kindle a fire, and offer eight thousand oblations of *varuṇa* wood; it will rain an *āḍhaka*.
In this manner, it rains up to ten *āḍhakas*.
Having consecrated a *pippalā* fruit with mantras and taken it in his hand, in whichever direction he throws it, there the food is transferred.
This same procedure applies even for setting fire [to property]. One should likewise perform the descent into water in this manner.
He drives away the nāgas;
having fashioned a clay serpent, he causes whichever [nāga] he desires to bite.
This is the very same procedure for a charcoal serpent.
Furthermore, it liberates [from snake venom]:
one should cast mustard seeds over which the mantra has been recited seven times in the four directions;
the snakes will come.
The binding of the maṇḍala should be performed.
Having sprinkled it with water, one should dismiss [the deities].
For the release by means of water: having empowered a clod of earth with the mantra, one should draw in the nāgas and cast it into the water; they become free from poison.
Taking up a bow, four arrows made of non-metal should be shot in the four directions. When the snake comes, moving along with the arrows, it should be addressed as follows:
"Drink this poison! he said.
The bitten man drank it and rose up.
Then, when he sprinkled water upon the snakes in order to extract their barbs, the barbs of each one fell out.
The snake remains unhurt.
One should fashion four mongooses out of earth from an anthill.
Having consecrated water with a mantra, one should sprinkle it; having gone [to the site], the snakes will abandon it and depart.
When they have arrived, one should say to them, "Drink the poison!
They drink it, and the dead person rises up.
Having consecrated charcoal and drawn a line, one should strike with an *arka* creeper; then a snake, being dragged along by executioners, comes forth.
One should say, "Drink the poison," and he drinks it;
the one who has been bitten becomes free of poison.
One should consecrate either a banner or a parasol with mantras.

Upon seeing as many corpses and those who have drunk poison as there may be, they all become free from poison; one should play a musical instrument after consecrating it with mantras, and by hearing it, they become free from poison.
Having drawn a mandala with five-colored dust, the sound of a palm-clap should be struck.
Then the nāgas and sarpas will come from the four directions;
they enter the maṇḍala.
One must not be afraid.
One should perform the binding of the topknot and the protection of oneself. Having consecrated the eyes with mantras and looked at the two angry ones, one should press the left thumb;
at that very moment, [the object] falls.
Like a serpent, it acts through its form;
when released, there is liberation.
Thus, by means of speech, one causes [the poison] to enter or releases it, whether bitten or unbitten.
Having consecrated the remains of Viṣṇu’s offerings (nirmālya) with mantras, wherever one casts them—whether on a street or in a house—at that very moment a serpent will bite a human.
Those [serpents] sprinkled with water become free of venom.
By raising the hand [over them], there is paralysis for six months.
Having consecrated oneself with mantras, one may allow oneself to be bitten by snakes at will;
the poison does not affect him.
He adorns himself with bracelets, armlets, and earrings.
Having consecrated dust with a mantra, one should whisper it into the ear.
Whether by means of water, a fan, or even mentally, having recited the mantra for success, one should cast the dust upon the ground;
the deceased then rises.
Incense made of human flesh together with clarified butter brings about nourishment (*puṣṭikaraṇa*).
Incense made of powdered human bone and the feathers of crows and owls brings about killing (*māraṇa*).
Incense made of *madana* and chaff seeds brings about eradication (*utsādana*).

Incense made from mustard seeds and *rājikā* causes fever; *kodrava* grain and cat excrement cause enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). Having combined skull-powder and *madhūka* powder together with honey, this incense is used for eradication (*utsādana*). *Moraṅgī* and castor stalks are an incense for eradication.
Cow-bile and human bone mixed with clarified butter are an incense for the killing of an enemy.
A fish-egg, clear liquor, and cotton seeds—
this incense quickly brings back a man who has gone to another country.
Split lentils and the flesh of a hen—this incense should be offered to one who is entering; after this, there is no further summoning.
One should combine the seeds of *bhallātaka* with sesame oil;
this is the "attraction incense," which one should offer for the purpose of attraction.
One should offer ghee and guggulu;
this incense destroys disease.
Having offered incense made of sesame and mustard seeds, one should likewise sacrifice those very same substances.

For seven nights, at the three junctions of the day, one should offer eight thousand oblations of salt and black mustard seeds under the name of whomever one desires to bring under control; by doing so for seven nights at the three junctions, one brings even a great man under one's power.
Having consecrated powdered skull with a thousand recitations, one brings whoever one desires under control by touching them with that powder.
Combined with cremation-ground ashes, if one grinds [the powder] over someone, one causes them to be seized by fever; [if one performs the rite] to release them, they are freed.
If one burns incense made of mongoose hair, mustard seeds, and a snake’s slough while reciting the name of someone, that person becomes hated by the whole world.
One effects subjugation with sesame seeds and brings about the production of wealth;
with sesame and rice grains smeared with ghee, one brings a woman under control. One should offer oblations for three nights at a site sacred to the Nāgas using barley, frog-fat, and marrow.
He causes the gods to send rain.

Having fashioned a clay Garuḍa and holding it with cupped hands, one should descend into water reaching the shoulders and recite the mantra at midnight; he by whose name this is done becomes submissive.

Having scattered rice grains in a cremation ground and established the *devahṛdaya* [mantra], one should recite the weapon-mantra (*praharaṇa*); this provides a livelihood for oneself along with one's retinue.
Incense made from the hair of a mongoose and a rat, along with cotton seeds and bones, brings all beings under one's control.
Incense made from poison (*viṣa*) and *bhallātaka* together with honey is a means of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
Incense made from the shells of hen’s eggs together with pungent oil (*kaṭutaila*) is a means of subjugation.
Palāśa, seeds of *surasā*, and *madana* flowers constitute an incense for subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
An incense made of *śatapuṣpā*, *devadāru*, the excrement of a frog, and that of a sparrow is for the purpose of subjugation.
Barley, sesame, and *dūrvā* grass mixed with cow’s urine form an incense for subjugation.

Haritāla and kākajihvā mixed with blood constitute an incense for rendering someone mute. Human hair combined with cow meat and oil constitutes an incense for causing disease. Crow feathers and owl feathers mixed with nimba oil are used for eradication (uccāṭana).
This incense, consisting of guggulu resin mixed with ghee and sidhu liquor, brings joy to all sentient beings.
Incense made from patra, tvak, and turuska causes one to be followed by all sentient beings;
it becomes obedient to one's command.
Turuṣka, sandalwood, camphor, and collyrium bring a king under one's control.

Having performed the ritual of worship and offerings before an image of Viṣṇu, one should offer eight oblations of *mahāmāṃsa* and recite the mantra eight thousand times for three nights; one will obtain whatever wealth one desires.

Having fashioned an effigy with ashes from a cremation ground and offered incense of *mahāmāṃsa*, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and recite the mantra eight thousand times at night in the cremation ground; one brings whoever one desires.
He issues a command.
For the purpose of eradication, one should offer oblations of cotton chaff with crow feathers; eradication occurs in an instant.
Having kindled a fire in a cremation ground with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, seated upon a skull, one should offer oblations of snake sloughs.
Food becomes inexhaustible.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of powdered charnel ground bones mixed with mustard seeds while reciting the name of a person; that person will come from a hundred yojanas away.
This may be performed for all desired objects.

One should have a deity fashioned by a craftsman observing the *poṣadha* vow upon a wooden plank, a wall, or a panel that is sufficiently deep; [the deity] with white sandalwood wings spread out, adorned with all the ornaments of a nāga, fierce and sharp, with a distorted face and deformed claws, seated upon a lotus, with his gaze cast downward.
Having made it one span in size, one should perform all rites before it.

One desiring nourishment should use *palāśa* wood; for the sake of subjugation, *bilva*; for one desiring a son, *udumbara*; and one desiring cattle should have it made of *śirīṣa* or *madhuka* wood, according to the prescribed rule for those desiring wealth.
With pork, one who desires fruits [of success]; with horse meat, there is offspring;

with the meat of a black antelope, one seeking prosperity, or one desiring extensive renown, or one desiring a woman, or one desiring the earth; for one seeking victory in legal disputes, tiger meat; for one seeking clothing, "great meat" (*mahāmāṃsa*); for subduing a king, *hastibalā*; for subduing a royal minister, *atibalā*; and for [subduing] a king, one should offer *aśvagandhā*.
For eradication, elephant hair; for malevolent sorcery, picumarda—these are declared to be the ultimate materials.
The preparation of the cloth occurs;
for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), the material is gold ore;
for the increase of fame, silver and so forth.
One causes destruction through the homa-offering of crow feathers;
one kills with vulture feathers;
one causes enmity with hawk feathers.
One causes enmity with peacock feathers;
one should give wealth with peacock feathers;
with partridge feathers, a woman; with quail feathers, sons; with crow feathers, gold; and with *ṭiṭṭibha* bird feathers, enchantment.

One effects eradication with dog meat; one performs attraction with buffalo meat; in rites of sorcery (*ābhicāruka*), with human flesh; in rites of pacification (*śāntika*), with deer hair; for one desiring a maiden, with owl feathers; for one wishing to destroy a country, with throat-hair; for inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), with human hair; in rites of sorcery, with the hair of a human female; and for the destruction of enemies—with all of these, there is a seven-day fire-oblation (*homa*) performed at the three junctions of the day.
By mere remembrance, I perform all poisonous rites; by constant recitation, I perform all rites.

O Blessed One, for whoever shall recite my mantra three times a day while practicing its accomplishment according to this King of Rituals (Kalparāja), I shall provide him with medical treatment for all afflictions caused by poisons and I shall remain constantly following behind him.
Then, at that time, he meditated upon the Svarūpa-mudrā:
having made the two thumbs entwined with each other, the remaining fingers should be positioned like wings;
this very Garuḍa-form was declared by Pinākin to be my mudrā.
Upon seeing this, the nāgas, afflicted by fear, flee away;
with their fingers pointing downward, the knower of mantras [acts] with this mantra.
Oṃ jaḥ.
Known as Nāgadamanī, she destroys the pride of the nāgas;
her fingers, resembling the buds of a lotus, are positioned at her sides.
Placing the two thumbs in the middle and pressing the fingers firmly with effort, this is known as the *nāgadamanī* [mudrā], divine among divine rites.
The ring finger and the index finger are well-positioned together with the middle finger;
the two thumbs are placed at the opening, while the remaining fingers are situated on the sides.
Renowned as the Garuḍanāda, it terrifies all the nāgas;
and whatever [mantras] have been taught by me in the practice of all mantras, [it surpasses them].
In the worldly science of Garuḍa,
all those [rites] should be performed by him alone out of compassion for all sentient beings.

All [rites], whether having some specific purpose or being without remainder, accomplish the goals of the Root Tantra; they are eternally present in this supreme tantra, which describes the welfare of all sentient beings.
All purposes of ritual action are well-established and abundant in their benefit for all sentient beings;
these indeed should be employed within the extensive rites of the preeminent mantra.
In this supreme kalpa, at its very root, your foundation is established upon the surface of the earth through all beings here, by means of the qualities produced by the path of mantras.
Known in detail through universal vision, it is for the compassion toward all sentient beings;
it is well-established for those desiring accomplishment, being based upon logical reasoning.
They shall bring about success in all respects for embodied beings in all mantras;
and all sentient beings shall be present within the ritual manuals according to one's mental desire.
Through the conjunction of mantra, mudrā, and breath-control, they recount history, ancient events, the present, and the future.
This mantra is irresistible and draws in all beings;
it is Rudra, the lord of all beings, worshipped by the gods.
Tambaka is to be known by the three-syllable name; he dwells in the Kalpa on the surface of the earth, eternally residing in the Himālaya mountains as Umāpati Maheśvara.

He should be known as the trident-bearer, the sword-wielder, the wielder of the Pināka bow, and the one whose banner is the bull; he is the leader of the Gaṇas, the bearer of the trident, the one called Maheśa, and the possessor of great supernatural power.
They call him the Imperishable, the Imperishable; he is Kapardin, whose weapon is the mace.
This mantra is of great significance, it causes all beings to tremble for their welfare, and it performs all rites as the means for accomplishing all actions.
This deity is indeed the Great-Souled One, celebrated as Mahādeva;
he is renowned for the purpose of all rites, always bestowing the causes and fruits [of action].
I shall proclaim his mantra; listen, you who desire prosperity.

Oṃ sthaḥ! Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded, the teachers of the three worlds, who possess inconceivable and wondrous forms! O source of the arising of auspiciousness, you who are worshipped by the three realms of existence! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ!
This mantra is a great mantra that instills fear in all enemies;
it bestows long life upon all beings and is effective for rites of pacification and nourishment.
Indeed, this mantra born of the mind should be employed in all ritual actions whatsoever.
One shall attain the knowledge of the cries of all beings, the activity of the knowledge of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*),
and likewise mastery over the superknowledges; one shall equally attain the thorough knowledge of all treatises and abundant goals arising from causes and fruits.
Whatever worldly mantras there may be, all of them in their full abundance— the wise practitioner who has mastered the mantra shall attain them all.
As many worldly mantras as there are, and even those of Śiva that are well-honored,
as well as the mantras belonging to the Great Self (Guru), are oriented toward the fruit of the accomplishment of the fire-oblation.
All worldly mantras, however, originate from Indra and Rudra;
they all become kings of mantras when bound according to the rules of ritual procedure.
Yama, Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Kubera, the Mothers, and Dayā—
this group consists of twelve, including Brahmā and Īśāna as the completers;
[and] Savitṛ, Śakra, the gods, and the Grandfather (Brahmā) as the great worshipers.
All those known as lords of the desire realm, who move among the gods of the mantra deities,
all come under control when the name of the Lord of Mantras is uttered.
I am the self-ruler of those who dwell in fire, of the denizens of heaven and the inhabitants of the waters,
and of those who take refuge in the palaces of the cardinal directions as well as those who roam in the intermediate quarters.
Furthermore, those great-iddhi serpents who dwell in the vault of the sky above and in the realms of the underworld below have taken refuge in the paths.
Situated within the lap of the Himālaya mountains, she rests upon the slopes of the Vindhya range,
on that famous great mountain, a wondrous and excellent repository of great minerals.
It was crowded with various hosts of gods, frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*,
filled with the songs of throngs of *apsarases*, and as radiant as Mount Sumeru illuminated by the sun.
Whatever nāgas reside here, whatever hosts of spirits take refuge here,
those of diverse forms, or those who have gathered from that place—
all of them come under control when joined with this mantra.
And whatever divine hosts of mantras there are that cause fear to all beings,
they all come under control when joined with this mantra.
In mountain caves and difficult strongholds, with various interior recesses,
they dwell upon the earth in palaces resembling gold.
The various captivating people, presiding over hosts of all beings,
[are found] in their dwellings as proclaimed.
Presiding over hosts of divine beings, they possess diverse forms;
indeed, all these hosts of beings roam upon the surface of the earth.
They possess various primary forms and diverse bases consisting of material shapes;
they abide in various modes of contemplation and wear diverse garments and ornaments.
All those [beings] were seen by him on the path as he proceeded with the foremost mantra—
the leader of all worldly mantras of great supernatural power.
The supreme Lord who brings all beings under his control wanders about;
he is the chief among all lords of mantras, including Yama, Rudra, Indra, and Vāsava.
Then the Lord of Mantras, the foremost one, the leader of all worldly beings,
sustains from all sides the mantras and the most abundant ritual manuals (kalpas).
This Lord Mantreśvara is the sovereign and king of all mantras;
he, the master of all obstacle-lords, should be remembered by all reciters of mantras. He alone is proclaimed as the fierce lord of fierce mantras.
In all the Śaiva tantras, one should always recite the conduct of all beings and even their cries through all worldly activities; indeed,
this should be employed at all times by practitioners who desire spiritual accomplishment.
Then the bird Vainateya, the king of birds endowed with great power, having bowed to the daughter of the Supreme Victor,
as well as to Mañjuśrī and all the sons of the Buddhas,
spoke these sweet words.
Speak, speak, O Great Being, you who are well-ascertained in the profound meaning!
You are established in the supreme Dharma, the reality of the selflessness of phenomena.
I have spoken of the extensive ritual manual, which is the domain of the meaning of the root mantras;
it should be known that, in brief, this is the most supreme among all mantras.
This mantra, which is praised by all, was spoken by me for use in all ritual accomplishments even among worldly mantras; it is not an internal mantra.
By the sons of the Victors, the great heroes, and by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas,
no other mantra more supreme than this is applied with their intelligence toward me.
With a face adorned by a slight smile, the steadfast one then spoke with a gentle voice;
he then uttered sweet words, which were beautified by being the very foundation of both sound and meaning.
This Suvarṇa has been described to you as the Lord of Dharma, the supreme among men;
he is the one who intends to release all mantras and the teacher of the selflessness of phenomena.
The Teacher of the World, the Great Hero, the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun,
the promulgator of all mantras, the supreme Lord of Mantras, the Excellent One.
The Lord, whose sole purpose is the welfare of others, the Sovereign of the Dharmadhātu, the Guru,
acts out of compassion for all sentient beings and for the arising of our own happiness.
Having reached the limit of phenomena, he is the ultimate, the non-abiding limit of reality;
this one of great splendor quickly proclaims [the truth] to you regarding all mantras.
This is the thirty-ninth chapter, the *Garuḍapaṭala*, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now follows the forty-second detailed chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Mañjuśrī, there exists within the ritual procedures for the mandala that serves as the means for all your accomplishments, and within all mantra-tantras, a secret chapter on mudrās and the commitments (samaya). By means of these, one does not transgress any of the commitments; one becomes one who has entered and been impelled by the commitment into all mundane and supramundane mandalas. In all mantra-tantras that serve as the means for general accomplishment, all [practitioners] are well-awakened to that which is most supremely secret, most supremely auspicious, and most supremely wonderful and marvelous. Without these, it is impossible to propitiate or accomplish any mantras.
In the past, all the Tathāgatas have spoken it;

now I too shall speak it for the sake, benefit, and happiness of all sentient beings, out of compassion for the world, for the sake of the great mass of people, and so that all reciters of mantras may enter the cloud of the Dharma of the Great Vehicle—which is the treasury of great mantras, eternal, zealous, inconceivable, and characterized by selflessness—into the Dharmadhātu. And what is that which I shall speak?
Listen, Mañjurava, to the secret mudrā accompanied by all [the mantras],
which is to be spoken by oneself exactly as it was formerly sung by the supreme sages.
Indeed, one who seeks the secret mantras should always employ this supreme host of all mudrās at all times and in all rites within the maṇḍala.
Then the glorious Mañjurava, with eyes like lotuses, smilingly gazed upon the Sugata, the most excellent, the Lord and Master of all dharmas.
With palms joined in reverence, the heroic son of the Jina, possessed of great supernatural power,
spoke these sweet words adorned with divine sounds and meanings.
Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! You who proclaim for the Lord the mantra that follows the Wheel of Dharma and which consists of the true meaning of the reality of phenomena.
Having thus spoken to the Sugata, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men,
the glorious Mañjurava then remained silent in that interval.
Thus spoke the Blessed Buddha, the Lord of the Dharmadhātu, at that time:
"Listen, O hosts of spirits, and all you assemblies of gods of great supernatural power!"
For those mortals on earth who draw mandalas on the ground— whether they be poor or suffering—
you shall be present for them as the mudrās drawn upon the earth.
And those mudrās which have indeed been taught by the best of sages for all the Buddhas, for the Pratyekabuddhas, the Arhats, and for the Śrāvakas;
The mudrās of all worldly beings belong to the Victors, the Lotus family, and the Vajra-holders;
indeed, all mudrās are to be employed everywhere in all rites. I shall now describe them in brief for the sake of all practitioners of mantra.
Whatever mantra was previously taught for all mandalas and ritual activities—
whether it be the site, the fire offering, the recitation, or the rite— one should employ that very same one accordingly.
At the beginning of the maṇḍala, this seal manifested by the Buddha should be drawn:
a white parasol for the Buddhas, blazing all around, and then the ornaments.
It is adorned all around with five-colored powders and embellished with jewels;
it is most excellent, radiant with various colors, and possesses a splendor like that of a rainbow.
This is the seal, the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), the supreme head-born [emanation] of the Buddhas;
to its right is the bowl, encircled on all sides by a garland of light.
Immediately following that, the khakhavaraka, the fang, the jīvarajas,
the śrīvatsa, the svastika, and also the wheel and the water-pot are described.
The sages, the best of the world, have declared that the book is the banner (*dhvaja*), the cloth (*patākā*) is in between them, and the bell is the mudrā born of the west.
To the left of the parasol is a lotus, between them is a jewel-seal, and within that is a vajra; they say it arises in the form of a three-pronged trident.
Utpala is indeed Gatāmudra; he is Salila, who is supported by water;
and Toya is at the end of that, truly supported by the streams of water.
At its end, two earrings are to be known, beautiful ornaments and likewise splendid;
at its end, moreover, is a great mountain, radiant with four jewels.
At its end, a great ocean should be drawn, variegated and radiant with colors;
at its end, moreover, a great tree, bearing fruit and adorned with leaves.
This tree is the Mahāmudrā; on the left side is the Jāntajā.
Then there is the Sitātapatra, which is declared to be the most excellent and powerful mudrā of the Buddhas.
In the case of mantras, the excellent one for the Khaḍgins is to be known as that of the Pratyekajinas;
indeed, the excellent mudrā of the robe is said to belong to all the Śrāvakas.
In the world, the fang of the noble Arhats is indeed celebrated;
the Śrīvatsa is intended as the mudrā representing the attainment of the fruit thereof in the world.
The *khakharaka* is the great seal (*mahāmudrā*), and another is that born from the solitary victors (*pratyekajina*).
Then there is the seal of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*), which indeed shatters all views;
this is declared to be the seal of Dharma, and it is known to arise from the casting away of the agent.
In this world, the Perfection of Wisdom, the relics of the Victor, the seal, and the book,
as well as the banner and the flag— these two great seals— are proclaimed as honored by the world.
The two of great heroism are for the attraction of all; both originate from the uṣṇīṣa.
The bell is the final mudrā, and the hair on the crown belongs to the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
In the Buddha-mudrā, however, there is indeed a lotus in the left hand, born from Lokeśa;
likewise, the Muni-mudrā is to be known for one who has attained Samantajyotis.
The vajra is the mudrā of the wise Vajrin;
the utpala is that of Mañjughoṣa; and the earring is that of Kṣitigarbha.
The mudrā called Mahātoya is taught in the Gaganālaya;
then there is this Mahāśaila mudrā, which destroys all views.
Mahodadhi is likewise a seal, O son of the Sugata; Sāgara is likewise a seal, proclaimed as renowned throughout the world. Mahāvṛkṣa is likewise a seal, celebrated and famous in the world.
And one should draw all the sons of the Victors in the abode of the three realms; this mudrā, as described by the Victorious One, should be drawn in the place situated near the bell.
The seal of all seals, arising from a square shape,
variegated, endowed with colors, beautiful in hue, and resplendent.
Adorned with jewels on all sides,
garlanded with flames, blazing, radiant with five colors, and auspicious.
Rising in the form of a mass, auspicious and resembling the sun and moon,
shining with great splendor—
this mudrā is of great heroism, the auspicious abode of all mantras.
For the three types of mantras— superior, middling, and inferior—
this place is declared to be the foremost mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all rites;
within this, one should draw the maṇḍala containing the great mudrā.
Whichever mantra is prescribed for a particular maṇḍala renowned in the world,
that very one should be drawn in the center, like a parasol upon the surface of the earth.
In the center of that mandala, one should likewise depict either an image or a mudrā;
the images should be painted as granting boons, as well as the manifestation of Mañjughoṣa.
Indeed, all the lords of mantras and the meanings of all mantras always [reside] on earth; otherwise, one should not draw the mudrās as prescribed by the ritual procedures.
The wise say that when those two [hands] are placed upon it with full jars, it is called "Victory" (vijaya);
moreover, the practitioner should draw the mudrā on the outside of the maṇḍala.
In the second mandala, the reciter should remain in all the aforementioned previously designated places, throughout every direction and intermediate direction.
The wise one should draw the mudrās of all the gods, sages, yakṣas, and garuḍas; he should also draw those of the piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
He [overcomes] the established views of the non-Buddhist heretics, the Kinnaras, the Kaṭapūtanas,

the Kravyādas, and the Vyantaras, along with the Kūṣmāṇḍas; he overcomes the Dūṣakas and those who exert themselves in the hells, all sentient beings, the Bhūtas, and those born in the realms of form, formlessness, and desire.
In the second mandala, one should always draw the supreme, eternal mudrā arising from the gods of the formless realm (ārūpya), which originates from the shape of a triangle.
Extending toward the eastern direction and embracing a brilliant line—
this is said by the primordial Buddhas to be the mudrā born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) belonging to the great-siddhis of the foremost gods of the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
Then, O Lotus-born Brahmā, they say that the mantra situated on the two lines further to the north is the Rūpāvacara within the abode of the three worlds.
That very same line extending from the center of the maṇḍala toward the outside,
resting upon the southern direction, is the excellent Mudrā Kāmaja.
This mudrā was taught by the foremost of sages for the supreme lord of the desire realm; it has been manifested in the world within the abode of all the gods.
[She is] the one who has Rudra, Indra, and Vasu as her foremost [disciples], whose disciples are Viṣṇu and Tīrthya, who is sky-clad (Digambara), who possesses the Sun,
Vāsava, and medicinal herbs, and who is marked by the signs of the Sun and Yama.

One should likewise draw all those world-protectors outside in their respective directions according to the orientation of the temple, and one should apply the corresponding mudrās in the same manner.
Whosoever is renowned as the vehicle of another, the mudrā representing that [deity] is prescribed by those honored by the world as bearing the same weapon and attire.
This group of mudrās has indeed been taught as entirely supramundane and auspicious;
furthermore, it is effective for all mundane activities everywhere.
The principal mudrās and all the mudrās for practitioners of mantra have been taught;
they should be drawn upon the ground by mortals who recite mantras and desire spiritual accomplishments.
"One who desires to obtain the essence of enlightenment."

Thus concludes the "Means for Accomplishing All Rituals" from the forty-first chapter of the Great King of Ritual Manuals, extracted from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the forty-third chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Pure Dwellers (*Śuddhāvāsabhavana*), addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Mañjuśrī, in your maṇḍala ritual, for all rites, for all tantras and mantras, and in all activities such as summoning, dismissal, recitation, observances, fire-offerings, accomplishments, and protective rites—there is a single Great Seal (mahāmudrā) which is the sole Great Hero, spoken of and rejoiced in by incalculable millions of Buddhas. And what is that?
Listen, O glorious Mañjurava, whose intellect perceives the profound meaning and the supreme reality;
by binding this, all practitioners of recitation [attain their goal].
The Mahāmudrā is of great merit, esteemed as a supreme auspiciousness;
its merit is equal to that of Great Brahmā, purifying and destroying all evil.
The supreme state of great security, the unshakable realm of nirvāṇa— auspicious, peaceful, most excellent, cooled, and the ultimate refuge.
He is renowned as the Lord of all mudrās, born from the crown of all mudrās;
he is known as the Protector, the Lord of all tantras, within the abode of the three worlds.

And it is powerful, threefold, and divine; even among those [relics] that are terrestrial and celestial, it is the manifest sign of the Buddha himself, the all-pervading refuge for all sentient beings.
O King of Mudrās, you who are eternally nourished within the three worlds by all mudrās,
you should always provide protection for those who recite mantras in all their ritual activities.
This renowned anti-demon elixir is auspicious and a destroyer of sins;
it is preeminent in all rites and a warder-off of malevolent beings.
This Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is proclaimed in the world as the tamer of those difficult to tame;
it is indeed effective for all mantras belonging to practitioners throughout three lifetimes.
He destroys all obstacles for practitioners in every rite everywhere;
at that very moment, he causes the mantras residing in the three sources to descend.
It leads that world back again and indeed destroys it;
it causes everything to fall everywhere across the entire surface of the earth.
Furthermore, the mudrā is fixed by means of actions such as binding and obstructing;
it is known among practitioners in the abode of the three worlds as the mudrā of crushing, uprooting, drying up, destroying, and likewise reviving the life-force.
And in rites of pacification, this Great Seal (mahāmudrā) is employed;
it is auspicious among all mantras, pure, stainless, and a destroyer of sins.
It accomplishes all aims in the world, renowned and supreme above all.
The supramundane mantras are superior to mundane ones;
they are the most excellent for all purposes, as well as for rites of pacification and enrichment.
The *mudrā* that leads to eternal security is employed by all mantra-practitioners;
for this *graha*, when joined with all mantras, is indeed said to be eternally invincible.
Established in the lineage, abiding at the limit of reality, the sovereign of the realm of phenomena, self-born, ineffable yet expressible, the syllable-less, eternally the syllable-less.
Abiding in the selflessness of phenomena, unarisen yet the source of what has arisen,
free from passion, immovable, and ultimately established as empty by its very nature.
Likewise, Akaniṣṭha is the eldest; it is auspicious for those going to nirvāṇa, the path to unsurpassed awakening, and the source of the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats.
Likewise, he is the cloud of Dharma, peaceful, and from whom the waters of the army have issued;
he knows the ultimate reality and the supreme truth, and fulfills the purpose of both aims.
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), possessed of great majesty, arisen from all the Buddhas;
he of great purpose and great heroism, the solitary hero of great supernatural power.
It accomplishes the purpose of all activities;
it is endowed with many excellent forms and arises in many forms.

It is the knower of the state of omniscience, the object of knowledge that is entirely without remainder, the ultimate, the wisdom, the knowable, the great destroyer, proclaimed, and adorned by the best of sages.
Worshipped by all beings and gods, and honored by the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats,
this is the supreme Dharma of the Great Seal, the unshakeable, highest state.
First of all, in a pure place— whether at a solitary tree, on a great mountain,
or on the delightful shore of the great ocean— one should resort to a consecrated sacrificial ground.
Whether by a river, at a well, or on a sandy bank, in a beautiful temple of the gods,
in the abode of the Enemy of Māra, or in a monastery, a dwelling, or a palace;
In a secluded place, sprinkled and swept clean, adorned with heaps of flowers,
sprinkled with fragrant scented water, and perfumed with excellent incense;
For rites of pacification and enrichment, one should face either the east or the north;
however, for fierce rites in the south, that direction is always avoided by the Jinas.
For the sake of attaining prosperity, good fortune, and subjugation, one should always perform the goat-sacrifice without cause;
thereafter, one should bind the supreme and most excellent Mahāmudrā with its face turned westward.
When a practitioner, holding high views for the sake of attaining a physical body, rises toward the Buddha,
he may descend to the netherworld (pātāla) and attain the state of a lord of the asuras.
With pure bodily conduct, possessing pure mantras and knowing the application of mantras,
one should then employ the supreme mudrā after bathing, sipping water, and having performed the recitation with a focused mind.
Both hands should always be washed with pure water that is clean, free from insects and small creatures, and scented with clay, cow dung, and fragrant substances.
When both hands have been washed with fresh water and purified, and are thus honored,
they should be joined together in a fist-like position, formed into the gesture of a hollowed casket.
Slightly hollow on all sides, six finger-breadths in height,
situated between both thumbs, and bent by the little fingers.
Then, having placed it upon the region of the heart covered with a white cloth,
one should show it in all ritual actions for the sake of accomplishment.
Indeed, for all beings, whatever is desired is quickly accomplished merely by drawing [this seal];
this is the Mañjurava mudrā, the accomplisher of the purpose of all rites.

Thus concludes the second chapter, the extensive section on the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which serves as the means for accomplishing all supreme rites, from the forty-first chapter of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the forty-fourth detailed chapter.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again surveyed the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, [proclaimed] this most secret chapter on mudrās, which is the seal of the countless Victors established at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), adorned with the inconceivable array of excellent qualities of the Dharma-treasure of all Tathāgatas; which serves as the sign for all sentient beings; which is fashioned according to the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of all worldly and transcendent auspicious mantras and tantras; which has become the path for the engagement of all sentient beings in the vision of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); which is common to all mantras and all designations; which fulfills all hopes of all sentient beings in this very life; which is the cause of supreme bliss through the propitiation of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and the completion of the equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*); which effects the summoning, dismissal, and the offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, garlands, and gifts; which brings about the entry of the sciences (*vidyā*) and the manifestation of the sciences; which accomplishes all purposes and goals; which subdues and governs all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, and kūṣmāṇḍas—whether fierce or gentle; which reveals the presiding lords of all functions, the blazing [powers], the ability to travel through space, invisibility, and the power of subjugation; which is a marvelous and wonderful cause for the equipment of enlightenment; which is guided by the purpose of all mantra-tantras; which is honored by all the Kings of Sciences (*vidyārāja*); which accomplishes all sciences; which is invoked by the mothers of all Buddhas; which fulfills the desires and wishes of sentient beings according to their needs; which produces the causes for the immediate realization of all mantras—in short, however it is applied and however it is practiced, it accomplishes accordingly.
"Mañjuśrī, I shall speak this chapter on the ultimate truth, which is the most profound secret of all the Buddhas.
It was spoken by all the Buddhas of the past, and the Blessed Buddhas of the future will speak it;
now I shall speak it—listen, O Mahāsattva, for I shall speak."
"Listen to that, O Mahāsattva; I shall speak.
Pay close and careful attention, Mañjurava! I shall speak—of wondrous eloquence, I shall speak!"
The Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men, the perfectly awakened one, the supreme among sages,
