having realized the welfare of beings, perceives the ultimate reality.
O bull among sages, you indeed speak of the secret mudrās for the sake of the essential meaning,
in the delightful city of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, which is inhabited by pure beings.
Then, in that excellent assembly of the foremost sages, in the abode of those free from passion,
when the King of Rituals (*Kalparāja*) concerning the reality of Mañjubhāgīna was being spoken.
Then the sons of the Buddha, those ministers who were wise and knew the ultimate truth, said to the assembly:
"Listen to this discourse!"
The Son of the Buddha, the eldest, who possesses the supreme dharma of the Mahāyāna, indeed spoke these excellent words: "He is truly named Samantabhadra."
"You are described by the Victors as a youth, possessing both the form of a child and a great form;
born in the lineage of the Śākyas, skillful and glorious, you are beheld as a Buddha."
For you, O one of universal great wisdom, out of a desire to favor the world,
have [revealed] this extensive collection of ritual manuals of yours, which is sealed with mudrās.
O son of the Buddha, possessed of great supernatural power, entreat the Great Hero,
who is the very essence of this eon and endowed with great supernatural power.
Thus addressed by the heroic and wise son of the Buddha,
Mañjuśrī quickly manifested himself as a child engaged in play.
Having prostrated before the Sugata, the Protector, the sole eye of the world,
he spoke these sweet words with a voice moistened by compassion.
May the Blessed One, the Buddha, who knows the reality of the power of wisdom,
explain how all mantras are certainly accomplished for those who recite them.
How indeed do they go unfailingly for living beings through non-conceptualization? How could they achieve success when merely cast or muttered, without being applied to all purposes?

From the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, and all those living beings who depend upon these realms within the threefold world— half of which consists of the desire realm— they are all included.
They are summoned, restrained, and possessed while being watched;
and they are employed for all ritual actions through the means that cause satisfaction and nourishment.
Those who abide on the ten stages and stand upon the path of the Sugata— the awakened Bodhisattvas, or those who rely on the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha— [all pay homage].
The great-souled ones who have transcended passion are summoned when they are well-honored;
they are joined by mantras and sealed with these mudrās.
The yogins speak according to reality— whether independent or seeing— concerning what has occurred in the past, what has not occurred, and what is occurring in the present.

The inconceivable accounts of the heavenly realm, as well as those concerning other bodies, have been described; likewise, the future has been depicted exactly as it truly is, along with illustrative examples.
When impelled by mantra and mudrā, they speak according to the proper rule; likewise, when worshipped with mudrās, they swiftly bestow accomplishment.
Endowed with ministers who are experts in mantras, and having been well-honored with offerings and oblations,
the Buddhas and likewise the sons of the Buddha will bring about accomplishment most swiftly.
Even the great-souled Arhats, as well as the Khaḍgins, are always bestowers of success;
this applies both to worldly mantras and to other, transcendent ones.
And those who are Siddhas, as well as Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kinnaras;
Asuras, Suras, and always Sattvas—all beings are established in these three categories.
In these infinite directions and within the various world-systems,
there are sentient beings throughout the five destinies who are always engaged in what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
They shall swiftly attain accomplishment when well-sealed with these mudrās;
this is known as the "Stainless" [mantra], proclaimed by the Sugatas, the knowers of mantras, and the sages.
The *viṭaka* should be known according to the rule, as well as the *visara*, the supreme chapter;
these were proclaimed by all the Buddhas in the world for the sake of the highest good.
The wise Mañjughoṣa declared this five-crested mudrā, revealed by all the Buddhas for the sake of the welfare of living beings.
It should be known that [hair] growing everywhere is "head-born," while that which grows from the crown belongs to the Tathāgatas;
it should be known that this bestows all goals and fulfills the treasury of the Dharma.
Furthermore, for the purpose of fulfilling the mantras and mudrās, there is that which possesses great supernatural power—
the most excellent among all mundane and supramundane [practices] at all times.
In the Mañjughoṣa tantra, however, this [practice] is considered the foremost and most excellent;
by its power, one shall swiftly accomplish all activities according to their purpose.
Having become pure, one should bind the supreme Lord mudrā in a pure place;
first, indeed, having made the two hands hollow and joined like a casket.
With the thumbs slightly separated from the palms and the thumbs placed [on the fingers], it is indicated by "tha";
with the five fingers arranged as five prongs, it becomes the *pañcaśikhā* mudrā.
Always placed at the location of the head with one finger-breadth [of space],
the Evacīrā mudrā is indeed applied to the locations on the crown of the head.
The little fingers are placed together, the two middle fingers are likewise closely joined,
and both thumbs are extended like needles.
From the union of the three needle-like forms, the triple-crested mudrā is proclaimed.
With all the fingers joined together, hollowed out by the formation of a cavity,
when this mudrā is always placed at the position of the head, it becomes the supreme head-mudrā.
That same [mudrā], with the fingers raised and their tips slightly bent, is to be known as Mahāvīrā; it is a great mudrā of great supernatural power.
These five great mudrās were previously taught by the excellent Victors;
thus do the two wise ones declare regarding all mudrās.
Jyeṣṭhā is the foremost among those with sealed faces;
she is indeed transcendent, surpassing all worldly ones in every respect.
These five great mudrās are the applications that cause accomplishment;
they are well-accomplished and most perfectly accomplished, for they have been declared as supreme and foremost,
possessing the power of Mañjughoṣa’s crest-jewel and his wondrous activities.
As many as there are mudrās of the Sugatas, all of which are causes for accomplishment—
what is renowned as "mudrā, mudrā" is the glorious Kisalayodbhava.
The hair-tuft of Mañjughoṣa is supremely meritorious and auspicious;
by binding it, great beings will certainly attain enlightenment.

One should always perform ritual actions according to the rules for that faithful person, whose faculties are unimpaired, who is adorned with great leaders, and who is ever joined with wisdom through sacrifice.
When properly joined with a being endowed with such qualities,
this mudrā indeed accomplishes all desired objectives in abundance.
However, through instruction, those who are wise, discerning, and effective in achieving their goals—
such disciples approved by the teacher should always be accepted in this world.
In this world, by a person who has observed the ritual actions and is endowed with devotion,
this mudrā is always employed by those who have entered the Mahāyāna.
When applied to mantras in three ways,
all these mudrās are indeed the foremost and most excellent in the world by virtue of their power.
For the sake of accomplishment for those desiring success, these [mantras], when properly joined with other mantras,
quickly fulfill one's purpose and bestow the fruit of all happiness.
Mañjughoṣa himself abides, composed in these mudrās;
in whatever place one performs these, Mañjurava himself is always present.
The Son of the Conqueror, possessed of great supernatural power, should indeed arrange this supreme protection;
he is a Great Being appearing in the form of a child, yet possessing great supernatural power and assuming various forms.
He appears in many forms for sentient beings, and in the form of mudrās for those embodied ones;
yet for foolish beings wandering in the ocean of saṃsāra, he appears as such.
Acting for their benefit, he quickly remains in the form of a seal (mudrā),
born from the head of Mañjughoṣa and established upon the crown of every head.
For by merely reciting these, joined with the root mantra or followed by the heart-mantra, all goals are indeed accomplished.
All those mantras belonging to the Lotus family,
as well as those of the Vajra-holder and the one with matted hair, are well-united with the Saugati mantras.
When joined with all worldly mudrās as well, they bestow the fruit of the intended purpose;
these five great mudrās, when joined with mantras, bestow the fruit of the intended purpose.
Having abandoned that which is to be conceptualized as residing in mantras, it yields fruit through mudrās;
it is a great protection and a source of great merit for embodied beings by its mere binding.
By merely recollecting these great mudrās, great protection is established;
how much more so when they are employed while reciting the mantras and relying upon the mudrās?
Or rather, all those who perform the recitation shall certainly attain enlightenment;
furthermore, there are other great mudrās originating from the trident and the spear.
Now, among the mudrās, the Great Spear (Mahāśūla) is declared to be most terrible and fierce;
it is employed here by the principal Wrathful King, Yamāntaka.
He performs various dreadful deeds that deprive living beings of their lives and bestow great terror, even upon a high-souled Vipasvin.
Created for the destruction of wicked beings within the three realms of existence,
various mantras have been joined with those very [beings], relying upon diverse mudrās.
These were always created by the supreme Victors for their very destruction;
they were devised for the purpose of the teaching, endowed with the meaning of mantra practice.
The mudrās, which reveal the meaning of the tantras, have been taught by the Lords of the World as a remedy for the poison,
sin, and diseases employed by wicked beings.
It was taught for the very purpose of destroying them, performing all rites;
for the destruction of Yama’s command and for liberation from the noose of death.
This mudrā, when employed constantly in conjunction with the mantra, is known as the destroyer of the messengers of Yama;
it is meritorious and the annihilator of death.
She is known as the giver of life who brings back those led by the command of Yama;
for the sake of destroying all diseases, she even strikes fear into Yama himself.
Likewise, this life-sustaining [practice], when joined with the foremost sages, is beneficial;
for those who have faith in this teaching, protection is ordained for their welfare.
The Goddess Mahāmudrā is celebrated as fruitful, destructive of the wicked, delightful in sound, beneficial, and the bestower of all goals.
Regarding the great weapon, they say there is another, the supreme among mudrās:
likewise, having placed the hands together, the two index fingers should be formed into a noose.
The two little fingers should always indicate [the deity] when joined by the fist-method;
the hands are always joined in the hollowed-cup gesture (sampuṭita), with both thumbs raised.
This mudrā is of great merit; it is joined with the Great Spear (mahāśūla) and arises from various weapons produced by the Lords of the World.
If a practitioner of recitation should think of the weapons of an enemy, by that very thought he would cut off the enemy's limb; it would happen simply from the arising of that thought.
When applied together, mudrās and mantras will certainly destroy the enemy;
they shall strike down all hosts of enemies, even those possessing great supernatural power.
The hosts of Yama’s messengers, obstacles, and planetary spirits, along with the Mothers,
Pūtanās, Skandas, Rudras, and highly powerful pretas.
Having recited [this] over the worlds of Vaivasvata and the entire realm including Indra,
one should employ no other mantra than the wrathful king Yamāntaka.
One should employ these mudrās, which are equal to great thunderbolts;
they would instantly destroy even Vaivasvata Yama—how much more so mere humans on earth?
This is the seal (mudrā) that wields all weapons, which destroys all that is evil;
it was established by the World-Leaders, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, the supreme among bipeds.
In that same way, having placed the hands together, one should form [the mudrā] by relying on the middle fingers;
likewise, having positioned the hands here, one should form it by means of the fist-union.
The tips of the two thumbs are pressed together,
joined by the fingers with their hollows facing downward, while the middle fingers are raised.
Likewise, with the two index fingers always resting upon the tips of the needle-like [middle fingers],
this excellent and formidable mudrā is called "the Trident" by the best of sages.
When both index fingers are slightly bent, it is the Mahāśūla;
when extended, it is known as the Paṭṭiśa—the supreme and excellent Great Mudrā.
When those same fingers are contracted at the tips and raised by three finger-breadths,
the wise declare this to be the *triśūla-mudrā* (trident mudrā).
These should be known as various weapons when both thumbs are raised;
for they are like great tridents, possessing great power and being terrifying.
In this supreme Mañjurava Tantra, for the sake of destroying evil beings,
these Great Mudrās of wondrous activity have been taught to subdue those who are difficult to tame.
They are fierce, life-taking, and born of deformed shapes;
most exceedingly terrible, they are wrathful and established in extreme cruelty.
The most formidable and excellent Jyeṣṭhā goddesses, possessing many forms, have been revealed;
everywhere, those Buddhas who recite their mantras are freed from old age and disease.
These perfected reciters always traverse these worlds;
they were ordained for the destruction of death by the perfectly awakened ones, the preeminent sages.
One should employ these, which destroy old age and disease, for the sake of destroying death;
when applied by practitioners of mantra, they are terrifying even to Death himself.
The glorious and supreme Lord created this mudrā in the excellent city of Śuddhāvāsa for the Lion of the Śākyas, the best of men and the son of the most excellent sage.

The Buddhas do not speak mantras, nor do they [teach] mudrās for those who perform cruel deeds; rather, out of affection for the sake of sentient beings and for the purpose of fulfilling the goal of omniscience, [they teach them].

Whether for the purpose of sporting with supernatural powers, as a cause for the equipment of enlightenment, for the sake of training beings through skillful means, or for the purpose of establishing them in the supreme Mahāyāna.
It fulfills the great saṃsāra; by the power of their resolve, it proclaims mantras and mudrās for sentient beings.

Even that which is called "space" is neither a Buddha nor conceived by speech; for those who are endowed with the reality free from conceptual proliferation, how could it be within the scope of discursive thought?
The ultimate limit is equal to the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and equal to the pinnacle of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);
for those joined with mantra, this is the ultimate seal (*mudrā*) that is thoroughly sealed.
They declare that it is always the cause for the liberation of the factors of existence;
it is called the seal of the Omniscient One, which fulfills the purpose of all-knowledge.

The seal and the sealing have been proclaimed by the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas— who possess inconceivable and inconceivable spheres of activity— for the purpose of honoring the meaning that is endowed with reason.
The mudrās of the All-Knowing Seer, such as the Uṣṇīṣa and others, have been manifested;
then there is the Avalokita-mudrā of Vajrapāṇi, and those that are worldly.
For the sake of the welfare of embodied beings, they have been spoken and will be spoken,
as long as the mudrās have been taught by the sons of the Buddha and the most excellent sages.
The seal that fulfills all aims is conceived through inconceivable power;
indeed, mantras have been taught in three ways for the sake of the conceptualization of beings.
There is but one mantra which has been spoken by the Buddhas; for the sake of the Sugatas' purpose, indeed, this single mantra is proclaimed among all mantras.
The glorious Lord of the Uṣṇīṣa is always of one color;
he becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin) eternally when the letter *ta* is joined with the letter *ra*.
Constantly joined with the letter *ū*, he is then proclaimed as the one endowed [with power];
he shall become the glorious Cakrin, the supreme head-born son of the Buddhas.
They say that the letter *ma* is the supreme mantra of the wise Son of the Buddha;
by its power it should be known as equal to that [mantra], and it is sung as having the meaning of the final syllable.
This renowned heart-essence of Mañjughoṣa, born from the crown of the Buddha's head,
should be known for its extraordinary power, great merit, and vast supernatural efficacy.
The mantra fulfills all aims;
the mudrā, when accompanied by the five-crested [gesture], fulfills the aims of both.

Either the five-crested mudrā or the two joined at the letter *ma* will cause one to realize the ultimate meaning; indeed, they grant both the goal in this very life and the enjoyment of worldly pleasures.
They say there is another mantra:
the letter *ja* joined with the letter *ra*, honored by the meaning of the *ava-uṣma* [vowels and sibilants].

This is indeed the supreme and foremost mantra, born from the head of the Lotus-bannered One; when joined with the excellent lotus mudrā, it is for the noble purpose of generating nourishment for those who seek prosperity.

It shall bring about the accomplishment of the rites for those who recite the mantra, as well as the fulfillment of all aims; furthermore, for the Vajrin, there are the mantras beginning with the syllable *Hraṃ* produced from the base of the arm and the head.
This most excellent and supreme mantra is indeed proclaimed as Caṇḍa;
when employed with the Vajrālaya mudrā, it shall accomplish the desired aims for those engaged in ritual action.
This mantra is a formidable tamer of the difficult-to-subdue and a cause of destruction;
one should perform the prescribed rite according to the stated meaning and for the purpose of the teaching.
One should not perform evil deeds out of a zeal for the suppression of sentient beings;
one should never employ the supreme mantra against those who are gentle-natured.
One should not abandon a being who has offended due to a minor fault, causing the destruction of that being's life;
one should not, out of delusion, act with such disregard toward creatures for their small transgressions.
For those with malicious minds toward the teaching, for the sake of inspiring faith in the faithless,
and for the sake of disciplining beings and subduing the flesh-eaters.
This supreme and foremost mantra has indeed been taught for the purpose of subduing the wicked and for the pacification of those with gentle natures; one should never employ it to take a life.
This supreme and excellent mantra is declared to be the foremost of all worldly mantras, even for the wielder of the vajra who possesses great supernatural power, among all worldly deities.
This other supreme mantra is indeed known as the crown of all worldly deities' mantras; therefore, Śiva is the single-syllabled one.
The Lord is the master of all worlds, yet he is the sovereign of worldly mantras;
the wise know him as Parameśvara, and the learned understand him as Svakāra.
All mantras whatsoever that are known as worldly are indeed bound within this mantra; thus they are honored everywhere.
These mudrās, prescribed by the best of sages, when applied everywhere,
are considered most auspicious, supreme, the foremost in the world, and composed.
Indeed, they include Īśvara and others, as well as the mothers of the planets such as Vipaśyin,
and the flesh-eating Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Kaṭapūtanas, Yakṣas, and so forth.
These mudrās have been proclaimed for Viṣṇu, whose banner is Garuḍa, and also for Brahmā; indeed, they are prescribed as beneficial for subduing those who are difficult to tame.
For these mudrās have been declared by the wise to be praiseworthy and auspicious;
they are the causes for subduing, enchanting, and attracting spirits and beings.
In a secluded place, always beautifully adorned with white flowers,
well-swept, and scented with the perfumes of the Siddhas, white sandalwood, and saffron;
Having worshipped the Lord Sugata, the Lion of the Śākyas, the one of great merit, the sovereign master of all mantras, with garlands of *jātī* flowers;
Having prostrated with devotion at all times before the Tathāgata, the Omniscient One,
as well as the Lord of Mantras, Lokeśa, and Vajrin, according to one's ability;
With a concentrated mind, one should pay homage in due order to the great-souled Mañjuśrī, the Lord of the Dharmadhātu, the Guru, as well as to all the Buddhas and their sons.
Seated upon a beautiful, moist bundle of *kuśa* grass or a sprout accompanied by milk, he, being pure, faces the east.

In rites for peace, one should face north; however, in the subsequent invocation, one should not face that direction. One should perform all ritual acts in accordance with the temple of the respective deity.
Engaged with all beings and compassionate in the performance of mudrās, one who has applied mudrās everywhere shall accomplish every sādhanā.
Facing east, one should certainly perform rites for prosperity and the summoning of mantras;
however, facing west, one should perform all rites for subjugation and for the sake of worldly beings.
One should know that when facing north, it is for pacification (śāntika) rites which destroy all diseases;
however, one should never perform sinful acts or those that cause the end of life while facing south.
Above, there is the destruction of obstacles; arise, O Lord of Pātāla, you who grant the highest siddhi! At that time, perform the rite in the city of the Asuras.
And she should face downwards everywhere, being unopposed by anyone;
and in all intermediate directions, wherever she may have resorted.
One should perform these in each respective case; they bring success for all embodied beings.
One who has performed the recitation should perform the ritual of the mudrās everywhere, together with the fire sacrifice.
Those situated therein attain accomplishment, as do those who are sealed by its mouth;
let the supreme procedure be told—listen to it!
Having become pure in body and pure in clothing, composed in the purity of happiness,
one should employ this mudrā, which accomplishes all aims and is perfectly concentrated.
Raising both hands, one should [anoint them] with fragrances such as white sandalwood and saffron,
and with excellent incenses free from animal products, including camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.

One who knows the ritual should prepare excellent incense with *yukti*, saffron, and other primary ingredients; having offered various oblations, one should always perform the rites according to the prescribed rules.
One should perform the ritual previously specified as taught in all the ritual manuals;
then, facing eastward, one should place both hands together in the gesture of a hollowed cup.
Then, having joined them together one with another, they stand with the fingers interlaced;
the middle, ring, and little fingers are joined at their tips.
The two thumbs should be known as motionless, equal, and firmly established;
then, one should place them with devotion at the forehead, in the region of the head.
The salutation, as well as the mantra joined with the six syllables:
the word "Oṃ" followed by the word "Namaḥ," devoid of the utterance of "Svāhā."
One should always recite the heart-mantra, which is free from the sound "huṃ," supreme, eternally free from the sound "phaṭ," pure, auspicious, and foremost.
O Mañjuvara, this most excellent [mantra] for the one of beautiful form in the guise of a child is proclaimed as my heart-mantra, which subsequently assumes all forms.
These six are to be known as the six-syllable mantras, the most excellent and supreme among heart-mantras; indeed, this one is the foremost of them all, effective in all ritual actions.
One should employ this supreme mudrā-mantra in all ritual actions;
having placed it on the crown of the head, one should apply it to the region of the forehead with due skill.
One should move the middle fingers for the sake of subjugating all spirits;
and for the sake of attracting a deity, both tips of the thumbs should be bent inward.
Having constantly dismissed those very ones, one should dismiss the deity of the mantra,
as well as the middle and eldest [deities], the disciples, and the best of sages.
With the two index fingers perpetually bent, one summons without doubt the Bodhisattvas born from the vajra and those who are lords of the ten stages.
By joining the little fingers and contracting them at the call of Sarāh,
one [subdues] yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas.
When this mudrā is fully worshipped, it treats the hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, as well as the Yakṣiṇīs beloved by Kubera, like a mother.
That which eternally bestows gain and loss, as well as desirable and undesirable fruits,
is renowned as Mahāmudrā and is sung of throughout the abode of the three worlds.
The wise one who has bound this Mudrā and Mahāmudrā upon his head becomes invincible to all beings; of this there is no doubt.
From afar, all obstacles and hindering spirits pay homage from afar;
possessing merit equal to that of Great Brahmā, one will certainly attain awakening.
Thus concludes the forty-second detailed chapter on the Great Mudrās from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the forty-fifth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni again addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and spoke to the entire assembly of gods gathered in the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.

Listen, O assemblies of gods! This is the chapter on mudrās, which demonstrates the playful display of the great supernatural power, transformations, and miracles of Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; which satisfies beings according to their inclinations by manifesting his form as a youth; which brings about the attainment of the supreme Dharma of the Mahāyāna; which effects the ripening of sentient beings and joins them with the power of mudrās and mantras; and which fulfills their intentions. It is the most secret of all, the seed and the essence within all mantra-tantra rituals, the supreme mystery, and the greatest secret among the highest tantras. It is not to be revealed among all mundane and supramundane [teachings], but is to be strictly guarded and must not be given to those who are not disciples, nor to those lacking faith, those who have not generated the bodhicitta, the miserly, those devoted to other heretical systems, those who hate the supreme Dharma of the Mahāyāna, or those who have shown no respect for any of the mantra-tantras.

It is said that for those who understand the commitments (*samaya*) and have entered the Buddha’s teaching—those who are well-formed and well-attired, endowed with faith, possessing an unimpaired continuity of mind, and great enthusiasm; who are respectful toward all mantras; who show reverence toward all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, all gods, and their fellow practitioners; who are filled with esteem for sentient beings; who are girded with the great armor; who are exerting themselves in the endeavor to deliver the entire realm of sentient beings; who are greatly compassionate; and who possess patience, gentleness, and sweet speech—for these [the mantra] should be given, but for others it should not be given. And they say:
A single group of mudrās, when properly applied and joined with mantras,
performs various activities desired by the mind when directed by the practitioner.
Those who recite it and desire accomplishment should employ it at all times;
he is renowned throughout the three worlds by name as the "Unconquerable" (Ajita) among the Buddhas.
For this mudrā, known as Śrīvatsa, is renowned among all beings as a bringer of female fortune; it is the foremost among the eight hundred mudrās on earth.
O Mañjughoṣa, listen to me: one should know there are eight hundred mudrās, which were sung by the excellent Jinas of old and preserved by the sons of the Buddhas.
I shall speak daily of what is present and what is yet to come;
for the sake of the welfare of all, I shall rejoice in it and protect it throughout the three worlds.
Mañjughoṣa, likewise thrilled, spoke to the best of speakers:
"May the great-souled Buddhas, who are honored everywhere, please teach!"
Having heard this, wise men will certainly take recourse to awakening;
it is for all those engaged in recitation, fire-offerings, and vows.
"Mantras will certainly be accomplished when they are sealed by these mudrās.
I shall now entreat the Great Hero, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men."
For the sake of our sentient beings, it fulfills the purpose of the treasury of Dharma;
for the sake of the supreme teachings of the Mahāyāna, it accomplishes the purpose of mantra practice.
May the great heroes teach this meritorious, pure, and sin-destroying chapter concerning the origin of mudrās, which tames those who are difficult to tame.
It is for the sake of completing the mudrās, for the sake of indicating the deity,
and out of compassion for those who recite mantras.
Having spoken thus, Mañjuśrī, the Youth in the form of a child,
gazed upon the most excellent Sugata with a pleasant and beautiful voice.
O Vināyaka, that glorious and best of sages, whose voice was like the song of the kalaviṅka bird and whose resonance was like the thunder of clouds, spoke these sweet words.
With a voice like that of Brahmā, he addressed the assembly with these words:
"Listen, all you hosts of beings, to the mantra-deity for the sake of the kalpa."
The commitment of all the gods is supreme, as are their mudrās and deities;
[these are] for those who have transcended the Buddhas, namely the Pratyekabuddhas and the practitioners of Arhatship.
How much less, then, could it be known by other beings, whether they be worldly deities of knowledge or others;
for this one is proclaimed as the foremost among all mudrās.
All those who recite [this] in such a manner will certainly attain accomplishment from the deity:
first is that named Kisalaya, and the second is Mekhalā.
The third is Sumekhalā, the fourth is born of Sumanas,
the fifth they call Saṅkalā, and the sixth is proclaimed as Rekhā.
The seventh is to be known as Suvarṇā, and the eighth is Mālā;
the ninth is called Aṅkuśī, and the tenth has seventeen petals.
The eleventh day shall be Kuntā, the twelfth day Sukuntā;
the thirteenth day shall be Kardamī here, and the fifteenth day Paṭahī.
The sixteenth is the *yaṣṭi*, while the seventeenth they know as the *muṣṭi*;
the eighteenth is proclaimed as the *vajramālā*.
Hemamālā is the nineteenth, while Padmamālā is the twentieth; Nāgī and Nāgamukhī are indeed the [twenty-first and twenty-second], and Mahāmukhī is the third [of the three].
Vaktrā, together with Vaktra, becomes Lohitā the umbrella-bearer;
Lohitā is the twenty-eighth, while Sinī is blue-red.
The thirty-second [tīrtha] on earth is said to be Jyotsnājanitāmasī;
[the others are] Tārā, Sutārā, Tārāvartā, and Sumudrajā as well.
She who is renowned on earth as Locanā is the mudrā known as Mahāprabhā; she is of terrible form, famous as the night that is ever terrifying.
The number of mudrās is indeed proclaimed to be thirty-seven:
Śvetā, Paṇḍarā, Avalā, and Māmakī;
The goddess Bhrukuṭī is celebrated as the remover of great fear;
she is renowned as Ajitā, Aparājitā, Jayā, Vijayā, and Parājitā.
She is celebrated as Sādhakī, Sādhanī, and Śvetatārā; they call her Ghaṭakarparā, the Sugatī who purifies one's destiny.
The Lotus-Bearer and the Daughter of the Lotus, the Vajra-Bearer and she born from the Vajra-Mind—
their number as women is proclaimed as the host of mudrās for men.
The auspicious mudrā-seat, as well as the throne, the seat, and the bed upon the ground; the self-arisen wheel of Śambhu, and likewise the vajra and the mace.
The Svastika, the Liṅga-mudrā,
and the King of Birds, Garuḍa— these are to be known as the mudrās of Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Indra respectively.
Brahmā, born from the lotus, the glorious one, and Śrīsampuṭa;
likewise Tathya, Yamalamudra, and Mayūrāsana.
Known throughout all directions, the wise one who always bestows the aims of Kārttikeya should be understood as a follower of Mañjughoṣa, the Youthful One.
His seal is of great heroism; the wielder of the spear always employs those various seals, and this very peacock-seat seal is applied to him alone.
By binding this mantra of Kārttikeya according to the proper method,
one [subdues] as many worldly mudrās as there are, including those of Śiva and even those of Indra.
Indeed, by binding all [fingers], it is employed for the purpose of subjugation;
this hand-gesture (mudrā) brings about abundant and well-performed results.
He is pleased with the wise son of the Buddha, Mañjughoṣa;
having entered the teaching of the Buddha, he possesses great supernatural power while appearing in the form of a child.
Then Kārttikeya, renowned for his preeminence among both the primary and worldly mantras,
should be employed by all, and especially by the ignorant.
She was seized by the grahas, mātṛs, and kūṣmāṇḍas, by the kaṭapūtanas,
and by the daityas, dānavas, yakṣas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
He is the constant liberator from flesh-eaters and humans alike,
as well as from fierce beings, the wicked, and the flesh-consuming *vyantara* spirits.
When applied by humans who have been consecrated with seals, this seal is liberating;
it is joined with the welfare of all sentient beings, and when employed, it always bestows happiness.
This has been explained both briefly and in detail;
now I shall proclaim another mudrā, by binding which one becomes happy.
For the practitioner engaged in all rites, even when the mantra-recitation is not fruitless,
there is proclaimed the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) named Buddhāsana;
it is recited in detail across all tantras— understand it!
Having bound this, all reciters are destined for awakening as a certainty;
how much more so those who desire accomplishment and are intent on attaining enjoyments?
As before, being pure and of clean conduct, standing facing the east,
one should join both hands together in the form of an añjali;
then, with palms opened wide, one should extend both thumbs forward.
With the middle fingers joined together and marked by the shape of a coil,
one should then place them at the region of the navel while seated in the paryanka posture.
This supreme and most excellent of mudrās, when employed in all rites— whether superior, inferior, or middling— will bring about success.
For this, when accomplished, swiftly accomplishes one's aims and is applicable in all circumstances;
it is of great merit, purifying, auspicious, and the destroyer of evil.
This meritorious mudrā, which removes all sins, is the cause of spiritual accomplishments;
next, another mudrā is proclaimed, known as the Mahāmudrā.
Known by the name Śatruñjayī, she is the destroyer of all obstacles;
having bound this [mudrā], one will bring all enemies under control, without a doubt.
All desires come to exhaustion, or else they lead to servitude;
likewise, passion, hatred, and delusion, along with their own factions and their retinues.
Worldliness, envy, pride, doubt, and skepticism; negligence, deceit, laziness, seeking gain through others, and following wrong paths.
False view, pride, anger, arrogance, and greed—
these ten unwholesome paths of action are all remembered as enemies.

This host of enemies has been described by the Buddhas and those well-awakened ones; it consists of those living beings who rely upon various paths and states, and who destroy the teaching of the Buddha. Against them, the mudrās are employed.
This mudrā is the Great Mudrā (Mahāmudrā), which was always sung by the Buddhas of old;
it should indeed be employed for the sake of subduing living beings, as it destroys evil.
Standing in the same manner before [the deity], with both hands joined together and placed in a state of embrace,
having formed the shape of a hollowed palm (añjali),
one should quickly place both index fingers upon the pair of thumbs.
One should rest the two [fingers] joined in the shape of a coil upon the third joint;
this second mudrā, which accomplishes all aims, was taught by the Victors. It swiftly destroys the hearts of enemies who harbor malice.
I shall now proclaim the third mudrā; listen to it, Mañjughoṣa!
Known by the name Śalyaharī, it is divine and destroys all thorns [of affliction].
When applied everywhere, this mudrā is a healer of all diseases.
The defects caused by poison and weapons, those arising from water and fire, those produced by the wind, and those inflicted by malevolent beings and artificial poisons— [all these he neutralizes].
[It neutralizes] flesh-eating [beings], humans, and those with poison, whether stationary or moving;
and whatever thorns are located within the bodies of women who are about to give birth.
For other living beings who delight in saṃsāra and are afflicted by faults, he is the guide for all; likewise, while they are like thorns, he is indeed the one who extracts the thorn.
This seal, the Mahāmudrā, when remembered by all living beings, quickly becomes free from pain and brings happiness; of this there is no doubt.
By the power of this mantra, those mortals, through its mere name,
roam upon the surface of the earth completely freed from all diseases.
And as before, being of pure conduct, clean, and with clean garments,
one should then bind the third, most excellent and supreme mudrā, which destroys evil.
Joining both hands together so as to form a reversed shape,
with palms even and clearly visible in the form of an *añjali*, one should place them at the location of the heart.
This is the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), which wards off all calamities;
by binding it, all practitioners of recitation are destined for enlightenment.
But one should designate the fourth as Mahāmudrā, the great yakṣī;
she is to be known as possessing great power among all mantras for those who recite them.
Here, all the hosts of yakṣas and yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power—
whether among all the deities of mantra they be superior, inferior, or middling— are to be worshipped by all sentient beings; this mudrā is proclaimed for that purpose.
Having first bound [the mudrā], one should recite the mantra during rites for performing fire offerings;
thus applied everywhere, this meritorious [mudrā] shall accomplish all mantras.
Vajrapāṇi, as well as the mantra-master, is indeed the sovereign of all mudrās;
this was recited in the past by the ancient and supreme Lords of the World.
In the same way, having become pure and standing facing north,
the reciter should then bind the most excellent and supreme mudrā for all rites,
for the sake of subduing all spirits.
Just as he quickly performs this, which is the activity of a sentient being on earth,
one should then place both hands joined together in the shape of a hollowed casket.
One should form the shape of a three-pronged needle with the thumbs, the little fingers, and the middle fingers; these four should be joined together and then bent toward one another.
One should indeed perform the excellent mudrā as described, positioned at the location of the head;
upon seeing it, all beings will undoubtedly flee.
But the fifth is Mahāmudrā; listen always, O Mañjurava, for she is known by the name Trisamayā, most meritorious and auspicious.
She who constantly subdues the difficult-to-tame, who accomplishes the welfare of all sentient beings,
who possesses a formidable form and great majesty, and whose radiance is like that of the Night of Doom.
She is the embodiment of the end of time, terrifying even to Yama,
fierce and of fierce form— difficult to behold and always unbearable.
The Rudras, Vasus, Yakṣas, Īśas, Rākṣasas, Grahas, Mātṛs,
and the gods who follow them— all these chief mantras of great supernatural power.
Likewise, she is eternally beneficial to all beings as the subduer of the difficult-to-tame;
she is indeed beneficial for the destruction of untimely death and for the vanquishing of death itself.
Created by all the Buddhas, it is terrifying even to Death itself;
having bound this [seal], men who know the pledge (samaya) shall indeed become eternal.
And those who are constantly devoted to mantras, being intent on recitation, they too are liberated;
indeed, for such embodied beings, mantras are accomplished without even effort.
Even one who does not recite may become a reciter; the impure may become pure, if they are joined here with the mudrā of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath.
For this [mantra], when joined with those who see reality, performs all actions;
it is for the purpose of destroying all obstacles and for the healing of all diseases.
It was established by the best of sages in the past for the sake of the equipment for the welfare of all beings, for the warding off of all that is evil, and for the fulfillment of all [aims].
This mudrā is beneficial in the world and serves to restore one who has fallen from their commitment (samaya).
By binding this most excellent and supreme mudrā, one who knows the commitment becomes [perfected] at that very moment.
It should be known that one has entered the mandala of all mantras, both worldly and supramundane, when one is impelled by the mudrā and mantra.
In the same way, having become pure as before for all rites,
one should form the vajra with the fingers in the shape of a triple-pronged needle.

One should place the thumb together with the middle and index fingers upon the head; then, having performed this, one should rotate it in a counter-clockwise direction (apasavya). This most excellent and supreme mudrā, when employed, is effective for all rites.
These five great mudrās have been taught by the Protectors of the World;
having bound them, the best of men will certainly touch the pinnacle of perfect enlightenment.
These fulfill every mental aspiration of those who recite the mantra;
they reveal all that is true and real exactly as it is, according to one's desire.
Furthermore, five other excellent and supreme mudrās have been revealed:
the head, the face, the body, the lotus, and likewise the armor.
These divine and excellent mudrās belong to the wise Mañjughoṣa.
In the past, this was proclaimed by the foremost of the world’s best, those who perceive reality;
and I, Mañjuśrī, shall now speak it—let it be understood as it is being told.
Listen with a one-pointed mind always to this mudrā, the most excellent of the best mudrās;
having maintained pure conduct as before, stand before the supreme relic.
One should always bind the mudrā known as Pañcārtha within the hollowed palms;
both tips of the palms should be formed into the shape of a bud.
One should always place the seal known as *śirasudrā* upon the head;
and just as the *utpalamudrā* is always placed upon the *duravara*.
And that body-seal (gātramudrā), when cast out from all sides, is performed; how indeed is it to be known? It should rather be the face-seal (vaktramudrā).
In the same manner, having placed the hands together, one should place them at the region of the navel;
with the index fingers slightly bent, one should touch one's own navel.
That shall be the armor mudrā, and that shall be for one's own protection;
for when these are applied everywhere, they are fruitful and accomplish all aims.
These seals are the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), auspicious and the destroyer of misfortune;
they should be employed at all times by those who recite [mantras], for they are fruitful and beneficial.
Possessing great heroism and great merit, it wards off all misfortunes;
by binding themselves with this, men are eternally destined for enlightenment.
There are five other great mudrās of the ascetic Lord of the World:
for the Sage Śākyasiṃha, and likewise for Ratnaśikha the Guru.
To Supuṣpa, to Sukeśa, likewise to Sumanasorava,
to the Buddha Saṅkusuma, and to the excellent Padmottara.
To the Perfect One, the One with Beautiful Eyes, to the Pure One, to the Teacher of the World,
to the Grandfather, to the Liberated One, and to the One who has cast off the world’s finest raiment.
And of these Buddhas, as well as of other great-souled ones—
of the self-arisen ones who have passed away, those yet to come, and those existing in the present.
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), which possesses great power and is garlanded with flames on all sides, arises upon the crowns of the heads of all the Buddhas as the characteristic of their manifestation.
Known as Uṣṇīṣā, she dwells within the abode of the three realms;
she is a universal monarch of great merit, auspicious, and the destroyer of calamities.
And he is remembered as the sovereign lord of all vidyās, the king of vidyās;
joined with the single syllable, this mantra is born from the crown of the Sugata’s head.
The knower of that [mudrā] should be known as the Lord of the Single Syllable;
born in the family of the Victors, he is the Wheel-Turner, the Mudrā, the Supreme Lord.
Having joined both hands together, marked by the form of a hollowed casket,
and having bound them with the fist-mudrā, the two middle fingers should indeed be well-pointed.
Having slightly contracted [the fingers] as if drawing them back, displaying them in the form of earrings—
this is the mudrā of the All-Pervading One, known as the Lord of all Mantras.
Having formed the head-gesture (*mūrdhāna*) deity with the fingers in the shape of a hollow bud,
one should slightly bend the two index fingers while the little fingers are well-honored.
This most excellent and supreme mudrā is taught for Tejorāśi;
that same [mudrā], when joined in a hollowed form, is known as the foremost "parasol-shaped" [mudrā].
With all the fingers spread wide, it is known as the White Parasol;
the Jayoṣṇīṣa mudrā, beneficial for the deity, is formed when the two middle fingers are well-pointed.
That same [mudrā], when spread out at the front with hands extending in all directions,
is to be known as the *uṣṇīṣa-saṃbhava* by those who perceive the meaning in every respect.
The supreme mudrā is proclaimed as being born from the hair of the Sage;
that fifth one, moreover, arises from all the uṣṇīṣas.
By this [mantra], indeed, all the uṣṇīṣa-hairs of as many Buddhas as there are come together, joined to all ritual activities.
Whatever mudrās have been sung by the best of sages throughout the three worlds,
this mudrā is the supreme sovereign of them all.
With this [mantra] one should summon the mantras, and with this very same one one should dismiss them;
with this, the reciter should perform all rites in every circumstance.
These five great mudrās were sung of old by the best of sages; they are indeed endowed with all purposes of action and are effective for accomplishing all uṣṇīṣa mantras.
However many *uṣṇīṣa* mantras have been proclaimed by the best of sages throughout the three worlds,
all of them everywhere fulfill these five purposes.
All the innumerable mudrās should be known as belonging to the Uṣṇīṣa;
among them, five are declared to be the most excellent for accomplishing all Uṣṇīṣa rites.
These five excellent mudrās belong to Avalokita;
they are preeminent in the Lotus family and are the most sublime mudrās upon the mandala of the earth.
The uṣṇīṣa and the lotus-face mudrā are also described;
the goddess Tārā, born of great compassion, is the fifth.
Having previously maintained pure conduct, wearing washed garments, and being well-recited in prayer,
the man should touch his head with his hand and stand with his arms raised.
One should draw [the lines] on the palm of the left hand and encircle them with the fist-position;
this is the Uṣṇīṣa mudrā of Avalokiteśvara.
Placing those very [fingers] upon the crown of the head, the Śira-mudrā is proclaimed;
those same [fingers], moreover, when contracted and established at the region of the navel, [form the Nābhi-mudrā].
Having extended all the fingers, that is known as the Padma-mudrā;
the two hands are positioned above the face, not resting against it.
The two hands joined together with the fingers slightly spread apart—
this very one is proclaimed as the Padmaketu face-mudrā.
The mudrā which is proclaimed in the world of the Nāgas as the Lotus Banner is formed by the joining of both hands in the manner of a fist.
When both index fingers are raised and formed into needles,
well-marked and pressed by the thumbs, this excellent mudrā is called Tārā.
"This is the supreme and most excellent mudrā, Karuṇā, belonging to the wise one whose banner is the lotus.
Thus, O Padmālayā, these five great mudrās have always been described.
For the Bodhisattva Lokeśvara, the Great-Souled One, these [mudrās] are primary;
herein, in the Lotus Family, they constitute the binding for all ritual actions.
The lords of the mantra-nāthas, the vidyās, and the worldly deities—
all of them indeed enter into this mudrā, becoming well-sealed by it.
And those lords of yakṣas who are celebrated as Vajrapāṇi of great supernatural power,
as well as those of great mantras who are fierce and intent on their purpose, and likewise those wrathful ones who take away life;
And whatever other worldly deities there are, preeminent and endowed with mantras,
they all come together when well-sealed by these mudrās.
These mudrās are the Great Mudrā, pure and the destroyer of evil;
by binding them, all practitioners of recitation quickly attain their goal with great swiftness.
The Tathāgata mudrā is liberated; it is the supreme sovereign for others in the healing of all diseases by the Lord Avalokiteśvara.
Through the mudrās, the five great enjoyments circulate upon the surface of the earth;
having assumed the form of women, they are dedicated to the welfare of all sentient beings.
O wise one, having bound this, men will certainly be intent upon awakening;
this is another great mudrā, O Vajrapāṇi of great supernatural power.
He who is the glorious Vajreśvara, the lord of all mantras, the sovereign,
the illustrious ruler of the ten stages, and the dispeller of all misfortunes.
He bestows great fear, he is fierce, and he is the repeller of wicked beings;
he is the tamer of the untamed, wise, and skillful in accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
In the form of a yakṣa, moving about on earth by his own power for the sake of sentient beings,
he should cause them to enter the Dharma while engaged in activities for the benefit of beings.
For the sake of the equipment for awakening, those who moved about in the form of yakṣas were beings who acted for the benefit of the world, yet were deluded by a yakṣiṇī.
For them, there will be no success with mantras uttered through speech characterized by misconduct;
[for such a person], the Bodhisattva—possessing great merit, many forms, and great supernatural power—is [the only one who can grant it].
If one harbors a hostile mind toward the Lord of Mantras, how can human beings achieve accomplishment?
These five excellent mudrās have also been proclaimed by the Buddhas of great supernatural power.
Vajrapāṇi, who possesses great merit, should quickly join those [hands] together;
likewise, having rubbed the hands with white sandalwood and saffron.
In the same way, formed like a hollowed cup and wrapped like a bud,
they are likewise placed and well-positioned at the location of the head.
That is to be known as Vajraśirā, the Mahāmudrā beneficial for the wise;
the second mudrā is Mūrdhajā, belonging to the Yakṣa general.
The Uṣṇīṣa mudrā is beneficial in the world; the Uṣṇīṣa is beneficial for the Lord of Yakṣas.
That same [mudrā] is the Vajra-śiras mudrā when the añjali is placed facing upward.
This mudrā, the Great Mudrā, is proclaimed as the "Uṣṇīṣa."
The third is named Vajrodbhavā; it should be placed in the region of the forehead.
With the palms joined in full añjali, the ring fingers are positioned between the eyebrows.
This is Vajrodbhavā by name, O Vajrapāṇi, which accomplishes all aims.
The fourth, however, is the Mahāmudrā, which is sung as Vajravaktrā;
it is formed by placing the palms of the hands face upward, joined together in the shape of a braid.
Having likewise placed [the hands] at the location of the chest with the middle fingers well-pointed,
this mudrā is the great mudrā, the excellent one, beneficial for the best of yakṣas.
She is the abode of all vajras;
she is the fivefold great mudrā, Vajrapāṇi of great supernatural power.
In the same manner, having placed the two hands at the region of the navel,
one should form them by bending the index fingers and pressing their tips against the thumbs.
On the third [finger], having embraced the two little fingers well-positioned,
one should then bind them in the form of a braid with the remaining fingers.
This is proclaimed as the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) named Vajrālayā;
herein indeed reside all seals, both those of the mundane world and those belonging to the Vajra-holder.
The Śaivas, the Śakras, and even the ṛṣis of great supernatural power are benefited by it;
for that supreme and foremost mudrā of Matanga has been proclaimed by the Great-Souled Ones.
The Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, Kūṣmāṇḍas, and Kaṭapūtanas—
those excellent mudrās which were proclaimed by Viṣṇu, Indra, and those called Vanaspati.
Also by the mothers of Īśāna, by the world-graspers,
and by the suns— the Bhāskaras, Indus, and Vivasvats— along with the well-worshipped Vasus who are protectors of the self.
Those who have been created as the most excellent mudrās by the hosts of all beings always come together in this Vajramālā mudrā.
Indeed, the most excellent and supreme mudrā is renowned in this family called Vajra;
likewise, there is the mudrā of the Tathāgata and that of the great-souled Avalokiteśvara.
For some hold that one mudrā belongs to others;
this mudrā, however, is known as the Mahāmudrā of Vidyot, the general of the Yakṣa army.
Having bound this, all men will certainly be destined for enlightenment;
the Tathāgatas have declared that this mudrā is the most excellent, the supreme, and the ultimate.
These five great mudrās of the illustrious Vajrapāṇi should always be recollected by those who recite [mantras], especially in times of great danger.
Indeed, the flesh-eating and meat-consuming beings quickly perish—
the yakṣas, rākṣasas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and kaṭapūtanas.
Gods, gandharvas, humans, and kinnaras together with the siddhas;
the foremost and most excellent of the grahas, the garuḍas, and the mothers of great supernatural power.
Even those who are the leaders of the world— Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara— as well as all sentient beings in the world, upon whom everything everywhere depends.
Upon merely seeing them, they all flee without a doubt.
These were the mudrās of the Jinas, O Vajradhara, Lord;
[they belong] to the Lord of Mantras, the Lord of Yakṣas, and the Great-Souled Lord of the World.

Therefore, all reciters who are intent on seeking accomplishment must constantly remember this mudrā during the time of recitation for all mantras, as it bestows success; it is that which they call "Kisalayā," which was sung of first.
In that same manner, the wise one should place the hands upon the chest;
having first formed that braid-like shape with the fingers on all sides.
That knowledge is the seal upon the sprout; it is the worldly mantra-deity.
A wise person should first employ that [seal] swiftly in minor rites.
It destroys all those afflicted by the disease of fever; there is no doubt about this.
That very same [mudrā] is to be known as Sumanas when the little finger is bent.
The *paṭahī* [mudrā] is formed by bending the middle fingers;
the *kandarpī* is formed when both thumbs are raised;
and the *ghaṭakharparikā* is known to be formed by well-bending the tips of the ring fingers.
In the same way, having formed a bud with the well-adorned tips of the hands,
the mudrā marked by the shape of a blue lotus is called the *utpala*.
With both hands opened and the fingers extended on all sides, this is indeed the Padma-mudrā; when the two [hands] are joined together, it becomes the Jyotsnā.
In that same manner, when all [fingers] are joined with the tips of the fingers touching the tips of the fingers,
this is the mudrā of Suparṇin, which is proclaimed as "Suparṇī."
That very form of Lampuṭā, with its inverted appearance and gestures,
becomes the Yamala-mudrā, which belongs even to the great-souled Garuḍa.
In the same way, having placed the two hands joined in the form of fists,
with both thumbs positioned in the middle, this is proclaimed as the *liṅgamudrā*.
When the two hands are raised with the thumbs positioned in the middle, that is known as the Śaṅkha;
by releasing the hands from that very position, it becomes the renowned Jayā.
When the little fingers are wrapped around [the thumbs], it becomes the Vijayā mudrā; when joined with the ring fingers, it becomes the Ajitā mudrā, which fulfills [all desires].
Having joined the two hands together, one should close them with the left hand;
the wise person here should form a fist by bending the tip of the thumb downward. This is to be known as the Aparājitā mudrā, which is highly honored.
The four maidens are to be known as the prescribed sisters among them;
this Tumburu, however, is renowned as the elder brother.
For these inhabitants of the ocean, relying upon boats as their vehicles,
wander through this place of great merit and great supernatural power.
For the sake of subduing all beings, they were created by the knower of Brahman;
indeed, when joined with secret mantras, these are honored everywhere.
These are unfailing; when applied to all rites, they bring success.
They swiftly accomplish one's aims, they are perfected, auspicious, and destroyers of misfortune.

By one who is pure, [the practice] should be accomplished through pure rites by the most excellent; for the sake of bodily accomplishment, [one should employ] a fire that has arisen and is blazing, or one that is extinguished and moves in the sky. For middling rites, a middling [fire] is used; for impure acts such as those involving defilement, an impure [fire] is used.
Furthermore, for those embodied beings who are indeed evildoers and constantly consume leftovers,
even minor rites always succeed for them without effort.
In the same way, having restrained the two hands, one should bring them together at the region of the navel;
from the middle fingers, one should wind them in the shape of a braid like a needle.
That mudrā is *sumekhalā*, and when it is unwound, it becomes *mekhalā*.
When those same two hands are placed at the level of the navel, it is the *sampuṭā* mudrā;
when that same [mudrā] is raised to the neck, it is called the *śrīsampuṭa*.
Then, having placed it at the location of the navel, one should rotate it counter-clockwise;
for this is the excellent Mudrā of Rajanī, which wards off wicked beings.
Raising the right hand and forming it into a fist, one should not rely [on anything else];
they call this the "Supreme Fist Mudrā," which pulverizes all mantras.
Releasing that very finger and employing both hands,
this is called the "excellent fist mudrā," which destroys the flesh-eaters.
That [mudrā] is to be known as *saṅkucitā* when the tips of the fingers are well-curved;
it is to be understood as the *sukuntā* mudrā, and as the *kuntā* when the fingers are extended.
Tārā and Sutārā are to be known through their ritual procedure; both should be of a single form, with the index fingers well-joined and placed in the shape of a blue lotus.
When the two hands are wrapped in the shape of a casket, it is called the "single-needle" [mudrā];
when those same hands are extended, it is proclaimed as the Tārā [mudrā].
Placing the two hands together in the form of a joined palms-mudrā,
the two index fingers are joined and positioned at the third joint.
When the two thumbs are at the ends, it is the Locanā mudrā;
releasing those very fingers, the two index fingers are joined together.
That very same mudrā, when employed as the mudrā of Māmakī,
is called the "Excellent Mudrā" (Mudravara) by those who well-bend the middle fingers.
The Śvetā mudrā is indeed formed by the hands extended here;
the Paṇḍarā mudrā, however, is formed by fists firmly clenched.
Both index fingers raised high constitute the Mahāprabhāvā, which possesses great power and great merit.
Then, having joined the two hands together in the form of a hollowed casket and formed the shape of eyes with the two index fingers, one should press them;
this is known as the excellent *bhrūkuṭī* mudrā, which always removes great fear.
Thus, these eight mudrās have indeed been proclaimed by the supreme Victors of old;
they possess great power, great merit, great majesty, and great supernatural efficacy.
In all mudrās and everywhere, and especially with mantras, these are indeed honored everywhere; when remembered, they bestow the fruits of one's goals.
They are great protections, purifying, auspicious, and destroyers of evil;
they are honored everywhere by the Buddhas and shall accomplish all mantras.
Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, Śvetā, Paṇḍaravāsinī,
Māmakī, Locanā, Sutārā, and Tāravartinī.
Thus these great mudrās have been recited by those who know the reality of the world;
this procedure for protection has been proclaimed and is taught among the great protections.
For these great mudrās, which remove great sins, belong to the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū),
as well as to the Hero Lokīśa and likewise to the Great Lord of Yakṣas.
These mudrās are of great merit and are certain causes for accomplishment;
they have been taught by the world-leaders, the illustrious Perfectly Awakened Ones.
In the same way, placing the hands so that they take the form of lute-players and pressing them together in reverse, this becomes the Saṅkulā mudrā.
In the same way, the tip of the needle is described as being like a hook;
likewise, the palms joined together with the head raised upward while positioned at the crown of the head.
By extending all the fingers, it becomes the beautiful parasol;
by clenching the two hands into fists, it becomes the deity Rātrī.
In truth, the *tāmasī* mudrā is formed by the fingers being constantly extended;
likewise, the fingers are bent while the thumbs are raised upward.
The poison-subduing [mudrā] was created by the illustrious ones as the *rekha-mudrā*;
it is to be known as being mentally bowed by those who are sealed with the *mahāmānasa* [mudrā].
In the same way, having extended both hands, one should join them with one hand;
one should encircle the two index fingers around the middle fingers—this is the mudrā of Garuḍadhvaja.
When both hands are joined together with the middle fingers resting upon the braid (veṇī),
this mudrā is celebrated everywhere by the name Haṃsamālā.
When those same two hands are extended and wrapped in the form of three prongs, that shall be the Vajra-mudrā; it is the most excellent and beneficial mudrā.
The supreme among all mudrās, when concentrated, belongs to Vajrapāṇi;
that same mudrā, with the fingers extended, becomes the Lotus Garland (Padmamālā). Known as the most excellent mudrā of Jyeṣṭhā, it is equal to that of Padmakeśin.
This supreme, divine mudrā is of great merit and great origin;
when employed in all rites, it brings accomplishment to embodied beings.
Renowned upon the earth as a maṇḍala, it is established as effective in all activities.
The crookedness of the mouth and the meaning should be understood; both [hands] are on the palm, level, with the tips of the fingers placed together, and the index finger raised.
The mudrā is to be known as "the face"; it has half a face when performed by those who are virgins.
The palms of the fists should be known as level, with the thumbs raised and bent upward.
They call it the Lohitāmudrā; the middle finger, being very red, and the blue-and-red [ring finger] are to be known as the mudrā born from the head of Rudra.
The goddess who possesses great power and is renowned throughout the circle of the earth,
she is the remover of all obstacles and the warder-off of malevolent beings.
That mudrā is described in the world; listen, you who desire prosperity!
Likewise, having restrained the two hands, one should first form a fist.
The two middle fingers should be known as extended, slightly contracted, and then pointed;
this mudrā, renowned as Mahāmudrā, is the destroyer of fear.
In the same way, when those two hands are clearly joined at the tips of the index fingers like a needle,
this is known as the *viṣṇu-mudrā*, which is honored everywhere.
When both [thumbs] are joined at the bases of the little fingers in the manner of Brahmā,
that mudrā, likewise shaped like a bud, is called the Vaindrī.
That shall be the Māheśvarī mudrā when both little fingers are raised;
releasing those very hands, one should resort to it through the yoga of dance.
Then, the left arm is always positioned with both ends extended,
embracing the right arm which is encircled by the index finger.
This Vajradharā is eternally conceived as Varāhī;
her two arms are likewise fashioned through the yoga of dance.
When both hands are formed in the shape of the index finger and cast forth, it is called the Vajracāmuṇḍī mudrā;
that same gesture, when both hands are extended and joined together, is likewise [the Vajracāmuṇḍī].
The gaze directed upward and fixed is called the Ghorā-Cāmuṇḍī mudrā;
the Kaumārī mudrā, however, belongs to Kārttikeya, the great earth.
Placing the hands in that very same way, one should join the tips of the index fingers;
with the other fingers extended, this is the *sarvamātṛ* mudrā.
This is the most powerful among all mudrās and mother-deities;
by means of this, one may indeed perform all rites for those who are ignorant.
And for women who have recently given birth, for the womb-places of embodied beings,
and regarding the protection and liberation through mudrās, from the defilements of pretas and vyantaras;
For the sake of liberation, one should employ the Nairṛta Graha-mātṛ;
for the welfare of living beings in the world, this mudrā brings about happiness.
This [mantra], which is the most excellent of all mantras, when employed for beings, bestows happiness and is beneficial;
the reciter should employ it everywhere in all minor rites.
One should always employ these mudrās with these very mantras;
likewise, having positioned the two hands so that they are encircled by the expanse of one's own earrings.
The mudrā formed by the fingers all around is indeed sung of as the "Nāgī";
likewise, with the middle fingers placed together, the tips of the index fingers are brought close.
The mudrā known as Nāgamukhī is preeminent in all rites;
that which is to be known as the supreme mudrā is designated in the world as the garland (mālā).
In the same way, having placed the two hands together, one should bind them all around with the fingers in the shape of a braid and then form the shape of a fist.
In the same way, with the two thumbs joined in the shape of a hollowed casket and the middle fingers slightly bent,
that shall be the Māla-mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all rites.
In the same way, with seven fingers always held perpetually erect,
that is the Saptacchada mudrā, which is celebrated throughout the three worlds.
These supreme and foremost mudrās have been shown as previously described;
indeed, these mudrās were explained in detail before.
For all [these] are to be known as one, as they are indicated and shown by the prescribed method;
for these meanings of conceptualization, along with their details, extend to the full range of extensive meanings.
All these are known as mudrās, sealed by all mudrās;
one should know that there are eight hundred mudrās, declared to be the accomplishers of all aims.
Among them, there should be only one that fulfills the purpose according to the sequence;
indeed, standing by means of the yoga of dance, the reciter should look upward.
Placing the fingers on the forehead, having joined the index finger with the little finger,
and applying the gaze of the eyes, one should remain standing and place [the mudrā] with the palms joined (añjali).
The mudrā named Sarvatrādarśanī consists of eight hundred [syllables];
by means of this, the mantras taught by the All-Knowing Seer are accomplished.
All mudrās indeed should be employed right here without conceptualization;
for this collection of mudrās as they have been described has thus been stated in summary according to the mantras.

From the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, this is the forty-third chapter, being the fourth [section] on the array of mudrās, sealed with the seal of the inconceivable dharma-realm of all Tathāgatas.
Now begins the forty-sixth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa deities, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:

Listen, Mañjuśrī, to this fifth chapter on the array of mudrās belonging to you, which has entered into the Dharma-treasury of all Tathāgatas, which is most supremely secret, sealed with the mudrās of the Dharmadhātu that are incalculable and inconceivable, which has entered into the practice of all mantras, which is most supremely esoteric, most excellent among all supramundane things, and most joyful among all mundane conducts; what is it that I shall speak?
It is that which was previously spoken by the Tathāgatas.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose again from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

"It would be well, O Blessed One, if you would teach for the benefit of all beings and out of compassion for us, the fifth extensive chapter on the Great Mudrās, consisting of the five Great Mudrās themselves, in brief—[teaching] the fulfillment of the conduct for approaching the seat of great enlightenment, the great accomplishment, and the great vow, for those who have entered into the practice of all mantras."

And the boundless seal of abiding is for the sake of fulfilling all activities, purposes, desires, and hopes through summoning and dismissal; for the sake of entering into all mantras, tantras, and great mudrās; and for the sake of entering into all seals of the great samaya that satisfy all sentient beings—for this, I consider it now to be the right time.
Thus addressed by the Blessed One, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men,
the wise Mañju-pratibha then remained silent for a moment.
This entire earth trembled in six ways;
all hosts of beings were terrified, and even the abodes of the ṛṣis were shaken.
At that very moment, beings from the three realms arrived;
seeing that they had come, the best of sages spoke these words to the beings:
Born in the Śākya clan, the skillful one taught the mudrā at that very moment;
by binding which, wise men certainly become intent upon awakening.
All mantras shall be accomplished— both those of the Sugatas and those that are mundane—
and the five great mudrās bound by the foremost Sages of old.
Now, having bound these [mudrās] within the abode of the three worlds, the Blessed One, the Teacher Śākyamuni, should himself perform the gesture of raising the hand.
Having wound them into the shape of a braid, the wise one should bend the middle fingers; he should touch the two little fingers together and raise both thumbs.
Bending [the fingers] into the shape of a *añjali*, one should display the form of Mañjuravehitā.
This is the *mudrā*, the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is praised by all Buddhas. When accomplished in every way, this goddess is also celebrated as Pūrṇā.
Having rotated those very hands, one should place them at the region of the navel;
it quickly fulfills all hopes, is highly meritorious, and indeed beneficial.
Known as "Manoratha," it is always the subduer of the unsubdued.
Placing the hands together in that very manner, one should encircle them with the fist-mudrā;
always placing it upon the chest, this third [mudrā] becomes perfectly pure.
The fourth, however, should be in the position of the head with the excellent mudrā;
the fifth would be Jyeṣṭhā, having released all pervasive qualities.
She should be known as Lokadhātrī, renowned for all ritual actions;
this very constant yoga is to be employed in all rites.

By drawing back the index fingers of both hands, subjugation is achieved; by flicking them apart, one should perform dismissal; but with the mind alone, liberation is attained. One should display all [these gestures] quickly, for they accomplish the purpose of all ritual actions.
Thus concludes the forty-fourth chapter, the extensive section on the Great Mudrās, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the forty-seventh chapter.

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods and that great assembly circle, entered the samādhi named "The Practice of All Mantras, the Infinite Secret, the Most Secret of All, Manifesting the Radiance of All Stars through Infinite Adornments.
Immediately upon the Blessed One’s entering this state, rays of light issued forth from the circle of hair between his eyebrows.

Having illuminated everywhere in all directions—above, below, and across—with a great radiance, and having exhorted all the mantras, [the light] again vanished into the Bhagavat’s circle of hair between his brows.

Immediately upon the vanishing of those rays, in the four directions, below, and above, four maidens together with their brother were established by the Buddha’s empowerment within that very great assembly circle, near the king of mountains, Sumeru, below.

Having assembled and sat down, they did so for the purpose of demonstrating the miraculous play of the Great Bodhisattva Kumārabhūta, for the purpose of accomplishing the practice of the great mantras, and for the purpose of entering into the mastery of the playful practice of all mundane and supramundane mantra-practices, including the practices of summoning, attracting, and consoling.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having slightly gazed upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi, who was assembled in that very assembly, as well as the entire host of Bodhisattvas, [spoke].

Then that entire assembly, and this great earth surrounded by hosts of deities—the abode of the single mantra of the great elements—shook the medicinal herbs, the great luminaries, and the mountains; it trembled, quaked, resounded, was agitated, and was thoroughly convulsed. The southern direction rose up while the northern direction sank down; the western direction rose up while the eastern direction sank down; it sank down at the edges and rose up in the center, and rose up at the edges and sank down in the center; and a great radiance appeared in the world.
Furthermore, other immeasurable, incalculable, marvelous, and wondrous miracles were displayed.

Those hosts of gods entered the samādhi called "The State of Peace through the Knowledge of the Great Object Free from Conceptual Elaboration," which cannot be known even by all the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Mahābodhisattvas.

What need is there to mention entering into meditative absorption for the sake of surpassing all other mundane and supramundane shrines of the non-Buddhist traditions, for the sake of penetrating all mantra-tantras, for the sake of fulfilling all dharmas of liberation, for the sake of leading all sentient beings to the state of peace, and for the sake of leading all beings to compassionately ascend and abide upon the Vajra-throne at the seat of awakening—the limit of reality, suchness, and the inconceivable—Blessed Śākyamuni remained absorbed in meditation.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva, addressed the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas: "Speak, speak, O Son of the Victor! Speak of that which enters into all mantra practices, which is the essence of all worldly mantras, the supreme secret, the entry into the commitments (*samaya*) of all beings and sentient beings, the fulfiller of all intentions and desires according to their inclinations. You have been authorized, O Son of the Victor, by all the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present, for the sake of fulfilling omniscience through the treasury of Tathāgata mantras; and for the sake of displaying here, in this extensive section of the King of Rituals (*kalparāja*), the inconceivable, marvelous, and wondrous miraculous transformations of playful sport; and for the sake of manifesting the knowledge of the Omniscient One."
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

Listen, O Dharmadhara! I shall explain the ritual procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) together with its secret teachings, the fire-oblation (*homa*), recitation (*jāpa*), timing, and observances (*niyama*) of the four maidens along with their brother; the construction of the image, the mandala, and the commitments (*samaya*); the rites of invocation, dismissal, and worship; the offering of water, lamps, perfumes, incense, garlands, ointments, powders, garments, food-offerings, banners, flags, bells, necklaces, and lamps; the sequence of rules for the methods of accomplishment and the goals to be achieved; the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and subjugation (*abhicāruka*); the practices of invisibility, traveling through the sky, walking on foot, bringing others under control, possession, causing enmity, destruction, withering, delusion, paralyzing, and killing; the various means of assuming the forms of diverse beings, inflicting pain, threatening, reviling, and creating many-footed or footless creatures; the display of paths and the fruits of actions as desired; and the application of binding, climbing, making [actions] fruitful, and the employment of all ritual acts, mantras, and tantras—culminating in the fulfillment of success (*siddhi*).
Listen to this, O son of the Conqueror!
Then the glorious Vajrapāṇi, having prostrated to the Sugata, the all-pervading Lord,
spoke these sweet words, adorned with both sound and meaning.

It brings about what is not for one's benefit, yet it is pleasant to the ear, sweetly modulated in meaning, and productive of many benefits; it is desired, the foundation of all mantras, and resonates with the sound of the voice of Brahmā.
With a voice like the song of the kalaviṅka bird, clear, deep, and self-controlled,
she elucidates the subtle reality of the meaning.
Then the Holder of the Vajra spoke these words concerning the Sovereign of all Mantras:
"Listen, O hosts of spirits, and you multitudes of gods of great supernatural power!"
Likewise, [he taught] the ritual manual (kalpa) to be described in detail, which accomplishes all rites;
it possesses great majesty through its four forms, with assemblies in the four directions,
endowed with the four castes, and adorned with four syllables.
That man, endowed with the four mantras, takes refuge in the fifth;
