he attains the majesty of the fourth state and the convergence of the four elements.
With his brothers as the fifth, he is the eldest, born from the space of the great elements;
unimpeded everywhere, supreme, and the means for accomplishing the purpose of all mantras.
It performs all rites, is worthy of worship, the eldest, auspicious, and the destroyer of evil;
it has proceeded for the welfare of all beings in the form of mantra.
She is renowned as the Four Maidens, with the Youth as her fifth constituent;
she consists of wind, water, fire, earth, and space as the fifth.
For those embodied beings, the ripening [of karma] occurs in the form of mantras.
The fifth is the preeminent lord of mantras, the foremost of blessings, appearing in the form of a brother.
I shall proclaim their mantras; listen to me regarding these others as well.

Then all those beings indeed became joyful in mind; having understood the nature of reality (dharmatā), they sat with gentle hearts and composed minds. Desiring to hear, everyone remained motionless with wide-open eyes.
Then the glorious Mañjuvara, looking up at the son of the Sugata,
Vajrapāṇi, the great yakṣa and abode of all lords of mantras, said:
In the meantime, another appeared whose heart was drawn by compassion:
all the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas.
The Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas who abide on the ten stages,
as well as all those in the world who are foremost and most eminent among all beings.
Seated everywhere, they are joined with all five destinies;
they are the foremost among living beings, supreme, and honored by others.
Indeed, from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, all those residing in the infinite realms—
extending as far as the limit of the three births and presiding over the ten supreme stages—
desiring to hear, gathered together for that assembly.

Then Vajradhara, the presiding lord, having perceived that all the sentient beings and bodhisattvas had arrived— all those who dwell as lords of mantras— as well as the gods, the eldest of the Suras, and the masters of the ten stages;
Having understood all these beings to be well-disposed toward the Buddha's teaching,
the wise Lord of the Mantra Sovereigns should then recite the mantra.
Homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded, who possess inconceivable and marvelous forms!

Oṃ tura tura hulu hulu! Do not delay; remember your pledge! Accomplish my purpose! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā! This mantra performs all rites. This is the heart-mantra of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and the root-mantra of all mundane and supramundane lords of diseases and kings. By means of this, one should perform all activities.
One should accomplish all substances; the omnipresent Lord performs all rites.
One should always perform rituals with this [mantra] for the swift accomplishment of one's aims.
In that regard, O hosts of gods, listen to my words as I proclaim the mantra.
Oṃ deva svāhā! This is the mantra of Sārtthavāha-Astumburu.
Oṃ jaye svāhā!
Oṃ ajite svāhā / Oṃ parājite svāhā / These are the root mantras that constitute the hearts of the four sisters together with their brother, who are honored by the world.
Of these, *om rūpiṇī om virūpiṇī viśvātmane*—these are the heart-mantras arising from Tumburu; they become the mantras in the heart of Tumburu. *Om deveśāya svāhā*.
There are subsidiary heart-mantras: *Oṃ vāmani piśāci oṃ mahārākṣasi svāhā* / *Oṃ vikṛtarūpiṇi svāhā* /
Oṃ prakīrṇakeśī kṛtāntarūpiṇi svāhā!
Oṃ vajrarūpiṇi kṛtāntarātri bhayānaki svāhā! This is the upahṛdaya (near-heart mantra) of Tumburu, the caravan leader.
Oṃ, you whose form is adorned with four faces, three-eyed, pot-bellied, and multiform—svāhā!
Oṃ dhu dhu, cause all directions to blaze—svāhā!
May this mantra be divine for all sisters together with their brothers.
Oṃ hūṃ, the crown-protection (śikhā) of all; oṃ hrīḥ jaḥ, the head (śiras) of all;
oṃ dhyāyini svāhā.
The mantra for all is:
Oṃ dṛk, the eye of all.

Oṃ, the glory of the sisters together with their brothers, who are anointed with sandalwood and saffron, protected by the *samaya*, wandering across the Himalayas and the oceans, firm in their vows, and authorized by the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha.
Hrīḥ / Rīm / Vrīḥ.
Bhujaḥ!
This is the great mantra upon the body of all sisters together with all brothers;
it is effective for all purposes and renowned for all rites.
The most supreme secret:
Oṃ āyāhi mahādeva viśvarūpiṇe svāhā!
Oṃ tumbure! This is the invocation mantra of the caravan leader Sārthavāha.

Oṃ gaccha gaccha mahādeva viśvātmane svāhā! This is the dismissal mantra for the caravan leader Tamburu: Oṃ āyāhi devi kumārike kiṃ cirāyasi samayam anusmara! (Come, O goddess Kumārikā; why do you delay? Remember your pledge!)
"Accomplish my task, svāhā!"—this is the invocation mantra for Jayā. "Oṃ, come, O possessor of great enjoyment! Accomplish my task; remember the pledge, svāhā!"
Oṃ mahāyogāndhari vistīrṇadhanapriye svāhā! This is the invocation mantra of Ajitā. Oṃ śmaśānavāsini rūpaparivartini dehānucare svāhā!
Furthermore, by means of the invocation mantra of Aparājitā, one may again draw all mandalas, both mundane and supramundane,
and employ them in all rites; even according to the procedures of other tantras, one shall accomplish one's desired aim.

Within this very cycle of kalpas, in the chapter of the *Mūlakalparāja* recognized for its equality, the mantra of the four maidens together with the youth is proclaimed first. This mantra, which the son of the Buddha desires, is said by the sons of the Buddha, who possess great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), to be effective for all rites (*sarvakarmika*).
It is the foremost of families, the chief of mantras, the sovereign of all mantras, and the all-pervading Lord.
He performs various and manifold deeds praised by the virtuous,
and he forcibly captivates the minds of beings born among the three realms of existence.
Having emerged from the various states of existence and wombs, one forcibly performs actions that result in the birth of offspring, driven by the necessity of the destiny one is subject to.
They are renowned as the Four Sisters,
who always dwell together with their brother in the great ocean.
Embarked upon a ship were five sisters together with their brother;
the helmsman of their minds was known by the name Tumburu.
Intent on benefiting sentient beings, they wander over the entire earth,
assuming various forms and adorned with diverse ornaments.
Their fruit is indeed manifold; honored with various requisites, they wander over the entire earth, including its mountains and thousands of oceans.
The mantra of those [goddesses] is held to be the great eldest, named Tumburu; indeed,
the mantra of Tryambaka, the caravan leader and lord of people,
consists of a combination of four syllables together with the fivefold Oṃkāra.

First, one should perform the worship of all mantras with special offerings of perfumes, incense, lamps, garlands, and food; having presented the bali-oblation, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) with clear words and syllables. Having taken up any one of these excellent mantras in a secret place, one should recite it three times a day, eight thousand times each.
Having offered the *argha* to her who has arrived, one should perform all the rites.
And here is the *argha*-mantra: *oṃ pravigṛhṇatu bhaginyaḥ sabhrātṛsahitāś cārghamayamadhiṣṭhāntu svāhā*.
The *argha* mantra for all [the deities] together with their brothers consists of the mantras for all the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).
*Oṃ jvala jvala mahāhutāśārci mahādyutīnāṃ svāhā*.
This is the lamp mantra for all.
Oṃ dhūṃ dhūṃ!
O you who dwell in the forest, crest of incense, charming with fragrant scent, may the goddesses together with their brothers accept it; may they meditate upon it, svāhā!
This is the incense mantra for all.

Oma! O you who dwell in flowers, O you who are rich in flowers, O you with fragrant garlands, O you who are sweet-smelling and enchanting! In this forest, flowers have been born—delicate and fragrant.
Having offered them with devotion, may you, who are as swift as thought, accept them! Svāhā!
This is the mantra for flowers.
With this one should perform the worship:
*oṃ gandhagandhādhivāse svāhā*.
This is the mantra for incense.
Oṃ balite balini svāhā / This is the mantra of Bālī. Oṃ lālāvati svāhā /
The mantra for the offering:
oṃ sū. The mantra for the garment: [oṃ sū].
Oṃ phaṭ:
the mantra of the bell. Oṃ: the mantra of vowels and consonants.
Oṃ, protect! The mantra of the parasol.
Oṃ, it is shaken, it is fanned, svāhā!
The mantra of the fly-whisk.
Oṃ keli-mahokali-hṛdayaṅgame svāhā! This is the mantra for all substances, implements, collyrium, gorocana, mirrors, and ornaments. Oṃ samastavyāpini svāhā!
The mantras for the vajra-fence that binds all directions:
*oṃ maṇḍaline svāhā*. This is the mantra for binding above and below.
And it becomes a bond that completely and universally binds all things without exception.
Om, homage to all Buddhas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Om hūṃ haḥ!

This great king of vidyās, named Śāsana, is effective for all rites. He holds mastery over all bhūtas and the four sisters together with their brother; he is their afflicter, witherer, obstructer, and binder. He is the subduer, delighting in both restraint and favor. His command is unimpeded in all activities against the mothers of all bhūtas and grahas. When recited in a secret place or a private chamber, he causes the four sisters together with their brother to do whatever one desires. However, when one makes a request, one should ask for whatever boon one desires; being thus requested, she quickly grants that boon.
In this way, they perform such acts as binding, beating, threatening, killing, and so forth;
yet when tormented by this very King of Vidyās and recited together with it, they accomplish all their tasks.
Their mantras are as follows:
They perform the rites of dismissal, supplication, and so forth. *Oṃ rūpiṇī gaccha gaccha samayamanusmara svāhā*.
This is the mantra for the dismissal of Jayā.
*Oṃ vāmane piśāci prakīrṇakeśi viśvarūpiṇi gaccha gaccha mama kāryaṃ sādhaya svāhā*.
The dismissal mantra of Vijayā: Oṃ lahu lahu rūpiṇi gaccha gaccha samayamanusmara mama kāryaṃ samādāya svāhā.
The dismissal mantra of Ajitā:

Oṃ, O you of universal form, O transformed one, O you with a transformed face, O warder-off of all evil ones, go, go; accomplish my purpose, svāhā! These are the dismissal mantras for Aparājitā, the mantras for requesting her departure.
Whatever task one desires to accomplish,
having filled one's joined palms with various flowers, one should make a request and propitiate them before the goddesses together with their brothers;
then they will be released.
Together with their brothers, they manifest their presence and grant boons as desired;
they move about according to their pleasure.
This must be spoken with words and performed every day. Even when thus constrained, they do not abandon their presence until liberation is attained.
Constant practice, if otherwise obstructed, does not persist as that which ought to be done.

Then those sisters, together with their brother, trembling and oppressed, overcome by a shudder and seized with fear through the power of the Bodhisattva, approached from the four directions and uttered these words: "Save us, O Blessed One, Vajrapāṇi! Save us!
We are oppressed, O Blessed One, we are utterly oppressed;
no other refuge exists."
"You alone, Blessed One, are our refuge; you alone are our protection."

In the meantime, all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as all sentient beings included within all states of existence, having been well-governed and well-disciplined in the teaching by the King of Vidyās, remained there—those sisters together with their brother—terrified, well-disciplined, and wailing with piteous cries through the power of the Lord of Vajras, the Great King of Vidyās.
Then, Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, addressed those deities together with their brother.
Do not fear, sisters; do not be afraid!
Go for refuge to the Buddha, the foremost of bipeds. Go for refuge to the Dharma.
Go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the foremost of those free from passion;
the most excellent of assemblies.
Then those sisters, with their brother as the fifth, went for refuge to the Buddha;
they went for refuge in this way,
and they went for refuge to the Saṅgha.

Then they became possessed of happiness and gladness, endowed with the highest happiness and gladness. Perceiving themselves as released from their tight bonds, filled with joy and bliss, having attained serene faith and experiencing the utmost thrill such that the hairs on their bodies stood on end, they uttered this inspired exclamation:
Oh, what a marvel has been attained here at the source of the Three Jewels!
Having gained this for a moment, we are made happy, forever freed from all miserable rebirths,
and our minds are ever established in the higher realms, heaven, and liberation.
Then, with a contented mind, gazing upon Mañjughoṣa, they prostrated their heads at his feet and uttered these words:
"O Protector from all sufferings! You are the refuge, O one of great splendor!"
O Protector, you who teach the profound, syllable-less state of all phenomena— you who have become a kinsman— to you we pay homage.
Command me, O Great Hero, Lord of Mantras, Son of the Conquerors! What have we been brought here for by the Lord? What command shall I carry out?
Thus addressed, the heroic and all-pervading Lord, the son of all Buddhas,
being urged by the deities, spoke these sweet words.
Go once more for refuge, O son of the Conqueror, to Vajrapāṇi;
indeed, the irreversible Saṅgha arises from the foremost of Bodhisattvas.
Having first established the Three Jewels, the lineage-born son of the Supreme Victor,
you should direct your mind toward awakening; be intent on the world with a mind of loving-kindness,
and then, having pervaded everything, strike down the state that is the basis of self-composure.
Then all those deities, having prostrated before the Son of the Conqueror and having fulfilled his command in its entirety, turned toward where the Wielder of the Vajra was.
Having quickly paid homage to that Vajrapāṇi of great splendor and having praised him, they all remained there, facing his face.
Then, having observed that, the maiden, together with her four brothers as a fifth,
stood gazing at Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas;
those goddesses became a permanent refuge for the sake of the eternal truth, adorned by the purpose of the impermanent truth.
I utter sweet words, beautiful with the meaning of my own mantras:
"Homage to you, to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power!"
O one of great splendor, we shall explain the Pratyekabuddha-saṅgha, the community of non-existent yogins, and the extensive meaning of the mantra of the Self.
For the sake of the people on earth to understand reality as it truly is,
and for the purpose of protecting the secret mantras that have issued from your mouth along with their esoteric secrets,
[compose] this ornament which serves as the foundation for the meaning of those mantras.
When this had been said, the Lord of Mantras, Vajrapāṇi of great splendor,
his face breaking into a slight smile and his countenance beaming, looked upon him.
He honored that maiden along with her brothers and circle of friends, saying,
"Permitted by me, you shall remain free from all apprehension."
Having proclaimed the extensive ritual manual together with its secrets and mandalas,
you who are constantly worshipped by living beings shall always grant boons to you.
You are honored by the ṛṣis, by the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and kinnaras,
and also by the garuḍas, devas, gandharvas, and the asuras of great supernatural power.
Together with the Kūṣmāṇḍas and all the Mothers, as well as the Moon and the Sun,
the World-Protectors, the Lord of Wealth, and the Vasus who were falling [from the sky].
By those very lords of the gods, by the piśācas, uragas, and humans;
by the lords of bhūtas, the lords of night, and the flesh-eating vyantaras;
and by the chief lords of the rākṣasas—those of fierce minds who cause harm.
And by hosts of Daityas and Dānavas, by Yamas and Pretas of great supernatural power,
by humans and non-humans, and also by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara.
"You shall be worshipped by the foremost of the gods, the great elders, the siddhas, cāraṇas, and pūtanas, as well as by yogins and the sons of the Conquerors."
There is no doubt regarding the powers of Jayā; they say her mantra is of excellent sequence, as described in the extensive details of the ritual manual (*kalpa*).
There are ninety million mantras with their extensive tantras and ritual manuals;
furthermore, sixty victorious mantras are proclaimed to have been obtained.
For Ajitā, however, there would be sixteen hundred thousand [mantras] arising;
for the maiden Aparājitā, four crores are proclaimed.
If the caravan leader Tumburu were to sing for nine koṭis [of years],
the eons would last for that same duration, honored by humans, gods, and asuras.
All this is known as Śaiva by all the inhabitants of the earth;
it was previously proclaimed by me in detail in this very Kalpa.
Afterwards, other people spoke of the various kalpa-mantras separately:
those of Tumburu, of the caravan leader, and of the wise Tryambaka.
The expansion of eons for this Śarva, who wears matted hair, is infinite;
by its power, the mantras shall attain accomplishment upon the earth.
Now you are indeed authorized by the King of Kalas; therefore,

always speak at length upon the mantras and tantras, together with their secrets, their detailed expositions, their hidden meanings, and even their most profound mysteries, which bring about the arising of happiness for all sentient beings.
Having spoken thus, the glorious Vajradhṛk, resting his vajra with ease,
remained silent for a moment upon the raised jewel-lotus.
Then those maidens, together with their brothers as the fifth, quickly prostrated before the Lord of Mantras, the Lord of Yakṣas, the son of the Supreme Victor.
He addressed the great hero Vajrapāṇi, the all-pervading lord of the masters of mantra,
with sweet words, one by one in succession.
I shall now describe briefly the mandala consisting of two arms;
they call it the Jyeṣṭha-maṇḍala, for Jayā sang the Jyeṣṭha.
In a secluded, private place, when the great crowd has departed, in a hidden spot free from the pressure of others, on a riverbank or a mountain peak.
In a secluded and delightful forest, in a dwelling once inhabited by a Buddha,
in an empty temple, or in a purified, empty house.
At a single, auspicious, and delightful tree standing by the great ocean;
at a solitary *liṅga* in a cremation ground free from smoke and dust;
and at the most meritorious Vajrāsana and the beautiful Dharmacakra.
Where the Buddha attained peace, where the Great Sage was born—
these places are preeminent and auspicious for the drawing of mandalas; as are the banks of the Gaṅgā, and everywhere along the shores of islands and sandbanks.
And on all those banks of the foremost rivers that have been celebrated and are renowned throughout the world, one should constantly draw the maṇḍala.
On all sides, reaching to the ends of the waters and submerged in the great ocean,
the rivers originating from the Himavat and Vindhya mountains flow toward the sea;
on the banks of these most excellent of rivers, one should prepare and draw the mandala.
Or else, in a secluded spot on the ground, or in a beautifully adorned dwelling, in delightful temples of the gods, or at a very lofty stūpa,
or likewise at a shrine containing relics, or at ponds, wells, and pathways.
On all those banks and in their midst, they were beautifully adorned with cattle-pens,
lotus ponds,
and various other excellent sites, which were constantly graced by monasteries and pleasure groves.
On this earth frequented by sages, there is satisfaction for those whose minds are as they wish;
it is marked with mountain peaks, planets, and caves along with their surrounding slopes.
With divine dwellings that were peaceful and devoid of living creatures,
which were conducive to meditation, praiseworthy, and frequented by the foremost of sages;
Or rather, one should draw the mandala wherever there is satisfaction of the mind;
indeed, in these places, it should always be well-worshipped according to the instructions given.
The deities swiftly descended and established their presence in that place;
there, the ritual procedure consists of the constant performance of recitation and fire-offerings.
Those mantras to be accomplished— whether they be of the highest, lowest, or middle grade—
all such mantras indeed attain accomplishment here in the siddha-fields that have been described.
All mantras—whether superior, middling, or inferior—are indeed accomplished;
for there are various attainments in this world, and the ritual procedures are likewise of three kinds.
Mantras are of three types according to the threefold division of time;
at the three junctions of the day, all mantras are oriented toward the fruits of their respective actions in three ways.
Peaceful rites are prescribed in the auspicious mandala called Jaya;
those for the sake of nourishment in the one called Vijaya; and malevolent rites in the one called Ajita.
Likewise, for minor rites, the one known as Aparājita is always prescribed;
for all rites, the knower of mantras should draw the one known as Tumburu.
Five mandalas are to be known for those dwelling in the ocean;
one should dig into the earth a square shape on all sides, according to the prescribed measure.
Having cleared an area of four or eight cubits with his hand, he should remove gravel,
charcoal, husks, hair, and refuse.
Then, having personally cleared away the impurities of skulls, bones, and excrement with one's hand,
one should likewise cause others to recite the mantra over all the refuse there.
The practitioner, having diligently cleansed [the area] infested with worms and insects,
should fill it with pure and fragrant clay from the forest.
[One should use] pure clay produced on a riverbank, or from the top of an anthill, or from between the ground of a cow-pen and the earth, or from other such sources originating from the earth.
Having covered it on all sides with sand, or else with earth mixed with cow dung, one whose mind is serene should do so on every side.
One should quickly smear it all over with various unctuous substances mixed with fragrance, combined with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and anointed with saffron.
Having carefully smeared the ground all around with clay to form a mandala on every side, the knower of mantras and the knower of the mantra-tantras should proceed.
With various powders of five ingredients, perfumed with incense,
one should draw the divine maṇḍala, measuring four cubits on all sides.
A mandala measuring eight cubits is called the largest;
four cubits is the smallest, while that which is in between is proclaimed as the medium.
Then the renowned [mandala] of five cubits, and that of six cubits for those who have renounced the left;
this is declared to be the measurement of the mandala for all the goddesses, together with their brothers, being square on all sides.
One should draw the divine maṇḍala, which has four doors, four corners, and is adorned with four archways; it is praiseworthy and beautiful in form.
In the center, one should draw the Youth (Kumāra), beautifully adorned with the ornaments of childhood,
possessing a complexion like the hue of saffron, situated in the middle of the left side,
and graced by a blue lotus held in his hand on all sides.
The great lord Mañjughoṣa, the deity who bestows boons, has his right hand placed upon a long, auspicious *śrīmāla* fruit.
With eyes slightly opened, one should indeed draw the deity of the slight glance all around with the right hand, as well as the great ocean.
Standing there, one should draw the goddess seated upon a boat with her brother as the fifth,
well-attired and of beautiful form, together with the mantras and vidyās.
Adorned with various ornaments and brandishing diverse weapons,
she possessed the appearance and gestures of a young maiden, yet exhibited the prowess of a young prince accompanied by his brothers.
Tumburu [beheld] the caravan leader’s wife, who had embarked upon a ship with her four brothers as the fifth member, accompanied by a helmsman.
The great ocean stands indeed all around within the mandala,
filled with creatures such as fish and others, abounding in bubbles and honored by the waters.
The wise one should draw the maṇḍala in a secret and secluded place on all sides,
exactly as prescribed by the ritual rules and as the reality has been proclaimed.
One should perform all that quickly and apply it specifically to worldly matters;
whatever [is taught] in this Śaiva Tantra and also in the Gāruḍa Tantra.
By Brahmā and the other foremost sages, by Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Kāśyapa, and also by the best of munis, Mārkaṇḍeya, as well as those born of Pulastya and Agasti;
By the Vasus and the Śakra-devas, by Rudra, Indra, and the Sun,
by various eminent beings, and by Yama and others who possess great supernatural power among the pretas.
Together with the planetary mothers and the kūṣmāṇḍas, who are worshipped by yakṣas and rākṣasas,
they are the lords of mind, possessed of great supernatural power, in the world of humans and non-humans.
Worshipped by Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Savasa throughout the expanse of the kalpas,
they have related the majesty of the kalpas in their entirety upon the surface of the earth.
In that mandala, they should be applied; they will be accomplished here, there is no doubt, through various primary wombs and various forms of activities.
They have spoken and will speak at length concerning the ritual manual of the goddesses;
at that time, they should be appointed in the mandala called Jaya as the earth.

Thus concludes the first chapter from the forty-fifth section of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, entitled "The Most Secret Chapter on the Entry into the Maṇḍala of the Four Sisters and its Samaya."
Now begins the forty-eighth chapter.
Then, indeed, the goddess named Vijayā, having assembled and taken her seat right there in that assembly,
spoke the ritual procedure for the accomplishment of her own mandala-observance:

First of all, in a secluded place, hidden and in private, one should draw a mandala on the fifth day of either the auspicious bright or dark fortnight using five-colored powders—white, black, yellow, red, and green—or on the fourth day.
It should measure four cubits in extent, be square on all sides with four corners, and adorned with four archways.
Throughout the center of the mandala, one should draw a great ocean, decorated with four mudrās.

In the center, the seal of the Sārthavāha is in the form of a maṇḍala, with the luster of the color of the moon. In the northeast corner, the seal of Jayā is in the shape of a half-moon and white; in the southeast corner, the seal of Vijayā is triangular and radiant yellow; in the southwest corner, the seal of Ajitā is in the shape of a knot and has a red radiance; and in the northwest corner, the seal of Aparājitā is in the shape of a vajra and has a black radiance. Furthermore, all the seals must be depicted as being garlanded with flames.
Having first become pure in conduct, one should place four full jars at the four corners, their mouths covered with mango sprouts and their interiors filled with all kinds of grains and jewels.
In the center, however, the fifth jar for the caravan leader Tumburu should likewise have its mouth covered with mango sprouts and be wrapped in fresh cloth;
and in that same manner, the offerings of bali, flowers, and so forth should be prepared, just as were the mudrās.
The colors, flowers, incense, perfumes, and so forth—all of that must be prepared in exactly that manner.

An offering (bali) should be cast in the four directions. For malevolent rites (abhicāruka), it should be performed at midnight or midday; for nourishing rites (pauṣṭika), at dawn; for pacifying rites (śāntika), in the afternoon or when the sun has set. Furthermore, these three types of ritual actions should be employed according to the prescribed times during the construction of the maṇḍala, the fire sacrifice (homa), the recitation (japa), and the accomplishment (sādhana).

Pure men and women who are skillful in character and free from distress should be admitted; likewise, young maidens who uphold secret mantras should be admitted first. Having positioned them facing the east, one should consecrate water with the root mantra of Vijayā, and having performed the consecration seven times, one should sprinkle it upon everyone.

Having fasted for one day and night and being clothed in clean garments, he should cause eight or more individuals—up to as many as one—to enter through the western door facing eastward. Having covered their faces with fresh cloths, having each person bind the *vijayā* mudrā and join their palms, and having offered yellow flowers, he should cause them to cast [the flowers]. Having recited the *vijayā* mantra and wiped their faces, he should cause them to behold the maṇḍala and have them perform a circumambulation.
One should show the mudrās to all of them;
then, they should be admitted one after another in succession until eight have entered.
First, one should invoke the goddesses with their respective invocation mantras and [the disciples] together with their brothers with the root mantra, using appropriate flowers.

Having first offered incense and performed the appropriate salutation, the disciple—whether a woman, a man, a boy, or a girl—should be consecrated outside that maṇḍala like a king, with all necessary implements or whatever is desired. One should consecrate him with whatever would please the Maṇḍalācārya or by which he might be satisfied.
Having been consecrated, one or three may be consecrated with the Noble Consecration (āryābhiṣeka).
And one thing must be said:

"Listen, noble son or daughter of good family! You have received initiation and are authorized by all the deities, together with their brothers, within your own mantra-tantras; having drawn the mandala as you desire, you may bestow the extensive rituals, rules, conduct, and procedures for your own mantras.
Those others should be consecrated with the initiation of knowledge (vidyā-abhiṣeka).
Or there may be two or three people;
as for the rest, having instructed them in the practice of their own mantras, they should be dismissed.
Then the mandala master, having sprinkled [the deity] with sandalwood water and offered the *argha*, should dismiss the deity with his own mantra using incense, flowers, and so forth.
All the ritual implements should be taken by himself;
having taken them, he should give his own share—the third part—to all those who are destitute.
The remainder should be washed away in water.
Having well-smeared that area of ground, making it beautiful, free from dust, one may go wherever one desires.
They should also be instructed in accordance with their own mantra practices.
All the disciples should be made to bind the mudrās of their respective deities in secret, in private, where there is no movement of people;
for by those very mantras previously specified, all mantras attain accomplishment with particular excellence.
Especially regarding the mantras for rites that bring swift accomplishment,
it has been stated in the Jayākhyamaṇḍala for the reasons previously specified.

That which is prescribed by the rules of ritual action in the auspicious mandala called Vijaya is called the second mandala; thus it has been taught by the practitioners of mantra who know the true meaning of reality.
She should be known by the name Vijayā, the accomplisher of all rites and purposes;
the knower of mantras shall achieve all desired aims through her among all mantras.
When a mantra has been previously recited by a person for all rites,
it is proclaimed that its presiding deity provides protection for victory.
There is the defeat of obstacles and the commencement of undertakings facing fruition;
this occurs in the second mandala, known as Vijaya, which accomplishes all aims.
Through seeing [the deity], a person is released from all long-standing sins;
through recitation and yoga, the knower of mantras attains purification from evil.
And there shall be the defeat of other mantras on this earth—
those belonging to opposing factions, whether born of evil or non-evil wombs.
At that very moment, the mantra-practitioner destroys the enclosures of the mandala known as Vijaya;
they call this "the all-accomplishing" [mantra], which brings about subjugation, attraction, and prosperity.
In this world, that which is born of ritual action is fruitful, accomplishing nourishment, pacification, and all goals;
for this [deity], born from the ocean of the mandala, is the accomplisher of all aims.
In the place called Vijaya, he is highly esteemed, meritorious, praiseworthy, honored by Soma;
he is eternally eternal, pure, auspicious, and the destroyer of calamities.
"By writing [this], practitioners quickly become handsome, possessed of beauty, fortunate, and an achiever of all aims; it leads upward and swiftly accomplishes one's purpose."
Thus they spoke with faith in the Buddha's teaching: "The single mandala of Ajita is indeed proclaimed as one that is honored by the world."
This was previously taught by the foremost sages, distinguished throughout the world;
now I shall proclaim the mandala named Ajita.
Or rather, one should employ it exactly as follows:
however, the best color is red, and it should also be [colored] with red powders.
In the same manner, with offerings of oblations, flowers, and so forth, and by means of perfumes, incense, and other rituals,
the exterior is entirely composed of red, its beauty enhanced by limbs consumed by blood.
In the same way, one should everywhere separate the *mudrā* and the *sarvatra* as well as the *bhīmā*; the application of the ritual of *bali* and *homa* should also be performed with red substances.
One should likewise cause water-pots of a reddish hue to be given, along with red garments;
and similarly, a face-covering or a red parasol.
One should employ a seat, a bed, a vehicle, and likewise red unguents; for the sake of attaining the goals of both women and men, one should likewise use red mantras.
Mantras for the sake of passion are appropriate only for one who possesses passion;
the knower of mantras should not direct his mind toward other mantras that belong to those who act [with such intent].
The wise practitioner, always disciplined in yoga and knowing the mantra, should utter the mantra for the sake of desire and to attain prosperity, as a means for subjugation and attraction.
One shall obtain all wondrous prosperities within the mandala named Ajita;
for the purpose of bringing all beings under control, this mandala is released upon the earth.
It has been constantly declared by the ministers that, for the sake of preventing mental distraction,
one should draw forth the great power of karma— the activity of material beings— into subjection.
A mortal whose mind is distracted indeed becomes possessed by her, who gazes with unblinking eyes;
he arrives as a slave, accepting all that she commands.
Seeing such a human being— helpless, fallen into subjection, and under the control of the *kiṅkara* servants— one should set him free once again.
Whether it be a woman, a man, a boy, or even a girl,
one should release them once again by means of the very root-mantra of Ajita.
On the surface of the earth, the wise one should draw the maṇḍala with the previously specified rites performed according to the rules, and he should employ it at all times.
Action accompanied by mantra is declared to be fruitful in the performance of mantra-rites;
one should accomplish this supreme procedure through the preliminary applications of other methods.
For all the hosts of Maheśvara, when being accomplished, are indeed perfected through the knowledge of the ritual procedure,
as well as form, mudrā, mantra, and the essence of the tantra.
The measure of the ritual yoga, which would be too extensive if described in full, should be understood according to this measurement; learn it now regarding this mandala.
A mandala arises when it is seven cubits, or six, five, or four cubits, or even two cubits or just one cubit in measure.
Eight cubits is the largest, while seven, six, and five are the middling sizes;
four cubits, two cubits, or even a single cubit is the smallest.
One should perform rites for pacification (śāntika) in the superior [mandala], and likewise rites for enrichment (pauṣṭika) in the intermediate one;
one should perform rites of sorcery (ābhicāruka) within the inferior mandala.
For the sake of bringing all beings under control, and for their constant subduing and deluding,
the reciter who is always devoted to the mantra should perform all rites.
The mandala named Ajita has been taught, which liberates one from all seizing spirits;
therein dwell the bhūtas, piśācas, grahas, mātṛs, and pūtanās.
Merely upon being seen, they always come under one's control, deluded by yawning;
through constant sight within the maṇḍala, they quickly attain subjection.
Then the goddess Aparājitā, having bowed down to the Son of the Best of Jinas,
[honored] Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, Mañjughoṣa, and Subhūṣaṇa.
And to all the sons of the Buddha, who possess great majesty,
as well as to this goddess together with her five brothers, one should utter these words:
"I too shall perform such a task for the sake of the mandala," he said,
and he chose a virtuous song composed of logical reasoning and the union of meaningful words.
It is considered to possess great majesty and great power, the subduer of the unsubdued;
it is accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, has the luster of a dark complexion, and a radiance equal to the Night of Doom (Kālarātri).
Resembling the color of the so-called messengers of Yama,
he was like the sun itself— terrible, a taker of others' lives, and fearsome.
Just as it was previously specified for the goddesses in the mandala,
one should perform all of that in exactly the same way, with the exception of the colors.
It should always be drawn in a cremation ground, or always in the city to the south,
where there is smoke, which is embraced by garlands of flames and surrounded by skeletons of bones.
In a neutral place where sisters dwell, upon that very ground of the earth,
one should draw [the diagram] with cremation ashes on the black-colored surface of the earth.
Just as the sequence of the ritual for worship has been previously specified by the mantras,
the practitioner of mantra should swiftly apply all of that in its entirety.
One's own mantra, the Lord of Mantras, Tumburu the caravan leader,
and the one surrounded by the great ocean.
In the Ajitā [mandala], Vijayā is quickly designated as holding a sword in her hand;
one should always designate that goddess Jayā as holding a bow in her hand.
For these [goddesses] possess various weapons, are adorned with various ornaments,
are known as beings of various movements, and have various appearances and gestures.
Having indeed drawn this black-colored mandala here upon the ground,
this mandala practiced on earth is truly a destroyer of the life-force of others.
The mantras that give rise to various purposeful activities and ritual actions—
having performed all of those as previously described, one should thereafter commence the rite.
Mantras are exhausted by recitation and fire-offerings, as are the mandalas;
for entry into this mandala occurs through the rites that arise from those preliminary procedures.
Thus, this mandala of the foremost goddess, the youngest one, has been described in brief, though it could be told at great length.
It is to be known by the name Aparājita, a mandala renowned on earth;
it was previously unconquered from all sides by the lords of the rākṣasas and the kinnaras.
Together with the Bhūtas, the chief Daityas, Yama, the Mātṛs, and the Sagrahas, as well as the Kūṣmāṇḍas, Vyantaras, Piśitāśas, and Pūtanās.

But in the Tantra, it is said: "On all sides, with mantras consisting of flesh-eaters accompanied by impurities, with the most terrible lords of the asuras, and with the great manifestations of all bhūtas."
Then Tumburu, the caravan leader, spoke to the entire assembly:
"O mortals, understand him who is called Tumburu on the left, the wielder of the vajra."
Having bowed their heads to the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, they spoke once more on the surface of the earth, saying, "It has been previously declared," and they learned this speech.
The entire previously described mandala has four risings;
the first concludes all ritual activities, while the second is now being explained here.
Thus, through skillful means, the fourfold mandala— which brings about the propitiation of all beings— has arrived here in its sequential order as an intermingled whole.
Always in an empty house, or always in an empty temple; in a secluded and private place, in one's own home, or even in a small hut.
With various colorful garments and ornaments, with diverse beautiful full bowls,
and with powders of five colors or various substances derived from fruits.
With various bright powders made from ground rice,
combined with white powders and perfumed with the incense of sandalwood and agallochum.
With blended powders of sandalwood joined with saffron and agallochum,
sprinkled with camphor and musk, and [mixed] with priyaṅgu, keśara, and other such substances.
One should always draw the mandala with powders of various fragrances, combined with *spṛkkā* and *sīra*, and well-perfumed with black *agaru*.
Bathing three times a day, performing recitations and fire-offerings, and changing his garments three times;
likewise, the mantra-practitioner [should act] during the mixed night-watch, clearly distinguished by white and black.
On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, one should always draw the mandala according to the prescribed ritual,
measuring four cubits in size.
The wise one should carefully draw all of that with a focused mind:
a square with four doors and joined by four archways.
One should always draw Śāriputra in the center of this maṇḍala,
seated upon a lotus in the middle, turning the wheel of Dharma.
The minister should paint the Buddha, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Great Hero;
he should quickly depict him together with his four brothers as the fifth, accompanied by the excellent mudrās.
The mantra-practitioner should draw [the design] on all sides, with four corners on every side.
On the excellent lotus, he should stand as the eldest; below the Buddha, who is like an ocean, Tumburu’s mudrā should be drawn, white in color on all sides.

All have the luster of white color, with the radiance of the kunda flower, the moon, and the hare-marked moon; they resemble the form of the white water-lily and are perfectly white in all their features.

The mantra practitioner, knowing the ritual procedure, should perform all of that for the goddesses according to the previously described yoga; this is the means for accomplishing the purpose of all rites.
Just as one should apply the mandala upon every cloth,
so too should one employ the threefold mandala prescribed for the cloth according to the ritual rules.
The remainder should be performed as desired on a cloth mandala or on the ground,
according to what is prescribed in this system of mantra-tantra.
On a wooden plank or a tablet, all the deities should be painted according to their appearance in wood, together with their brothers as the fifth.
Just as everything [prescribed] for the maṇḍala, all that should be drawn upon a cloth,
or even in the sky, as specified according to its appropriate origin;
this has been taught by those who know the mantras of the cloth, while for images, it is proclaimed as follows.
Those who know mantras should always employ sandalwood from the Malaya mountains, saffron along with its filaments, and the *punnāga* tree in the making of images.
One should find the *piyāla*, *padmaka*, and *rodhra* wood upon the earth,
as well as *sarala*, *devadāru*, and *kāśmīra* together with the *ghaṇṭaka*.
A cloth made from *kuṭaja*, *arjuna*, *jambu*, *priyaṅgu*, and *uḍumbara* wood,
or specifically from *raktacandana* wood, is prescribed.
Wood from the Plakṣa and Udumbara trees, and especially from the Sahakāra; as well as the Puṇḍarīka, Sarja, and Sinduvāra, which originates from the Siddhas.
The *vakula*, the *tilaka*, the *kāṣṭha*, and likewise the *saptacchada*—
these and various other species of trees are of male, female, and neuter types.
All parts should be taken from the wood; from the root and the rhizome, those that grow upward;
and from the branches, all parts should be taken from both the Madhuka and the bitter wood.
One should know that *picumanda* wood is for [rites of] subjugation (*abhicāruka*), as are *kāṣṭha*, *ariṣṭa*, and *bhūtataru*; likewise, the wood of *putrañjīvaka* is always used for subjugation.
One should employ *aśvattha* wood for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), whether on the ground or in a wooden vessel.
For the purpose of nourishment, it is said that one should use wood, or specifically the head of an *aśoka* tree;
one should employ all types of wood for all rites in every situation.
The root-end of the wood for the image should be joined with the Root (Mūla) lunar mansion;
then, for the wood used for the pillar, one should join it with the Jyeṣṭhā lunar mansion;
thereafter, for the wood used for the branches, one should join it with all the lunar mansions.
Thereafter, one should have [the rite] performed under the asterism Revatī on a Monday;
indeed, under the asterism Mūla on a Sunday, the pillar is observed by Śukra and the others.
Accompanied by all the primary attendants and all the hosts of grahas,
he would go to the root of Rasātala and enter the body of Āsuri.
Then, by means of wood produced from the *tamba* tree and also from the *gāṇḍa* tree,
[one achieves] the subjugation and attraction of spirits, as well as their paralyzing, immobilizing, and deluding.
One should indeed perform an act of sorcery; the image shall enter into them, and thereafter it shall ascend to the vault of the sky by means of upward-pointing wooden splinters.
O Goddess, one should employ an image that rests upon a divine vehicle;
by means of it, one may go everywhere through the branches [of the tree] and experience the arising of the bliss of invisibility.
The mantra practitioner may also commence the rite in any direction as desired;
however, all the cardinal points have been specified, and they are intended as the defining characteristics for the image.
They were mounted upon a ship, beautifully adorned with the appearance of goddesses;
they bore the marks of the form of maidens, and their hair was arranged in five locks.
In that very way, we were indeed awakened within this mandala placed upon the hand;
Tumburu is truly the caravan leader, and the one of great splendor is the helmsman.
With a sword placed in the left hand,
the mantras— consisting of three or two finger-breadths in height— are recited while moving obliquely across the vessel.
One should have a boat well-constructed, either one *vitasti* in length or longer;
it should be beautifully finished, white in appearance, and as bright as a conch shell or the moon.
The wise one should especially cause Jaya to be made, as well as Tumburu;
Vijayā, shining with a golden hue, and Ajitā, who is intensely red.
One should designate Aparājitā as being black in color, the ring finger as white,
Prasannā in the form of Tumburu, and Jayā likewise.
The goddesses Vijayā, Aparājitā, and Ajitā, with slightly furrowed brows and gentle attire, should be depicted on all sides.
Whether the size is that of a thumb-joint or that of the little finger,
all these measurements and appearances have been declared by all the mantra-practitioners.
The *dantī* is known as the "mace of enjoyment," produced from gold or earth;
one who desires sovereignty over the earth should fashion this very beautiful [image].
An image made of silver or even copper is renowned for bringing about subjugation;
indeed, one made of bell-metal is said on this earth to effect the summoning of spirits.
Indeed, it is said that for malevolent rites, the image should be made of tin, lead, or iron;
or likewise of various precious gems, such as coral and crystal.
Those who desire swift accomplishment should fashion a gentle image; however, rites arising from foul states should be performed with images made of skulls and bones.
Just as those who have attained their goals succeed through various principal peaks and other such places,
so indeed do all mantras and even minor mantras on this earth achieve success.
Gains occur according to possibility, and the attainment of goals occurs according to what is possible;
these are accomplished from all sides when performed through the application of images.
Thus it is said.
Then Tumburu, the caravan leader, explained the general procedure for the accomplishment of all [deities]:

having fashioned an image of the goddesses made of ivory, measuring the size of the little finger, one should summon them in a very secret place with the root mantras. Offering incense with the left hand, one should recite the root mantra of Jayā.
Having performed the recitation eight thousand or eight hundred times, whatever is desired will be told entirely in a dream.
Recitation should be performed three times a day for seven days;
it accomplishes everything according to one's desire.
It performs all minor rites, such as subjugation, summoning, and the liberation from planetary afflictions.
Or, for the purpose of subjugating sentient beings according to one's desire, he shows the signs and rituals for the supreme means and other practices:
one should strike an image of the goddesses with *jātī* flowers;
the king will become submissive.
One should strike an image of the goddesses with jasmine buds—
five buds for each repetition— one hundred and eight times at the three junctions of the day for seven days.
Whichever princess one desires, endowed with great wealth and possessing an excellent form and beauty, she shall obtain her.
One should strike each individual image with five *jātī* flowers at the three junctions of the day for seven days, one hundred and eight times.
One obtains whichever beautiful woman one desires;
taking that very image, one should carry it upon one's head.
Having covered [her] with hair, her husband stands before her as a servant;
he should place [the substance] between her thighs;
she obtains supreme good fortune.
Having taken the path, one proceeds with the vajra;
one is not robbed by thieves,
and upon seeing an enemy force, one paralyzes it.
He may enter into battle; he is not struck by weapons;
he bewilders the enemy.
It paralyzes an enemy army moving about with elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having consecrated collyrium with mantras, one should recite over the eyes;
whoever one looks upon becomes his servant.

Having consecrated *gorocanā* with mantras and applied it as a *tilaka* on one's own face, whoever one looks upon becomes subject to one's will. As long as the *tilaka* remains, one will experience uninterrupted passion in sexual union.

In this manner, having consecrated seven times various excellent articles such as garments, incense, perfumes, garlands, flowers, sacrificial threads, staffs, water-pots, wooden items, sandals, beds, vehicles, seats, food, and all other such specific requisites, one should perform the rite oneself or cause others to do so.
All sentient beings will become submissive, acting as servants and following one's will.

Having consecrated a *māṣa*-bean and a *jambūlika* fruit seven times, one should offer eight thousand oblations into the fire before the goddesses in a secluded place during the three junctions of the day for seven days; then all *raṇḍās*, all *ḍākinīs*, all *bhūtas* and *grahas*, and all *kaśmalas* will become submissive. They will follow one’s commands as servants, and one will be able to travel to and from a distance of a hundred *yojanas*. Furthermore, having ground [the substances] with cow urine in the forenoon, and having taken a *piṇḍāraka-bandaka* and an *āmra-bandaka*, one should prepare them by repeating the mantra a thousand times and smear them on the foot.
One should employ either divine water or *jyeṣṭha* water in all rites and in all rituals that involve worship, even according to the supreme mantra procedures;
however, there is this distinction:

in whichever maṇḍala the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, the Buddha Śākyamuni—the Caravan Leader, the foremost of all beings—is depicted, it is in that maṇḍala that the rites should be performed by one who has seen the *samaya*.
"All rites are swiftly accomplished.
Ten thousand recitations for the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) should be performed.
When Jayā speaks her own ritual manual.

Having fashioned an image of the goddesses out of emerald, sapphire, ruby, crystal, and so forth; or from special gems such as coral sprouts, stone, lapis lazuli, or made of gold and silver; or having fashioned an image the size of the little finger, or the size of a barley grain, or even a pearl; and having placed them upon a boat together with the four sisters along with their brother—at least having fashioned their images—one should, as before, prepare a mandala in a clean place sprinkled with water of sandalwood, saffron, and camphor, using those very same materials for the specific ornaments and weapons of the goddesses. In a very secret location, during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, or on the full moon of Kārttika, or in another bright fortnight, during the appearance of the Prātihāraka flowers, or on another auspicious day in the light half of the month, on a praised lunar date, under the days of the Moon or Venus, and under the constellations Rohiṇī, Revatī, Anurādhā, or Jyeṣṭhā, subsisting on alms-food, or eating only water and barley flour, or consuming sacrificial ghee, fruits, bananas, mangoes, and coconut, one should first recite the mantra of Jayā one hundred thousand times.

Having performed the recitation and completed the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), Tumburu, having beheld the maṇḍala arising from the image of the Tathāgata, and having established his protection, wearing white garments, adorned with garlands, and with his head bound with *mālatī* flowers, shall remain fasting for a day and night and then enter the practice of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Having offered the water-offering (*argha*) as before, he should perform a great worship using a profusion of *jātī* flowers, or *mahākṛpā*, *piṇḍītaka*, *nāgakesara*, or *punnāga*—or any one of these—or with fresh flowers. Taking five *mālatī* flowers at a time, he should strike the goddesses along with their brothers three hundred thousand times.
Within six months, one becomes a vidyādhara;
in an instant, one even goes to the world of Brahmā;
possessing a divine form and moving according to one's will, one lives for an intermediate kalpa.
It is accomplished even by means of the ritual procedures of other kalpas and by all mundane mantras.
Ajitā likewise speaks her own ritual manual as a mantra-practitioner;
both of these great goddesses perform all rites as previously described, being born from the source of their own mantras.
However, this is their distinction.
One should accomplish all rites with yellow flowers for Vijayā and red flowers for Ajitā, as well as with various ritual implements of those respective colors.
Regarding Vijayā, they also say this:
her image should be made yellow and red.

Having prepared the Tathāgata maṇḍala as before, one should fashion an image of Tumburu the caravan leader and Ajitā; [the former] should be made of copper or red sandalwood, while according to my ritual manual it should be made of silver-gold and have a yellow luster, smeared with gorocanā and saffron.
Everything else is exactly as previously described. Both goddesses spoke thus to one another:
Vijayā and Ajitā shall accomplish all rites according to one's desire and what is sought by the mind.
Aparājitā spoke thus:
"I too shall speak for a kalpa; everything that has been uttered by me in this mandala must be performed exactly so with one's own mantra."

Having drawn an image of the goddesses with charcoal from a cremation ground or with cremation ash, and having worshipped it with black flowers, one should recite [the mantra] while holding the name of the enemy in a secret place or in a cremation ground;
at that very moment, the enemy dies or becomes insane.
Or he is seized by epilepsy,
or he causes the destruction of his lineage;
at the will of the practitioner, one should offer oblations of human flesh (mahāmāṃsa) right there in that cremation ground.

It destroys enemies, paralyzes them, withers them, causes them to be seized by a great rākṣasa, or brings about the destruction of their lineage according to the will of the practitioner. It causes the entire population of all regions and districts to be afflicted by a great epidemic, and then restores them to health again.
In this way, it performs all such cruel rites that take the lives of others and cause immediate injury.

Rites should be performed on the fourteenth, ninth, eighth, sixth, fourth, and other such lunar days of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). All rites achieve success on the days of the sun, Mars, and Saturn. Without any effort, one should take charcoal from a cremation ground and write the name in a skull belonging to a *caṇḍāla*, or draw the image of a woman or a man.
At that very moment, they become impassioned.
By placing a finger upon the vulva while [visualizing] a reflection in a skull-cup, a woman who is burning with passion comes from even a hundred *yojanas* away at that very instant.
Holding the skull-cup and reciting the mantra, one becomes invisible.
Taking collyrium, one should apply it to the eyes;
a woman, being consumed by the fire of passion, will come.
All rites are to be performed in this manner.
Thus addressed, the goddesses entreated the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One, the Buddha, the Lord of Dharma, speak his own mantra;
and for the sake of compassion toward us and for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, [speak] the practice of his own mantra."
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the son of the King of the Śākyas, having looked slightly at that maiden together with her brothers, spoke these words:
"O maidens, you five including your brother are not capable of hearing the greatness of the qualities of the Tathāgata, nor the power of the practice of mantras, nor of undertaking the conduct.
Who else in this world, including the gods, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, would be able to hear it or undertake the conduct?"

Excluding those Bodhisattvas who have generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and are established on the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), who are lords, and who possess a supreme head distinguished by the illusion-like wisdom of all Tathāgatas— the entry into the accomplishment of all mantra practices— who else is capable of hearing or knowing this instruction, of explaining the entry into mantra practice, or of revealing it to all sentient beings?
Excluding the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, as well as those sentient beings who have entered that path and generated the mind of awakening— you maidens are not capable [of this].
Therefore, generate the mind of awakening;
toward all sentient beings, be possessed of a mind of loving-kindness and a mind of benefit.
Having spoken thus, those maidens, having taken up the three refuges and generated the mind of enlightenment, sat down in silence to listen to the Dharma.

Thus concludes the chapter on the four maidens, which is the second ritual procedure for entering the maṇḍala as an aid to accomplishment, from the forty-sixth detailed section of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter.

Then those deities, having circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni, all the bodhisattvas, and all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas three times, bowed their heads in prostration and stood gazing at the Buddha, the Blessed One, while also gazing at the extensive rituals of the mantras and tantras.
They spoke of their own mudrās and medicinal herbs, speaking according to their respective intentions.

Authorized by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, for the benefit of sentient beings, he spoke the entire extensive collection of chapters on mudrās and mantras; each [deity] then spoke their own respective chapter on mudrās and the ritual manual for medicinal herbs.

Tumburu, the caravan leader, spoke thus: "First, having rubbed one's hands with perfume—either mixed with sandalwood or other fragrant substances—one should stand before the goddesses facing either east or north. Grasping the thumb of the right hand with the left hand using a fist-like grip, one should rotate it counter-clockwise and place it at the region of the navel; or, using the fist-grip, one may place it at the position of the head. O Blessed One, this is my *samayamudrā* of Tumburu, the caravan leader."

In that same manner, for the purpose of accomplishing ritual actions, one should place the two hands at the region of the navel using the fist-gesture (*muṣṭi-yoga*), having inserted the thumb of the left hand inside and firmly grasped it.
This, O Blessed One, is my *Jayā* mudrā, which performs all rites. In that same manner, having opened the fist with the index finger, one should threaten.
In the southern direction, all obstacles are destroyed.
This is the second great mudrā. Having raised the second finger, one should direct it toward the western direction.
This is the second great mudrā; it paralyzes all wicked *nāgas* and should be employed for the purpose of neutralizing poison.
Raising the third finger and directing it toward the northern quarter, all yakṣas, yakṣīs, kinnaras, mahoragas, and kūṣmāṇḍas become submissive;
this is the third great mudrā, which effects summoning and fulfills all hopes.
All activities will also become manifest.
Having spread the fourth finger and contracted the thumb which remains within, one should direct [the hand] toward the eastern quarter of the palm;
all gods will become submissive.
Standing before the gods and facing the east, one should display it;
all spirits will become submissive,
and one will become beloved by all sentient beings.
This is the fourth Mahāmudrā, which bestows the fruits of all desires.
Having joined both hands and spread all the fingers, one should touch the crown of the head with the palms in the shape of an añjali;
then one should gaze upward and downward.
From the peak of Brahma down to the base of the pillar, and below to the netherworld of Rasātala,
it brings all the gods and dānavas under its control.
This is the fifth great mudrā, which accomplishes the purpose of all activities.
O Blessed One, this very [mudrā] is the five great mudrās that bestow the fruits of all desires.

Vijayā spoke thus: "O Blessed One, there are indeed five great mudrās of mine. Having placed the left hand inside [the right] so that the nails are not visible, one should form a firm fist and, by means of the yoga of striking and wiping, look downward.
This is the first great mudrā."
The second is for looking upward;
the third for looking toward the southern direction; the fourth for grasping all directions;
and the fifth is placed upon the head.
These very five great mudrās become the bestowers of the fruits of all desires.

Ajitā spoke thus: "Having restrained both hands and inserted both thumbs into the middle [of the palms], forming the shape of a hollowed *añjali*, one should make the middle fingers like needles and the little fingers raised in the shape of a noose, while likewise pressing down the index and ring fingers; this is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) named Ajitā.
It is a merit-bestowing subduer of the difficult-to-tame, accomplishing all ritual purposes.
One should turn that same seal toward the southern direction."
The second great mudrā is named Vijayā;
in this manner, one should attract [the deity] from the western direction.
The great mudrā is named Jayā.
In this way, one should not turn back toward the northern direction;
this is the great mudrā named Aparājitā.
In this way, one should not turn back toward the eastern direction.
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) named Mahāsārthavāha exists; these very five Great Seals fulfill all aspirations. Thus it is said.
Aparājitā spoke thus: "O Blessed One, there are exactly five great mudrās of mine.
As before, having washed one's hands, they should be bound during the dark fortnight.
They are to be applied according to that very same procedure as in this sādhana."

Standing facing south in front of the goddesses, join both hands together; with the middle, ring, index, and other fingers, form a trident in the shape of three needles. Then, inserting the little fingers, the middle [fingers], and the thumbs into the center, place this upon the surface of the hand at the position of the head.
This is first the great mudrā named Aparājitā; in this manner, all [mudrās] are to be employed, just as in the case of Ajitā.
The sisters who bear the same names as the brothers, together with them, are the *mahāmudrās* of all.
That which is on the palm of the hand is this ocean;
that which is the thumb belongs to the brother Tumburu; and these fingers are all the sisters known by their successive names.
The index finger is Jayā, the middle finger is Vijayā, the ring finger is Ajitā, and the little finger is Aparājitā;
these should be applied to the two feet in this sequential order.
When meditated upon and honored, they provide their presence.
Seals (mudrās) become effective whether they are visualized or not visualized;
they perform all actions and fulfill all hopes. When one is in a state of distress, the great seals (mahāmudrās) should be visualized;
then no fear will arise.

Tumburu, the caravan leader, spoke thus: "Now, there is a general designation for these as 'remedies' (agada). And such is the power of our medicinal herbs by which all spirits (bhūta) are brought under control.
What, then, is that?"

Having taken a shoot from an *aśvattha* or *nyagrodha* tree, one should grind it with milk and stir it with cow’s milk. During the bright fortnight, under the asterism of Aśvinī, on a Monday, on the seventh lunar day, in the forenoon, one should recite the Sārthavāha mantra seven times over [the mixture] for a woman who is in her fertile period and not subject to miscarriage. Having likewise formed the mudrā, one should cause her to drink it while facing the east;
thus the woman will conceive a child and give birth to a long-lived son. She should sleep together with her husband.
Taking the root of those very [plants] under the constellation of Mūla, when the moon is in the northern direction, one should have fine powders prepared on a Sunday.
Whomever one gives these to becomes submissive; they should be applied to food, drink, meals, and the like, as well as to perfumes, garlands, betel, and so forth.
It should be done in such a way that it enters the bodies.
One touches it with the tongue and attends upon it with one's being.
That very [substance], by that same procedure, one should drink as if from a woman, or likewise from oneself.
One may even go to a hundred women without one's semen being interrupted.
Likewise, it brings about the development of a large phallus even in a woman.
A *gorjaruka* or a centipede, or the fruits of the *naraśakra*, as well as this powder, should be drunk with milk by one who has a hundred women in his house.
In this manner, having excluded the *pūrvamūla* and one's own *mudrā* when accompanied by mantras, everything else—both poison and secondary poison (*viṣam* and *aviṣam*)—may be employed.
And in all ritual actions, it is the supreme means for subjugating all beings, and these are the things to be accomplished.
Jayā said: "Taking the root of *jayantī*, one should perform it in such a way that it accomplishes all the rites of Tumburu.
Now, if one should desire to travel through the sky:

having wrapped the root of *jayantī* with the three metals, one should place it in the mouth after mixing it with saffron. This should be done by one who has fasted for three nights, is pure, and performs the rite under the conjunction of Puṣya on a Monday, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight, on the full moon, or on the fourteenth or eighth day."
When the lunar eclipse has ended, it becomes invisible.

Having recited one hundred thousand syllables of one's own mantra and cast in the pill, once the lunar eclipse has ended, one becomes a *vidyādhara*, able to assume any form at will, moving wherever one desires, and lives for twenty thousand years.
Upon vomiting it up, it becomes visible again.
Furthermore, in the human realm, he performs all actions in this manner.
Vijayā spoke thus: "However, there is this distinction:

having taken *agastivandāka*, one should grind it with *jyeṣṭhodaka* water or divine water (*divyavāri*), consecrate it with one's own mantra, and smear it on the feet; then one can travel back and forth for a hundred *yojanas*.
One remains untiring as long as one does not abandon [the practice]."
Taking the root of Vijayā, one should perform the rite in the same manner;
likewise, taking the root of Jayā, one accomplishes everything.
Ajitā spoke thus: "Having taken the root of Ajita, one should proceed exactly as before;
it accomplishes everything.

Aparājitā spoke thus: "Having taken the root of Aparājitā, together with its white and black leaves, fruits, and roots, everything should be performed just as the Caravan Leader [Sārthavāha] instructed."
However, this is the distinction:
that which acts swiftly (*āśukārin*) is accomplished quickly.
*Putrañjārī*, *kṛtāñjali*, *sahā*, *sahadevā*, and *mahoṣadhī* [are such].
Likewise, the goddess Chatrādhicchatrā, the renowned Mahākāla, Nākulī, Gandhanākulyā, and Saṅkucitakarṇikā.
Taking the roots of these [plants], one should have powders of *śūrpa* prepared;
by this, living beings come under one's control as soon as they are touched.
The husks of red śāli rice, saffron together with sandalwood,
combined with musk, and immersed in divine water.
The knower of mantras should fashion a pill from the three metals as prescribed;
having made that pill the size of an *akṣa* fruit, he should then place it in his mouth.
Or during a lunar eclipse, or at night, one should recite the mantra with a concentrated mind;
at dawn, the embodied being, having mastered the mantra, goes wherever he desires.
The pill always remains in his mouth as he performs the recitation;
or, assuming whatever animal form he desires, he wanders everywhere across the earth.
Likewise, when [the mantra] has been uttered, the practitioner becomes one whose intellect is fixed on recitation;
otherwise, if it remains in the mouth, it would always be of universal form.
One who has performed the recitation is distinguished by performing self-protection with their own mantra;
otherwise, the pill is stolen if the reciter does not perform protection.
All mantras, including the king of mantras belonging to all worldly realms,
are accomplished through the worship of all ritual manuals (kalpas) spoken by all [the Buddhas].
Those mantras and tantras that have been proclaimed attain accomplishment within this [system].
They wander over the entire earth, assuming various guises; existing in different states of existence and wombs, they take the forms of dogs,
crows, cats, owls, mice, frogs, and scorpions.
Crowded with all types of origins, bodiless yet dwelling within bodies,
they wander the entire earth, capable of uttering the cries of all living beings.
When all beings are under control and the welfare of all creatures arises as something dear,
and mortals always act accordingly, then one should employ them.
It is not spoken of to others in the world, for it is honored by the deities;
it is to be known as all-knowing in every respect and the accomplisher of all mantras.
Whatever has been spoken, and whatever other men on earth shall speak— all that extensive collection of ritual manuals (kalpavisara) has been declared here by the Mothers of the World.
Thus addressed, the gods, together with Sūtrāntasaṃpañcama,
then stood silent, having bowed to the Bull among Conquerors.
He sat down in that most excellent assembly to hear the Dharma,
[to receive] the empowerments of all the Buddhas and the sons of the Conquerors without exception.
Having requested the Great Hero, they remained silent thereafter;
then the glorious Vajradhṛk honored the deities.
Out of a desire to benefit those beings, he gave them his approval, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Therefore, O maidens, remain diligently established in the pledge."

Thus concludes the third chapter from the forty-seventh detailed section of the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra belonging to the Bodhisattvapiṭaka-avatamsaka, titled "The Detailed Section on All Rituals, Seals, Medicines, Tantras, and Mantras, Together with the Rules for Recitation and the Means of Accomplishment for the Four Maidens."
Now begins the fiftieth chapter.
Then indeed, the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi, the general of the yakṣas, was present in that assembly.

Having sat down, he rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, regarding that King of Wrath named Yamāntaka who was spoken of by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, its ritual manual (*kalpa*) has not been revealed by the Blessed One in detail."
Nor was it by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.

"O Blessed One, observing future generations, when the time for the disappearance of the teaching has arrived after the Blessed One has passed into parinirvāṇa, during the most terrifying period, in the lowest of ages—a time when the Buddha-field is devoid of all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—I shall [act] for the sake of protecting the Tathāgata’s teaching, for the sake of the long endurance of the Dharmadhātu, for the sake of warding off all wicked kings, for the sake of subduing those who harm the Three Jewels, for the sake of fulfilling the inconceivable bodhisattva conduct through skill in training sentient beings, and for the sake of accomplishing the inconceivable ripening of sentient beings. O Blessed One, in that final time, in that final age of the Sugata, when the destruction of the teaching is occurring, whoever shall employ this King of Wrath named Yamāntaka according to the ritual prescribed in the *kalpa*, for him there will be success."

This King of Wrath must certainly be employed against wicked kings and those beings who harm the teachings, as well as against great yakṣas who possess great energy and are intent on both punishment and favor, yet are devoid of great compassion; it is not to be used against others.
Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called "The Empowerment of the Buddha’s Miraculous Transformation" through silence.
Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta also remained in silence.
And the entire circle of the assembly experienced a sixfold earthquake.
The hosts of gods were terrified, and all the lords of the children were struck with fear;
so too were all the gods, the nāgas, the lords of the dānavas, and the mātṛs.
All the hosts of gods, headed by the chief grahas, trembled;
humans trembled with divided minds, and the pūtanas were filled with evil intent.
Then those kings, distressed and terrified, with their hearts filled with rage,
sought refuge in the command of the King of Dharma.
Terrified of the Lord of the Guhyakas, the Yakṣa Vajrapāṇi of great splendor, and of Mañjughoṣa the Youth himself— the King of Mantras—
then made a solemn pledge in the presence of Mañjughoṣa.
Save us, O Child, you who have compassion for all sentient beings!
Today we shall consume you with extremely terrible and cruel mantras;
for today, overcome by wrath, we stand upon the surface of the earth.
Then the Bodhisattva, possessing great splendor, appearing in the form of a youth, said:
"Do not fear, O all you gods, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and dānavas!"
Indeed, this pledge has been declared by me to you; it is not to be transgressed by any deities, nor by humans or non-humans, nor by any beings whatsoever.
Always maintaining a mind of loving-kindness, one should constantly recollect that mantra—
the Fully Enlightened One, the foremost among bipeds, the Lion of the Śākyas, the supreme among men.
By him alone were spoken the mantras of Uṣṇīṣa and the others, together with Locanā;
they are the teachers of the three worlds, the wheel-turners, the mass of splendor, and the source of victory.
Vijayoṣṇīṣa and the other mantras, Padmapāṇi together with Lokita, the Lord Avalokiteśvara, Bhṛkuṭī, Tārā, and Yaśasvinī.
And the goddesses Sitavāsinī, Mahāśvetā, Yaśovatī,
and Bhogavatī, as well as Hayagrīva, the king of mantras.
For these mantras, issued from the Victors, are preeminent within the Lotus family;
the single-syllable mantra is the sovereign lord and master of all mantras.
Having recollected the God of gods, the Lord of Mantras of great splendor,
there arose from him a wrathful manifestation known by the name Yamāntaka.
The thoughts of Avalokiteśvara, which give rise to compassion,
were revealed by former Buddhas whose minds were drawn forth by great compassion.
That Tārā, spoken by Avalokita, delivers sentient beings;
she is the noble vidyā born of samādhi, designated as "woman," and possessing the form of a name.
Then the bodhisattva practices the supreme conduct of awakening throughout thousands of world-systems, indeed many incalculable ones in various ways.
Then the Goddess, wandering for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings,
assumed the form of a woman and appeared before embodied beings in the form of a mantra.
One should establish beings who are to be disciplined by means of ritual rules in the vehicle of enlightenment;
thus has the inconceivable conduct of the Bodhisattvas been revealed.
One should likewise recollect the heroic Vajrapāṇi, the sovereign lord of mantras,
and the goddess Māmakī, the mistress of the family, who is honored throughout the three worlds.
Śaṅkulā, Mekhalā, the illustrious Vajramuṣṭi,
Krodhendratilaka, Śatru, Nīladaṇḍa, and Bhairava.
These hosts of female messengers and wrathful deities are proclaimed as the presiding lords of the vidyās;
they are all preeminent in the Vajra family, for they are indeed protected by us.
Likewise, Gajagandha in the world, the Bodhisattva of great supernatural power;
and Mahāsthānagata, the wise Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
But whoever at that time remembers Samantabhadra, the most beautiful and foremost of sons, for them no fear exists.
As well as Māṇibhadra, Jambhala the supreme Yakṣa,
and all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas— whence could there be any fear?
Through the recollection and worship of them, great protection is proclaimed;
then, O gods, there is vast fruit and meritorious splendor that is beyond conception.
