To the goddess who assumes a female form, who is free from passion and possesses great supernatural power,
who indeed offers worship to the Three Jewels and is devoted to the teaching of the Jina;
When they have no fear whatsoever regarding friend or foe,
that is said to be the "pledge" (samaya) there, which must not be transgressed by any practitioners of mantra.
This is proclaimed as the supreme wrathful [deity] Yamāntaka;
when beings abide in his commitment (samaya), all humans shall not eat them.
Then all those gods, who were indeed superhuman, with joyful minds,
all stood at their post according to the agreement, following the wisdom of the Son of the Jina.
Then the Yakṣa general, enraged at those words of defeat,
caused all the incalculable world-systems to tremble.
Why was this King of Wrath revealed by the Sons of the Conquerors in the past? Was it not for the sake of disciplining sentient beings? Why then is it now shown to be purposeless?
"The power of the King of Wrath and his ancient emergence have been proclaimed.
Having spoken thus, the wielder of the vajra then set down his vajra and stood still.
Then, having laughed, the wise youth Mañjughoṣa, possessing great supernatural power and appearing in the form of a child, indeed uttered these words.
Do not be angry, O great yakṣa Vajrapāṇi of great supernatural power;
for this king of wrathful deities of great supernatural power has been revealed by me.
I shall give you the mantra itself; reveal it as you wish.
It was not possible for you to fully describe the power of Krodha.
For he is seen here, situated within this very body;
indeed, by him you were drawn toward yourself, if that is what you ask of me.
For it is not possible to turn back one who is possessed by anger here, O Lord;
therefore, having granted permission, reveal as you wish, setting aside the [usual] convention.

When he has not bathed, when he is fast asleep, when he is engaged in sexual intercourse with a village woman, when he is anointed with oil, when he is unprotected, or when his mind is always corrupt; |||
Abandoned by all the best of mantras within the teaching because they are not serene,
such mortals are full of doubt and lack faith among those who are ill-situated.

They should be shunned by one who is composed when encountering those who reject the jewel of the True Dharma and the Saṅgha, as well as the naked ascetics who are always impure, defiled by leftovers, and whose conduct and sphere of activity are unholy.
Indeed, in an unprotected place, one devoid of mantras, constantly impure, and merciless;
or in the dwellings of the gods, at shrines, or in the courtyards and mandalas of monasteries.
There, those who delight in sexual intercourse will be destroyed by anger;
they have fallen from their commitments, yet they remain complacent, ignorant of the application of mantras.
Their gait and conduct will be faltering, and anger shall fall upon them;
among all humans in the world, no heedfulness is found.
Those who delight in negligence and do not guard against the breach of their commitments are slain by the King of Wrath, if they are practitioners who have failed to apply themselves correctly.
In every way, all fools are subject to negligence, with the exception of those who have transcended passion— the Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, and Śrāvakas— who are always liberated.
"All indeed are to be slain and punished in every way by the King of Wrath.
Thus was it spoken by Mañjuśrī, whose mind was permeated with compassion.
"The conduct of the Buddhas and the great supernatural powers of the Bodhisattvas are inconceivable.
Having spoken thus, they all then remained silent.
Then the glorious Vajradhara again grasped the vajra;
having taken up the vajra, he was pleased and, having received permission, spoke thus.

Thus concludes the forty-eighth chapter, the detailed exposition on the description of the wrathful king Yamāntaka, his mantras, his greatness, and the rules of discipline, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the fifty-first chapter.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas, having surveyed the entire great assembly circle, addressed all those hosts of beings seated above the Pure Abodes:

Listen, noble sirs, to the procedure for the cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*) at the outset of the Great Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, as spoken by the Great Bodhisattva who is Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, possessed of immeasurable strength and prowess, the tamer of the unsubdued, the ender of Vaivasvata’s life, and intent upon the subjugation of wicked beings.
Neither a specific lunar day nor a constellation is prescribed, nor is fasting enjoined;
when fear of enemies has arisen, one should have this painting executed.
Having taken a corpse on the fourteenth or eighth lunar day during the dark fortnight of the month of Kṛṣṇa, one should obtain the garment of a Brāhmaṇa from that [corpse].
Then, having taken it at night, one should dye it with blood;
thereafter, one should perform a purification with water and then cause it to be thoroughly dried.
One should have a fierce, wrathful, and terrifying painter depict [the image] in a cremation ground during the dark fortnight; one should complete it in just three nights.
On the nights of the eighth and fourteenth days,
the painter, stationed there and always facing south, should be illuminated by a lamp of human fat.

Having performed the protection ritual and being composed in mind, the mantra-practitioner— himself afflicted by the suffering and fear caused by his enemies— should either have [the image] drawn upon a human skull or draw it himself while seated upon one.
When the first watch of the night has begun, even an enemy experiences great fear;
when the second has begun, he is seized by a high fever and the enemy falls into a swoon.
If he releases his life-breaths on the third day, he will have gone to the next world;
how could there be peace for him when the mantra-practitioner is displeased?
The body of the enemy indeed withers away and the destruction of their home occurs from painting such a cloth [mandala] of Yamāntaka during a great danger.
One with six faces and six legs should be depicted as black in color, with a protruding belly,
wrathful, and clad in a tiger skin.
He wields various terrible weapons, holds a staff in his hand, and is fearsome;
he has red eyes, is full of wrath, and is marked by the movement of the three-eyed one.
With hair standing erect and matted, smoke-colored in some places and resembling black collyrium in others, he was terrible, with a luster like a rain-cloud in the monsoon.
One should depict him resembling the form of Kṛtānta (Yama), mounted upon a buffalo,
performing cruel deeds, most terrifying, fierce, and the slayer of Rudra.
Indeed, it destroys both twins—life and vitality;
it rises up as a slayer of beings, cruel and exceedingly violent in all its actions, terrifying and most dreadful in its onset.
Having drawn this supreme wrathful one, the terrifier of Māra and the source of fear even for fear itself for all embodied beings, using pigments made from one's own blood;
One should draw the intermingled [deities] with brilliant colors mixed with human fat and cow's ghee,
using skull-bowls fashioned from human bone.
Having drawn [the deity] himself or by means of a painter, using brushes made from the hair of a corpse, while fasting; |||

One should first cause the excellent cloth [painting] to be adorned with abundant offerings of food, flowers, and the like, with red garlands, choice sandalwood, incense of human flesh and fat, and lamps of fat; and worship should be performed at the beginning, the end, and the middle.
Having clearly performed the *phaṭ* [mantra] and having given wealth to the artisan— indeed,
even a great price by which he is always satisfied—
one must ensure that he is not harmed and that his duty is performed with safety.
In brief, one should fulfill his every desire as the price for the hero;
the work for the artisan should be fruitful, and one should avoid that which is devoid of reward.
One should employ [the ritual] in such a way that he becomes fully satisfied;
furthermore, great protection must be provided, for otherwise he will die.
The practitioner, together with his family, perishes; therefore, he should protect himself.
This rite is to be performed by one who has recited the vidyā; it is not prescribed for others.
Having made the cloth-painting clearly manifest, or having seen it as desired by the mind,
one should perform all rites that are fierce and destructive to enemies.
Taking the excellent cloth, one should go wherever one desires,
even to the great yakṣas, the great kings, who are proud of their vast wealth.
[It is not for those] possessed of great pride and arrogance, the cruel, those who perform cruel deeds,
those who harm the Three Jewels, the nihilists, those devoid of mantra, those who do not worship mantras, nor those who revile the truth and its devotees.
And for those who revile mantra-reciters, their downfall shall be brought about;
one should employ the ritual against them according to the procedure prescribed by the rules.
Against those who are most unrighteous, perpetually so, and who cause suffering to all living beings,
one should employ a rite that immediately obstructs their life-force.
One should take the leaves, bark, and fruit of the *gṛhyāriṣṭa* plant, including the roots,
along with sour gruel (*kāñjika*) mixed with acidic substances and powdered human bone.
Pungent oil, poison, amlavetasa, fresh ginger, black mustard,
and blood originating from human beings;
Having taken all the necessary materials and placed the cloth [painting] in a secluded place,
one should face south while the cloth faces north.
Having prepared a fire-pit as desired with white wood produced from pungent trees,
and having kindled it with pungent branches, one should, being composed, offer into that pit the oblation prescribed by the ritual rules, consisting of all [the necessary] ingredients.
Furthermore, having summoned Agni with the mantras of the Wrathful King,
one should bind the trident mudrā for all rites here.
One should offer eight thousand oblations into the fire-pit with wrath;
when that [rite] is performed, the death of a son shall occur for the first time.
In the second [dream], his wife indeed; in the third, his attendants along with their leaders; and in the fourth, death for him for whose sake that [rite] was performed.
When the recitation is performed at midnight in the presence of the cloth-painting for the purpose of slaying enemies, it proceeds exactly in that manner.
The destruction of his kingdom shall occur, and misfortune shall arise within his army;
fire, great winds, and heavy rains shall break forth.
The entire wheel [of his realm] is struck down from all sides by the wheel of an enemy;
he is beset by various calamities and overwhelmed by great diseases.
The entire body of that king will surely wither away, there is no doubt;
his entire house will be crowded and agitated by non-human beings.
He finds no peace upon his bed and tosses about upon the ground;
his house is surrounded by rākṣasas, pretas, and flesh-eating demons.
Afflicted and deeply distressed by intense sufferings, he fears everywhere;
the gods on earth, such as Maheśvara and others, are powerless to protect him.
Brahmā and the other guardians of the world, Śakra and the other lords of the thirty-three gods,
all mantras, all deities, and all that arises in the mundane world.
For one who is wicked, arrogant, and enraged, his life ends there;
for at midnight or at midday, wherever the reciter speaks,
the wrathful Vaiśvānara is manifest as Yama, the King of Death.
Having installed the cloth painting on the ground at will during the dark fortnight,
one should perform a grand worship and an offering made from materials found in a cremation ground or a forest.
Likewise, under a single tree, at a linga, on a mountain, on the edge of a forest, or in caves,
one should always undertake ritual action alone and without a companion.
In the great forest, in a secluded place, in empty temples,
in an empty mansion, by a river, or on the shore of the ocean.
In that place, or nearby, or residing there as desired,
one should always cause rituals to be performed within a range of up to a hundred yojanas.
One should always have these ritual acts of measurement performed by a pure person;
or else, one who stands in the immeasurable state, having gone to the limitless regions, is pure.
In the realm of inconceivable mantras, the sphere of mantras is inconceivable;
the supernatural power of mantras is inconceivable, and the success of those who recite them is inconceivable. The activity seen is inconceivable, and the fruit as well is inconceivable.
The activity, the miraculous domain, and the transformative power of the great-souled Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath,
as well as the inconceivable accomplishment of those possessing form, are seen here upon the surface of the earth.
All Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power are unable to protect [it],
let alone worldly mantras, along with the Grahas and those Mothers.
Īśāna, as well as Viṣṇu, Skanda, and Purandara— even they,
along with the Jinas and the sons of the Jinas, have been bound by you under oath.
Even the great-souled Bodhisattvas who have attained the ten stages,
as well as the Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who are free from passion and possess great supernatural powers,
were unable to protect the commitment previously made by them.
I shall speak briefly; listen, you who desire the welfare of beings!
No one else is capable of turning back [the obstacle] when the reciter is displeased. How then could there be peace for him here, while the supreme mantra remains unsatisfied?
When the mind of the practitioner of the great-souled Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, becomes clear and moist with compassion at any time,
then first he attains peace, fortitude, or the preservation of life.
Picumanda, pungent oil, sour gruel, and poison as the fifth;
human blood, human flesh, salt, and again the three pungents (trikaṭuka).
Black mustard, conch-shell powder, amlavetasa, fresh ginger,
the roots of dhurdhūraka, and likewise those of kośātakī.
Castor root, barley alkali, safflower, and also thorn-apple;
likewise, the root of the madana plant, garlic, and gṛñjanaka.
Having prepared equal portions of palāśa wood, śākhoṭaka wood, liquor, and spirituous extracts, one should offer them as oblations into the fire in the presence of the cloth painting.
When eight thousand oblations have been offered, there is the destruction of enemies along with their very roots;
indeed, one may destroy the entire assembly of messengers, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Its eradication along with the roots occurs for one who offers oblations during the second junction;
when the third junction has arrived, it occurs for the reciter who offers oblations.
Famine shall prevail for him, as well as among the people and the guilds; there shall be drought and great pestilence, with the land everywhere swarming with rākṣasas.
Fire, falling rocks, thunderbolts, and lightning will strike the country,
the region, or the territory of that king.

In his country, calamities arise in many ways and of various kinds— such as the occurrence of railway disasters and likewise the arrival of hostile armies— due to the destruction of Great Fortune (*Mahālakṣmī*).
If one offers a single oblation of *dhurdhūraka* root, madness arises for him;
by constantly offering pungent substances, he is seized by a great burning fever;
and by offering extremely sour substances into the fire, a great fever born of cold occurs.
For one who dwells within the body of wicked kings who are arrogant in their power,
of great yakṣas, of the wealthy, of the cruel, or of those supported by vast armies,
death will come to his life within two nights or seven nights.
Whichever deity or lunar mansion (nakṣatra) someone is devoted to, one should write its name;
having fashioned a figure from the charcoal of a cremation ground, placed upon the ground in front of the cloth painting,
and standing upon its head with one's foot, one should perform the recitation while filled with wrath.
Suddenly, O lord of men, that king is seized by various piercing pains;
overcome by a great disease, he may even die at that very moment.
Furthermore, one is slain by a beast, or becomes deformed,
or is devoured by cruel rākṣasas born of impure human origins.
He is slain at that very moment by flesh-eaters, Pūtanas, Piśācas, Pretas, and Mātṛs, as well as by his own servants.
Then the glorious Vajradhara, having spoken thus to the assembly,
paid homage to all the Buddhas and remained thereafter in silence.
Desiring the welfare of the worlds, he spoke thus once more:
[this] mantra for all the hosts of yakṣas and for all the yakṣiṇīs everywhere.
Then the Bodhisattva Yakṣasenāpati spoke;
he chose a chapter on yakṣīs that included all ritual actions:
the summoning of all, the subjugation of all, and the extraction of all thorns.
When a practitioner of mantra is desirous of sexual union, blinded by passion, or of deluded intellect,
he cannot be restrained by antidotes or by the commands of the Sugatas.
In this beginningless saṃsāra, those who have practiced [evil] while deeply afflicted have been told by the Tathāgatas that their destination is from suffering to even greater suffering.
The celibate student who has conquered his senses attains an auspicious state;
through the recitation of the mantra, he shall obtain what is declared to be beneficial, auspicious, and peace.
Having ascended to the equality of the three vehicles, one shall attain perfect nirvana;
whereas those who are perverted, blinded by passion, and seized by evil destinies— those wretched ones wander in the five realms of existence within the terrible thicket of saṃsāra.
For the sake of those who are suffering, the enjoyment of sensual pleasures is described;
yet they are liberated from all evils, having turned away from the threefold faults.
Possessed of the Teacher’s command, they are released from all bonds.

Thus concludes the second detailed chapter, the forty-ninth [section], the "Regulations for the Malevolent Rite of Yamāntaka, the Wrathful King," from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra that is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Now begins the fifty-second chapter.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Śāntamati was present, seated among that very assembly.

Rising from his seat, bowing to all the Buddhas, and standing in the midst of the circle of the assembly, he circumambulated the Blessed One Śākyamuni three times, prostrated at his feet, and looking toward Vajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas, he uttered these words:
"You are exceedingly cruel, O Vajrapāṇi, you who proclaim mantra-tantras that cause injury to all beings and are associated with sensual desires.
Indeed, O Son of the Conqueror, this is not the way of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.

For the great Bodhisattvas, impelled by great compassion, practice the conduct of a Bodhisattva for the sake and welfare of all beings; having set out with a resolute intention for their benefit, they do not seek release from the bonds of existence."
Furthermore, O Son of the Conqueror,
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones do not preach a teaching that harms sentient beings with reference to all beings, because they are endowed with great compassion;
rather, they act with the resolute intention for the welfare of all sentient beings.
Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajrapāṇi addressed the Bodhisattva Śāntamati:
"In this way, Śāntamati, a bodhisattva should train; in this way should they practice."
Just as you speak and just as you proclaim,
so do all the Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power;
thus shall I explain it according to the ultimate truth.
Relying upon the limit of reality, one is liberated at the limit of phenomena;
indeed, the inconceivable limit of sentient beings is likewise inconceivable in its ripening.

The qualities of a Buddha are indeed inconceivable, and the conduct leading to enlightenment is likewise inconceivable; for, having regard for the beings to be trained, their conduct is truly inconceivable.
The conduct of the bodhisattvas is proclaimed to be inconceivable;
this tantra among all mantras is likewise inconceivable due to its power.
The sphere of supernatural power and the greatness of the movement of the Great-Souled Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, and his mantra are inconceivable and beyond thought.
For, Śāntamati, the accomplishment of the manifestation of the realm of sentient beings through the conduct of Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas is indeed inconceivable.
Thus, Śāntamati, a Bodhisattva who recites mantras should generate the thought:
"Even if for the sake of this single being I were to produce much demerit."
And there would be rebirth in the great hells; yet this being would not produce such a vast heap of demerit that he might become incapable of attaining the three types of enlightenment.

Thus, Śāntamati, a bodhisattva who recites mantras should apply his mind in this way and employ skillful means as well as rites of sorcery (*abhicāruka*). In all ritual actions, he should be one who perceives the signs (*nimitta*), yet not one who grasps at what is unwholesome; and he should train himself with regard to the conversion of sentient beings.
With a mind permeated by compassion.

Moreover, O Son of the Conqueror, all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, realize that there is no distinction between dharma and non-dharma, the auspicious and the inauspicious, the greatness of the states of the wholesome and unwholesome, the means for training sentient beings, and the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu); they likewise realize the skillful means for teaching the Dharma to sentient beings.
In that very same way, O Sons of the Conqueror, we must train ourselves.

That is to say, noble sons of the Conqueror, you who are seated here in this great assembly of the mandala for the sake of disciplining and for the instruction that ripens sentient beings—there, all of you together must listen and have faith; you must become seekers of what is wholesome and unwholesome;
that is to say, you must become those who delight in the Dharma teachings of the Tathāgata.
Then the bodhisattva mahāsattva Śāntamati, having looked toward Vajrapāṇi, the general of the yakṣas, became thirsty and sat down upon his own seat;
reflecting that "the qualities of a Buddha are inconceivable," he gazed upon the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Then Vajrapāṇi, the lord of the Guhyakas, having surveyed that entire assembly circle, spoke again the ritual manual of the Wrathful King.

Listen, O assemblies of gods, and all you hosts of beings who have issued from the realm of sentient beings! First, having performed the protection rites, one should take that cloth-painting of the Wrathful King to a secluded place. At a site with a single linga in a temple of Maheśvara, one should smear that linga with human blood, black mustard seeds, and sour gruel (*kāñjika*). One should worship it with *picumarda* leaves, make a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) for oneself out of a string of human intestines, and holding a human skull-cup in the right hand, strike at it. Threatening the linga with the left hand, overcome by supreme wrath, with a mind filled with great contempt because of being insulted by wicked kings, or by other rogues, great yakṣas, very wealthy men, fierce men, or great leaders, one should close the door securely. Naked and with hair disheveled, treading upon the linga of Maheśvara with the left foot, one should recite the wrathful mantra until the linga of Maheśvara splits in the middle, becomes split into two pieces, and a great sound of "HŪṂ" is heard.
Therefore, one should not be afraid;
at that very moment, whether it be that wicked king himself or any other great yakṣa, he will be seized by fever,
or he will be seized by non-human beings such as rākṣasas and the like.
One should recite there for a mere moment until, in an instant, the life of the enemy comes to an end in death;
if one recites until the end of the night, the entire family perishes.
There is yet another rite:
at midday, having gone likewise to a temple of Maheśvara, one should worship with nimba leaves, offer incense of *mahāmāṃsa*, and recite the mantra.
Until the enemy's house is consumed by fire, and the enemy suffers from a great fever and trembling.
If he does not abandon the recitation, or if he remains enraged, the enemy of Dakṣiṇāmūrti shall die and his lineage shall be destroyed. Then, if one performs the rite of restoration,
one should again wash the image with water and bathe it with very cool milk.
Furthermore, by means of cow's products,
one becomes healthy.
There is yet another rite:

having kindled a fire with thorns of the *madanakaṇṭaka* at the southern face of the Liṅga of Maheśvara, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *vaikaṅkata* wood fuel smeared with poison, blood, and mustard seeds.
All enemies will be seized by a great disease.
They become powerless in all their actions.
On the second day, they are seized by a great fever or a great pain, or by various diseases, or by non-human beings intent on taking their lives.
On the third day, at the three junctions of the day, they abandon their life entirely in every respect.
To bring about reconciliation, one should offer milk as an oblation;
peace will prevail,
and all enemies throughout all lands will become well-disposed.
In this manner, one may subdue whichever among all the gods or all the spirits is devoted to a particular deity;
having stepped upon the constellation, mantra, or name of that being with the left foot, one should perform the rite— excepting, however, the vidyās belonging to the Tathāgatas.

Grasping the big toe of all [the deities] with the left hand, one should perform the rite; one must never move [the deity] even by way of stepping upon it. One may step upon and employ all worldly mantras. Even while unaccomplished, the King of Wrath performs rites merely through recitation: he destroys all mantras, slays all enemies, and causes all magical diagrams (*yantra*) to fall.
In brief, however it is employed—even according to the ritual procedures of all worldly and transcendent mantras—he accomplishes all of that.
It accomplishes everything;
by mere recitation, it fulfills all hopes.
This King of Wrath is perfected through recitation alone and bestows the supreme accomplishment.
By the mere will of the mind, one causes an enemy to be slain; when joined with the Great Spear Mudrā, one performs all rites.
There is another ritual:

at midday, having stayed for one night in a cemetery by a funeral pyre on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should kindle a fire with wood from the cemetery and offer as oblation mustard seeds smeared with poison and blood.
Then all the *preta*s arrive, crying out "Hā! Hā!"
One should not be afraid.
Then one should say, "Kill my enemy.
Having said, "So be it," they vanish.
Then, having traveled even a thousand yojanas in a mere moment, they cause the enemy to be slain and destroy entire lineages;
they perform such actions as these.
There is another rite as well:

in a secluded and pure place, having entered an empty house while clothed in clean garments, one should offer eight thousand oblations of cotton seeds. Then, taking that ash with both hands, one should bind it separately in two pieces of clean cloth.

Having made two *poṅgalikā* pills and placed them in a hollowed-out earthenware bowl (*śarāva*), and having performed great protective rites for oneself and one’s belongings, one should not enter the house but go to a great cremation ground. On the night of the fourteenth or the eighth day of the dark fortnight, standing upon a funeral pyre and facing south, holding the earthenware bowl, naked, with hair disheveled, and becoming enraged and fearless, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
It becomes accomplished.
If any non-human being requests that ash as a possession, it must not be given.
If one employs force, one should recollect the King of Wrath and utter the syllable *huṃ*;
at that very moment, [the obstacle] perishes.
This is the procedure for all obstacles.
One should apply the mark of ash held in the left and right hands.
Having performed protection with vigilance, one should return.
At dawn, at sunrise, having bathed, being pure and clothed in clean garments, one should enter one's own home.
Or one may go wherever one desires, even if it is not the proper place.

Then, with the ashes held in the right hand, if one strikes the heads of humans, bipeds, quadrupeds, and all living beings—including gods, nāgas, and yakṣas—they become submissive. Or, with the ashes held in the left hand, if one strikes the heads of all humans and non-humans, and all women, they become submissive.
If one takes the ashes with the right hand and strikes them upon the navel region of men,
they become eunuchs;
and if one crushes them against the private parts, he becomes impotent.
If one is intent upon a woman who practices vulgar acts, one should sprinkle her private parts—the region of the genitals—with ashes.
She becomes incapable of serving another man;
her wounds disappear until she encounters that very same man again.
Once again, that opening of her wound appears,
so that he is unable to engage in sexual misconduct;
the same applies to the man as well.
One should sprinkle the male organ with ashes;
it will then become incapable,
and when approaching another's wife, it remains as if withered.

Then, by the power of the one who gave it, that very organ of his—whether female or male—reappears. It functions or does not function according to the will of the person to whom that ash was given, or he may make it act as he desires.
However, if they force it upon those to whom it was given, worms appear in their private parts.
By these [beings], they are devoured and deprived of life;

within a month, they become putrid, resembling foul-smelling corpses. Men are seized by human diseases such as the great discharge (mahāpradara) and other ailments, and a great swelling (mahāśvethu) arises.
By that very affliction they meet their end;
or else they become unable to indulge [in their desires] according to the slave's wish,
for he makes them perform everything exactly as he desires.
If, upon being merely touched, one does not obtain physical contact—whether standing within the range of vision or out of sight, or when facing with the wind—one should scatter ashes.
Just as he is slightly dusted by those ashes, the giver, having mentally visualized it, should scatter the ashes;
whatever he has intended, all those actions are accomplished by it.
Whether by the hand of another or by oneself, one performs all those actions as desired; and they do not fail to bear fruit.

Then, one should sprinkle with ashes all these various items: beds and seats, coverings and garments, diverse and excellent ornaments, various clothes, vehicles, carriages, sandals, umbrellas, and so forth; all specific utensils; all bodily requisites such as food, drink, and edibles; and all vessels and implements; as well as flowers, betel, fruits, perfumes, incense, and the like.
Consequently, the bodies of the enemies will become completely infested with lice, bugs, and worms, and they shall be consumed by them.
He is afflicted by various sufferings and dies within seven nights;
all physicians and all gods are powerless to prevent it.
All mantras are powerless to protect [the person],
except for that which has been bestowed by him.

Now, as for the method of restoration: having combined licorice (*yaṣṭīmadhu*), blue lotus (*nīlotpala*), and white sandalwood (*śvetacandana*), one should grind them with cold water and smear that upon the body, starting from the head down to the soles of the feet, while reciting the root mantra of Noble Mañjuśrī.
The person will then become healthy.
There is another rite as well:
having gone upwind from women, one should employ this against all wicked *ḍākinīs* and haughty women where desired, but not against others.
Standing upwind of them, one should scatter ashes.
Having contemplated with the mind, all the private parts and breasts are removed;
even in the case of a man, the male organ, the beard and body hair, and the breasts appear.
In this way, one performs many various and diverse actions,
or causes others to perform them,
or causes them to be performed by whatever brings about joy.
Whether by a woman or by a man,
wherever the manifestation of the mind arises, having given ashes to that person, one causes them to act as desired;
and through application, one should cause them to train.
In this way, one causes [the victim] to be seized by great diseases:

having visualized it with the mind, from touching the head, a headache arises; from touching the mouth, a mouth-inflammation arises; and in this sequence, up to the heart, a heart-ache or a stomach-ache arises.
Likewise, one causes [the victim] to be seized by diseases arising from the feet and the shanks, such as those caused by corrupted blood and the like.
In brief, it kills, withers, causes to ripen, attracts, and subjugates; in whatever manner it is employed, it performs all those actions accordingly.
It performs rites of affliction, attraction, and subjugation even when situated at a great distance.
Having gone near a wall in a difficult place and standing with the wind at one's back, one should cast that very ash.

Both [the enemy forces] fall upon the ramparts, the gateways, and the watchtowers that have been seized by hand; then a great conflagration breaks out in the administrative headquarters and the palace,
and a rout of the army occurs.
He will be afflicted by great calamities;
having abandoned everything, he will either flee or fall into captivity.
In the same way, one should scatter ashes against an enemy army when the wind is blowing from behind them.
The great army will suffer defeat;
it will be seized by a burning fever,
and the elephants, horses, chariots, banners, and the general will all meet with destruction.
Or he approaches for capture;
in this way, he performs various kinds of rites as desired for the destruction of enemies,
as well as great protection for himself, his own army, or his friends.
Then he performs the propitiation:
in every case, before all the paintings, one should offer a thousand oblations of milk;
they will become healthy and invincible.
Now, for one desiring to accomplish the practice of a yakṣiṇī:
Naṭī, Naṭa, Bhaṭṭa, and the renowned Revatī; likewise Tamasurī, Lokā, Mekhalā, and Sumekhalā.
These are the eight yakṣiṇīs who accomplish all desires.

The mantra of Naṭikā is: *Oṃ naṭi mahānaṭi āgacchāgaccha divyarūpiṇi svāhā*. The ritual procedure for this is as follows: having drawn her on a wooden board or a cloth, the vidyā should be recited eight thousand times while subsisting on either meat or milk. She should be depicted adorned with all ornaments, dark-complexioned yet radiant, leaning against a tree, wearing a single garment, with her hair loose; her eyes slightly reddened, her face bearing a gentle smile, threatening the practitioner with her right hand, while her left hand clings to a branch of the tree; she is beautiful in every limb and dressed in variegated silk.

In front of that very cloth-painting of the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*), one who is free from mental distraction should stand facing north, kindle a fire with *palāśa* wood, and offer eight thousand pills of *guggulu* resin smeared with curd, honey, and clarified butter at the three junctions of the day for seven days.
Then, on the seventh day, having prepared a magnificent sacrificial offering (*bali*) and lit lamps of clarified butter, one should remain reciting the mantra until midnight.
Thereupon, that *yakṣiṇī* herself, emitting a great radiance, will come in her own form.
When she has arrived, she asks,
"What must I do?
Then the practitioner should say, "Become my wife."
Having said, "So be it," she vanishes.
From that time forward, she becomes his wife;
she grants all desires and leads him to her own abode.
He bestows an elixir (*rasāyana*);
having drunk which, one becomes possessed of a divine form and rivals even the great yakṣas.
If he does not come on the first occasion, one should recite [the mantra] together with the King of Wrath (*krodharāja*) on the second occasion; then he will certainly come.
If it does not wither, it dies.
The mantra of Naṭṭā: Oṃ naṭṭe, wearer of white garments and garlands, lover of sexual union, svāhā!
This is her very ritual procedure.
The mantra of Bhaṭṭā: Oṃ bhaṭṭe bhaṭṭe, illuminator, why do you delay? Come, come! Arrive, arrive! Accomplish my task, svāhā!
This [rite] is accomplished even without a cloth.

Having prepared a mandala in the place of the head and burning guggulu incense, one should recite the vidyā eight thousand times while remaining silent, alone, pure, and having closed the door. Within a month, she will certainly arrive at night.
Once she has arrived, she should be desired; as a wife, she grants all desires.
If she enters his abode, he lives for five thousand years;
otherwise, she wanders right here in Jambūdvīpa.
She lives for five hundred years;
he sports with her and carries out all her commands.
He goes wherever he desires with him;
he bestows upon him an elixir of rejuvenation (rasāyana);
and like a beloved wife, she maintains an attentive and resolute disposition toward him.
The mantra of Revatī: *Namaḥ sarvayakṣīṇām / oṃ rakte raktāvabhāse raktānulepane svāhā*.
Revatī is the most excellent of yakṣiṇīs; she is playful and fond of sexual union.
With slightly reddened garments and dark, curly hair, she stands.
A yakṣī beautiful in all her limbs, always delighting in sensual enjoyments,
who constantly grants desires and wealth— one should designate her as the bestower of boons.
Having painted the cloth as before, this is its specific distinction: she is dressed in red silk garments, wears a red silk upper robe, and is red in complexion.
The mantra of Mekhalā is: *oṃ mekhale mahāyakṣiṇi mama kāryaṃ sampādaya svāhā*.
The mantra of Sumekhalā: Oṃ mekhale sumekhale mahāyakṣiṇi sarvārthasādhani oṃ samayamanusmara svāhā.
The mantra of Ālokinī is: oṃ lokini lokavati svāhā.
For these [deities], the ritual procedure is exactly the same.
The mantra of Tamasundarī is: *oṃ ghuṇu guhyake ghuṇu ghuṇu guhye ehyehi guhyake svāhā*. There is no ritual service (*upacāra*) for this.

Regarding the procedure for her cloth-painting (*paṭavidhāna*): first, one who is pure and dressed in clean garments, on the full moon day, having closed the door in a secluded place that is dark and devoid of light, should recite the vidyā ten thousand times.
The preliminary service has been performed;
thereafter, one should begin the practice (*sādhana*).
Starting from the first day of the month until the next full moon, within this interval, the ritual action takes place.

At night, at the time of sleep, having ascended his bed in a secluded and hidden place alone, having closed the door, having mixed *saṅkucitakarṇikā* and *vānapuṣpa* with pungent oil, having washed his hands and feet, and having empowered his right arm one hundred and eight times with mantras, he should sleep in silence. Thus, day after day until the full moon,
she will certainly arrive at midnight.
Once she has arrived, one should not converse with her;
rather, one should desire her through silence for six months.
When she initiates a conversation, then one may speak with her.
From that time forward, she becomes perfected;
she becomes his wife, granting all desires.
And through her divine, pleasant touch, she accomplishes all his tasks even while remaining invisible.
He bestows elixirs and rejuvenators;
having placed [the practitioner] upon his back, he carries him even to Mount Sumeru;
and at night, he causes him to traverse Jambūdvīpa.
It causes even an enemy situated a hundred *yojanas* away to be slain;
it accomplishes everything exactly as commanded,
with the sole exception of approaching another's wife.
This is the rule for all: one must not approach another's wife;
one should dwell together with her alone.
If one should approach her, they bring about either death or madness.
This is the yakṣiṇī named Andhārasundarī,
surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs;
day after day, she dispatches one yakṣiṇī as a messenger.
Once accomplished, she becomes the one who grants success to all practitioners; she is surrounded by a retinue of many mantras and all the yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power.
This procedure is exactly the same for all of them.
What, then, is their appearance?
There is no vision of this.
The yakṣiṇī named Andhāravāsinī possesses great supernatural power;
she dwells in caves, is a hero among men, and is renowned throughout the world as a maiden.
Madhuyakṣī, Manojñā, and the seventh, Surasundarī—
these are the seven yakṣiṇīs who act for the benefit of sentient beings.
They wander through this world and indeed across the entire earth;
in just a moment, they fly up to the abode of the gods.
In the battle between the gods and the daityas, those of great supernatural power fought;
they were most righteous, filled with compassion, desiring the welfare of beings, and very affectionate.
They roam upon the surface of the earth out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings;
nothing is difficult for them to accomplish, for they are auspicious performers of all rites.
They were spoken of by the Bodhisattva for the sake of the enjoyment of sentient beings.
The mantra of Guhyavāsinī is: *oṃ guhile guhamati guhavāsi ānaya bhagavati mayāntikaṃ samayamanusmara svāhā*.
Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand *priyaṅgu* flowers smeared with ghee at the three junctions of the day for one month;
thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished.

Thereafter, one should begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*). On a wooden board, a cloth, or a wall, using non-sticky pigments and brushes made from new vessels, one should first have Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, drawn: square in shape, with four peaks rising high, and encircled by a range of seven mountains.
At the edge of those mountains, a cave situated within a mountain should be drawn.

Therein, a single Yakṣiṇī named Guhavāsinī should be caused to be painted, possessing a divine form, adorned with all ornaments, dwelling in the cave, clothed in silk garments, with a silk upper robe, golden-hued, and of variegated, beautiful appearance. Having had such a cloth-painting (paṭa) executed, one who is pure, subsisting on a diet of milk, should recite the mantra ten thousand times in a clean place.
Having performed a great worship according to one's ability, then at the conclusion of the recitation, after creating a great radiance, the Yakṣiṇī herself arrives in a divine form.
When she has arrived, an *argha* offering should be given with jasmine flowers mixed with water scented with white sandalwood.
Then she says: "Child, what must be done?"
One should say, "Be my mother," and having done so,
he vanishes;
and one must not harbor a corrupt thought toward him.
Nor should one pray for anything connected with sensual desires; for if that noble lady, who possesses great supernatural power, prays for sensual desires, it will not be accomplished.
From that time forward, she performs all tasks like a mother.
He provides food and clothing for a retinue of eight hundred;
he protects one who is in danger;
and even for one situated atop a great forested mountain, he accomplishes all tasks.
He provides whatever food is desired;
he bestows all things such as elixirs and rejuvenators;
and he complies with his wishes in every way.
He creates huts, houses, and the like,
and he bestows a thousand pieces of gold every day;
all of it must be spent on that very same day.
If one does not perform it, one becomes cut off;
it occurs in every single respect.
Furthermore, there is another function of this [karma].

In front of this very cloth, having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood until it is free of flames and smoke, one should draw an image with red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*) on the palm of the right hand for a man, or on the palm of the left hand for a woman, and heat it upon that same heap of embers while reciting the mantra.
She brings a woman even from a hundred *yojanas* away;
she causes everything that is commanded to be done.
This ritual is to be performed at night,
not by day.
The mantra of Naravīrā is: oṃ naravīre svāhā.

In the same manner, having had her image painted on a cloth, one should have it depicted as residing in an aśoka tree, excluding the cave-dwelling. This is its specific distinction: the entire ritual procedure is exactly the same as that for Guhāvāsinī.
And she should be addressed as "sister."
There is another rite for this [mantra]:
during a lunar eclipse, one should wrap gold ochre in birch bark, place it in one's mouth, and recite the mantra as long as the moon remains eclipsed.
Then, by writing the name of whichever woman or man with that gold ochre, one brings them forth, even if they are situated a hundred *yojanas* away.
At dawn, she leads [the practitioner] to that very place;
she performs tasks like a sister;
and in times of calamity, she provides great protection.
By merely reciting [the mantra] over all women, one brings them under control;
this is the ritual procedure for Naravīrā.
The mantra of the Yakṣakumārikā is: *oṃ yakṣakumārike svāhā*.
This is its ritual procedure (*upacāra*): it should be caused to be written on birch bark with *gorocanā* [cow-gallstone pigment].

A young maiden (*kumārī*) with hair half-bound in braids, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a single garment, holding a citron fruit in her right hand, and grasping a branch of an *aśoka* tree with her left hand [should be depicted].
Such a birch-bark leaf should be placed above the location of the head.

One should sleep alone in a secret place. Having made a mandala with white sandalwood and having scattered *jātī* flowers at the three junctions of the day while burning *guggulu* incense, one should recite the vidyā eight thousand times for the duration of one month.

Then, on the full moon day, having performed a great worship with *jātī* flowers and having offered lamps of ghee and sacrificial oblations, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and recite the mantra throughout the night until the daughter of Vaiśravaṇa herself, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred maidens, arrives. Having surveyed that entire quarter of the sky, she stands in the air in her own form and says: "What should I do?"
Then the practitioner should say: "One of these three boons—whether as a mother, a sister, or a wife—should be requested. If she becomes a mother...
One must not corrupt the mind;
for one who corrupts it, destruction arises.
One should behave toward it as toward a mother.
And that mother provided food, clothing, and various excellent ornaments for her retinue of five hundred simply by thinking of them;
she gave a thousand dīnāras every day,
providing everything for those wandering throughout this very Jambūdvīpa.
When she becomes a sister, then even from a distance of a hundred yojanas, she brings a woman;
she leads her right there and accomplishes all tasks just like a sister.
Then she becomes his wife, and he comes to possess his own celestial abode; he lives for a thousand divine years,
and when he dies, he is reborn into a wealthy family.
She carries out every command like a wife.
The mantra of Vadhuyakṣiṇī is: *oṃ niḥ*.
This is Vadhuyakṣiṇī.

The ritual service (*upacāra*) for her is as follows: having smeared the right arm with white sandalwood paste, and having consecrated saffron with a thousand recitations of the mantra, one should, alone and observing silence at night in a secluded place, close the door, place five or eight *vibhītaka* fruits into sesame oil, and recite [the mantra].

Having taken that oil and discarded the *vidhītaka* fruit, one should place it in a new vessel—whether of gold, silver, copper, or clay—at the foot of the bed. Having consecrated it one thousand times with this very mantra of the One-Syllable Yakṣiṇī, one should sleep in a secluded, dark place upon a bed strewn with flowers. Then a non-human female will arrive and anoint one’s feet;
she possesses a divine countenance and palms of hands as soft to the touch as silk.
By the mere touch of which a divine sleep of pleasant contact arises;
by which one awakens with pain at the end of the night even at sunrise;
and having awakened, one should contemplate that very thing.
She must neither be desired nor spoken to [with lustful intent].
Within six months she becomes accomplished;

then, possessing a divine form, appearing like a young bride, surrounded by female attendants, with a lamp in her hand, illuminating the world with her own radiance, holding a bed and seat, and blazing with various ornaments, she arrives and converses with him.

Embracing the implements for enjoying sensual pleasures, she comes and embraces the practitioner around the neck; from that time forth, she follows him like a beloved wife. Having arrived, she is to be desired; after attending to him at night, she disappears at dawn.
Leaving behind his pearl necklace on his bed— worth a thousand pieces of gold— he departs day after day, casting it away;
everything must be spent without remainder,
for if he were to set aside anything, there would be nothing left.
It must not be told to anyone;
if one tells it, [the recipient] will not come again or will cause harm.
For these are indeed the supreme secret-holders; they are to be kept strictly hidden, and it is not permissible to reveal them to a second being.
One must not disclose them even to one's mother, father, friends, masters, or kinsmen.
At the very least, they must not be imparted even to animals or living beings belonging to the animal realm.
This is the supreme secret;
it is the very procedure for all the Guhyakas and all the Yakṣiṇīs. Even those who have attained accomplishment become unaccomplished [if they neglect this].
If he confesses [his transgression],
he should always avoid sexual intercourse with other women and with his own wife.
The mantra of Manojñā is: *oṃ manohare madonmādakari vicitrarūpiṇi maithunāpreye svāhā*.

Regarding her ritual service (*upacāra*): having had a well-proportioned hut constructed beneath an *aśoka* tree in a garden grove—one that is most secret, provided with artificial doors, bolts, and high walls—a pure practitioner should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Thereafter, one should begin the ritual action (*karman*).
Having gathered human fat and made a wick with a cotton rag from a cemetery, one should close the door and light a lamp.
One should place a garment with its fringe intact and free of hair outside the door.
At night, a fresh woman, having become a human female in form, will come naked, put on that garment, and enter.
Then the practitioner enjoys himself with her as long as the lamp burns;
when the lamp is extinguished, she disappears.
Having tied a piece of gold to that garment, he leaves the bed, discarding the garment.
Then the practitioner takes her by the hand;
having loosened a single ring, she steps forward.

Then from his neck he takes a divine pearl necklace, then from his arm a bracelet, from his waist a girdle, from his feet anklets, and from his head a jewel. In this manner, whichever single divine ornament is taken from here or there, she hands it over right there.
He goes and comes without being hindered;
in this manner, it should be spent entirely every day.
When he consults [with others] after such a number of months have passed, then he should be consulted.
She becomes his wife;
remaining constantly present, she bestows an elixir (*rasāyana*) which, when drunk, enables one to live for a long time.
Having meditated upon her in the mind, one should drive a stake of *khadira* wood into the ground.
A divine celestial palace appears;
once it has been raised, it vanishes.
This second mantra belongs to her.
"Oṃ mahānagni nagnije svāhā. Having lit a lamp with that very [substance] and having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with this mantra, one should employ it;
she will certainly come.
Furthermore, having consecrated a ritual stake (kīlaka) with the mantra, one should drive it into the ground.

When the lamp has been raised and extinguished, the human stake (*mānuṣakīlaka*) and the fat-stake (*vasākīla*) vanish. One should carry them on the horns of a *gavala* or a buffalo, wrapped in a cloth from a cremation ground, to another country;
there, one gives them wherever one desires.
Or he performs it himself;
however, the mantras must not be given away.
If he does give them, his knowledge becomes severed.
Whatever one gives, that very thing accrues to him;
wherever he desires it, or in whatever secret place he performs it—
this accomplishment, once turned back, does not depart.
Or he may cause another woman to take pleasure;
however, he does not converse with them.

This is because he is intent on seeing other women and desires them in his mind, and thus he approaches such a person who is suitable for him, due to the power of the practitioner and as something unprecedented.
The mantra of Surasundarī is: *oṃ surasundari svāhā*.
The ritual procedure for this is as follows: having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations of clarified butter.

At the three junctions of the day for one month, on the full moon of the bright fortnight, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, pure and in a clean place, one should recite the mantra in secret until, at midnight, she certainly arrives.
Then the mother, sister, and wife act exactly as they did before; all of that should be told in full detail.
These seven yakṣiṇīs, by the command of Vajrapāṇi,
roam throughout the entire earth and the three worlds, including the gods and asuras.
Some compassionate ones moved among mortals, fond of sexual union;
others were noble women, as well as young girls, fools, and other yakṣīs.
Likewise, at night, she wanders about, intent on her desire for lions;
greedy for meat-eating, she seeks to destroy the lives of children.
Likewise, drawn by the scent of blood, that yakṣī— who constantly takes life and is ever fond of gore— has indeed come to Jambūdvīpa.

They roam through all the houses, including those under protection, those with a death-impurity, and those with a birth-impurity; this is declared to be their suppression, and this is the samaya that has been revealed.
Just as attachment to gathering and binding the foolish in this world [is taught],
so all this has been proclaimed for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings.
Just as a practitioner of mantra, desiring sexual union and blinded by passion with a deluded mind,
might summon and enjoy a yakṣī or a rākṣasī through mantras,
or likewise a nāgī, a gandharvī, a daitya woman, or a kinnarī.

The wise practitioner of mantras should enter the delightful subterranean abode, the supreme city of the asuras, where there are countless women; having gone there, the knower of mantras who recites them may dwell for an eon.
When the Perfectly Awakened One named Maitreya becomes a Buddha, then he shall hear the True Dharma, and having heard it, he will be liberated.
Having summoned a daughter of the gods, a goddess, or even the excellent wife of a vidyādhara by means of mantras, he should then enjoy the delight of divine happiness.
The practitioner residing in Jambudvīpa always brings [the deity] right there;
he should remain in a pure and secret place, always devoted to the practice of ritual purity.
For the deluded, the supreme accomplishment may sometimes arise through that;
[yet] feces, urine, and impure places are always foul-smelling and putrid.
One should not touch a human woman, for she is a vessel of suffering— of the pain of disease, of grief, of separation even from those joined in pleasure, and ending in death.
Impermanent, suffering, likewise empty, void, insubstantial, and non-eternal;
it is a mere deception of the foolish, arising from the production of conceptual construction.
The mantra-practitioner should not pursue any desires born of beginningless craving;
the cessation of those [desires] is called liberation, and within them lies the state of accomplishment.
Indeed, his mantras are accomplished if he is free from desire;
even one smeared with feces, urine, and blood, when thus worshipped.
One should not touch a human body, which is subject to old age, death, and great sorrow;
nor should one indulge in sexual union there, for those whose minds are blinded by delusion and possessed by passion.
Success is not obtained by those who are always impure and devoted to mantras;
rather, one who knows the mantras, recites them, possesses wisdom, has conquered the senses,
is steadfast, and delights in pure conduct will indeed succeed with every mantra at all times.
Padmoccā, Samodā, and also Ajitā and Jayā always,
as well as Śyāmāvartā— the yakṣī— these are the yakṣīs of great supernatural power.

The mantra of Padmocchā is: *oṃ padmocce svāhā*. The ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for this is as follows: On the bank of the Gaṅgā or on the shore of the ocean, having constructed a hut in the middle of a garden or flower grove, one should become exceedingly pure oneself and prepare a clay structure in the shape of a stone slab. Having closed the door there at night and brought all necessary articles for enjoyment and pleasure, one should arrange a bed for the Yakṣiṇī right there near oneself. Then, one should recite the vidyā ten thousand times.
In this way, she will certainly arrive within the space of a month.
And having arrived, she becomes a wife who enjoys sensual pleasures;
at dawn, she departs after leaving behind her divine pearl necklace and bed.
In this manner, day by day, she becomes permanently present after six months.

One must not accept that pearl necklace; if one accepts it, one will be reborn as exactly that. When six months have passed, that necklace, worth a hundred thousand dīnāras and adorned with precious gems, becomes a permanent wife who grants all desires.
Having assumed whatever form is desired, she appears;
she manifests herself in whatever way is pleasing.
This is the procedure for all yakṣīs according to the wish of the practitioner, as has been taught here and elsewhere.
The mantra for victory is: *Oṃ jaye sujaye jāpayati sarvakāryāṇi kuru me svāhā*.
The goddess Kanakābhā has variegated limbs and dark, curly hair;
she is beautiful in every limb, auspicious, fortunate, and sublime.
One should point out Jayā as a woman who is pleasant-spoken, the best among women, beautiful and lovely to behold,
with praised limbs and fair skin, highly honored by all the world,
and wearing a slightly reddish garment.
The ritual procedure for this is as follows: first, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
thus the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) is accomplished.
Then, having entered a great forest and subsisting on fruit, one should recite until she appears in her own form.
And when she has arrived, she asks, "What shall I do?
If she is one's mother,
she fulfills all hopes like a mother.
It bestows sovereignty;
it makes one a master of great wealth;
and it consecrates one with long life.
Then the sister brings a woman as desired, even one residing a thousand *yojanas* away; she gives a hundred thousand *dīnāras* day after day,
and that [wealth] must be spent.
Then she becomes his wife; he leads her to his own abode, mounts a divine celestial chariot with her, and sports with her for a long time—thirty thousand years—wandering as he pleases.
He becomes like a great yakṣa.
The mantra of Pramodā is: Oṃ ṣṭhrīḥ hrīṃḥ mahānagni hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Her ritual procedure is as follows: at midnight, an immeasurable number of recitations (jāpa) should be performed.
One should fall asleep again;
within a month,
she will certainly come and become one's wife, granting all desires.
Day after day he gives him twenty-five dinars; moreover, he provides for his own livelihood and enables him to live for a long time.
In this way, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of yakṣiṇīs;
likewise, there are piśācas, piśācas of great supernatural power, nāga maidens, asura maidens, apsarases, celestial women, and daitya maidens.
In this same manner, there are mantras for all the vidyādharīs, from every quarter, and for both human and non-human females.

Likewise, there are innumerable mantras of the yakṣas, gods, nāgas, ṛṣis, gandharvas, asuras, pretas, and rākṣasas, as well as those of Mahābrahmā, Maheśvara, Mahāviṣṇu, the Mothers, and the goddesses headed by Aindrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍī, and Vārāhī; all these exist individually. And they have all been summoned here at the proper time by the Wrathful King Yamāntaka, brought forth, seized, established in the pledge (*samaya*), and presented to Mañjughoṣa. Together with their retinues, standing in succession, they are all attendants. In brief, wherever there is an image, or having made a likeness oneself, one should recite the mantra of the Wrathful King Yamāntaka until the reflection trembles, moves, or perspires.
These come in their own essential form;
whatever is spoken, they accomplish it all.

Likewise, for those four maidens who are great yakṣiṇīs, accompanied by their brother Tumburu, possessing divine forms, dwelling upon the ocean, mounted upon a boat, honored by all the world, and acting for the benefit of sentient beings— the ritual procedure for them is exactly this: namely,
they should be depicted either as a crowded scene on a cloth, a wall, or a wooden panel.
Having boarded a ship, she was led away by her elder brother.
Having placed a maiden who resembles Caturā within the ocean,
and having stationed her there in secret, one should begin the recitation of the mantra while suppressing one's anger.
Trembling, shaking, and likewise perspiration arise everywhere;
then, knowing "they are accomplished," the reciter of mantras should cease the recitation.
At the end of the night, they declare the auspicious and inauspicious by their very nature;
indeed, those practitioners become entirely successful through the recitation.
Commanded by the excellent planets beginning with Soma, as well as by the ṛṣis and likewise by the rākṣasas, they perform everything when drawn forth and overcome by wrath.
Those of great supernatural power are well-honored by the Piśācas and the Garuḍas;
those of great supernatural power are likewise honored by Maheśvara and others of such a nature.
And by these [deities], the rituals and the tantras of the mantras have been spoken in full detail;
all of them, along with their ritual manuals and extensive manuals, should be put into practice.
All those mantras whatsoever that are parched or born of dejection remain effortlessly under the control of the King of Wrath.
All those noble mantras that are indeed distinguished and all-pervading have been assigned to the King of Wrath and revealed by him.
Indeed, they have been described by the supreme Victors as excellent, preeminent, and foremost;
likewise, O mantra-holder, these mantras have been proclaimed by me as well.
And furthermore, those other principal mantras belonging specifically to the five families,
which were spoken by the sons of the Conquerors, as well as the worldly ones possessed of great supernatural power.
Having drawn them all together, the King of Wrath, possessed of great supernatural power,
binds all of them here within this teaching by means of the mantras, tantras, and weapons.
Whichever procedure has been prescribed for them, by that very same [procedure] this Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath, is to be employed; he is supreme and effective for all ritual actions.
And Tārā, Bhṛkuṭī, as well as Pāṇḍaravāsinī,
Mahāśvetā, the Vidyā, Māmakī, and she who is born from the vajra.
To Uṣṇīṣaprabhā and the deity Sarvalocanā,
to every Tathāgata-vidyā, and to the wise Mañjughoṣa.
Mahāsthāman, Samanta, and likewise the Lord Padmavara—
just as there is the Bodhisattva Yakṣeśa of great supernatural power in the world.
As it was said: "The Son of the Victor (Jinaputra), renowned throughout the world in all his limbs, as well as Vajrasena, Suṣeṇa, and my own wise sons."
The reciter should not show contempt for those mantras spoken by me;
he should always honor them all, for they were spoken as inviolable.
The reciter should not employ the well-worshipped King of Wrath there;
he should never effect the severance of the vidyās within those mantras.
And likewise all worldly mantra-deities according to their respective rites,
such as Umā, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, and others, as well as Hari who is well-worshipped.
Just as it has been done for all mantras in the tantras,
so too should one undertake every mantra from every source;
indeed, the activity of all mantras is seen to arise from the Wrathful One.
This mantra is a great wrathful one known by the name Yamāntaka;
having drawn forth even the great-souled Yama, it shall swiftly cause him to be slain.
Indeed, Śakra and even the high-souled Kṛtānta, son of Vivasvat, were drawn forth by him;
he is the Lord, the subduer of the unsubdued, who wears the wise as his garments.
This mantra, a great mantra, has been proclaimed by Mañjubhāṣin;
it performs all rites, is fierce, and accomplishes all mantras.
Having spoken thus, the glorious Vajrapāṇi, possessed of great supernatural power,
bowed to the Buddha, the Great Hero, the Lion of the Śākyas, the Supreme among Men; and relying upon the mantra, the wielder of the vajra uttered the mantra of great supernatural power.
"May all sentient beings indeed listen, as well as all the auspicious hosts of spirits;
I, the presiding lord of the entire host of Maitreyas, shall proclaim this supreme mantra."
This was spoken by the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa—
the formidable subduer of the difficult-to-tame, which wards off all that is evil.
It was spoken by the Bodhisattva for the sake of training sentient beings;
and I, too, speak here in the midst of this assembly that which is most formidable.
Homage to all Buddhas, who have arisen from the nature of non-existence!
Homage to the Pratyekabuddhas and the noble Śrāvakas! Homage to the Bodhisattvas, the Great Beings, the lords established on the ten stages!

Namely: *Oṃ kha kha khāhi khāhi, O subduer of wicked beings, you who hold a sword, mace, noose, and axe in your hands; four-armed, four-faced, six-legged, go, go! O destroyer of great obstacles, you of deformed countenance, you who cause fear to all spirits, you who utter loud laughter, you who are clothed in tiger-skin, perform, perform all rites! Cut, cut all mantras! Attract, attract all spirits! Grind, grind all the wicked! Cause them to enter, cause them to enter into the center of the maṇḍala! O ender of the life of Yama (Vaivasvata), perform, perform my task! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Do not delay, do not delay! Remember your pledge! *Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*! Shatter, shatter all hopes! O Blessed One, why do you tarry? Accomplish all my aims! *Svāhā*!
O worthy ones, all you hosts of gods, this is he, the wrathful king named Yamāntaka, who brings even King Yama himself, slays him, withers him, cooks him, and subdues him.
In this way, he [subdues] all mantras and all gods; how much more so a miserable human being?
He brings even those bodhisattvas established on the ten stages.
How much more so, then, worldly mantras?
Thus, this King of Wrath possesses immeasurable strength and prowess;
likewise, he performs all rites even among those spoken in all mantra-tantras.
Just as it is employed among all mantras, so does it act;
this King of Wrath named Yamāntaka is accomplished through mere recitation and is thus complete.

Thus ends the third detailed chapter, the fifty-first [chapter] from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra which is an ornament of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, entitled "The Complete Rules for All Procedures of the Wrathful King Yamāntaka."
Homage to the Buddha!
This concludes the ritual manual (kalpa) of Yamāntaka, the King of Wrath.
Now begins the fifty-third detailed chapter.

Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having arisen from that samādhi, while teaching the Dharma to the ocean-like assembly circle, sat down before all sentient beings and all hosts of spirits. There, he addressed the many thousands of incalculable bodhisattvas headed by Vajrapāṇi; the many thousands of incalculable arhats headed by Śāriputra; the incalculable sons of the gods of the Four Great Kings headed by Vaiśravaṇa; the incalculable sons of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven headed by Śakra; and the gods of Suyāma, Santuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmitavaśavartin, Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahma, Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, Ābhāsvara, up to Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha. He addressed these deities, saying:
Listen, O venerable hosts of gods, all bodhisattvas, and noble śrāvakas:
all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, subject to the nature of arising and passing away.
Having arisen, they indeed cease; their complete stilling is bliss.
All things arise with causes through the power of ignorance;
indeed, the aggregates, together with their origin, are said to be the root of suffering along with its cause.
The knowledge that brings about their cessation—the cause of happiness and the activity of happiness—is called the abandonment of suffering; in brief, it is the prevention [of the defilements].
That very threefold vehicle has been taught by me here:
that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and are momentary.
It has been taught that the entire bond of existence is always and at all times empty;
through detachment from that, those beings who have emerged from their spiritual lineage proceed in three ways.
At that time, the Bodhisattvas, the Buddhas, and those relying on the enlightenment of the Pratyekabuddhas—
as well as others who have abandoned passion, possess great supernormal powers, and come day after day— [assemble].
Relying on the awakening of the śrāvakas, they have indeed attained the threefold peace;
this dharma, both auspicious and inauspicious, has been taught by me in brief.
One should always avoid what is unwholesome and always practice what is wholesome;
non-violence toward all living beings is how the Dharma has been revealed.
There is but a single path for all phenomena within the five destinies:
that which is untainted and rests upon the limit of reality.
This very path was taught by the ancient primordial Buddhas;
I too have explained it all, leading to the peace of nirvana.
By relying upon the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is attained;
the limit of all phenomena is declared to be the limit of reality, which is itself without a limit.
This Dharma has been revealed in brief as being of two kinds;
let all the gods and the Bodhisattvas of great supernatural power listen!
When my śrāvaka arhats attained nirvāṇa upon this earth,
it occurred in the midst of a sāla grove growing on the slopes of the Himalayas.
Near the river Hiraṇyavatī, in the vicinity of the Mallas,
amidst the Yamakaśālaka grove, my final nirvāṇa will take place.
As long as I possess perception, my nirvāṇa shall then take place on this earth at the city of Makuṭabandhana, at the Caitya, and always by the delightful bank of the river.
Indeed, all the bodhisattvas and śrāvakas of great supernatural power,
as well as the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and world-protectors of great supernatural power.
Śakra, Brahmā, Suyāma, and others such as those of Akaniṣṭha—
all of them will indeed assemble in that place.
There, in the Yamakaśālaka grove,
the funeral rites for the Mallas were performed on the northern bank of the Ganges, that great river.
On the southern side of the Himālaya, in a forest of Sāla trees,
my final resting place shall be in that very spot.
Likewise, on the delightful bank of the river, at the auspicious shore named Hiraṇya,
there will be a gathering of all the hosts of gods and others.
Then, by all men, the best of kings, and those born of both human and non-human origins;
likewise, by all beings, both mortals and the ignorant as well as the wise.
In that place, amidst a great festival and with great enthusiasm,
I performed a divine mantra upon my own body while it was still possessed of flesh.
But having set aside that which is free from worldly desire, one then attains peace and liberation;
having relinquished the limit of phenomena (dharmakoṭi), one enters into the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
"This is my final birth; in the city of Kapilavastu, within the preeminent clan of the Śākyas, I have been born in this prison of existence."
Then, having abandoned my miserable self, I likewise departed from my home;
having served many sacred fords, I did not attain [liberation] and died once again.
And difficult practices were performed by me, having tormented this body; for six years I dwelt there, even with my body emaciated and utterly dried up.
And I did not obtain anything by which my knowledge might have been obscured;
therefore, having risen there, I partook of a meal of auspicious rice.
Following the path indicated by the deities, I went there to the ground at the foot of a magnificent king of trees on the bank of the Nairañjanā River.
Then, on the ground in that forest, which was strewn with various flowers,
endowed with the fruits of great woods, and filled with diverse trees;
Then, having encircled the great river, I stayed at the foot of a tree; for as soon as I beheld that portion of the earth which was my own, I attained steadfastness.
In that very same way, having seen that tree—
a great tree with vast shade, adorned with leaves and branches, and beautified by its hidden roots— [I approached it].

At the *aśvattha* tree, one should attain the state of the *aśvattha*; indeed, sitting at the foot of that tree, I found there steadfastness (*dhṛti*) as well as meditation and supreme concentration (*samādhi*). There, at the end of the night, I attained the hope-free state which brings an end to birth.
Māra had employed many obstacles in various forms;
having his army shattered, he turned back and returned once more to his own abode.
For that purpose, mantras and tantras have indeed been taught in many ways; furthermore, various applications, meditations, and forms of knowledge have been taught.
Furthermore, there are three vehicles therein, and all conduct is practiced within them;
for the remedies against the faults have indeed been revealed in three ways.
Then, rising up and returning once more to Pāṭaliputra, he bathed in its auspicious waters and there initiated the sage along with his disciples into the wandering life.
Having performed manifold deeds for the benefit of sentient beings, I departed from there once again; then, in due course, I entered the delightful city of Kāśī.
Having gone to that place, those of supreme awakening and great supernatural power remained there;
I myself stayed in that region among the people of Kāśī,
having set in motion the wheel that brings about peace through the true Dharma and leads to Nirvāṇa.
For the sake of the happiness of all beings, the Dharma was revealed there concerning the destiny of the worlds of gods and asuras, which issues from the five vital breaths.
In the past, the wheel of Dharma was turned there by the primordial Buddhas;
and by me as well, the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma has indeed been turned in that direction.
For the sake of the bliss of liberation from existence and for the removal of the defects of sentient beings,
he indeed set in motion the Brahma-wheel, which is secure and has peace as its ultimate goal.
For the sake of destroying the path of existence, [he taught] the Noble Eightfold Path, born from the meditative concentration on the Four Truths, and adorned by the four divine abidings.
It possesses dependent origination enacted in twelve aspects,
joined with the cessation of ignorance, and produced by the wheel of the arising of knowledge.
The ultimate reality is indeed whirled around, born from the most excellent pinnacle of the limit of existence;
it arises from the greatness of movement through the forward and reverse sequences, like the rim of a wheel.
The wheel of instruction is auspicious, and many beings have attained liberation;
having left the delightful city of Kāśī, I shall then go to Śrāvastī.
Likewise, one should avoid the heretics by displaying miraculous transformations;
having thus performed wonders in the countryside, they were then made to feel doubt.
Then, having fully satisfied many sacred fords and shrines,
he again performed the auspicious descent of the gods by placing them within the vessel of fire among the people.
Having joined Śakra with the nature of reality among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven,
[he likewise joined] the gods beginning with Akaniṣṭha, as well as Brahmā, Īśa, and Purandara.
Together with Vaiśravaṇa, the lord of yakṣas, and the gods of the Four Great Kings' realm, who are always like intoxicated elephants,
[there were those] bearing three lutes and wearing garlands.
All the hosts of gods— those of the earth, those of heaven, and those of the intermediate space—
as well as all the noble ones together with their leaders of the hosts, and indeed all the gods and asuras.

Having made her devoted to the fruit of the Dharma and inclined toward the path leading to Nirvana, she should then be joined with that which is truly beneficial for the sake of many living beings who lack wisdom.
The calculation of those [worlds] is incalculable, extending infinitely to the end of saṃsāra;
it comprises the great trichiliocosms, including their realms and their innermost depths of mind.
Having indeed always established many beings entirely in truth and in the ultimate reality,
I have come here and am now stationed above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.

Having set in motion the true Dharma of mantras which accords with the three vehicles, and having brought about the discipline of sentient beings, he then proclaimed this King of Rituals (Kalparāja) in many ways throughout the world and entrusted it to Mañjughoṣa.
But when I have passed away and the world has become empty upon the surface of the earth,
Mañjuśrī will then perform the Buddha-deeds for sentient beings.
For the sake of protecting the true Dharma of the Lords of Jinas who have entered parinirvāṇa,
Mañjughoṣa will be a constant and perpetual protector.
However, for the sake of manifesting the power of the mantra, this extensive ritual manual has been told;
indeed, at that time, during the most terrible and dreadful end of the age.
In that lowest age, at that time, the lords of men will be great killers, delighting in mutual slaughter; they will be evildoers of wicked conduct with meager enjoyments— of this there is no doubt.
And having come to me for the sake of worship, he was present in the Sālavana grove and at the Makutabandhana Caitya on the bank of the river Hiraṇyavatī.
When I have entered final nirvāṇa, lying upon my bed, having attained the realm of peace,
and when my body has been placed upon the funeral pyre, free from all enjoyments in the sambhogakāya.
