Having seen that very deed of mine, performed with such wondrous conduct, I myself have brought it under control through an act of conversion by a Buddha, which was otherwise inaccessible.
Having remembered that auspicious and wondrous deed, all the lords of men,
together with the gods, asuras, and humans, will all perform worship.
Then all the kings, having assembled, will undoubtedly perform a great festival of worship in my presence at that time.
When the body, together with its flesh and the arising of the qualities, has been placed upon the funeral pyre—
at the end of the impure and even at the pure, when all is devoid of merit—
the peaks of existence (*bhūtakoṭi*) are then empty within the convergence of the five aggregates.
But many beings, upon seeing him, were engaged for the sake of great merit;
likewise the great śrāvakas, the high-souled ones who were free from passion and possessed of great supernatural powers,
and all the bodhisattvas who had indeed taken their stand upon the ten stages.
They all stood surrounding him, all full of compassion;
indeed, all the hosts of gods, both noble ones and ordinary worldlings.
And all of them, having gathered together in one place at this site of great merit,
attained clarity of mind, taking refuge in the meaning of impermanence and suffering.
All the hosts of spirits stood nearby at the edge of the shrine;
they performed a great worship and cried out and wept.
They shed tears with drops of water, moved by compassion,
and all of them cried out thus: "The Buddha has now taught the Dharma on this earth regarding impermanence, suffering, and emptiness."
O best of sages, he is that very same one, now the seventh and most excellent bull among seers;
born of the Śākya clan, the foremost of all beings—this is my final vision of him.
This Blessed One lies here— he who spoke of impermanence and suffering,
who proclaimed the emptiness of the ultimate truth, and who taught the meaning of primordial peace.
O hosts of gods, for what reason do you not awaken that Lord?
All these sons of the Buddha, possessed of great supernatural powers, have indeed come here;
as well as the great heroes who seek the Dharma and the disciples endowed with great supernatural powers.
All beings indeed suffer— humans, gods, and asuras alike—
for this is the time for turning the wheel of Dharma.
May the Blessed One arise quickly, following the Buddha’s timely hour; for those who have set out upon the path of the Sage must cross over the surging great ocean.
One should not despise many sentient beings, but for a long time remain equanimous toward them, and should cultivate meditative concentration and liberation on the path to peaceful nirvana.
Or the Sage [is unable] to describe it as it truly is; for he has already spoken much in this manner, uttering many kinds of idle chatter.
Then all the hosts of gods of great supernatural power became silent; having uttered incomparable cries of lamentation, they stood there with prostrations.

Then Brahmā and the others, together with the gods and asuras, humans and all the lords of men, having opened their eyes, sat there upon the earth with tearful throats, faltering voices, and hearts overwhelmed by grief.
Another Śākyan-born was liberated, free from passion, and possessed of great supernormal power;
he belonged to the Great-Souled Buddha, the God of Gods, who possesses primordial wisdom.
The monk named Aniruddha was his younger brother,
a virtuous man who was extremely subtle, skillful, and discerning, and was an expert in the principles of song;
he was surrounded by many eminent sages and lords of men.
With a heart softened by compassion, he spoke these sweet and well-composed words, addressed to the Mallas along with their king as they sighed deeply.
"O worthy ones, do not set fire to the funeral pyre here until the Blessed One’s son, who has arisen from the nature of reality, appears before us."
This disciple, known by the name Mahākāśyapa, possessed great supernatural powers;
he was a Brahmin born with the foremost wisdom of the Great Sage, free from worldly desires.
Born among the people of Magadha, he dwells there on Mount Gṛhapippala in the excellent city of Rājagṛha, composed in meditative concentration.
He himself will surely come quickly and not otherwise;
however, if the deity residing there is devoted [to another], he might ward off the meteor.
Do not yet kindle the funeral pyre with futile labor,
as long as that one of great supernatural power remains— the foremost disciple, the true son of the Sage.
Having circumambulated the Teacher, the Buddha, who is honored by the three worlds,
he bowed his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, which are worshipped by the world.
Then you shall all perform this for the sake of the funeral pyre;
at that time, these [women] will become like blazing shrines.
"Do not all of you here exert yourselves in vain!
Thus addressed by the wise Aniruddha,
all those wrestlers, along with the human kings, sat down.
I was born among humans and was nurtured by humans with various kinds of enjoyments and other auspicious accomplishments in the arts and crafts.
I attained enlightenment for human beings at the foot of a tree upon the earth;
I have taught the Dharma for human beings, which is beneficial to all sentient beings.
For this very reason, the funeral pyre of humans is prepared for the purpose of lighting lamps;
"I am a human" and I have attained preeminence among all beings.
In the world of humans, my peace is conceived as final nirvana.
Whosoever are all the Buddhas indeed existing in the past and the future,
they are all humans born in bodies within this world of men.
Just as with birth, awakening, and the wheel, there is a commonality in practicing the auspicious;
all Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats likewise enter into peace in three ways,
having relied upon a human body and attained unsurpassed tranquility.
For inconceivable eons, I have rendered service to them; and finally,
when [the world] has become peaceful, cooled, ceased, and the surface of the earth has become empty, I have established the relics there.
For the benefit of human beings, and out of a desire to bestow honor and grace upon the worlds of gods and asuras, as well as upon the sages, yakṣas, and garuḍas.
The rākṣasas, pretas, kūśmāṇḍas, piśācas, and pretas of great supernatural power;
indeed, all beings together with the grahas and the mātṛs.
And all the worlds as well, inconceivable and innumerable realms,
and all living beings— these relics were established by you at that time for the purpose of worship, when the surface of the earth had become empty.
Some were brought by mortals possessing wealth, others by kings of the gods,
and still others by inhabitants of the netherworld, by lords of the dānavas of great supernatural power,
as well as by nāga kings and daityas; they brought my minerals one by one.
Then those who are virtuous and possessed of great supernatural power, having carried away those whose wealth has been stolen,
will perform worship after bringing them back to their own abodes once more.
There is no doubt that all Buddhas of great supernatural power will arise—
whether superior, inferior, or middling— from the threefold clarity of mind.
They will appear in the world in three ways, having attained the states of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats;
likewise, the vehicle in the world is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
At that time, there will appear in the world those who follow the path described in the Mahāyāna, yet who have departed from its practice and rely instead upon the awakening of a Pratyekabuddha.
And there will be other disciples there who have transcended passion and possess great supernatural power;
at that time, they will appear in the world, adorned by the threefold lineage.
Those protectors of the earth, possessing great enjoyments and great gentleness, as well as the wielders of the discus,
having long experienced divine and human prosperities,
eventually reached the threefold peace at the end of their time.
This very path has indeed been fully revealed by all the Buddhas— those of the past, those of the present, and likewise those of the future— just as it is now.
There, all the deities were indeed seated upon the ground of nirvana;
with distracted minds and agitated, they spoke with voices choked by sobs.
Then they all said: "Alas, how painful is impermanence!
Even the Buddha, possessed of great supernatural power in the world, has now entered final nirvana."
Thus addressed, all those kings of the gods, possessed of great supernatural power,
remained silent and stood still.
Among the Magadhas, the best of people who dwell in Kuśāgrapura,
there is a mountain near that city known by the name Vārāha; there,
in a cave belonging to the descendant of Pipala, that monk dwells absorbed in meditation.
My son, the foremost disciple, born of my own breast and arisen from the Dharma—
known by the name Mahākāśyapa— was then seated in that excellent cave.
Having then eaten that alms-food, he sat down and thought to himself:
"For a long time I have paid homage to this Buddha, the Great Sage;
now I wish to go to that Self-Existent One, the Supreme among Men."
"Where does the Blessed One, the best of sages from the Śākya clan, reside? Standing there, he is mindful of Mahākāśyapa, the king of brahmins."
Having thus reflected with his mind upon the Sage as the Sage,
he should survey the world and all beings with his divine eye.
Likewise, having illuminated the worlds beginning with Akaniṣṭha,
he illuminated all the world-systems arising within the great trichiliocosm, including all those designated as containing sentient beings.
With his divine eye, he perceives as far as the range of the disciples—
the teaching that is extinguished, peaceful, cooled, and free from worldly taints.
He was indeed surrounded on all sides by hosts of gods possessing great supernatural power,
as well as by humans, lords of men, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
all the multitudes of spirits, and bodhisattvas of great supernatural power.
Then there were also wise śrāvakas of great renown who had become bearers of the burden,
both those still possessed of passion and those free from passion, as well as divine beings, noble ones, and humans.
Then [they saw] the hero, the Buddha, the kinsman of the sun,
the god of gods, the most excellent, the lord, and the best among sages, placed upon the funeral pyre.
He was indeed surrounded on all sides by kings dwelling in the islands,
as well as by wrestlers and lords of men, who held bundles of grass torches in their hands.
They were unable to set it on fire, being restrained by the deities and by the monk Aniruddha, who was observing his vows and had spoken thus.
With a throat choked with tears, he raised a loud cry that resounded throughout the earth—a terrible sound of "Alas! Alas! mingled with the booming of kettledrums.
That forest was divine, crowded with hosts of sages, praised by throngs of apsarases, and resounded with the songs of siddhas and vidyādharīs as well as the high-singing of kinnaras.
The auspicious crying of birds resounded with sweet warbling;
there was a wonderful and charming music of instruments, resonating with both divine and human sounds.
The Sāl forest became a place where the Apsarases sang in chorus, a setting befitting the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, and which was filled on all sides by yogins.
Then, sighing deeply and filled with grief, he who was once free from sorrow gazed upon that supreme bull among sages lying there, surrounded on all sides.
Then the śramaṇa Kāśyapa, my foremost disciple, shed a single tear as he rolled upon the earth.
And he quickly utters these words: "Alas, what a tragedy unfolds!
For even those Buddhas who have become free from outflows (anāśrava) must indeed pass into final nirvāṇa."
"Impermanent, suffering, and empty—this very thing was taught by him here;
I have not seen anything eternal in this universe that persists through other births."
Then, rising up from there quickly, one should go to the king of the Magadhas,
Ajātaśatru, who is afflicted by suffering and overwhelmed by grief for his father.
Having then gone to his house, he said to that lord of men:
"O Great King, that Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among bipeds, has passed into final nirvana."
"Quickly harness the chariot; let us go into the presence of the Teacher,
who lies upon the earth, free from fever, with his consciousness departed,
having transcended all enmity and fear— the one to be enjoyed, with the body as the seventh."
Having heard those cruel words, the king was once again deeply distressed; then, lamenting within himself and weeping aloud, the monarch spoke these words.
I have fallen away from both the Teacher and my father; abandoned by all my kinsmen, I am likewise untrustworthy among people. Having fallen into a terrible hell, whom shall I choose as my refuge?
Save me, O Great Hero, foremost disciple of the Teacher!
Mahākāśyapa of great majesty, there is no life for me here.
Having spoken thus, the king, the preeminent lord of men among the Magadhas,
fell at that very moment to the earth at the feet of the foremost disciple;
motionless and fainted, he suddenly lay upon the ground.
At that time, O youth Mañjughoṣa of great supernatural power,
you wander everywhere throughout the worlds with the desire to benefit sentient beings.
When my body had been placed upon the funeral pyre in that forest grove,
you, O Mantra, were seated there, surrounded by a multitude of Bodhisattvas.
"Indeed, having placed your own body here on the earth for the sake of worship, you look all around at living beings; for who is suffering, and whom can one deliver?"
Thus I, the prince of profound and true intellect, have fallen to the ground;
therefore, O Mañjuśrī, you must surely [act] for the sake of this king who is in extreme distress.
Even though he was staying there, you alone were able to discipline him;
for he is one who can be understood only by a Bodhisattva, and cannot be reached even by gods of great supernatural power, nor by other sages, nor by Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, or Śrāvakas.
Remaining there, one shall see Mañjughoṣa, the lord of men, as if in a dream.
Empowered by you alone, that king, fainting from grief,
then beheld in a dream Bāli manifest before his eyes,
as well as the youth Viśva himself, Mañjughoṣa of great supernatural power.
Through your grace, O Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva, together with the boy, is thus manifesting the Dharma and displaying various inconceivable miraculous powers.
The king's descent into Avīci and his swift emergence,
as well as various states of existence, the miserable realms, and destruction that appears beautiful.

Then, having extensively explained the qualities of the greatness of his destiny, which are entirely beyond those of all śrāvakas, he performed the destruction of the wicked deeds of the sūtra-makers.
This very extensive diversion of King Ajātaśatru has been told in brief, yet adorned with the meaning of its detailed significance.
This detailed ritual manual has been spoken by all the Buddhas— those who abide in the beginning, the middle, and the end—
for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings.
At that time, O Prince Mañjuśrī, you shall everywhere discipline the rulers of the earth who follow after evil deeds.
Inconceivable is the range of your supernatural power, and inconceivable is the number of those to be converted;
you shall indeed become the guide of all the hosts of living beings.

Having spoken thus, the Great Hero, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Best of Speakers, and the Supreme among Bipeds, then addressed Mañjughoṣa of great splendor— who was situated above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven— at that time, for the sake of the Buddhas.

After many eons have passed— eons that are inconceivable, beyond calculation and numbering, and equal to what cannot be measured by human reckoning— you shall become a perfectly awakened Buddha; indeed,
you will appear in the world as the Buddha named Mañjudhvaja.
Then, having performed the work of a Buddha for you all in due succession, you shall always liberate many sentient beings, and your final nirvana will come to pass.
Thus addressed, the prince, who possessed great supernatural power though appearing in the form of a child,
sighed deeply and became agitated, his mind filled with compassion.
Having gazed upon the Perfectly Awakened One for a long time, he shed teardrops;
then, with palms joined in salutation, he sat down once more.
Then, standing upon the surface of the earth, the excellent king named Ajātaśatru bowed his head to the wonderful Brahmin Mahākāśyapa.
Having awakened and regained consciousness, the leader prostrated at his feet;
then, sighing for a long time, he explained the matter in detail.
Then the son of the king, the Lord of Magadha known as Ajātaśatru, being seated,
chose Mahākāśyapa, saying, "Let us go to that place of the funeral pyre."
Having been honored while residing in a shrine or an image, and being worthy of assistance by humans,
that foremost disciple, staying there, approached me thus through his supernatural power.
His mind was carried away by that; it was not appropriate for me to go by means of my supernatural power. I desired to go on foot to the great assembly of the Citta mountain.
"I have come for the sake of seeing the Teacher for the very last time.
Then, at the midpoint of the road, that practitioner stood still at Saṅghārāma.
There he saw a resident of the monastery,
an elderly monk who was actually a young being, deluded by Māra.
Having seen him, the elder approached that long-absent one,
who was of great renown, highly fortunate, a pure being free from affliction.
Having approached and bowed at the feet of that brahmin, he then said to that illustrious man, "Welcome; for what purpose have you come?"
"Where will you go quickly, or why do you stand here so agitated?
He said to that young seer, "Venerable one, have you not heard?"
The Teacher indeed is the Fully Awakened One of all the world, the supreme among bipeds;
my father, the Buddha of foremost wisdom, has passed into nirvana like the flame of a lamp.
The Great Hero has set; the earth has indeed become empty.
All worlds are likewise empty, and the quarters have become empty for me.

Likewise, the Uṣṇīṣonnata was accomplished by Māndhātṛ in the world;
similarly, Jayoṣṇīṣa was accomplished by Dhundhumāra, the best of kings.
Likewise, the victory-ushnisha of King Kandarpa is described;
Prajapati was indeed his son, and Locanā was his daughter on earth.
The son of Prajāpati was Nābhi, and his son was called Ūrṇamukha;
the son of Ṛṣabha was Lābhina, who was firm in his vows and had accomplished his task.
For him as well, the yakṣa Māṇicara was perfected on the Himavat mountain;
he too, Bharata, the son of Ṛṣabha, then recited those mantras.
In due course, that great hero attained success upon the earth;
and these and many other world-renowned kings,
having mastered the mantras and ruled their kingdoms, departed for heaven.
Those kings of vidyās of great supernatural power who were spoken by the Lords of Jinas—
all of them, being experts in the meaning of mantra and tantra, will achieve accomplishment in the auspicious age of eighty thousand years.
These and many other world-renowned kings,
having ruled for eighty thousand years or even a hundred, will then go to heaven, being destined for enlightenment.

At that time, during the middle period, the mantras— possessing divine, wondrous, and great supernatural powers— attained accomplishment when recited by those such as Padmapāṇi, by the foremost of men who are practitioners of mantra,
and by those adorned with ornaments dwelling on the earth.
And King Brahmadatta, indeed, in the great city of Vārāṇasī,
was a perfected one (siddha) with a lotus in his hand, a lord of the world renowned throughout the world.
Possessing great heroism, that Great-Souled One, exceedingly compassionate and sublime,
bestowed the teaching of the Dharma upon sentient beings in the form of mantras.
King Brahmadatta experienced human happiness;
thereafter, having perfected his mantra, he entered heaven in his own physical body.
And his son was the wise Puṇyakarman, firm in his vows;
his son was the accomplished and greatly heroic one, renowned by the name Harya.
By the power of that mantra, Śakra was then defeated;
his son, a king named Śveta, was then a giver of all things.
The mantras that grant boons to him are known by the name Mahāśvetā;
having accomplished that mantra, one shall live for three hundred years.
By the power of that mantra, he goes to Sukhāvatī;
his attainment of enlightenment is certain, as are those other [benefits] which have been proclaimed by me.
At that time, during the middle period, one should accomplish the middling mantras;
even in the lowest and most difficult age when I have attained Buddhahood,
the mantras of the Vajra and Lotus families will attain accomplishment.
"O Kumāra, those mantras which were previously spoken by you on earth shall indeed attain accomplishment; for these mantras possess the quality of being a portion [of the supreme].
As for other mantras, as well as various worldly ones, they are likewise [subject to this]."
The Kaśmalās, those of deformed appearance, and the sky-dwellers of the intermediate space; the Yakṣiṇīs of the earth, as well as various Piśācīs;
the Garuḍas, Kinnaras, Pretas, and those spoken of as Rākṣasas.
In this difficult age, the lowest of eras, the mantras of the piśācas, uragas, rakṣasas, and the highly powerful nāginīs shall attain accomplishment.
Mantras that have the form of youths and those that have the form of maidens will indeed attain accomplishment during that terrifying time.

Mantras are of three kinds, and the methods of accomplishment (*sādhana*) are likewise of three types; through these very three times, a threefold success (*siddhi*) is desired. I shall speak in brief, for what is being told is exceedingly extensive.
After that King Śokamukhya,
there will be a king known in the world as Viśoka, a follower of the Dharma.
These mantras were mastered by him; having accomplished them, the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī, free from sorrow, bestowed them upon the inhabitants of heaven.
Having experienced happiness for a long time on the summit of heaven, that great king,
being wise and virtuous by nature, returned once again to the human state.
Having experienced sovereignty and manifold prosperity,
that glorious one of great splendor worshipped the supreme relics for seventy-six years;
thereafter, overcome by fever, his body dissolved, he went to heaven.
Immediately after him, King Śūrasena is proclaimed;
he was renowned as a practitioner of Dharma and was always devoted to this teaching.
By him also, through the great glory of the Devī Stūpa, the mantras were accomplished; by him also, a very great monument was then caused to be built for the Teacher,
so that the entire earth, as far as the edge of the ocean, was adorned with stūpas.
Through the ripening of that karma, a disease born of his body will arise; having wasted away for one fortnight, he will pass away from this body.
Having ruled the kingdom for seventeen human years,
he passed away and entered heaven, destined certainly for enlightenment.
His immediate successor will be a king named Nanda,
glorious, possessing a great army and great strength, in the city called Puṣpa.
By him also was accomplished the mantra known as Piśāca-pīlu;
through the power of that mantra, he shall possess great wealth.
Consequently, he will become renowned in the world as both lowly and preeminent;
having obtained that wealth, the practitioner of mantra will attain the status of a sovereign in this world.
At that time, there will be Brahmins who are logicians on this earth;
residing in the city of Magadha, they will be greedy for the pride of supernatural powers,
and without a doubt, they will be conceited with false arrogance.
Surrounded by them, that king—
though virtuous in character and righteous in soul— will bestow that wealth upon them;
and having approached a spiritual friend, he will worship the most excellent relics.
But solely through that practice, and by reason of his unflagging generosity,
sixteen and eight monasteries were built by that wise one.
At that time, in the city of Puṣpasaṃhati,
there will indeed be a high-souled chief minister, compassionate, virtuous, and likewise a twice-born brahmin.
He will be a righteous soul for that king, the supreme Śākya;
and she, the Yakṣiṇī Vīramatī, will have her mantras perfected upon this earth.
By him also was made the most excellent reliquary of the Jinas upon the earth;
for he was exceedingly wise, being protected by the power of a yakṣiṇī.
Impelled by that karmic impression and driven by former impressions,
the wise one will, in due course, attain enlightenment which is difficult to find.
"Due to a fault committed by a woman, men shall meet their death;
at that time, one renowned as Vararuci will become excessively lustful."
The illustrious King Nanda, too, due to the transgression of his past karma,
caused his ministers to become alienated within the city named Pāṭala.
But one who belongs to the class of detached mantras, though true to his word and possessed of great strength,
will become afflicted with a major disease due to the transgression of past karma.
Afflicted by suffering through a great fever at midnight,
the lifespan of that king will indeed be sixty-six years; furthermore,
that king will certainly attain enlightenment as a disciple.
Among his friends, there will be a young brahmin named Pāṇini,
who will certainly be prophesied by me as a śrāvaka.
That twice-born man, having mastered the mantra of the great-souled Lord of the World, and desiring wisdom, should accomplish the Hālahala wrathful deity.
Another king of that [lineage] shall be known as Candragupta;
having attained success through the Yakṣa Japendra, he shall rule a kingdom free from thorns.
That lord of the earth was a great yogi, true to his word, and righteous in nature;
yet, having encountered an evil friend, he committed many killings of living beings.
Due to the ripening of that karma, he has fainted from poisonous eruptions.
Having wept at midnight, he should establish his son upon the earth—
the youth known as Binduvāra, who is a wicked minister.
Then, having passed away from the time of Candragupta and fallen to earth,
he reached the realm of the *preta*s— a destiny devoid of human company. However, through his application to the practice of mantras, he abandoned that state and went to heaven.
O Lord of Men, through the arising of the cause of mantras, that king gradually attains individual enlightenment by means of volition directed toward a wholesome object.
Furthermore, in a previous existence, King Bimbasāra, while still a child with an unrefined mind, had a caitya constructed by Siṃhadatta.
By the power of that karma, he indeed went to heaven irreproachable;
for five thousand births, he enjoyed happiness among the immortals.
Having descended from the heavenly world, he was reborn as a lord of men,
born into the royal family of the wise Candragupta.
Then, while still a youth, the king attained no small amount of happiness;
as he grew mature, he became bold, confident, eloquent, and pleasant of speech.
Thus, with the kingdom entirely under his own control, he ruled for seventy years.
O King, when the mantra named Keśinī has been mastered by him,
then those mantras of yours, O Prince, will attain success.
At that time, the mantra-siddhi spoken by you will come to pass;
the Soul of the Universe, the Lord of the worlds, will appear in the form of a youth.
It will undoubtedly exist for embodied beings in the form of mantra,
out of a desire for their welfare.
At that time, the mantras recited on earth will always be successful for that wise king Bindusāra.
The man known as Cāṇakya was one who had attained mastery over the Krodha-siddhi;
indeed, the Krodha named Yamāntaka was mastered by that evil-minded man.
Overcome by anger, he deprived living beings of their lives;
having committed that intense evil, he indeed [ruled] for three reigns at that time.

That contemptible twice-born shall become a long-lived one; by the power of that mantra, he shall inhabit an asura body while still in his own form. Having entered an asura body, he shall live for a long time.
Then, with his body shattered, he departs from the hells;
having thus experienced the suffering of hell, he falls into an evil rebirth here.
Then, having exhausted for one eon those various undesirable sufferings born of karma in the hells— incited by the mantras of anger—
he falls from that painful hell and is reborn among the animals.
Having entered the womb of a nāga, he will become one of terrifying form;
a king of nāgas, exceedingly wrathful, possessing great wealth, and arrogant with poison.
And being a performer of cruel deeds,
that man of wicked karma, having passed away, went to the world of Yama.
This Sunīda is King Yama, the king of the pretas, possessed of great supernatural power;
having thus experienced thousands of sufferings again and again, [he has become so].
In due course, that dull-witted young man will come to this earth; having attained a human birth, he will be of fearsome appearance,
poor, prone to anger, and of little renown.
Those Pratyekabuddhas in the world who are free from desire and wander like rhinoceroses,
who move upon the earth out of compassion for the lowly and the wretched,
have entered the practice of wandering for alms for the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings.
Seeing that evil-minded person, those who knew the minds of others at that time became intent upon him there, out of compassion and for no other reason.
Then, overcome by anger and incantations, he took those pieces of boiled grain for the purpose of eating, and at that time, he revealed the underlying cause.
He would offer alms there to one of those great-souled ones, saying:
"O all you renunciants, eat this as you please.
Out of compassion for them, he then displayed his supernatural power before the Buddhas.
Then, overcome with wonder and his mind uplifted by that power,
he prostrated himself from all sides with his head before the Buddhas who were like swords;
they all departed through the sky at will, free from all defects.
By that very merit, may I too conceive the thought of individual enlightenment;
for just as these great beings are— possessing peaceful appearance and great supernatural power—
may I likewise become such in the world, neither suffering nor falling into an evil rebirth.
Having exhausted the remainder of his karma, he will always pass away and go to heaven;
that righteous-souled one will, in due course, attain the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha.
Therefore, one should not perform malevolent rites for the sake of attaining power through mantras.
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have prohibited malevolent magic (*ābhicāruka*).
For the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are exceedingly compassionate and possess great supernatural power (*maharddhika*);
however, for the sake of demonstrating the efficacy of mantras that accomplish all rites, such [practices] have been shown.
The Tathāgatas have indeed spoken mantras that are like wish-fulfilling gems;
yet those who are childish in form, deluded in mind, and overcome by anger and greed employ these mantras against one another for malevolent purposes.
Thus, it has been prohibited by the Buddhas and by the wise Bodhisattvas in every respect to increase the enjoyments of sentient beings through mantras.

Arise now, O you who are the cause of prosperity, for the sake of protecting me and my kingdom! One should indeed accomplish the mantras for the purpose of attracting beings who have taken various forms of birth, but never by means of depriving them of life.
At that time, there will be monks of mine who are highly learned;
those known by the name Mātṛceṭa, having composed a hymn of praise to me alone,
shall speak according to the form [of reality] through descriptions of my actual qualities.

Having pacified the mind in every respect and delighting in the teaching of the Buddhas, one who has attained success through mantra is difficult to perceive; this applies especially to you, Mañjughoṣa.
Virtuous, endowed with moral discipline, a speaker of Dharma, and deeply learned—
even while formerly in the state of an animal, he spoke this hymn of praise.
In the delightful city named Nṛpa and in the forest called Khaṇḍa,
I dwell at ease together with my assembly of disciples.
While staying there, the crow sat and caused my mind to become serene;
having serenely focused his mind upon me, he passed away and went to heaven.
Having passed away from among the gods, he will be reborn among humans;
and having been reborn among humans, he shall go forth into homelessness within my teaching.
Having gone forth, that great-souled one, the observer of vows named Mātṛceṭa, will at that time praise me as I truly am.
He composed this well-spoken hymn of praise, which is true to its meaning and supported by various illustrations and reasons, solely for the benefit of all living beings.
For the sake of favoring sentient beings, he will then, at that time during the end of the age (yugānta) which is censured by the world, become intent upon exhorting [others] with hymns of praise;
through the ripening of that karma, his body having dissolved, he went to heaven.
Thus, that wise one, having experienced various pleasures in succession,
shall attain omniscient awakening, the supreme goal, which is inconceivable.
When four hundred years have passed after I, the Tathāgata, have entered parinirvāṇa,
there will be a monk named Nāga who delights in the welfare of this teaching;
having attained the stage of Muditā (Joy), he shall live for six hundred years.
The *māyūrī* spell was mastered by that great-souled one,
who understood the meaning of various treatises, the meaning of verbal roots, and the reality of the lack of intrinsic nature.
When he has cast off his body, he shall be reborn in Sukhāvatī;
there, in due course, he will certainly attain Buddhahood.
At that time, there was a monk named Saṅga, who was skilled in the true meaning of the treatises;
he further analyzed the definitive and interpretable meanings of the sūtras in many ways.
One who speaks of the world, whose mind is disciplined, and whose conduct is humble, shall have Śāladūtī accomplished; thus it is said.

Through the power of that mantra, an excellent wisdom arose in him regarding the essential meaning of the Sūtras for the sake of gathering [the teachings] so that the Dispensation might endure for a long time;
he lived for one hundred and fifty years, and having cast off his body, he went to heaven.
Having experienced happiness for a long time while wandering through the long cycle of existence,
this very self will, in due course, attain enlightenment.
"O monks, in this way, during that era, there were many who within my teaching possessed various forms of wisdom and were virtuous in their conduct."
Then, at that final time, there will be one named Nandana;
he too will have his soul united with the meaning of the mantras, will be a knower of the tantras, and highly learned.
For him, the *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious jar) will be accomplished, impelled by the mantra of the yakṣas.
In the past, in that very Mahāyāna-sūtra, I myself spoke;
at that time, the one of great asceticism drew it forth from that jar.
Since he had previously seen this book in the form of a mantra there,
no protection was performed for that jar which had been empowered by the yakṣa.
Due to a lapse in mindfulness caused by lack of vigilance, the jar was taken from his head;
consequently, that monk became a master of mantras, one who had perfected his mantra-asceticism.
He gazed at the banyan tree, yet he did not see anything there. Then, his limbs red with rage, he spoke while thundering.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including Śakra and the others up to Maheśvara—all these are drawn forth by the mantra;
I am neither the practitioner of the mantra nor the king of mantras.
Those mantras which were spoken by the sons of the Buddha, as well as by the supreme Victors, for the purpose of subduing or for taming those who are difficult to tame;
"If all of them do not come forth, I shall drag [them] out by force.
Then the mantra-practitioner, firm in his vows and having accomplished the rite, rose up from there.
But since the mantra had been prescribed,
he— intent on swift attraction— employed it in all directions as the cause for drawing [the target] toward him.
By merely recollecting this in an instant, he who performs swift action brings even Brahmā and the other gods down to earth with a single utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*.

All the gods, beginning with Brahmā and including Śakra, were drawn forth; uttering cries of "Alas! Alas!", they were distressed and made a terrifying noise, saying, "What shall we do? Why have we been brought here, we who are guilty of an offense against the mantra?"
Then the wise and confident monk, acting with haste and speed, addressed the inhabitants of heaven: "Return the jar from here to that place."
That monk addressed all the gods one by one:
"Quickly speak, may it be well with you; which of you has taken this jar?
Those gods looked all around, but they would not admit it.
"The Lord of Gods is taking heed: by whom has this pitcher been stolen?
The glorious Bodhisattva of great splendor beholds the wielder of the thunderbolt."
He has a son who is fierce, greatly wrathful, and very terrible;
manifested in the form of an obstacle-maker, he wanders everywhere throughout the world.
Therefore, that jar was brought; the Lord of Gods spoke:
"There is an obstacle in the Vajra family who sports playfully upon the earth."
"I have been honored by these," he said, and for that reason he killed the potter;
having spoken thus, the Lord of Gods returned once more to heaven.
Then all those gods were dismissed by means of their own respective mantras;
in a mere instant, indeed, they vanished even more swiftly than a moment.
Then, by his own power, he brought that obstacle along with its jar;
thereafter, that obstacle took up the jar of the pretas.
But when the obstacle was removed by that which was brought [there], she spoke these words:
"The jar was taken to the world of the hungry ghosts; we are not at fault in this matter."
Enraged, that great minister addressed the obstacle:
"Go, go, O great obstacle! Do not act in this manner ever again!"
Then, at that very moment, those hungry ghosts were brought by him;
their minds were agitated and overwhelmed, and they were wretched, for they had needle-like mouths.
They cried out with piteous voices, for they were most exceedingly terrible; they uttered a mournful cry: "Save us, O Great-Souled One!"
We have brought this jar here for you; do with it as you wish. O mantra-practitioner of great compassion, let trembling arise within you.
With a mind moistened by compassion, he spoke these words:
"What suffering is there for you in this world? Speak it without delay."
With dejected minds, they said: "O Great-souled One, hunger oppresses us; we have been parched with thirst in this world of pretas for a long time."
The monk Mahākāruṇika gave that very jar to them.
Then, with contented minds, they went to their dwelling places;
by the mere thought of them, food and drink appeared in the jar.
In this world, during that wretched time when it has arrived, there will be a monk named Nandaka, adorned with sandalwood garlands; he shall live for three hundred years.
A great-souled one who is inclined toward awakening, he will swiftly attain that which is difficult to find.
There is no doubt that at that time, in the lowest of ages,
there will be a king named Gomimukhya who shall cause my teaching to disappear.
Starting from the eastern direction, that fool will then destroy even the gateway in Kaśmīra, as well as the monasteries and the excellent relics.
That evil-minded one will cause those endowed with perfected virtue to be slain;
taking refuge in the northern direction, death shall come to him.
"Overcome by a wrathful non-human being, that evil-minded one, along with his kingdom, cattle, and kinsmen, shall be crushed by a fragment of a mountain and go to the netherworld."
Then his destination shall be downward, from hell to a more terrible hell; he will undergo intense, dreadful suffering, more painful than pain itself.
The hell known as Avīci is renowned for those who commit evil deeds;
that wicked Gomiṣaṇḍa shall remain there for a great eon (mahākalpa),
having committed most terrible sins by following an unvirtuous friend.
Therefore, with every effort, you should clarify your entire mind toward this teaching of the Tathāgata; thus you shall enjoy all prosperity.
All of you shall always travel upon the path leading to certainty in Buddhahood, following the eightfold way, to the city that is free from sorrow and devoid of decay.
Immediately after him, there was a protector of the earth known as Buddhapakṣa;
he was a great yakṣa, possessed of great generosity, and devoted to the teaching of the Buddhas.
There will be no doubt that in that time, during the lowest of ages,
the king will be exceedingly joyful and devoted to the Teacher’s instruction,
[constructing] monasteries, groves, shrines, and unsurpassed images of the Teacher.
Having caused various ponds and wells to be constructed, O Great King, one whose life has reached its end shall go to heaven.
On this earth, the Bodhisattva Mahātman, whose banner is the lotus, has attained success and possesses great heroism; he seeks the protection of the world.
By the power of that mantra, he shall live for three hundred years;
through the remainder of that karma, he shall swiftly attain awakening.
And his son was the king Gambhīrayakṣa, renowned throughout the entire earth, possessing a great army and great strength.
Then, at that time, that king will be disciplined in soul;
that highly resplendent monarch will, without a doubt, cause many monasteries, dwellings, shrines, ponds, and wells to be constructed.
By him also was accomplished the mantra of the wise Mañjughoṣa,
known as the six-syllabled speech, which is of great significance and increases prosperity.
By the power of that mantra, he shall indeed become one of great wealth;
gradually, being wise, he will swiftly be intent upon enlightenment,
performing various kinds of deeds within this teaching of the Tathāgata.
At that time, he will appear dwelling in the northern direction,
in the renowned region of Nepal, situated within the lap of the Snowy Mountains.
But King Mānavendra, born of the Licchavi lineage,
having also accomplished the purpose of the mantra, will become a possessor of great enjoyments.
O lord of men, the vidyā named Bhogavatī was mastered by him;
having ruled for eighty years, his kingdom was free from thieves.
Then, when the king’s life was at its end, he departed for the heavenly world;
there, the mantras—Śītalā, Śāntika, and Pauṣṭika—were swiftly accomplished.
And Tārā, world-renowned, and the goddess Pāṇḍaravāsinī,
and Mahāśvetā, who is ever intent on the welfare of others with an untiring mind.
In this manner and others, many kings were then proclaimed;
they were described in manifold ways, in various forms, and with diverse characteristics.
Those Mleccha kings were also worshippers of the Teacher:
Vaviṣa, Suvṛṣa, Bhāvasu, Śubha, and Sustathā.
The Bhākrama, the Padakrama, and the Kamala are proclaimed;
then the Bhāgupta and the Vatsaka, which is the last.
At the end of the Mlecchas, there will be various uprisings in Jihnu; having overstepped their bounds, they will fall from the ocean and live outside, subsisting on the wealth of the wise.
Then, the Lord of Nepal will be shattered by the falling of weapons;
his knowledge will be lost, his kings will be ruined, and he will serve barbarians and thieves.
Many kings and various beloved brahmins will appear at that time, having reached China from all directions.
King Hiraṇyagarbha, however, possessed a great army and great strength;
he was extensive in his lineage and had many subjects and kinsmen.
Bowing down to the Mlecchas, victorious, and devoted to the teaching of the Teacher,
he too accomplished the mantra of the Greatly Resplendent Kumāra.
The eight-syllable king of vidyās,
renowned by the name Mahāvīra, is the great abode of all accomplishments.
Therefore, for the sake of sovereignty, even a king of dull intellect who is concentrated upon this [mantra] will attain the state of Buddhahood as a certain goal by merely remembering it.
Thus, while appointing him to minor tasks for the sake of the kingdom,
the lord of men desired such an unsurpassed boon.
He always commands the entire host of deities, beginning with Brahmā;
how much more so the humans in the world and other beings who are contemptible?
Having lived for a hundred and fifty years, that great king, a righteous soul, will go to heaven and,
in due course, attain supreme enlightenment.
In that region, these vidyās which were spoken by the Kumāra will be accomplished quickly; no other vidyās will ever succeed there.
The Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa, the greatly courageous and immensely radiant,
indeed dwells visibly in that place in the form of a child.
Then, a king named Turuṣka, residing in the northern region, will accomplish that supreme, divine field of accomplishment for human beings.
Possessing a great army and great heroism, he will be in that place,
as far as the gateway of Kaśmīra, including Baṣkala and Kāviśa.
Then that king shall enjoy the surface of the earth for seven hundred *yojanas*.
That lord of the earth will possess two lakhs and seventy-seven thousand [subjects];
of this there is no doubt at that time, in the lowest age.
Having mastered the mantra, he shall live for three hundred years;
the Keśinī vidyā has been accomplished by the wise lord of men.
For the sake of his own ultimate welfare, he should cause many monasteries to be built,
and likewise, he should construct eighty-six thousand excellent stūpas.
Furthermore, the Perfection of Wisdom, the supreme dharma of the Mahāyāna and the mother of the Buddhas, is established in that region in this world.
When that king’s body has perished, he will go to the heavenly realm;
in due course, that lord of the earth will attain supreme enlightenment.
In the interval of that king, there was one known by the name Mahāturuṣka;
he was wise, highly esteemed, renowned, and devoted to the worship of his gurus.
He, too, always practiced the mantra of the goddess Tārā, who possesses great supernatural power.
He too, possessing well-known mantras, for the sake of sovereignty upon the earth,
was a king named Maheśākṣa, a great yakṣa with a vast army.
He shall also become a king, esteemed by his circle of kinsmen;
at that time, there will be eight thousand monasteries.
By the power of that mantra, he shall live for two hundred years;
when his body is cast off, he is reborn among the Tuṣita gods as a son of the gods, an intoxicated Bodhisattva of great supernatural power.
Thus, that righteous one, having gradually fulfilled the factors of enlightenment,
shall attain incomparable awakening through gradual effort.
In that region, the most excellent and abundant [teachings] always remain;
they were previously proclaimed by the Victors, and now they exist on earth through practice,
frequented by those free from passion as well as by *nāgas* of great supernatural power.
At that time, the world-protectors and the yakṣas who guard the Teacher’s dispensation will become protectors of the true Dharma on earth.
Thus have been proclaimed many kinds of kings, world-renowned;
they have been told of, and they will also be told of, in that most dreadful time.
Beyond that, as far as the border of the country, and further from Ujjayinī as far as the shore of the ocean, likewise in the region of the Lāḍas.
A king named Śīla, devoted to the teaching of the Buddhas,
will arrive at the city of Valabhī and become a Dharma King.
That king, devoted to righteousness and disciplined in soul, will cause to be built monasteries and various excellent reliquaries for the welfare of living beings.
One should perform various kinds of worship with beautiful images of the Victors;
one should honor the supreme and foremost relics for the sake of the illustrious Lords of the World.
Such a person is not merely a master of mantras, but is the highest among those whose success arises from ritual action.
In that region, there was a well-known monk who lived on alms;
he was virtuous, endowed with wisdom, and devoted to the teaching of the Buddhas.
That great-souled one, moving at the proper time, entered the alms-round and beheld the excellent royal palace, vast and crowded with people.
Having entered there seeking alms, possessed by hunger,
thirsty, and with a weary mind, he did not obtain any food at that time.
Having seized him, those men quickly departed from that house;
thereafter, he remained with an anxious mind, protected by the king's soldiers.
They departed from that city and at that very moment returned to their own abode;
hungry, thirsty, and suffering, they fell into a state of despair.
Then, his meal having been cut off as midnight approached, that ascetic of feeble mind gave up his life;
at that time, he made this aspiration: "May I become the lord of the Lāḍas."
Then, having passed away, that great-souled monk will be reborn into the family of a king named Dhara, as a worshiper of the Teacher’s dispensation.
Having ruled a kingdom free from thorns for thirty years,
he— greedy and overcome by the indigestion of his final illness— was brought to his end through the machinations of his own kinsmen.
Then, his body having perished, the king passed away and went to heaven,
to the excellent Tuṣita realm where Maitreya dwells.
That great-souled one, a listener of the Dharma, will be reborn there;
he will listen with reverence to the Dharma of Maitreya, who possesses great splendor.
He will gradually attain enlightenment, which is difficult to find;
when King Śīla has passed away, Capala will come to rule there.
Having ruled for half a year, one fortnight, and likewise five months,
he was killed by the king's officers who subsist on weapons.
Indeed, due to a fault committed by a woman, he was pierced by a weapon and went to the lower regions;
his younger brother, named Dhruva, likewise attained the state of being fixed and immovable.
The ruler of the Lāḍas shall be a servant, a miser, and a fool;
all other lords of men, however, shall have their heads as servants.
And when Śīlāhva has passed away, their ancestral lineages will all become kings in Ambhoja, residing on its shores.
Nṛpa, Indra, Sucandra, Dhanu, Ketu, and likewise he named Puṣpa— these are said to have been born in the city of Vāravatī.
Having first arrived at Balabhī, there are thousands named Prabha and likewise thousands named Viṣṇu, following this sequence.
It is said that there will be infinite kings born from the lineage of the Yādavas;
among them, the last king shall be named Viṣṇu.
But when the wise king, overcome by the sage’s curse, had set out with his citizens, people, and kinsmen, the city was submerged in water as he departed.
Then, in Dvāravatī, situated upon the great ocean,
it was everywhere in the northern direction, amidst various undertakings and mountain slopes.
It is said that there will be infinite kings belonging to various lineages; now, learn of the thirty lords of men who will belong to the Śaka dynasty.
Eighteen kings are renowned, with Sārdhabhūtika as their middle one;
at the end, however, they were all destroyed by the Nāga army.
Then Viṣṇu, Hara, Kuntanāmā, Ajita, Para, Īśāna, Sarvapaṅkti, Graha, Suvra, and another.
Then those kings, having lost their sovereignty and being forever fallen from the bounds of propriety,
became wealthy with great enjoyments there, originating from Viṣṇu.
Then those two foremost of mantra-practitioners, beginning with the letter *bha*, were from the middle [lineage];
both were wealthy, illustrious, renowned in this teaching, and devoted to its welfare.
Having thus recited the mantra, O Kumāra, you are the King of Mantras.
Thereafter, O King, three hundred and eight sons were born to those two lords of men, and they then resided in Śrīkaṇṭha.
The Vaiśyas shall indeed be named Ādityas, and their place will be the abode of the Lord;
of this there is no doubt. At the end, the sovereign of all lands, a lord of men, will be proclaimed by the name beginning with the letter *Ha*.
In that region, these mantras spoken by the King of Dharma— these vidyās for pacification and nourishment— will indeed attain success at that time.
Various riches consisting of the objects of enjoyment,
as well as various yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power who assume diverse forms.
In that lowest age, there will indeed be those who attain perfection,
taking refuge in the southern direction and the earth together with its oceans.
King Śvetasucandra was indeed Sātavāhana;
likewise, Mahendra was Śaṅkara, and Vallabha was the lord of the earth.
Sukeśī and Keśī are renowned in the southern direction;
Maṅgala is said to be the beloved, while Govinda is the banner of Vṛndāvana.
Then there were Mṛtpāta, Pota, Mahendra, Candra, Gopendra, Indrasena, Pradyumna, and Mādhava.
Gaṇaśaṅkara, Vyāghra, Siṃha, and likewise Budha;
Śuddhabudha, Kumbha, and Nikumbha are also celebrated.
Mathita and Sumita,
Bala and Pulina, as well as Sukeśin and Keśin.
Countless many kings are renowned in the southern direction;
understand that they include those of the past, the future, and the present.
For in this world of manifold deaths, these beings are overwhelmed by various diseases;
some, having died through the falling of weapons or by famine, have gone to heaven.
Thus all these kings have been described, as well as Vipuṣa;
the king at the end of Mahendra has been declared, as well as Asahati.
At that time,
in that place, for those who desire the accomplishment of mantras, it will have come to pass.
These mantras, beginning with the wrathful ones and appropriate for the vajra, are to be accomplished;
they are likewise beneficial for rites of sorcery as well as for the purpose of subjugation.
Then Mañjuśrī, the great-souled youth appearing in the form of a child,
shall indeed attain accomplishment in that land when the Kali age has arrived.
Residing on Mount Vindhya by the salt waters of the ocean,
he is celebrated as Kārttikeya, the bestower of boons upon all beings.
"O, by the command of the wise Bodhisattva Mañjughoṣa,
for the sake of desiring the welfare of sentient beings, you shall dwell in the southern direction."
Whatever mantras of Kārttikeya have been spoken by Mañjubhāṣin, in that region at that time, success will be achieved; of this there is no doubt.
At that time, it was proclaimed throughout the region of Śrīparvata, on the slopes and ridges of the Vindhya mountains, on all the islands, and in the coastal regions of Kaliṅga.
In the lands of the Mlecchas, characterized by the three gunas, there are kings known as infinite in number, extending everywhere to the shores of the belly of the ocean.
Indeed, many kings known as Kāmarūpa and Kalā, who reside within the womb of the Himālaya mountains, are said to always dwell among the Udra peoples.
The leaders of various mleccha tribes were devoted to the worship of the Teacher;
O King, Indra, Sucandra, and Mahendra were rulers dwelling among the mlecchas.
Both kings there, devoted to the teaching of the sixteen [Arhats],
shall be worshippers of the images of the Teacher through your grace.

There is no doubt that many excellent kings, who have resided in the eastern direction— whether of the past, the future, or always those of the present— will become devoted to the teaching of the Jina. Thus it has been proclaimed.
I shall describe the first of the best of kings, born on earth from the lineage of the Gauḍas; he was born in the beautiful city of Vardhamāna to a renowned father.
That king named Lokākhyo, the increaser of Gauḍa,
shall become a contemplator of the Dharma when I have not yet appeared in this world.

Many kings have passed away, engaged in various livelihoods; in the intermediate period, there were those who found solace, being middling and possessing middling qualities. Listen now to the truth concerning the lords of men in this endless age.
The king named Samudra and Vikrama are also celebrated;
the preeminent and foremost Mahendra, the best of kings, is considered to follow those beginning with the letter Sa.
In this lowest of ages, there will be a king named Devarāja,
the best of rulers, wise and devoted to dharma.
His younger brother was likewise a commander-in-chief, devoted to the king’s commands and to his welfare;
he ruled the eastern region as far as the ocean, which was beautiful, adorned with shrines.
At that time, he will undoubtedly cause the entire earth to be adorned with monasteries,
groves, ponds, gardens, and pavilions at all times.
Then that illustrious builder of the bridge will construct the steps;
he shall worship the images of the Teacher and worship those who are devoted to him.
Having ruled a kingdom free from rivals and thorns, the protector of the earth shall live for thirty-six years; at the age of thirty, the king should renounce the world.
Then, brooding and utterly overwhelmed, tormented by grief for his son, and having adopted the conduct of an ascetic, the king sought to take his own life.
Then, with his body shattered, he is reborn from the hells;
having dwelt for three and one days in that hellish state, he departs.
Having cast off his body, the king shall always go to heaven;
the world of the virtuous gods is known as Śuddhāvāsa.
There, with a pure soul and inclined toward awakening, he shall become a king of the gods.
Having experienced happiness in heaven by the hundreds and thousands,
and having returned once more to the human state, one becomes a Buddha again in a subsequent existence;
for it is by that very same karma that embodied beings are led through various births.
At that time, in the city of Ujjayinī, which was famous among the people as Kālavatī,
there lived a merchant who was exceedingly wealthy and preeminent in his profession.
In a time when Buddhas do not appear, in a world that is empty and without refuge,
Pratyekabuddhas of great supernatural power dwell in this world.

Desiring the welfare of sentient beings, they wander upon the surface of the earth; having reached the city of Ujjayinī, those great-souled ones, moving in groups, entered it for alms and descended onto the street.
Then Vāṇyājeya, seeing the sage standing before him,
invited him and led him to his own home with food;
having quickly brought the excellent sage there, he invited him to take a seat.
"Be united; the time for your meal has arrived.
Yet those great-souled ones remained silent and did not utter a word at that time.
And he offered his alms-bowl to a merchant who was always [generous] toward him;
for merchants are then wise and capable of discerning intentions.
He filled the bowl with various kinds of food and then,
with his own hands, carefully offered it to them.
Having taken it up, they all then departed through the sky in every direction;
appearing like a row of lamps, they remained supported by the form of the firmament.
Then, with his hair standing on end and filled with great spiritual urgency,
he fell upon the ground there, his mind divested of pride in his supernatural powers.
And then he made a vow, as clear as a verbal utterance:
"By this root of merit which I have obtained today..."
O best of sages, this foremost one shall indeed become an unsurpassed Buddha;
for ten thousand births thereafter, he will be a universal monarch (cakravartin) upon the earth.
Then, having cast off that body and having experienced happiness for a long time among sixty million celestial beings, he relinquished his birth as a denizen of heaven.
Then, being under the power of others, one would obtain birth among human beings here;
however, in this world, one's birth will always be within a royal family.
That king named Bālākhya shall be the ruler of the eastern region;
for thousands of births he will enjoy long-lasting, unobstructed happiness,
and finally, that illustrious monarch will attain omniscience.
Having thus reflected upon these various and abundant prosperities,
who indeed would then perform worship, entreaties, and meritorious deeds for the Teacher that are conducive to and lead toward the path of awakening?
After him, there will be a king of the Gauḍas known by the name Kumāra; he too will be exceedingly devoted to the Dharma.
After him, there was the illustrious one known as Ukāra;
after that, their mutual separation is intended.
For these Gaudas are indeed great separatists and fierce-minded;
therefore, the king known as Deva is remembered as the ruler of Magadha.
He too will be surrounded by those who have struck down and destroyed their enemies;
then another king named Candra shall exercise sovereignty under him.
He too, pierced by weapons due to karma impelled in a previous life,
shall have a son who lives for twelve successive months in that same manner.
At that time, even as a child, he was struck down by a different weapon while those fierce beings,
whose minds were intent on mutual harm, delighted in doing injury.
At that time, there will be an eminent king named with the letter 'Bha',
a leader of the Gauḍa people, who will be afflicted by a great disease.
Afflicted by that very same disease, he passed away and went to the lower realms;
after him, another named Dakāra remained for about ten days.
In this land of Gauḍa, there will be one residing on the bank of the Gaṅgā;
after him, one called by the letter Bha shall cause [the rite] to be performed for three days.
Then the cowherd shall become king; at that time he will be a giver of all things, a speaker of kind words, compassionate, and indeed possessed of great strength.
Subjugated by women, wretched, and foolish, you two may become conquerors of enemies;
yet, by approaching a virtuous friend, you will then become great renouncers.
At that time, he established monasteries, excellent and delightful shrines, various pleasure groves,
ponds abundant with water, and most beautiful almshouses.
Many strive for his fame and renown as he serves,
constructing delightful temples for the gods and dwellings for those endowed with virtue.
It was overrun by heretics and inhabited by various sectarians;
it extended across all directions, reaching as far as the shores of the ocean.
That king Kṛpībhogī, who is fond of dharma, will be prosperous in the eastern direction; of this there is no doubt. He will be negligent as well.
When he was afflicted by acute dysentery in his old age,
having retired to the banks of the Gaṅgā and ruled the kingdom for twenty-seven years, he died at eighty years of age.
Then, when his body had perished, he was reborn among the animals;
from there, he became a glorious Naga king, a lover of the Dharma,
by whom this beautiful shrine containing an image of the Teacher was caused to be made for him.
At that time, he also had monasteries built here on earth for the sake of the Saṅgha;
by the ripening of that karma, when he reached his final existence—
One shall attain the state of Buddhahood, the certain path, the immovable station;
thereafter, beyond that, on earth, there will be a city of the Gauḍas overrun by heretics.
In this eastern region, in the city known as Tīrthika,
there was a king renowned as Bhagavat, the sovereign of the Gauḍas.
Having been consecrated by a powerful southern king and having ruled there, he then proceeded toward the western direction.
Having entered the beautiful city of Sāketa according to his desire, he returns once again, having become free from his enemy.
Surrounded by thieves across the eastern region as far as the ocean,
he died, shattered by the blows of weapons, and passed into the state of a preta.
Having ruled a small kingdom for three years,
that king was seized by bandits; he died and became a preta of great supernatural power (*mahardhika*),
and for three years he exercised sovereignty over the pretas in that very place.
Having abandoned the body even from that state, he goes to the most dreadful world of the hungry ghosts;
once liberated from there, he shall always go to the celestial realm.
The king known by the name Samudra shall be his successor;
that dull-witted and evil-minded one will obtain the kingdom for three days.
His younger brother was also famous by the name Bhasman;
he was a lord devoted to taking life, a perpetrator of great sins,
merciless, and yet diligent in exerting effort over his own body.
This was not done for the sake of the next world, but rather here and now;
having encountered an unwholesome friend, he committed much evil karma.
That kingdom was overrun by twice-born men and by wretched logicians;
likewise, humans and ancestors [were deprived] of enjoyments of various kinds.
That king likewise obtained manifold prosperity;
having traveled by stages, that lord of the earth reached the western direction and then took his stand in the northern direction as far as the gateway of Kaśmīra.
There too, having conquered in battle and ruled the kingdom for twelve years and fifteen months everywhere, he then—
On the earth, he was afflicted by disease and fainted again and again;
overcome by great suffering, his body shattered, he went downward.
Driven by greed for the sake of sovereignty, they harbored mutual hatred toward one another; having brought forth a great downpour of weapons, they [attacked] each other.
Then, having consecrated the boy named Sakara as king,
and having made him a mere figurehead, he returns once more;
by him even those who were divided among the foremost of the twice-born are brought together.
Having reached the Magadhan country at the city named Udumbara,
he himself consecrated two boys and a preeminent brahmin upon the earth.
Then, traveling by stages, he reached the eastern direction;
having arrived at the Gauḍa country, he was indeed without rival there at that time.
Those two chief ministers, Bāla and Mukhya, were caused to be slain by that evil-minded king of Kaliṅga;
having resorted to an unwholesome friend, he committed a great slaughter of living beings.
But those who had previously been honored by kings proud of their martial prowess,
he caused all of them among the inhabitants of Gauḍa to be slain.
Then King Somākhyo will become a peerless hero,
[ruling] as far as the banks of the Gaṅgā and beyond Vārāṇasī.
The one of dull intellect will destroy the beautiful image of the Teacher and the abundant bridge of Dharma previously proclaimed by the Victors.
The one of dull intellect, delighting in the words of a sectarian teacher, causes [the body] to be burned;
thereafter, being angry, greedy, falsely proud, and indeed disrespected, he [suffers].
At that time, he will destroy all monasteries, groves, shrines, and the dwellings of the Nirgranthas on the earth, acting as an obstructer of their livelihood.
And at that time, there will be an excellent king in the Middle Country,
whose name begins with the letter 'Ra', who possesses a self endowed with splendor, and who is steady in the conduct of a Vaiśya.
In this teaching, there will likewise be a capable king equal to the one named Soma;
he too shall come to an end at the hands of the king of the Nagna caste.
His younger brother will be a solitary hero named Hakāra;
he will be a brave man endowed with a great army and possessed of transcendent valor.
I determine that the king known by the letter *ha* will be the one renowned as Soma;
thereafter, there will be a king of Vaiśya conduct, possessing a great army and great strength.
Then, resorting to the duty of the Kṣatriyas, they went to the eastern region to that excellent city named Puṇḍra, being devoid of pride, anger, and ill conduct.

One who is compassionate, devoted to dharma and artha, and learned might commit the slaughter of many beings; intent upon causing pain to living creatures, he would be solely devoted to their suppression.
He defeated the one named Soma, who followed evil deeds;
thereafter, being forbidden, the one named Soma remained within his own country.
The king known as Hakāra, honored in the kingdom of the Mlecchas, turned back [the enemy]; having performed pleasing deeds, King Hakāra brought prosperity to those devoted to wealth and dharma.
Whether he departed by his own power or with a gait as he desired,
those [beings], filled with joy for the kingdom, performed the deed.
Having now obtained enjoyments based upon the status of kingship,
he previously gave food and clothing to a Pratyekabuddha.
Then the sandals were given, adorned with a parasol and chowries;
by the power of his merit, these two became the deities of his great kingdom.
Having always enjoyed the abundance of pleasures among gods and humans,
he shall indeed become a twice-born named Soma, a possessor of great enjoyments.
Having bestowed enjoyments upon the twice-born and having ruled the kingdom at that time,
he likewise [reigned] for seven [years] together with [them].
Afflicted by diseases of the mouth, he will remain so for seventeen years, one month, and seven or eight days.
Being devoured by worms, he met his death and went to a downward rebirth;
at that time, that city was overrun and destroyed by non-human beings.
Afflicted by a fever and overwhelmed by disease through a purely human fault,
that king then died and passed away by means of the application of a mantra.
There is a hell renowned as Avīci for evildoers;
there that person who has practiced the extremes of unwholesome karma will be reborn.
Then that person of evil mind is cooked in hell for a great eon (mahākalpa),
and thereafter in the Ṭaṭa, Hahava, Sañjīva, and Kālasūtra hells.
Having experienced the terrible Forest of Sword-leaves again and again,
one likewise dwells in the realms of animals and hungry ghosts.
Thus, as one wanders again and again through thousands of births in saṃsāra,
one finds no happiness and shall always be a partaker of suffering.
Therefore, with every effort, having made your entire mind serene toward this teaching of the Tathāgata, proceed toward the perfection of agelessness.
Toward the Buddha, both service and harm result in infinite karmic consequences;
therefore, one should cultivate serene confidence toward the Buddha, as well as toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
In this world, those kings who worship [the Buddha] for a long time become supreme;
they possess great sovereignty over a vast kingdom, enjoy great pleasures, and become lords of wealth.
O King, by worshipping the foremost of the world, one shall obtain various forms of happiness and vast prosperity; indeed, one shall attain lordship over the world.
They repeatedly attain the state of Śakra, the state of Yama, and the state of Brahmā;

they attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, Buddhahood, and the state of a Śrāvaka on this earth. Among those who have reached the excellence of the three vehicles, two have gone to a state free from longing.
For thus are the Buddhas inconceivable, and the knowledge of the Buddhas is inconceivable;
for their fruit is inconceivable, and their maturation is inconceivable.
After this, even when the king named Soma has set on the earth,
the Gauḍa kingdom will be characterized by mutual strife;
its people will always have their weapons raised and will show no regard for one another.
For seven days in this manner, and likewise for another month,
that *gaṇajya* shall always exist on earth according to the tantra.
On this bank of the Gaṅgā, in a dwelling occupied by a monastery,
there lived thereafter the son of that man named Soma.
Then, for a child of the Vaiśya caste, the period of impurity lasts for eight months and five days, including the day of birth and the night.
A king of Gauḍa named Nāgarāja will arise;
at the end of that king's reign, Jayāditya and others will appear in his lineage.
Surrounded on all sides by Vaiśyas,
those Nāgas named Āhveya were then afflicted by the calamities of famine and oppressed by foreign armies.
Their kingdom, not yet attained, was thrown into turmoil by great bandits;
they, having fallen from the bounds of propriety, [ruled].
For one period of five years, he indeed lived there in great distress;
at that time, they brought about his death by committing the slaughter of many living beings.
Due to the transgression of their past karma, those people, following the livelihood of Vaiśyas,
will at that time become prone to mutual agitation.
Then, relying on the conduct of a Kshatriya, he will become a powerful lord of men in the Gauḍa kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, some kings, pierced by weapons and overwhelmed by diseases,
passed away and thereafter went from there to the hells.
There, the king was again dominated by women and possessed a child;
thus, after one fortnight, he was pierced by weapons and slain.
There will be a great onset of famine and the land will be agitated by foreign armies;
the eastern provinces will be scattered, terrified, and dispirited,
and there will be no doubt that the rulers of men in that region [will likewise suffer].
In Madhurā, there will be a merchant of noble lineage; Sūrvī will be an excellent king, his form honored, and he shall become the ruler of the Māgadhas.
His younger brother, named Bhaka, took refuge in the eastern direction.
His son, named Paka, was born in the eastern regions;
he is declared to be a preeminent Kṣatriya who follows the bonds of childhood.
Having been held in captivity for seventeen years by the king named Gopa, that Blessed One was bound and then released in the city called Bhagavat.
Later, a great king named Akāra arrived from the western region and established himself on the banks of the Gaṅgā as far as the eastern horizon.
A great king of the Śūdra caste, possessing a vast army and great strength,
took his stand upon that shore and remained there on all sides.
Having seized the city known among the Gauḍas as Tīrtha,
that renowned and mighty king remains stationed there.
There, a young kṣatriya and likewise a merchant entered at night; and there, at the end of the night, the Tathāgata was honored.
The king, known as Śūdravarṇa, having returned once more to the city named Nanda, [ruled] as far as the banks of the Gaṅgā.
Having reached the city of Vārāṇasī, he then established that child Kāśin on the throne as the king of the Magadhas.
Then the mighty king, a member of the Śūdra caste,
afflicted by suffering and filled with great passion, entered and consecrated him at that time.
Having then consecrated the young boy named Graha to the kingdom,
he was overcome by a great disease and rolled upon the ground.
Then, sighing deeply and with great effort, even though his body was broken, he crossed over;
he dwelt among the animals for fifteen months at that time.
Then, having been liberated from birth, he is reborn among the gods;
indeed, for twenty births at that time, he enjoys various divine prosperities.
Then, in due course, that righteous one shall attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
for he had acquired that very karma in former births.
The great-souled Pratyekabuddha was indeed completely covered with garments; they offered him sandals for the sake of [providing] elephants, horses, and chariots,
and then, with diligent minds, they gave him food.
By the ripening of that karma, he shall become Śatakratu, the king of the gods,
in this world of the deities for thirty koṭis of births; then, having come down to earth, he shall become a king in this present life.
He will enjoy a kingdom acquired by others,
and his son, too, shall be a king established in Vārāṇasī.
His kingdom will be utterly destroyed, shattered, and plundered on all sides;
at that time, that kingdom will be largely overrun by enemies and occupied by brahmins.
That king, being negligent and acting according to his own desires, was marked by the planets;
indeed, in his final time, he died later struck down by an enemy.
When King Soma had passed away, the Māgadha king [ruled] over them all, who were mutually opposed,
throughout the eastern region on every side.
Then, extending as far as the banks of the Gaṅgā and beyond Vārāṇasī,
there will be a Kṣatriya king known by the letter *pa*;
he will be one who was honored by that person of the Śūdra caste known by the letter *a*.
In a city called Nanda, situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
there will be a Kṣatriya king impelled by his past deeds;
he himself performed that karma, and he also rejoiced in it being done.
Long ago, when the Teacher named Kanaka had appeared,
there was a very wealthy merchant in the great city of Vārāṇasī.
That merchant’s young son, surrounded by foolish children,
went out onto the street for the purpose of playing in the dust.
Having seen the excellent stūpa in his own home, worshipped by his father and mother,
he dwelt upon that very stūpa in his mind and constructed one out of dust.
Then, with flowers from the remains of previous offerings, he performed worship;
with faith, recollection, and understanding, he praised that stūpa for its Buddhahood.
There the boy played, surrounded by children;
at that time, he was the sole foremost disciple of the Jina Kanakaśāstu.
Free from fault, with a disciplined mind and a wisdom liberated from the three realms, he,
being thus free from fault, then wandered for alms.
And then he entered the most beautiful city of Vārāṇasī,
free from passion, at that command, to where those fools were upon the earth.
Where all those children of yours were gathered on every side, [he said:
"Come, monk; come here! Pay homage to the reliquary of the Teacher.
Do you not see the beauty of that which was constructed by us with great effort?"
Then the young son of the merchant, taking a roll of grass,
playfully bound the one who was free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power.
There, that one free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power (maharddhika) took heed;
standing there upon the earth, he beheld the stupa (caitya) constructed by them.
Then, placing his hand upon the head of the fool, the noble-minded one spoke thus:
"Release the boy; let us go where you had the monument made.
Then they all returned to the place on earth where the receptacle for the relics was located.
Having paid homage, that great-souled hero, free from passion, set out once again for alms as he desired, together with his children and attendants.
Then the young son of the merchant, taking hold of the edge of the robe,
led him to his own home and had food prepared for him.
Then that chief merchant, seeing that fool,
took hold of the hem of the robe of the one who was free from passion and possessed of great supernatural power.
Terrified and with his hair standing on end, my elder brother came to my house; as soon as he fell at my feet, he quickly caused the boy to be released.
Having taken his son, he diligently sought forgiveness from the Victorious One,
the foremost conqueror, who is intent on the welfare of others, while holding out his alms-bowl.
He filled that vessel with rice, condiments, and various foods, and addressed his son: "Take this, my son, and give the mantra."
Then, having diligently washed his hands— whether he be a child or one possessed of wisdom—
and having taken a bowl full [of food], he should offer it to one free from passion.
Having quickly bowed him down, he prostrated at his feet on the ground; then,
having been taken hold of by the one free from passion,
