he ate, and indeed, being free from passion, he then experienced a state of pleasant touch.
Another there, indeed a fool whose mind was possessed by envy, on the following day,
with a heart full of anger,
took a great quantity of solid and soft food and gave it to him.
If there is any merit whatsoever in me, by giving this alms-food,
may I become the wealthiest person on earth through this son of a merchant.
Then all those heretics and the wives of the twice-born gathered together and, having engaged in a dispute, reviled Nindaka.
"You are a fool; you do not know where the destination of these shaven-headed ones lies. For they themselves do not abide [in truth], so how can there be liberation for others?"
Such hatred arose in that young being;
he caused them to destroy what had been described by the Teacher.

One should always cause to be built a bridge of Dharma, a monastery for fame, and excellent shrines on earth; and one should likewise cause a slaughterhouse to be built for the son of the chief merchant.
Having given alms to these beggars, what destination will there be?
For those whose minds are seized by evil destinies, I shall now bring about their destruction.
That very boy who was most wicked, even he who became the king named Soma—
having experienced suffering for a long time, that was the ultimate ripening of his karma.
This son of the preeminent merchant, his body having perished, went to heaven;
there he experienced for a long time the various pleasures of the celestial dwellers.
Having passed away from there, he will be born in this world of the gods;
then, from that birth onward, he will always achieve liberation from bondage.
A mortal who has undergone three births will again become a lord of the earth;
yet, by the power of karma, he shall fall again and again from time to time in various places.
He who, out of childish fickleness, has offered a faded flower-garland at a stūpa, shall become a king on this earth in this world of living beings and exercise sovereignty over the land.
Therefore, his enjoyments were indeed afflicted; that was the fruit of his afflicted giving.
Having obtained those enjoyments with great difficulty, that king was like one whose joints are exposed and naked.
Because of instability, because of being like a child, and because of a mind that is always wavering,
one should constantly perform great worship toward the Teacher’s excellent relic on earth.
By the ripening of that karma, one's royal sovereignty shall become unstable;
having been a king, one becomes [otherwise], and having not been a king, one returns [to that state].
He who has released himself from the bonds of intellect, who is liberated again as a child, shall exercise sovereignty on earth over the northern, western, and middle regions.
Bound by the ripening of that karma, the fool was liberated;
for five hundred births indeed, the fool was bound and liberated.
Then, in his final birth, he will forever sever all bonds;
at fifty-five or seventy-seven years of age,
he will become a king on earth extending as far as the eastern ocean.
All those border-dwelling barbarians and thieves settled within the belly of the Vindhya mountains shall be brought under control when there is a king on earth known by the letter 'Pa'.
At that time, this Kṣatriya king will enjoy all the territories situated within the lap of the Himālaya mountains and resting in the northern direction.
Having built a stūpa out of dust through ignorance and in his childhood state,
he shall become the king of Magadha, without rivals and free from thorns,
extending as far as the forest boundaries and reaching the eastern ocean.
To the west of Lauhitya is the wise one, and likewise the Himavat to the north;
to the west is the delightful city of Kāśī, or indeed the city called Śṛṅga.
In the meantime, the protector of the earth, the upholder of the Teacher’s dispensation,
having defeated those two kings named Pañcakesarin;
He ruled his own kingdom;
and all those sons of Siṃha were likewise then destroyed and uprooted.
O, in the eastern part of the Himālaya's lap, the Daśānūpa king shall take refuge on the shore;
at that time, this Kṣatriya king will enjoy the people and the provinces.
As his birth increases, his enjoyments shall also increase;
and when old age is reached, those enjoyments shall attain stability.
They shall live for eighty years, and likewise seven times seven more;
then, overcome by old age, having met his end, he went to heaven.
Having experienced long-lasting happiness in this world of the gods, the king likewise fell again by virtue of his previously defiled karma;
he dwelt for a month among the animals as a nāga king of great supernatural power.
Then, having passed away from that broken body, he is reborn among humans as a wise Kṣatriya, born into a merchant family and skilled in his livelihood.
Having approached a spiritual friend, that enjoyer within the teaching of the Jina shall accomplish the Queen of Vidyās, the goddess Tārā of great supernatural power.
That Jina is not one whose mantra has been mastered [in the ordinary sense], for he moves according to his own will;
at that time, the Sugata will become the king of the Vidyādharas.
Then he was known as a universal monarch by the name Citraketu;
likewise, that wise one was renowned for his deeds among the Vidyādharas.
For eighty-nine and seven [times] ten million years—
divine and human— the first universal monarch shall have a retinue of sixty million maidens born to him.
Then, his body having been dissolved, impelled by the goddess Tārā,
he shall go to the lord of the gods and there teach the Dharma.
O protector of the earth, he, being destined for enlightenment, will swiftly proceed by stages;
and at that time, during the degenerate age, when the king named Pakāra has passed away.
There, having resorted to a great conflict with one another,
his servants shall exercise royal sovereignty for seven days.
Then, after seven days have passed in due order, the king named Vakāra likewise,
being unslain and having destroyed [the enemy], shall set out from that direction toward the quarters.
When the king named Pakāra has passed away, the one beginning with Bhakāra is considered the next;
he too shall exercise royal sovereignty for three years.
His younger brother, named Vakāra, who has been consecrated by the ascetic,
shall rule for four years, O Rājyavardhana.
Both of them, suffering from indigestion and overcome by sudden diarrhea and fainting,
passed away and were reborn in the world among the yakṣas.
Thereafter, those virtuous ones gradually attained the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
His younger brother, a Kṣatriya named Dhaka who is devoted to righteousness,
will also become king for three years;
he shall be the lord of men.
Furthermore, his younger brother, a king renowned by the name beginning with the letter *Dha*,
shall become a sovereign ruler over the entire earth in this land.
With elephants, horses, chariots, and boats on all sides,
he shall be the conqueror of all enemies encountered in battle.
He adorns this entire region and the whole earth with images of the Teacher,
monasteries, and likewise with reliquaries of the Jinas,
beautifying indeed the entire earth in its totality.
Likewise, his predecessor was a king; he himself was a twice-born Śākya by birth, proud, sharp-witted, wise, inclined toward awakening, and possessed of a mind free from pride.
At that time, during that lowest of ages (yuga), even he attains a state of happiness;
the Kṣatriya is declared to be of foremost intellect, and the king indeed becomes a lover of dharma.
Through diligent effort, he shall live for one hundred and twenty-seven or eighty years.
Having passed away due to a fault committed because of a woman, that wise one went to heaven; in due course, he shall attain supreme enlightenment.
After him, there will be a world-renowned lord of the earth named Śrī;
he will be a great king in the Gauḍa kingdom and a lover of righteousness.
And in the excellent city of the Gauḍas, among the great people beginning with the letter 'ba',
he shall indeed exercise sovereignty there, having conquered all around.
There, that foremost of the twice-born, Śākaja, established seven and eight monasteries, which were properly endowed with all necessary provisions.
When he has obtained his assistance, the lord of men shall rule the kingdom on all sides and live there for eighty-one years.
Due to the fault of his servant, that righteous-souled one passed away and went to heaven;
in due course, he likewise ruled even over the kingdom of the gods.
Then, with his body dissolved, he shall go from heaven to the most excellent of heavens,
having fulfilled the wholesome dharmas that are the causes of his awakening.
His very servant shall indeed become the king and rule a kingdom free from thorns;
he will be a protector of the earth whose name begins with the letter *ya*.
At that time in the Yuga, he shall rule the kingdom for eight years;
yet he himself will be slain by women, and having been killed, he will go to the lower realms.
Furthermore, there will then be a Kṣatriya king from the Pakāra lineage;
by him, that entire circle of servants will be slaughtered without interruption.
Having encountered an unwholesome friend, he committed the slaughter of many living beings;
he will become one who is intoxicated by the power of his majesty throughout this entire world.
Acting with haste, fickle, a drunkard, and fond of deceivers;
utterly deluded by the intoxication of liquor, he then lies upon the ground in his bed.
He was pierced by blows from weapons and by his enemies who were fully prepared;
then, with his body thus mangled, he met his death and went to the lower realms.
One of his brothers, known by a name beginning with the letter 'Ra',
will likewise always rule as king upon the earth for forty-eight days.
Having bestowed wealth upon the twice-born, he shall pass away; of this there is no doubt.
Thereafter, O protector of the earth, he will then become one who enjoys delicious foods.
He was indeed of the Śūdra caste, deformed and truly contemptible;
he was preponderantly unrighteous, ill-behaved, and always delighted in strife.
He indeed causes all those of the twice-born classes, the feudal lords, the self-restrained, and likewise the renunciants to fall away, for he is always intent on their suppression.
He is the one who inflicts severe punishment upon thieves and murderers,
and he is the restrainer of all the wicked who have taken refuge in heretical vows.
Having ruled the kingdom, being both liberated and a donor,
that lord of the earth shall indeed live there for seventeen years.
Overcome by the suffering of leprosy, he then passed away and was reborn as an animal;
from among the animals, he became a Naga king with a great hood, wise and confident.
Then, having experienced for a long time the ultimate suffering resulting from his own karma, he became manifest in a physical form that was most loathsome and full of swelling pride.
Such kings, who cause the world to flourish, have been described;
they are known throughout this entire world as those who abide in their former bodies.
Then, from the lineage of the king named Pakāra, another Kṣatriya was born, heroic and valiant, who became the sovereign of the three oceans.
In this eastern land, there will arise one of great army and great power,
[adorned] with divine monasteries, residences, and temples containing the relics of the Teacher.
With various gardens, ponds, wells, pavilions, and bridges,
as well as perpetual almshouses, he constantly beautifies the earth.
Devoted to the most excellent voice of the Jina, he relied upon the supreme vehicle;
indeed, it was by means of the Śākya renunciant alone that he then reached his final goal.
He should avoid all forms of ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), yet he should manifest the power of the dakṣiṇā itself;
renowned by the name beginning with the letter 'Ka', he shall be possessed of mindfulness and learned.
Having ruled the kingdom for twenty-one years,
that protector of the earth then met his end through cholera and departed for heaven.
Thus, that wise one, swiftly destined for enlightenment, proceeds by stages;
meanwhile, his remaining lineage becomes dependent on others for its livelihood and dwelling place.
Thereafter, O kings, there will undoubtedly be cowherds living as servants; people will become wretched, even among the twice-born.
At that time, when the teaching of the Teacher has perished and the world is most unrighteous,
one should employ beings toward the goal of virtue through the practice of mantra.
Furthermore, those mantras for increasing enjoyment which were taught by the Prince should then be practiced at that time for the sake of royal sovereignty.
At that time, however, the supreme accomplishment is not to be achieved in that region,
nor in the delightful Dharmacakra, nor likewise in the Mahābodhi forest.
Wherein that Blessed One entered into peace and the state without substrate, there these two mantras are to be accomplished: the deity Tārā and the deity Bhṛkuṭī.
Likewise, on the shore of the ocean, at the Visphūrjī— the best of rivers—
and everywhere along the banks of the Gaṅgā, the practice originating from the lotus should be performed.
That Bodhisattva who is renowned by the name Candra is indeed called Tārā, the Queen of Vidyās of great supernatural power.
Assuming the form of women, the goddesses wandered everywhere throughout the world with hearts moistened by compassion, desiring the welfare of sentient beings.
And the one residing in the Sahā world-system is called Taimbya;
however, a Bodhisattva of great supernatural power (maharddhika) is the master immediately following the tenth stage (bhūmi).
Tārā the goddess is proclaimed as the one to be trained by all sentient beings; she brings about effortless accomplishment for his protection, defense, and concealment.
Through diligent effort, the Goddess— who increases enjoyment and sovereignty— is accomplished,
as well as the cause for the equipment of awakening.
Then the Goddess, filled with compassion for embodied beings,
became closely associated with them in the form of mantra, as the cause for the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment by sentient beings.
For the sake of the satisfaction and nourishment of all, he took his stand in the eastern direction,
having again divided himself into many forms, numbering five hundred.
He wanders over the entire earth for four periods of time;
thereafter, success is achieved either in the east or beyond Vārāṇasī.
The eastern region of that goddess’s field is proclaimed as the place where Jambhala, the king of yakṣas and possessor of great splendor, attains accomplishment.
At that time, in that lowest of ages, beings desiring enjoyments should accomplish the Yakṣarāja and Tārādevī for the sake of nourishment.
Furthermore, wrathful mantras should be accomplished in the southern region,
or among the Mlecchas, thieves, and islands, or even in the midst of the ocean.
And then Tārā is accomplished, as well as the King of Yakṣas of great power,
in Harikele, Karmaraṅga, Kāmarūpa, and the place called Kalaśa.
All the various hosts of female messengers and the yakṣiṇīs of great supernatural power—
those mantras for the sake of enjoyment which were sung by Mañjughoṣa—
attain accomplishment in that region as they do not in other places.
In the eastern direction and in the intermediate directions, various mantras with diverse purposes were taught at that time; these are to be accomplished by embodied beings.
Likewise, in the Middle Country, there were various ministers and kings;
understand that due to the weakness of beings, their intellects were limited. A summary of the principal kings is now being stated, along with their enumeration.
It is proclaimed as beginning with the letter *ma*, beginning with the letter *na*, and beginning with the letter *pa*;
it begins with the letter *da*, begins with the letter *i*, begins with the letter *sa*, and begins with the letter *a*.
That which is called *graha*, that which is called *kīrti*, and that which begins with the letter *ha* is proclaimed;
then there shall be that which begins with the letter *śa*.
That which begins with the letter *ja*, that which begins with *ba*, that which begins with *la* and is marked by the moon,
that which is renowned as beginning with *ha*, and likewise that which begins with *a*.
The letter *sa* and that which begins with *la* are known as female and are hated by the world;
that which begins with *sa* and is called *ma* is the sovereign power over the worlds.
Gradually, the Brāhmaṇas will bear the marks of worms, adopt the livelihoods of Vaiśyas,
be mostly engaged in unrighteous acts, become objects of hatred, and be lustful toward women.
In that time of the lowest age, there will undoubtedly be rulers of men, lords of the earth, in the Middle Country, who possess vast retinues.
In that lowest age (yuga), the lifespan of humans will be one hundred and twenty years;
at that time, this is proclaimed as a long life.
Among those who were otherwise preeminent, there was a disparity of high and low status;
indeed, it is said that at that time, in that age, all the kings were short-lived.
Likewise, on the banks of the river Gaṅgā, on the slopes of the Himālaya mountains,
and in the land of Kāmarūpa, there will be kings.
It is said to be at the beginning, the middle, and likewise at the end, as well as in the regions of the limbs;
that which is at the beginning is called Vṛtsudhāna, and he is celebrated as Karmarāja.
Formerly, Aṅgapati, his son Subhūti, and Bhūtireva,
as well as Sadaho and Bhavada, were all born in Kāmarūpa.
From Subhūmi down to Mṛgakumāra, these were the [former] names in Vaiśālī;
there, in that supreme city named Kapila, this Sage was born.
The Śākyas born of the inner harem are said to be kings descended from the Ikṣvākus;
they are renowned as ending with Śuddhodana, the Śākyas who cause the Śākya lineage to flourish.
Indeed, those mantras spoken by the foremost beings of the world have been described as having little power;
however, those mantras proclaimed by the Jinas, as well as all the hosts of servants, [possess great power].
Likewise, all the various hosts of female messengers belonging to both the Vajra and Lotus families are accomplished when practiced by those who are skilled in the meaning of mantra and tantra.
All those worldly mantras are accomplished here in this central region;
specifically, those spoken by the Jina which are to be practiced should be accomplished while staying in the Middle Country.
Through various types of signs and various types of causes,
and by employing various applications, there are various attainments for embodied beings.
Likewise, mantras belonging to the middle class are indeed to be accomplished for the increase of enjoyments,
as well as for protection, rescue, subjugation, and the summoning of embodied beings.
The kings of the Middle Country who have passed away and those yet to come have been described according to their various forms and marks, as well as their diverse lifespans and lineages.
All kings are said to be of three types—superior, inferior, and middling;
likewise, success is of three kinds, and one should apply them according to the three times.
Likewise, three kinds of mantras have been taught by the best of sages;
furthermore, infinite kings are said to reside in the Middle Country and in the West.
Likewise, in all directions— namely the north, west, east, and intermediate points—
as well as on all the outer continents, it is marked in four ways.
Infinite are the lords of the earth who have been proclaimed; infinite are the practices for accomplishing mantras;
infinite are those who take refuge in the various directions; and infinite are the accomplishments of mantra.
When the Sage’s teaching had disappeared and the Muni had passed away, Mañjughoṣa indeed spoke these mantras to kings at that time for the sake of restraint and favor.
The practice of the [proper] time is taught for the purpose of playful protection and miraculous transformations,
regarding the greatness of mantra and the destinies and births of sentient beings called "kings."
For those desiring to accomplish the mantra as proclaimed for specific places and times,
kings have been mentioned incidentally in the case where the path has disappeared from the teaching.
The qualities, majesty, and results of the mantras have been explained at the end;
O King, the two supreme vehicles previously taught have also been declared.
There is no doubt that all those kings who have been described as occupying the various directions will be firmly established during that lowest of ages.
Then, having firmly established themselves in the renunciant life within the teaching of the Śākyas,
they will act for the sake of the doctrine, being constantly devoted to the practice of mantra.
O Prince, when that best of sages, the supreme worldly eye, had passed away, I shall speak of them; listen then with a one-pointed mind.
And at the end of the age, when the Teacher’s teaching has vanished from the world,
there will undoubtedly be ascetics who live by means of kingship.
Namely, the renowned ones called Mātṛcīna and Kusumāra;
and those called Makāra and Kukāra, who were exceedingly devoted to the Dharma.
He is known as Nāgāhva, and by the name Ratnasambhava;
he is called Gakāra, Kumāra, and Vakāra, the contemplator of the Dharma.
This great-souled one, known by the letter A, upholds the teaching of the Teacher; he is esteemed for his virtues and is wise, proclaimed as the one known by the letter La.
He whose name begins with the letter *ra* and is proclaimed to begin with the letter *na* is the king on the side of the Buddha, the illuminator of the Teacher’s dispensation.
There was a renowned ascetic named Akāra, a twice-born who had likewise gone forth as a renunciant;
he resided in the city of Sāketa and was eighty years of age.
Likewise, there will be a wise monk named Kāvya, beginning with the letter 'A', who possesses passion; he will reside in the southern direction, live for sixty years, and dwell in a city.
The ascetic beginning with the letter *tha* is renowned in the southern direction;
he is a refuter of the arguments of opponents and likewise an ascetic accomplished in mantra.
Another excellent renunciant was a resident of the city of Saihnika;
though ignoble, he perceived himself as noble, and he lived on the island of Siṃhala.
At that terrifying time at the end of the age, he will indeed be a refuter of the proponents of other doctrines and a critic of the heretics.

The ascetic (yati) is said to begin with the letter *va*, and the one celebrated as beginning with *la* is likewise mentioned; the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) begins with *ra*, and the renunciant (*pravrajita*) begins with *vi*.
There will be no doubt that one devoted to the teaching of the Teacher will appear as a monk whose name begins with the letter 'Sa', during the reign of the king known as Bālāka.
He always constructed monasteries, groves, and shrines, as well as ponds and wells;
likewise, images of the Teacher, symbols, bridges, and causeways.
There will be no doubt; he is remembered as one who has ascended above, distinct from the Teacher.
Beyond that, those beginning with the letter *ma* and those beginning with the letter *ka* have been proclaimed.
Nakārādya, Sudatta, Supeṇa, Senakīrtita,
Dattaka, and Dinaka— these were the revilers of the doctrines of others.
One was formerly a merchant and the other formerly a physician; both were concerned with the welfare of the poor.
The first became a renowned ascetic beginning with the letter 'ca', while the other was known as one beginning with the letter 'ra'.
The one whose name begins with the letter *bha* will be renowned for his faith and will commission the making of images of the Teacher;
likewise, the one whose name begins with the letter *ma* will be born wise and will also be a faithful ascetic.
Various ascetics will be proclaimed, and they shall be infinite at that time;
all those ascetics will be renowned as illuminators of the Teacher’s dispensation.
And when this teaching has perished and is without light upon the earth at that time,
he will undoubtedly fashion beautiful images of the Teacher.
All have indeed been prophesied for enlightenment and have always attained the highest state;
they are likewise worthy of offerings in the world and bringers of an end to the three realms of existence.
Those who are devoted to the application of mantra and tantra are known and remembered as bringers of fame;
now, however, I shall speak of those twice-born ones who are characterized by their devotion to dharma.
In this most terrible time, she will resort to the conduct of royalty through the application of mantras and tantras throughout this entire world.
An excellent brahmin named Vakāra, wealthy and a master of the Vedas,
wandered over this entire earth for the sake of debate.
Delighting in the refutation of rival sects throughout the great expanse bounded by the three oceans,
he who recites the six-syllable mantra indeed becomes one who is face-to-face through his speech.
Out of a desire for the welfare of sentient beings, the Prince was carried by song; through this extensive collection of kalpas, he remained vigilant in his awakened wisdom.
Jaya and Sujaya, Kīrttimat, and beyond him Śubhamat;
then Kulīna, Dhārmika, Udyata, Sādhu, and Mādhava.
Madhu and Samadhu were then established;
they were of the Śūdra varṇa, while others were born of the Śaka lineage.
All those reciters here, by the word of the Youth,
were likewise practitioners, wise and learned in the scriptures.
And those ministers were brought face-to-face with him, being occupied with the affairs of the kingdom;
and another famous brahmin named Vikāra was likewise present.
Known as Puṣpa, he will become an adept in wrathful rites;
indeed, he will exercise suppression over kings due to poverty and humiliation.
Mañjughoṣa is proclaimed here as that King of Wrath, Yamāntaka,
who is indeed the tamer of those beings who are wicked and difficult to subdue.
For the purpose of preventing what is harmful, for the sake of what is beneficial, for its increase,
and solely for the benefit of sentient beings, even when it involves the obstruction of one's own body and life.
For that foolish young man, impoverished and incited by anger,
turned back that wrath of the king which would have brought about the end of his life.
After him, there was a renowned twice-born man whose name began with the letter 'Sa',
who was skilled in the meaning of mantras and possessed a disciplined mind.
Then the Lord, renowned as a great reciter of mantras,
accomplished that mantra for the purpose of subjugation and for no other reason.
When the elements have been brought under control, one then becomes possessed of wealth;
thereafter, he is indeed renowned as a twice-born man who contemplates both dharma and artha.
He who begins with the letter *śa* will become preeminent among the people of Mālava at the end; for when the teaching is propitious, he shall indeed be the foremost reciter of mantras on earth.
And those afflicted by vetālas and grahas, the brahmarākṣasas and rākṣasas,
all the pūtanās and bhūtas, as well as various kinds of flesh-eaters (kravyādas).
All poisons, both stationary and mobile, are under his control;
indeed, all are under the control of that one who bears the marks of a twice-born, provided he is established in his duties.
Thereafter, a renowned brahmin appeared in the southern region;
he was known as Vakāra, and he was devoted to the teaching of the Teacher.
With monasteries, groves, shrines, and delightful images of the Teacher,
he indeed adorns the entire earth bounded by the two oceans.
To his west was a renowned and very wealthy preeminent brahmin,
known as Bhakārādya, who resided in the southern direction.
The great-souled one, whose form is mantra, is certainly destined for enlightenment;
he is renowned in the Middle Country as a twice-born named Sampūrṇa.
Vinaya and Suvinaya are the two sons of Pūrṇa, who dwells in Madhura;
Bhakāradya is the lord of wealth and the priest of kings for the performance of mantras.
Thus have these twice-born ones been described, who honor the teaching of the Teacher;
they are distinguished by their middling, final, and initial qualities, and are born from various lineages and clans.
Those who worship the twice-born from various lands are themselves surrounded by the twice-born;
they belong to various sacred sites and lineages, and their spheres of conduct are manifold.
Ascetics from all quarters have been proclaimed, as well as men of great learning;
yet the Buddha himself is the King of Dharma, the accomplisher of the welfare of all sentient beings.
The four great kings have been proclaimed as the protectors of all beings and of the three gods; they are celebrated throughout all the worlds.
Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra the king of the yakṣas,
and Śakra— these are proclaimed as having a fixed lifespan among the gods.
Sujāma and the son of the gods Sunirmita are the lords of the Vaśavartin [heaven];
Santuṣita is declared to be the king, another lord of the desire realm.
From Śakra onwards, let there be those with a single name who are likewise lords of the desire realm;
they too shall always have a single support, perform a single recitation, and possess great supernatural power.
Those gods are said to be infinite and they assume various forms;
from this point upward, they are all equal and possess great supernatural powers.
Thus, O best of gods, these perceptions are proclaimed as being designated by their names;
no sovereign power could prevail over them, for they rely upon an equal mode of conduct.
Therefore, as far as the Avīci hell, no king is found there;
the eight hells and their sixteen secondary regions are also proclaimed to extend to that limit.
The kings of karma are the non-kings; Yama the King is the sovereign of the departed spirits.
Suvarṇa is the king of birds; he is Garuḍa, possessed of great supernatural power.
Among the kinnaras, Drumu is renowned; among the bhūtas, Rudra is said to be the leader.
Among the vidyādharas, the king is Vidyā-citraketu, who possesses great supernatural power.
Likewise, Vemacitrin was the best among the Asuras;
Vyāsa was said to be the best among the Ṛṣis; and Mahāratha was the best among the Siddhas.
Soma is designated as the lord of the constellations, and likewise Bhāskara of the planets;
similarly, Īśāna is proclaimed to be the king of the Mothers.
The day is said to be the counterpart of the zodiac signs, and the maiden (Kanyā) is said to be their [counterpart].
The ocean is said to be the counterpart of rivers, while the excellent lotus (supuṣkara) is that of clouds.
Airāvata is proclaimed as the king of elephants, Harivara likewise of horses,
and Prahlāda everywhere as the king of beasts.
Infinite are the destinies said to exist, and infinite are the kings;
yet among them all, everywhere, the Buddha is the supreme being in the world.
Among those [islands], there is no sovereign superior to the first Kurus;
likewise, among the surrounding islands to the east and west, there is none.
In the eastern [direction] of Jambūdvīpa, that lord of men [resides];
and endless activities are proclaimed for the four continents along with their lords of men.
These lords of beings on earth, who are born from the three classes of gods and asuras, have been described in brief, for they would be too extensive to describe in full detail.
Residing in infinite world-systems, with infinite expansions of virtues,
those inhabitants of this earth have indeed been described as infinite within this eon.
These have been taught for the sake of attaining mantra-siddhi despite the lapse of place and time;
thus, the various kings of mantras as well as the hosts of messengers achieve success.
This Dharma has been briefly explained by the preeminent sages;
indeed, it was now spoken by those residing above the Śuddhāvāsa heaven.
The great hero Mañjuśrī questioned the Leader of the World:
"Regarding this rite that has been described, how indeed should I maintain it?"

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*—the own ritual manual for all kings—should be performed in detail, as an extensive expansion. O Mañjuśrī Kumāra, best of sages, you have spoken at length on the mantras for the sake of the Bodhisattvas;
for the sake of the meaning of the path to enlightenment and the goal of awakening, it is known as the *Dharma-sūtra*.
The enumeration of the lifespan of beings on earth according to the rituals of the Kalpa-mantras,
as well as the proclamation of the duration of the lives of kings.

The Piṭaka named Dharmasaṅgrahaṇa, which is directed toward awakening and flows toward enlightenment, has been taught through the application of mantra and tantra; you, O wise one, should always uphold it as that which fulfills the purpose of mantra and tantra.
Thus it is said.
Thus concludes the fifty-first chapter, the Prophecy of the Kings, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a compendium of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, an extensive Mahāyāna sūtra.
Now begins the fifty-fourth chapter.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having again gazed upon the abode of the Śuddhāvāsa gods, addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta.
"Mañjuśrī, this Dharma discourse shall circulate in this place;
therein, he himself should be understood in this way."

Surrounded by the assembly of all bodhisattvas, honored by the community of śrāvakas, and attended by all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, garuḍas, gandharvas, kinnaras, mahoragas, siddhas, and vidyādharas—both human and non-human—I should be known as dwelling here.
One should know that the Tathāgata remains right here for the sake of protection, defense, and guardianship.
Mañjuśrī, O youth, ten benefits are to be known [from this].

In whatever place this treasury of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas—whether existing in the form of a book—is written down, read, maintained, honored, and attended to with one-pointed mind, or is worshipped, revered, and respected with various yak-tail whisks, full parasols, banners, flags, bells, musical instruments, garlands, ointments, incense, and fragrant perfumes;
in that place, what are the ten [blessings]?
There shall be no fear of foreign armies, nor shall there be famine.
There, no great calamity of pestilence shall afflict him, nor any fear of non-human beings; he shall have no fear of fire, nor any fear of adversaries;
and there he shall have no fear of drought, nor any fear of excessive rain.
And there he has no fear of great whirlwinds, nor fear of any flesh-eating demons (kravyāda);
he has no fear of Śakra, nor fear of any rogues or thieves;
and he has no fear of death, nor any fear brought about by King Yama.
Furthermore, he has no fear of asuras, nor fear of any devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or asuras;
he has no fear of mantras, nor fear of any poisons or venom;
and he has no fear of disease, such as fever, dysentery, or ailments of the major and minor limbs.

These ten benefits are to be known in this regard: wherever this great treasury of Dharma of the Tathāgatas, contained in this *Mahākalpaviśara*, may remain as a book, or where we perform its writing, reading, worship, preservation, and recitation.

This treasury of Dharma of the Tathāgatas is most secret by virtue of following the mantras; furthermore, it is for those who have entered the samaya of the masters from all sides. It must not be revealed to those who do not know the samaya.
For what reason?
This is a secret;
this is a hidden teaching.
This is the word of the Omniscient One:

lest beings should reject it, despise it, fail to honor it, fail to revere it, and thereby produce great demerit; lest they perform acts that cause harm to sentient beings through secret obstructions, provide counsel to kings, and bring about calamities that shorten the lifespan—therefore, this must not be disclosed to others.

This should be disclosed to those beings who have entered the practice of the secret mantras of the *samaya* secrets, who are well-trained and well-established in the training of the Tathāgata’s teaching, who are skilled in the meaning of the Dharma, who abide in the Dharma through their entry into the *samaya* of the sense-bases and elements, who are true to their word, who possess firm vows, and who are compassionate ones having entered the path of the conduct of beings; it is not for others.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva, rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the name of this Dharma-discourse, and how should I remember it?
The Blessed One said: "Remember it as 'The Bodhisattva-piṭaka of the Roaring of All Bodhisattvas.'"
You should also remember this as "The Chapter on the Teaching of the Marvelous and Wondrous Dharma";
you should also remember it as "The Instruction for Bodhisattvas Who Have Entered the Practice of the Treasury of All Mantras";
and you should also remember it as "The Marvelous and Extensive Exposition of the Mahāyāna."
"Remember it also as the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*;
remember it also as the *Sarvadharmārthapūraṇanirdeśa*."
You, who are a Bodhisattva of great supernatural power, have wandered everywhere throughout all the worlds in their entirety, investigating both dharma and adharma.
You do not perceive this supreme secret, this most excellent and sublime Dharma—
the faultless teaching on the destinies and the meanings of the mantras, tantras, and sūtras.
O Hero, you do not perceive the excellence that is dedicated to the awakening of Dharma,
such as this Secret Sūtra adorned with the sense that requires interpretation.
The meanings of the sūtras in their various forms and the practice of the mantra-tantras—
there exists nothing here that has not been found within the extensive ritual manuals (kalpavisara).
One shall obtain the great enjoyments and the riches of great kings as well as those of the celestial dwellers, and likewise abundant fame, both divine and human.
One should avoid the eight non-leisure states among the faculties and cultivate the [eight] leisures; for such a person, Buddhahood is certain, as is their threefold rebirth among living beings.
By upholding this sūtra, there shall be these merits and benefits:
neither poison nor fire can affect his entire body.
Neither vetālas nor grahas, nor pūtanās, nor the mātṛs, nor thieves and rākṣasas [can harm] him.
Furthermore, the piśācas shall not harm him who recites this sūtra,
or who retains it, or who honors it repeatedly in various ways.
Whether one worships with musical instruments or with offerings of worship,
the wise man who performs such worship obtains these human blessings proclaimed here.
The sick shall be freed from disease; the sorrowful shall become happy;
the poor shall obtain wealth; and the bound shall be released from their bonds.
Having fallen into this suffering of saṃsāra consisting of the five destinies,
may he attain the secure, auspicious, and immovable state of nirvāṇa.
By reciting this sutra, one attains the state of a Pratyekabuddha, the state of a Śrāvaka, and the ultimate state of Buddhahood itself.
O supreme Victors, by reading this sutra here, one obtains all that merit which is gained by worshipping the infinite [Buddhas] who are renowned as white as the Ganges.
As many inconceivable millions of fields as there are in this world,
may one always worship that many Buddhas, each as numerous as atoms.
They should always provide various kinds of food and drink, as well as medicines for the needs of the sick, and various types of seats and beds in every respect.
With various kinds of robes, as well as powders, garments, and ornaments;
with parasols, sandals, and cloths; and with fragrant garlands and ointments.
Or by offering various incenses and lamps on all sides,
a living being shall obtain that merit through the upholding and reciting of this [text].
In this world, there are Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas of great supernatural power,
and the supreme Bodhisattvas of great soul who abide on the ten stages.
By that measure, all those [merits] and likewise their worship would belong to that mortal who holds the book in his hand; he shall obtain that merit.
As many beings as are spoken of in the world, all those who are said to reside within the world-systems— may they all be freed from their fever.
And whatever being should again and again perform their worship with reverence,
that wise person would obtain that merit by worshipping this supreme Dharma.
Even if one were to constantly worship this supreme treasury of Dharma of the Lords of the World with jewels for ten million eons, it could not be equaled by those most excellent Victors.
And for the sake of jewels, this supreme Dharma shall be like a wish-fulfilling gem;
through recitation and retention, the mantras in this ritual manual spoken by Mañjughoṣa [shall grant their fruits].
He who, with an untiring mind, should accomplish this on earth, shall possess a cow of plenty that grants his desires and the perfection of great wealth and enjoyments.
The mantras spoken by the Sages, which possess the definitive meaning, the interpretable meaning, and their fruits,
shall accomplish the state of a Vidyadhara on earth through the conjunction of ritual action and time.
His fame was renowned in all directions; his success was filled with an abundance of jewels.
His course of action, resulting from his greatness, was described as fruitful and well-praised by the virtuous.
O King, whoever among us shall hold even a single mantra from this collection of kalpas,
his royal prosperity shall bear fruit and he shall possess the excellence of long life.
Or may he obtain various enjoyments and activities under the protection of the best of kings;
and may he not be harmed by weapons, nor by poisons, whether stationary or mobile.

Furthermore, in this world of mortals, which is defiled by those intent on malevolent rites against others, there are mantras for the accomplishment of *vetāḍas* produced through the power of the *paravidyās*.
For him there is no fear of fire, nor of enemies, spirits, or others;
neither the body of that king nor even that of any living being is harmed.
Furthermore, if one should uphold or recite this supreme and foremost of sutras,
then when a battle has arisen, that king shall be honored with his head bowed low.
Having placed an umbrella over his head, one should pay homage again and again;
neither bandits nor those with various weapons raised will strike him.
One should cause him— who has mounted the back of an elephant, who appears in the form of a youth,
and who is well-seated upon a peacock throne— to descend into battle.
Seeing him in the form of a child, adorned with the ornaments of a divine youth, all those hostile people and others turned back.
Having mounted upon flags and banners a golden or silver [image] that has been honored with colored powders, it should be well-placed and properly composed.
At that time, one should indeed cause him to descend into the entirety of a battle crowded with enemies, where various weapons are raised and encountered in combat.
Upon merely being seen, humans and non-humans alike, as well as kings and even the lords of the gods, are either destroyed or utterly bewildered on all sides.
There were also accomplished vidyādharas who relied upon mantras and tantras,
as well as powerful rākṣasas and the mātṛs known as kaṭapūtanas.
Various kinds of flesh-eaters, as well as yakṣas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and pūtanas,
are truly unable [to harm] one upon merely seeing the raised banner standing there.
To the youth Viśvakarman, who possesses manifold forms,
the noble Mañjughoṣa, the sovereign of the ten stages, the Lord.
The great king, a Kṣatriya, was a protector of the earth for those dwelling upon it;
he was faithful, free from lack of conviction and doubt, and beloved of the Dharma.
Having generated the pure state of a Sugata and with minds permeated by compassion,
they indeed proceeded with this rite described here, desiring to effect a reconciliation.
For these have been taught in the scriptures by the Victors who have realized the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
concerning the ritual application of mantras, the practice for an eon, and the principles of the tantras upon the earth.
In the past, by countless supreme Victors who were established within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
this treasury of Dharma was indeed spoken for the sake of human beings upon the earth.
Long ago, while a terrifying war between the gods and the asuras was taking place,
his city was then indeed left with its armies destroyed by his enemies.
Then, while beings were alone and deprived of their chariots upon the earth,
he questioned that best of sages, Kāśyapa, the supreme Victor.
"What should be done? the Lord of Śacī uttered these words:
"I have been defeated by the terrible asuras and have taken refuge here."
Thus addressed, Maghavān Śatakratu, bowing his head with his crest to the feet of that best of sages, then spoke to the dwellers of heaven.
For in former times, Kauśika was indeed the thousand-eyed Indra;
thus addressed, that best of sages, Kāśyapa, became a Brāhmaṇa.
Then the youth Viśvasambhava uttered a voice with the melody of a kalaviṅka bird, a song formerly sung by the supreme Jinas.
This great-souled Mañjuśrī is difficult to encounter, endowed with a hundred thousandfold vigor;
he is proclaimed as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) and is the teacher of the profound meaning.
He taught the Dharma and other truths to sentient beings as being free from conceptual proliferation, formless, devoid of intrinsic nature, and without abode; remember that, O Lord of the Gods!
Then, having been thus remembered by them, the youth Viśvarūpin, who has realized the true nature of reality, arrived there at that very moment.
Where the Blessed One was staying, as well as Maghavan, the lord of the gods, he approached and, having paid homage to the supreme Jina, then spoke these mantras.
Having prostrated before all the supreme Jinas and the greatly radiant Kāśyapa,
he then spoke these mantras after having received the permission of the Sage.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas whose teachings are unimpeded!
Oṃ hana hana all fears! Destroy! Annihilate! Terrify! Crush! Cut! Split! Blaze! Blaze! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!
As soon as this mantra was spoken by the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta...
This great earth, bounded by its mountains and oceans, shook in six ways;
and all the Blessed Buddhas, throughout infinite and boundless fields and the limits of every direction of the world-systems, empowered these mantra-words.

Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, his fear and horripilation vanished, struck with wonder and amazement, his eyes wide open, rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and having looked upon Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta face-to-face, took those mantra-words and fixed them in his mind; then, mounting his chariot once more, he fled toward where those asuras were, and all the asuras set out toward their own city in the great ocean-abode of Pātāla.

With his mind struck down and shattered, his pride vanished from his face which was dejected, overwhelmed, and agitated by fear of the army, and seeing that Lord of the Gods who was like a blazing fire, he cast aside his weapons and returned to his own abode.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, addressed the Trāyastriṃśa gods:
"Do not fear, sirs! Do not fear!
By the power of the Buddha, we have conquered the asuras; let us go to our own city."
"Come, sirs! Play, enjoy yourselves, and amuse yourselves, having gone each to his own excellent palace. With joyful minds, those gods returned once more to their own abodes.

Then it occurred to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "What if I were to fashion an image in the form of that boy and place it upon the tip of my banner? Then I would have no fear of the Māras. Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, taking hold of a great jewel-gem called *Mahatā-maṇiratna-dyotigarbha-prabhodyotana*, had an image made in the likeness of the boy. He then erected and firmly fixed that banner atop the palace roof, in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, in the center of the great city of Sudarśana, and established it there.

Then those asuras, headed by Prahlāda and Vemacitrin, did not ascend to the netherworld (pātāla), nor did they attack the gods, nor were they able to approach him as he displayed his supernatural powers (ṛddhi-vikurvāṇa) or to face him in battle.
This continued for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years by human calculation,
and there was no fear of the asuras.
Thus has this been proclaimed by the Blessed Buddhas and the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas in the past: it possesses immeasurable qualities and benefits, increasing longevity and health;
thus has this detailed expansion of immeasurable qualities and benefits been taught since of old as being infinite and boundless.

The generation of immeasurable merit leads to birth in the great hells, among animals, hungry ghosts, or in the world of Yama—a state of contempt for those who revile this Dharma-discourse, or who doubt it, or who reject it with a distracted mind, or who say, "This is not the word of the Buddha," or "These are neither mantras nor medicinal herbs"; or who, thinking that even the extensive majesty, supernatural powers, and transformations of the Bodhisattvas, as well as the extensive elaborations, have been spoken by the ignoble, abandon them, cast them aside, disregard them, or are unable to hear them; they depart from that place, and for them there will be great demerit—thus he said.
Those men who, with deluded minds, shall indeed reject this supreme Dharma proclaimed by the best of sages and by the wise sons of the Conquerors.
By that [karma], men go to hell, including its elevated regions and the animal realm:
namely, Kālasūtra, Sañjīva, Kṣuradhārā, and Gūthamṛttikā.
Then the corpse-pit, the river of caustic liquid, the torrent of fever,
and furthermore the terrible forest of sword-leaves, as well as the Avavaṃhahava hell.
People go to that hell known in the world as Aṭaṭa, for those who have committed evil deeds— those men who are corrupters of the Dharma.
That place is known as Avīci, terrible and renowned throughout the world;
it is the abode of evildoers, filled with loathsome iron walls.
Those people who would violate this Dharma are cooked therein;
they are cooked in all those hells, from Avīci on up, along with their festivities and their very foundations.
Having gone to the endless depths of the hell realms, such a person of doubt will always be a rejecter of this extensive sūtra, the very essence of all the Dharma.
They incur contempt in the world;
then, having fallen under the power of others, they go helplessly to the hells ending with Avīci.
For he who, relying upon the *Siddhicitragata*— which is adorned with mantras and tantras, known as the *Saṃsūtrakalpa*, and which is the unobscured limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)— [attains it].

The body has the dharma-realm as its object; it is a meditation without an objective support, extensive, supreme among chapters, accompanied by conceptualization, and vast in its conceptual elaboration.
Well-arranged by Mañjughoṣa, perfectly accomplished, and honored by Śrīmati,
this extensive Root Manual has indeed been taught in great detail.
It is free from the extremes of eternalism and nihilism, as well as from both [extremes] and their opposites;
it is taught through a gradual progression of transition, and is raised high in the form of mantra.
One who constantly rejects the wind, the blue sky, and well-cultivated emptiness will then go downward, to the lowest state.
Then, having fully accomplished awakening through various kinds of merits acquired over incalculable eons, I [attained it] under the most excellent Victor.
He has spoken the meaning of the mantra-tantras, which concerns the destination of rebirth and is free from fault;
it is indeed the Root Ritual Manual, pure, auspicious, and the destroyer of evil.
This extensive chapter has been proclaimed, beautiful with its blue thread-conclusion,
describing the greatness of the qualities of kings as applied according to time and place.
The true Dharma for the sons of the Victors on this earth, as well as for those born of the three [vehicles],
was taught by the Jina, the seventh Sage, to the leaders of the world.
The detailed exposition of the ritual procedures has been spoken, which increases glorious prosperity;
it is complete with its root, known as the *Visarapaṭala*, and is honored within the mantra-tantras.

Indeed, those mortals on earth who reject this supreme, foremost sutra— the treasury of Dharma empowered by the Victor— will dwell in the Avīci hell until the end of time for many great eons, as has been described.
When, at some time or other,
mortals may become poor, diseased, or foolish, they are born among the mlecchas;
they incur contempt in the world and suffer from leprosy.
Foul-smelling, loathsome, maimed, and indeed blind, he appears on earth with a terrifying form, always hideous and as harsh as a hungry ghost (preta).
He will be skillful yet dejected in mind, with deformed nails and likewise loathsome; he will be devoured by worms and overwhelmed by ringworm and itching.
He is born homeless, utterly loathsome, and unable to converse;
with his mind seized and his intellect corrupted, he wanders again and again.
Furthermore, he will be a rejecter of the Dharma-treasury of the Victors, which is worthy of worship as their relics;
he will be beset by many sufferings and fatigues, and though having many friends, he will be without a protector.

The mortal is born in many ways, overwhelmed by grief and suffering; wherever his destination leads, there he is born with a corrupted mind. By rejecting this sutra, one is reborn in those very places.
Thus it was said.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground. With palms joined in reverence, his eyes wide open and unblinking, and perceiving all those sons of the gods in the Śuddhāvāsa heaven and the many hosts of beings assembled to hear the Dharma, he addressed the Blessed One Śākyamuni in this way:
"It is marvelous, Blessed One! How exceedingly well-spoken is this Dharma-discourse!"

Therefore, Blessed One, in the future time there will be beings overcome by uneven greed, beings whose minds are intensified by the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*), lacking faith, deceitful, harsh, and of immoral conduct. They will have no faith in the course, majesty, and worship of mantras, nor in the rules regarding time and place, the practice of mantras, the fire-oblation (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and the detailed ritual manuals (*kalpa*). Thinking, "This is not the word of the Buddha," they will reject them;
with afflicted minds, they will pass away.

They will experience painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations; they will be reborn in the great hells. Blessed One, how should one act toward those suffering beings? For the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are possessed of great compassion. Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, stroking Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta on the head, addressed him: "Excellent, excellent indeed, Mañjuśrī! You who have set out for the sake and welfare of all sentient beings."
Excellent, Mañjuśrī, that you ask the Tathāgata about this matter.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, listen well; pay close and careful attention.

I shall speak for the sake, benefit, and happiness of all sentient beings, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of gods and humans who have entered into the practice of all mantras, who are intent upon the path to enlightenment, and who desire to rely upon the supreme embodiment of the dharmadhātu. At the time of death, this King of Vidyās, the supreme secret, should be remembered; O Youth, it belongs to the extensive section of your own Root Ritual Manual. And what is that?
Homage to all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones!
Oṃ, you who possess the form of a youth, source of the universe, come, come!
Quickly, quickly! Bhrūṃ bhrūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Jina-jit Mañjuśrī, you of beautiful glory, deliver me from all sufferings! Phaṭ phaṭ! Pacify, pacify!
O you who have arisen from that which arises from the dead, destroy my sin; svāhā!

"Mañjuśrī, as soon as this supreme heart-mantra of yours— which brings about all peace, destroys all evil, liberates from all suffering, generates longevity, health, sovereignty, supreme good fortune, and eloquence, and which rouses all the vidyā-kings— was spoken by the Buddha, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, this great earth, including its mountains, oceans, sentient beings, and the entire collection of the vessel-world, shook in six ways. Furthermore, all states of existence— the realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and the world of Yama— and the sufferings of all sentient beings therein were completely stilled."
And this King of Vidyās, Mañjuśrī, should be kept in mind;
at that time, their minds will not be inclined toward the rejection of the true Dharma,
nor will the wicked Māras find an opportunity to enter.
All obstacles and obstructing spirits shall depart.
Furthermore, one should generate this thought:
"How could I possibly conceive of or reject the inconceivable enlightenment and qualities of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones? The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will know [this]."

Thus concludes the fiftieth chapter, the detailed exposition on the benefits, censures, and majestic powers, from the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, a Mahāyāna Vaipulya Sūtra that is a treasure-trove of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Now begins the fifty-fifth chapter:
If one offers eight hundred oblations of white mustard seeds before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) of the noble Mañjuśrī, directed toward a specific person, that person becomes submissive.
To bring a woman under one's control, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations; she becomes submissive.
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should strike the forehead of Noble Mañjuśrī with eight thousand white flowers; the wife of a king becomes submissive.
Having fashioned a Śiva-liṅga out of unfallen cow dung, one should offer seven oblations before it of white mustard seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, using a trident made of cow dung.
He for whose sake this is performed for three days comes under one's control.
For the purpose of subjugating a maiden, one should offer eight thousand *araṅgaṇa* flowers to the noble Mañjuśrī;
she will come under one's control.
Having fashioned a small figure out of beeswax and placed it upon one's own thighs, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times; whoever is targeted by this rite shall become submissive.
Furthermore, one should offer eight hundred white flowers before the cloth painting.
Whoever one desires becomes subject to one's will.
One should grind together conch-shell navel, rocanā, and tagara;
having empowered it eight thousand times with mantras, whoever it is given to—whether with food or drink—that person becomes subject to one's will.
For the subjugation of a Brahmin woman, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *bilva* flowers before a painted image; she becomes submissive.
With ashes over which the mantra has been recited seven times, whichever woman one sprinkles becomes submissive.
Standing before a woman or a man, one should offer eight thousand oblations; he or she becomes submissive.
One should take a four-finger-width piece of wood over which the mantra has been recited eight thousand times; by means of it, one attracts Yama, and he becomes submissive.
One should offer eight hundred or eight thousand white flowers.
There, taking a single flower and seeing a woman, one should turn it toward her.
He comes and becomes subject to one's will.

Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should fashion an image made of clay from an anthill; sitting upon it, one should recite the mantra until Vāsuki trembles, at which point he is accomplished. He then gives food to oneself as the twelfth.
One speaks of the past, the future, and the present.
Subsisting on a diet of milk and barley gruel, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one will obtain wealth and enjoyments.

For one month subsisting on alms, having fasted for one night on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, and having performed a great worship before the cloth painting, one should grasp the feet of the image and recite the mantra until it moves or becomes immovable, whereby one becomes invisible. One becomes the king of all *siddhas*,
and food arises by the mere thought of it.
One lives for five thousand years. Having descended into the Ganges River, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Afterwards, having constructed a sand stūpa upon that very spot and having placed honey and milk together, one should perform the fire offering.
All the nāgas come;
they perform everything that he commands.
Having ascended a mountain peak and installed the cloth painting, one should offer oblations of sandalwood sticks smeared with oil.
The yakṣas will come;
they will do everything that one commands.
Having installed the cloth-painting in a forest and having placed honey and long pepper together in one place, one should offer eight thousand oblations.
All the vidyādharas will come and become obedient to one's commands.
Having established a caitya containing the essence of dependent origination beneath a single tree, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

Upon the completion of one hundred thousand recitations, a goldsmith observing the *poṣadha* vows should fashion a trident out of *aśvattha* wood endowed with the proper characteristics. Having consecrated it with the *sapāta* offering, on the full moon day, having smeared it with fragrant perfumes and performed worship before the cloth painting according to his means, he should hold it in his right hand and practice throughout the entire night until it blazes.
When it blazes, he becomes Mahādeva.
One becomes the lord of spirits,
a tamer of the difficult to tame, and unimpeded among all sentient beings;
having entered the ocean, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
Starting from Sāgara, whichever nāga king he desires, he sees him;
or he gives him a jewel-gem (maṇiratna).
By taking that, one becomes a vidyādhara.

One becomes the king of all nāgas and vidyādharas. Having had a copper vessel fashioned by a smith who observes the poṣadha vows, one should perform a grand worship during the fortnight of miracles on the full moon day; having established it before the cloth painting, one should recite the mantra until it blazes with light.
Then, having placed his hand therein, whatever he desires, all that appears.
This is the sādhana of the auspicious jar (bhadraghaṭa).
Having descended to a river flowing to the ocean, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.

On the full moon day, having constructed a caitya made of clay or sand, and having installed the cloth-painting (paṭa) right there and performed a great worship, one should sit in the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka), take hold of a crystal, a gem, or a clay [image] with the right hand, and recite [the mantra] until it blazes.
One becomes a Vidyādhara who possesses the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi).
Having installed the cloth-painting in a caitya containing relics (sadhātuka), one should recite it one hundred thousand times (lakṣa).

On the full moon day of the fortnight of miracles, having performed worship according to the ritual and having prepared a magnificent garland of lamps, one should take hold of a banner draped with white cloth with the right hand and recite the mantra until it blazes. One then becomes a Vidyādhara of the Banner,
unimpeded everywhere.

On the full moon day during the fortnight of miracles (*prātihārakapakṣa*), having performed a great worship before the cloth painting, one should smear a book of the Blessed Prajñāpāramitā with fragrant perfumes, wrap it with garlands of fragrant flowers, and holding it with the left hand while seated in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), recite [the mantra] until it blazes. One becomes a king of the *vidyādharas* and goes wherever one desires.
One becomes a practitioner of the conduct of a bodhisattva.

Having prepared a beautiful maiden who is well-bathed and adorned, one should perform worship before the cloth painting according to one's means; then, holding her with the left hand while standing, one should recite the mantra until it blazes forth together with her.
Together with her, one becomes a vidyādhara.
Placing one's hand upon a solitary linga, one should recite [the mantra] until one's companions no longer see [one].
Thus, one becomes invisible, inaccessible to all accomplished masters (siddhas), and gains the power of invisibility.

On the thirteenth lunar day, during a lunar or solar eclipse, having placed yellow orpiment behind a leaf of the Bodhi tree at a shrine containing relics in a temple of Maheśvara, one should recite [the mantra] until it emits smoke.
Having applied the *tilaka* mark, one becomes invisible.
Subsisting on milk and barley gruel, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times at the root of a tree on the shore of the ocean during the three junctions of the day for seven nights;
one then beholds the jewels that dwell in the ocean.
One may take [the substances] as desired.
Having eaten mung beans and ascended a mountain peak, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times for twenty nights;
then the jewels and gems situated on the mountain will become visible.
Then, having placed it upon the head of the hand, one should sit upon it and recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
thus for seven days.
He becomes submissive.
Desiring to bring under one's control a king or a high official, one should fashion an image of him from beeswax and cast it into smokeless embers; after seven nights, he becomes submissive.
Desiring clothes, one should recite the mantra once over white flowers that have not been crushed and cast them into water for seven nights;
one obtains a pair of garments worth eight thousand [pieces of gold].

Having recited the mantra eight thousand times over cow's ghee, one should apply it to a woman; she becomes free from all pain. Having consecrated fresh butter with eight hundred recitations, one who is anointed with it may enter the fire.
And it is not given;
anointed with that very [substance], he enters the water and becomes immobilized.
Reciting the mantra as long as he has energy, he consumes alms-food.

Having fashioned an iron sword the size of a span and having installed a cloth painting in a reliquary containing relics, one should perform a grand worship. Having placed the sword upon *aśvattha* leaves that curl to the right, one should recite the mantra until it blazes.
When it is grasped by him, he flies up together with his retinue.
Surrounded by a thousand *vidyādharas*, he becomes invincible to all *vidyādharas* and lives for ten million years.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should perform a grand worship of the cloth painting (*paṭa*). Having fed the monks designated for the *saṅgha*, one should draw a hundred-petaled lotus with red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*) upon the ground and sit upon the pericarp of that lotus. One should recite the mantra until the lotus pierces the earth and rises up.
Then, twenty *vidyādharas* appear, seated upon the petals of the lotus.
Surrounded by them, one flies upward.
He goes together with as many beings as he sees and by whomsoever he is seen;
that lotus is adorned with many jewels,
and he lives for an eon equal to the lifespan of a Brahmā.
When the body has been separated [from life], one may take a lover at will.
If one sprinkles a withered tree with water over which the mantra has been recited eight thousand times,
it will blossom and bear fruit.
Having descended into a dry riverbed, one should recite [the mantra]; it becomes water.
One should recite while crossing a river;
for one who is weary, dry land appears.

One who desires to bring a king or a high official under one's control should, beginning on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, offer eight thousand flowers before the cloth painting and perform eight thousand oblations of salt;
the king will certainly become submissive.
Starting from that very eighth day, one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred times at the three junctions of the day with *gorocanā* until the eleventh day.
Having made a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with it, whoever one looks upon becomes submissive.
If one desires to bring a boy or a girl under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of white mustard seeds before the painting.
Taking the foot-dust of those [images] and fashioning it into a statuette, whoever one mentions by name becomes subject to one's will.
One desiring rain should take cow-ghee and, during a lunar or solar eclipse, place it in a copper vessel; one should recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment occurs.
When it begins to steam, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing; whatever one hears, one grasps.
When it begins to smoke, one obtains the elixir of taste;
when it blazes, one becomes a rememberer of past lives.
One should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *arkapuṣpa* flowers.
He gives a hundred thousand dīnāras. If one offers eight thousand arka flowers before the cloth painting,
one obtains a hundred dīnāras.
In front of the cloth painting, one should offer eight thousand oblations of rice grains smeared with ghee;
one will obtain five dīnāras.
Having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), one should offer eight thousand oblations in front of the cloth painting of [materials] smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One obtains three hundred dīnāras.
One should offer eight thousand black sesame seeds;
one obtains more than a hundred dīnāras.
Desiring to bring a patriarch (*kulapati*) under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* wood before the painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights;
the patriarch will become submissive.

Desiring to bring a lord of the world (*lokapati*) under one's control, one should offer eight thousand oblations of young *dūrvā* shoots before the painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
He exercises the leadership of the *kaula* for as long as he lives.
One who desires to bring the noble Saṅgha under his control should offer eight thousand *arka* flowers before the cloth painting for seven nights.
Whatever purpose one undertakes, one seeks that; by constant recitation, one obtains the desired object.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of guggulu resin pills before the cloth painting;
one will obtain a thousand pieces of gold.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of kunduru incense before the cloth painting for seven nights.
One obtains a treasure.
Before the cloth painting, one should offer a thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee at the three junctions of the day;
one obtains a thousand *dīnāras*.

To bring enemies under one's control, one who observes the *poṣadha* vows should offer eight thousand oblations of royal mustard seeds before the painting at the three junctions of the day for seven days;
all enemies will become submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of lac for seven days.
One becomes beloved by all people.
One should offer eight thousand grains of *śāli* rice three times a day for seven days;
one will obtain a hundred *kārṣāpaṇa* coins.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take the corpse of a man whose limbs are intact, bathe it, adorn it with ornaments, and worship it with fragrant flowers and incense. Then, having stepped upon its chest with the left foot, it should be struck on the head.
Thereupon, it rises.
It should likewise be struck with a sword made of *puṣpaloha* iron.
One obtains gold of natural luster;
then, if one does not desire it, one should say,
"Vomit it out," and then the wish-fulfilling gem emerges.
Having placed it on one's head or neck, or having tied it elsewhere, whatever one contemplates appears before one.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for a day and night, one should descend knee-deep into a river flowing to the ocean and cast ten thousand *jāti* flowers into the current;
one will obtain ten *māṣakas*, or a thousand pieces of gold.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer ten thousand lotuses into a river flowing toward the ocean for seven nights;
one will obtain a treasure-chest.
Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should descend into that same river and set adrift ten thousand flowers for seven days.
One obtains ten villages.

Having made a pill the size of a chickpea with *aśoka* flowers, one should offer eight thousand oblations of it, smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, before the cloth painting at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
Whatever one seeks, that one obtains.
This is the procedure for *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.

One obtains a thousand pieces of gold by offering ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga* husks mixed with *aśoka* pills, consecrated three times, before the cloth painting. By uttering the name [of the person], one obtains a princess within a single month.

Desiring to bring a king together with his ministers under one's control, one should kindle a fire before the cloth painting with *aśoka* wood and offer ten thousand oblations of *aśoka* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee;
that minister will come under one's influence.
Having kindled a fire before the cloth painting, one should offer ten thousand oblations of *apāmārga* wood and *śatapuṣpā* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
One sees a treasure in one's own house.
Having entered knee-deep water in a river flowing to the ocean, one should offer ten thousand [flowers];
those who smell them [attain success].
Having formed a fist with the left hand, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
then it becomes accomplished.
Upon releasing [the fist], it is seen.
Having installed the cloth painting at a shrine containing relics, or on a riverbank, or on a mountain, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses;
one will behold Śrī.
By this very same procedure, one should offer a hundred thousand blue lotuses.
He sees the ritual procedures.
One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of guggulu pills;
one obtains one hundred thousand dīnāras.
One should offer one hundred thousand fragrant flowers;
one obtains ten million garments.
With guggulu incense offered in eight-hundredfold measure, one fulfills whatever is desired by the mind.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of sesame and mustard seeds before the cloth painting every day for three days;
one will obtain twenty-five dīnāras.
By this very same procedure, one should offer oblations for seven nights.
One obtains a hundred dīnāras.
Having cut a figure made of salt again and again, one should offer it eight thousand times;
whoever one desires, whether woman or man, becomes submissive.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of mustard seeds moistened with both hands and smeared with ghee for three days;
this pacifies all obstacles.
Having placed one foot in water and keeping the other on dry land, one should recite the mantra until the foot that was in the water becomes light.
Thereupon, one becomes liberated from evil.
Having kindled a fire with *arka* wood, one should offer eight thousand *rājikā* seeds for seven days;
thus, the karmic obstructions are exhausted.
Having made equal parts of the powder of *brāhmī*, *guḍūcī*, and *pippalī*, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-one times over it with honey before the noble Mañjuśrī and lick it for seven days;
one becomes intelligent.
For fourteen nights, one becomes supremely intelligent.
Through the practice for two months, one becomes a possessor of the power of retention (*śrutidhara*).
Having performed eight thousand recitations before a cloth painting (*paṭa*) or an image, one should afterwards drink [the water].
Thus, remaining silent, one should recite day after day.
One becomes possessed of great intelligence;
whether bound or imprisoned, one is liberated by recitation alone.
Upon seeing thieves, one should recite.
One will not be robbed by thieves.
Having consecrated oil eight thousand times with mantras, one should smear it on the head;
one will become beloved by all people.
All those who touch [the image] in the presence of the Blessed Buddha become submissive.
By this very mantra, one should smear the wound of a man struck by a weapon with oil consecrated eight thousand times; the wound will vanish and no pain will arise.
Having recited this over a clod of earth, one should throw it into the water seven times;
thus the mouths of crocodiles, turtles, and other such creatures will be bound.
On the full moon day, having fasted for three nights and entered water reaching up to the navel, one should offer one hundred and eight white flowers.
One obtains a pair of garments worth five dīnāras.
During a lunar eclipse, at a shrine containing relics, one should prepare pills from finely ground guñjā seeds mixed with ghee and honey;
having covered them with seven *aśvattha* leaves and shielding them with the hand, one should recite the mantra until they burst into flame.
If one eats it, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara).
By means of this, one should perform rites for all the sick.
Having consecrated oil with this mantra, it should be given to those suffering from colic, burning sensations, hemorrhoids, dysuria, or gout; they will become free from disease.

Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, having fasted for three nights, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *yūthikā* buds—anointed with ghee, curd, and milk—beneath an *aśvattha* tree.
One obtains one hundred *rūpakas*.

If this does not succeed, one should perform the ritual; one then obtains one hundred *rūpakas*, or sees [the results]; it destroys *piśācas*, fevers, spirits, and planetary seizures, and one releases [the afflicted] with a thread.
For a woman who is not giving birth, one should recite [the mantra] over oil one hundred and eight times and smear it on her navel or the region of her waist;
she will become free from the obstruction.

By holding a *kumbhīra* [stone], one should empower a clod of earth with the mantra one hundred times and, while gazing at the moon at a shrine containing relics, recite it until one is released, using a mixture of *anantā*, *vetasī*, *brāhmī*, *vacā*, *bṛhatī*, and honey.
It swells;
having consumed it, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara).
In battle, having consecrated a *pratisarā* cord eight hundred times and tied a knot on the wrist, one’s strength remains unassailable.
Having fasted for a day and night, one should accomplish [the rite] in the presence of the Blessed One.
