For one who is not being cured, having kindled a fire with milk-wood fuel, one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of the mantras mixed with curd, honey, and ghee.
One should perform a fire offering (homa) with red or blue lotuses, or with jasmine flowers.
Before the cloth painting (paṭa), one should subsist on a diet of milk and barley gruel, perform increasing offerings,
and feed the monks.
By this rite, even that which was previously unattainable becomes accomplished.
One who desires wealth obtains riches by performing a homa with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks;
through a homa of clarified butter, one achieves pacification and nourishment.
Or, by offering eight thousand oblations of lotuses smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, or oblations of guggulu resin mixed with ghee,
all goals are accomplished in this way.
If black rice is offered after reciting the mantra over it for a specific person's sake, that person becomes submissive.
Subjugation is accomplished with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks.
Having kindled a fire before the cloth-painting with *bilva* wood, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *agaru* fuel-sticks;
it grants all objectives.
If one performs ten thousand oblations at a reliquary containing relics,
one obtains a kingdom;
by performing one hundred thousand oblations with lotuses, one becomes possessed of great wealth.
Having performed worship for all the fire-offerings with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should begin the homa.
Having kindled the fire with eight hundred *bilva* fuel-sticks, one should offer eight thousand *bilva* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Whomever one desires shall become submissive.
Having kindled a fire with milk-wood (*kṣīrakāṣṭha*), one should offer a hundred thousand oblations of *agaru* fuel-sticks;
this grants all aims.

Having performed worship with perfumes, flowers, and incense at a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics, rising early in the morning and becoming pure, one should kindle a fire and offer eight thousand oblations of *nāgakesara* and *priyaṅgu*.
Within one month, one obtains wealth.
Having kindled a fire with *vaikaṅkata* fuel-sticks and *palāśa* wood smeared with curd, honey, and ghee, one should offer oblations;
one obtains a thousand pieces of gold.
Having kindled a fire with *udumbara* wood, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *vāsaka* fuel-sticks smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Having consecrated it one hundred thousand times and bound it upon the hand, one becomes unconquerable in battle;
by binding it on the head, one becomes invisible.
On the fifth day of the dark fortnight, having gone to a river, one should cast eight thousand white flowers into the current;
as a result, one obtains eighty-eight thousand dīnāras.
This ritual is also known as the *kunduruka* rite.
This *bilva* is also a ritual action (*karma*);
it bestows enjoyments (*bhoga*).

On the fifth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a day and night before a painted image (*paṭa*), one should place yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*) upon a white cloth and recite the mantra until the threefold accomplishment (*siddhi*) is attained.
By walking on foot, one lives for seven thousand years;
when it blazes, one becomes a resident of the eon;
it is a remedy for all diseases.
Binding and releasing with clay constitutes the binding of the mandala.
One should offer eight thousand oblations of lotuses before a painting at the three junctions of the day for seven days;
one will then behold a treasure.

In front of the cloth painting, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of *śatapuppā* flowers smeared with curd, honey, and ghee; one will obtain a kingdom. One should offer one hundred thousand oblations of ghee.
One obtains five villages.
One should offer eight thousand arka flowers;
one obtains a thousand gold coins.
When being recited, it grants everything,
with the exception of that which is connected to sensual desires.

Having fasted for a night on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should offer ten thousand oblations of flower-offerings (nirmālya) smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before the noble Mañjuśrī during the night.
One obtains great fortune.
Beneath a Bodhi tree, one should offer eight thousand oblations of Bodhi-tree wood;
one obtains a thousand pieces of gold.
One should offer eight thousand *jātī* flowers at the three junctions of the day for seven nights;
one will obtain a thousand pieces of gold.

Having fasted for three nights, one should perform these rites beneath a Bodhi tree, kindling a fire with fuel-sticks of milk-tree wood, and offer eight thousand pills of *guggulu* resin, each the size of a cotton seed.
One obtains a thousand dīnāras.
For eye diseases, fever, abdominal tumors, headaches, and sciatica, one should recite [the mantra] and then apply it.

Protection must be performed by means of this very [mantra] against all fears and calamities caused by wolves, tigers, buffaloes, crocodiles, elephants, bears, thieves, snakes, piśācas, bhūtas, and brahmarākṣasas, as well as against those that move in water.
Having gone to a lotus pond, one should offer a hundred thousand lotuses;
one obtains an ordinary kingdom.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścara�ņa*), one should take realgar (*manaḥśilā*), grind it with human milk, and perform a thousand oblations (*sahasrasampātāhuti*). Being observant of the *poṣadha* vows, one should make five pills, place them in a casket made of agallochum, and during a lunar or solar eclipse, having performed a ritual offering (*balividhāna*) together with white mustard seeds, one should place the casket before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) and recite the mantra until the mustard seeds crackle and pop.
Then, one effects the subjugation of all sentient beings. If it emits smoke, one becomes the king of all those who possess the power of invisibility and lives for infinite eons.
Then, when it blazes up, one becomes a king of the Vidyādharas, a divine youth with a radiance equal to the rising sun, remaining for a great eon (mahākalpa).
Rocanā, yellow orpiment, and other such substances are to be accomplished by this very same procedure.
For all of them, there are three kinds of accomplishment.
One who desires to bring about peace should have the sacrificial fire kindled with fuel-sticks by officiating priests and offer eight thousand oblations of fine rice (*paramānna*) for three nights;
peace will ensue.
For oneself or another, or for a village or city in the event of drought, one should offer the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*) for seven nights.
Having empowered conch shells, banners, and other objects with mantras, one exhausts [negative] karma;
within seven days, one exhausts even the five deeds of immediate retribution and becomes capable of all ritual actions.
A binding of knowledge (*vidyābandha*) should be performed by tying a knot with a thread over which the mantra has been recited twenty-one times.
A binding of the mandala (*maṇḍalabandha*) is performed with mustard seeds.

During a lunar or solar eclipse, having smeared a mandala with sandalwood paste, one should place equal portions of ghee, honey, and *āmalakī* juice in a copper vessel; then, sitting in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), one should recite the mantra until it becomes warm.
Having drunk it, one becomes a possessor of the power of hearing (śrutidhara).

One who observes the poṣadha vow should, at the improper time, recite [the mantra] seven times over a mouthful of water and drink it. Whatever one contemplates while performing this, he declares in a dream.
Having recited the *śvetavacā* mantra seven times and placed it between the teeth in the mouth, whatever one requests, that one obtains;
one becomes a superior debater.

Whatever state of being one has in mind while reciting, having offered flowers, incense, and so forth before the Tathāgata, one should cast a directional offering (*diśābali*) toward the four quarters.
Then, seated upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass, one should recite [the mantra] eight thousand times;
this fulfills all hopes.

Having fashioned a lion from anthill clay and anointed it with *gorocanā*, one who has performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) should place it before the cloth painting, prepare a sacrificial offering (*piṇḍaka*), and recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times.
Then he moves;
as soon as he has moved, he becomes accomplished. At that very moment, while reciting the mantra, one should mount a lion.
With his hair curled in locks, having the appearance of a sixteen-year-old though being twice eight years of age, he flies up as the sixteenth [emanation] of himself.
Having arrived among all the vidyādharas, possessing the lifespan of Brahmā, and upon death, he is reborn among the gods.
By seeing or hearing him, he paralyzes the enemy army.

Having prepared a jar completely filled with water scented with all kinds of rice and having covered its mouth with mango sprouts, bathe Vināyaka with it after it has been consecrated eight thousand times;
he will quickly release [the child].
One should also bathe a pregnant woman.
She gives birth with ease;
one should bathe the child,
and it becomes liberated from all seizing spirits.
By this consecration, she becomes completely liberated and becomes equal to the sādhana itself.

For the subjugation of great vassal kings, one should offer eight thousand oblations of *arka* wood fuel smeared with curd, honey, and ghee before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) for seven nights at the three junctions of the day.
One becomes master over [the person] together with their retinue.

For a princess, one should offer eight thousand *priyaṅgu* flowers for seven days, and she will be given [to him]. One should offer eight thousand oil-cakes at the three junctions of the day for seven nights.
One brings those standing before one under control.
Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times at a reliquary containing relics while subsisting on alms-food.

Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for one night and performed worship of the cloth-painting according to one's means, one should offer eight thousand oblations of black sesame seeds smeared with curd, honey, and ghee.
Then, at dawn, he obtains a village;
twelve [villages]. If the rites are not yet accomplished, he obtains a village of a thousand households.

Having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*), one should set up the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) facing west on the bank of a river. Subsisting on water and barley-meal, having performed worship according to one's means and lit twenty-one lamps of ghee, one should offer an outer oblation (*bali*) for all spirits. Sitting in the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), one should recite the mantra until the divine son Aruṇa arrives;
he grants a boon.
Alternatively, subsisting on alms-food, one should recite it for three months beneath a *vaṭa* tree.
Then, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having smeared a sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide and offered an oblation (*bali*) consisting of all flavors,

and having given an oblation for all spirits outside, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and offer eight thousand pellets of *guggulu* resin, each the size of a jujube pit, into smokeless embers. Thereupon, the yakṣiṇī Paṭavāsinī arrives.
One should offer her an *argha* oblation with scented water.
She asks, "What shall I do?"—whether she says "I am your mother," "your sister," or "your friend"—one of these [titles] should be accepted.
She bestows a medicinal elixir (*rasāyana*).
Having consumed that, one attains a lifespan of an eon and gains the strength of a yakṣa.

Having performed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) and having made offerings according to one's means at a shrine containing relics, one should bathe three times a day and perform an immeasurable recitation (jāpa) during the three junctions of the day for six months.

Subsisting on alms-food or a diet of milk and barley-gruel, one should then begin the ritual practice (*sādhana*). During the dark fortnight, under the asterism of Puṣya, having purchased *karavīrikā* realgar from a hero-seller, one should purify it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Having given the medicinal herb to a Brahmin girl, having bathed and adorned her, and having entered facing the east, one should grind it at an auspicious lunar day, division of the day (*karaṇa*), and moment (*muhūrta*).
With the ring finger, [one should apply] the uneven [substance].

Having made a pill the size of a jujube seed and placed it in a casket made of *aśvattha* wood, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) before the cloth painting (*paṭa*) with a thousand oblations. Having stayed there for seven nights, at the end of that period during the bright fortnight, one should perform a grand worship and present a most magnificent offering (*bali*). Having honored the casket with perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should place it upon four *aśvattha* leaves and cover it with three more. Pressing it down with the hand and paying homage to all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one should sit upon a bundle of *kuśa* grass and recite the mantra until substances such as elixirs and rejuvenators appear.
Again it goes out;
half is to be used for the Three Jewels,
and then it remains right there.
There will be no fear of the discus of Viṣṇu;
one beholds the Blessed Maitreya.
Having made a vow, one should enter.
It is a warding off of all [obstacles].
In a clean place, one should place a house of dust upon mustard seeds;
thus, the warding off of all [obstacles] is accomplished.
If one desires to bring about an excessive movement,
one should say, "Go!
Having fashioned a clay seal on the hem of a garment and empowered it with eight thousand recitations, one should place it upon the bitten person and summon [the venom].
Even a corpse will rise up.

Having purified substances such as realgar (*manaḥśilā*) and so forth, as well as swords, discuses, and *musuṇḍī* spears, with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should perform a thousand oblations (*sahasrasampātāhuti*). Then, taking any one of those substances and having drawn the *sādhana*-maṇḍala on the full moon day, one should place the substance upon a cloth and sit cross-legged; one should recite [the mantra] until success is attained. Alternatively, having written the name of whichever substance one desires upon a wooden board and having consecrated it eight thousand times, one should throw it into a lake where a *nāga* resides.
The nāga fulfills everything for him;
within seven days, he certainly accomplishes the desired object.
Having written the name of the desired thing on a wooden plank along with the substances and so forth, one should likewise cast it into a well or a lake.
Then the person should be immersed in the water;
he hears a great voice there, saying,
"In such-and-such a place, wealth and other things are located."
Then it should be grasped.
When crossing a river and so forth, or in the ten [situations], one should remember it in an assembly, in a royal court, or in a dispute;
everywhere one becomes unconquered.
If one wishes to bring someone under one's control, one should visualize Noble Mañjuśrī in that person’s mouth and engage in some conversation;
before long, they will come under control.
Alternatively, having placed water in a vessel, one should meditate upon Noble Mañjuśrī.
One should contemplate the bitten person with that water consecrated eight thousand times;
he becomes free from poison.

Having entered the maṇḍala according to the prescribed rite, one should take cow dung that has not fallen [to the ground] from a bull in full vigor, and, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya) and observing silence, having prepared the maṇḍala, one should recite the mantra starting from the full moon until one has recited it a third time, reaching one hundred thousand repetitions.
A celibate student (brahmacārī) should observe this vow for six months;
success is attained here within a month.
After six months, the black world becomes directly perceptible.
One attains supreme accomplishment even with the body;
in brief, one accomplishes every mantra.
From the *Mahākalparāja*, the *Āryamañjuśrīmūlakalpa*, the fifty-fifth chapter, the section on the accomplishment of gold (*hemasādhana*), the detailed exposition, the complete cycle, is finished.
And thus concludes the ritual manual (kalpa) of the noble Mañjuśrī as it was obtained.

May there be well-being! Written by Paṇḍita Ravicandra, the lord of the illustrious Mūlaghoṣa Monastery, who has departed from the Middle Country for Śrībo; it was completed on the day of the lunar mansion *Ardra* during the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, while Jupiter was situated in Leo. Thus ends the Mañjuśrī-kalpa.
May there be auspiciousness!
